title: A huge new London Museum tells the city's story from the Romans to Banksy
summary: Britain's capital city is getting a new attraction that bills itself as the world's largest city museum
story: Britain's capital city is getting a new attraction that bills itself as the world's largest city museum
LONDON -- A Roman mosaic, a bloodstained shirt, a bagel filled with barbecued pork, a sewer-clogging chunk of fat.
These are just a few of the objects that help encapsulate Britain’s teeming capital at the London Museum, which bills itself as the world’s largest city museum.

The museum opens Saturday after a yearslong, 437-million-pound ($573-million) refurbishment of Victorian buildings that were once part of the city’s Smithfield meat market. It replaces the notoriously hard-to-find Museum of London, which was located half a mile (800 meters) away and closed in 2022.

The London Museum sits in a much more prominent location, between London’s financial district and the creative Clerkenwell area and next to the wholesale meat market, which is due to move elsewhere by 2030 after more than 800 years on the site.
Museum Director Sharon Ament says change has been the one constant in London for two millennia.

“The great thing about London is it’s always been a mashup,” she said. “A defining feature of London is people coming and going. It started with a load of incomers creating (the Roman city of) Londinium, and it’s been ever thus. And London has always been a place, I think, where you can come and go, be yourself, and take opportunities.”

The museum’s airy ground floor covers the market’s former trading hall, and explores the London of living memory. Exhibits include the gilded State Coach used by the Lord Mayor of London, the former telephone switchboard from Buckingham Palace and a police sentry box decorated with piranhas by the street artist Banksy in 2024.
There are signs from iconic London buildings including an Odeon cinema, the now-closed Walthamstow greyhound-racing stadium and local fried-chicken chain Morley’s.

A temporary exhibition explores London’s food, including the changing face of Brick Lane, a street that has housed generations of immigrants and produced Jewish delis, South Asian curry houses and new fusions such as char siu bagels that reflect the area’s burgeoning population of Chinese students.

On the museum’s vast lower floor, exhibits trace the city’s history from Londinium through the Middle Ages, the devastating Great Fire of 1666, boom-time as the capital of the British Empire and the waves of immigration and social movements, from suffragettes to Black Pride, that transformed London during the 20th and 21st centuries.
Like the city, the museum’s collection is dizzyingly eclectic.

There is a chunk of the Whitechapel Fatberg, an 820-foot-long (250-meter-long) lump of hardened fat, oil, diapers and baby wipes found clogging a sewer in 2017. Elsewhere is the bass guitar smashed by Paul Simonon of The Clash on the cover of the punk band’s album “London Calling.”
Pieces of clothing include the shirt reputedly worn by King Charles I when he was executed in 1649, Queen Victoria’s black mourning dress and Olympic diver Tom Daley’s swim trunks.
One large gallery is devoted to the Cheapside Hoard, a trove of gold and gemstones from a 17th-century jeweler’s workshop discovered by workmen demolishing a building in 1912.
Senior curator Hazel Forsyth calls the hoard “a time capsule of contemporary taste, culture, innovation, craftsmanship” and 17th-century global trade.
“It literally takes you on a voyage of discovery,” she said.

The hoard includes priceless items, such as a tiny watch made from a single Colombian emerald crystal. But there are also some highly accomplished fakes — showing that crime and scams have long been part of city life.
At the back of the exhibition space is one more surprise: a 20-foot (6-meter) window with a view of trains thundering past on London Underground tracks into nearby Farringdon station.
The museum is due to get even bigger, with a set of underground vaults scheduled to open in 2027, followed by expansion into a former poultry market building in 2028.

Like many modern museums, it aims to be a place to eat, drink, hang out and shop as well as to learn. It contains four eating and drinking venues and a gift shop where visitors can buy fridge magnets, hair clips and all manner of other merch adorned with the museum’s mascot: a pigeon.
A museum spokesperson said pigeons were chosen because they are an “unlikely hero of the city”: ubiquitous, sometimes unloved and somewhat misunderstood.
“They’re really smart, they’re actually quite beautiful, and they’re everywhere.”

title: Resurgent ‘Hunger Games’ goes big at box office, despite 'Grand Theft Auto VI'
summary: "Sunrise on the Reaping” debuted with estimated $120 million in North America.
story: "Sunrise on the Reaping” debuted with estimated $120 million in North America.

NEW YORK -- Fourteen years and six movies in, “The Hunger Games” movie franchise rediscovered its box-office might, as “Sunrise on the Reaping” debuted with $120 million in North American theaters over the weekend, according to studio estimates Sunday.

The sun had seemed to be setting on “The Hunger Games” as a cultural force. After the original blockbuster run of four movies led by Jennifer Lawrence, Lionsgate’s 2023 prequel, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” topped off at $361.8 million worldwide — a decent sum but about half what each of the first four movies grossed.

Yet “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” has restored the Suzanne Collins adaptations to blockbuster status. The film, a sequel to “Songbirds and Snakes” and set 25 years before the original series, launched with $225 million worldwide on its opening weekend. Lionsgate produced and distributed the movie, budgeted at about $150 million.

“It’s obviously not common for a film in its sixth installment to completely reverse the trajectory, but it’s awfully satisfying to be a part of it,” said Adam Fogelson, chairman of the Lionsgate Motion Picture Group.

At a time when movie series longevity is far from assured, “Sunrise on the Reaping” managed to notch the year’s fifth $100 million-plus domestic launch — something only accomplished in 2026 by some of the most bankable franchises: Spider-Man (“Spider-Man: Brand New Day”), Toy Story (“Toy Story 5”), Super Mario (“The Super Mario Galaxy Movie”) and whatever Christopher Nolan makes (“The Odyssey”).
And it did it while a significant portion of potential moviegoers were locked at home playing “Grand Theft Auto VI.”

Yet Gen Z again powered a big weekend in theaters. Some 74% of the audience for the “Hunger Games” prequel-sequel were aged 18-34. Several of 2026’s box-office hits — including “Obsession,” “Backrooms” and “You Can See Everything” — have likewise succeeded by packing theaters with the most potent demographic in moviegoing.

While “Sunrise on the Reaping” includes a supporting cast of well-known veteran stars (Ralph Fiennes, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Jesse Plemons), the movie largely belongs to a new generation of young actors: Jo Zada, Mckenna Grace, Ben Wang and Whitney Peak. The film, directed by Francis Lawrence, is centered around teenage Haymitch Abernathy (Zada), the role originally played by Woody Harrelson.

Fogelson credits several things to the “Hunger Games” turnaround. “Songbirds and Snakes” was an origin story of a villain, and thus a darker tale. “Sunrise on the Reaping” has the Hunger Games themselves more front and center. It focuses on the backstory of a beloved character in Haymitch. And the cast, a mix of newcomers and veterans, elevated the film.

“It’s consistent with how ‘The Hunger Games’ has always operated. Jennifer Lawrence wasn’t the mega movie star when this franchise started with her,” Fogelson says. “There is no question that part of the incredible resurgence we’ve seen at the box office has been Gen Z and Gen Alpha demonstrating how much they love going to movie theaters.”

Reviews were OK (67% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes), but audience scores were better. “Sunrise on the Reaping” earned an “A-” CinemaScore from moviegoers, a tick up from the “B+” received by “Songbirds and Snakes.”

In its first weekend of wide release, Amazon MGM Studios’ “I Play Rocky” came in second with $9.3 million from 2,477 locations. Peter Farrelly’s comic drama about the making of “Rocky” stars Anthony Ippolito as a young Sylvester Stallone. It has previously played in limited release for two weeks.

The biggest win for “I Play Rocky” — a potential Oscar contender — wasn’t its bottom-line gross, but its CinemaScore: an A+. Such a high mark is rare. (Even “The Odyssey” didn’t score so well.) But Farrelly has managed it before. His best picture-winning 2018 film “Green Book” got the same score.
Ticket sales were down about 10% from the same weekend last year, when “Wicked For Good” came out, according to data firm Rentrak. But they were up 84.9% from last weekend.

From the earliest stage of dating “Sunrise on the Reaping,” Lionsgate analyzed the benefits and risks of going up against “Grand Theft Auto.” Ultimately, the studio believed both could coexist. Some 67% of the audience for the “Hunger Games” film was female.

“Many have speculated as to whether the release of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ would hurt ‘The Hunger Games’ at the box office this weekend, and I think the marketplace has already spoken,” said Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends for Rentrak. “Both can do just fine.”

Last week's No. 1 film, “Ebenezer,” starring Johnny Depp, dipped 60% in its second weekend with $7.7 million. The Paramount release has grossed $32.5 million domestically and $45.9 million internationally.

Hollywood will now turn its attention to a Thanksgiving holiday weekend full of intrigue. “Sunrise on the Reaping” will be competing with a variety of new releases: Universal’s “Focker in Law,” the Disney animated film “Hexed,” Netflix’s IMAX release of “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” and Neon’s wide release of James Gray’s crime drama “Paper Tiger.”
With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak:
1. “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” $120 million.
2. “I Play Rocky,” $9.3 million.
3. “Ebenezer,” $7.7 million.
4. “The Cat in the Hat,” $6.9 million.
5. “Godzilla Minus Zero,” $2.7 million.
6. “You Can See Everything,” $2.5 million.
7. “Wild Horse Nine,” $2.5 million.
8. “Ghost Soldier,” $2.4 million.
9. “Wildwood,” $2.3 million.
10. “Ramayana,” $2.1 million.

title: Josh Allen teams up with Oscar-winning director to produce ‘The Buffalo Miracle’ documentary
summary: Bills quarterback Josh Allen and two-time Academy Award-winning director Ben Proudfoot have teamed up to deliver an uplifting documentary titled “The Buffalo Miracle.”
story: Bills quarterback Josh Allen and two-time Academy Award-winning director Ben Proudfoot have teamed up to deliver an uplifting documentary titled “The Buffalo Miracle.”

BUFFALO, N.Y. -- Ben Proudfoot’s first encounter with Josh Allen came in the form of seeing a large cardboard cutout figure of the Bills quarterback erected inside a McDonald’s franchise in suburban Buffalo.

Unassuming as the setting seemed, the fast-food restaurant would serve as the centerpiece for a documentary the two-time Academy Award-winning director was filming to highlight the unlikely heroes and communal spirt that emerged during a deadly two-day blizzard which paralyzed the region over Christmas weekend in 2022.
“I said, ‘Who’s that?’” Proudfoot recalled with a laugh. “And they said, ‘That’s Josh Allen. He’s our hero.'"
Store manager Kristin Kosha chuckled at the memory.
“I thought he was trying to get a rise out of me,” Kosha said. “But no, he genuinely didn’t know.”
Little did Proudfoot realize he'd soon get the opportunity to meet Allen.

By sheer coincidence, Allen had just launched his production company, Out of Pocket Studios, and was searching for the ideal initial project to back when Proudfoot's film crossed his desk. With Allen as executive producer, they teamed up in making “The Buffalo Miracle,” a 37-minute documentary premiering on HBO on Tuesday night.

“I think it speaks volumes that the story he chose to inaugurate his company with is about the goodness of the people of Buffalo,” Proudfoot said. “He could do anything. He decided to make a film about the heroism of everyday folks from Buffalo."
For Allen, who grew up on a farm in central California, the film serves as a holiday love letter to his adopted blue-collar home.

“Who knows the reason that I started Out of Pocket,” he said. “Maybe it was for this exact moment to push this film forward and for the world to see because of what I think Buffalo and western New York stand for, the grittiness, the care for one another. We’re called the ‘City of Good Neighbors,’ and this totally encapsulates that.”
Tragic as the blizzard was with Erie County's death toll reaching 47, the film captures those braving the harrowing conditions and opening their doors to save others.

Kosha and assistant Jeffrey Spengler defied McDonald's policy in keeping their restaurant open. They eventually sheltered and fed some 50 people — and one pet dog — during a two-day storm that ended on Christmas morning, brought near-hurricane-force winds and dumped more than 4 feet (1.2 meters) of snow.

It’s a story of Amherst police officers Thomas Brown and Derek Westbrook navigating treacherous whiteout conditions to rescue those who were stranded in cars and in homes without power by transporting them to McDonald’s and other shelters.

And it’s a story that, as survivor Paache’ Spikes-Redding says in the film, is about people and community and even sports, with those gathered at the McDonald’s uplifted by the Bills' AFC East-clinching win at Chicago on Christmas Eve.

“Race, religion and politics, they might divide us. Sports brings us together,” Spikes-Redding says in the documentary. “What was the odds that we all ended up here and what was the reason, people from all walks of life.”
With their car stranded, Spikes-Redding, her son and then-fiancé broke into a closed restaurant and gathered around a gas stove to stay warm before being rescued by Brown.

It’s a story of rekindling friendships, with Westbrook rescuing Jimmy Bessing, who has Down syndrome and was living on his own when the power went out in his apartment. They recognized each other immediately as former high school classmates and took a selfie before trudging back to Westbrook's truck.

And it’s a story about giving back. Immigrants Tan and Lili Zhao were among those who sheltered at McDonald’s. They own a beauty salon and one of the closing scenes shows Kosha and Spengler — “Heroes," the Zhao's called them — enjoying a relaxing spa treatment.

“It’s been absolutely surreal. We never thought what we did would reach the audience that it has. And we most certainly didn’t do it for that reason at all,” Kosha said. “But it’s nice to see a little act of kindness and taking care of your neighbor could hopefully pass on a nice message.”
This is the community Allen has grown to cherish, and a city he watched rally from other difficult moments that year.

That May, 10 Black people were killed in a hate-motivated mass shooting at a Buffalo supermarket. A week after the storm, Bills safety Damar Hamlin had a near-death experience when he went into cardiac arrest and needed to be resuscitated on the field during a game in Cincinnati.
“It’s a fantastic story and it’s very special to me,” Allen said of the film. “If you’re not brought to tears at the end of this, I just don’t know what to tell you.”
Proudfoot is from Halifax, Nova Scotia, and now lives in California, and this is the America he’s grown to know and sought to emphasize.

“What was reaffirmed for me really in hearing about this story is that there are callings greater than your job, greater than your political affiliation, greater than your race, ethnic identity, religion,” Proudfoot said. “It brought out the best in people. And so I think that speaks to the people of Buffalo, it speaks to humanity, it speaks to America.”
His one regret is Spikes-Redding not being alive to see the finished product. Shortly after filming completed, she was killed in a hit-and-run accident.

“It’s hard to make sense of how somebody like that would be taken away from her family,” Proudfoot said. “So I’m happy that she lives on. She’s really the star of the show. And she had the last word.”
In the final scene before the closing credits, a smiling Spikes-Redding appears on screen and playfully says: “Merry Christmas to all. And to all a good night.”

title: Tom Jackson, Broncos star and ESPN 'Sunday NFL Countdown' analyst, dead at 75
summary: Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the Orange Crush defense with the Denver Broncos who went on to even more fame as an ESPN broadcaster, has died at 75
story: Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the Orange Crush defense with the Denver Broncos who went on to even more fame as an ESPN broadcaster, has died at 75

Tom Jackson, a fiery cornerstone of the Orange Crush defense with the Denver Broncos who went on to even more fame as a beloved broadcaster on ESPN, has died, his family and the network announced Sunday. He was 75.

Jackson's family informed ESPN that he died Friday, but it was their wishes that his death not be announced until the start of the network's “Sunday NFL Countdown” show by Jackson's longtime friend and on-air partner Chris Berman. A cause of death was not given.

“Tom was so much more than an accomplished NFL analyst. There was nobody kinder, more thoughtful, more loyal or more engaging than him. And when it came to laughter, Tom’s was frequent and unmistakable,” Berman said. “Tom was my best friend professionally and personally. If you ever met him or just knew him from watching ESPN, he was your best friend, too.”
Berman said Jackson made a surprise visit a couple of weeks ago to ESPN, where he worked for 32 years over two stints after playing 14 seasons for the Broncos, and that the two talked on Tuesday.

A fourth-round draft pick out of Louisville in 1973, Jackson was an inspirational leader of Denver’s first Super Bowl team in 1977. He started 177 games for the Broncos between 1973-86, retiring after the team's second Super Bowl appearance. He was a first-team All-Pro in 1977 and a second-team All-Pro the following season; he also was a three-time Pro Bowler.

The Broncos held a moment of silence and showed a video tribute to Jackson before their game against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. After the Broncos won 38-24, coach Sean Payton said the team would give a game ball to Jackson's family.
Following his playing days, Jackson had a second career at ESPN from 1987-2016 and was featured on “Sunday NFL Countdown” and “NFL Primetime.”

Before the internet, and before NBC took over the Sunday night package in 2006, “NFL Primetime” was must-see viewing for fans and players because it showed highlights from all the games, as well as the interaction between Berman and Jackson, who often finished each other’s sentences.

“I can remember coming from games and waiting in a rush to get home, to watch ‘Primetime’ because all I wanted to know was, what were you and Tom Jackson gonna say about one, the team?” ESPN analyst and Hall of Fame wide receiver Randy Moss said to Berman.

NBC's “Football Night in America” paid tribute to Jackson Sunday night. Host Maria Taylor said: “Before there was a ‘Football Night in America’, there was ‘NFL Primetime,’ where TJ and Chris Berman set the standard for an NFL highlight show. It’s a standard that we look to every single Sunday.”

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, who was in Mexico City for Sunday night's game between the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings, said Jackson was “an outstanding player whose toughness and leadership helped define an era of Broncos football. He brought credibility, passion and humor to everything he did, and generations of fans came to know him through his work at ESPN.”

Jackson briefly returned to ESPN in 2019 and reunited with Berman to do an online version of “NFL Primetime.” He was awarded the Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award from the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2015.

“In my lifetime there was Howard Cosell doing ‘Monday Night Football’ halftime highlights and then there were Boomer and TJ doing ‘Sunday NFL Countdown.’ I am not here as a colleague but as one of million who watched, learned from and idolized the two of you,” ESPN host Mike Greenberg said during Sunday’s show.
ESPN’s studio crew wore orange ties in honor of Jackson during the three-hour show.
Berman said Jackson was the last of seven people interviewed for the studio analyst job and that the last person rarely gets the job. But Jackson nailed the interview.

“Tom Jackson was one of the most influential and beloved figures in ESPN’s history. He brought the credibility of an All-Pro NFL player, the insight of a gifted analyst and a warmth and authenticity that connected with generations of football fans. Alongside Chris Berman, he helped make ‘NFL Primetime’ an iconic part of our football weekends,” ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro said in a statement. “Away from the set, Tom was a trusted colleague, generous mentor and dear friend to many. ... His legacy at ESPN, throughout the NFL and among the countless fans who admired his incredible work will endure.”
ESPN’s NFL studio in Bristol, Connecticut, is named the Chris Berman-Tom Jackson Studio. It is the only named studio on ESPN’s campus.

“The Denver Broncos are heartbroken by the passing of Ring of Fame linebacker Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the legendary Orange Crush defense and one of the most beloved players in franchise history,” the Broncos said in a statement.

“An inspirational leader and fierce competitor, TJ was a proud member of the Broncos’ first Super Bowl team that helped establish a winning tradition in Denver. Off the field, Tom carried himself with class, warmth and humility, forging deep connections and lifelong friendships with teammates and throughout Broncos Country.”
Jackson is survived by his wife, Jennifer, and daughters Taylor and Morgan.
AP Pro Football Writer Arnie Stapleton in Denver contributed to this report.

title: Amy Poehler returns to TV with 'Dig' — just in time for Thanksgiving
summary: Amy Poehler returns to TV comedy for the first time in over 10 years with new show, “Dig” which is set on an archaeological excavation in Greece
story: Amy Poehler returns to TV comedy for the first time in over 10 years with new show, “Dig” which is set on an archaeological excavation in Greece
Amy Poehler’s back on television and that’s a big deal.

Despite the fact that she’s never been away — whether it’s charming guestson her “Good Hang” podcast, presenting at awards shows or starring in movies — it’s been 11 years since she's starred in a TV series.

As the irrepressible Leslie Knope on “Parks and Recreation,” Poehler corralled a team of office workers to do good for the community and each other, picking up six Emmy nominations and building a beloved fan base.
Now “Parks and Rec” fans can rejoice that she’s reunited with co-creator Mike Schur to lead the cast of “Dig,” their new show set on an archaeological excavation in Greece.
“The big deal is Amy deciding to act again, honestly,” says Schur, with Season 1 arriving in full on Monday.
“If you survey a thousand people and say, ‘What do you think of Amy Poehler?’ — 999 of them swoon and laugh. So just her being back on TV is a delight.”
Poehler admits it’s significant.
“I’m at a point in my life, and lucky to be, where the only way I see my friends is by working with them. And I have the most talented and funniest friends.”
And while her cynical “Dig” character Elise is very different from the positivity of Leslie Knope, the show does have the same vibe as “Parks and Rec,” according to co-star Geraldine Viswanathan.

“You just feel like these people are your friends and they’re so distinctive," says Viswanathan. "It’s a very unlikely group of people who kind of are thrown together in this workplace comedy and actually have a lot to learn from each other.”

Based on Kate Myers' novel “Excavations," the show follows a summer expedition to discover history in the Greek dirt, bringing together people from different generations, all soul searching while looking for rare artifacts in the ground.
The show, which also stars Hugh Laurie, Antonia Thomas, and Fina Strazza, premieres on Peacock in the U.S. on Monday.

Poehler spoke about the show, how a meeting of her “Dig” and “Parks and Recreation” characters might go, and navigating family gatherings with The Associated Press. The conversation has been edited for clarity and brevity.

POEHLER: Archaeologist is kind of like the fake job you think you want to have when you’re 10 years old. I did not think that I had any interest in it until I started studying and learning about it and then realizing, oh, this is such an amazing metaphor for who gets to tell their story, what do you have hidden, what stuff do you wanna dig up?
Now I’m obsessed, and all I do is read stories about when people find things on the beach and discoveries that have changed the way we think about science and nature and dinosaurs.

POEHLER: We were only there a short amount of time, a few weeks, but boy, I had never been to Athens. I absolutely loved it. The people, the Greek people are so fun, kind. They’re my kind of people because I enjoy direct people. Little bossy and direct, but kind.

POEHLER: It is because exactly that, 11 years later, getting to be back on set with Mike and getting to work with his amazing talented wife, J.J. Philbin, who’s an incredible writer, worked on “Only Murders” and was at “SNL” with us. That reunion is as important to me almost as the work.
POEHLER: Leslie would be a little intimidated by Elise, because Elise would think Leslie was a lot.

I think they would respect each other, but they have very, very different energies. And it was nice to play somebody who was kind of still and quiet, and people projected stuff on her rather than a person who just constantly projected stuff out.

POEHLER: I’m so bad at this. Kayvan (Novak), who plays my love interest, he’s really that tall. He is so tall and that is all his real hair, beard and hair. He has the hair of a horse. He’s incredible.
I think that the dirt would be that in the very beginning when we were all pretending to not like each other, we actually did.

POEHLER: You just have to have a sense of humor about yourself. If you can take life and what you believe in seriously, but not yourself seriously. When we all start to take ourselves seriously, we get into trouble. And then also just lock yourself in the bathroom. Just go in the bathroom and lock the door and play on your phone. Or you volunteer to go do an errand and then pretend your car broke down and just lie in the back seat and never come back.

title: Miley Cyrus marries rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate Palm Springs wedding
summary: Singer Miley Cyrus has married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate ceremony in Palm Springs, California
story: Singer Miley Cyrus has married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate ceremony in Palm Springs, California
Pop culture icon Miley Cyrus married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate weekend wedding in Palm Springs, California, according to a post on the singer’s Instagram account.

The post said Cyrus, 33, and Morando, 28, were wed on Saturday. Photographs show the couple embracing in front of a white backdrop with a palm tree characteristic of the Palm Springs desert in the background, a large dog lying at their feet. In one photo, the couple kisses standing in an aisle of white roses.

The “Party in the U.S.A.” singer wore a long-sleeve silk Saint Laurent gown by Anthony Vaccarello and elegant white silk kitten heels, according to a statement from Saint Laurent. The dress had a low back, and she wore flowers in her hair, which was pulled back into an updo.
Morando wore dark, square shades. His single-breasted tuxedo was also made by the French luxury fashion brand.

The pair have been together since 2021, meeting after they were set up on a blind date, according to an interview Cyrus gave Vogue in 2023. Morando proposed to her while the couple were in Japan late last year, he said in a separate interview with Wonderland Magazine.
“I could feel my heart pounding” before popping the question, Morando said for a profile in the magazine.
Morando is the drummer of the rock band Liily.

title: 'GTA VI' finally reveals the actors, voices and familiar names behind Vice City
summary: Rockstar Games has finally revealed the cast behind "Grand Theft Auto VI," ending years of secrecy
story: Rockstar Games has finally revealed the cast behind "Grand Theft Auto VI," ending years of secrecy
LOS ANGELES -- After years of secrecy, “Grand Theft Auto VI” is finally giving up some of its biggest mysteries.

Rockstar Games kept much of the cast behind its blockbuster video game under wraps before launch, including the performers behind protagonists Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval. Now that players are roaming Vice City and the wider fictional state of Leonida, actors who spent years bound to secrecy are revealing themselves.
The gaming company's newly released credits are filling in an unusually deep roster of performers, musicians, comedians and broadcasters.
Manni L. Perez plays Lucia and Dylan Rourke portrays Jason, confirming years of fan speculation over the actors behind the game’s central couple. Rockstar’s official credits list both as the leads.
Rourke and Perez marked the reveal together on social media, writing about the years they spent watching developers build the game before finally being able to publicly connect themselves to it.
They are hardly alone.

Former “Saturday Night Live” cast member Bobby Moynihan plays Cal, while Stephen Root, who had previously acknowledged appearing in the game without revealing his role, voices Brian Heder. Taryn Manning, Roselyn Sanchez and Denzel Curry are also among the names buried throughout Rockstar’s sprawling cast list.
For years, Rockstar allowed Lucia and Jason to become globally recognizable characters without publicly identifying the actors portraying them.

That created an online guessing game as fans analyzed voices, facial features and past acting credits while Rockstar released trailers but little information about the performers. The official credits finally ended the speculation with Rourke as Jason, a former soldier pulled deeper into Leonida's criminal world, while Perez plays Lucia, his partner after her release from prison.
The reveal also puts two actors who were hardly household names at the center of one of entertainment's largest launches.

Rourke said in a joint Instagram post with Perez that they had spent years witnessing what he called some of the hardest-working craftspeople in game development, adding that the pair were honored to be part of the project.

Other actors have described similarly long periods of secrecy. Edwina Rai, who appears in the game, said on Instagram that she first auditioned in April 2022 without even knowing what the project was. She went through three callbacks and a chemistry read before landing a role in what she described as the biggest project of her career.

The sports world also turns up inside Leonida. NFL star Tyreek Hill revealed that he voices Maleek Rivers, a wide receiver for the fictional Vice City Manatees. The character draws on Hill's real-life persona and Miami connections, including a nod to one of his touchdown celebrations.
Some of the biggest surprises are not walking Vice City’s streets at all. They are coming through its radios and talk shows.

“Weird Al” Yankovic revealed that he hosts Vice City FM, the game’s ’80s station, alongside Brigitte Nielsen. He also wrote in-game commercials and voices Burger Shot advertisements. Rockstar’s credits list Yankovic not only as DJ Al but among the game’s additional writers and original-music contributors.

Charlamagne tha God and Ivy Rivera host the in-game “Early AF” program, while “GTA VI”’s larger radio lineup includes musicians, actors and comedians ranging from Bad Bunny and Burna Boy to Lana Del Rey,Jeremy Irons,Keith Richards and Jason Sudeikis.

The effect is bigger than a conventional video game soundtrack. Rockstar has constructed fictional stations that operate almost like real media ecosystems, with hosts, commercials, talk segments and personalities embedded into the world around the player.
That approach has long been part of the franchise’s satire, but “GTA VI” appears to have expanded it considerably.

title: What to stream on Thanksgiving week: 'Dig,' Jennifer Lopez and 'Way of the Warrior Kid'
summary: Amy Poehler's new series “Dig” and Jennifer Lopez’s concert show are among the new streaming releases this week
story: Amy Poehler's new series “Dig” and Jennifer Lopez’s concert show are among the new streaming releases this week
The Amy Poehler-led series “Dig” and a new concert show from Jennifer Lopez are some of the new television, films, music and games headed to a device near you.

Also among the streaming offerings worth your time this Thanksgiving week, as selected by The Associated Press’ entertainment journalists: “The Mosquito Bowl,” “Blade Runner 2099” and a new project from Peter Gabriel.

— In “The Mosquito Bowl” (Wednesday on Netflix), Peter Berg directs a World War II drama about four college football stars who enlist in the Marines after the attack on Pearl Harbor. Based on a true story, the movie matches two passions – football and war films – for Berg, the filmmaker of “Friday Night Lights” and “Lone Survivor.” The cast includes Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson and Tom Francis.

– “The Magic Faraway Tree” (Friday on HBO Max) adapts Enid Blyton’s classic children’s book series. Claire Foy and Andrew Garfield star as parents of a family that relocates to the English countryside. There, their three children discover a magical tree full of enchanting fairies with branches that lead to fantastical lands.

– In “Way of the Warrior Kid” (Wednesday on Apple TV), a bullied middle school kid named Marc (Jude Hill) experiences a life-changing summer with his uncle, Jake (Chris Pratt), a recuperating Navy SEAL. Jake’s teachings, dubbed “Operation Warrior Kid,” go beyond hand-to-hand combat. With Linda Cardellini.
— AP Film Writer Jake Coyle

— Struggling to think of what to watch with your loved ones this Thanksgiving holiday? Strain no more. On Thursday, “The JLO Show: Live in Las Vegas” will premiere on CBS and stream on Paramount+. It’s a concert spectacular, capturing Jennifer Lopez’s “Up All Night Live in Las Vegas” residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace. It’s all the hits, at home.

— On Friday, Peter Gabriel will release “o(backslash)i,” a companion record to his 2023 release “i/o.” The album's 13 new tracks bring the joint project to a total of 25. “This record has been more of a marathon than a sprint,” he said in a press statement about the prolific work.
— AP Music Writer Maria Sherman

— Amy Poehler and Hugh Laurie star in “Dig,” a summer-in-Greece comedy about archaeologists and the college students working beside them. All 10 episodes arrive Monday on Peacock. The series reteams Poehler with “Parks and Recreation” co-creator Mike Schur. Writer J.J. Philbin, who is also married to Schur, joins as co-showrunner.

— A three-part docuseries on the Karen Read story arrives Monday on Netflix. “The Trials of Karen Read” examines the death of Boston police officer John O’Keefe. Jurors and members of O’Keefe’s family speak on camera in the three-part series, which revisits both trials.

— In Prime Video’s “Clashing Through the Snow,” rivals up for the same publishing job end up sharing a rental car after a snowstorm strands them. It stars Chris Briney (“The Summer I Turned Pretty") and Michelle Randolph (“Landman”) with Lukas Gage, Julia Fox and Paris Hilton. It streams Monday on Prime Video.

— Set 50 years after “Blade Runner 2049,” a new sci-fi limited series called “Blade Runner 2099” comes to Prime Video on Wednesday. It stars Michelle Yeoh as the replicant Olwen and Hunter Schafer as Blade Runner Cora in a Los Angeles remade by someone other than humans. All eight episodes drop at once.

— Instead of watching football on Thanksgiving, you could go full camp and binge “The Hunting Wives” Season 2. The series, loosely based on a novel of the same name, stars Brittany Snow and Malin Akerman as Sophie and Margo, whose friendship in an East Texas town turns messy and murderous. The series was originally intended for Starz but ultimately landed at Netflix, where it became a breakout hit and even got its own “SNL” sketch. In Season 2, Sophie and Margo go from friends to foes. WNBA star Angel Reese also joins the cast. A third season has already been ordered.
— AP Writer Alicia Rancilio

— If you’re looking for something to download to your laptop after Thanksgiving dinner, check out “Appulse.” It combines two types of arcade classics: pinball and space shooters like “Asteroids.” The gimmick here is that the pinball itself is a spaceship with guns, and whenever you fire them the recoil sends you in the opposite direction. Meanwhile, enemies are landing, so you need to shoot or ram them to conquer the leaderboard. French indie developer Le Rado promises multiple tables and the ability to upgrade your craft as you bounce your way through. Pull the plunger Thursday on PC.
— Lou Kesten

title: In the unflinching 'Josephine,' Beth de Araújo transmutes tragedy into art
summary: The central character of Beth de Araújo’s shattering film “Josephine” is an 8-year-old girl modeled on Araújo as a child
story: The central character of Beth de Araújo’s shattering film “Josephine” is an 8-year-old girl modeled on Araújo as a child

NEW YORK -- The central character of Beth de Araújo’s shattering film “Josephine” is an 8-year-old girl modeled on Araújo as a child. While walking in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park, she and her father interrupt a rape, an experience that has taken Araújo much of her life to process.
But one of Araújo’s biggest influences, when turning autobiography into drama, was Travis Bickle of “Taxi Driver.”

“It’s so complicated because you see the world through his eyes,” Araújo says. “The world is dark and dangerous, and there’s some really horrible people in it. He’s like, ‘Well, I’m going to do something about it.’ You’re like, ‘But the darkness has taken over you. You can’t be the vigilante you want to be.’ ”

In “Josephine,” which opened in theaters Friday, point of view plays a big role. Starring Mason Reeves as the 8-year-old protagonist and with Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan as her parents, the film is largely told from Josephine’s perspective. After her glimpse of a grim adult world, we watch her struggle so much so that she, like Travis Bickle, is nearly overtaken by darkness.
But that’s not what happens to Josephine, and it wasn’t what happened to Araújo. She became a filmmaker instead.

“There is a way to find true resilience,” Araújo said in a recent interview. “It's in the way — how do I say this — I've become an artist. For me, the ‘Taxi Driver’ ending isn't true. At one point, the incident did almost completely overturn me. But it didn’t.”

It has taken time for Araújo, 41, to get to this point. Her memory of the incident was only triggered in adulthood. In 2014, she recounted her experience in a “Moth” talk. For a time, Araújo also volunteered for a rape and battering hotline in Los Angeles. Eventually, she, in a fit of catharsis, poured out what she calls “a vomit draft” of 70 pages.

But as she developed it, “Josephine” became both about Araújo’s own story and about moving beyond it. When the film premiered earlier this year at the Sundance Film Festival, it won both the grand jury prize and the audience award.

“Josephine” is by any measure a triumph. It’s one of the most searing and memorable films of the year: an uncommonly accurate portrait of childhood and the rare film to unblinkingly confront sexual abuse. But it hasn’t been easy.

“To make this career work, to make money on your films about things that people don’t deem a moneymaker, it’s daunting. Somehow I’m suited for it,” Araújo says. “I don’t mean this in a good way. Go be happy and be a dairy farmer in Ireland. I don’t know if I wish this on people.”
Araújo has carved out an uncompromising start as a filmmaker. Her first movie, 2022’s “Soft & Quiet,” followed a female white supremacist and elementary school teacher. It caught Tatum's attention.
“Beth’s first movie was just …,” says Tatum, clapping his hands. “It was singular. I watched it and I was like: (Expletive), that is someone who made a choice.”

In “Josephine,” the parents struggle with how to talk to Josephine about what she has seen. Tatum’s father, Damien, believes in training Josephine to protect herself. Her mother, Claire (Chan), longs for more sensitivity. But they both struggle, unprepared for the sudden onset of adult horrors in their young daughter’s life, or their churning repercussions.

“When I read the script, I found myself going back and forth, at times empathizing more with Claire and other times with Damien, and other times just wanted to shake the both of them,” says Chan. “They’re two people who are just trying their best but they bring their own flaws and traumas with them, and the way they were raised.”
For Tatum, the father of a 13-year-old daughter, the connections were profound. He has learned, he says, that there is no handbook for parenthood.

“I could see a lot of my dad and a lot of myself in how to handle moments like that,” says Tatum. “I’m a mix of both of us: the uncompromising rage but also trying so very hard to be a softer person than maybe what Beth had. That exploration, I didn’t know what would come out of it. Each scene was kind of an unfolding moment.”

That includes the widely hailed performance by the nine-year-old Reeves, whom Araújo discovered at a farmers market. Given the nature of the film, efforts were made to shield her from the story’s uglier aspects. She never read the script; her mother read it aloud to her. At the Sundance premiere, she arrived midway through the movie, after the park scene. But again and again, Reeves impressed Araújo by her instincts as an actor.
“Sometimes when you’re talking to Mason, you feel like you’re talking to your grandmother. She’s ageless,” says Araújo. “The biggest difference was that she needed snacks.”

After Araújo’s experience as a child, her parents’ solution was to avoid any discussion of it. Araújo doesn’t know when children should be talked to about sexual assault. But she believes ignoring it isn't the answer.

“I will say for me, silence was really not helpful,” she says. “It left me to spiral into this dangerous imagination without some clear guidance. Some adult guidance could have been very helpful to me. I didn’t get it not for lack of love but for lack of understanding. We hope kids aren’t retaining as much as they are sometimes.”

Araújo’s experience fielding calls on the Los Angeles hotline helped her see the patterns of sexual assault. It only fueled her anger in how little public funding there is in studying rapists or in educating young men.

“We have decided that we’re OK telling young girls: ‘It’s sort of your job to keep yourself safe because no one else is going to do it. You have to not go into the woods alone. You have to not get into the Uber late at night,’” Araújo says.
“Look at the mess we’re in,” she adds, citing the lack of charges related to the Jeffrey Epstein case. “We’re telling all the little girls in the world: It is on you to keep yourself safe.”

Araújo tries to compartmentalize her reactions. She grants that “Beth, the citizen, is infuriated.” But as a filmmaker, she's not a policymaker. And making “Josephine,” and selling it, has been hard enough.
“It’s a tough space to live in. It’s an incredibly tough film to edit. I’m looking forward to challenging myself and moving on,” Araújo says. “I’m kind of ready to keep making art.”

title: Trump administration urges judge to lift order blocking Kennedy Center's closure
summary: President Donald Trump’s administration has urged a federal judge to lift a court order blocking its plans to close the Kennedy Center for two years of renovation work on the cultural and arts venue
story: President Donald Trump’s administration has urged a federal judge to lift a court order blocking its plans to close the Kennedy Center for two years of renovation work on the cultural and arts venue

WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump's administration on Thursday urged a federal judge to lift a court order blocking its plans to close the Kennedy Center for two years of renovation work on the cultural and arts venue.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper didn't immediately rule from the bench after hearing arguments on the government's request to dissolve the preliminary injunction that he issued in May. In that order, Cooper ruled that the Kennedy Center board’s vote to close the facility was “ill-informed and seemingly preordained” with no regard for its legal obligations.

A Democratic member of Congress sued to challenge Trump's takeover of the Kennedy Center — a key piece of the Republican president's campaign to leave his personal stamp on some of the most iconic landmarks in the nation’s capital.

In August and September, the center’s board voted twice to close its main building for two years to complete the planned repairs. Government lawyers said in a court filing that the center has become “dangerously dilapidated and decrepit,” with a ceiling partially collapsing in early September.
Justice Department attorney William Jankowski argued that the court's review of the board's decision must be “very, very deferential.”
“Plaintiff does not dispute the need for construction at the Kennedy Center,” Jankowski told the judge. “The board's decisions here were reasonable, and they must stand.”
At the close of Thursday's hearing, Cooper — who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama — didn't specify how soon he would rule.
Cooper asked an attorney for the plaintiff, Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, how keeping the injunction in place indefinitely would benefit the center and the public.

Beatty's attorney Nathaniel Zelinsky warned the judge that lifting the order now would “embolden future breaches and misbehavior” by the administration. He urged Cooper to appoint an independent monitor to protect the center if he does dissolve the injunction.
“There’s a monumental breach of fiduciary duty that is ongoing,” Zelinsky said.
The judge asked what authority he has to appoint a monitor to oversee the center's operations.
“It's pretty standard trust law,” Zelinsky replied.
Beatty, an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board, sued last December to prevent the addition of Trump’s name to the center. Beatty subsequently challenged the closing plans, too.
In May, when Cooper initially blocked the administration from closing the center for renovations, he also ruled that Trump’s name was illegally added to the building.

Beatty’s attorneys urged the judge to keep the injunction in place. The center’s closure plan is a “Band-Aid” designed to cover up officials’ mismanagement and to please Trump, they argued in a court filing.

Last year, Congress appropriated roughly $257 million for maintenance on the main building at the center’s request. Performing the work in phases, with partial closures spaced out over four years, would allow the center to remain open to patrons, Beatty's lawyers argued.

A center official who consulted with Trump concluded that a total closure over two years would be the "most cost-effective and efficient path" to addressing the center’s infrastructure needs, government lawyers counter.

title: Dozens of inmates in Romania step onto the stage for the 15th edition of a prison theater festival
summary: A drama festival in Romania gives dozens of prison inmates a brief respite from life behind bars as they perform on stage at a renowned theater in the capital
story: A drama festival in Romania gives dozens of prison inmates a brief respite from life behind bars as they perform on stage at a renowned theater in the capital

BUCHAREST, Romania -- A drama festival in Romania gave dozens of prison inmates a brief respite this week from life behind bars as they stepped into the limelight, performing on stage at a renowned theater in the capital.

This year’s 15th edition of the “Dana Cenusa — Unshackling through Culture” Multiart Festival, organized by the National Administration of Penitentiaries at the Nottara Theatre in Bucharest, brought together 59 inmates from seven different prisons across the country.

Launched in 2009, the prison theater festival offers inmates a route toward integration and hopes to combat stereotypes by giving theatergoers an opportunity “to discover the human being beyond their legal status.”

Madalina Iosif, spokesperson for the prison administration, told The Associated Press that social reintegration is not just about prisoners serving custodial sentences but also engaging inmates in educational and social activities to prepare them "for a fresh start.”

The performances — collaborations between 12 theater professionals — showed off a range of themes, from an adaptation of Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot” drawing on the memoir “The Silent Escape” by the late Romanian political prisoner Lena Constante, to productions titled “Locked Within Myself” and “The Sweetness of Doing Nothing LTD.”
Patricia Prisacariu, director of “Waiting for Godot,” said it was a sometimes difficult but memorable and worthy experience.

“I won’t lie to you, it was hard at first. It was a challenge for me,” she said. “But I think I’ve learned to see their sensitive side and to bring out what is pure within them. I’ve come to understand that ‘Godot’ means something different to everyone … I am truly glad to have met these wonderful people.”
Since 2009, the festival has taken place every year except 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, and hundreds of inmates have performed in scores of plays penned by both professionals and prisoners.

While participation doesn’t guarantee a shorter sentence or other privileges, it can earn inmates selected for the performances bonus points, which they can apply toward extra visitors or faster access to parole.
Tuesday wasn’t the first time stepping onto the stage for 32-year-old inmate Pavel Alexandru Cristian, who appeared in “Locked Within Myself.”

“I was selected three years ago. This year, we will be performing a piece — a monologue-based performance — centered on our inner fears,” he said. “I will play the role of a police officer, tasked with drawing certain conclusions by the end.”

Maria Caramalau, a prison police inspector at Vaslui Prison in eastern Romania, said the productions give inmates opportunities to show a side of themselves that even they might struggle to see beyond.
“When you are someone deprived of your liberty you tend to see yourself as having only flaws,” she said.

“But in the moment you receive applause on stage, when a person’s positive side is revealed, it becomes clear that … whether free or behind bars, art has the power to help us escape, in a sense, from our own fears.”
McGrath reported from Leamington Spa, England.

title: Activist archivists are bringing back old home movies
summary: Archiving activists who roam from town to town in France are making people's forgotten home movies great again by preserving them digitally
story: Archiving activists who roam from town to town in France are making people's forgotten home movies great again by preserving them digitally
ANTIBES, France -- They flicker on a small screen — grainy, almost ghostly images of lives and times that Romain Gimenes has heard about from family for years but is too young to have known himself.

Slowly hand-winding reels of decades-old Super 8 film through a viewing machine — lent to him by archiving activists who have made it their mission to save home movies like these from being tossed out as trash — Gimenes marvels as loved ones and places that his grandfather filmed in the 1970s dance back to life in sepia tones.
“Oh! That’s my grandfather,” the 30-year-old French Riviera school teacher exclaims. He inherited his middle name, Gabriel, from the man whose bearded face appeared fleetingly and whom he never met.

Interspersed among more images — of his mother, his 94-year-old grandmother, even a great-grandmother and others — pops up a prized find: Footage of a service station the family used to own, since demolished and replaced by a bakery, in the Riviera town of Antibes.
Gimenes whips out his phone and snaps a photo, a digital copy of an analog image to show and remind his mother of halcyon days.

“A photograph of a photograph,” he says, reflecting on his Instagram-era reflex gesture. “Today, we film everything and photograph everything. But who takes the time to look at it all? Who takes the time really to see things, really to look?”
“It’s that gesture of our time — the swipe.”

Just 200 years ago, only one human being — also a Frenchman — had the power to freeze time and our world into a photographic image. The father of photography, Nicéphore Niépce, knew back in 1824 that he'd invented something special, writing to his brother that the image he'd taken of the view from a window was “vraiment quelque chose de magique” — really something magical.

The world's fastest cameras today capture trillions of frames per second. Never have so many people been armed with the ability to immortalize children's first steps, to unmask abuses by filming them, to distort truths by altering or inventing images, to edit instances into reels and stories, to sear joys and horrors, beauty and ugliness onto our retinas and our brains.
And never have humans been so addicted — but also, perhaps, so inured — to that power.

On the clouds of Google Photos alone, users have stored more than 9 trillion photos and videos. Images take up so much digital space that it has to be measured in zettabytes, which are mind-blowingly gigantic. Just one zettabyte is equivalent to 250 billion DVDs and if each of its 1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 bytes of data were a liter of water, a zettabyte would fill more than 7,000 Pacific Oceans, according to U.S. technology company Cisco Systems, Inc.
Boston-based data research company IDC estimates that photos and moving images will have generated about 144 zettabytes of data worldwide in 2026.

“That includes captured, streamed, broadcast and replicated copies. By 2030, that figure is forecast to reach about 234 zettabytes as higher-resolution smartphone cameras and video-first social platforms put more content in more hands, and as AI-generated images and video add a new source of data on top of what people capture,” says Adam Wright, an IDC senior research manager. He answered questions via email.
But then there are images that make up no zettabytes — yet — and that are, those archiving them say, crying out for rescue.

For Stephanie Ange, Pierre Bouchut and Margot Lestien, who roam from town to town in France, collecting home movies and digitizing them for archives, image preservation is a battle waged reel by reel.

The name that the trio chose for their group, Ofnibus, plays off the French word for UFO. They can never be sure what they might find on the films and video cassettes that people bring them, often without much of a clue of what they show. Rummaged from garages, attics, cupboards and drawers, and often filmed by people who have since died, they are, quite literally, noninventoried cinematic objects until Bouchut runs them through his film-scanner or pops them into his VHS machines.

In their 23 residencies over five years, Bouchut has seen “everything there is to see in life”: Marriages, baptisms and birthdays galore but also an A-to-Z from farmers butchering prized pigs to the forcible shaving of women's heads during World War II to punish and shame them for suspected relations with German soldiers.
He’s had plenty of surprises, not all of them pleasant, including what today might be called sex tapes — or as he more delicately puts it: “Births, and the stage before births.”
“I love picnics,” he says. “And the Tour de France — everyone filmed that.”
The more he watches, the more he's struck by how “everything changes, but nothing changes.”

“Children apparently weren’t better behaved in the past. People enjoyed themselves just as much as they do today,” he says. “There’s a universality that comes through, something that gives you a little faith in humanity.”
But as time passes, so do the people who know what the images show.

“Finding the material, being able to watch it again and digitize it is one thing, but you still need to be able to interpret and understand it,” Lestien says. “That’s where the urgency lies: the people who still remember the events and what’s on the films are dying.”

The introduction in 1965 of Kodak's Super 8 mm format democratized moviemaking with hand-held cameras that whirred through cartridges containing 50 feet (15 meters) of film. But ever-fewer families still have the functioning projectors (followed later by VCRs) that would be fired up occasionally to watch their home movies together. Films that were treasured can, for the generations that inherit them, become unwatchable clutter.
“Eventually they throw it away because it takes up space, it’s starting to smell bad, and they can’t really see what they could do with it,” Lestien says.
The projectors and video-viewing machines that the Ofnibus team carts around France are making forgotten home movies great again.

In Antibes, they digitized 22 hours of images for archiving and reconnected their donors with memories and family histories. They also commissioned an editor who boiled down selected images into a 30-minute movie for a public viewing that 50 townspeople attended. It included rediscovered footage of Brigitte Bardot, the cinema icon who lived on the French Riviera and was filmed with a basket of roses.

Retired 65-year-old travel agent Sophie Roux-Nantas brought 16 reels of film from the 1930s to the '60s that were languishing in her garage. She saw herself as a 3-year-old on a beach “playing just as children play, just as the new generation does. We made sandcastles. That hasn’t changed, and we swam in the same way.”
On one of his 28 videocassettes “that were all sleeping in a box,” 41-year-old physiotherapist Yohan Chabert was transported back to the 1990s and a family game of Monopoly.
He snapped a photo of the screen.
“It’s moving,” he said. “And, I think, it’s something to share. Because having reels at home and leaving them in a cupboard is a bit of a shame.”

title: CDC director draws doubts from employees and ire from legislators
summary: Dr. Erica Schwartz, head of the CDC, is facing scrutiny from House Democrats and calls for her resignation
story: Dr. Erica Schwartz, head of the CDC, is facing scrutiny from House Democrats and calls for her resignation

NEW YORK -- Three months into her tenure as head of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. Erica Schwartz is being investigated by House Democrats, facing a call to resign, and drawing ire from both within and outside the agency.
What's been happening at the nation's top public health agency has alarmed outside health professionals. It also has alienated staff, leaving morale as bad as ever, employees say.

Schwartz, 54, took the helm of the CDC at a very challenging time: the worst U.S. measles epidemic in more than three decades, a large dengue fever outbreak in Florida and the fastest-growing overseas Ebola outbreak in history.
She reports to U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who is a longtime critic of vaccines and federal public health policy and who played a role in decimating CDC staffing last year.
“She has a tough job, at a tough time, and a tough boss,” said Noel Brewer, a University of North Carolina public health professor.

In an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday, Schwartz defended her work, saying she's trying to restore trust in the CDC — including by changing how measles-associated deaths are being reported. She said some of the criticisms are based on misperceptions and argued she is making progress on her goals.
“I do understand why people have concerns," Schwartz told the AP from her home in Naples, Florida. “Have I made mistakes? Certainly. But I'm here to work on the behalf of the American people.”

Some experts say she has made the situation worse. And critics are seizing on the Pan American Health Organization’s declaration last week that measles is continuously spreading here, marking the re-establishment of a public health threat that was eliminated in the last century.
“I have no confidence that she will do what it takes to course-correct at the CDC, and she should resign immediately,” said U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet, a Colorado Democrat.
When President Donald Trump nominated Schwartz to be the next CDC director in April, he called her “a STAR!” on social media.

She holds both medical and law degrees. She was chief medical officer for the U.S. Coast Guard, where she oversaw 41 clinics and 150 sick bays. She served as deputy surgeon general in the U.S. Public Health Service, helping to lead uniformed medical and health professionals posted at the CDC and government health agencies.
Many public health leaders were cautiously optimistic, noting the CDC badly needed steady leadership after enduring more than a year of turmoil and months of being led by interim directors.

Schwartz was the third Trump nominee for CDC director in less than 18 months. The first was a former Florida congressman whose nomination was pulled an hour before a Senate confirmation hearing. The second was Susan Monarez, who won Senate approval but then was ousted less than a month into the job when Trump administration officials said she was not aligned with the president’s agenda.
Under Kennedy, the agency has seen around 30% of its staff leave, mostly through layoffs, resignations and retirements.

At her nomination hearing, Schwartz pledged “radical transparency” to rebuild public trust in the agency, which she noted declined during the COVID-19 pandemic and which has eroded further under Kennedy.
“I will always stand on science and speak the truth, even in difficult moments,” she testified.

Meanwhile, public misperceptions about vaccines have persisted. A recent Annenberg Public Policy Center survey found that about 1 in 6 Americans said they believed that “vaccines given to children for diseases like measles, mumps and rubella cause autism” — even though dozens of studies have determined there’s no causal link. Roughly another 1 in 5 said they didn’t know whether it was true.

Schwartz started at the Atlanta-based agency in mid-August. A week later, she held her first “all hands” staff meeting, during which she promised to advocate for the agency and said she wouldn’t hesitate to disagree with Kennedy — but only privately.
Some say that’s when their optimism for Schwartz began to fade.

“I don’t have a clear sense of what is important to her, what are her red lines,” one CDC health scientist told the AP. “If we’re talking about radical transparency,” it is appropriate to know on what issues and what messaging she will not compromise, the scientist added. The employee spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution.
Asked about that assessment, Schwartz said: “I would never do anything unethical or illegal. ... That is a red line.”

Despite that transparency pledge, CDC and HHS officials for months would not release Schwartz’s salary — even though it is public information. Schwartz is paid about $375,000 a year, CDC officials finally told the AP this week, above the typical range for previous CDC directors.

So far she also has been less visible than some predecessors. She has not held any news conferences, and has not used her bully pulpit to try to persuade more Americans to get vaccinations — including for measles, the flu and COVID-19.
Schwartz told the AP that, concerning measles, she doesn't believe a federal health official on TV will sway most of the unvaccinated.
But with the nation experiencing its worst measles epidemic in decades, many public health and medical leaders say Schwartz should be strongly urging Americans to get vaccinated.

“I hope to see her display independence from the vaccine rhetoric and challenges that have been part of this administration,” said Dr. Wendy Armstrong, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. “I don’t think we have seen that yet.”
Kennedy continues to back Schwartz. The Health and Human Services Department issued a statement in response to Associated Press queries, quoting Kennedy as saying she had his full support.

“Dr. Schwartz brings the judgment to make hard decisions and the courage to see them through. She is reforming CDC and sharpening its focus on its core mission: protecting Americans from disease,” the statement said.
Some Democratic legislators accuse Schwartz and Kennedy of downplaying measles.

Kennedy has challenged health officials’ accounts of measles deaths. And the CDC has stopped quickly relaying state reports of measles deaths. It adopted a new policy requiring the review of death certificates, which has resulted in CDC counting only about half the measles-associated deaths that states are reporting.
Schwartz said that was her decision, and stemmed from her desire to have a uniform definition of what counts as a measles death.
Democrats on the House Energy & Commerce Committee have questioned why CDC changed the policy.

“As the crisis worsens, we are concerned that you continue to direct an effort at CDC to downplay the outbreak and artificially reduce the number of deaths that CDC reports,” according to a statement from Reps. Frank Pallone Jr. of New Jersey, Diana DeGette of Colorado and Yvette Clarke of New York.
“We are expanding our investigation to examine the threats your actions pose to Americans’ health and whether changes to your statutory authority are required,” they added.

The statement followed a briefing at which Schwartz was supposed to answer congressional staffers' questions about the measles data. The committee leaders described Schwartz as unresponsive and, at times, misleading.
Schwartz argued that she was “fully transparent. And I am really concerned that they think there is more to the story. There isn't.”

The AP interviewed eight current CDC workers about Schwartz's tenure. They all spoke on condition of anonymity, saying they feared retribution for speaking frankly about what’s going on within the agency.

Some said they never had high expectations. Others said they initially were hopeful but lost confidence, some of them blaming her handling of the measles death count. One said it’s still too early to judge her.
Several said they had hoped for more improvements and stability. Announcements about leadership appointees coming, going and changing titles have continued in a blur, the employees told the AP.
Some mentioned Caroline DeBerry, a former vice president at a conservative think tank and author of independently published novels including one titled “Esther: The Woman Who Didn’t Know Her Place.”

DeBerry got a job as acting director of communications, starting in August. Employees said she gained notoriety within the agency when all CDC website updates ground to a halt while awaiting her approval.

Asked about it, Schwartz said: “There was a bit of clunkiness that happened one day.” She also said DeBerry is on “terminal leave” and her last day will be in December, but did not immediately offer additional detail.
None of the agency veterans interviewed by the AP said they have spoken with Schwartz. But some said they had seen her around the CDC campus accompanied by a group of security guards.

Security has been a sensitive topic at CDC, especially since an August 2025 shooting outside the entrance of CDC’s main campus. A Georgia man who had blamed the COVID-19 vaccine for making him depressed and suicidal opened fire, killing a police officer and spraying bullets into 150 windows.
(The slain officer, David Rose, is widely held up as a hero by CDC employees, and some expressed irritation that Schwartz referred to him as “Officer Stone” during a recent health summit appearance.)

Dr. Tom Frieden, who served as CDC director in the Obama administration, said he occasionally had an escort outside the CDC campus after he received death threats. But Schwartz moves with a large security team inside CDC, and agency staffers said they don’t recall seeing that before.
“It feels like they’re afraid of us,” one health scientist said.

Schwartz acknowledged that early in her time at CDC, she walked the halls accompanied by about a half dozen guards at the recommendation of security leadership. The security details have been reduced to one plainclothes guard, she said.
A directive about research publications shows just how far apart CDC staff feel from the political leadership.

Two CDC scientists told the AP that they were directed in a recent meeting to stop submitting their research to journals run by organizations that have sued Kennedy. The prohibition would cover Pediatrics, one of the most-cited journals for doctors who specialize in children’s medical care, and Clinical Infectious Diseases, a highly regarded publication for doctors focused on germs.
The scientists said the directive was clearly stated but not written down in a memo or email.
HHS and CDC officials are adamant that neither Kennedy nor any other HHS or CDC official ever issued such a directive.
At the health summit, Schwartz acknowledged that CDC employees have lost trust in the political appointees who have been put in charge of the agency, “and I’m trying to earn that trust every day.”
She talked about work going on to stabilize the agency’s leadership and develop a “strategic hiring plan” for 2027.
CDC employees look around and see burned-out colleagues.
“I think everyone is just exhausted,” one health scientist said. “There’s just a sense that we can’t go on like this anymore.”
