title: Democrats supporting abortion rights won in the midterms, but changes unlikely soon
summary: Democrats who ran on abortion rights platforms won big in elections for Congress and state government jobs
story: Democrats who ran on abortion rights platforms won big in elections for Congress and state government jobs

Democrats who ran on abortion rights platforms won big in elections for Congress and state government offices. But it's not likely that they'll be able to impose quick and vast abortion policy changes.
That’s because Democrats did not take full control of the legislatures and governor's offices in states with the strictest laws — those that ban abortion at six weeks or all stages of pregnancy.

And in Congress, Democrats who will control both the House and Senate could attempt to bar states from adopting some kinds of abortion bans, but any move would likely meet a veto from President Donald Trump, which couldn't be overridden without GOP help.

Abortion has been primarily a state government issue since the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2022 ruling that struck down Roe v. Wade allowed states to enforce bans. Now, 13 states ban abortion at all stages of pregnancy — with some exceptions — and four more do so after about the first six weeks.

In 2027, Democrats will have control of both legislative chambers and the governor’s office in six states where they currently share power with Republicans. Those states — Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — already allow abortion through until at least fetal viability, which is generally considered to be sometime after 21 weeks of pregnancy.

Abortion is currently allowed through the first 20 weeks from fertilization, or about 22 weeks' gestation in Wisconsin and 23 in Pennsylvania. Democrats kept the governorships and gained full power in the legislatures in the elections in both states.
Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro are both calling for leveraging that power to amend their states’ constitutions to create a right to abortion.

Voters in a dozen states already have passed similar amendments, including two — Nevada and Virginia — this year. Voters in November also kept such protections in Missouri but defeated an initiative to add them to state law in Idaho.

In Georgia, where Democrats gained the House and the governor's office, abortion is banned in most cases after fetal cardiac activity can be detected — around six weeks into pregnancy and before many women realize they’re pregnant.
Josh McLaurin, the incoming Democratic lieutenant governor, is optimistic that one Republican state senator would be willing to join Democrats to repeal that law.
The measure could get at least a vote in the Senate, he said, because Republicans will have a 29-27 majority and may not take a “hyper-partisan approach” to block it.

McLaurin said that voters see the ban as a healthcare issue, especially after a state review board in 2024 found that two women died in Georgia after doctors were hesitant to perform abortions that could have saved their lives.
Still, Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms acknowledged that a GOP-held state Senate could be an obstacle.
“If we see a pathway to do something about it this session, then we’re going to take that opportunity," Bottoms said at a news conference. “And it may not be this session.”

After winning the attorney general election in Texas, Democrat Nathan Johnson said he would not sue out-of-state medical providers who prescribe abortion pills via telehealth and ship them to patients in the state as the outgoing attorney general, Republican Ken Paxton, has done. Paxton dropped his suits in November.

Those pills often come from states that seek to protect medical professionals who prescribe them through telehealth and ship them to patients in places with bans. That practice is why the number of abortions has been higher since the fall of Roe. It's also the heart of the current abortion legal battles.
Johnson could also withdraw Texas from a lawsuit challenging federal policy on the abortion pill mifepristone and decide not to defend the state's abortion restrictions against lawsuits.
“It is deeply gutting that now we don’t have Texas to be fighting with the pro-life side on this,” said Kelsey Pritchard, spokesperson for SBA Pro-Life America.

Pritchard and other anti-abortion activists are pushing the Trump administration to make mifepristone harder to get by persuading the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which is studying the drug, to bar filling prescriptions through the mail or at pharmacies. The FDA has said it'll have more information by March.
They're also counting on remaining Republican state attorneys general to keep up the fight.

Ohio lawmakers this month passed legislation to bar telehealth prescriptions for mifepristone sent into the state and to reimpose a 24-hour waiting period before obtaining an abortion. It’s not clear whether outgoing Republican Gov. Mike DeWine will sign them into law — or how courts would rule on legal challenges. Voters passed a constitutional amendment protecting abortion access in 2023.

Ingrid Duran, state legislative director at the National Right to Life Committee, said her group will keep pushing measures that Democrats sometimes support — such as supporting ways for women to anonymously and safely give up newborns for adoption. And, she said, it will encourage anti-abortion bills that may not have much of a chance of passing now as a way to build for the future.
“We're not going to give up just because it's going to be more challenging,” she said.

Some congressional Democrats are planning to push forward a measure that would bar states from banning abortion before viability and rescind restrictions that some states have — such as requiring multiple doctor’s visits or ultrasounds.
With a Trump veto expected if it reaches him, the effort would be aimed largely at forcing him to reject a policy that has public opinion on its side.
About 6 in 10 U.S. voters said abortion should be legal in all or most cases, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters in all 50 states.
Associated Press journalists Scott Bauer, Kate Brumback, Marc Levy, Amelia Thomson-DeVeaux and Anna Wilder contributed to this article.

title: A converted shipping container became an unexpected source of mental health help in South Africa
summary: In a South African township, a sensory room in a repurposed shipping container was initially designed for young children but has since become a mental health haven for teenagers and adults
story: In a South African township, a sensory room in a repurposed shipping container was initially designed for young children but has since become a mental health haven for teenagers and adults

JOHANNESBURG -- Sisanda Hani enters a former shipping container at a community center in South Africa, slips off her shoes and plunges into a sea of blue plastic balls. The 40-year-old mother of a teenager with ADHD and epilepsy lets the balls envelop her and screams.
For Hani, that howl is a release.

The shipping container is now a “sensory room” opened in April by youth-focused non-profit Afrika Tikkun in Orange Farm, a low-income township south of Johannesburg. Initially designed for young children with developmental conditions, it surprisingly also became a place of relief for parents and caregivers in a neighborhood where professional therapy is hard to find.
“We had a lot of stress,” Hani told The Associated Press. “No one was asking us how we were doing.”

The room is an assortment of sights and textures. Fairy lights thread through beaded curtains. Foil fish, tiny mirrors, a hammock and a burlap cushion fill the underwater world, with shapes resembling amoebas and coral covering a wall. Outside are balancing logs, sand and water pits, and a swing.
Locals helped design it, making sensory items from recycled materials in workshops led by Afrika Tikkun and its partner, Sensory-Space.

Hani was among those who helped. Caring for her 19-year-old son makes it difficult for the single mother to hold down a job. Even temporary work can be interrupted by a call about a seizure, sending her rushing home. Encounters with people who do not understand his conditions add to her stress.

She initially thought the room was only for children. A social worker encouraged her and other mothers to try it, and she says now she leaves feeling less burdened and better able to talk calmly to her son instead of shouting. She says he also becomes calmer and more playful during visits.
“We bottle it inside, but when you come here, everything comes out,” she said.

Afrika Tikkun describes the space as South Africa’s first community sensory facility. Program participants and their parents can book free sessions. Its usage records list 450 school-going children aged 6 to 18, 67 young adults and 56 parents and caregivers.

Tegan White, an occupational therapist with the program, says the room’s textures, lights, sounds and movement help users explore sensations and regulate their responses. The ball pit, for example, provides full-body contact that can help users sense where their limbs are.
For adults under stress, it offers somewhere to settle without having to explain their feelings.
“It doesn’t require words. Maybe you aren’t ready to talk,” White said.
The room provides sensory activities beyond her appointments, but she stresses that it complements professional care.
“Therapy is absolutely essential. Having access to ongoing intervention is important,” she said.
Annelize Kruger, an independent occupational therapy lecturer at the University of the Free State, says sensory rooms can help children and adults manage distress, although research remains limited.
“Our sensory needs do not disappear as we get older,” she said.

She distinguishes time spent exploring a sensory room from clinical sensory integration therapy, which involves individually tailored activities guided by an occupational therapist. Guidance can help users identify calming strategies to use beyond the room, Kruger said.

But professional care remains difficult to obtain for many in South Africa. In 2023, then-Health Minister Joe Phaahla said fewer than 30% of people with mental health problems in Africa's biggest economy received treatment. The government’s 2023–2030 mental health policy acknowledges staff shortages and uneven services across provinces.
And across Africa, mental health services remain underfunded and fragmented, particularly in underserved communities, according to the World Health Organization.

At the center, teenagers ask to return simply to sit and relax, says disability inclusion manager Bridget Gumede. Some children have shared troubles at school and home, prompting referrals to social workers. Staff admit up to five people at a time for sessions lasting less than 30 minutes.
“I didn’t know that it can do this much,” she said, adding they now need a bigger space.

The container and its sensory contents cost about $4,700 to $5,300, said Lana Roy, who leads Afrika Tikkun’s Disability Inclusion program. The organization has opened another sensory space in Cape Town and hopes to expand further.
Dee Blackie, the designer of the sensory space, says they invite adults to do something they may have left behind: play.
“So it doesn’t matter if you say, well, playing is not for me. When you get into the space, you immediately start playing,” she said.
For Njabulo Ntombela, 19, that play offers relief from worries about finding work and continuing her education. She says she's afraid she will be unable to support her family.

She visits the sensory room once or twice a month when she feels overwhelmed. Before discovering the room, she said she would withdraw and spend the day without speaking to anyone. Afterward, she feels more comfortable approaching others and asking for help.
The ball pit also gives her a chance to experience play she says she missed growing up.
"When I’m here, I feel like I’m back to 7 years old,” she said.

title: South Korea confirms its first case of cholera in 10 years
summary: South Korea has reported its first cholera case in 10 years
story: South Korea has reported its first cholera case in 10 years

SEOUL, South Korea -- South Korea on Friday reported its first case of cholera in 10 years, with health authorities urging people to take precautionary measures, use only safe water and wash their food properly.

The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency said health workers confirmed cholera from test samples of a person who had visited a hospital emergency room in the southeastern port city of Changwon earlier this month, showing symptoms of vomiting and diarrhea.

The agency said the unidentified person, who recovered and was discharged on Tuesday, had not traveled overseas in the past two months. It said health workers were trying to trace the source of infection and the people the person had been in contact with.

It was the country’s first case of cholera since 2016, when authorities identified three cases suspected to be caused by contaminated seafood. At least 162 people got sick in a larger outbreak in 2001.

Cholera spreads mostly through contaminated water and food and can also spread through contact with an infected person’s stool or vomit, according to the agency. Diarrhea is the most common symptom, and severe illness can lead to dehydration or shock that could potentially be fatal if treatment is delayed.

The agency issued guidance urging people to stick to safe water and cooked food and to wash and peel fruits and vegetables. It also urged medical facilities to promptly test and report suspected cases

title: Experts debunk Thanksgiving food myths, from turkey 'coma' to risky leftovers
summary: Experts say turkey was likely on the table at the first Thanksgiving in 1621, but there's no word on whether anyone took a nap afterward
story: Experts say turkey was likely on the table at the first Thanksgiving in 1621, but there's no word on whether anyone took a nap afterward
CONCORD, N.H. -- Was turkey on the table at the first Thanksgiving? Probably. Did anyone take a nap afterward? Unclear.
Among the many myths associated with Thanksgiving is the notion that today's traditional menu harkens back to what the Pilgrims and Wampanoag people actually ate in November 1621.

While no oral history has been passed down by the Native people, Pilgrim Edward Winslow briefly described the three-day feast in a letter to a friend, said Malka Benjamin, director of colonial interpretation and training at the Plimoth Patuxet Museums in Plymouth, Massachusetts.

According to Winslow’s letter — the only surviving record of the celebration — the Wampanoag leader Massasoit provided five deer, while the Pilgrims killed enough fowl in one day to feed the entire colony for nearly a week. He didn’t mention turkey specifically, but it frequently shows up in other firsthand accounts of the time period, Benjamin said.
“I feel very confident saying that it’s highly likely there was turkey on the table, in addition to duck and goose and other kinds of birds,” she said.

The menu also probably featured seafood, she said, along with squash and nasaump, a porridge-like Wampanoag dish made with ground corn and berries. Potatoes? Nope. And while cranberries were available, there was no sugar to turn them into sauce.
Here are some other more modern myths about Thanksgiving food and what experts have to say about them:

Unless you’ve been asleep for the last few decades, you’ve probably heard that tryptophan in turkey makes you sleepy. While the amino acid does spur the creation of feel-good brain chemicals like serotonin and melatonin, there’s not enough of it in turkey to make you nod off, said Kimberly Dong, associate professor of public health at Tufts University School of Medicine. Chicken and beef have similar levels; cheddar cheese has even more.

“What’s happening is that people are eating a lot of carbohydrate-rich foods that are really quickly absorbed into the bloodstream,” she said. That causes a spike in blood glucose levels followed by a rapid drop. It’s that roller coaster that contributes to fatigue, she said, not the “turkey coma.”

Overeating in general also makes you sleepy because blood gets diverted to the gastrointestinal tract to deal with digestion, leaving muscles tired, said Susan Roberts, a professor and nutrition scientist at the Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth.
“I’m not one of these punitive nutritionists. I think if you have overeaten and you do feel tired, fine, take a nap,” she said. “Enjoy it.”

That said, both Dong and Roberts take issue with the idea that overeating is a given. Skipping breakfast on Thanksgiving might sound smart, but trying to “save” calories for a big dinner usually backfires, Dong said, “because you are so ravenous by the time the food is served.”

Instead, she recommends eating a light breakfast and staying hydrated early in the day. Roberts, meanwhile, suggests a multi-day strategy: eating high fiber foods for two days before Thanksgiving to keep hunger in check.

The experts disagree when it comes to leftovers, however. Dong says setting aside leftovers can counteract the “this is my one chance to eat this” mentality that leads to heaping helpings. But Roberts says hosts should pare back from the start, and that guests who feel they can’t decline leftovers should throw most, if not all, of them away at home.
Willpower doesn’t work when a plate of food is in front of you, she said, because the sights and smells activate the body to receive a big meal.

“A better place to use your willpower is before it ever comes in the house, when you’re still full from the Thanksgiving meal,” she said. “You can throw half or three-quarters of it away now and it’s easy, but if you put it in the fridge, it becomes a whole different matter.”

If you do end up with leftovers, be careful, says Anne Suelzer, a registered dietitian and licensed dietitian with Health Loft. Properly stored leftovers will be safe for three or four days, but don’t rely on your senses to judge.
“The bacteria that make you sick usually don’t change how food looks or smells,” she said.
Leftovers should be refrigerated within two hours, and the clock starts when the food comes out of the oven, not when you’re done eating.
“It helps to start packing things up while people are still at the table,” she said.

title: Scientists report strong new evidence that specially bred mosquitoes can fend off dengue
summary: There is new evidence that breeding a special kind of mosquito could help fend off dengue infections, rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten
story: There is new evidence that breeding a special kind of mosquito could help fend off dengue infections, rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten

WASHINGTON -- Children who lived in Brazilian neighborhoods buzzing with a special kind of mosquito were far less likely to catch dengue or another worrisome virus, chikungunya, researchers reported Saturday.

The major study of more than 5,700 children in one of the world’s dengue hot spots offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit these viruses can be a viable strategy rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten.

In neighborhoods populated by these so-called Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes, researchers found about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections in schoolchildren compared to similar neighborhoods — an effect sustained even during Brazil’s severe 2024 dengue outbreak, said Dr. Sri Edupuganti of Emory University, part of the international research team.
The researchers reported the findings at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene.

“This is really exciting,” said Dr. David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who wasn’t involved with the Brazilian study. He predicts that pairing more use of these Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing steps to fight mosquito-borne disease could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places.
The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any U.S. state since at least the 1940s.

Usually in the continental U.S., dengue is found mostly in people who traveled internationally. But as of Friday, Florida health officials had tallied more than 650 locally acquired cases, about three-quarters of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa.
Outside the U.S., the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy.

How it works: Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia. It is harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The bacteria dramatically reduce the mosquitoes’ ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects — males and females — into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population.

Field trials and other studies in Indonesia and elsewhere have shown the strategy can significantly lower dengue diagnoses. But because people with mild symptoms may not be diagnosed, the new study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, went further. Researchers tested blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya or the Zika virus.

The four-year study compared children living in neighborhoods that all got the same pesticide and other mosquito-control interventions, but half were randomly assigned to have Wolbachia mosquitoes released into the area. There were too few cases of Zika to calculate if the special mosquitoes had any effect on that disease.
AP Medical Writer Mike Stobbe contributed to this report.

title: Britain's Princess Catherine reflects on life after cancer diagnosis in a new documentary
summary: The Princess of Wales opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary reflecting on life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024
story: The Princess of Wales opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary reflecting on life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024
LONDON -- Britain's Catherine, Princess of Wales opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.

“Heal” follows 44-year-old Kate as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours. She completed the feat in June to raise money for the cancer charity of the Royal Marsden Hospital, where she was treated.
In a trailer released Saturday by Prince William and Kate’s Kensington Palace office, the princess reflects on her cancer journey and speaks to others about their experiences.

Kate, who is married to the heir to the British throne, announced in March 2024 that she had cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy following major abdominal surgery. She did not reveal what type of cancer she was treated for.
Kate disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission and has gradually resumed her public duties, visiting India with William earlier this month.
In the trailer, Kate says cancer changes people profoundly, and “healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew, and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.”
She adds that “it’s clear we’re not meant to carry life’s challenges alone” and “often, it is through pain that we realize there’s a greater beauty that lies beyond that.”

“Heal” will be broadcast by the BBC in Britain on Nov. 29, by NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30, on Australia’s Channel 9 Dec. 1 and Canada’s CTV and Noovo on Dec. 7. Kensington Palace said proceeds from its distribution will go to the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

title: Palestinians victims of a third of violations against children worldwide, Save the Children says
summary: Save the Children warns that children in the Gaza Strip face severe dangers after three years of war
story: Save the Children warns that children in the Gaza Strip face severe dangers after three years of war

AMMAN, Jordan -- The children of the Gaza Strip face unmatched dangers after three years of war, a prominent non-governmental organization warned Thursday, as they suffer from repeated displacement, loss of family members, lack of healthcare and education, and abysmal living conditions.

Save the Children said almost one third of the tens of thousands of attacks and violations against children recorded worldwide last year took place in the Palestinian territories. The danger was especially high in Gaza, the tiny enclave with a population of 2 million where at least 20,000 children have been killed, according to local health authorities.
The psychological and physical impact on Palestinian children in Gaza will “live for many years to come,” Save the Children Regional Director Ahmad Alhendawi told The Associated Press.

In its annual global report, Save the Children said that one in four children, some 589 million, lived in conflict zones in 2025, the highest number documented since the end of the Cold War in 1990. The vast majority are in the Middle East and Africa.
The number is expected to increase this year with the ongoing war in Iran and the wider Mideast, and renewed war in Lebanon and Yemen in 2026.

Save the Children reported nearly 12,500 cases of violations against children in the Palestinian territories, mostly attacks on hospitals and schools and deprivation of aid. It said the situation was especially critical in Gaza, where Israel continues strikes despite an October 2025 ceasefire agreement with Hamas.
Although the latest report focused on 2025 figures, Alhendawi said conditions have shown little improvement this year.

“Lots of children who have survived themselves are injured themselves and are without surviving parents,” said Alhendawi. “This report is showing very clearly that what happened and what continues to happen in Gaza are violations at a scale that we haven’t seen and needs to be prioritized by the international community.”

Israel launched its war in Gaza in response to Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attacks. It says its ongoing strikes, including one on a hospital in the southern town of Khan Younis last week, target militants and are responses to Hamas violations of the ceasefire agreement.

While Israel has killed most of Hamas’ senior leadership, the conflict has devastated the territory and taken a heavy toll on Gaza’s civilians. The vast majority of people live in crowded tent camps or in the ruins of their former homes, with little access to food, water, or electricity.

“The children of Gaza are deprived of the bare minimum in life,” said displaced Palestinian Riad Abou Shamel, 65, surrounded by children playing in an open lot in Khan Younis filled with rubble and remains of pancaked buildings hit in airstrikes.
“They go to the market and can barely bring back half a cucumber or half an apple.”
Israel's military did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.

The report shed light on the surge of cases of abductions, sexual violence, and recruitment of children by armed forces in Africa, in conflict areas in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Nigeria, Sudan, and Somalia, and attacks on hospitals in Ukraine.
The data and figures in Save the Children's report of violations against children and children living in conflict zones come from the United Nations and the Peace Research Institute Oslo.
Chehayeb contributed from Beirut. Associated Press Senior Producer Wafaa Shurafa contributed to this report from Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip.

title: Scientists are fighting for their halted funds. Trust of Black communities may be harder to win back
summary: In Pittsburgh, a study aimed at understanding why Black Americans are twice as likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease has been abruptly halted
story: In Pittsburgh, a study aimed at understanding why Black Americans are twice as likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease has been abruptly halted

People in a historically Black corner of Pittsburgh took memory tests, tracked their sleep and blood pressure and shared stories of their past to help scientists unravel risks for Alzheimer’s disease.

But they may never get answers. The study was among broader research into why Black Americans are twice as likely as their white peers to develop Alzheimer’s, but the Trump administration abruptly halted it in its final stretch.

Researchers say the move not only wasted more than $8 million in taxpayer money already spent but also is a blow to the hard-earned trust of anxious study participants who won’t even learn if their brain tests showed signs of trouble.

“The community will look like, ’Oh, they came in here, they took all our stuff, they checked us out. Now they’re gonna leave us hanging,'” said Roderick Blair, 70, who had participated in the study for four years.

Trust in U.S. health institutions has long been strained in the Black community, stemming from the nation’s long-standing racial health inequities, unequal access to care and bias within the nation’s medical system. The legacy of the Tuskegee study, which withheld treatment from Black men who had been infected with syphilis in the 1930s, still casts a shadow.

The Pittsburgh study overcame that mistrust. Getting people involved in the city’s Hill and Homewood communities helped get people talking about memory loss, dementia and Alzheimer’s and helped challenge misconceptions about it, according to La’Vette Wagner, the Pittsburgh study’s field coordinator.

Families who once dismissed memory loss as depression began asking about dementia, and people outside the study called her to ask if family members could join, she said. More than half of Black Americans, or 55%, believe that a significant loss of memory or cognitive abilities is a natural part of aging rather than disease, according to the Alzheimer’s Association.
As Blair said, "You start forgetting things and you start to wonder, do you have Alzheimer’s? You wonder, do you have dementia?”

Then the study, which had been near completion in its fifth and final year, was stripped of funding last year by the National Institutes of Health, on the grounds that it was “not science,” according to the study’s researchers, despite a rigorous review and vetting from a community advisory board.
“It wasn’t a Black study or a DEI study,” Wagner said. “It was something that was happening that was real.”

Similar terminations happened all over the country. Negar Fani, a neuropsychologist at Emory University in Atlanta, was two years into a five-year, $2.9 million project on how daily experiences of racial discrimination affect the brain and body of Black Americans when NIH terminated it in July.
While Fani tries to find the roughly $2.3 million she needs to complete the study, she and her team were left to try to explain the situation to participants who feel abandoned.
“It takes a lot to restore trust with the Black community, who has experienced so many different betrayals,” she said.
Like the Pittsburgh study's funding, Fani’s grant had been terminated for being “not scientific” and “subjective” — after the study had been approved and had enrolled 66 of the 220 people it needed.
“It’s simply brain science research,” she said.

In Pittsburgh, study lead researcher Andrea Rosso is one of numerous scientists in a recently filed lawsuit against NIH and its parent Department of Health and Human Services, one of a growing body of legal actions as the administration continues to hunt for and halt medical grants with descriptions that include the words “disparities,” “minority” and “racial.”

Ann Cohen, a director of Pittsburgh’s Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center, also is part of that lawsuit after her separate, complementary study of Alzheimer’s risk also was halted -- after spending $5.2 million over three years. She, too, has a troubling ethics question: What to do with blood samples collected from the participants?
“You lose trust a hell of a lot faster than you build it,” she said.

A spokesperson for HHS said “Massive amounts of DEI grants have failed to translate into better health outcomes for minority populations. Following President Trump’s directives, NIH is shifting money into rigorous research that will help Americans — including minority populations — live longer, healthier lives.”
This year, the NIH has awarded 2,000 fewer grants for multiyear studies worth a total of $200 million compared with 2025, according to an Association of American Medical Colleges report.

“It’s unprecedented. Many of the decisions are based on political biases and based on what politicians think is valuable rather than peer review processes, evidence-based decisions about where to invest our research dollars,” said Jill Rosenthal, the director of public health policy at the Center for American Progress.
“We’re wasting resources, we’re wasting the opportunity to identify cures for diseases,” she said.

Researchers in Pittsburgh are especially concerned that promises made to the community will remain unfulfilled. The study, 15 years in the making, would’ve helped identify participants at a higher risk for Alzheimer’s — and for potential doctor’s visits and care.
Now, Wagner said, the findings are “stuck on a shelf,” and worse, over a decade of trust built with study participants has been breached.
Blair, the study participant, said reinstating trust within their communities will be an uphill battle. “It’s going to take years to reestablish something that was moving pretty good,” he said.

title: Canada's defense minister says his country answers to no one in Washington
summary: Canada’s defense minister says that his country answers to no one in Washington, asserting Canadian sovereignty after the Pentagon accused Ottawa of failing to meet its military commitments
story: Canada’s defense minister says that his country answers to no one in Washington, asserting Canadian sovereignty after the Pentagon accused Ottawa of failing to meet its military commitments

TORONTO -- Canada’s defense minister said on Tuesday that his country answers to no one in Washington, asserting Canadian sovereignty a day after the Pentagon accused Ottawa of failing to do enough to defend North America.

The Pentagon said Canada lacked a credible plan to meet NATO’s spending targets, accusing Ottawa of relying for decades on American taxpayers to foot its defense bill. Relations between the two neighbors have been strained by U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st state.
“Canada is a sovereign nation. I’ll be very direct. We don’t report to the United States,” Defense Minister David McGuinty told reporters.

He insisted Canada remains on track to spend 5% of gross domestic product on defense and related security investments by 2035, while emphasizing that NATO allies had agreed to review the spending pledge in 2029.
“We also said by 2029 we would be examining that 5% commitment,” McGuinty said.
McGuinty said Canada’s plans would bring spending to 4% of GDP by 2030, a “significant, significant step” from 1.25% of GDP 14 months ago.

NATO’s 2025 agreement calls for at least 3.5% of GDP for core defense and up to 1.5% for related security investments by 2035. The scheduled 2029 review will examine the pace and balance of spending against security threats and military needs.
The Pentagon’s unusually blunt fact sheet on Monday accused Ottawa of postponing its largest spending increases until after the 2029 federal election.
“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves,” it said. “Canada must get serious and focused.”

The Pentagon said U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was “laser focused” on modernizing Canada’s military. The U.S. criticism followed a classified directive from Hegseth that Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said largely restricts officials’ participation in Canadian think tank events and social engagements.

The Trump administration barred Pentagon officials from attending the Halifax International Security Forum under restrictions imposed in 2025 on think tank participation. Now in its 18th year, the gathering draws about 300 military officials, U.S. lawmakers, diplomats and scholars annually. Previous administrations of both parties sent senior Pentagon officials, including defense secretaries.
Democratic U.S. Sen. Andy Kim, who attended the Halifax forum this past weekend, criticized the restrictions in a social media post.
“Hegseth did not allow a single American servicemember in uniform to show up,” he wrote.
Rounds said Saturday that the directive was not expected to affect joint military operations or intelligence sharing.

Canada reached NATO’s previous 2% target. Its latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by 2027-28, including 2.6% for core defense. Canada’s parliamentary budget watchdog has questioned how the government will reach 5%.
McGuinty said cooperation with Washington through the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, and work with NATO remained unchanged.
“We’re making the investments we announced. We’re executing on those plans,” he said.
The Pentagon also criticized Ottawa’s review of its planned purchase of 88 American-made F-35 fighters, warning that a mixed fleet could worsen personnel shortages and create uncertainty for NORAD.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered the review as Trump threatened Canadian sovereignty and imposed tariffs. Canada has examined Swedish-made Gripen fighters, which could bring manufacturing jobs.

title: Armed men take hostages in Cartagena, one of Colombia's top tourist destinations
summary: Colombian police say that a group of armed men have seized a super market in the city of Cartagena and taken an unknown number of people hostage
story: Colombian police say that a group of armed men have seized a super market in the city of Cartagena and taken an unknown number of people hostage

BOGOTA, Colombia -- A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday and are holding an unknown number of hostages, Colombian police said.

Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the Exito supermarket in Cartagena’s La Castellana neighborhood Tuesday, while local media have shown footage of snipers on nearby buildings in what appears to be a standoff appears between the armed men and police.

Cartagena is one of Colombia's main tourist destinations. The city of a million people is famous for its well preserved 18th century architecture, and the thick stone walls built to defend it from pirate attacks.
Cartagena’s airport temporarily suspended its operations on Tuesday following the incident. But it later said in an X message that operations were slowly returning to normal.

title: Russia backs tax rises as 2027 budget sees military spending soar
summary: Russia’s lower house of parliament has approved a 2027-2029 state budget and passed tax increases to fund the war in Ukraine
story: Russia’s lower house of parliament has approved a 2027-2029 state budget and passed tax increases to fund the war in Ukraine
Russia’s lower house of parliament approved a 2027-2029 state budget Tuesday and separately passed a series of tax increases to fund Moscow’s war in Ukraine.

The budget allocates approximately 17.15 trillion rubles ($208.9 billion) for national defense in 2027, up from the 12.93 trillion rubles ($157.5 billion) in 2026. The amount is also a marked increase from the 13.6 trillion rubles ($165.7 billion) forecast for expenditure in 2027 in last year’s budget.
The government seeks to help cover rising military costs with additional taxes on mining companies and income from citizens’ investments.
Deputies approved the bill with 396 votes in favor and 37 abstentions. It now goes to the Federation Council, Russia’s upper house of parliament, for approval.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has increasingly sought to squeeze tax revenue out of businesses and consumers to support his nearly five-year war in Ukraine, even as the country’s economy increasingly skews toward military spending at the expense of civilian needs.

Russia’s budget deficit has swelled beyond forecast this year because of heavy military spending and sluggish economic growth. The economy has also been strained by sanctions, high interest rates for nonmilitary companies, labor shortages and Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and export terminals.

Dmitry Kobylkin, head of the parliamentary faction for the ruling United Russia party, hailed the bill as a “victory budget,” writing in a statement that it included spending on national defense and care for veterans and their families, as well as state social support.

Additional funding for veterans' programs was added before the bill’s second reading, Russian state news agency Tass reported. The programs include Time of Heroes, a Kremlin-backed program that seeks to prepare former soldiers for careers in government.

Russia has previously implemented broad tax increases that proved unpopular among small businesses. The new hikes, part of the 2027-2029 budget bill, are more selective in scope, including a 20% to 30% windfall profits tax on mining companies that have benefited from rising prices in iron ore, nickel and gold.

Another measure imposes higher rates of 13% to 22% on income from interest, dividends and proceeds from selling property. Such income is currently taxed at 13% for amounts under 2.4 million rubles ($29,800) and 15% above that.

Other proposals taking effect Jan. 1 include a 100-ruble per parcel charge and a 22% value-added tax on online purchases of foreign goods worth less than 200 euros ($219), which are currently tax-exempt.
The changes will allow the Kremlin to raise more revenue from its domestic financial resources as sanctions continue to bar Moscow from international bond markets, foreign banks and investors.

Russia has enough financing to cover its budget deficit in 2027 and probably 2028, Chris Weafer, CEO of consultancy Macro-Advisory Ltd, told the Associated Press in October. “But that is at the expense of raising taxes, of increasing costs for households as well as businesses,” he said.
Weafer said that the Russian budget now prioritizes the military over normal economic development or infrastructure, creating an image of growth only by boosting state-linked defense industries.
On the streets of Moscow, most people linked rising taxes and other economic pressures to Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Homemaker Oksana Savitskaya said she believed the situation would worsen until the end of the “special military operation,” the Kremlin’s preferred term for the invasion.
“It seems to me that the economic instability right now and the rise in taxes is bad for development, for small businesses, for example. It’s bad for the everyday person,” she said.
Retired journalist Boris Khizhnyak said that Russia’s economic situation in the upcoming year would be “complicated.”
“You know that we have a “special military operation” underway, and that first and foremost will bring economic adjustments,” he said.

title: Gisèle Pelicot condemns publisher for using nude images from her rape case in book promo
summary: Gisèle Pelicot says she is shocked that a Paris publisher used nude images taken by her rapist ex-husband to promote a book about her case
story: Gisèle Pelicot says she is shocked that a Paris publisher used nude images taken by her rapist ex-husband to promote a book about her case

PARIS -- Gisèle Pelicot says she is deeply shocked that a Paris publishing house used nude images taken of her by her rapist ex-husband as promotional materials for a book that examines her watershed fight for justice.
The 73-year-old Pelicot became an icon of courage and feminist causes during the drugging-and-rape trial in 2024 that convicted all 51 of the accused men, including her ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot.
In a statement to BFMTV, Gisèle Pelicot denounced the book, “Emprises,” and the publisher’s use of intimate photos in promoting it. The broadcaster published extracts of the statement on Monday.

“I am deeply shocked that images of the most private aspects of my life could be exhibited and exploited for commercial gain," the statement said, according to BFMTV. “I refuse to let my private life be used as a selling point."

The nude images of Pelicot were apparently taken by Dominique Pelicot and were part of the court case that saw him sentenced to 20 years in prison, said Christophe Bigot, a lawyer for Gisèle Pelicot, speaking Tuesday to The Associated Press.

Bigot said he has seen the images and that they show Gisèle Pelicot alone, without the men convicted for rapes and sexual assaults while she was unconscious, knocked out with drugs that Dominique Pelicot slipped into her food and drink.
Gisèle Pelicot's statement also criticized the book itself, saying it “describes scenes of me being raped and gives an interpretation of my life that is unbearable.”
“Above all, I refuse to let my story be re-written to suggest that I was complicit with what I was subjected to,” she said, according to the statement extracts.
“Today, I find myself humiliated, exposed and hurt once again. As if the ordeal of the trial hadn’t been enough!”

The publisher, Éditions Tinbad, didn’t respond Tuesday to emailed questions. On its website, Tinbad acknowledged that promotional efforts had been “unfortunate and ill-suited." It offered “our sincerest apologies” to Pelicot and to author Sabine Prokhoris.

It said that it won’t print any additional runs of the book beyond the 280 copies now in the hands of its distributor, and that it will stop promoting it. But it said that “absolutely no images of her being raped or video of a pornographic nature were sent to the press."

The weekly newspaper Le Canard enchainé first reported last week that the publisher sent photos and videos of Gisèle Pelicot to several media outlets. The newspaper described the images as pornographic and said they were taken by Dominique Pelicot.
It quoted Tinbad's publisher as saying: “Of course we don’t have Mrs. Pelicot’s permission to distribute these photos. That is why we sent them to you solely for private, informational purposes.”

The police evidence against Dominique Pelicot included his library of images documenting years of abuse — more than 20,000 photos and videos in all, stored on computer drives and catalogued in folders marked “abuse,” “her rapists,” “night alone” and other titles.

He and all but one of his co-defendants were convicted of sexually assaulting Gisèle Pelicot over a period of nearly a decade. The other co-defendant was convicted of drugging and raping his own wife with Dominique Pelicot’s help.

Gisèle Pelicot became a hero to many in France and beyond for courageously demanding that all the evidence be heard in open court, waiving her right to anonymity as a survivor of sexual abuse and insisting that shame should fall on her abusers, not her.

title: South Africa convicts Zimbabwean who tried to travel to Russia to fight against Ukraine
summary: A Zimbabwean man has been convicted in South Africa of trying to travel to Russia to fight in its war against Ukraine
story: A Zimbabwean man has been convicted in South Africa of trying to travel to Russia to fight in its war against Ukraine

JOHANNESBURG -- A Zimbabwean man was convicted and sentenced on Tuesday for trying to travel to Russia to fight in its war against Ukraine after being arrested in South Africa with eight others earlier this month.
Tafadzwa Sithole was sentenced to five years in prison, suspended for five years, and he is set to be deported back to Zimbabwe.
He told a South African court that he had agreed to fight for Russia in the war in exchange for “remuneration” after successfully applying online in Zimbabwe.
Sithole said a person he identified as “Albina” contacted him after he submitted the application, arranged accommodation in South Africa and provided a flight ticket to Russia.

His admissions were detailed in a plea agreement with South African prosecutors. He pleaded guilty to violating the Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which prohibits mercenary activity and regulates military assistance to parties in foreign conflicts, including recruitment and training.
The law also applies to foreign nationals.
Sithole, who described himself as an unemployed third-year student at a university in Zimbabwe, appeared in court with four other accused who are also negotiating plea agreements with prosecutors.
He said he entered South Africa legally on Nov. 4 and stayed in accommodation in Kempton Park, east of Johannesburg, in preparation for his travel to Russia.
He was arrested at O.R. Tambo International Airport on Nov. 8 while attempting to board a flight to Russia.

“He agreed and offered to serve as a member of the armed forces of the Russian Federation in return for remuneration. He knew that the Russian Federation was engaged in an ongoing armed conflict with Ukraine and that the military service he intended to render would be performed in the context of that armed conflict,” his lawyer told the court.
Zimbabwe is among several African countries where Russia has been recruiting fighters for its war against Ukraine. Others include South Africa, Kenya, Botswana and Ghana.
Zimbabwean authorities said in March that 15 citizens had been killed in the war in Ukraine and that they were seeking the return of 66 others.
The government said recruits were promised well-paid jobs but had their travel documents confiscated and were forced into combat.

An investigation by Code for Africa, a nonprofit data journalism and technology organization, identified 289 websites, domains and social media profiles used to lure recruits through false advertising and promises of generous benefits. South Africa’s Institute for Security Studies cited the findings.

Kenya’s government said in February that more than 1,000 citizens had been recruited to fight for Russia. Families protested in Nairobi in March, demanding their relatives’ return and the prosecution of those responsible.

South Africa has helped repatriate some citizens it said were lured into the conflict and police investigated allegations that Duduzile Zuma-Sambudla, a daughter of former South African President Jacob Zuma, helped lure 17 South African men to fight for Russia under promises of security training.
She denied wrongdoing and resigned from Parliament in November 2025 following the allegations.
A tenth suspect who is a Botswana national also appeared in court on Tuesday on similar charges.

title: Car bomb in central Colombian city injures 23 as violence spreads to urban areas
summary: A bomb exploded outside regional government offices in Villavicencio, Colombia, injuring 23 people
story: A bomb exploded outside regional government offices in Villavicencio, Colombia, injuring 23 people

BOGOTA, Colombia -- A bomb exploded outside regional government offices in the Colombian city of Villavicencio, injuring 23 people, authorities said Tuesday, as a wave of violence involving rebel groups and drug gangs spreads to urban areas.

The explosion occurred Monday night in Villavicencio, a city with a population of half a million people. Authorities initially reported 19 injuries before raising the toll to 23. They said the attack remained under investigation.

During the first three months of his term, President Abelardo de la Espriella has increased the use of air strikes against drug gangs and rebel groups in rural areas and acted on military intelligence to capture several midlevel commanders.

Rebel groups have responded with drone attacks on police stations and military bases around the country, and have also attacked their targets with rockets made from gas cylinders and by detonating roadside bombs.

Villavicencio is a major agricultural and commercial hub on the edge of the Amazon rainforest, where rebel groups have long fought over control of drug trafficking routes, as well as legal businesses like cattle ranches and palm plantations.

Alexander Baquero, the mayor of Villavicencio, told Colombian radio station Blu that he believed the attack could have been waged by a FARC holdout group that operates in Meta province and was seeking retaliation for strikes conducted against it by the military.

Colombia this week is marking the 10th anniversary of a historic peace agreement between the government and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, in which more than 14,000 fighters laid down their weapons.

The peace deal initially brought relief to rural communities that had been caught in the fighting between the military and the rebels. But violence has once again increased in some rural areas, as smaller drug gangs and rebel groups attempt to take over territory that was once controlled by the FARC.

On Tuesday, President de la Espriella vowed to intensify operations against rebel groups. In a post on X, the conservative leader said that the “narco-terrorists” behind the attack in Villavicencio will “pay for every drop of blood they have shed, and for every building they have destroyed.”

title: Dozens killed in latest land dispute attacks in Nigeria's Niger state
summary: Dozens of people were killed in attacks in north-central Nigeria, advocacy groups and local authorities said
story: Dozens of people were killed in attacks in north-central Nigeria, advocacy groups and local authorities said

ABUJA, Nigeria -- Dozens of people were killed in attacks on communities in north-central Nigeria, advocacy groups and local authorities said, in the latest violence linked to longstanding disputes between herders and farmers over grazing land and other resources.

The Miyetti Allah Cattle Breeders Association of Nigeria, or MACBAN, which represents mostly herders from the predominantly Muslim Fulani ethnic group, said that 64 people from Fulani communities were killed over the weekend in the Borgu area of Niger state.

“The tragic incident, which reportedly claimed the lives of men, women, children and elderly persons, is a painful and devastating loss,” MACBAN special assistant Yusuf Abubakar said in a statement Monday. He called for an investigation to “bring the perpetrators to justice.”
Amnesty International Nigeria said it had obtained videos and images showing “children lined up and slaughtered, one by one, while their mothers and fathers lay in the pool of their own blood.”
Amnesty said the raid was believed to have been a reprisal for an earlier attack on Saturday.

The state’s information commissioner, Obed Nuhu Nana, said an attack on the Lumma Ba’are community in the Borgu area early Saturday left five people dead, including the village head. Five others were injured and taken to hospital, and some houses were reportedly set ablaze, Nana said in a statement.
Local resident Hassan Kafobe Dodo said Lumma Ba’are residents “assumed” the attackers who killed their village head were Fulani.
“They usually blame attacks on (the Fulani),” he told The Associated Press on Tuesday, adding that more than 300 people from Lumma Ba’are attacked Fulani communities in retaliation.
Local media reported that one of the attackers who killed the village head of Lumma Ba’are had been arrested, but police have not commented.
Such attacks among farmers and herders over land resources are not rare in this part of Africa’s most populous country — a problem worsened as climate change turns grazing lands into barren desert.

Fulani herders have been accused of carrying out mass killings across northwestern and central Nigeria, where decades of conflict over grazing land and water have deepened divisions between Christians and Muslims.

The disputes have compounded security challenges in these regions, where banditry, kidnapping and other armed violence are widespread, including attacks by Islamist groups such as Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province.

title: Thousands of Sikh pilgrims flood Pakistan shrine for founder of Sikhism's birthday
summary: Thousands of Sikh pilgrims from India have gathered in eastern Pakistan to celebrate the 557th birthday of Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism
story: Thousands of Sikh pilgrims from India have gathered in eastern Pakistan to celebrate the 557th birthday of Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism

NANKANA SAHIB, Pakistan -- NANKANA SAHIB, Pakistan (AP) — Thousands of Sikh pilgrims from neighboring India gathered in eastern Pakistan on Tuesday to celebrate the 557th birthday of Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, officials said.

More than 5,000 worshippers attended ceremonies at a shrine in Nankana Sahib, a town in Punjab province where Guru Nanak was born. According to a government statement, Pakistan has issued visas to more than 3,000 Indian Sikhs for the occasion.
Dressed in orange, blue, yellow, and white, pilgrims filled the shrine complex with color. Men covering their heads with turbans and women with scarves, offered prayers and sang devotional hymns.

Many Sikh holy sites are in Pakistan after the British partitioned the subcontinent into separate nations in 1947 following two centuries of colonial rule. Pakistan and India have a long history of strained relations, largely centered on the disputed Himalayan region of Kashmir. They have fought multiple wars since partition, including two over their rival claims to the territory.

title: China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
summary: The Chinese Communist Party is investigating Chen Jining, the CCP's secretary in Shanghai, in connection with violating party discipline, state broadcaster CCTV reported
story: The Chinese Communist Party is investigating Chen Jining, the CCP's secretary in Shanghai, in connection with violating party discipline, state broadcaster CCTV reported
BANGKOK -- Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, state media reported Tuesday.
The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping’s long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement provided no further details.

The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong’s rule.

“The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping’s anti-corruption campaign has no limits,” Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. “This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented.”

Other Politburo members purged include Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.
The post of Shanghai party secretary has traditionally been viewed as a stepping stone to China’s top leadership. The country’s current premier, Li Qiang, previously held the position.
Chen has served as Shanghai party secretary since 2022. He previously held senior positions in Beijing’s municipal government and headed the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

title: British officials warn UK firms aiding Ukraine to brace for Russian sabotage threats
summary: British security officials have warned U.K. companies supporting Ukraine's military to brace for potential sabotage attempts by Russia
story: British security officials have warned U.K. companies supporting Ukraine's military to brace for potential sabotage attempts by Russia
LONDON -- British security officials on Tuesday warned U.K. companies supporting Ukraine’s military to brace for potential sabotage attempts by Russia.
The rare public alert came after a series of attacks and attempted attacks across Europe, amid warnings from European officials about Moscow’s hybrid attacks on digital and physical infrastructure.
Estonian authorities have said that Russia’s security services were behind an August arson attack on a defense company that provides military vehicles to Ukraine.

Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1 after authorities disrupted another attack on a defense company. Eight Latvian citizens were detained on suspicion of arson, which was ordered by Russian military intelligence, the Estonian and Latvian domestic security services said.

A U.K. court also convicted several men over a 2024 plot to set fire to a London warehouse that contained supplies for Kyiv. In September, a British man was charged with plotting with Russian spies to sabotage a drone factory, and an American soldier at a base in England was arrested earlier this month on suspicion of spying for Russia.
Authorities in Poland, Romania and other NATO countries also say they have disrupted multiple Moscow-backed sabotage plots.

The National Protective Security Authority, part of Britain’s MI5 domestic security service, and the Defense Ministry told firms providing “material support” to Ukraine’s armed forces that they may be a target for Moscow.
Chief executives from defense and critical infrastructure companies were being briefed privately by government ministers, the Defense Ministry said.

The alert says that Russia has increased sabotage attempts against European defense facilities in recent months, usually through proxies “employing low-sophistication sabotage methodologies, such as arson.” It warns of other hostile activity, “including intimidation of individuals, espionage and information operations,” all aimed at eroding support for Ukraine.
It advises companies to reduce their online presence, beef up security at their sites, identify “potential hostile observation locations” and teach employees to recognize suspicious activity.

The Associated Press has tracked more than 210 incidents across Europe that Western officials consider sabotage and malign activity linked to Russia since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022. The incidents include arson, sabotage, espionage, cyberattacks and attempted assassinations.

Officials say one goal of the attacks is to undermine support for Ukraine, spread fear and discord in European societies and drain investigative resources. Russia often uses proxies for such attacks, and some perpetrators say they have no idea they have been hired by Moscow.

MI5 Director-General Ken McCallum warned last month of a growing threat from hostile states, chiefly Iran and Russia. He said that Russia’s military and intelligence services are “escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare.”
“Russia is using tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict,” he said.
Emma Burrows contributed to this report.

title: Houthi rebels close in on Aden as Yemeni forces dig in behind a fortified line
summary: Iran-backed Houthi rebels have advanced close to Yemen's government seat in Aden
story: Iran-backed Houthi rebels have advanced close to Yemen's government seat in Aden

Iran-backed Houthi rebels have advanced to within about 60 kilometers (about 40 miles) of the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the southern city of Aden, but the forces fighting them have set up a fortified line to defend the city, a military official said Tuesday.

Iran reiterated Tuesday that it would not hold talks with the United States to end their conflict unless several conditions are met. It also said three oil tankers had struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire despite U.S. aerial protection.
Meanwhile, at least nine Palestinians were killed in several Israeli strikes in Gaza, local officials said.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Tuesday. Read our full coverage here.

The Houthis' advance toward Aden has come after forces allied with the government withdrew from areas on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, allowing the Houthis to consolidate their grip on territory around the crucial waterway.

Col. Majed al-Nuzaily, spokesman for the Yemeni army, said the forces that withdrew from the western coast are now stationed north and west of Aden “on a defense line built to stop the Houthi advance," as the rebels come within 60 kilometers of the city.
“Aden is a red line. It was a red line in 2015, when the Houthis came to the city and its people drove them out,” he said during a virtual briefing.

Speaking in the same briefing, Yemeni foreign ministry official Marwan al-Noman called for the United States and other Western countries to support the Yemeni coast guard in its efforts to intercept smuggled weapons to the Houthis, as well as provide training to Yemeni forces fighting the rebels on the ground.
“The Houthis are a terrorist organization. They threaten Yemenis first, and then every nation whose ships cross the Red Sea,” he said.
Yemen’s Interior Ministry said Tuesday that shelling of areas in Taiz province in southwestern Yemen killed three civilians, including a child, and wounded two other children, citing local police.
The ministry, which is aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government, blamed the Houthis for the attack.
The Houthis and the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen continue to trade accusations that civilians in their respective territories have been targeted in recent hostilities.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said Tuesday that 11 people were injured when one of the towers in the financial district of the Saudi capital Riyadh came under what it described as a “terrorist attack.”
It was the second incident targeting the capital’s financial district in less than a week. There was no immediate claim of responsibility.
The Houthis have in the past claimed responsibility for attacks on Riyadh, including last week’s strike. The Houthis have said their attacks are in response to Saudi strikes in Yemen.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said Tuesday that the kingdom won’t “tolerate any infringement” of its sovereignty and would “defend its resources with all our strength and resolve.”

Iran’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said Tuesday that Tehran wouldn't negotiate with the U.S. "until Iran’s seven conditions are met,” according to Iranian state television.

Iranian authorities haven't publicly disclosed those conditions, but Iranian state media have said they include the lifting of sanctions, the ending of the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and the release of seized Iranian assets.
He also warned that Iran would “shift the geographical scope of the conflict should the enemy make a mistake.”
The naval arm of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said the three oil tankers struck the naval mines because they were “in violation of regulations” regarding passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Guard’s navy said in a post on Telegram Monday that the strait “is not a place to test unauthorized routes or to disregard maritime warnings.”
It said the tankers were “engulfed in flames” after hitting the mines despite being under U.S. aerial escort.

At least nine people were killed in four Israeli strikes Monday night and Tuesday morning, officials in Gaza said. Among those killed was a senior security official in the Hamas-run government’s Interior Ministry.

The ministry said Na’im Abu Nahl, director-general of its internal security service, was killed in a strike west of Gaza City on Tuesday. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the killing and said Israel would continue targeting Hamas security forces.

Hospital officials across Gaza reported at least eight other deaths in the four strikes, including a child killed in an airstrike in central Gaza on Tuesday and three police officers killed in Khan Younis.

Israel’s military did not immediately respond to questions about the strike that killed the officers. Since last year’s ceasefire, Israel has repeatedly targeted police stations in Hamas-controlled areas of Gaza, viewing them as instruments of the group’s rule.
Hamas maintains that police are needed to preserve order amid persistent shortages and instability.

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed in the three-year Israel-Hamas war, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-led government, maintains casualty records regarded as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts, but does not distinguish between civilians and militants.
Hadjicostis reported from Nicosia, Cyprus, AlJoud from Beirut and Metz from Jerusalem.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

title: Malaysia to repatriate another 6,803 Myanmar nationals despite ICJ genocide ruling
summary: Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says the country plans to repatriate another 6,803 Myanmar nationals next month
story: Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says the country plans to repatriate another 6,803 Myanmar nationals next month

KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia -- Malaysia will repatriate another 6,803 Myanmar nationals next month, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Tuesday as he defended the government's engagement with Myanmar's military leadership, despite a landmark international court ruling finding the country responsible for genocide against Rohingya Muslims.

The International Court of Justice, based in The Hague, Netherlands, last week found Myanmar guilty of genocide against its Rohingya minority, with evidence showing Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya in a 2017 military operation that included mass rapes and killings, and the destruction of thousands of homes.

Myanmar’s government has dismissed the ruling as unfair. Anwar told Parliament that Malaysia respected the ICJ's ruling, but would continue to engage Myanmar's leadership to facilitate the repatriation of refugees.

Malaysia hosts nearly 200,000 refugees from Myanmar, including Rohingya who fled a military crackdown and members of other ethnic minorities. Anwar said that efforts to resettle them in third countries had been unsuccessful and Malaysia couldn't continue bearing the burden indefinitely.
He said that talks with Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing, who visited Kuala Lumpur last month, had helped bring progress to the long-standing issue.
Another 1,500 people will be sent back on three Myanmar naval vessels on Dec. 6 and 7, while another 5,303 will return throughout next month by air, with all costs borne by Myanmar, Anwar said.
A total of 10,476 Myanmar nationals have already been repatriated this year, including 1,476 who were taken home aboard a Myanmar naval vessel on Sept. 29, he said.
Malaysia had secured a guarantee of a “safe and dignified return” for those repatriated, Anwar said.
“So far, based on monitoring by Malaysian intelligence, none of the 10,476 individuals have been subjected to any form of pressure,” he said.

Despite the engagement with Myanmar, Anwar said that Malaysia remained committed to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations' peace plan on ending violence and resolving a prolonged crisis in Myanmar after the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021. It had sparked widespread opposition that plunged large parts of the country into conflict.

The 11-nation regional bloc has renewed diplomatic pressure on Myanmar for failing to implement its peace initiative and restricted the country’s top leaders from major regional summits. Myanmar has slammed ASEAN for unfair treatment.

title: Serbian police arrest a 17-year-old after shots fired at a high school
summary: Police in central Serbia have arrested a teenager after he fired a small-caliber rifle in a high school hallway
story: Police in central Serbia have arrested a teenager after he fired a small-caliber rifle in a high school hallway
BELGRADE, Serbia -- Police arrested a teenager in central Serbia on Tuesday after a small-caliber rifle was fired in a high school hallway, injuring two women, authorities said.
The shooting happened around 8 a.m. at the First Technical School in Kragujevac.

Police said the teenager fired at an office near the entrance, shattering the glass and injuring two women inside. A 50-year-old woman suffered a gunshot wound to the leg, while the other was injured by flying glass.
Police later arrested the teenager’s father on suspicion of illegally possessing a weapon linked to the incident.
The women were taken to a local hospital, where doctors said their injuries were not life-threatening.
Principal Nemanja Joksimovic told local media that the 17-year-old was a student at the school.
“This happened during the first class, so other students were inside the classrooms, which is good under the circumstances,” he said.

School shootings are rare in Serbia. The country’s first school shooting occurred in 2023, when a 13-year-old boy killed nine children and a school guard at an elementary school in Belgrade and injured six others.

title: Global land mine casualties hit a 5-year high, driven by Myanmar’s brutal civil war and Syria
summary: Casualties from land mines and unexploded ordnance reached a five-year high in 2025, with Southeast Asia seeing a significant number of those killed or wounded
story: Casualties from land mines and unexploded ordnance reached a five-year high in 2025, with Southeast Asia seeing a significant number of those killed or wounded

BANGKOK -- Casualties from land mines or unexploded ordnance reached a five-year high in 2025, with Southeast Asia making up a disproportionate number of those killed or wounded, largely due to Myanmar's civil war, a report released Tuesday showed.

The annual global report by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines found civilians were the most affected, making up some 84% of the 6,929 casualties recorded in 2025, and half of them were children.

In Myanmar, where both government military forces and the militias fighting against them make widespread use of mines, 1,891 casualties were recorded in 2025, the highest number of any country for the third consecutive year.

“Myanmar has gone beyond crisis to catastrophe, and has claimed the ignoble title of top producer of land mine victims for a 3rd year in a row,” said Yeshua Moser-Puangsuwan, a co-author of the Landmine Monitor 2026 report. “There is now contamination at some level in almost 2/3 of the townships of the country.”
On average, five people are killed or wounded by land mines daily in Myanmar, the report found.

Driven by the Myanmar figures, Southeast Asia, where there is also widespread mine contamination in Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam and elsewhere, accounted for 27% of global casualties in 2025 despite having just over 8% of the world's population.

Syria, which experienced a large-scale return of civilians after the fall of the Assad government at the end of 2024, saw a spike of more than 50% to 1,602 casualties in 2025, a testament to the ongoing dangers of mines and leftover ordnance even after fighting has stopped.
“Syria is huge, but it is a post-war crisis,” Moser-Puangsuwan said. “People are now returning and that is driving the casualty figure. They need to radically scale up their clearance capacity.”

In addition to posing dangers long after conflicts are over, land mines and unexploded ordnance also impede access to food, water, schools, hospitals and other basic needs and restrict freedom of movement, the report said. They also endanger transit and prevent the safe return of refugees, and impede the delivery of humanitarian aid.
Economically, they take a toll by contaminating farmland, and countries also have to divert funds that could have been used for other pressing societal needs to remove mines
Children have made up 36% of all civilian casualties, where the age of the victim was known, recorded by the organization since 1999, the report said.

“Driven by curiosity, a lack of awareness, or high-risk behavior and bravado, children in general are more likely to deliberately handle explosive items than adults, often mistaking them for toys or other play objects,” the report said.

The International Campaign to Ban Landmines urges more countries to join the 1997 Mine Ban Treaty and respect its requirements for the immediate end of the stockpiling, production, and transfer of antipersonnel mines.

This past year saw the opposite happen, however, with Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland — all with borders next to or near Russia — pulling out of the treaty, citing the “security situation in our region.”
Ukraine, meanwhile, notified the United Nations it had decided to suspend the implementation of the treaty, even though such a move is not allowed under its provisions.
Russia, not a party to the treaty, has been making widespread use of mines in its invasion of Ukraine, and Landmine Monitor found that Ukraine had been using them as well.
Lebanon, the Marshall Islands and Tonga all joined the mine ban treaty during the reporting period, and 162 countries are now bound by it.

In addition to Russia, Ukraine and Myanmar, the study found new use of antipersonnel mines by North Korea and Iran. It also reported new use by non-government groups in Colombia, India, Pakistan, Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Mali, Niger, Nigeria and Togo.
There was also evidence of use by unconfirmed actors in the border region between Thailand and Cambodia, as well as in Bangladesh and Sudan.

Landmine Monitor noted a report by Netherlands-based investigative group Bellingcat suggesting the United States, which is also not a signatory to the mine ban treaty, had deployed mines by air in Iran during the early days of the ongoing war, based upon satellite imagery. The White House has refused to comment on the report.

title: Hanoi eatery blast kills 6 and injures more than a dozen
summary: An explosion suspected to be from a gas leak at a hot pot eatery in Hanoi has six people and injured more than a dozen others
story: An explosion suspected to be from a gas leak at a hot pot eatery in Hanoi has six people and injured more than a dozen others

HANOI, Vietnam -- An explosion at a hot pot eatery in Vietnam's capital on Tuesday, suspected to have been caused by a gas leak, killed six people, injured more than a dozen others and damaged nearby houses.

VnExpress, an online news outlet, said that the early morning blast in Hanoi shattered windows, cracked walls and tore metal shutters from their frames, while corrugated roofs and awnings collapsed. The report said that the explosion damaged nearby houses and shook neighboring apartment buildings, with debris scattered across the street.

Police are using detection equipment to search for survivors and hydraulic machinery to lift concrete slabs, amid concerns that more people may be trapped under the rubble as the eatery was packed when the blast struck, the report said. Authorities have also relocated residents from neighboring buildings deemed structurally unsafe, it said.
