Hanoi police were cited as saying that investigations were ongoing. But preliminary findings pointed to a gas explosion that brought down part of the building. More than 14 people, including one with a traumatic brain injury, have been hospitalized, the report said.
Lan Phuong, 26, told VnExpress that the blast jolted her and her younger sister awake, sending their balcony door flying about three meters (10 feet).
“Luckily, we were both covered by blankets at the time and were not seriously injured. But we were terrified and could only scream,” she said.

title: Most victims of factory fire died trying to reach emergency exit, rescuers say
summary: Indonesian authorities have confirmed 26 workers were killed in a fire three days ago at a candy factory where rescuers said most victims died on the second floor trying to reach the emergency exit
story: Indonesian authorities have confirmed 26 workers were killed in a fire three days ago at a candy factory where rescuers said most victims died on the second floor trying to reach the emergency exit

SERANG, Indonesia -- Indonesian authorities confirmed Tuesday 26 workers were killed in a fire three days ago at a candy factory where rescuers said most victims died on the second floor trying to reach the emergency exit.

More than 600 rescuers, including soldiers, police officers, Red Cross personnel and volunteers, were searching the burned three-story building for eight more workers missing since the fire Saturday at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in Serang district of Banten province near the capital, Jakarta.
Teams focused on the rear of the factory, where debris, lingering smoke and occasional flare-ups complicated recovery efforts, said Al Amrad, head of the Banten search and rescue agency.
Many victims were found near an access route leading to an emergency staircase close to the area where the fire is believed to have started.
“Most victims were recovered from the factory’s second floor, and many of the remains were severely burned,” said Jajuli, a search-and-rescue worker who uses a single name.

He said workers trying to reach the emergency exit had to navigate corridors and turns, while the staircase’s proximity to the fire may have made escape difficult as flames spread through the building. Some victims were found clustered together, apparently trapped while attempting to flee. Elevator problems also may have hampered evacuation efforts, he said.

Preliminary examinations showed the remains recovered from the site so far belonged to 26 victims, Banten Police medical chief Commissioner Dr. I Gusti Gede Dharma Arimbawa said. Seven were men and nine were women, while 10 others were too badly burned for visual identification. DNA samples would be used to match the remains to the list of missing.
During a meeting with families Monday, company officials apologized and pledged support for affected workers and relatives.
“The company will take responsibility for helping victims and their families,” chief executive Steven Erwin Wijaya said.

About 300 workers were inside the factory when the fire started, possibly in a cooling unit on the second floor. Many of the workers escaped, and rescuers saved 29 of them, five of whom were hospitalized with injuries.
The workers said no alarm sounded and their fellow workers shouted warnings that allowed them to escape.
Police have opened a criminal investigation after finding preliminary evidence that negligence may have contributed to the fire.

“We have found indications of a criminal offense related to negligence,” Zain Dwi Nugroho, deputy chief of Banten police, told reporters Tuesday, adding that investigators have questioned 19 witnesses and seized safety records, permit documents and camera equipment as they seek to determine who could be held criminally responsible.

The company earlier said the factory regularly conducted evacuation drills and maintained evacuation routes and that its fire-safety systems, including hydrants and emergency exits, were functioning when the fire occurred.

Indonesia’s ombudsman urged the company and authorities to clarify issues involving wages, employment status, social security benefits and workplace accident compensation, and called for a review of workplace safety standards.
The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products exported to more than 40 countries.
Karmini reported from Jakarta, Indonesia.

title: North Korea reviews Switzerland relations after sanctions on youth camp linked to war
summary: North Korea has threatened to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month
story: North Korea has threatened to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month

SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea threatened Tuesday to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month, condemning Switzerland for imposing sanctions on a youth camp in eastern North Korea over its alleged role in the transfer of children from Russia-occupied areas of Ukraine.

Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, described the Swiss sanctions on the Songdowon International Children’s Camp in the coastal city of Wonsan as an “open hostile act” and a “serious infringement” of the North’s sovereignty, according to a statement carried by state media.

Kim Yo Jong, one of Pyongyang’s top foreign policy officials, said the camp supported “legitimate” cooperation between North Korea and Russia. She didn't directly address Western accusations that some Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces were sent there to be reeducated.

North Korea has closely aligned with Russia over the war in Ukraine, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons in recent years to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, possibly in exchange for economic assistance and military technology transfers.
Strengthened ties with Moscow and Beijing have been key drivers of Kim Jong Un’s increasingly assertive foreign policy as he positions North Korea as part of a united front against the United States.

Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis traveled to North Korea in late October as Switzerland opened a diplomatic office in Pyongyang and held talks with senior North Korean officials, including Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui, on “promoting dialogue and cooperation,” North Korean state media said at the time.

Kim Yo Jong said that North Korea would need to “comprehensively reconsider the relations with unreliable Switzerland” following the sanctions on the camp and called on North Korean diplomats to take unspecified “corresponding” countermeasures.

“It is my view that the Swiss diplomatic office has spontaneously lost justification for its existence, which was opened in Pyongyang under the pretext of improving the relations, given that the Swiss Confederation has clarified its stand not to respect the sovereignty of the DPRK,” she said, using the initials of North Korea’s formal name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

In adding the Songdowon camp earlier this month to its broader sanctions related to Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine, Swiss authorities held the camp responsible for the “forced assimilation, including indoctrination, and militarized education of Ukrainian minors,” according to a document by Switzerland’s State Secretariat for Economic Affairs.

It said the camp participates in programs involving the transfer of Ukrainian children from Russia-occupied territories to North Korea and exposes them to propaganda and activities designed to promote pro-Russia narratives.

The United Kingdom in May and the European Union in September imposed similar sanctions on the Songdowon camp, freezing its assets and prohibiting financial transactions with the facility, although the practical impact of such measures is unclear given North Korea’s limited financial ties with European countries.

Switzerland established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974 and is one of the few Western countries to maintain dialogue with the country, which has aggressively expanded its nuclear weapons program since Kim Jong Un took power in 2011.

The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation opened a “cooperation office” in Pyongyang in 1997 that mostly focused on humanitarian programs, but the office closed in March 2020 as North Korea shut its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Swiss government has said that the new diplomatic office in Pyongyang, which reports to the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, would help strengthen direct contacts with North Korean officials and promote dialogue.

In a statement to The Associated Press, the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said that it had taken note of North Korean statements. But it said that neither the Swiss Embassy in Beijing nor its diplomatic office in Pyongyang had been officially contacted about the matter. It said that Switzerland aims to “maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues.”

Kim Yo Jong's statement came a day after North Korean state media reported that Kim Jong Un received credentials from the newly appointed ambassadors from several countries, including Russia, Sweden, Indonesia, Vietnam, Brazil and India, in Pyongyang on Sunday.

During the ceremony, Kim Jong Un defended his efforts to strengthen his nuclear-armed military as necessary to protect the North’s security amid what he described as an “unstable security crisis and political and economic chaos round the globe,” Pyongyang's official Korean Central News Agency said.
Jamey Keaten contributed to this report from Geneva.

title: Officials backtrack after 24-hour hunt for Istanbul lioness, saying she never existed
summary: Turkish officials say a lioness that was subject to a 24-hour search and sparked panic among Istanbul residents does not actually exist
story: Turkish officials say a lioness that was subject to a 24-hour search and sparked panic among Istanbul residents does not actually exist

ISTANBUL -- A 24-hour search for a lioness in the Istanbul suburbs that sparked panic among local residents was thrown into fresh confusion late Monday when Turkish officials said the animal did not exist.

Istanbul’s governor mobilized teams of animal welfare experts, police and army commandos in the hunt for the lioness after it was “identified” – even releasing two videos of the animal prowling around the upmarket neighborhood of Uskumrukoy.
Residents were warned to stay home, and the 54-square-kilometer (about 20 square miles) Belgrade Forest to the north of Istanbul was sealed off.
By Monday evening, however, officials backtracked and said in a statement new images had been examined that showed the animal was “not a lion or any other large cat species.”

“The area has been scanned from the air with a drone equipped with thermal cameras and from the ground by our teams,” the statement said. “Baiting was also carried out and motion-sensor camera traps used."
“Fieldwork has not yielded any concrete evidence of a lion being present in the area.”

The abrupt change left many bewildered, wondering what animal could have been mistaken for a lioness, with some suggesting it was a large dog. Others posted mocking videos of domestic cats on social media, asking if it was the lioness.
Even after the governor’s office statement, media outlets published another video of an animal emerging from bushes and asked readers if it could be a lion.

title: Pope Francis' diary details profound spiritual crisis and encounters with the devil
summary: The Vatican has released excerpts of Pope Francis' private diary
story: The Vatican has released excerpts of Pope Francis' private diary

VATICAN CITY -- Pope Francis saw the “gates of hell” when he realized the depths of the clergy sexual abuse scandal and experienced mystical visions of the devil throughout his ministry, according to excerpts of his personal diary published Tuesday by the Vatican.

“The Private Diary of Pope Francis” also reveals the Argentine pope suffered a profound spiritual crisis in 2021-22, connected to his own temptations to exercise power omnipotently. He overcame the crisis by entrusting himself entirely to God’s mercy.

The book, released globally in several languages, offers a deeply personal view of Francis' mind and heart, revealing his innermost fears, insecurities, dreams and temptations. It shows him as incredibly hard on himself, lamenting his own sense of worthlessness and shame, and his utter trust in God to lead him, even from the depths of despair.

The book was curated by a close aide, Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, the Argentine theologian who heads the Vatican’s doctrine office and writes that Francis wanted the papers published. Fernández is listed as the author, as his comments contextualize Francis’ diary entries.

Written in a leather-bound calendar used as a notebook, it starts in 1992, when Jorge Mario Bergoglio was auxiliary bishop of Buenos Aires. It continues through his time as cardinal in the Argentine capital and finally pope. The last entry is Aug. 18, 2024.

The most moving sections are Francis’ revelations of his own spiritual torments and what he described as encounters with the devil — visceral, tangible and seemingly terrifying visions. Two occurred in Buenos Aires, and the third after his disastrous 2018 trip to Chile.

“A few days after returning to Rome, I was in a meeting. I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant possessing everything. ‘Now I’ve gotten everything I wanted,’” Francis quoted the devil as saying in a Jan. 24, 2021, entry. “Just as I can’t forget his eyes from the previous two, in this case, I can’t forget the powerful raspiness of his voice.”

During the 2018 Chile trip, Francis created an uproar by discrediting victims of Chile's most notorious abuser. After journalists, including from The Associated Press, challenged him during the in-flight news conference returning home, Francis commissioned an investigation and realized the victims were right, that he was wrong and had been misled by the Chilean hierarchy.

“Devastated because of the situation in Chile and the dialogue with the journalists on the airplane,” Francis would write later. “I became aware of how serious the problem was. … It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn’t think it was so serious.”
Francis wrote on June 7, 2018, that in the Chile scandal, he “saw the entrance to hell. Pagan seduction in full force.”

As he dealt with the fallout in the next two months, he wrote: “What shame and evil this has brought on the church!” and “Once more the gates of hell. … May holiness and conversion abound in the midst of so many scandals.”
But Francis’ spiritual crisis wouldn’t come until 2021.
The book dates the onset of the crisis to Jan. 24, 2021. The day before, Francis canceled several public appearances due to what the Vatican said was a bout of sciatica.

Fernández reveals, however, that Francis was suffering from “insupportable” pain from an intestinal problem that in July 2021 landed Francis in the hospital for 10 days for surgery to remove 33 centimeters (13 inches) of his colon.
In January 2021, amid the COVID-19 pandemic, the Vatican was in utter upheaval over a massive financial investigation authorized by Francis.

In September 2020, he had fired a onetime close collaborator, Cardinal Angelo Becciu, convinced Becciu had embezzled money from the Holy See. The scandal — and Francis’ belief that a web of corruption had engulfed the Vatican’s secretariat of state — led to an unprecedented Vatican investigation and years of legal proceedings through which Francis sought to show his willingness to crack down on financial misconduct.

The trial resulted in some convictions, including against Becciu, but much of prosecutors' theory of a vast conspiracy of corruption was thrown out. The appeals process is ongoing, with Francis' own role in the investigation a key question for the defense.

There is no mention of the trial in Fernández’s text, though he hints at it by revealing Francis’ later musings that the 2021-22 spiritual crisis was “mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation.”

Fernández writes that the crisis was primarily related to Francis’ exercise of power, the temptation to omnipotence and belief that he was above the world. It’s a vice Francis admitted to publicly in 2013, in his first interview as pope, when he acknowledged a tendency to wield power in an “authoritarian” way.

It is significant that Francis was tormented by something his critics often faulted him for: an authoritarian, go-it-alone governing style in an absolute monarch and supreme leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics.
For Francis, the temptation to omnipotence was the devil tempting him to “reductive curiosity,” or believing he alone could solve everyone’s problems, and essentially thinking of himself as God.

By Dec. 30, 2022, Francis had apparently overcome the crisis, by entrusting himself to God. Fernández writes that Francis realized that what began on Jan. 24, 2021, “was a powerful invitation from the Lord to become aware of an accumulation of interior darkness that he had to overcome so he could be free.”

Fernández notes that the final two major teaching documents of Francis’ life, a 2023 text on confidence in God’s merciful love, and a 2024 encyclical on Christ’s human and divine love, are deeply spiritual texts borne out of the crisis. They differ in tone and content from the texts often associated with his pontificate.

While the book reveals some of Francis' innermost thoughts, Fernández says Francis wrote his most confidential thoughts in an indecipherable code, which is not reproduced, presumably to prevent anyone from trying to decipher it.
The reader is also left wondering what Fernández left out of his selection of diary entries, and what more context he could have provided as one of Francis' most trusted advisers.

Fernández writes that the diary includes hardly any information about church matters, and is truly a spiritual repository. He said he omitted entries affecting third parties, though he does include some of Francis' personal musings, including about then-Cardinal Robert Prevost, now Pope Leo XIV: “A great pastor, a generous missionary and an irreproachable man.”

Francis had shown Fernández the diary and told him, “From this, you will all see,” essentially entrusting the writings to him after his death on April 21, 2025. Fernández said Francis wanted them known because he thought they would help others.
Fernández said he mentioned the writings to Leo after his election, and feared they would end up in a Vatican warehouse with Francis' other personal items that were sealed upon his death.

“I added that I wished to study these materials — to make them known and interpret the exact meaning of their contents,” Fernández wrote. “The Holy Father showed interest and, a few days later, sent me the cardboard box with those texts, so I could care for them and do the work I hoped to do with them.”
The posthumous publication of a pope's innermost spiritual musings is not unusual.

Pope John XXIII’s autobiography, “Journal of a Soul,” was published in 1960. St. John Paul II had wanted his personal notes burned after his death, but his secretary defied his wishes and had the writings published in 2014.
Associated Press religion coverage receives support through AP’s collaboration with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc. The AP is solely responsible for this content.

title: Bangladesh's ousted leader Hasina plans to return home from exile on Dec 16
summary: Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return home from exile in India on Dec. 16
story: Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return home from exile in India on Dec. 16

DHAKA, Bangladesh -- DHAKA, Bangladesh (AP) — Sheikh Hasina, who was ousted as Bangladesh's prime minister more than two years ago, said Tuesday that she plans to return home from exile in India on Dec. 16, the day the country celebrates as Victory Day when it won independence after a war with Pakistan.

Hasina went into exile in India on Aug. 5, 2024, after a student-led mass uprising forced her to end her 15-year rule. She was sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity involving the uprising in which hundreds of protesters were killed. Hasina rejected the verdict and has said she is ready to fight the case once she is back.
Abu Abdullah M Saleh, press secretary to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told The Associated Press that the government would stick to its position on Hasina's extradition as a convict.
“My government's stand is very clear. She has been convicted in a tribunal. We have sought her extradition,” he said by phone.
The junior minister for foreign affairs, Humaiun Kobir, told reporters in a briefing on Tuesday that Hasina could return only “in handcuffs or under strict surveillance.”
“The reality is that no terrorist will ever be allowed to return this way without extradition,” he was quoted as saying by the country's leading English-language Daily Star newspaper.
It is expected that Hasina would be arrested upon her return and sent to jail.
A prosecutor had earlier said that Hasina wouldn't be able to appeal her death sentence as she missed the required deadline, and that there would be no legal basis to stop her execution.
In Bangladesh, presidential clemency is allowed, but Hasina has never sought that in earlier statements and has rejected the verdict outright.

After her announcement of returning home, political tensions have gripped the South Asian nation, which has a history of unrest. Explosions of crude bombs, arson and road blockades have returned in recent weeks. Unidentified people set fire to the ancestral home of an interim leader, while in Hasina's ancestral home in another part of the country, people took to the streets.
The government blamed Hasina's supporters for attempting to create chaos before her planned return.
In the statement Tuesday announcing the planned date of her return, she urged current Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to arrange for her return on the national airline.

“Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5th, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka,” spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali said in the statement.

“It is deeply symbolic that she has chosen 16 December, our Victory Day, for her planned return to Bangladesh. We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people, honoring the great victory achieved under the leadership of her father, Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman,” Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, told the AP.
“We are equally confident that she will definitely return and under her leadership post- return, Bangladesh will once again advance towards peace, stability and prosperity,” Arin said.

Hasina's father led the war against Pakistan and was the first leader of the country. He was assassinated in a military coup in 1975, along with most of his family members. Hasina and her younger sister survived because they were outside the country at the time.
Earlier this month, in an interview with the AP, Hasina said that she would return to the country in December at any cost, and even the possibility of death couldn't prevent her from returning home.

Also this month, Hasina urged the government to provide her with a new passport and national identity card to facilitate her return, but the government said that she wouldn't get that. Her documents were canceled by the interim government.

Three days after Hasina's fall, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus took over as head of an interim government and later handed over power to the elected government of Rahman's Bangladesh Nationalist Party. The Yunus-led government banned Hasina's Awami League party, and it wasn't allowed to contest the election in February.

The Jamaat-e-Islami party, the country's largest Islamist party, which sided with the Pakistani military junta in 1971, returned to politics in the February election and is now the main opposition party in Bangladesh. Under Hasina, many top leaders of the party were executed on charges of war crimes.

title: It's a race to find Cyprus' disappeared, hindered by a construction boom and fading memories
summary: A group of dedicated Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot experts have for two decades worked hard to unearth and identify the remains of ethnically split Cyprus' missing persons
story: A group of dedicated Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot experts have for two decades worked hard to unearth and identify the remains of ethnically split Cyprus' missing persons

LAPITHOS, Cyprus -- The construction worker in Cyprus spotted human bones jutting out from the muddy trench where he had been preparing to pour concrete for the foundation of a new luxury hotel. His alerts went unheeded and the remains were entombed beneath tons of concrete.

They stayed there, a stone’s throw from the island nation’s northern coastline, for 38 more years — until the hotel's recent demolition presented Cyprus' Committee on Missing Persons with the rare chance to act on the decades-old eyewitness account.

Comprised of a Greek Cypriot, a Turkish Cypriot and a United Nations appointee, the CMP employs a bi-communal forensic team of more than 60 archaeologists, anthropologists and geneticists who have spent two decades unearthing and identifying bodies from the conflict that consumed Cyprus and led to its ethnic division.

There were 2,002 people on an official list of those who disappeared during 1960s clashes after Cyprus gained independence from British colonial rule and when the island’s population split in 1974. The CMP has exhumed and identified 1,085.

Such achievements offered closure to relatives waiting decades for word about their loved ones' fates, and chiseled away at mistrust and enmity between the two communities. And this has helped to provide impetus for a negotiated peace deal, despite numerous failed U.N.-mediated rounds of talks.

But 745 Greek Cypriots and 172 Turkish Cypriots are still missing, according to the CMP — and recovering bodies like the one beneath the L.A. Hotel is increasingly difficult as eyewitnesses die and old memories blur, while high-rises and hotels luring foreign buyers and vacationers are built atop makeshift graves.

“Time is our biggest enemy at the moment because our witnesses are disappearing, families are leaving us, buildings are going up everywhere,” Leonidas Pantelides, the Greek Cypriot member of the CMP's hierarchy, told the Associated Press in an interview at the demolition site. “So it is a struggle against time, but it’s one that we cannot give up on.”
Before the foundation for the L.A. Hotel in Lapithos was laid in 1988, there was little there but citrus orchards and pristine beaches.

It had been the scene of fierce battles between Turkish forces and Greek Cypriot defenders during Turkey’s 1974 invasion, which was triggered by a Greek junta-backed coup that aimed at union with Greece.

As Turkish troops advanced to seize the northern third of the island, hundreds of Greek Cypriots were buried in hastily dug mass graves while tens of thousands more fled. Many Turkish Cypriots also disappeared in the south. The island's ethnic split was entrenched in a 1975 deal to swap populations stuck on either side of a United Nations-controlled buffer zone.

The bright pink L.A. Hotel sought to draw European tourists to the island's north, where Turkish Cypriots declared a separate state recognized only by Turkey. But the business collapsed under the strain of COVID-19 travel restrictions. A new owner tore it down this year to make way for a swankier hotel.

The CMP seized the moment and got the owner's consent to dig at the site for the body spotted almost four decades earlier — a rare reprieve as construction marches ahead on both sides of the buffer zone. Excavation began this month, with hopes that finding at least one body beneath the concrete slab could prompt searches on other developed or condemned property in the north.
“We hope that we will have the chances for more old buildings to be demolished so that we can excavate the whole area, which is a focus area actually for us,” archaeologist Irene Papadopoulos said.

Since unearthing 177 bodies in 2015, the CMP's success rate has dwindled. So far this year they’ve found just eight. What was once an open field where a witness described someone being buried near an olive tree could now be the site of a strip mall or apartment complex. Ground-penetrating radar has brought only mixed results.

Even the slightest clue can help piece together disparate strands of information, according to Pantelides: “A topographical detail that a witness knows may help us to locate a place of interest more specifically, because our biggest problem is accuracy."

For Ali Culluoglu, team leader of the Lapithos dig, the work is deeply personal. His grandfather had been among the missing until his remains were found in 2015 near the town of Paphos, on the island’s southwestern corner. The CMP will keep searching until "the last missing person" is found, he said.
A half-dozen skeletons are laid out atop white tablecloths in the CMP's anthropological laboratory, where Alexandra Mouski painstakingly pieces together tiny fragments of a shattered skull.

Collecting tooth and bone samples for identification through DNA analysis is a laborious process, since most remains have been found comingled in mass graves. Many samples must be taken to properly identify the bones before returning the most complete remains possible to relatives, laboratory coordinator Istenc Engin said.

DNA collected from remains is checked against a genetics database containing samples from relatives of most of the missing on both sides. DNA samples are occasionally taken from deceased relatives, when the missing person had no family members still living, identification coordinator Katerina Papaioannou and colleague Gulbanu Zorba said.
Forensic teams also search for any artifacts that could help identify the bodies — like a ring engraved with a wedding date and the initials of a spouse.
"This is very important for the family members, because this they can remember. They cannot understand the bones, but they can understand the artifacts,” Mouski said.

Among the Cypriots still waiting for results is schoolteacher Panayiotis Efstathiou, who was 10 when his parents and younger brother were caught behind enemy lines after Turkish forces landed. He never saw them again.

His amateur sleuthing turned up details about how his family disappeared — including the name of the now-deceased man who killed them. But his years of gathering testimonies haven't revealed just where they were buried outside their village of Vasileia.

“I believe they must all accelerate their work, because most witnesses have died, others are in very old age; they’re suffering from dementia and I see this daily. I search for them, speak with them. They won't say,” Efstathiou told the AP. “It will be very difficult, unfortunately, to find those who are left. From this side and from the other side.”

title: Meet the major players in Spain's general election
summary: Spaniards will vote in a general election Sunday, when Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will try to defy the polls that point to a combined victory for conservative and far-right challengers
story: Spaniards will vote in a general election Sunday, when Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will try to defy the polls that point to a combined victory for conservative and far-right challengers
BARCELONA, Spain -- Spaniards will vote in a general election Sunday, with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez seeking to fend off conservative and far-right challengers to earn yet another term.
Sánchez’s main rival is conservative Alberto Núñez Feijóo, while the far-right’s Santiago Abascal is vying to play kingmaker to Núñez Feijóo and usher in a right-wing coalition.
Here's what you need to know about the top candidates.
Pedro Sánchez of the Socialist Party has led Spain’s government since 2018, making him one of Europe’s longest-serving leaders.
With his polished appearance and command of English, Sánchez has become a darling of the global progressive movement.

He has staked out strong positions against U.S. President Donald Trump and the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, as well as Israel’s military operations in Gaza. He has remained firm on his pro-migration policies amid a wider anti-immigration mood sweeping the developed world. He has overseen Europe's fastest growing major economy for several years, but greater wealth has not helped extinguish anger over rising housing costs.
Sánchez, 54, is a fierce campaigner who has outwitted adversaries both inside and outside his party and repeatedly beaten the odds, earning him the reputation of a political escape artist.

The most recent example of his electoral savvy came in 2023 when Sánchez’s Socialist Party took a beating in regional elections. Instead of licking his wounds, the very next day he stunned the country by calling for a general election, and he campaigned on fears of the far right entering government. The audacious move worked, and voters let him stay in office after forming another left-wing coalition.

Now the trained economist arguably faces his greatest challenge. He is dogged by legal cases involving corruption by a former minister and top officials in his party as well as his wife — who denies wrongdoing.
Sánchez’s fate will most likely depend not only on his Socialists rallying but also a group of smaller parties to the Left outperforming polling that predicts they will lose votes.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the Popular Party is a lifelong civil servant-turned-politician who has avoided scandal and projects himself as a sensible, moderate and effective center-right administrator.

Known nationally by his second last name, Feijóo won election after election in Galicia during the 13 years in which he governed the rural northwest corner of Spain. Despite being a less-developed region, Galicia has a long tradition of producing strong politicians. Among them were 20th-century dictator Francisco Franco and former Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy, who ran Spain from 2011 until 2018 — the last time the Popular Party led Spain.
Feijóo, 65, wants to reduce government regulations and lower taxes while, like Sánchez, is staunchly pro-European Union. If he wins, Feijóo is expected to mend bridges with the U.S. and Israel.
Feijóo made the leap to take over his party in time to lead it during the previous general election, when he failed to oust Sánchez.
That means the pressure is on Feijóo to make good on the broad support the Popular Party has maintained since then.

While the low-key Feijóo may be overshadowed by his rivals, he is in charge of the Popular Party's finely tuned vote-winning machine that's entrenched in the capital, Madrid, as well as many of Spain's rural provinces.

Bearded and barrel-chested in his tailored suits, Santiago Abascal is a member of the global populist right who exudes macho toughness, and his candidacy could ensure Feijóo has a coalition to govern.

Abascal, 50, is from Spain’s northern Basque Country. Like many politicians from across the spectrum in Spain, his ultranationalist ideology was shaped in response to the violence of the region’s separatist group ETA, which disbanded in 2018.

The first part of Abascal’s political career was as a rank-and-file member of the Popular Party before he and others splintered off to found Vox in late 2013. He quickly took over as its leader and has maintained firm control of the party ever since.

His ideology fits within the wider populist right movement, from the U.S. to Europe. He is a staunch defender of Israel and has strongly criticized Spain's position under Sánchez toward the country. He wants to slash government regulations for business and cut taxes, and is an open admirer of Argentina's chainsaw-wielding President Javier Milei.

Like Milei, Abascal slams progressive causes, including feminist thought, while dismissing climate change. Vox is not openly hostile to the EU, unlike other far-right European parties, but he blames immigration for Spain’s cost-of-living pains.

Far-right parties like Vox have been boxed out of government in Spain since the return of democracy following Franco's death in 1975. After losing seats in the 2023 election, Vox is aiming for a rebound that would afford it the leverage to demand ministries as a junior member in what Abascal hopes will be Feijóo's triumphal government.
Right-wing voters who find Vox too mild can opt for “Se Acabó la Fiesta" (The Party Is Over), the political vehicle of a far-right social media influencer.

On the other end of the spectrum, in-fighting impeded smaller progressive parties from remaking an electoral coalition that helped the left stay in power in 2023. This time, the Frente Amplio (Broad Front) will compete with Podemos (We Can) for the most left-leaning of voters. That will hurt both their prospects, as well as Sánchez's shot at forming another left-wing coalition.

There are also traditional parties that focus on influencing how policies and laws impact their home territories. These regionalist parties in Catalonia, the Basque Country, Galicia and the Canary Islands could play a role in forming a ruling coalition if the results are close.

title: Pentagon sharply rebukes Canada over defense spending and the F-35 fighter jet review
summary: The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets
story: The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets

TORONTO -- The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets.
In an unusually blunt fact sheet, the U.S. Defense Department on Monday said Ottawa had failed to make the tough decisions needed to modernize its military and meet NATO commitments.
“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves,” it said. “Canada must get serious and focused.”

Simon Lafortune, a spokesperson for Canada’s defense minister, said Canada had committed 81.8 billion Canadian dollars ($56.9 billion) over five years to rebuild its armed forces and reached NATO’s 2% defense spending benchmark five years ahead of schedule.

“Canada is also on track to meet NATO’s new commitment to invest 5% of GDP annually in defense by 2035 and is taking concrete steps to build the capabilities needed to meet that goal,” he said in a statement.
The Pentagon said U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was “laser focused” on modernizing Canada’s military after decades of American taxpayers footing the bill for its defense.

Canada reached NATO’s previous target of spending 2% of gross domestic product on defense and joined allies pledging to reach 5% by 2035, including related security investments. Its latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by 2027-28, but only 2.6% of GDP would go toward core defense.

The Pentagon accused Ottawa of having no credible, fully costed plan to meet NATO’s 5% target and postponing the largest spending increases until after the 2029 federal election. Canada’s parliamentary budget watchdog has also questioned how the government will meet the target.

The criticism follows a classified directive from Hegseth that Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said largely restricts U.S. military officials’ participation in Canadian think tank and social events. Relations have been battered by President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st state.

Wesley Wark, a Canadian national security expert and former government adviser, titled his Monday newsletter “Pentagon Pete strikes again,” calling the criticism “insulting and infuriating.” He suggested Washington was discounting Canada’s NATO deployment in Latvia and its support for Ukraine.
In May, Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby paused a U.S.-Canada defense advisory board established in 1940, accusing Ottawa of failing to make credible progress on its military commitments.
The Pentagon said only 41.9% of Canada’s air force fleet and 53.9% of its naval fleet were serviceable in 2025-26, while army readiness stood at 48%.

It also criticized Ottawa’s review of its planned purchase of 88 American-made F-35s, warning that a mixed fighter fleet could worsen personnel shortages. The Pentagon accused Canadian leaders of putting domestic economic interests ahead of military effectiveness, creating uncertainty for the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, which the countries operate jointly.

Prime Minister Mark Carney put the F-35 purchase under review as Trump threatened Canadian sovereignty and imposed tariffs. Canada has examined Swedish-made Gripen fighters, which could bring manufacturing jobs.
Carney has acknowledged readiness problems, saying only one of Canada’s four submarines was seaworthy. His government plans to buy up to 12 replacements.
“We should no longer send three-quarters of our defense capital spending to America,” Carney said in June.
Other NATO allies also remain short of the new 5% target. Yet Colby praised Germany’s military buildup Sunday as a “tectonic shift” and called Poland a “true model ally.”

The Trump administration had already barred Pentagon officials from attending the Halifax International Security Forum under restrictions imposed in 2025. The forum’s president, Peter Van Praagh, previously served as a senior adviser to a Conservative government in Canada.

Before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Van Praagh warned that Trump might undermine the results if Republicans suffered major losses. If those efforts succeeded, he said, it would mean “the end of the United States as we know it.”
Speaking at the Halifax forum Saturday, Rounds said Hegseth’s directive was not expected to affect joint military operations or intelligence sharing.

title: South Korea says several Russian aircraft flew into its air defense zone
summary: South Korea’s military says it scrambled fighter jets when several Russian aircraft flew inside the country’s air defense identification zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan
story: South Korea’s military says it scrambled fighter jets when several Russian aircraft flew inside the country’s air defense identification zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan

SEOUL, South Korea -- South Korea scrambled fighter jets Tuesday to chase away Russian military aircraft that flew inside the country’s air defense identification zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan, Seoul’s military said, correcting earlier government statements that the planes had violated the country’s territorial airspace. An alert for an eastern island was quickly lifted.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff’s announcement followed a statement by the Ministry of the Interior and Safety, which relays military information for such public alerts, that Russian aircraft had violated South Korean airspace and instructed residents of Ulleung island to evacuate. The provincial government had issued another alert saying the planes were suspected to be North Korean.

Joint Chiefs’ spokesperson Jang Do-young said the Russian aircraft entered the country’s air defense identification zone and flew close to the airspace of Ulleung island, which prompted the military to coordinate with the government over the evacuation alert.

Jang did not provide a specific answer when asked whether there had been a miscommunication with the Safety Ministry that caused the agency to alert that the Russian planes violated South Korea’s airspace, saying the military needed to look into the matter further. He said the North Gyeongsang provincial government may have alerted a training text by mistake.

The Safety Ministry ordered Ulleung Island residents to take shelter in underground facilities or buildings around 7:52 a.m., but lifted the order three minutes later, saying the aircraft had left the danger area.
The Joint Chiefs said the country scrambled fighter jets in preparation for contingencies before the Russian aircraft withdrew.

An air defense identification zone refers to a buffer zone extending beyond a country’s territorial airspace, giving a military more time to identify, track and repel foreign aircraft approaching its territory.

Jang said the Russian aircraft had breached the country’s air defense zone several times this year and that the military planned to lodge a protest with Moscow through the Russian military attache over the latest incident. The military did not say how many Russian planes it detected or what types of aircraft they were.

No major disruptions were reported on the island, which has a population of around 9,000. It had a major scare in 2022, when North Korea fired more than 20 missiles into the sea during heightened inter-Korean tensions. One missile headed toward the island, triggering air raid sirens and prompting residents to evacuate.

In 2019, South Korean fighter jets fired warning shots after a Russian A-50 airborne early warning aircraft, flying alongside Russian and Chinese bombers in a joint patrol, entered South Korea’s territorial airspace near the island of Dokdo. Moscow then denied violating South Korean airspace.

Tuesday’s incident came a week after South Korea scrambled fighter jets to repel several Russian military aircraft that it said temporarily entered the country’s air-defense zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan. Japan the same day protested to Moscow after saying that two suspected Russian aircraft had entered the country’s airspace off its southwestern coast.

title: US flew drone over Mexican territory to help capture drug lord in Sinaloa
summary: Mexican security officials say the United States flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to help the government track down and capture a top drug lord over the weekend in Sinaloa
story: Mexican security officials say the United States flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to help the government track down and capture a top drug lord over the weekend in Sinaloa

MEXICO CITY -- The United States flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to help the government track down and capture a top drug lord over the weekend in Sinaloa, Mexican security officials said Monday.

The recent detention of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro” illustrates increasing law enforcement cooperation between the neighboring countries, but U.S. involvement in Mexican security operations has long been a touchy subject.

U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to crack down on cartels, while Mexico has repeatedly underscored its sovereignty. On Monday, Sheinbaum emphasized that U.S. forces were not allowed to operate on the ground in Mexico and the governments were only sharing intelligence.
“This case in particular demonstrates the capacity of the armed forces” of Mexico to make major detentions, Sheinbaum said.
The U.S. has sought to line up allies across Latin America to allow U.S. forces to operate in their territories, with mixed responses from across the region.

The weekend detention of the capo, who was one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives, triggered a burst of violence in the northern state of Sinaloa that left 20 people dead in the city of Guasave. Among them were four soldiers and 16 suspected criminals, Mexican officials said Monday.

Defense Secretary Gen. Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said Monday that the capture of Meza Flores and 16 members of his criminal group was the result of “very important intelligence sharing” with U.S. authorities over the past three months to pinpoint Meza Flores’ location in Guasave.

In the week leading up to Meza Flores’ capture, that included authorizing the U.S. to fly intelligence drones over Mexican territory to assist Mexican law enforcement to later surround the capo and go in for the capture, Trevilla Trejo and other Mexican officials said. They emphasized that the intelligence mission was carried out in compliance with Mexican law.

On Monday, Mexico's prosecutors' office announced that it had formally charged Meza Flores and two other alleged cartel members with illegal possession of firearms and possession of methamphetamine with the intent to sell, adding that the three were flown to Mexico City over the weekend following their capture.

Authorities also highlighted that the U.S. has an existing extradition request for Meza Flores for drug trafficking charges, leaving open the possibility that the cartel boss may be sent north to face justice.
His capture was celebrated by Mexican and U.S. law enforcement as a major blow to criminal groups in the region.
The U.S. government highlighted its intelligence support in the operation, but did not immediately provide more details about the use of the surveillance drone when asked on Monday.

Meza Flores led the Beltran Leyva organization and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. He was also a key ally of a Sinaloa Cartel faction known as “Los Mayos," which is locked in a brutal territorial war against another cartel faction in the Mexican state.

The capture of Meza Flores was the latest in a string of targeted operations against cartel kingpins by Mexican authorities, the largest of which was the February killing of Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho."
While the captures show that the government is doubling down on its fight against crime, many experts were quick to emphasize that the strategy could backfire.

In previous anti-crime offensives in Mexico and other parts of Latin America, knocking out cartel leaders without debilitating the entire criminal structure around them has largely only fueled bloody power struggles between cartel factions. That has been the case in recent years in Sinaloa.

title: Australia set to pass digital duty of care law, fines up to 5% of global revenue
summary: Australia is set to create new online safety laws that would make tech giants potentially liable for multibillion dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms
story: Australia is set to create new online safety laws that would make tech giants potentially liable for multibillion dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms

MELBOURNE, Australia -- The Australian government clinched a political deal on Tuesday to introduce online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms. The United States warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech.
The Digital Duty of Care Bill would require Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement.
The legislation is similar to the European Union’s Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom's Online Safety Act passed a year later.

The proposed legislation would set minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said.

“We can’t cure the internet, but this is providing some basic safety standards and saying if you build it, you are responsible for its risks,” Communications Minister Anika Wells told reporters at Parliament House in Canberra.

Wells announced on Tuesday her center-left Labor Party government had accepted amendments proposed by the minor Greens party to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority.
Greens leader David Shoebridge confirmed his party had agreed to support the amended bill.

“Today we are taking power back from a handful of billionaire-owned, largely U.S. corporations and giving it back to Australians who have been paying too high a price for their profits,” Shoebridge said in a statement.
The Senate will likely pass the bill on Wednesday and the House of Representatives, where the government holds a majority, would pass it into law before Parliament rises for the year on Thursday.
The Greens' amendments include increasing maximum penalties for breaches from 109 million Australian dollars ($72 million) to 5% of a tech company’s global revenue.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration expressed “serious concerns” in a submission in September to a parliamentary committee examining the draft law. U.S. concerns included how Australia would designate what constitutes “foreseeable harm.”
U.S. Ambassador to Australia David Brat said he had conveyed his government’s objections to the amended legislation to Wells on Tuesday.
“Vaguely defined ‘harms,’ backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” Brat posted on social media.
“As Australia’s largest foreign investor, the U.S. is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors,” he added.
Wells said of their conversation: “There are points of difference and we’re ironing them out.”

The conservative opposition Liberal Party shares U.S. concerns that the bill empowers government ministers and the nation's online safety watchdog to judge what was harmful. Opposition lawmakers oppose the legislation.
“This bill undermines both the online safety of Australians and our freedom of expression,” senior opposition senator Sarah Henderson told reporters.
The Greens' amendments would also give people a legal right to sue social media companies in Australian courts for harms suffered online.
It follows Australian mining magnate Andrew Forrest having to go to U.S. courts to sue Meta over scam ads on its platforms that use his likeness without permission. The case is not yet resolved.

In October, a U.S. judge ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.

Australia's bill would also let social media users opt out of algorithms that send them content and empower Australia’s online safety watchdog to remove apps and websites that fabricate naked images from genuine images of people.

It would also require protections for children against content that promotes eating disorders, hostile ideas about women, pornography, crime or dangerous stunts, or causes serious mental health distress.
Lisa Given, an information sciences expert at RMIT University in Melbourne, described the draft legislation as “very good” and largely in line with European laws.

“It’ll be very interesting to see what happens now globally,” Given said. “I’ve always been of the view that if countries can band together and put through similar legislation, collectively we have a better chance of actually pushing Big Tech to make real changes in terms of the design of their systems.”

title: US consumer confidence soars as election uncertainty ends, gas prices fall
summary: Americans’ confidence in the economy jumped this month as gas prices continued their steady decline and election-related uncertainy ended
story: Americans’ confidence in the economy jumped this month as gas prices continued their steady decline and election-related uncertainy ended
WASHINGTON -- Americans’ confidence in the economy jumped this month as gas prices continued their steady decline and election-related uncertainty ended.

The Conference Board said Tuesday that its consumer confidence index soared to 103.3 this month, from a reading of 91.9 in October. It’s the second straight increase after the index fell in September to its lowest level since April 2014, even lower than during the pandemic.
Consumer confidence is closely linked to gas prices, and the Conference Board also said Americans see the job market improving.

The improvement could signal a pickup in consumer spending in the months ahead, though Americans have been spending at a solid pace this year even as consumer surveys have been lackluster. Economists say the surveys are not as reliable a measure of consumers' behavior as they have been in the past.

title: Utah asks to drop charges against Kalshi, founders after Kalshi halts trading there
summary: Utah is asking asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against Kalshi and two of its executives, accusing the prediction market operator of running an illegal gambling enterprise
story: Utah is asking asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against Kalshi and two of its executives, accusing the prediction market operator of running an illegal gambling enterprise

Utah asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, citing Kalshi's decision to halt trading in the state that had accused it of running an illegal gambling enterprise.

The one-sentence motion filed Tuesday in a Salt Lake City-based court by state Attorney General Derek Brown referenced a “change in circumstance." Brown’s office noted that it could refile the case if Kalshi resumes offering trades on its platform there.
“Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges,” Brown said in a statement.

Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across more than 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the U.S. Supreme Court.
The felony charges filed by Utah include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.

The state’s charging documents name Kalshi and its co-founders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara. They are due in court in Salt Lake City on Dec. 4, unless a judge agrees to dismiss the case.

Utah law prohibits gambling, and Utah considers prediction markets gambling, Brown's office said. Many other states contend that the platforms’ sports trading activities are flouting their laws that regulate sports betting and casino gambling.

Utah's felony charges represented a new tactic in how states are trying to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity. In a separate case, Brown's office is still asking a state court to make Kalshi give up the profits it made in Utah.

Kalshi, the nation's largest prediction market operator, said Monday it had halted trading in Utah after it became clear that a federal judge hearing a case brought by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission wouldn't immediately stop Utah's attempts to shut it down there.
A Kalshi spokesperson called it an “unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi" but said the company will continue to fight in court for the right to operate in Utah.

Kalshi didn’t close open positions or void contracts when it blocked any new positions from being taken in Utah. It also let Utah traders close out their open positions and withdraw their funds, Kalshi said.

Kalshi, like the CFTC, argues that prediction markets offer “event contracts” that should be considered swaps under a federal law that grants exclusive regulation to the federal agency. Utah and at least 42 other states have opposed that view.

Kalshi sued Utah in February, asking a federal judge to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling restrictions on the platform. A federal judge rejected the request, and an appeal is pending at the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which declined to halt Utah’s regulatory enforcement during Kalshi’s appeal.
Trading activity on Kalshi is halted in Nevada and partially in Michigan and Washington, according to Kalshi.
Follow Marc Levy at http://twitter.com/timelywriter

title: Federal agency boosts size of most single-family loans the government can guarantee to $855,400
summary: The Federal Housing Finance Agency is increasing the size of home loans that the government can guarantee against default as it takes into account rising housing prices
story: The Federal Housing Finance Agency is increasing the size of home loans that the government can guarantee against default as it takes into account rising housing prices
The Federal Housing Finance Agency is increasing the size of home loans that the government can guarantee against default as it takes into account rising housing prices.
Beginning next year, mortgage buyers Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will be able to acquire loans of up to $855,400 on single-family homes in most of the country, the agency said Tuesday.
The new conforming loan limit amounts to a roughly 2.7% increase from its 2026 level.
FHFA oversees Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which buy home loans from banks and other lenders, guaranteeing them against default. The loans are then bundled into securities sold to investors.
But FHFA sets limits to the size of the loans that Fannie and Freddie can buy. Such loans are known as conforming loans, while mortgages above the conforming loan limit are known as jumbo loans.
FHFA adjusts the limits of a conforming loan annually to reflect changes in U.S. home values, which have been rising nationally, albeit more slowly.

Rising mortgage rates have weighed on home sales this year, deepening a national housing slump that dates back to 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. They declined last month to their slowest annual pace in more than 16 years as mortgage rates surged.
The FHFA’s latest House Price Index shows that, on average, U.S. home prices increased about 2.7% in the July-September quarter compared to a year earlier.

The 2027 single-family home conforming loan limit will apply to most of the country, though the FHFA allows higher loan limits for certain states, such as Alaska and Hawaii, and in counties where the local median home value is more than double the conforming loan limit.
For example, the conforming loan limit in 2027 for single-family homes in Los Angeles County will be $1,283,100, while in New York County it will be $1,224,750.

title: UN climate talks break down over bitter disagreements on fossil fuels
summary: Climate talks in Turkey failed to reach an overarching agreement.
story: Climate talks in Turkey failed to reach an overarching agreement.

ANTALYA, Turkey -- Chaotic United Nations climate talks in Turkey couldn't reach an overarching agreement on Sunday because of disagreements over whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming.

Expectations had already been low heading into the two-week negotiations, but discussions about explicitly including fossil fuels — the chief cause of global warming — and other issues including money proved irreconcilable.

The talks, called COP31, continued without a main agreement known as a cover decision. The meeting had already made progress on smaller issues that nibbled at the process and the warming problem and continued to go on after the failure on the cover decision.

Any pact approved at the talks has to be by a near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they couldn't accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership that didn’t mention fossil fuels.

A considerably larger number of nations said that consensus on something was more important and accepted the decision, often reluctantly. Russia and Saudi Arabia pushed to keep fossil fuels out of the document.

“It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks, which ran nearly 48 hours overtime at the Turkish resort town of Antalya.
For most of the first 25 years of the United Nations climate talks, outcomes didn’t explicitly mention fossil fuels, until three years ago.

That’s when in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates a groundbreaking agreement called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels,” but since then there’s been no explicit mention of fossil fuels. The Turkish-Australian proposal recalled the Dubai deal entirely, but that wasn’t enough for many nations and environmental groups.

Adding to the disagreement was the fact that the draft included explicit language and a goal for carbon capture and storage for industrial polluters, which many nations and activists said would run against efforts to reduce overall emissions.

“The failure of this COP to deliver ambitious, fair, science-based outcomes falls squarely on the shoulders of richer nations, petrostates, and the disgracefully incompetent duo of the Turkish and Australian COP presidents,” said Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists.

As the proposed deal fell apart in the plenary session, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, the president of COP31, was absent, leaving it to Elchin Allahverdiyev of Azerbaijan to announce the failure.

“Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that’s disappointing, very disappointing,” said Australia’s Chris Bowen, the president of negotiations in the unusual joint leadership.

Bowen said the explicit call in the Dubai agreement to wean away from coal, oil and natural gas that cause climate change is still in force: “Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is happening. It’s happening. It’s happening at speed and it’s irreversible.”
Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland, Delgado from Bangkok and Arasu from Bengaluru, India.
