title: Issue with automation system causes Delta flight delays in Atlanta
summary: An issue with Delta Air Lines’ weight and balance automation system was causing flight delays Sunday at its hub in Atlanta and nationwide
story: An issue with Delta Air Lines’ weight and balance automation system was causing flight delays Sunday at its hub in Atlanta and nationwide
ATLANTA -- An issue with Delta Air Lines' weight and balance automation system was causing flight delays Sunday at its hub in Atlanta and nationwide.

Delta said in a statement that its teams were using manual workarounds to get flights off the ground while they continued to work to restore automation. The delays come as Americans begin traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday this week.
The Federal Aviation Administration said on X that Delta was working to resolve the issues, and that the delays weren't related to any FAA air traffic systems.

Earlier this month, a malfunction in the FAA’s network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers canceled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days after that, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights.
As of midday Sunday, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 48% of Delta's flights were delayed.
FlightAware said that 38% of flights out of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport — Delta’s hub — were delayed while about 36% of flights destined for the airport were delayed.

title: Small US trucking firms scramble to survive mounting diesel costs
summary: High diesel prices have put pressure on small U.S. trucking businesses
story: High diesel prices have put pressure on small U.S. trucking businesses

NEW YORK -- When diesel prices topped $4 a gallon early in the U.S.-Iran war, Kevin Otto thought he could manage by telling his Minnesota trucking company's 16 drivers to slow down. He estimated that traveling at 65 miles per hour would allow Otto Transfer's fleet of flatbeds to squeeze two-tenths of a mile more from every gallon and save him $7,000 per truck.

Instead, prices kept climbing. After diesel surpassed $6 a gallon in September, Otto added a fuel surcharge to every job for the first time. He based the surcharge on the government's weekly Midwest diesel average, beginning at 5% and eventually raising it to 12.5%.
“To me, it’s drastic, but it’s the only way to survive," said Otto, who took over the 80-year-old company from his parents in 2002.

High diesel prices this year have put new pressure on the small businesses that make up most of the nation's motor carriers. The war drove up one of their largest and least avoidable daily expenses just as the highly fragmented U.S. trucking industry showed tentative signs of recovery from a yearslong slump marked by weak demand and depressed rates.

Small trucking companies usually have fewer financial buffers against surging fuel prices than their larger competitors. Big fleets typically have greater cash reserves, often buy diesel at bulk discounts and tend to negotiate long-term contracts with adjustable fuel surcharges. Many smaller operators negotiate rates one load at a time and must absorb higher pump prices while waiting three to four weeks for spot rates to catch up, freight data provider DAT Freight & Analytics said.
Even when a rate includes a separate line item for fuel, carriers may wait 30 to 90 days to be paid.

“Those lags in the rates catching up to fuel are even more challenging if you’ve got to put food on the table and you don’t have a large company that’s helping carry over that difference,” Alex Leslie, senior research associate at the American Transportation Research Institute, said.

On-highway diesel reached a record national average of $6.53 in September, according to the Energy Information Administration. The price was $5.94 a gallon for the week of Nov. 16, about 56% more than before the war, EIA said. Gasoline averaged $3.81, about 30% higher.

Getting goods hauled around the U.S. and Canada costs substantially more than it did a year ago. Spot rates paid by freight brokers for individual loads were 44% to 48% higher in September, depending on the type of trailer, according to DAT. The company estimated that diesel costs accounted for at least two-fifths of the year-over-year increase.

The rest of the increase didn't necessarily translate into profit. Insurance, maintenance, equipment, tolls and other expenses were going up as the industry began to emerge from the lows of a “freight recession,” the American Transportation Research Institute said.

The average cost of operating a truck reached a record $2.34 per mile in 2025, a 3.4% increase from the year before, while nonfuel costs rose 4.2%, the industry research organization reported in July.

Profit margins were also exceptionally thin last year. Truckload and refrigerated carriers reported average operating margins of less than 1%, while flatbed carriers averaged a 0.5% operating loss, according to ATRI.

The downturn started in early 2022, when a pandemic-era surge in freight demand faded and too many trucks were left chasing fewer loads. Industry data suggest that a shrinking supply of trucks, rather than a renewed boom in shipments, is contributing to this year’s higher freight rates, obscuring how strained many trucking businesses are.

At October’s average diesel price, a tractor-trailer that gets six miles per gallon would have used $521 worth of fuel traveling 500 miles a day, compared with $310 in February, DAT calculated. Yet monthly freight volumes were lower for all three major trailer types than a year earlier, the company said.

“Demand actually hasn’t increased that much, and the market for the last few years has been quite depressed,” Adam Parish, director of trucking procurement at supply chain management company Flexport, said. “And so there’s been a lot of pricing pressure from customers.”

Wes Oberman’s company in Huntingdon, Tennessee, works with 14 drivers who own their tractor-trailers but operate under Oberman Logistics’ federal motor-carrier authority as they haul steel and consumer goods across the South.

The owner-operators handle jobs at individually negotiated flat rates and buy diesel on the road with company discount cards. They are allocated 85% of each load’s gross revenue, from which Oberman deducts their fuel purchases and fixed expenses.

As diesel consumed more of each load's revenue, he became pickier about the jobs he accepted. Sometimes that's meant waiting a day for a better-paying load or one requiring fewer “deadhead” miles, when the truck travels empty between jobs.
“We just got to keep trucking, as they say, save every penny we can and just weather the storm until this diesel crisis goes away,” Oberman said.

President Donald Trump sought to ease the pressure in October by directing the Internal Revenue Service to suspend federal penalties and reporting requirements through Dec. 31 for using dyed diesel on highways. Federal excise-tax payments were deferred, but state taxes and restrictions can still apply.
The restricted diesel normally is reserved for tax-exempt off-road uses such as farming. The fuel is dyed red to make improper use easier for law enforcement to spot.

David McKinney, the owner of McKinney & Sons Transfer in Lexington, Alabama, called the dyed diesel plan “absurd.” He doubted it would provide meaningful relief for small trucking companies. After selling two trucks in September to preserve cash, he worried that residual dye in the tanks of his company's remaining 15 trucks could expose him to fines after the temporary policy expires.
The IRS is considering a grace period.

McKinney, who has been in the trucking business for 30 years, has a fueling station at his shop so he pays less for diesel than he would if his drivers filled up at truck stops. Yet given the complicated calculus of trucking, his company is only breaking even, he said.

“Our bottom line is: For the past four months, we have survived. We have not profited any money,” McKinney said. “Rates need to be higher, but the trucking business is so competitive, it keeps it down."
In Delano, Minnesota, Otto worries his new surcharge will cost him customers. He previously adjusted his freight rates only once a year, but his long-term clients have accepted the added charge.

Otto usually gives the drivers who haul utility poles around the country for his company a bonus at the end of the year, but since his costs have risen so much, he isn’t sure if he is going to be able to do that this year.

EIA expects diesel prices to ease next year as more Middle East oil production outside Iran recovers. But the agency raised its 2027 forecast by 54 cents in November, to an average of $5.03 a gallon, citing continued constraints on global refined-fuel supplies. It warned that shipping disruptions could still produce short-term price swings.
“It’s a five-alarm fire, absolutely,” Otto said. “It is unsustainable, and I fear that it will only get worse.”

title: Crowdstrike to acquire Zscaler in $44B deal that would create a cybersecurity giant
summary: CrowdStrike is acquiring cloud security company Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at about $43.9 billion
story: CrowdStrike is acquiring cloud security company Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at about $43.9 billion

CrowdStrike is buying cloud security company Zscaler in an all-stock deal worth about $43.9 billion, the companies said Monday, in a major acquisition that combines two of the cybersecurity industry's biggest names.

The all-stock deal arrives after a string of high-profile hacks hit banks, supermarket fridges and crypto platforms, forcing the White House to shake up its cybersecurity leadership and raising alarms with officials around the world.
Cybersecurity experts have warned that artificial intelligence is being used to turbocharge cyberattacks by making it quicker and easier to find software flaws.
“Security used to be about keeping the adversary out," George Kurtz, CEO of Austin, Texas-based Crowdstrike, said in a statement. “Today, safety is required to let AI in.”
Reports of advanced artificial intelligence models deploying agents working on their own to break into other organizations have also raised alarms.
“In the AI era, Zero Trust security has become non-negotiable, and AI agents are rapidly becoming the new weakest link," Zscaler CEO Jay Chaudhry said.

Crowdstrike's focus has been on so-called endpoint security, with services to protect laptops, mobile devices and desktop computers. Santa Clara, California-based Zscaler, meanwhile, specializes in cloud-based network protection.
Zscaler shareholders will get 1.135 shares of Crowdstrike for each Zscaler share they own, under the deal's terms, which represent a 34% premium to Zscaler's closing price on Friday.
Shares of CrowdStrike tumbled more than 7% before the opening bell Monday. Shares of Zscaler rose 20%.
Existing CrowdStrike shareholders will own about 84.1% of the combined company, while existing Zscaler shareholders will hold the remaining 15.9%.
CrowdStrike and Zscaler were already working together in a partnership that included 2,000 shared customers. The deal would expand the combined company's market by more than $185 billion by 2029.
The transaction is expected to close in the second half of Crowdstrike's fiscal 2028 year, which begins in February.

title: Honda recalling more than 810,000 vehicles due to airbag inflator issue
summary: Honda is recalling more than 810,000 vehicles because their airbag inflators may rupture
story: Honda is recalling more than 810,000 vehicles because their airbag inflators may rupture
Honda is recalling more than 810,000 vehicles because their airbag inflators may rupture.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said that the recall includes 810,592 Honda Civic vehicles with model years 2012 to 2013, Honda CR-V vehicles with model years 2012 to 2013, Honda Accord 2013 models and Acura ILX and RDX vehicles with model year 2013.

The NHTSA said that the vehicles have certain Takata front and passenger air bag inflators. The inflators may rupture due to propellant degradation occurring after long-term exposure to high absolute humidity and high temperature variation.
If an inflator ruptures, it could result in sharp metal fragments hitting a driver or other vehicle occupant and result in serious injury or death.
Tens of millions of Takata airbags have been recalled, one of the largest ever product recalls.

Dealers will replace the front driver or passenger air bag inflator for free. Interim letters notifying owners of the safety risk are expected to be mailed Dec. 18. Additional letters will be sent once the final remedy is available.

Owners may contact Honda’s customer service at 1-888-234-2138 for more information. Individuals may also contact the NHTSA vehicle safety hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the agency's website at www.nhtsa.gov.

title: Climate talks in overtime as nations wrestle with response to worsening global warming
summary: Negotiators at the United Nations climate talks in Turkey are working an extra day in an attempt to reach a final agreement to address global warming
story: Negotiators at the United Nations climate talks in Turkey are working an extra day in an attempt to reach a final agreement to address global warming

ANTALYA, Turkey -- Work crews boxed up the venue for this year’s United Nations climate talks in Turkey, as negotiators went into overtime on Saturday in an attempt to reach a final agreement on global warming. But hopes are slim that additional discussions will produce concrete plans to slash fossil fuel use.

The added day of talks came as the two-week annual summit, or COP31, drew strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels in a draft of the final agreement. The document is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which drives heat waves, floods and other disasters.
To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut emissions from the use of coal, oil and gas.

In a letter sent on Saturday to this year's co-hosts, Turkey and Australia, 100 civil society groups warned that they were “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs” the U.N. has ever held. The letter stated there were only hours left “to save this COP from becoming a low point of three decades of climate negotiations.”

In the lead-up to these talks, the U.N. announced that the world will likely blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.
“No one knows what is happening behind closed doors, or what the outcome of COP31 will be,” said Teresa Anderson, global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International.
Inside an area of the COP31 venue known as the pavilions, where countries showcased innovations and hosted panels, workers were seen packing up electronics and boxing up belongings on Saturday.
The hallways, previously bustling with tens of thousands of participants, stood largely empty, with only a handful of security guards seen taking photos by deserted pavilions.

“COP31 is in a bleak overtime, with dwindling food and water, and no sign of any progress since the alarmingly underwhelming texts we saw earlier,” said Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at the venue in the Mediterranean coastal city of Antalya.

Earlier during the summit, the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker warned that progress on slowing global warming has stalled for the past five years, even as disasters — including this year’s heat waves in Europe and flooding in Nepal — become more deadly.

Countries most vulnerable to climate change, including small island nations whose lands are battered by rising seas, also say wealthy nations that caused the climate crisis must contribute more to U.N. funds to help them recover from disasters and adapt to a warmer world.

“Every year there seems to be a greater discontent, a mistrust and frustration for civil society, indigenous people and countries that are more climate vulnerable,” said Tuvalu's Minister of Environment Maina Talia, during a Saturday press conference.
“I am still holding the line, trying to be very optimistic until we see the text," he said.
The United States, a major polluter and the world’s largest economy, did not participate directly in this year's talks.
The next climate summit will take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.

On Friday, a protester wearing a red noose around his neck and a vest emblazoned with the slogan “you are killing the future” interrupted official proceedings by clambering onto a table and shouting: “You take out fossil fuels. You killed 1.5. There is no money. Just kill me now. The Global South cannot wait.”

The Global South isn’t a geographical term, but a reference to developing countries in general. As the protester was escorted out by security, he shouted: “You keep doing nothing at all. Nothing at all. Kill me now. Kill me now."
The demonstration interrupted Turkey's Minister of Environment and COP31 co-president Murat Kurum, who said “let’s try to maintain the peace in the room" before continuing with his scheduled remarks.

“Yesterday, of course, this place was buzzing and today it’s nearly empty. But all the key negotiators are here, civil society is here, watching the negotiations,” said Harjeet Singh, a strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, who has attended 18 climate summits.
“We are still stuck with many, many disagreements and nobody knows how long this will go on,” he said.

Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland, Delgado from Bangkok, Arasu from Bengaluru, India, and Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan. Associated Press journalist Tammy Webber contributed from Fenton, Michigan.

The Associated Press’ climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. The AP is solely responsible for all content. Find the AP’s standards for working with philanthropies, a list of supporters and funded coverage areas at AP.org.

title: After a 13-year wait, 'Grand Theft Auto VI' arrives with enormous hype and expectations
summary: The global rollout of "Grand Theft Auto VI" is underway, taking players back to Vice City
story: The global rollout of "Grand Theft Auto VI" is underway, taking players back to Vice City
LOS ANGELES -- After a 13-year wait, “Grand Theft Auto VI” has begun its global rollout, sending players back to Vice City and kicking off one of the most anticipated entertainment launches in years.
Players in New Zealand were among the first to enter Rockstar Games’ sprawling Florida-inspired world as midnight Thursday arrived, hours before the game becomes available across the United States.

Internet providers there had prepared for a massive surge in downloads. Chorus New Zealand expected about 35 petabytes — 35 million gigabytes — of additional traffic across its network as players downloaded the massive game.

“The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” said Kurt Rodgers, the company’s network strategy manager. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.”
In Wellington, Adam Simmons launched the game from his living room as soon as it unlocked, keeping the volume low so he wouldn’t wake his wife and daughters.
“The gameplay dynamics are just amazing and the graphics are great and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep,” he said after about half an hour of play.
Shares of Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, rose more than 8% Wednesday as the rollout continued.

In the Dallas area, Bryan Banuelos, a mobile auto detailer, told customers he wouldn't be taking calls Thursday so he could focus on “GTA VI.” His social media post actually drove some business beforehand, with customers trying to get their cars detailed before he disappeared into Vice City.
“Tomorrow will be the beginning of a new era for the gamers that like GTA,” Banuelos said.

The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days.

Rockstar returns to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following one of the most successful entertainment products ever released.

At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida.

Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy.
The focus on their relationship marks a major departure from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists.

Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, extending beyond Vice City to beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida.

Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area’s history and architecture.

Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game’s arrival as a marketing opportunity.

Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game’s release.

The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity.
Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding “GTA VI” gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight.
In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game’s soundtrack.
Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation.

The first “GTA VI” trailer drew more than 93 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, while Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has said the second trailer generated more than 475 million views across platforms in a day.
The game also has attracted awards attention before most players have had a chance to explore it.

“GTA VI” received eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.

The long wait is partly a product of the extraordinary staying power of its predecessor. “Grand Theft Auto Online,” the multiplayer component of “GTA V,” has kept players engaged for years through updates, activities and in-game purchases.
Music has long been woven into the “Grand Theft Auto” experience, with fictional radio stations and carefully curated soundtracks accompanying players as they drive through the series’ cities.
“Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album,” a 34-track collection of original songs tied to the game, is scheduled for release Friday.

A separate 30-track “Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score” by Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice is scheduled for release Dec. 11. The adaptive score is designed to shift depending on where players are and what they are doing and includes collaborations involving Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
Despite years of trailers and promotional material, Rockstar has kept significant portions of “GTA VI” under wraps.

The full voice cast has not been revealed, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. Actor Stephen Root has confirmed to The Associated Press that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly identified his role.
Questions also remain about the full range of characters, locations, activities and gameplay systems waiting inside Leonida.
Associated Press journalists Charlotte Graham-McLay in Wellington, New Zealand, and Tong-hyung Kim in Seoul contributed to this report.

title: Iran strikes 3 tankers as it shows off missile launchers, and other Mideast news
summary: Iran has unveiled a new missile launcher at an underground facility
story: Iran has unveiled a new missile launcher at an underground facility
Iran unveiled a new missile launcher at an underground facility, touting what it says is its continued capability to strike if the war with the United States and Israel accelerates once more.
Meanwhile, in the Gaza Strip, an Israeli airstrike hit a truck carrying food, killing three men, the head of Shifa Hospital said. The Israeli military said that it struck Islamic Jihad militants.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here.

Iranian state television aired footage from an underground missile facility where the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard unveiled a new launcher that it said was capable of firing two liquid-fueled missiles.

The launchers appear to be an advance over a dual launcher that Iran previously used that fired two solid-fuel missiles at a time. Liquid fuel is more efficient and gives operators some capability to adjust the missiles’ speed and trajectory.
The location of the missile site wasn't revealed, but the broadcast aimed to tout Iran’s missile capabilities and counter statements from Washington that the U.S. has destroyed the missile program.
During the unveiling of the launchers, Brig. Gen. Seyyed Majid Mousavi, commander of the Guard’s Aerospace Force, said that Iran’s “capabilities have expanded significantly."

Separately, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Saturday that Tehran remained in contact with mediators from Qatar who visited Iran on Friday to explore “whether another opportunity can be given to diplomacy.”
At least three oil tankers were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday in what appeared to be the latest Iranian strikes on shipping through the strategic chokepoint.

The U.K. military’s maritime security center said two tankers were struck separately by projectiles early Saturday while exiting the Persian Gulf through the strait. There were no reports of casualties, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center reported.
There was no immediate comment from Iran on the center’s report.

The Iranian navy said in a statement carried on state media that a tanker hit a naval mine east of the strait and caught fire. State media also said that the military carried out its most “intense and varied” operations yet in the strait overnight to stop vessels.

Iranian forces have been attacking shipping through the strait in a campaign aimed at hiking global energy prices to pressure the United States, which has imposed a crippling blockade on Iranian ports.
An Israeli strike hit a truck carrying food in Gaza City’s Tel al-Hawa district on Saturday, killing three men, Mohamed Abu Selmiya, the director of Shifa Hospital, told The Associated Press.

Videos circulating online showed a pickup truck reduced to twisted metal with boxes of cooked rice torn open in the back. It wasn't immediately known where the food was being taken or whether it was connected to an aid organization. Most of Gaza's more than 2 million people are homeless and dependent on food distributions by the United Nations and other aid groups.

The Israeli military said later Saturday that it had struck Islamic Jihad militants who were traveling in a vehicle used to transport food and logistical supplies to fellow militants. The vehicle wasn't visibly marked as belonging to a humanitarian aid organization, the military said.

One of the men had been fired from such an organization after Israel's military notified it of his militant role, a military official said on condition of anonymity in line with military regulations. The men were targeted because they had “advanced attacks” against Israel's military and civilians in recent weeks, the military added.

Since a ceasefire deal with Hamas came into effect in October 2025, Israeli strikes have killed more than 1,650 people, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn't distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll, but says women and children make up around half the dead.

In a Saturday address to mark Lebanon's independence day, President Joseph Aoun said that the country faced two “fundamental obstacles”: Israel’s occupation and “foreign interference in our affairs — specifically by certain influential elements within the Iranian regime.”
Aoun said that Israel should withdraw from Lebanon, but defended the two countries’ first direct talks in decades, saying “diplomacy is not surrender.”

He said: “The era of weapons outside state control has come to an end” — a reference to Iran-backed Hezbollah militants, who began firing on Israel right after the start of the Iran war. The group has refused to hand over its weapons while Israel is occupying parts of southern Lebanon.
Sally Abou AlJoud reported from Beirut, and Wafaa Shurafa from Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip.

title: (Not) up in the air: Travelers' trepidations spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups abound
summary: At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing— crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses
story: At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing— crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses

NEW YORK -- At this point, it's practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses.

And for 2026's busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there's another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a nationwide ground stop last week — the first since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation.

The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She's pretty sure she's not the only one.

“For a lot of people, especially as they’re paying attention and because it’s in the news where they’re tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we’re having ... I think more and more people are now getting anxious,” said Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel.
It's an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days' tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it's a familiar one, too.

Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it's one they're likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic.
But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.

“For the most part, air travel still remains strong,” said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People “might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it.”

In some ways, the country's aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute.

“Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy ... and frankly, it is taken for granted,” said Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum.

“You've got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places,” he said. “But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It’s a commodity. There's nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that’s a clear sign of its success — that you’re in a bus.”

At this point, as a traveler, Michelle Jolene says she's used to the delays, the cancellations, the rerouting of flights. So while she's not thrilled at the idea of adding infrastructure issues to the list of potential problems, she's not rattled by it.
“I literally haven’t had a normal flight in so long and I fly a lot. So I’m like, just, okay, here’s another thing,” said Jolene, who lives in Miami.
She did think it would make some people reluctant to get on a plane, “the people who fly maybe once a year for their holiday.”

And instead of flying this year, they’ll drive to "Disney or the beaches in North Carolina or something," she said. “But those of us who have to fly to work and to live our lives, there’s just not much choice. What are you going to do?”
If anything, a more disruptive aspect to flying than the potential for delays might be the cost — another anxiety trigger for many that can't just be stuffed into the overhead compartment.

Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas travel are up 31% and 23% from the same time last year, according to estimates from the travel-booking company Hopper. For travelers, that means dealing with the highest holiday airfares in a decade.
Some of increases to fares and fees are linked to higher jet fuel costs tied to the war in Iran. In September, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index.
It led Jolene, 50, to find a creative way to get her daughter's flight home to Miami for Thanksgiving: toilet paper.

She saw a promotion on American Airlines’ online shopping portal earlier this year that awarded 10 miles for every dollar spent. She bought 10 boxes of 48 rolls, earning her about 8,500 miles — which was enough to cover the entire flight from Washington, D.C., where her daughter attends college.
The upfront cost was worth it, she said, because it’s a product she would have bought anyway and one that doesn’t go bad. She's keeping the rolls in her garage
“The funny part," she said, “is we have to buy toilet paper anyway.”
AP Airlines and Travel Writer Rio Yamat in Las Vegas contributed to this story.

title: Walmart raises its outlook for the year for the 3rd time after a solid quarter
summary: Walmart reported solid sales for the fiscal quarter as the discounter continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices
story: Walmart reported solid sales for the fiscal quarter as the discounter continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices

NEW YORK -- Walmart reported solid third quarter sales gains as the retailer continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum that are seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices.

The company topped Wall Street’s profit and sales projections, and it raised its annual guidance for the third time this year, but the outlook released Thursday was more conservative than industry analysts had expected.

Comparable sales, which include digital channels and stores, rose 2.9%. That is better than last quarter's 2.6% increase, when Walmart reported its weakest comparable sales growth in six years. But it's still a slowdown from the 4.5% growth registered during the same period last year.

Still, slowing comparable sales, particularly in Walmart stores, also reflect a strategic shift toward e-commerce, Walmart+ memberships and advertising. Global e-commerce sales rose 17%, while U.S. e-commerce sales increased 23% during the latest quarter, the company said.

Walmart said that more than 80% of U.S. e-commerce orders are being fulfilled from stores, including its third party marketplace orders. Stores enabled faster delivery speeds on a wide range of assortments, the retailer said.
Shares rose nearly 1% before the opening bell Thursday.

“We delivered strong results, growing our core business and gaining market share,” Walmart's CEO John Furner said in prepared remarks. “The strength of our omnichannel model gives us room to do even more.”

Walmart is considered a barometer of consumer spending given its vast customer base. More than 150 million customers use its website or visit its stores every week, according to Walmart. Analysts look to the massive retailer for clues about what to expect from the industry as a whole during the critical holiday shopping season.

Consumers in the U.S. have remained resilient in the face of painful inflation, but they have also grown more selective about what they buy. Many rely on retailers like Walmart as a one-stop shop for low-priced household goods, groceries and pharmaceuticals.

The latest U.S. retail sales data revealed that shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as Americans pulled back on a variety of purchases, from cars, clothing and furniture and even their own hobbies.
Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a 0.8% gain in September, according to Commerce Department data released this week.
Walmart has been hammering its low price message while refining its store label fashion brands like Scoop and Free Assembly.

Walmart is also trying to increase subscriptions to its shipping programs. During the third quarter, Walmart launched a combined Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus annual membership bundle for $120 per year. The package saves shoppers nearly $100 compared to buying both plans separately, it said.

Walmart, based in Bentonville, Arkansas, has begun to capture a larger share of wealthier consumers. The biggest gains in market share for Walmart have been coming from households with annual incomes over $100,000, the retailer has said.

Walmart’s quarterly net income was $4.94 billion, or 62 cents per share, in the three-month period ended Oct. 31. Adjusted per-share results were 65 cents, higher than the 64 cents Wall Street had expected, according to FactSet. In the year-ago quarter, the company earned $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share.
Sales rose 5.2% to $188.8 billion in the latest quarter. Analysts were predicting $187.38 billion, according to FactSet.

The company said that comparable sales were driven by groceries and general merchandise categories like furniture and toys. But the figure was once again hit by federal legislation that requires pharmacies to dispense some high-cost Medicare drugs at capped prices, the retailer said.

For the full year, Walmart now projects earnings per share to be in the range of $2.84 to $2.89, up from the prior guidance of $2.80 to $2.87. Sales should be up anywhere from 4.9% to 5.2%, up from the prior forecast of 4% to 5%. That would mean a forecast for sales in the range of $748.12 billion to $750.25 billion, according to FactSet.
Analysts expected $2.89 per share and sales of $752.68 billion for the year, according to FactSet.

title: Suspects charged in brazen train heist ring that netted $22 million in cargo from major retailers
summary: Authorities have charged more than a dozen people for allegedly orchestrating a massive train heist operation
story: Authorities have charged more than a dozen people for allegedly orchestrating a massive train heist operation

LOS ANGELES -- More than a dozen people were charged Thursday with allegedly orchestrating a massive train heist operation to steal over $22 million in cargo — from popular shoes to power tools — from major retailers.

A federal indictment unsealed on Thursday paints a picture of an organized group that targeted more than three dozen trains carrying Nike sneakers, Crocs footwear, power tools and other consumer goods that were imported into the United States through Los Angeles and Long Beach, which are home to the busiest ports in the country.

Trains that shuttle goods to stores and customers around the country have become a prominent target for large-scale theft in recent years, especially at large ports in the U.S. that receive hundreds of millions of dollars of shipments every day. The relatively low-tech robberies have demanded attention from the world's largest retailers, including the likes of Amazon.

The men would disable the trains at a planned location by busting the brakes, the indictment alleged, at which point the goods would be offloaded onto trucks. The goods were then peddled to an unnamed company that would resell the stolen merchandise for profit.
“The scale of the theft is staggering,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli, promising to prosecute any future efforts to steal the merchandise.

In group chats, the men shared numerous photos and videos of themselves busting into the hulking train cars, and posing with wads of cash and stolen merchandise. They also shared AI photos of themselves captioned “Los Trenes,” which means the trains in Spanish, beneath glamorized photos of men throwing boxes of shoes off trains into nearby cars while police helicopters descended overhead.
The 13 men were indicted for conspiracy and theft of interstate railroad cargo. Two were also charged with violence against railroad carriers.
If convicted, the men could face anywhere from five to 20 years in federal prison.

title: Trump administration auctions deep-sea mining leases near American Samoa in first sale of its kind
summary: The Trump administration has auctioned deep-sea mining leases for millions of acres of the federal seafloor near American Samoa
story: The Trump administration has auctioned deep-sea mining leases for millions of acres of the federal seafloor near American Samoa
The Trump administration on Thursday auctioned deep-sea mining leases to millions of acres of the federal seafloor near American Samoa, giving a controversial industry a foothold in U.S. waters.

The two 20-year leases are the first of their kind in the U.S., following President Donald Trump’s directive last year to leverage deep-ocean minerals to counter growing competition for resources from China. The leases are already the source of several legal challenges.

The two lease areas each sold for the minimum bid amount of $3 million to deep-sea mining startup Wetstone U.S. Ventures, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. While there were two bidders at the auction, only Wetstone placed bids. Wetstone did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press.

The leases grant the company the ability to begin initial surveys of the seafloor to explore for minerals and prepare their testing or mining plans. It has the exclusive right to mine those areas commercially if approved in further environmental reviews.

The auction moved forward despite passionate opposition from locals in the territory and three lawsuits seeking to halt the sales. The auction was held at the Ventura County Fire Department Headquarters in Southern California, where a few dozen protesters gathered outside.
“We had hoped it would never come to this,” Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, an American Samoa resident who has fought the auction for more than a year, said in a statement Thursday.

Globally, deep-sea mining is still at an experimental stage. A handful of other countries have allowed companies to start exploring their waters for deep-sea minerals, but no company has started commercial operations. The U.S. has never issued a lease for deep-sea minerals beyond a short-lived mining effort in California waters more than 60 years ago.

The federal interest in seafloor minerals stems from an April 2025 executive order, when the president directed his administration to search for and responsibly develop critical minerals on the ocean floor, both within and beyond U.S. borders. The Marine Minerals Administration is considering further auctions of the seabed near the Northern Mariana Islands, Virginia and Alaska, while the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is reviewing permit applications from companies that seek to mine in international waters.

It’s unclear if the leases will withstand legal challenge. On Monday, a court ordered the National Marine Fisheries Service to more thoroughly assess the impacts the mining activities could have on endangered species, saying the agency's “cramped, expedited, informal” review violated the Endangered Species Act.

The Marine Minerals Administration said in a statement that it had addressed the court's opinion by starting to consult with the fisheries service on another environmental assessment. But it did not cancel or delay the auction.

David Henkin, deputy managing attorney at the environmental law group Earthjustice, said the ruling made Thursday's auction unlawful. In order to issue the notice of sale, the government needed to comply with the Endangered Species Act, he said.

"We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided,” Earthjustice attorney Chris Eaton said in a statement. Earthjustice is representing Fa’asao Amerika Samoa, a group dedicated to safeguarding the territory’s culture, and the Conservation Council of Hawaii in the suit.

Another lawsuit filed Wednesday by the Natural Resources Defense Council and Finafinau, an environmental group founded by Suluai-Mahuka, similarly argues the environmental review process was rushed and is asking the court to strike down the leases.
A third lawsuit, brought by a council of local chiefs in American Samoa, the Faleula o le Manu’atele, is challenging the federal government’s authority to auction the waters near their islands.

Tony Romeo, head of the deep-sea mining startup Eco Minerals, which did not participate in the auction, said any company going into deep-sea mining needs to be prepared for pushback from environmental groups.
“If they can halt it through legal action, they will,” he said. “We’ll see how it ultimately plays out.”
Erik Milito, president of the National Ocean Industries Association, said in a statement that he expects industry interest and investment to grow in the coming years.
“Decades of environmental research and extensive assessments have helped lay the groundwork for responsible ocean mineral development," he said.

title: Japan's PM Takaichi says Russia and Japan will keep talking as ties remain chilled
summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi says that she met with Russian President Vladimir Putin for more than 30 minutes in the first such encounter between the two countries’ leaders in seven years
story: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi says that she met with Russian President Vladimir Putin for more than 30 minutes in the first such encounter between the two countries’ leaders in seven years

SHENZHEN, China -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on Thursday that she and Russian President Vladimir Putin held talks and agreed to keep communicating in the first such encounter between the two countries’ leaders in seven years.

Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, she said she raised the issue of Moscow’s treatment of Japanese businesses in Russia and urged Putin to release a Japanese journalist detained for alleged spying during their meeting late Wednesday in Shenzhen, China.
“We reached an agreement to maintain communication at various levels, including direct contact between the president and myself,” Takaichi said.
Japan's ties with Russia have long been strained by a territorial dispute dating back decades.

Japan lodged a protest with Russia in October over the arrest of a Japanese journalist working for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper on suspicion of spying, demanding that Moscow provide an explanation, consular access and humane treatment.

Moscow recently seized control of some local subsidiaries of Japan Tobacco, the largest cigarette maker in Russia, and the company reported it expects a 724 billion yen ($4.5 billion) loss for this year due to the takeover.

Earlier, Japan Tobacco had forecast a 662 billion yen profit for the financial year ending Dec. 31. The company said it has not given up legal ownership of the Russia-based subsidiaries or withdrawn from operating in Russia.

Tensions rose in August after Putin visited Iturup, one of four Russian-controlled islands off Japan’s northern coast that Tokyo also claims. Earlier this month, Tokyo protested after two Russian aircraft briefly violated Japanese airspace off southwestern Japan.

The last bilateral in-person talks between Japanese and Russian leaders were held between then-Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and Putin in September 2019, during the Eastern Economic Forum in the Russian city of Vladivostok.

Putin is attending the annual APEC summit for the first time in nine years. He, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump held a summit meeting Thursday after the APEC gathering, an event that seems to underscore Japan's diminished role as a global power.
Takaichi herself was given a very minimal reception on her arrival in Shenzhen, provoking speculation over a deliberate snub by her hosts.
When asked, Takaichi said she did not believe the summit between Xi, Trump and Putin would undermine Japan’s interests.

“We have been maintaining close communication with the United States and other allies while carefully monitoring the impact on the international situation and we will continue to respond appropriately,” Takaichi said. "We do not believe that Japan’s interests will be compromised.”
She did not elaborate on efforts to repair damage to Japan’s ties with China following remarks she made nearly a year ago about Taiwan.
“China is an important neighbor. Given the various issues and challenges that exist between Japan and China, I believe it is essential to engage in dialogue and maintain communication," she said.
Yamaguchi reported from Tokyo. Associated Press journalist Haruka Nuga in Tokyo contributed to this report.

title: UN climate talks in Turkey risk being ‘worst COP ever’ as fossil fuels go unmentioned
summary: Negotiators are still seeking concrete commitments for nations to transition away from fossil fuels, as this year's U.N. climate summit reaches its final day
story: Negotiators are still seeking concrete commitments for nations to transition away from fossil fuels, as this year's U.N. climate summit reaches its final day

ANTALYA, Turkey -- This year's U.N. climate talks are wrapping up in Turkey, with negotiators still debating how to address global warming and experts warning that only slashing fossil fuels can avert its most catastrophic effects.
Activists and country leaders were in an uproar Friday, the last scheduled day of the two-week summit known as COP31, after the term “fossil fuels” was left out of the final agreement’s draft.
Climate summits often end with a final text, meant to address how the world will deal with climate change. Such agreements — often adopted by nearly 200 nations — are still voluntary and non-binding.
Negotiators, who pulled an all-nighter from Thursday into Friday, said they expect COP31 to go into overtime on Saturday.

Past COPs have failed to agree on how to transition away from fossil fuels — coal, oil and gas — that warm the planet, heat the oceans and worsen air quality. Climate change also intensified several of this year's disasters, like Europe’s deadly heat waves and Nepal’s devastating flooding.
If phasing out fossil fuels don’t make it into the final agreement, this year’s summit runs the risk of being the “worst COP ever,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa.

In a rare move, Panama vowed to “formally object” if the final agreement doesn’t add climate finance, cap oil production, and acknowledge failing goals, among other demands. The country's Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks are being held hostage by a “petroleum mafia” and need to be reformed.
“The COPs have become an exercise in hypocrisy and futility,” he said. “What we have here is a contest to see who speaks the most, who blows the most hot air.”

In the lead up to COP31, the United Nations announced the world is dangerously close to missing its decades-old goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

“There is nothing on the table that protects people, or addresses the priorities of the Global South,” said Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International, at a Friday event, where attendees chanted and held signs that read “SHAME!”
One of the main deals on the table at COP31 is an electrification goal to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035.

But the final draft doesn't spell out that this should be reached with renewable energy sources, like solar and wind — leaving the door open for fossil fuel power plants to be counted as part of an electrification push.

“At a time when the climate crisis demands decisive action, weakening commitments on fossil fuel phase-out risks undermining progress,” said Ghiwa Nakat, executive director of Greenpeace in the Middle East and North Africa.
The U.N. has hosted climate talks for more than 30 years but it was only in 2021 during COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, that nations first acknowledged fossil fuels contribute to climate change.
Two years later during COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, countries explicitly called for a transition away from fossil fuels for the first time.
Turkey and Australia, co-hosts of COP31, are being roundly criticized for removing fossil fuels from the final text's draft.

“We are not here to discuss decisions at previous COPs,” said Turkey's Minister of Environment Murat Kurum, who is overseeing the summit held in the Turkish resort town of Antalya. The electrification push implies a transition away from fossil fuels, he said.

“Removing those words from a document will not remove the pollution from the atmosphere," said Adow of Power Shift Africa. “It simply exposes how far these negotiations have become detached from what is needed outside this conference center.”

Leaders from countries ravaged by climate change — mostly poorer, vulnerable nations that don't emit a lot of greenhouse gases — have said that rich countries are not providing previously agreed upon funds to deal with climate change.
They said that U.N. funds for adapting to climate risks, dealing with climate impacts and funds for clean energy infrastructure don’t match what the U.N. has said these countries need.

The draft agreement states the need to triple the amount of money for countries adapting to climate impacts, but it doesn’t specify how much. One of the draft's previous versions stated at least $120 billion would be needed annually.
Many of the world's most polluting nations did not participate directly at this year's talks, including the United States, the world’s largest economy and a major emitter.
It's richer nations, like the U.S., that vulnerable countries want funding from — and it's hard to ask for funds without American officials in the room.
Efforts to slow global warming have essentially stalled for the past five years, according to a recent report by the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker.

“Disappointment is rife," said Iskander Erzini Vernoit, an adviser to African negotiators in Turkey. Next year’s climate summit is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.
“Hope is not lost, but absent a course correction, we are headed toward a low-ambition set of outcomes at COP31,” he said.
Delgado reported from Bangkok, Arasu from Bengaluru, India, and Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan. Associated Press writer Tammy Webber contributed to this report from Fenton, Michigan.

title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
summary: A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year
story: A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year

NEW YORK -- A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.
The benchmark S&P 500 index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.

The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.

Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 8.5%.
The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.

AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.

The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.

“The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.”

Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.2%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.
Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.

Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 14% lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 30%.

The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 8.5% to $88.91, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.

Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.

Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.
Outside of tech, several companies managed to gain ground despite strong downward pressure on the market. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.
While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.

The University of Michigan’s latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists’ expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.

Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.
AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.
An earlier version of this story incorrectly reported the closing price and percentage change for Anthropic shares.

title: A rare EU-UK summit as Andy Burnham seeks to mend Brexit damage
summary: A decade after Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences and possibly pave a way to get back together
story: A decade after Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences and possibly pave a way to get back together

BRUSSELS -- A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together.

Burnham is scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners.

Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.
“The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained,” he said this week.

Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.

Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be “a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security.”

The two sides are expected to sign a trade deal for food and drink, an agreement on emissions trading and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU. Burnham says the deals could add a modest 0.4% to Britain’s economy.

The war in Ukraine, and the U.K.’s military strength, are drawing the two back together, and the summit provides the EU with an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.

“Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential,” Costa said ahead of the meeting. “By deepening our cooperation, we can strengthen our ability to address the challenges of our time, strengthen our resilience and promote stability in Europe and beyond.”

Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want real clarity about the country’s intentions.

Ireland’s ambassador in London, Sonja Hyland, said that when Britain voted for Brexit, “there was a lack of clarity as to exactly what that meant.” If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must “make a clear decision as to what it wants.”
Lawless reported from London.

title: Jayden Daniels rallies Commanders in final seconds to set up winning kick in 22-20 win over Bengals
summary: Jayden Daniels connected with rookie Antonio Williams on two long pass plays, moving the Commanders 64 yards in 34 seconds to set up Drew Stevens’ 26-yard field goal as time expired, and the Washington Commanders stunned Joe Burrow and the Cincinnati B...
story: Jayden Daniels connected with rookie Antonio Williams on two long pass plays, moving the Commanders 64 yards in 34 seconds to set up Drew Stevens’ 26-yard field goal as time expired, and the Washington Commanders stunned Joe Burrow and the Cincinnati B...
LANDOVER, Md. -- Jayden Daniels and the Commanders had scored on five consecutive drives, all of them covering 50 yards or more. But their last possession was the most daunting.

After the Cincinnati Bengals took a one-point lead on a 56-yard field goal by Evan McPherson, Washington took over at its 28-yard line with 39 seconds left and no timeouts. The Commanders' defense had kept them in the game, but now it was up to Daniels.

The third-year quarterback made two pinpoint throws to rookie Antonio Williams, moving the Commanders 64 yards in 34 seconds to set up Drew Stevens’ 26-yard field goal as time expired, and Washington stunned Joe Burrow and the Bengals 22-20 on Monday night.

“Win the game, do whatever it takes to win the game,” Daniels said. “I personally live for those moments. High-pressure situations. Being able to have the chance, back against the wall, 40-something seconds. ... It just means a lot.”

Daniels hit Williams over the middle for 22 yards, spiked the ball, then found him again for a 42-yard catch-and-run to the Cincinnati 8. The QB spiked it with 5 seconds left and Stevens converted his fifth field goal of the night, all in the second half.

Daniels finished with 283 yards passing and led the team with 55 yards rushing, and Williams had nine catches for 122 yards as Washington (4-5-1) remained in the NFC East race, two games behind the division-leading New York Giants.

The Commanders became the first NFL team in at least 30 years to end a game with six consecutive scoring drives that each covered more than 50 yards, according to OptaSTATS. Only one of them concluded with a touchdown.
“This was a full team win,” coach Dan Quinn said.

Burrow threw for 300 yards and two touchdowns for AFC North-leading Cincinnati (7-3), but the Commanders largely held in check a Bengals team that had won five straight, scoring 31 points or more each time. Washington's defense forced Burrow to settle for checkdowns all night and mostly prevented big plays from the dangerous receiving duo of Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins.
“They did their normal — we just didn’t pick it up and execute it the right way,” Chase said.
Chase and Higgins combined for just seven catches for 74 yards.
“This is an easy team to play zone and play it safe,” Quinn said. “If you do that, they're likely to rip you. It's hard to challenge, but in my opinion, that was what was best for us.”

Quinn made another questionable late-game decision when he sent Stevens out on fourth-and-1 to kick a 41-yard field goal with 2:26 left for a 19-17 lead. That left plenty of time for Burrow, who found Mike Gesicki for a 32-yard completion to move the Bengals into field goal range.
The Commanders' defense came through again with a sack to push the Bengals back, and McPherson made the long kick with 46 seconds left. As it turned out, that was too much time.
Chase said the toughest part about Cincinnati's winning streak ending was “losing when you know you're better.”

The game got off to a slow start in unexpected rainy conditions, but opened up in the second half as the teams traded scores throughout the third quarter. Burrow's 4-yard touchdown pass to Colbie Young put the Bengals ahead 17-10, and the Commanders rallied with three field goals by Stevens.

“At some point defenses are going to make plays too,” Gesicki said. “I think everybody was so accustomed to the Bengals scoring 30-plus and blah blah blah, everybody wants to talk about it. Listen, it’s the National Football League. They are going to make plays and stuff’s going to happen.”

There was an unexpected stoppage early in the third when the stadium lights went out with the Commanders in the red zone. After a delay that lasted about four minutes, Stevens converted from 36 yards to tie the game at 10-all.
The Bengals had already missed some key opportunities by then.

“I just thought we didn’t start very well,” coach Zac Taylor said. “They found some momentum early in the game and they came after us and we didn’t really do a great job providing the answers until the third, fourth drive.”

Washington held Cincinnati to three points on its first four possessions before Higgins' 31-yard touchdown catch that made it 10-0. Jacory Croskey-Merritt, activated off injured reserve earlier Monday, scored on a 1-yard run for the Commanders with 12 seconds left before halftime.
Bengals: Safety Bryan Cook suffered a right ankle injury but returned to the game.
Bengals: Host the New Orleans Saints on Sunday.
Commanders: Visit the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday.

title: Blackhawks center Connor Bedard has right shoulder surgery
summary: Chicago Blackhawks captain Connor Bedard had right shoulder surgery
story: Chicago Blackhawks captain Connor Bedard had right shoulder surgery
CHICAGO -- Chicago Blackhawks captain Connor Bedard had right shoulder surgery on Monday.

Team physician Michael Terry said Bedard is expected “to make a full recovery in an approximate timeline of four months.” Terry offered the same timeline when Bedard had surgery on his left shoulder July 8, and the center missed the first six games of the season before playing on Oct. 13 against Pittsburgh.
Bedard also hurt his right shoulder on a draw during a 3-2 loss at St. Louis on Dec. 12 last season. He missed 12 games before returning on Jan. 9.

The 21-year-old Bedard led the rebuilding Blackhawks with 45 assists and 75 points last season. The No. 1 pick in the 2023 draft became the second-youngest captain in the history of the Original Six franchise in September.

title: Even without big stats, Miami believes Mensah's game against Virginia Tech was his finest hour
summary: Those looking at stat sheets might think Miami quarterback Darian Mensah played the worst game of his season against Virginia Tech last weekend
story: Those looking at stat sheets might think Miami quarterback Darian Mensah played the worst game of his season against Virginia Tech last weekend
CORAL GABLES, Fla. -- Those looking at stat sheets might think Miami quarterback Darian Mensah played the worst game of his season against Virginia Tech last weekend.
The Hurricanes would say otherwise. They believe it was Mensah's finest hour.

Mensah faced constant pressure in two forms all night — from the Hokies' defense and from a scoreboard where Miami was losing for much of the game — and never flinched. He engineered a second half where Miami had the ball for 23 of the 30 minutes, converted seven of nine third downs and did just enough to beat the Hokies 28-20.
Was there a Heisman Trophy-sealing highlight? No.
Did it show why he should be a Heisman candidate? Miami thinks so.

“Stats don’t tell the whole story most of the time,” Miami offensive coordinator Shannon Dawson said. “That was one of the best performances I’ve seen (from) him this year, probably that I’ve had a quarterback do in a while based on how I view quarterback play.”
Keep in mind, Dawson said that after a game where Mensah's numbers were far from stellar for No. 4 Miami (10-1, 8-0 Atlantic Coast Conference, No. 7 CFP entering Tuesday night's rankings update).

Mensah — still playing without his top weapon, with wide receiver Malachi Toney sidelined after surgery to repair a high ankle sprain — finished the game against the Hokies with no touchdown passes, the first time this season that he hasn't thrown at least one. He had two interceptions, a season high. He averaged 6.5 yards per pass attempt, down 33% from his norm through the season's first 10 games.

But Miami won, on a night where little went right. And while Mark Fletcher Jr.'s three touchdown runs and Jake Weinberg's school-record 59-yard field goal commanded headlines — rightly so — the Hurricanes knew it was Mensah keeping drives alive that got them across the finish line.

“He gets better and better with each game and Saturday is no different,” Miami coach Mario Cristobal said. "He continues to get better and better and in the face of any situation — pressure, covered, uncovered, free hitter, have to improvise, have to change a play at the line of scrimmage with his feet — he just finds a way.
“As special as it gets, and I completely think that he’s just getting started.”

Mensah's first throw of the night was intercepted; it hit running back Javian Mallory in the hands, then ricocheted skyward for an easy pick. There was a point where Virginia Tech had scored as many touchdowns (two) as Miami had run offensive plays. It was 14-0 before Mensah and the offense did anything worth noting.
Score from that point: Miami 28, Virginia Tech 6. Yards in that span: Miami 394, Virginia Tech 118. Mensah was the calm in the eye of the storm, and it showed.

“If stuff doesn't go our way, we just try to go out there and execute the next play,” Mensah said. “It's always about the next play. I think our mindset as an offense is pretty elite. We just respond.”

Mensah — who leads the nation in completion percentage, is third nationally in touchdown passes and fourth nationally in yards entering this weekend — will get a chance on Dec. 5 to become the fifth quarterback in ACC history to win multiple conference championship games when the Hurricanes play Wake Forest in Charlotte, North Carolina for the league title. Mensah led Duke to that crown last season.

First, though, is Saturday's regular season finale at home against Boston College. Mensah insists all focus is on that, not the title matchup. And Dawson said it was that sort of thinking from Mensah — being focused on the next play, not anything else or any individual accolades — that got the Hurricanes over the top against the Hokies.

“I don’t know how many times in my career we would’ve won that game,” Dawson said. “He kind of willed us to win it. I think it was at least the grittiest performance I’ve seen — we were nine of 15 on third down and if it isn’t for him, we’re probably three of 15. ... To be quite honest, it was a damn good performance by a damn tough kid.”
