title: MLB drops player contract escrow provision that was in salary cap proposal
summary: Major League Baseball dropped its demand for an escrow provision that was part of its salary cap proposal, instead saying Tuesday that an overage or underpayment under a 50-50 revenue split would be accounted for in future seasons
story: Major League Baseball dropped its demand for an escrow provision that was part of its salary cap proposal, instead saying Tuesday that an overage or underpayment under a 50-50 revenue split would be accounted for in future seasons

NEW YORK -- Major League Baseball dropped its demand for an escrow provision that was part of its salary cap proposal, instead saying Tuesday that an overage or underpayment under a 50-50 revenue split would be accounted for in future seasons.

When MLB made its cap proposal, it included a provision used by other leagues in which a slice of an individual player's salary would be withheld and clawed back if the percentage of revenue going to players in a year winds up going over the percentage specified for compensation. The players' association objected, saying that mechanism would gut player contract guarantee provisions.

“For months, union leadership has attacked the escrow provision used in other sports and mischaracterized the issue as the end of guaranteed contracts," baseball spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "MLB took another step today by withdrawing our escrow proposal, removing any doubt that every single guaranteed player contract will remain fully guaranteed in the new salary cap and floor system.”

MLB said any underpayment or overpayment to players would be incorporated into future cap and floor calculations and that MLB would have the ability to have up to two years to account for a revenue lag.

“Instead of holding back player money each year, MLB’s new proposal is to take that same amount of money out of players’ pockets in the following year,” union head Bruce Meyer said in a statement. “It’s a different way of achieving the same objective of the salary cap — to reduce and suppress player salaries and freedom of movement. This is yet another example of how MLB’s salary cap proposal pits player against player, past, present and future.”

In another proposal Tuesday, players asked that money they donate to team charities be deducted from their salary for the purpose of calculating team luxury tax payrolls and for the new competitive integrity tax the union proposed be assessed to low-spending clubs.

title: Kuemper makes 29 saves as Kings beat Canadiens 2-1; Larkin picks up an assist in Montreal debut
summary: Darcy Kuemper stopped 29 shots as the Los Angeles Kings spoiled Dylan Larkin’s debut with the Montreal Canadiens with a 2-1 victory Monday night
story: Darcy Kuemper stopped 29 shots as the Los Angeles Kings spoiled Dylan Larkin’s debut with the Montreal Canadiens with a 2-1 victory Monday night
MONTREAL -- Darcy Kuemper stopped 29 shots as the Los Angeles Kings spoiled Dylan Larkin’s debut with the Montreal Canadiens with a 2-1 victory Monday night.
Alex Laferriere and Trevor Moore scored as Los Angeles (8-12-2) won for the third time in four games.
Alex Newhook scored for Montreal (14-7-4), which lost its second consecutive game in regulation. Jakub Dobes made 20 saves.

Larkin picked up an assist some 24 hours after Montreal acquired the disgruntled 30-year-old center from the Detroit Red Wings in a blockbuster deal. Larkin hadn’t played since Oct. 26, three days before he decided to sit out until he was traded. He forfeited more than $1 million in salary while the Red Wings suspended him without pay.
Adrian Kempe’s hooking penalty with 59.1 seconds remaining in the game put the Canadiens on the power play, but Montreal failed to capitalize.
Six weeks after Canadiens fans serenaded the former Red Wings captain with chants of “We want Larkin!,” the crowd broke out into “We got Larkin!” after puck drop at the Bell Centre.

Montreal carried that energy through the opening 10 minutes, but Laferriere quieted the building when he scored at 14:43 in the first. The Kings forward took a puck off the end wall and beat Dobes with a between-the-legs goal.

Newhook tied the game at 7:28 in the second when his shot hit Kuemper, bounced upward and crossed the goal line. Larkin earned an assist after the puck glanced off his skate while laying a hit to create a turnover.

Moore restored the Kings’ lead at 14:57, scoring after Canadiens defensemen Adam Engstrom and Arber Xhekaj let up, thinking the other would retrieve the puck. Instead, Moore skated into Montreal’s zone, controlled the puck and fired a shot past Dobes.

Montreal’s bench was sharp with coach’s challenges, overturning two goals: one for offside when Moore appeared to score in the first period, and another from Mats Zuccarello in the second for goalie interference.
Los Angeles captain Drew Doughty became just the second player to skate in 1,300 games with the franchise, joining longtime teammate Anze Kopitar (1,521).

story: Ben Roethlisberger and Rob Gronkowski are among the first-time eligible players who have advanced in the voting process for the Pro Football Hall of Fame Class of 2027
Ben Roethlisberger and Rob Gronkowski are among the first-time eligible players who have advanced in the voting process for the Pro Football Hall of Fame Class of 2027.
Adrian Peterson, Antonio Brown and Richard Sherman also advanced in their first year of eligibility.
A total of 52 players have reached this stage, including Ken Anderson and Eli Manning. The Hall of Fame selection committee will reduce the list to 25 candidates in two weeks.

Anderson was a four-time Pro Bowl pick and the 1981 AP NFL MVP in a 16-year career with the Cincinnati Bengals that ended in 1986. He led the Bengals to one AFC championship.

title: Myles Garrett, Micah Parsons ready for spotlight when Rams host Packers on Thanksgiving Eve
summary: Myles Garrett and Micah Parsons are two of the best pass rushers of their generation
story: Myles Garrett and Micah Parsons are two of the best pass rushers of their generation

INGLEWOOD, Calif. -- Myles Garrett and Micah Parsons are two of the best pass rushers of their generation, and they're set to share an NFL field for only the third time Wednesday night when the Los Angeles Rams host the Green Bay Packers.

If anybody still doubted whether Parsons plans to make his season debut at SoFi Stadium, Garrett inadvertently eased their minds when he was asked about the pregame communication between two superstars who have become friends.

“The dialogue was, ‘Hey, big bro, you got any extra tickets?’" Garrett said with a grin. "I said, ‘Yeah, I got you, man.’ I hooked him up, and I’m looking forward to him being out there and doing his thing, feeling healthy. I know he had to take some extra time, but the game is better when Micah Parsons on the field doing this thing.”
Thanksgiving Eve will mark a turning point for these players and their teams, which are both 6-4 and sitting on the outer edge of the NFC playoff bracket.

The Rams’ home fans finally will get to see Garrett play for their team for the first time, 11 games into a season that has shifted in focus from Super Bowl aspirations to mere postseason qualification.
Garrett missed seven games earlier this season while recovering from knee surgery, but Parsons hasn’t played since last Dec. 14, when his first season with Green Bay ended with a major knee injury.
While Parsons is listed as questionable by the Packers, he was activated from the physically unable to perform list Tuesday — and it's clear he's mentally ready to lead their late-season charge.

“I’m just so focused,” Parsons said. “I’m so locked in on what’s ahead of me, and I understand what this game Wednesday means to the organization ... and what it means for playoffs. And if I can be out there, I want to be out there and I’m excited for any time. We've only got seven games left, and I want to capitalize on those if I can.”

Quite appropriately for a game with this much pass rushing talent, the Rams are using this holiday spotlight to debut their Fearsome White alternate uniforms — a tribute to the team's 1960s “Fearsome Foursome” era, when it had one of the best defensive lines in NFL history.

The Rams' current line group is also formidable, with Garrett and Aaron Donald together alongside high-volume sack artist Byron Young and nose tackle Kobie Turner, who is expected to return from injury.
“When we go out there as one and play to the best of our ability, we're a very, very scary unit,” Turner said. “There will be opportunities for us.”

The Packers' offensive line appears to be ripe for disruption by Garrett and Donald: Green Bay is coming off a 30-10 loss to Minnesota in which Jordan Love was sacked eight times, the most allowed by this team since 2015.
But the Packers had won five of six before that loss, and they understand the meager margin for error in the NFC North.

“We’re definitely feeling the urgency,” Green Bay receiver Christian Watson said. “Just got to do our job and let everything else handle itself, but the urgency’s definitely there. We know what’s stake. We know the opportunity we have in front of us. We’ve just got to take care of it.”
Green Bay (6-4) at Los Angeles Rams (6-4).
When/where to watch: Wednesday, 8 p.m. EST, Netflix.
Latest odds: Rams by 2 1/2.
Against the spread: Packers 6-4; Rams 6-4.
Last week: Packers had a bye, lost to Vikings 30-10 on Nov. 15; Rams beat Cardinals 34-6.
Last meeting: Packers beat Rams 24-19 on Oct. 6, 2024, at Green Bay.
Series record: Packers lead 51-47-2.

Rams RBs Kyren Williams and Blake Corum vs Packers S Evan Williams and LB Isaiah McDuffie. Los Angeles likely must establish its running game to have any chance to thrive offensively while Puka Nacua, Davante Adams and Terrance Ferguson are all sidelined by injury. Green Bay is in the middle of the NFL pack in run defense, but Williams' stout play in the box as the Packers' leading tackler could lead a strong defensive effort.
— The Packers have won 10 of their past 11 meetings with the Rams, including each of the past five. Sean McVay is 0-5 against Matt LaFleur, his offensive coordinator in 2017.

— Despite their modest record, the Rams have outgained their opponents by an NFL-high 1,009 yards this season. That's the largest yardage differential for any team in Week 10 over the past three seasons.
— This is the only game the Packers are playing in a three-week stretch. They lost at home to Minnesota on Nov. 15 and don’t play again until a Dec. 6 trip to New Orleans.
— The Rams haven't allowed a first-quarter touchdown in 11 consecutive games going back to last season, the longest active streak in the league.

— The Packers are playing on a Wednesday in the regular season for only the second time, the first since 1938 against the Chicago Cardinals. The Rams are playing their third Wednesday game and the first since 1948.

— Green Bay has 20 takeaways, its highest total through the first 10 games of a season since 2014. The Rams have a minus-3 turnover differential with just nine interceptions and four fumble recoveries.

— Watson and Matthew Golden are the first Packers duo to have 50-plus catches for 850-plus yards apiece in the first 10 games of a season. They’re the first set of teammates to do it since Miami’s Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle in 2022.

title: Kaapo Kakko scores winning goal as Kraken beat Ducks 3-2
summary: Kaapo Kakko scored the go-ahead goal for Seattle with 2:25 left in the game, and the Seattle Kraken beat the Anaheim Ducks Monday night, 3-2
story: Kaapo Kakko scored the go-ahead goal for Seattle with 2:25 left in the game, and the Seattle Kraken beat the Anaheim Ducks Monday night, 3-2
SEATTLE -- Kaapo Kakko scored the go-ahead goal for Seattle (11-9-1) with 2:25 left in the game, and the Kraken beat the Anaheim Ducks (11-13-1) Monday night, 3-2.
Kakko’s goal was his fourth of the season, with Brandon Montour and Mackie Samoskevich each providing assists on the play.

Kraken center Ben Myers scored the first goal of the night, putting Seattle ahead 1-0 at 2:51 of the third period, but the Ducks tied it with a goal from top scorer Cutter Gauthier at 4:06 mark.

Morgan Barron also had a goal for the Jets (12-9-4). Kyle Connor picked up two assists. Stuart Skinner made 34 saves for Winnipeg, which is 8-1-1 in its past 10 games and finished a four-game homestand 2-1-1.

title: Wembanyama sits out against Kings due to back tightness, 2 days after 50-point, 19-rebound game
summary: San Antonio Spurs star Victor Wembanyama sat out Monday night’s game against the Sacramento Kings due to back tightness
story: San Antonio Spurs star Victor Wembanyama sat out Monday night’s game against the Sacramento Kings due to back tightness
SACRAMENTO, Calif. -- San Antonio Spurs star Victor Wembanyama sat out Monday night's game against the Sacramento Kings due to back tightness.
Wembanyama, coming off a 50-point, 19-rebound performance in a win over New Orleans on Saturday, was ruled out about 90 minutes before tipoff.

San Antonio was also without injured starters De’Aaron Fox (bruised shin) and Dylan Harper (hip) during a 123-107 victory. Stephon Castle had 28 points, 11 assists and eight rebounds, while Julian Champagnie made six 3-pointers and scored 22 as the Spurs (15-3) improved to 8-0 on the road and remained tied with the Los Angeles Lakers atop the Western Conference standings.

“We had some stretches last year when Vic didn’t play. Obviously, when he’s on the court it’s a whole different basketball game and we’re able to play better with him for obvious reasons,” Champagnie said. “But you know, 82 games, things happen.”
Champagnie hit four straight 3s in the second quarter to help the Spurs regain the lead and eventually pull away from the Kings (2-15).
“We've got to figure out ways to continue to be good without him on the floor, and I think tonight’s a good building block for us,” he said.
Backup center Luke Kornet got more playing time with Wembanyama sidelined and said his absence can provide a good chance for others to get into a rhythm with more minutes to spread around.
Kornet finished with 18 points and 11 rebounds.
“It’s honestly fun to have those games where everybody can kind of step in and contribute,” he said.
San Antonio coach Mitch Johnson said that even without Wembanyama on the floor, the Spurs still play their brand of basketball.

“We played a good amount of minutes last year without Victor, with a lot of the same cast we have, and time helps chemistry,” Johnson said. “We had some big puzzle pieces out, which means part of the style of play may look a little different, but we still try to uphold the brand and identity that we play with.”
Wembanyama also had five blocks and four steals in 32 minutes Saturday as San Antonio rolled past the Pelicans 114-91.

He became the first player with 50 points, five blocks and five 3-pointers since the NBA added 3s in 1979–80. He is also the first player since steals and blocks became official statistics in 1973–74 to record 50 points, 15 rebounds, four steals and five blocks in a game.

“I just want to keep stacking them up,” Wembanyama said of his historic night. “I don’t plan on doing those. They just come and we play the right way as a team. So, I just want to stack them up. Hopefully there’s many more coming.”

story: Adam Clark scored 20 points and Corey Stephenson added 18 to help Mississippi rally to a 73-63 win over No. 19 BYU in a Maui Invitational semifinal Tuesday
LAHAINA, Hawaii -- Adam Clark scored 20 points and Corey Stephenson added 18 to help Mississippi rally to a 73-63 win over No. 19 BYU in a Maui Invitational semifinal Tuesday.
The Rebels (6-0) overcame an 18-point first-half deficit with a furious second-half charge, fueled by a 21-0 run.
After shooting 11 for 31 in the first half, Ole Miss went 17 for 32 the rest of the way and held the Cougars (6-1) to just 5-for-25 shooting from the field after halftime.

BYU scored the first nine points of the game and padded its lead with runs of 13-2 and 10-0 to take a commanding 40-22 lead with 2:32 until the intermission. However, Ole Miss scored the final four points of the half, then the first 17 out of the break to storm ahead, punctuated by Ilias Kamardine 3-pointer at the 15:36 mark.
The Rebels seized the lead for good on a step-back jumper by Clark with 12 minutes remaining that put his team ahead 49-48.
Ben Henshall had 12 points and Kamardine and Santiago Trouet added 10 apiece for Ole Miss.
BYU was led by Collin Chandler, who scored 21 of his career-high 34 points in the first half.
The Cougars were plagued by a season-worst 23 turnovers, which Ole Miss parlayed into 27 points.
The Rebels had 18 steals.
BYU shot a woeful 4 for 28 from 3-point range.
BYU held a 40-26 lead at halftime, but opened the second half on a scoreless drought of 4:46.

title: Jannik Sinner undergoes 'minor' surgery on his troublesome right knee
summary: Jannik Sinner says he has undergone a “minor” operation on his bothersome right knee after it didn’t respond well enough to other treatments
story: Jannik Sinner says he has undergone a “minor” operation on his bothersome right knee after it didn’t respond well enough to other treatments
MONACO -- MONACO (AP) — Jannik Sinner has undergone a “minor” operation on his bothersome right knee after it didn't respond well enough to other treatments, the Italian tennis star said Tuesday.
Sinner hasn’t played since defending his Wimbledon title in July for his fifth Grand Slam trophy and recently lost the No. 1 ranking to Alexander Zverev.

“Over the past few months, together with my team we’ve tried everything to treat my injury without surgery,” Sinner wrote on Instagram. “After some very encouraging progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn’t respond as we’d all hoped, that’s why today I underwent a minor surgery to improve the condition of my iliotibial band. I really miss being on court and will now begin my recovery process together with my team.”
He did not say when he expects to return to the court but had already announced that he was done playing for the season.
“I have to respect the protocols at the moment because if we rush things we could have more serious problems,” Sinner said during a news conference in Milan this month.
When Sinner shut down his season last month, a statement from his management team said he “will follow a course of treatment for inflammation in his knee.”
It’s the second prolonged absence from the tennis tour in two years after Sinner accepted a three-month ban in a settlement with the World Anti-Doping Agency for a doping case in 2025.
The Australian Open, the first Grand Slam of 2027, starts Jan. 17. It could mark the second straight Grand Slam that Sinner sits out after also missing the U.S. Open.
The French Open, the year's second Slam, starts in late May.

title: Social media firms not liable for the 2022 Buffalo mass shooting, New York's top court says
summary: New York state's top court says Facebook, YouTube and other social media giants aren’t liable for the racist mass shooting at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York, in 2022
story: New York state's top court says Facebook, YouTube and other social media giants aren’t liable for the racist mass shooting at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York, in 2022

NEW YORK -- Facebook, YouTube and other social media giants aren't liable for the racist mass shooting at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York, the state's highest court ruled this week in lawsuits over the 2022 attack.
In a 4-3 decision Monday, the Court of Appeals upheld a lower court's decision to dismiss claims against the tech firms from survivors and victims' relatives.
The lawsuits accused the companies of offering platforms engineered to promote extreme content and encourage compulsive use and of helping to radicalize shooter Payton Gendron.

Gendron, who is white, absorbed racist conspiracy theories online before he killed 10 Black people and wounded three others at the Tops Friendly Market. The 23-year-old is serving a life sentence after pleading guilty to state-level murder charges.
He told a court in 2023 that he “believed what I read online and acted out of hate.”

The Albany-based Court of Appeals said the four lawsuits “fail to establish that the shooter’s actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence of these defendants’ decisions about how to design and operate their platforms.”

Three judges disagreed, saying the survivors and families had built enough of a case for it to go forward. Gendron described himself in his diary as an online “addict” whose “mental health has seriously degraded,” the dissenters noted in an opinion by Judge Jenny Rivera.

The ruling affected Facebook and Instagram owner Meta; Google and YouTube parent Alphabet; and Reddit. Under different reasoning, the decision also upheld the dismissal of claims against other messaging and social media apps as well as Amazon, which owns Twitch, the service that Gendron used to livestream the rampage.
Matthew Bergman, who represents victim Heyward Patterson's family and estate in one of the cases, said Tuesday they were assessing their legal options after the ruling.
“The families affected by the tragic May 2022 Buffalo grocery store attack deserve accountability when dangerous product design choices contribute to real-world harm,” Bergman said in a statement.
Messages seeking comment were sent to lawyers for the other plaintiffs and for the companies.
Jury selection is ongoing for Gendron's federal hate crime trial, which carries the possibility of a death sentence if he is convicted. He has pleaded not guilty in that case.

The people he killed ranged in age from 32 to 86. In addition to Patterson, they were Celestine Chaney, Geraldine Talley, Katherine Massey, Pearl Young, Andre Mackneil, Ruth Whitfield, Roberta Drury, Margus Morrison and Aaron Salter.

title: China unveils new space mission crew, with a Pakistani astronaut
summary: China has unveiled the crew for its Shenzhou 24 spacecraft, set to launch this week
story: China has unveiled the crew for its Shenzhou 24 spacecraft, set to launch this week
JIUQUAN, China -- China on Tuesday unveiled the crew for its Shenzhou 24 spacecraft ahead of this week’s launch, with a Pakistani set to become the first foreign astronaut to board its space station.

Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, will fly alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, the China Manned Space Agency announced, according to the official Xinhua news agency. The spacecraft is scheduled to launch Wednesday morning from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China.

Speaking at a news conference, Ali, a former air force pilot, thanked the Chinese government for helping him realize his dream. In Mandarin, he cited a line of Chinese poetry about climbing one story higher to see farther.
“It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights,” he said in Mandarin.

Speaking in English, Ali said the mission “is not a finish line” but a long path. He said he hoped the next chapter of space cooperation between the two countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint flights and to the Moon, Mars and beyond.
“To every child who’s watching while I’m in orbit: Look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams," he said.

The launch would mark the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China’s manned space program. It is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his best wishes to the astronauts ahead of their mission.
“Tomorrow, Pakistan will look to the skies with anticipation, pride and deep gratitude,” he wrote on X.

He praised Chinese President Xi Jinping, saying his “visionary leadership and steadfast commitment to Pakistan-China friendship have taken our All-Weather Strategic Cooperative Partnership to unprecedented heights.”

Sharif also credited Pakistani scientists, the armed forces and national institutions, saying their efforts reflected the country’s growing capabilities and determination to advance space exploration and science.
“Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space,” he said.

Ali will undertake a short mission as a payload specialist, state broadcaster CCTV reported. In orbit, he will primarily conduct experiments under the China-Pakistan partnership, alongside daily operations.
He is expected to carry out four scientific projects in biotechnology and materials science, including an experiment involving photosynthetic microorganisms, CCTV said.
Ali will return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, the broadcaster added.
While Ali and Wu will be making their first spaceflights, Tang has flown on two previous missions. He is set to become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong space station three times, CCTV said.
Tang told reporters that differences in language, culture and psychology had made learning to work together more challenging on this mission, but that both sides’ efforts were paying off.

“The labels and operating instructions aboard the spacecraft and space station are all in Chinese, and the Pakistani astronaut began training with virtually no foundation of the language,” he said, adding that he and Wu had also stepped up their English studies.
China is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030. The United States is widely seen as China’s main space rival, with NASA aiming to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.
Leung reported from Hong Kong. Associated Press video journalist Wu Jia contributed to this report in Jiuquan.

title: Scientists discover quasar formed within 630 million years of the Big Bang
summary: Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet
story: Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. -- Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its center dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.

The quasar formed within 630 million years of the universe-forming Big Bang, a German-led team reported Tuesday. That's considered a very early development in the 13.8 billion-year history of the cosmos, and it smashes previous records.

“This time the leap in cosmic time is huge!” the European Southern Observatory’s Julien Wolf, who led the study, said in an email. “The previous two records each took us back by about 15 million years or less. This one takes us back by nearly 40 million years, the biggest advance in nearly a decade!”

Wolf and his team spotted the quasar while digging through millions of observations made by the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope. Launched in 2023, Euclid is surveying galaxies in an effort to shed light on the dark matter and dark energy that fill so much of the universe and keep it expanding.

Finding a quasar so early in the universe is rare, according to Wolf. What makes this one even rarer, he said, is the massive size of its black hole, despite being such a relatively slow eater of everything around it. Scientists are seeing it as it was 13.1 billion years ago — when the universe was less than 5% of its current age.

Wolf nicknamed the quasar Dun Aonghasa after the prehistoric stone fort in Ireland's Aran Islands. His wife and daughter are Irish, and he was awestruck when they visited the fort — a frontier holding “the promise of a vast horizon still to explore,” just like this quasar.

His team's findings were corroborated by the Hubble and Webb space telescopes as well as other observatories on and off Earth. Thanks to Webb, scientists learned that the black hole powering this quasar is equivalent in mass to 360 million of our suns, an astounding amount so early in time. The final results appear in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

“Dun Aonghasa gives us a new deadline” for the early universe, Wolf said. “About 630 million years after the Big Bang, its black hole had already grown to about 360 million times the mass of the sun. But how?”
Their prowling of the cosmic dawn continues.
“Honestly, the record could fall again in a few months or it could stand for years,” Wolf said.

title: Mercury gets its first visitor in years as a pair of spacecraft loop into orbit
summary: The European Space Agency announced BepiColombo's arrival via social media.
story: The European Space Agency announced BepiColombo's arrival via social media.

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. -- A pair of spacecraft slipped into orbit around Mercury on Saturday after an eight-year cruise through the inner solar system to unravel our littlest planet's mountain of mysteries.

The linked robotic explorers — one European, the other Japanese — will separate from one another next month in order to map and study the scorching little planet from different altitudes. The $2 billion (1.7 billion euros) mission is known collectively as BepiColombo.

The European Space Agency announced BepiColombo's arrival via social media. A series of thruster firings slowed the spacecraft enough to be captured by the planet's weak gravity. But it took several anxious hours before flight controllers in Germany — 94 million miles (152 million kilometers) away — could confirm that BepiColombo had achieved orbit. Teams pored over the data streaming back; additional information was not immediately available.
BepiColombo is only the third spacecraft to visit Mercury — the sun's closest planet and barely bigger than our moon — and the first in more than a decade.

NASA's Mariner 10 flew past Mercury three times in the mid-1970s. The team included the late Italian mathematician Giuseppe “Bepi” Colombo, for whom this latest mission is named. NASA's Messenger spacecraft entered orbit around Mercury in 2011 and, after running out of fuel, crashed into the planet in 2015.

Launched in 2018, BepiColombo took a slower, more roundabout route to get to Mercury, flying once past Earth, twice past Venus and six times past Mercury for gravity-guiding assists. All those loop-de-loops put more than 6 billion miles (10 billion kilometers) on the odometer. The conjoined spacecraft shed their mother ship in September for the final leg of the journey.

Lead project scientist Geraint Jones said he and others can’t wait for all the new data to start streaming down in the spring. The mission will provide the ability to compare “unprecedented measurements taken by two spacecraft at the planet at the same time,” he noted.

Once orbiting separately, the European Space Agency's satellite and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s smaller craft will study Mercury’s dense interior and exterior magnetic field, as well as everything in between: impact craters, volcanic plains, mountain ridges and peaks jutting as high as 3 miles (4 1/2 kilometers).

The mercury at Mercury can hit more than 800 degrees (427 degrees Celsius), adding strain to electronic and engineering systems. Space agency officials want to keep the mission going for at least one Earth year — or the equivalent of four Mercury years.
“The spacecraft and its instruments need to be kept as cool as possible, which is a huge technical challenge in itself,” Jones said in an email.

Despite its relative proximity to Earth, Mercury is one of the solar system’s least explored planets. Only outer planets Uranus and Neptune have had fewer visitors — a lone Voyager 2 back in the 1980s.

title: NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from an awe-inspiring one light-day away
summary: NASA’s Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away
story: NASA’s Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. -- NASA’s Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away, humanity’s first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space.

Flight controllers received the spacecraft’s call Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent. That’s how long it took for the radio signals to traverse the more than 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) at the speed of light.
“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” the Jet Propulsion Laboratory’s director, Dave Gallagher, said in a statement.

It’s another day in the history books for Voyager 1, which launched in 1977. It swept past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, snapped the most distant photo ever taken of our “Pale Blue Dot” in 1990, became the most distant human-made object in 1998, and crossed from the sun’s sphere of influence into the vast void between stars in 2012.
NASA could not confirm this newest distance record until Thursday. But that didn’t stop the space agency from wishing everyone a “Happy Voyager light-day … day!” via social media the day before.
Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, are NASA’s longest-operating space missions, still churning out data despite powering down most of their instruments to keep exploring.

Voyager 2 actually beat its twin into space by two weeks. But its route to Jupiter and Saturn plus Uranus and Neptune was slower and longer, and it did not reach interstellar space until 2018. It won’t reach the one-light-day mark until 2035.

Both spacecraft are doing well for their 49 years of age, plowing through space at 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) with plutonium for power. Picture-taking ended long ago, but they send back bits of precious data almost every day on their never-before-explored environment.

Each carries a so-called Golden Record brimming with the sounds of Earth. The project was led by the late Cornell University astronomer Carl Sagan, who also coined the phrase “Pale Blue Dot” for Voyager 1’s farewell glimpse of Earth.
NASA expects the gold-plated phonographic records — time capsules for anyone or anything that might encounter them — to last more than 1 billion years.
“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler,” NASA’s Joe Westlake, the heliophysics division director, said in a statement. “

title: (Not) up in the air: Travelers' trepidations spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups abound
summary: At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing— crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses
story: At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing— crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses

NEW YORK -- At this point, it's practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses.

And for 2026's busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there's another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a nationwide ground stop last week — the first since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation.

The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She's pretty sure she's not the only one.

“For a lot of people, especially as they’re paying attention and because it’s in the news where they’re tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we’re having ... I think more and more people are now getting anxious,” said Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel.
It's an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days' tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it's a familiar one, too.

Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it's one they're likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic.
But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.

“For the most part, air travel still remains strong,” said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People “might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it.”

In some ways, the country's aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute.

“Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy ... and frankly, it is taken for granted,” said Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum.

“You've got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places,” he said. “But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It’s a commodity. There's nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that’s a clear sign of its success — that you’re in a bus.”

At this point, as a traveler, Michelle Jolene says she's used to the delays, the cancellations, the rerouting of flights. So while she's not thrilled at the idea of adding infrastructure issues to the list of potential problems, she's not rattled by it.
“I literally haven’t had a normal flight in so long and I fly a lot. So I’m like, just, okay, here’s another thing,” said Jolene, who lives in Miami.
She did think it would make some people reluctant to get on a plane, “the people who fly maybe once a year for their holiday.”

And instead of flying this year, they’ll drive to "Disney or the beaches in North Carolina or something," she said. “But those of us who have to fly to work and to live our lives, there’s just not much choice. What are you going to do?”
If anything, a more disruptive aspect to flying than the potential for delays might be the cost — another anxiety trigger for many that can't just be stuffed into the overhead compartment.

Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas travel are up 31% and 23% from the same time last year, according to estimates from the travel-booking company Hopper. For travelers, that means dealing with the highest holiday airfares in a decade.
Some of increases to fares and fees are linked to higher jet fuel costs tied to the war in Iran. In September, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index.
It led Jolene, 50, to find a creative way to get her daughter's flight home to Miami for Thanksgiving: toilet paper.

She saw a promotion on American Airlines’ online shopping portal earlier this year that awarded 10 miles for every dollar spent. She bought 10 boxes of 48 rolls, earning her about 8,500 miles — which was enough to cover the entire flight from Washington, D.C., where her daughter attends college.
The upfront cost was worth it, she said, because it’s a product she would have bought anyway and one that doesn’t go bad. She's keeping the rolls in her garage
“The funny part," she said, “is we have to buy toilet paper anyway.”
AP Airlines and Travel Writer Rio Yamat in Las Vegas contributed to this story.

title: Treasury secretary says no further restrictions needed for Nvidia chip exports
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says no further restrictions on older Nvidia chips to China are needed
story: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says no further restrictions on older Nvidia chips to China are needed

WASHINGTON -- Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that no further restrictions on the sale of older Nvidia chips to China are needed following the Trump administration's move earlier this week to block China's remote access to the latest semiconductors.

The ability of Chinese tech firms to access Nvidia’s technology came under scrutiny after CEO Jensen Huang stepped down amid allegations of his affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that uses advanced chips to generate computing power that Chinese firms access remotely.
“The proper chip restrictions are in place,” Bessent said in an interview with CNBC after returning from a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump. “And the remote access has been curtailed.”

Bessent's comments came a day after the House Foreign Affairs Committee released details of the Commerce Department's approval of the sales of more than 850,000 chips from Nvidia and its competitor AMD to Chinese companies. The Pentagon has identified some of those companies as having ties to the Chinese military.

The report tracked applications from Nvidia to sell its H200 chips — one of its more powerful products, though not the most advanced — and AMD's applications to sell its roughly comparable MI325X chip to companies that are either located or headquartered in China, or entities with parent companies based in China.

The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security approved the export, re-export, or transfer of 879,868 of these chips to companies with Chinese ties across 21 license applications as of May 11, 2026, the report said. Nvidia and AMD had requested to sell a cumulative total of more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese-tied companies across those applications, per the report.

The approvals, which don't necessarily indicate completed sales, included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent and its subsidiaries, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, according to the report. Each of those companies has been identified by the Defense Department as having ties to the Chinese military.

The report shows the Commerce Department has a “long track record of transparency with Congress about licensing activity for the H200 and equivalent chips, including both approvals and rejections,” a spokesperson for the Bureau of Industry and Security said in a statement Friday.

The spokesperson said the Commerce Department's approach to H200 licensing is based on a rule in the Federal Register that was published in January. The rule imposes “significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial,” the spokesperson said.

An Nvidia spokesperson said in a statement Friday that the “limited shipments we made under the H200 program were legal and authorized” by the BIS. “The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes," the company spokesperson said.
Earlier this week, Nvidia said it was no longer shipping H200 chips to China. The spokesperson said Friday that shipments had stopped despite prior approvals.

AMD said it complies with U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains “rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations” in a statement from a spokesperson Friday. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity,” the spokesperson said.
Chinese technology firms have been bracing for impacts on their ambitious AI development plans as scrutiny mounts on export controls in the U.S.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under intense scrutiny himself in the wake of the turmoil following the Huang affair. Last week, Bessent said he was frustrated with the Commerce Department’s delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed International, which is under investigation by the U.S. for potentially diverting restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. A former executive at the company who allegedly had an affair with Huang was reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being a spy for China.
In an unusually public rebuke of a fellow Cabinet member, Bessent said his department wanted to place export controls on Megaspeed, but Commerce was in charge of the matter.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Trump said he has “not lost confidence” in Lutnick. Calling him a “different kind of guy," Trump said he “has a natural business instinct” and has “done a very good job.”
Huamani reported from Los Angeles. Associated Press writer Meg Kinnard contributed from Columbia, South Carolina.

title: House Democrat probes agencies' use of messaging apps to discuss official business
summary: A top House Democrat is investigating the use of encrypted messaging apps by Justice Department employees to communicate official business
story: A top House Democrat is investigating the use of encrypted messaging apps by Justice Department employees to communicate official business

WASHINGTON -- A top House Democrat is demanding that multiple government agencies preserve communications created on nongovernment messaging apps and investigate whether any records related to official business have been deleted.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee and the panel's incoming chairman, said in a series of nearly identical letters made public on Friday that he was concerned that President Donald Trump's administration was circumventing record-keeping requirements by using apps like Signal that can be configured to automatically delete messages after a certain time period.

Raskin noted in the letters, which were sent to top officials at the FBI, the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security, the Bureau of Prisons and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, that the agencies were legally required to preserve all records related to their official business, policies and decisions.

But he said: “There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records, seemingly with the express purpose of circumventing federal record preservation laws. This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials.”

The Maryland Democrat cited as an example a Signal exchange that he said he had obtained between the FBI’s top lawyer and an associate of the Republican president's oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., in which a potentially ongoing healthcare fraud investigation was discussed.
The Associated Press made multiple attempts to get comment from the agencies cited by Raskin but didn't receive any immediate responses.

Signal is an app that can be used for direct messaging and group chats as well as phone and video calls. It uses end-to-end encryption for its messaging and calling services that prevents any third party from viewing conversation content or listening in on calls.
Encrypted messaging apps are increasingly popular with government officials, an Associated Press review from last year found.

Their prevalence was demonstrated in vivid fashion last year when journalist Jeffrey Goldberg revealed that he had been inadvertently added to a Signal group chat of U.S. national security officials coordinating plans for airstrikes.

The White House and the Pentagon have said that disgruntled former employees were spreading false claims about the use of Signal, a commercially available app not authorized to be used to communicate sensitive or classified national defense information.

title: Asian American women feel the impact of Nvidia CEO affair scandal and 'spy' accusations
summary: The reveal earlier this month that billionaire Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had extramarital affairs has sent shock waves through the tech world, particularly with Asian Americans who revered him as a once-in-a-generation talent
story: The reveal earlier this month that billionaire Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had extramarital affairs has sent shock waves through the tech world, particularly with Asian Americans who revered him as a once-in-a-generation talent

The reveal earlier this month that billionaire Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had extramarital affairs sent shock waves through the tech world, particularly with Asian Americans who revered him as a once-in-a-generation talent. But what has hit hard for Asian American women is the discourse around the allegation that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal, was possibly a spy.
Almost immediately, videos and memes reviving tired tropes fetishizing Asian women hit social media.

“So few Asian women in general make it to the news for positive things. This is just going to continue to perpetuate negative stereotypes or biases for Asian women," said Misa Chien, founder of a network for Asian American women leaders called The Authentic Asian. Whether or not the allegation is true, “just the news will definitely influence people's opinions of women who have broken the ceiling or are trying to.”

Asian American women working in tech, civil rights advocacy and academia have felt a sense of dread that this ordeal will diminish how their peers are viewed and treated in their workplaces. It's a reminder that no accomplishments will completely dispel centuries-old stereotypes.
Jensen Huang has since resigned. However, the U.S. Justice Department has not found sufficient evidence that Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, was a spy.
“I don’t know if that’s been determined yet," President Donald Trump told reporters this week.

Among the social media posts being spread was a collage of photos showing CEOs with Asian female partners. Author May-lee Chai, who has written about the treatment of Asian women throughout history, called it “disgusting.”
Depicting them like trophy wives "implicates these spouses like they’re somehow similar to this suspected spy,” said Chai, a creative writing professor at San Francisco State University.

The speed at which people glommed onto the Asian female spy narrative was shocking to April Moh, chief marketing officer for a financial technology company and board member of Stand with Asian Americans, a legal civil rights organization specializing in combating workplace anti-Asian discrimination. The chatter has also led to women sharing stories of uncomfortable interactions.

“I have women in technology who tell me that they get really weird looks and they get questioned about laptop security by their colleagues when they’re visiting China,” Moh said. “I have another person telling me that she has been jokingly asked, ‘So, are you a spy?’ by people who think that’s a joke now. It’s not funny to her or me.”

Many clients of Stand with Asian Americans are Asian women who have proved their competence yet are still accused of being fraudulent or deceitful, said Rachel Lee, the organization's president and general counsel.

"It is deeply disturbing to see this not just unique to the Nvidia Jensen Huang case, but as a part of a long-standing dangerous narrative that Asians are perpetual foreigners, untrustworthy, disloyal,” Lee said.

On top of their integrity being questioned, Asian workers also deal with misconceptions that they cannot lead. The annual Social Tracking of Asian Americans in the United States Index from The Asian American Foundation found at least half of U.S. adults characterized Asian Americans in the workplace as “respectful” or “reliable.” Only 1 in 10 viewed them as “assertive.”

“The No. 1 theme in onboarding interviews all last week were 'I’m mistaken for the secretary, I don’t look like the typical face of leadership," said Chien, talking about new members of her Asian leaders network.

Years before Chinese laborers were fully banned from entering the U.S. under the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act, the federal government targeted immigrant Asian women. In 1875, Congress passed the Page Act to control immigration from “any Oriental country.” It included a specific prohibition of women coming for prostitution.

“Chinese women were deemed — and East Asian women in general — as being untrustworthy," Chai said. "It was presumed that they would be coming for illicit means as prostitutes to the United States and that would cause harm to white men.”
By the early 20th century, the Asian woman as a seductress, spy or “dragon lady” started becoming an archetype on Hollywood screens, she added.

The headlines had Chien reflecting on when she played a spy in a building security ad in Hong Kong 20 years ago. She was instructed to wear three bras to resemble Angelina Jolie's figure. She wrote an Instagram post to point out “how the media enjoys putting Asian women in that kind of role" and urged women to not let people's assumptions keep them from success.
“So many followers messaged me saying ‘thank you so much for speaking up,’" Chien said.

Suspicion toward Chinese people in the U.S. has dramatically heightened geopolitical tensions. Over two dozen states in the last few years have proposed or enacted “alien land laws” to prevent Chinese nationals from buying property. The number of international students enrolling in American universities has fallen. And the first Trump administration created a plan known as the " China Initiative " to crack down on espionage by profiling Chinese professors.

Critics say that initiative contributed to the 2024 suicide of Jane Ying Wu. A neuroscientist at Northwestern University who had lived in the U.S. for 40 years, the 60-year-old came under federal investigation in 2019. She was never charged with anything.
“This type of pernicious stereotype can actually destroy lives,” Chai said. “It’s not in any way an accurate portrait of an entire race and ethnicity.”
Jokes rooted in stereotypes under the guise of being complimentary also do not help Asian female workers, Lee added.
"Whether it’s a compliment or not, a trope is a trope,” she said. “I don’t care if it comes out of the mouth of the U.S. president.”

Ideally, Lee said more companies should allow for education and training around the harm and history of stereotypes. She encourages any woman who has had uncomfortable interactions to reach out to advocacy groups such as Stand with Asian Americans if she has nobody to turn to at work. At Stand with Asian Americans, people do not need to have a legal case of discrimination or harassment to receive assistance including education on their rights and mental health support.

Individuals also have the right to draw boundaries and make clear what's not OK to say, Lee added. It's in employers' best interest to make sure no federal laws against discrimination and harassment are being violated.
“It's a win-win to have that conversation,” Lee said.

title: Anthropic's IPO caps an explosive growth period for the AI startup, filled with contradictions
summary: A mere five years before breaking the record for the biggest public stock offering ever, Anthropic began as a Silicon Valley startup when its founders broke away from OpenAI with their own ideas about how to develop artificial intelligence
story: A mere five years before breaking the record for the biggest public stock offering ever, Anthropic began as a Silicon Valley startup when its founders broke away from OpenAI with their own ideas about how to develop artificial intelligence

A mere five years before breaking the record for the biggest public stock offering ever, Anthropic began as a Silicon Valley startup when its founders broke away from OpenAI with their own ideas about how to develop artificial intelligence.

Today, the company that dedicated itself to prioritizing safety, building the Claude chatbot along the way, has been one of the loudest voices raising warnings about how the same technology could bring catastrophe.
It's one of the contradictions that mark the brief, colorful history of Anthropic, which emerged Thursday from its first day of trading on Wall Street with a market value of $1.75 trillion.

The company, which still pledges to prioritize humanity's benefit, now faces pressure from shareholders to wring profits from the technology its most senior leaders have described as posing existential threats.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei described the push and pull between safety and AI advancement as one of the “central tensions at the heart of the company” on Thursday.

In an interview with CNBC, he described the rapid pace of AI advancements — due in large part to advanced models helping to build the next, improved version of themselves — as akin to building something that lets a driver go 200 miles per hour when they had previously been driving at 60. His company, he said, is working to develop it safely.

“What we’ve done with pacing is essentially said, ‘Look, you know, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let’s only drive at 90 miles an hour, spend time figuring out how to do that safely,’" he said. "And the rest of that surplus, we spend building the model in the right way.”

The company's seven founders — Amodei, 43, his sister and Anthropic’s president Daniela Amodei, 39, and five other former OpenAI employees — left the rival company in pursuit of building one that more clearly prioritized safety in artificial intelligence development.
Anthropic publicly has been committed to safety and transparency around their AI models, but insiders have sounded alarm bells in recent months.

An Anthropic researcher resigned from the company in September, criticizing the safety practices of both Anthropic and OpenAI. Jacob Coxon, whose message spurred industry-wide conversations about the speed of AI's growth, wrote that both Anthropic and OpenAI are “gambling with our lives.” He warned that some working on AI development believe it could threaten human life by the end of the decade.

Dario Amodei responded with an essay calling for an industry-wide slowdown on the technology’s development. He enumerated detailed plans for slowing development and ushering in coordination across different companies and countries, and championed the idea of having independent evaluators embedded within Anthropic and other labs.

But the results from at least one of those independent evaluations underscored Coxon's concerns. A recent report from the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research found Anthropic is developing its systems around twice as quickly as it was a year ago, largely because of the help of AI itself.
Amodei said Thursday in comments at the Nasdaq opening bell that the company's “most difficult safety work lies ahead of us.”

“And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” he said.

Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, meaning it has a legal obligation to balance shareholder interests with the public good. But these types of companies are rarely public, and of the few that are, they are significantly smaller than Anthropic, so the company is entering uncharted territory.

The company has said it is working towards a future where “AI’s benefits are shared by everyone," but the initial public offering has created a concentration of extreme wealth for its founders, employees and other investors.

Before the IPO, the two Amodei siblings each had a net worth of just over $14 billion, according to Forbes. By Thursday afternoon, Dario Amodei's net worth was $22.7 billion and Daniela Amodei's was $22.8 billion.

The Amodeis and the other co-founders have said they are committed to pledging 80% of their equity to philanthropy, although that commitment is voluntary. The company has an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity, which Anthropic matches. Anthropic has also pledged at least 5% of its stock to a “public benefit” fund.
Speaking to CNBC Thursday, Daniela Amodei said the concept of a public benefit corporation “spoke” to the co-founders when they were initially creating the company.

“We’re really trying to do something that we do think can have this incredible economic value and impact, but we want it to be baked into essentially our structure that we also have to balance that against building things that are good for people,” she said.

In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission last month, Anthropic devoted an unusually lengthy 93 pages to the risk factors they must spell out for investors. Among the concerns were that advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

Some argue Anthropic has outlined the ways its technology and that of its competitors could have devastating consequences in the name of sheer transparency. But critics have questioned the emphasis the company has placed on these dystopian-like potentials while positioning itself as the logical solution given its safety-minded focus.

A “Saturday Night Live” sketch in September made this contradiction a punchline. Cast member Jane Wickline played Dario Amodei, saying: “Sam Altman, myself, all the major AI players, we have talked about this extensively, and we are all on the same page here: We do not condone what we are doing.”

The faux interview on "SNL" concluded with a line that seems to have resonated with skeptics, showing up on a protest sign outside of Anthropic's San Francisco headquarters on Thursday: “I urge you to urge me to stop.”
Associated Press business writer Wyatte Grantham-Philips contributed.

title: White House taps Kirsten Davies as cyber chief after outages rattle Americans
summary: The White House has picked a new national cyber director after widespread service outages disrupted life and unnerved many Americans
story: The White House has picked a new national cyber director after widespread service outages disrupted life and unnerved many Americans
WASHINGTON -- The White House named a new national cyber director Thursday after a series of widespread service outages disrupted life and unnerved many Americans.

Kirsten Davies, chief information officer at the Defense Department, will fill the role, according to social media posts by several members of Trump's cabinet. She will replace Sean Cairncross as the administration's top cybersecurity official.

“Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected,” Davies wrote in a post on X. “Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future.”

President Donald Trump faced a groundswell of criticism as Americans grappled with a cascade of service outages that snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications.

Even staunch Trump allies accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause of the disruptions. Over the past week, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there’s “zero” information that the technical failures are related to each other or to a malign actor.
The White House made the change as Trump returned from a three-day trip to Asia, where he downplayed the episodes, declaring that “things like that happen.”

“She has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional, and we are confident she will advance President Trump’s America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote in a post on X congratulating Davies.

title: California attorney general subpoenas Nvidia over chips, former CEO's affair
summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia related to former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy
story: California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia related to former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy
California Attorney General Rob Bonta has issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia related to former CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

The California Department of Justice said Thursday it is asking Nvidia whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public.

“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors. My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” Bonta said in a statement. “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors.”

On Tuesday, key House lawmakers said that Huang has voluntarily agreed to appear for transcribed interviews as the company faces intensifying national scrutiny over sales of its advanced computer chips.
Huang will appear before congressional committees on Dec. 1, followed by the company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, on Dec. 2.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a message for comment Thursday.

title: Trump says he plans to penalize companies that build data centers in other countries
summary: President Donald Trump says U.S. tech companies will face “a tremendous tax” if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries
story: President Donald Trump says U.S. tech companies will face “a tremendous tax” if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump says U.S. tech companies will face “a tremendous tax” if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries.

Trump did not provide details Friday and he said he hadn’t yet told his own officials about his plan. The Republican president urged Americans to welcome data center construction in their communities and extract concessions from the developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.
Trump says, “You ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off.”

With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers, America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses.
The new raft of promises from the world’s richest companies came as anti-data center sentiment was a potent issue in the midterm elections, in which Democrats took control of Congress.

Despite backing from Trump, the data centers powering the artificial intelligence boom have become politically toxic. Community opposition that blocks municipal permits has become a bottleneck, and tech giants could face even more challenges if voters next month elect more public officials who are skeptical of data centers.

title: Anthropic's record IPO raises hopes for a charitable windfall that has nonprofits preparing to scale
summary: Anthropic's record $1.5 trillion valuation is carrying hopes of a charitable windfall that could send billions of dollars to philanthropy
story: Anthropic's record $1.5 trillion valuation is carrying hopes of a charitable windfall that could send billions of dollars to philanthropy
NEW YORK -- It was philanthropy, the story goes, that first bonded two of the founders behind artificial intelligence giant Anthropic.

Jared Kaplan, the San Francisco company's chief science officer, and CEO Dario Amodei were doctoral students carpooling to an event organized by an academic fellowship. As Kaplan recalls, he and Amodei spent the ride discussing “this idea of thoroughly investigating what kinds of charitable causes could do the most good.”
“We had so much largesse to, sort of, disperse,” Kaplan joked at a Hertz Foundation discussion in April 2025.

Those once-hypothetical philanthropic ambitions gained new steam as Anthropic debuted on the stock market to a record $1.5 trillion valuation. The Claude AI tool maker already plans to dedicate 5% of its shares for a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. Its seven co-founders say they'll give away 80% of their equity — a $112 billion commitment based on its IPO price.

Now suddenly affluent employees, many of whom will become millionaires as they sell their vested stock, may wield enough capital to make transformative donations themselves — riches that are commanding the attention of nonprofits looking to direct some sliver toward causes from global health to animal welfare.

Silicon Valley has great expectations. The napkin math suggests leading U.S. AI firms' valuations could add at least $37 billion annually in intended philanthropy, according to a widely circulated May blog post by Nan Ransohoff, head of public goods at the payments company Stripe.
“This is a once-in-a-lifetime kind of opportunity for people to really make an impact on extreme poverty,” said Peter Singer, the moral philosopher whose writings influence many tech donors.

Nonprofits aren’t counting on an immediate charitable windfall, though. Many Anthropic employees cannot sell or gift the bulk of their shares until next spring. Questions persist about the charitable priorities of these potential philanthropists whose worldviews have been shaped by the increasingly powerful AI models advancing at breakneck speed. The sector's volatility — between high borrowing costs, recent turmoil at the chipmaker Nvidia and warnings about risks to humanity — leaves skeptics doubtful about the amounts actually available to redistribute.

“The challenge is that deploying philanthropic capital is hard,” said Renaissance Philanthropy president Kumar Garg, whose nonprofit matches funders with scientific initiatives. “That’s not an automatic step.”
Will the artificial intelligence wave of wealth creation differ from previous ones that created new philanthropy?

There's reason to believe so, according to Benjamin Soskis, a historian of philanthropy and senior research associate at the Urban Institute's Center on Nonprofits and Philanthropy, even if he finds the number of tech executives who have “actually managed to empty the safe” is low.

The modern philanthropic foundation stemmed from the post-Civil War wave of industrial capitalism. Titans such as oil magnate John D. Rockefeller Sr. and steel tycoon Andrew Carnegie established bureaucratic institutions intended to address the root causes of social problems. Those were followed by the turn-of-the-century technology wealth that brought a more data-centric, risk-taking approach. The Gates Foundation launched to address pressing crises in global health and poverty.
AI wealth, according to Soskis, carries a sense of “extreme peril” and “really transformative promise” that should spur even more urgent action from this emerging class of donors.

At least one of Anthropic's co-founders will donate in the coming weeks to the Trump Accounts children's savings program, according to comments made Friday by U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on CNBC.

Anthropic's explosive growth is also fueling some anticipation that its 5,300 employees will want to rapidly scale their charitable impact, too. A generous internal giving program adds another incentive. Employee equity gifts are matched by the company with shares of Class N common stock. Anthropic also partners with donor-advised fund vendors such as Daffy, which offer a tax-efficient tool for grantmaking without the hassle of a more sophisticated charitable foundation.
Daffy CEO Adam Nash expects this younger generation to give more quickly.
“The people working in AI see the impact AI is having already,” Nash said. “And they are giving now, right?"
One organization in particular appears poised to move those rising donation volumes.

Coefficient Giving was formed by San Francisco-based billionaire Cari Tuna and her husband, Dustin Moskovitz, a Facebook co-founder and early Anthropic investor. A spokesperson told The New York Times the couple transferred their Anthropic stake into an undisclosed nonprofit last year to avoid personally profiting.

The philanthropic funder — which has directed more than $8 billion since 2014 in support of global health, animal rights, AI safety and the effective altruism community — has been scaling its pledges. In July, Coefficient Giving increased its commitment to the grantmaker GiveWell to $1 billion.
The move reflected expectations of “considerably more future funding for this kind of work,” according to the announcement.

“We might grow a lot, in part because we want to spend faster in response to these trends,” Coefficient Giving CEO Alexander Berger said during a late July public discussion. "But there is a great deal of room for other organizations and approaches, and I do not expect us to play an overwhelmingly dominant role.”

GiveDirectly has spent months identifying the biggest barriers to rapidly growing its antipoverty work, according to Nick Allardice, its president and CEO. The tech-focused nonprofit sends cash straight to poor households with no strings attached.

Recipients must have mobile phones to receive the digital transfers. GiveDirectly offers phones for about $15, usually subtracted from recipients' first payment. So the nonprofit secured investments this year to build out a supply chain to support many more mobile phones going forward.
The group is betting that its preparations for a charitable boom will be worthwhile.
“I have this level of cautious optimism,” Allardice said. “But I can't foresee the future, and I don't know exactly what's going to happen.”
Wild Animal Initiative executive director Cameron Meyer Shorb shares those tempered expectations.

His nonprofit funds wild animal welfare research. It's the sort of work some observers predict will see the biggest upswings in support: nonprofits connected to effective altruism, a data-driven movement that prioritizes donations to causes with the greatest impact on the most living beings.

The movement's reputation took a hit when Sam Bankman-Fried, one of its leading proponents and financial backers, got a 25-year prison sentence for cryptocurrency fraud. But the ideas are rebounding in the same tech circles that could see big payouts as more AI companies go public.

Effective altruists have learned not to rely too heavily on any one funder, according to Shorb. He expects “quite a bit” of fresh support for animal advocacy and sees an outsize role for midsize donors.
He said he has connected with a couple of Anthropic employees. Perhaps more important, he said, are relationships with the philanthropic advisers who help plan donors' giving.

“As you can imagine, it’s a pretty tricky place for a soon-to-be billionaire to be to have all this potential power coming soon,” Shorb said. “As soon as anyone finds out about that, anyone who can possibly get their email or phone number will just be knocking down their door. So we’ve tried to be gentle and slow and respectful in our approach.”
