title: Chinese tech firms fear AI hits from US curbs after Nvidia fallout
summary: Chinese tech firms are facing challenges as the U.S. tightens restrictions on access to advanced chips
story: Chinese tech firms are facing challenges as the U.S. tightens restrictions on access to advanced chips
HONG KONG -- Chinese technology firms are bracing for impacts on their ambitious artificial intelligence plans as the U.S. tightens restrictions on China's access to the world's cutting-edge chips.

Chinese tech giant Alibaba, which on Thursday announced another quarter of strong revenue growth for its global AI cloud and compute services, warned that the new U.S. rules could affect some of its global data center expansion plans. It said it was still assessing the repercussions.

The Trump administration this week issued new rules in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, following the news that he’d had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

The rules now restrict remote computing access through data centers in third countries, the latest U.S. move to curtail China’s abilities to use advanced Nvidia chips to train its increasingly capable AI models.
As the technology race between the two superpowers intensifies, existing U.S. export restrictions already barred China from getting the world’s most powerful chips.
But some Chinese companies have been able to bypass those restrictions by renting remote computing access to train AI models, pushing the U.S. to close what some policymakers called a loophole.

As global AI usage grows, Alibaba has been expanding its capabilities across chips, cloud infrastructure and AI models. It launched its flagship Qwen4-Max AI model earlier this week. In September, Alibaba's CEO called its new Zhenwu V900 chip the “most powerful” AI chip in China, while it announced massive data center investment plans in China and abroad.

Alibaba Cloud’s AI-related revenue currently comes significantly from China and there’s still a lot of “untapped demand” from Chinese enterprises, said Jacob Cooke of the Beijing-based consultancy WPIC Marketing + Technologies.

For the latest July-September quarter, Alibaba reported a 53% year-on-year revenue surge for its AI cloud and compute services to nearly 61 billion yuan ($9 billion). Total revenue for the quarter rose 10% from the year before to almost 272 billion yuan ($41 billion), slightly better than what analysts had expected.
While the company has a strong cash buffer, capital expenditures jumped 60% during the quarter to 50.5 billion yuan ($7.6 billion) thanks to its increased spending on AI infrastructure buildout.
Chinese tech giant Tencent on Wednesday said the new U.S. rule on chip access “sets everyone back in China.”

“Everyone is actually having less compute, advanced compute, to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China,” Tencent President Martin Lau said on an earnings call. Training timelines for Tencent’s next versions of its AI models would probably be impacted, he said.

“Chinese AI firms are still heavily dependent on the most frontier Nvidia chips," said James Chai, a researcher at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, with new U.S. rules on remote access cutting off a huge portion of Chinese firms’ access to compute.

A study released in October by the Institute for Progress, a U.S. think tank, estimated that remote access to AI chips through overseas data centers could account for roughly one-third of China’s AI compute by the end of 2027.

Nvidia, meanwhile, said it is now “no longer shipping” chips including the H200, one of its more powerful chips, though not the most advanced, although the Trump administration greenlighted some sales to China, reflecting how Nvidia has toughened its stance on China following Huang’s ouster.

Analysts expect the U.S. will step up its chip export control policies against China after Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, raised U.S. national security concerns. Earlier reporting by The New York Times suggested that U.S. officials suspected Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited in part to potentially influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available to Chinese companies.
Beijing has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, and has called the new U.S. rules blocking Chinese companies' remote access to computing power overseas “economic coercion.”
Analysts and industry leaders in China say the U.S.’s tightening of chip export control measures would ultimately accelerate China’s push to make its domestic chip industry self-sufficient.

“Over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we actually see the industry is actually progressing very fast,” said Tencent's Lau.

title: Sales of 'Grand Theft Auto VI' skyrocket as the series makes its return
summary: Sales of “Grand Theft Auto VI” are skyrocketing, as gamers’ insatiable appetite for the series continues
story: Sales of “Grand Theft Auto VI” are skyrocketing, as gamers’ insatiable appetite for the series continues
Sales of “Grand Theft Auto VI” are skyrocketing, as gamers' insatiable appetite for the series continues.

The game, which launched on Thursday, has hit $2.36 billion in revenue with approximately 24.6 million units sold, according to Sensor Tower, which is a market research firm that tracks mobile apps, digital advertising and consumer behavior online.

Earlier this month, the PlayStation blog said that “GTA VI” was the most preordered game in the history of its namesake store. Due to the demand, PlayStation said that it was teaming with Rockstar Games to allow players to start preloading the game nine days early, so that they'd be ready to play on launch day.

“GTA VI” is the latest installment in the hyperviolent, open-world video game series that has skewered American culture with fictionalized versions of New York and Los Angeles and is now returning to its sun-baked version of Miami — Vice City.

It's the first new “GTA” game in 13 years, with the story of “GTA VI” centered on a couple trying to improve their circumstances through crime. Early reviews for the game have noted that it has a depth of relationship building that goes beyond the violent stickups and bank robberies.

The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units globally, according to publisher Take-Two Interactive. “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days.

title: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with AI's help
summary: A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude
story: A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude
A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.
It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.

Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”
Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.

Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about “my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.

A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.

Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute’s website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.
The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.

“This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics,” he said in a statement. “But the journey from today’s announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult.”
Alpöge said he is “presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics.” He said more than 250,000 pages came out of his work with AI.
In September, OpenAI said its technology was key in a similar breakthrough with Navier-Stokes, an equation that governs the flow of fluids.

“Navier-Stokes fell and now the Riemann Hypothesis,” said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University. “There’s some kind of out-of-body experience where I’m looking at myself saying, ‘Yes, the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved,’ and kind of trying to comprehend what the hell these words are coming out of my mouth.”
Anthropic made a blockbuster Wall Street debut this week, through which it raised a record-breaking $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.

Amodei has projected an optimistic vision for AI’s future in which the technology leads to significant advancements in math and science research while simultaneously warning about the potential risks AI poses.
AP Technology Writer Kaitlyn Huamani contributed.

title: Potential health effects of Army's detonation of nearly 5 tons of lead azide
summary: The U.S. Army is planning a controlled detonation of explosive material at an ammunition plant in rural Iowa on Wednesday. There could be potential health effects.
story: The U.S. Army is planning to perform a controlled detonation of explosive material at an ammunition plant in rural Iowa on Wednesday.
Last week, environmental groups filed lawsuits in an attempt to stop the controlled explosion, saying that detonating nearly five tons of lead azide could harm people and contaminate the environment.
The Army has insisted the stockpile is too unstable to be moved and that destroying it in place is the only responsible option.

"There's a humongous health threat already," ABC News medical correspondent Dr. Darien Sutton told ABC News Live on Monday. "When you think about lead, humans are exposed in two main ways: either through inhaling it or ingesting it. Now, with a detonation or explosion, the immediate effect is inhaling it."
What is lead azide?
Lead azide is an explosive chemical compound of lead used mainly in detonators, according to the National Center for Biotechnology Information.
When heated, lead azide can release highly toxic fumes containing lead and nitrogen oxides.

Lead azide is unstable, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. It explodes at 350 degrees Celsius, but it may also explode if shocked, heated or subjected to friction when dry.

Although lead azide decomposes during detonation, the lead itself does not disappear. The Army says the resulting dust plume will contain some lead, and lead-containing particles and residue may remain in the surrounding environment.
What are the health risks of exposure?
Lead does not biodegrade and can persist in the environment for many years unless it is physically removed.
"Lead damages nearly every organ in the human body, the brain, the kidney, the liver, also the reproductive system," Sutton said. "What many may not realize is lead accumulates in the body."
Sutton explained that when lead is inhaled or ingested, it gets stored in vital organs and in the skeleton, replacing calcium and bone mineral.
"Years or decades later, it can leach back into the blood, causing harmful outcomes for people," Sutton said.

Sutton added that there is a potential secondary effect of lead contaminating surfaces and a possible long-term effect of lead landing on the ground or in water, which could affect food or drinking water.
How much is required to become a health risk?
It's unclear how much exposure to lead azide is required to be considered a health risk.
However, lead azide is a highly toxic and extremely sensitive explosive compound, and no amount of lead exposure is considered safe.

According to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, airborne lead exposure of 30 micrograms per cubic meter averaged over eight hours triggers workplace safety requirements, while 50 micrograms per cubic meter is the maximum permissible occupational exposure limit.
These limits apply to the lead component, not specifically to lead azide, and do not guarantee safety below those concentrations.

"When you find out that someone has an elevated level of lead ... the only real treatment is to avoid exposure or continued exposure," Sutton said. "There's no easy way to extract that lead from the human body, and so that dangerous effect could have long-term effects after that initial exposure."
On Tuesday, federal officials recommended that local residents, especially children and pregnant women, evacuate. Residents are advised to remain relocated until Friday at the earliest.
"Evacuated individuals will be notified by phone once the all-clear is given and at that point may return home at their convenience," the Army said in an advisory posted Tuesday.
ABC News' Eric M. Strauss contributed to this report.

title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaving the US, self-deporting to Spain
summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was returned to the U.S. after being mistakenly deported to a Salvadoran mega-prison, is self-deporting to Spain, sources tell ABC News.
story: It comes nearly two years after he was mistakenly sent to a Salvadoran prison.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was returned to the U.S. after being mistakenly deported to a Salvadoran mega-prison, is in the process of self-deporting to Spain, sources familiar with the matter tell ABC News.
ABC News observed Abrego Garcia boarding a flight from a Washington, D.C.-area airport to Madrid, Spain, on Tuesday.
His departure marks a major development nearly two years after the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison as part of its ongoing immigration crackdown.

Prior to his boarding the flight to Spain, ABC News observed Abrego Garcia enter a Customs and Border Protection office at the airport before going through airport security -- in part, a source said, to have his ankle monitor removed after it was issued by federal immigration officers when he was returned to the United States over a year ago.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, where Abrego Garcia and his family live, said in a statement that the Trump administration was "forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar's will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation."

"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Abrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag. Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice," said Van Hollen, who traveled to El Salvador to meet with Abrego Garcia following his deportation. "I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free -- including from this Administration's constant persecution."

Abrego Garcia, who had been living in Maryland with his wife and children, was deported in March of last year to CECOT -- despite a 2019 court order barring his deportation to that country due to a fear of persecution -- after the Trump administration claimed he was a member of the criminal gang MS-13, which he denies.

After the Supreme Court upheld a ruling that Abrego Garcia should be returned to the United States, he was brought back to the U.S. last June to face human smuggling charges in Tennessee, after which U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis released him from ICE detention while he awaited trial.
In May, a federal judge dismissed the criminal indictment against him, finding that the government's investigation had been tainted "with a vindictive motive."

In October, Judge Xinis, who has been overseeing Abrego Garcia's immigration case, abruptly canceled a hearing on the matter. Last week, several sealed filings were filed in the case, including a sealed order.

In court filings, the Trump administration had been pushing for Abrego Garcia's deportation to a third country in Africa. Government officials had previously named the countries of Liberia, Uganda and Eswatini as potential destinations for removal.

title: Trump awards Medal of Freedom to former NYC Mayor Rudy Giuliani
summary: Trump pardoned Giuliani last year.
story: Trump pardoned Giuliani last year.
President Donald Trump awarded the Medal of Freedom to former Mayor of New York City Rudy Giuliani at the White House on Tuesday.
Giuliani said in a statement after the ceremony that he was "honored and humbled" to receive the Medal of Freedom from Trump.

"Any and all distinction I have received in public office is fully the result of following the advice of my boss, Ronald Reagan, who said: 'There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit,'" Giuliani wrote. "I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me -- particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together."
White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said that Trump recognized Giuliani with the highest civilian honor for his "lifetime of service to the American people."

Wales described Giuliani as a "dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our Nation," going on to reference his efforts to root out crime in New York City and his leadership in the aftermath of 9/11.
The White House press pool was not invited to cover the ceremony.
Following the White House event, Giuliani’s son, Andrew Giuliani, briefly addressed reporters on the White House North Lawn, saying his father’s Medal of Freedom ceremony was "incredibly special."
"To see your father receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom is an unbelievable honor. It’s tough to describe," Andrew Giuliani said.
Last year, Trump announced his plans to present Giuliani with the Medal of Freedom, after Giuliani suffered injuries in a car accident.

"As President of the United States of America, I am pleased to announce that Rudy Giuliani, the greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot, will receive THE PRESIDENTIAL MEDAL OF FREEDOM, our Country’s highest civilian honor," Trump said on Sept. 1, 2025.
Trump pardoned Giuliani last year for his alleged involvement in attempts to overturn the 2020 election.

Giuliani served as the president’s personal lawyer and was disbarred in two jurisdictions in 2024 over "false and misleading" statements on the 2020 election. Voting machine company Dominion settled its $1.3 billion defamation lawsuit against Giuliani over false allegations surrounding the 2020 presidential election.
Trump's pardon was largely symbolic as Giuliani -- along with others Trump pardoned at the time -- were not facing federal charges, and Trump does not have the ability to pardon states charges.

In his second term, Trump posthumously awarded the Medal of Freedom to conservative activist Charlie Kirk and 9/11 hero Welles Crowther. He has also announced plans to present the award to neurosurgeon and former Secretary of Housing and Urban Development Ben Carson, Team USA Hockey goalie Connor Hellebuyck, and baseball player Roger Clemens, a White House official confirmed.

title: They want to watch Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan die but the Army won’t let them
summary: Julia Wilson was nine months pregnant when she found herself caught in gunfire at Fort Hood in 2009. 'It's crazy how quickly things run through your brain," she said.
story: The Army is limiting witnesses to victims' survivors and those who were wounded.

Julia Wilson was nine months pregnant when she found herself caught in the gunfire at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. She had just returned from lunch and was shutting off her truck when she heard gunshots and watched a soldier nearby collapse after being struck by a bullet.

A civilian human resources employee at the base, Wilson repeatedly sounded her truck alarm, hoping to distract the gunman from shooting her colleagues, and called 911. As she ducked across the seats of her truck, she counted at least a dozen bullets flying in her direction.
"'I'm never going to see the face of my child. I'm never gonna hold him' -- it's crazy how quickly things run through your brain," she told ABC News.
She and her baby were unharmed.

Now, 17 years later, Wilson wants to witness the execution of the man who could have killed her. But the Pentagon has denied her request to attend the Dec. 3 execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 31 others. Nidal is set to die by firing squad at the same Army base where he carried out the attack.

Wilson is among multiple survivors of the massacre who say the Pentagon has denied their requests to witness Hasan's execution, despite assurances that victims and their families would be permitted to attend. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at one time said it would be livestreamed, though that plan was overturned by President Donald Trump.

On Nov. 5, 2009, Hasan, who was then an Army major, opened fire inside a medical processing building at Fort Hood in a rampage he described as a jihad in protest of U.S. wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Dozens of other soldiers and civilian employees, including Wilson, Dr. Kathy Platoni and Dr. C. Alan Hopewell, were caught in the attack.

All three had hoped to attend the execution, saying they wanted to be there for the friends and colleagues they lost and that watching the Army carry out Nidal's sentence might bring them some measure of relief after 17 years.

Though none were struck by gunfire, all three witnessed the attack firsthand and said they continue to live with its psychological toll. They say that they are appealing the Army's decision to Department of Defense officials and raising the issue with lawmakers.
The Defense Department did not respond to ABC News' questions about who is allowed to attend.

Wilson called the Army's decision an "institutional betrayal," arguing that its interpretation of its rules effectively dismisses the trauma experienced by those who survived the shooting but weren't hit by gunfire.

The Army's rules on who can witness an execution are relatively broad. They outline that prison staff, the condemned prisoner's attorney and family, and victims of the crimes that led to the death sentence may attend. Hasan was convicted of numerous charges of murder, premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder.

But the regulations also give the Army discretion to invite additional witnesses, including victims who might not meet the narrower definition of victims. Army rules also require the presence of at least two journalists, effectively as third-party witnesses, a common practice in civilian executions.
Army officials cited security concerns and limited space at the execution site in restricting attendance, correspondence reviewed by ABC News shows.
"The fact that I don't meet the category doesn't change the reality of what I experienced with my unborn child," Wilson said. "I continue to hear the screaming and smell the blood."

Platoni, a retired Army colonel and former chief psychologist for the Army Reserve, was undergoing routine medical processing ahead of a deployment to Afghanistan in an adjacent building when Hasan opened fire. She said she had never met Hasan but would have been his supervisor in Afghanistan.

Military bases can be heavily guarded at their gates while remaining relatively open once someone is inside, particularly someone in uniform. Troops carrying out ordinary duties outside combat zones do not carry weapons. Security falls largely to military and civilian police, who patrol installations.

Platoni, who tended to the wounded in the aftermath of the attack, argued that the Army is applying an unnecessarily narrow interpretation of its own regulations, which authorize victims of offenses punishable by death, including attempted offenses, to witness an execution.
"I've never been this angry in my life that they're doing this to us and telling us we weren't victims because we didn't take a bullet to the brain," she said.
Hopewell, then an Army major who oversaw the outpatient psychiatry clinic at Fort Hood and was Hasan's supervisor, was inside the facility when Hasan tried to force his way in during the shooting.
Armed with an FN-5.7 pistol equipped with a laser sight and a 20-round magazine and carrying a .357 Magnum revolver as a backup, Hasan moved through the halls, shouting for doors to be opened.
Hopewell and his colleagues had barricaded themselves inside a room just before Hasan reached them. Unable to force his way in, he screamed in frustration, Hopewell recalled.
"I was about two feet away from him when he was trying to smash into my clinic to kill me," Hopewell said. "You can't go through something like this and have it not affect you."

Hopewell said he was initially ambivalent about witnessing Hasan's final moments. But Sgt. Kimberly Munley, who was shot three times, asked Hopewell to accompany her to the execution. Hopewell had received communications from Army officials inviting him to attend but they subsequently rescinded that invitation.
"Since I was one of the senior officers, I feel it's my duty to represent the families and the victims and my clinic staff," Hopewell said.

For Platoni, attending the execution is not just about watching Hasan die but also supporting the people who survived his attack and the families who lost loved ones. Five soldiers in her unit were killed in the shooting and she still wears a hero bracelet that bears their names to commemorate them.

"It would mean that I could be there to support my fellow soldiers that were wounded and did survive. It would mean that I might be able to, as I did during the court martial, be there to support the families, and I want to witness this so that I know he's gone from the Earth," she said. "So I want to see justice served in some way. But all we've encountered is injustices, one after the other."
All three survivors say they have struggled with post-traumatic stress disorder since the shooting.

Wilson described years of living with a heightened sense of danger, even in otherwise ordinary situations. She said that she has grappled with depression and struggled to hold down a job due to difficulty with concentrating.
"You're constantly looking over your shoulder. You're constantly scanning for threats," Wilson said.

The decision to exclude them from Hasan's execution has compounded a longstanding frustration among the three survivors, who say the Pentagon has repeatedly failed to support those whose lives were upended by the massacre.
For Wilson, witnessing the execution would offer a "smithereen of closure and justice," after 17 years. She said she wants Hasan to see her one final time and recognize that she survived his attack.

"I need him to read from my eyes that you tried to victimize me, but I survived you, and you have destroyed my life and many other people's lives," she said. "And maybe, just maybe, with you ending here -- maybe my life might be able to start somewhat again."

title: Groups push back on Trump administration changes to historical monument
summary: Two Philadelphia groups filed a federal lawsuit against the Trump administration over the removal of panels at the slavery memorial at the President’s House site.
story: The site is where President George Washington lived and enslaved nine people.
Two Philadelphia groups filed a federal lawsuit against the Trump administration over the removal of the interpretative panels at the slavery memorial at the historic President's House site.

The memorial marks the site is where President George Washington lived for most of his presidency -- from 1790 to 1797 -- and where he enslaved nine people. It was born out of a community campaign and established in 2010 to tell their stories.

The lawsuit was filed on Monday in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania by Avenging the Ancestors Coalition (ATAC) -- a group that fought for years for the memorial to be established -- and The Black Journey, which runs the African American Walking Tour of Philadelphia.

"Right now is where we fight the good fight. What you have here is based on mythology. What you have here is based on half-truth," ATAC founder Michael Coard said at a press conference announcing the lawsuit. "What you have here is based on lies and nothing but lies."

The lawsuit names the National Park Service, the Department of the Interior (which oversees NPS), Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and acting NPS Director Jessie Bowron as defendants. Neither the Interior Department nor NPS immediately responded to ABC News' requests for comment.

Coard, who reflected on his years-long battle to fight for this memorial in a July interview with ABC News, accused the Trump administration of attempting to sanitize the brutality of slavery and downplaying the Founding Father's role in it.

He pointed to language contained in the new panels that focuses on Washington's "discomfort" with slavery and language that suggests people enslaved at the President's House received more favorable treatment than those enslaved elsewhere.

The complaint argues that the removal of the panels and the changes at the memorial that were made by the Trump administration violate the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution and the Administrative Procedure Act.

"NPS's actions are part of a coordinated effort by the Trump administration, not only to distort the past and manufacture an alternative narrative of the history of the United States, but also to disparage and denigrate the stories and history of Black people in this country," the lawsuit alleges.
This is the second federal lawsuit that was filed seeking to stop the Trump administration from making changes to the interpretive materials at the memorial.

The first lawsuit, filed by the city of Philadelphia and backed by Coard's group, was ultimately unsuccessful after a federal appeals court in July cleared the way for the Trump administration to replace the exhibit panels.

The Interior Department claimed that the content was "divisive" and "disparages" Washington. The court determined that the new panels installed by the Trump administration at the site were historically "accurate."

The White House did not provide specific examples of panels that they took issue with, but appeared to dispute the focus and tone of the exhibit. President Donald Trump asserted in the past on social media that institutions "across the country" focus too much on "how bad slavery was," instead of focusing about the "success" and "brightness" of the country.
The changes at the slavery memorials stem from orders outlined in Trump's March 2025 executive order, "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History."
The order called for the removal of "negative" and "divisive" materials from national parks and content that "disparages" Americans, living or dead.
"What we want to make sure we do is to restore the truth," Coard said. "What [President Trump] has done at this site created a dangerous precedent."

title: Army says lead explosives detonation will proceed after court denies bid to stop it
summary: Trump said he wants the OK from the federal appeals court and incoming Iowa governor to proceed.
story: President Donald Trump weighed in on the contested plan on Monday.
The U.S. Army said the planned detonation of nearly five tons of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Iowa will proceed as previously scheduled on Wednesday.
The announcement came after a federal appeals court denied an emergency motion to halt it, clearing the way for the controversial operation.
The Army said in a statement on X it would proceed with the "extensively mitigated, carefully controlled detonation" on Wednesday morning, "based on forecast wind conditions."
"This is a consensus decision," the Army said.

Earlier on Monday, President Donald Trump said in a post on his social media platform that he ordered the military to hold off on the planned detonation until the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals and the incoming Iowa governor signed off on it.

The controlled detonation of the degraded explosive material was most recently pushed to Wednesday. In denying the motion challenging the U.S. Army's permit, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals said that "every day of delay increases the risk of an uncontrolled explosion that will cause far greater public health and environmental harm than the planned, controlled detonation initiated under the protective terms of the Permit."
Trump had said that he believes the "proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem," but left the decision to the appeals court and incoming Governor-elect, Rob Sand.

"If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation," Trump said.

The controlled detonation is to dispose of degraded lead azide, which is highly sensitive to shock, friction and heat and extremely unstable. Due to the risks of accidental detonation in packing and transporting it, "safely destroying it in place is the only responsible option," the Army said.

Outgoing Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said in a statement Sunday that while the detonation is a federal operation, the state has been "engaged in the preparation process so we can support the work of our federal partners in responding to the needs of Iowans," including evaluating potential public health impacts and providing guidance to the public.

The Army's plan to conduct a controlled detonation of nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide at the military ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, has raised concerns from the public and medical groups over the potential health impacts, as well as a legal challenge from environmental groups. The Army said the detonation will cause a dust plume containing some lead, a known neurotoxin.
Sand, a Democrat and the incoming Iowa governor, deferred to the Trump administration on moving forward with the planned detonation while calling for greater transparency.

"The Administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks," Sand said on social media.

"Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward," he said. "That means they should have the same access to the information I've received in briefings from the administration, straight from the source. I've asked the federal government to share that information with the public as soon as possible."
Sand previously called for transparency regarding the operation and questioned why "we are rushing to demolition."

"All relevant federal, state and local government resources should be focused on protecting everyone that could be impacted," he said in a statement Sunday. "Iowans deserve transparency over how we got here, then answers and accountability to stop this from ever happening again."

Two rapid, controlled detonations were initially scheduled to take place at the Middletown plant midday Friday to safely dispose of degraded lead azide, according to the U.S. Army. Those plans were subsequently postponed twice, with the Army saying on Sunday, prior to Trump's announcement, that it had pushed the controlled detonation to Wednesday to allow for "optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced."

Lead azide is the primary explosive used to detonate munitions, such as grenades and artillery shells. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, which issued the permit for the detonation, the "recrystallization of the stored lead azide has increased the material's sensitivity to friction and shock, and disturbing the containers of lead azide could create an unacceptable risk of unintentional detonation."

The Department of Health and Human Services, the EPA and the Army previously said the agencies are taking "extreme mitigation measures to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized."

The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter filed an emergency motion on Thursday seeking to halt the detonation. The groups argued that the detonation could spread lead dust across a large area, potentially reaching communities more than 100 miles from the plant.

As of the filing, the Army's latest modeling projected that lead dust could settle across an area approximately 25 miles long and 5 miles wide, including homes and waterways, according to the motion. The groups further argued that people, livestock and wildlife could also continue to face exposures to lead once it settles into the ground.
The filing also questioned the Army and EPA's handling of public notification, alleging that some of the potentially impacted communities were not given direct or timely notice.

In an order filed late Thursday night, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals granted an administrative stay of the permit while the federal appeals court considered the emergency request to formally halt the detonation. The court lifted the administrative stay on Monday while denying the emergency motion.

Prior to Trump's statement Monday, the Justice Department said in a court filing Sunday that the Army intended to move forward with its detonation plan, citing an "immediate risk" that those materials could "spontaneously explode."

The Justice Department also argued that the Army has the authority to move forward without that permit, saying the EPA's regulations have an exemption from permitting requirements in events that require immediate action.
The Army said it plans to detonate 68 barrels -- approximately 9,700 pounds -- of lead azide, a highly toxic and extremely sensitive explosive compound.

Lead is a neurotoxin that can cause brain damage and reduced cognitive function, particularly in children. There is no established amount of exposure that can be considered universally safe, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Although lead azide decomposes during detonation, the lead itself does not disappear, and lead-containing particles and residue may remain in the surrounding environment, according to Iowa Health and Human Services.

Amid the detonation plans, the American Lung Association warned that lead dust from the plume could be spread "far from site of the detonation, depending on the wind and weather," and called on the U.S. Army to work with state and local health departments and "better communicate to residents the expected levels of exposure, the potential health impacts and how to protect themselves."

title: Attorney General Blanche sidesteps questions about DOJ probe into Nvidia's Huang
summary: Blanche described Nvidia as "a good corporate citizen."
story: Blanche described Nvidia as "a good corporate citizen."

Attorney General Todd Blanche on Tuesday seemed to downplay the Justice Department's role in investigating the ongoing controversy with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence believes could be a Chinese intelligence asset, dodging questions from reporters and saying Nvidia is a "good corporate citizen."

"I'm not going to talk about investigations," Blanche said when asked directly whether Huang had ever been the subject of an investigation. "What does that mean? Had Huang been investigated? For what?"

Just 12 days ago, Blanche acknowledged an export control investigation into the Nvidia AI chips was "ongoing." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a key question is whether Nvidia's chips were illegally being diverted to China.

In an interview with The New York Times on Monday, President Donald Trump said he consulted with Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton before he "recommended" reinstating Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO to its board.

Blanche's comments come after top administration officials gave assurances to the Nvidia board that Huang was not facing any criminal charges, sources familiar with the discussions between top administration officials and the board said. The assurances came before Huang was reinstated as CEO in a surprise move on Monday.

Top administration officials also told the board that they believed Huang was not a national security risk, despite U.S. intelligence showing that Huang allegedly had an affair with Alice Huang, a woman U.S. intelligence believed could be passing information back to China, sources said.
The New York Times was first to report on the assurances.

Asked how Blanche could rule out the Nvidia CEO's potential criminal liability when the DOJ's investigation into potential export control violations by Nvidia remained ongoing, he said, "When you say the export investigation is ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about."

Alice Huang is the former CEO of Megaspeed, a Singaporean company federal investigators are probing over alleged export control violations and the illicit transfer of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China.

Megaspeed said in a statement on its website last week that it "takes its compliance obligations under U.S. export control laws extremely seriously." The company also says it "has cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) and stands ready to cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority."

When asked by ABC News Justice Department Reporter Alexander Mallin about Blanche's previous comments about the export control investigation, the attorney general responded, "Yes. That's not -- that's not new information."
Pressed about whether he was satisfied with the cooperation from Huang and Nvidia in DOJ's investigations, Blanche described the company as "a good corporate citizen."

"Obviously if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that that the president is saying to the American people," Blanche said, later adding, "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen."
Blanche further declined to comment on the status of Huang's potential continued access to classified information in his dealings with the U.S. government.

Lawmakers said Huang will sit for a closed-door transcribed interview on Tuesday, Dec. 1, before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee. Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter will do so the following day, the lawmakers said.
Trump took credit on Monday for Huang's return as Nvidia's president and CEO. Trump told CNBC he spoke "directly and indirectly" to the company's board members about bringing Huang back.
"I spoke to them. Let me put it this way: And I convinced them. I made the deal," Trump said in a phone interview with CNBC.

Huang resigned earlier this month after allegedly having an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence believes could be a Chinese intelligence asset. Huang had admitted in an internal message to Nvidia staff that he had been "unfaithful to his wife."
Trump said in the CNBC interview that a "very thorough investigation" by the U.S. government "exonerated" Huang and determined that he "did nothing wrong."
Nvidia said on Monday that it will continue to carry out its own investigation into reports of an alleged foreign intelligence operation targeting Huang.

title: Trump owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock at the end of last year
summary: President Donald Trump owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock at the end of 2025, according to his annual financial disclosure report reviewed by ABC News.
story: His accounts continued to trade Nvidia in recent months, according to filings.
President Donald Trump owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock at the end of 2025, according to his annual financial disclosure report reviewed by ABC News.

His accounts have continued to trade Nvidia in recent months, including more than three dozen trades buying and selling millions of dollars of Nvidia stock this year through September, according to separate filings that disclose trades in his accounts.
The White House continues to maintain that third-party institutions manage Trump's accounts.

"President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000," said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle.

"Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers."
Trump has repeatedly vouched for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid the scandal surrounding his alleged afair with a woman U.S. intelligence alleges is a Chinese asset.
On Monday, he took credit for Huang's stunning return to Nvidia, saying in an interview that he spoke "directly and indirectly" to the company's board members about bringing Huang back as CEO.
"I spoke to them. Let me put it this way: And I convinced them. I made the deal," Trump, who had urged Huang's reinstatement publicly, said in a phone interview with CNBC.
Following the announcement, the major stock indexes rebounded sharply on Monday as Nvidia shares closed up more than 30%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 1,447.98 points, or 3.0%, while the S&P 500 jumped over 4.73%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq soared over 6.5%.
Shares of Nvidia surged, recovering nearly all of the losses suffered since Nov. 12, the day Nvidia announced Huang's resignation.
Nvidia develops the semiconductor chips, systems, and software powering artificial intelligence. In early October 2026, its market valuation reached $5.8 trillion.
Given its significant presence in the stock market, Nvidia is a common holding in many investment portfolios and Trump's shares in the company represent a small portion of his overall portfolio.

title: Trump granted new chance to potentially erase his hush money case
summary: An appeals court is giving President Trump a new chance to move his criminal hush money case into federal court, where he could then attempt to overturn his conviction.
story: Trump is seeking to move the criminal case into federal court.

A federal appeals court is giving President Donald Trump a new chance to move his criminal hush money case into federal court, where he could then attempt to overturn his conviction on grounds of presidential immunity.

The late U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein decided in August that Trump could not move the case into federal court, two years after a jury in Manhattan convicted him on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records related to a hush payment to adult actress Stormy Daniels.
On Monday, a three-judge panel of the Second U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals disagreed.

"First, the district court erred in holding that removal is categorically unavailable in a state criminal case after a federal officer defendant has been convicted," the panel said. "Second, the district court erred in holding that Defendant-Appellant failed to show 'good cause' to justify granting him leave to file a second notice of removal."
The ruling allows Trump, for a third time, to argue the hush money case rightfully belongs in federal court, where he would be able to argue he is immune from prosecution.
Hellerstein, who died last month at 92, previously decided that "paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity."

The appellate court's two-page ruling asked that "no further proceedings occur in the state courts" while Trump's petition is pending, effectively pausing Trump's traditional appeal of his conviction through the state appellate courts.

In May 2024, in between his two presidential terms, Trump became the first president in American history to be criminally convicted after Manhattan prosecutors alleged that he engaged in a "scheme" to boost his chances during the 2016 presidential election through a series of hush money payments to Daniels, then falsified New York business records to cover up that alleged criminal conduct. He denied all wrongdoing.

After Trump won the 2024 presidential election, he was sentenced to an unconditional discharge and later made his lead defense attorney from the trial, Todd Blanche, the attorney general of the United States.

title: Navy keeps Black war hero's name on carrier after weighing renaming it for Trump
summary: Navy officials had weighed renaming the vessel for Trump, sources said.
story: Navy officials had weighed renaming the vessel for Trump, sources said.

The U.S. Navy has dropped the idea of renaming an aircraft carrier now under construction for President Donald Trump, saying the ship will keep the name of Doris Miller, the Black sailor honored for his heroism at Pearl Harbor.
"There is no intention to change the name of the USS Doris Miller," Meghan Stoltzfus, a Navy spokesperson, said in a statement on Monday.

In August, sources familiar with the matter told ABC News that Navy officials were weighing whether to strip the name of one of World War II's most famed Black service members from the new aircraft carrier -- instead possibly naming it for Trump.

The carrier, under construction in Virginia, was christened in name during Trump’s first administration, when the Navy announced the Ford-class ship would become the USS Doris Miller, honoring Miller's heroic actions during the attack on Pearl Harbor, during a ceremony on Martin Luther King Jr. Day in 2020.

During the 1941 attack, Miller, serving as a cook aboard the USS West Virginia, helped move the ship’s mortally wounded captain to safety before taking control of an anti-aircraft gun, despite having no formal training on the weapon. He was credited with shooting down at least one Japanese aircraft -- a notable feat during an attack in which only 29 of roughly 350 Japanese planes were brought down.

The USS Doris Miller would be the first aircraft carrier named for a Black American and the first to honor an enlisted service member.It would also be the second Navy ship to carry Miller's name. A destroyer named for him entered the fleet in 1972 and was decommissioned in 1991.
Renaming a commissioned or planned Navy vessel is relatively uncommon; renaming the vessel for a sitting president would be unprecedented.

The Miller family said in a statement over the weekend that the family is "encouraged" that the ship will keep Miller's name ahead of several shipbuilding ceremonies -- the first of which is scheduled for Dec. 5 in Newport News, Virginia.

"Doris Miller’s legacy is not just our family’s history; it is American history. His courage deserves to be remembered, honored, and recognized for generations to come," Thomas Bledsoe, Miller's great-nephew and the family spokesperson, said in a statement.
ABC News' Tesfaye Negussie contributed to this report.

title: Rep. Jimmy Gomez to resign after House Ethics report he engaged in sexual misconduct
summary: Gomez lost his reelection bid in November.
story: Gomez lost his reelection bid in November.

California Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez said Monday that he will resign from Congress following a House Ethics Committee report that says the panel found "substantial evidence" that he "engaged in sexual misconduct … including making unwelcome sexual advances and sexual contact toward a House staffer."

"I recognize the seriousness of the Ethics Committee’s report and as I previously stated I take full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage," Gomez said in a statement.

Gomez, who lost his reelection bid in November, said he will resign on Dec. 1. Gomez represents California’s 34th Congressional District, which includes part of Los Angeles; he lost his race to Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres.

The committee said on Monday that it reviewed allegations that Gomez engaged in sexual misconduct in violation of the House’s Code of Official Conduct, including “engaging in inappropriate sexual contact with a House staffer." The report also said Gomez disregarded "the power imbalance inherent in his relationship with House staffers."
Gomez denied wrongdoing, saying his actions were "consensual" and that he did not violate House rules. Gomez also said he has "strong disagreements with the Committee’s report and its conclusions."

"Among other significant deficiencies and omissions, the report does not include key portions of my testimony that are essential to a full and fair understanding of what occurred," Gomez wrote in a statement. "I also have serious concerns about the process. In my interview, I answered the Committee’s questions only to see my statements selectively quoted, disparaged, and disregarded throughout the final report, to which I was given no opportunity to respond."
According to the report, however, the staffer testified that Gomez was "[p]retty forceful” and that an encounter between the two was "not consensual."

"Representative Gomez’s conduct caused this House staffer significant and ongoing distress and contributed to her decision to leave House employment altogether. Representative Gomez’s conduct also reflects a broader environment of sexual misconduct and toxic working conditions in some Capitol Hill offices which the Committee is determined to address,” the report stated.
The report said the committee reviewed "relevant documents" and interviewed 10 witnesses, including Gomez.
The report says that Gomez's behavior toward the staffer “could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse." There have been no criminal charges filed.
The committee found the staffer's account "credible in her assertions that his conduct toward her was unwelcome."
Attorneys Lisa J. Banks and Sarah E. Nesbitt of Katz Banks Kumin, who represents the staffer, praised the committee's report.

"Our client testified truthfully and at great personal risk. She sacrificed her own sense of safety and privacy to help reveal the ongoing misogyny and debauchery that permeates Capitol Hill.  Representative Gomez seems to believe that the power he wields, both as a man and as a member of Congress, makes him untouchable. Today’s findings are a meaningful step toward dismantling that belief,” the attorneys wrote in a statement.
The full House could still take action against Gomez before the end of the 119th Congress, although the committee did not make a specific recommendation.

"During the Committee’s consideration of this matter, Representative Gomez lost his bid for re-election to the House. In this circumstance, the Committee has observed that although there is not enough time for it to pursue an adequate House sanction, it remains essential that the Committee adopt and publish its Report so that the House is aware of Representative Gomez’s misconduct and so that the House may determine, in its judgment, whether to sanction Representative Gomez,” the report concludes.
Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries and top House Democratic leaders called Gomez's decision to step down “appropriate.”
“The report of wrongdoing and abuse of power by Rep. Gomez is serious and deeply troubling,” they wrote in a statement.
“Decisive action to set a new standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats,” they added.

title: Canada's defense minister says his country answers to no one in Washington
summary: Canada’s defense minister says that his country answers to no one in Washington, asserting Canadian sovereignty after the Pentagon accused Ottawa of failing to meet its military commitments
story: Canada’s defense minister says that his country answers to no one in Washington, asserting Canadian sovereignty after the Pentagon accused Ottawa of failing to meet its military commitments

TORONTO -- Canada’s defense minister said on Tuesday that his country answers to no one in Washington, asserting Canadian sovereignty a day after the Pentagon accused Ottawa of failing to do enough to defend North America.

The Pentagon said Canada lacked a credible plan to meet NATO’s spending targets, accusing Ottawa of relying for decades on American taxpayers to foot its defense bill. Relations between the two neighbors have been strained by U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st state.
“Canada is a sovereign nation. I’ll be very direct. We don’t report to the United States,” Defense Minister David McGuinty told reporters.

He insisted Canada remains on track to spend 5% of gross domestic product on defense and related security investments by 2035, while emphasizing that NATO allies had agreed to review the spending pledge in 2029.
“We also said by 2029 we would be examining that 5% commitment,” McGuinty said.
McGuinty said Canada’s plans would bring spending to 4% of GDP by 2030, a “significant, significant step” from 1.25% of GDP 14 months ago.

NATO’s 2025 agreement calls for at least 3.5% of GDP for core defense and up to 1.5% for related security investments by 2035. The scheduled 2029 review will examine the pace and balance of spending against security threats and military needs.
The Pentagon’s unusually blunt fact sheet on Monday accused Ottawa of postponing its largest spending increases until after the 2029 federal election.
“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves,” it said. “Canada must get serious and focused.”

The Pentagon said U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was “laser focused” on modernizing Canada’s military. The U.S. criticism followed a classified directive from Hegseth that Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said largely restricts officials’ participation in Canadian think tank events and social engagements.

The Trump administration barred Pentagon officials from attending the Halifax International Security Forum under restrictions imposed in 2025 on think tank participation. Now in its 18th year, the gathering draws about 300 military officials, U.S. lawmakers, diplomats and scholars annually. Previous administrations of both parties sent senior Pentagon officials, including defense secretaries.
Democratic U.S. Sen. Andy Kim, who attended the Halifax forum this past weekend, criticized the restrictions in a social media post.
“Hegseth did not allow a single American servicemember in uniform to show up,” he wrote.
Rounds said Saturday that the directive was not expected to affect joint military operations or intelligence sharing.

Canada reached NATO’s previous 2% target. Its latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by 2027-28, including 2.6% for core defense. Canada’s parliamentary budget watchdog has questioned how the government will reach 5%.
McGuinty said cooperation with Washington through the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, and work with NATO remained unchanged.
“We’re making the investments we announced. We’re executing on those plans,” he said.
The Pentagon also criticized Ottawa’s review of its planned purchase of 88 American-made F-35 fighters, warning that a mixed fleet could worsen personnel shortages and create uncertainty for NORAD.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered the review as Trump threatened Canadian sovereignty and imposed tariffs. Canada has examined Swedish-made Gripen fighters, which could bring manufacturing jobs.

title: Airline glitches, storms could make for a messy Thanksgiving travel week
summary: It’s shaping up to be a messy time for traveling heading into the Thanksgiving holiday
story: It’s shaping up to be a messy time for traveling heading into the Thanksgiving holiday

Traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past week, the threat of storms on both coasts and soaring airfares.
No wonder Americans are feeling jittery going into the busiest travel week of the year.
On top of all that, there's concern that a big storm brewing along the East Coast could ground the big balloons in the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.
The biggest unknown for travelers is whether airlines will be upended again by new system failures.

First there was the Federal Aviation Administration's network malfunction setting off the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. Then last week, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines saw their own outages, leading to hundreds of flight delays.
Delta said Monday that its operations were stable Monday, a day after over 1,000 of its flights were delayed after an automated system that calculates aircraft weight malfunctioned.
“Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers,” the airline said.
As of Monday morning, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 7% of Delta’s flights were delayed.
Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving are up more than one-third from the same time last year, according to estimates made in late October by the travel-booking company Hopper.

Holiday travelers can expect a rainy week on the East and West coasts and dry conditions in the nation’s mid-section, said Joe Wegman, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center.

Many eyes are on an East Coast system. Heavy rain and high winds are expected to start Wednesday night along the coast of the Carolinas, hit the New York City area on Thanksgiving Day and reach Maine by Friday, he said.

The windy forecast was causing concerns about whether the floats will be able to fly during the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. City law prohibits Macy’s from flying full-size balloons if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or wind gusts are over 35 mph (56 kph).
The weather service said it expected the rain in New York to hold off until after the parade ends, but winds could be an issue.
“This is poor timing with the storm coming up on Thanksgiving Day,” Wegman said. “Perhaps better timing that it’s happening on Thanksgiving Day rather on any of the travel days before and after.”

Rainy and windy weather also was expected on the West Coast. Moderate to major coastal flooding was forecast from Washington state to Southern California because of possible record-breaking king tides.

Rain was forecast for the Pacific Northwest on Monday, and expected to spread to northern and central California by Wednesday morning with snow possible in higher elevations, the weather service said.
Snow was forecast Monday for parts of the Rockies, northern Michigan, western New York state and northwestern Pennsylvania.

“Across the U.S., certainly check with your local airports and airlines for any possible delays,” Wegman said. “I think weather won’t be a significant factor except on Thanksgiving Day itself, and if there are any lingering impacts into Friday morning perhaps from delays that happen on Thanksgiving Day.”
Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio. Associated Press reporters Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; and Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

title: Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying flight
summary: Masked U.S. immigration officers have detained two people on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as passengers were boarding
story: Masked U.S. immigration officers have detained two people on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as passengers were boarding

Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a “distressing” scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.
Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who “overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws.”

During the confrontation, another passenger “hurled hot coffee on the officers,” the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.
Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.
Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

“We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306,” the airline said. “We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests.”
It added that the airline is committed to “treating every guest with dignity and respect.”
The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases look on.
ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities.”

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.”
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency's abolition.

“The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and local elected officials. “We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it. It is beyond reform.”
Ferguson also said he was looking into how ICE agents accessed the jet bridge and he believes they violated a state law he signed in March limiting facial coverings on law enforcement officers.

April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, representing over 600,000 workers, said union members were aboard the flight. She said the action disrupted travel during one of the busiest times and only days after flights were grounded nationwide due to a communications problem. “Airport workers are already managing extraordinary stress, passengers are already anxious and instead of restoring calm and confidence, federal agents introduced more fear and more chaos,” she said.

title: Alaska ends voter data agreement with Justice Department, which had been searching for noncitizens
summary: A Republican official who oversees Alaska elections says she has ended an agreement in which the state shared its detailed voter registration list with the U.S. Department of Justice and allowed the agency to flag voters for removal
story: A Republican official who oversees Alaska elections says she has ended an agreement in which the state shared its detailed voter registration list with the U.S. Department of Justice and allowed the agency to flag voters for removal

JUNEAU, Alaska -- A Republican official who oversees Alaska elections said she has ended an agreement under which the state shared its voter registration list with the U.S. Department of Justice and allowed the agency to flag voters for possible removal.

No voters were removed as a result of the agreement signed last December, and the Justice Department since then had not identified “any potentially ineligible voters or raised concerns regarding Alaska’s voter registration records,” the office of outgoing Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom said.

Dahlstrom said she notified the Justice Department that Alaska was terminating the agreement, effective Monday. That's also when Alaska officials announced that the results of the Nov. 3 general election, in which Democrats flipped a U.S. Senate seat and the governor's office, had been certified.

The Alaska Division of Elections directed the department to destroy the confidential voter information the state provided, Dahlstrom's office said in a statement released late Monday. A Justice Department spokesperson on Tuesday said the agency would send a formal response to the state.

The federal government's demand for detailed state voter information was part of a broader effort throughout the midterm election cycle to promote the idea that scores of noncitizens were on state voter rolls and potentially casting ballots illegally. In fact, years of research, state investigations and the Justice Department's own record of arrests showed the issue to be extremely rare.

The Justice Department sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for not complying with its demands to provide detailed voter registration data or other election-related records, with 28 of those lawsuits dismissed by courts, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. The department entered a settlement agreement with Oklahoma and dismissed its case with that state, the group said.

Alaska was one of at least 16 states to provide voter lists that included information such as driver’s license and partial Social Security numbers, dates of birth and addresses. Alaska and Texas also signed data-sharing agreements with the Justice Department, in which it outlined plans for its own analysis of voter files, its plans to flag voter list issues and directions for removing voters deemed ineligible.

Voting and civil rights groups sued Alaska elections officials earlier this year, alleging that sharing the state’s full voter registration list violated the Alaska Constitution and that terms of the agreement violated due process rights. That case is still pending.
ACLU Voting Rights Project, one of the organizations involved in representing the groups, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Dahlstrom said the Division of Elections “entered the agreement in good faith to cooperate with our federal law enforcement partners as permitted under Alaska law. The circumstances have now changed, the election has concluded and the agreement no longer serves a continuing purpose.”

She said Alaska "has strong list-maintenance procedures and will continue to protect both the accuracy of its voter rolls and the rights of eligible Alaska voters.” Her office said terminating the agreement “does not constitute an acknowledgment of wrongdoing by the Division of Elections."

Alaska state Sen. Bill Wielechowski, a Democrat and critic of the state's decision to hand over voter information, said Tuesday he believed the motivation for ending the agreement was to try to “make the lawsuit go away” before the administration of Alaska’s new governor, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, “could settle or produce discovery.”
He said he wants Kreiss-Tomkins’ administration to look into the circumstances surrounding the decision. Wielechowski also questioned the impact of the demand to delete the records.
Kreiss-Tomkins and his lieutenant governor, independent Zac Johnson, take office Dec. 7.

title: Records: Government, judge debated constitutional implications of searching Rep. Ilhan Omar's home
summary: A magistrate judge who authorized a search of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home by federal agents has ruled that the Minnesota Democrat was entitled to assert her right to privacy protections afforded to sitting members of Congress at the outset of the search
story: A magistrate judge who authorized a search of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home by federal agents has ruled that the Minnesota Democrat was entitled to assert her right to privacy protections afforded to sitting members of Congress at the outset of the search

WASHINGTON -- A magistrate judge who authorized a recent search of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar 's home by federal agents ruled that the Minnesota Democrat was entitled to assert her right to privacy protections afforded to sitting members of Congress at the outset of the search, according to court documents unsealed on Monday.

The unsealed filings reveal how Justice Department attorneys and U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh resolved their initial disagreement over the thorny constitutional implications of searching a member of Congress’ private residence for a criminal investigation.

The heavily redacted documents — released in response to a lawsuit filed by media organizations — do not appear to shed new light on the reason or outcome of the search itself or disclose new details of an immigration-fraud investigation that Omar claims is politically motivated.

Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, The Associated Press reported last month, citing a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.

The unsealed filings show that Sharbaugh — before authorizing the search of Omar's home — raised concerns about the “Speech or Debate Clause” implications of searching a private residence belonging to a member of Congress. The clause, which is designed to protect legislators from executive branch interference or intimidation, includes a privilege against compelled disclosures.
Sharbaugh said he disagreed with the government's argument that the privilege is limited only to official congressional offices and certain electronic devices.
“That logic does not hold,” the magistrate wrote.

Sharbaugh concluded that the government's law-enforcement interests needed to be balanced against Omar's constitutional rights as a member of Congress. He said the government ultimately agreed to a search protocol allowing Omar to invoke a privilege over any Speech or Debate Clause material before agents carried out the search.

Omar, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in Somalia, has been a target of anti-immigrant rhetoric by President Donald Trump and many Republican allies. She hasn’t been charged with any crimes and has denied any wrongdoing.

Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the partial unsealing of court filings related to the Oct. 12 search of Omar’s Washington, D.C., home by Department of Homeland Security agents. He ruled after over a dozen news organizations, including The Associated Press, argued that the public has a First Amendment right to access the records.

Boasberg agreed with the government that it would be premature to unseal a 67-page search warrant affidavit containing sensitive details of the government’s investigation. In a court filing last month, the government argued that it would jeopardize the investigation to unseal the court records before a charging decision is made.
An attorney for Omar didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment Monday on the unsealed documents.

Agents conducted the court-authorized search less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Omar won her reelection bid. The Justice Department historically has avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of an election.
Omar has said DHS agents seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift.
Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed to this report.
