title: Pacific Coast king tides could break decades-old records and flood communities
summary: High tides along the Pacific Coast could break records and flood low-lying areas, complicating travel during Thanksgiving week
story: High tides along the Pacific Coast could break records and flood low-lying areas, complicating travel during Thanksgiving week
SAN FRANCISCO -- High tides along the Pacific Coast could break 40-year-old records and flood low-lying coastal communities, complicating travel during Thanksgiving week.

In the San Francisco Bay Area, tides could reach 2.6 feet (0.8 meters) above normal Tuesday before peaking Wednesday at 2.8 feet (0.9 meters) above normal, said Dial Hoang, a National Weather Service forecaster.

The Bay Area’s highest recorded tide reached 2.9 feet (0.9 meters) above normal in San Francisco on Jan. 27, 1983, he said. San Francisco's famed Embarcadero waterfront, which flooded during heavy rain last week, is again at risk of flooding.

King tides, the highest tides of the year, occur when the gravitational pull of the moon and sun aligns to raise water levels. Their effects this year are being amplified by the ongoing super El Niño, which has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater.
The weather service issued a high surf warning in the Bay Area on Wednesday, when breaking waves of 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 meters) could overpower swimmers and sweep people into the ocean.
“Remain out of the water and stay off of jetties, piers, and rocks. Never turn your back to the ocean!” the agency said in a social media post.
Heavy rain forecast for Tuesday evening into Wednesday could worsen street flooding.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, who urged people over the weekend to consider avoiding holiday travel because of an “extremely serious” situation, later said the forecast had improved somewhat.

“As you make plans for Thanksgiving, keep the weather in mind. Check conditions before traveling, and avoid unnecessary trips when roads are flooded or winds are strong,” he wrote on social media on Monday.

Farther north, in Humboldt County near the Oregon border, the sheriff’s office ordered evacuations in a small coastal community where some buildings flooded on Monday, saying people needed to leave by Tuesday morning.

“The tides are expected to be higher by Tuesday, and the southerly winds will have been blowing for 24 hours by then, and so that will push the storm surge even higher,” said Matthew Kidwell, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Humboldt County.

National Weather Service offices in Portland and Seattle warned of coastal flooding through Friday. The most significant flooding could occur Tuesday through Thanksgiving Day as several weather systems bring strong winds and rising surf coinciding with high tides.
Waves can sweep people off rocks or knock them off their feet and pull them into the ocean, the agency warned.

Washington State Ferries has canceled several sailings because of high tides. About 300,000 people are expected to use the ferry system over the holiday weekend, and extreme tides could disrupt their trips.
Heavy snow in the mountains could slow holiday travel over passes, especially along Interstate 90 east of Seattle.

In South Florida, king tides are expected to cause coastal flooding from Palm Beach to Miami. Water levels could remain elevated for several hours before and after high tide Wednesday and Thursday mornings.
A storm arriving Tuesday night could increase the risk of flooding if it moves over land, the National Weather Service said.
Many South Florida communities were just beginning to dry out after slow-moving storms dumped more than 17 inches (43 centimeters) of rain less than a week earlier.

The St. Johns River has been above flood stage near Cocoa since Nov. 2. Last week, it broke a record set in 1953. The river is forecast to remain at least 2 feet (0.6 meters) above flood stage, according to the weather service.
Associated Press writers Martha Bellisle in Seattle and John Raby in Charleston, West Virginia, contributed.

title: How to make holiday travel less of an expensive hassle and get home safely
summary: The busiest week of the year for U.S. travel is getting off to a bumpy start
story: The busiest week of the year for U.S. travel is getting off to a bumpy start
The busiest week of the year for U.S. travel is getting off to a bumpy start.

Technology failures — including one earlier this month that led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years — are rattling air travelers. Bad weather is swirling around San Francisco and the East Coast.
“You start to get a little anxious,” said Debra Birnbaum, a journalist who lives in Los Angeles.
Birnbaum grew up in New York and planned to fly there Tuesday for Thanksgiving. She said she’s not an alarmist, but she still doesn’t feel like she fully understands the reasons for the ground stop.
“I wish the government had done a better job of explaining what happened and why,” she said. “If I could drive, I would drive.”

But driving has its own hassles. While gas prices have fallen over the last two months, Monday's national average of $3.64 per gallon for regular gasoline was still 18.5% higher than last year, according to AAA. Diesel, at $5.82 per gallon, was 54% higher than a year ago.
Here are some tips for easing travel headaches over the holiday season:
Motor club AAA predicted that 81.5 million people will travel at least 50 miles (80 kilometers) from home between Tuesday and the Monday after Thanksgiving. Ninety percent of them will travel by car.

Inrix, a transportation data provider, said that Tuesday and Wednesday would likely be the busiest days on U.S. roads, while next Sunday and Monday are busy as people return home. Major metro areas like New York, Washington, Los Angeles and Boston could see more than double their normal traffic congestion, Inrix said.

Motorists should consider hitting the road in the morning to avoid the heaviest congestion, Inrix said. The worst times for traffic will be in the afternoon and early evening, the company said. Another option, if time permits, is driving on Thanksgiving Day, when congestion is expected to be minimal.

U.S. gasoline prices are close to the Thanksgiving record of $3.56 per gallon, which was set in 2022, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, which tracks gas prices across the country.
“It’s still going to be one of the most expensive Thanksgiving Days that we’ve seen," De Haan said.

There is wide disparity in what stations are charging, he said, because some have been quicker to lower prices as the cost of oil drops. Some states, like Ohio, Georgia, Indiana and North Carolina, have also suspended their gas taxes, he said.
De Haan recommended that motorists use apps to check gas prices in their neighborhood and along their routes. He said other cost- and gas-saving measures include:
— Joining wholesale clubs and loyalty programs that offer lower gas prices.
— Using cruise control, which can decrease the amount of gas used during trips.
— Not exceeding 70 mph (113 kph).
— Traveling at off-peak times to avoid traffic jams.
— Removing items in vehicles to reduce their weight.
Think about the weather and emergency situations you might encounter, like traffic pileups in dense fog, as you put together an emergency kit for your vehicle.

The National Safety Council, a training and consulting organization, said drivers should check their emergency vehicle supplies every six months and replace expired items. Here are some items the group recommends:
— Mechanical: A properly inflated spare tire, wheel wrench, tripod jack, jumper cables, multipurpose utility tool, flashlight with extra batteries, duct tape
— First aid: Gauze, tape, bandages, antibiotic ointment, aspirin, non-latex gloves, scissors, thermometer, tweezers, instant cold compress
— Food: Drinking water and nonperishable, high-energy foods like nuts, dried fruit and hard candy
— Weather: Rain poncho, snow brush, shovel, warm clothing, cat litter for traction, windshield washer fluid
— Miscellaneous: Compass, reflective vest, fire extinguisher, cellphone charger

The Transportation Security Administration said it’s preparing to screen 17.6 million passengers nationwide between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30. More than 3 million people are expected to travel by air on Sunday alone.

The agency recommends arriving at least two hours before domestic flights and three hours before international flights to allow sufficient time for parking, airline check-in, baggage drop and security screening.

It also reminds travelers that containers with more than 3.4 ounces of liquids or spreads — think mayonnaise or chip dip — must be packed in checked bags. That includes cranberry sauce, gravy, maple syrup and canned fruit or vegetables. Holiday pies, meats and solid casseroles can be brought as carry-on items, the TSA said.

U.S. airfare prices have reached a 10-year high as airlines account for jet fuel cost increases in the wake of the U.S. war with Iran, according to travel booking site Hopper. As of late October, available flights for the Thanksgiving period cost 39% more than last year, while searches for flights around Christmas showed prices were up 40%, to an average of $466 for a roundtrip ticket, the company said.

To save money, consider shifting your itinerary by a day or two if you have the flexibility, Hopper's lead economist, Hayley Berg, advised. Flying on Thanksgiving Day and returning the following Monday or Tuesday can be hundreds of dollars cheaper than flying on Wednesday and Sunday, for example. Leaving the Monday or Tuesday before Christmas instead of the weekend before can also save money.

Berg also recommends considering different airlines and airports. This is the first holiday season since Spirit Airlines ceased operations in May, leaving consumers with one less ultra-low-cost option. But a handful of budget carriers, including Frontier and Allegiant, are still in business. Just factor in those airlines' extra charges for bags and seat assignments when comparing prices.
“If you’re going on a vacation rather than home for the holidays, shop around,” Berg said. “There might be deals from your local airport that you haven’t considered before.”
AP Airlines and Travel Writer Rio Yamat reported from Las Vegas. Dave Collins contributed from Hartford, Connecticut.

title: Miley Cyrus marries rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate Palm Springs wedding
summary: Singer Miley Cyrus has married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate ceremony in Palm Springs, California
story: Singer Miley Cyrus has married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate ceremony in Palm Springs, California
Pop culture icon Miley Cyrus married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate weekend wedding in Palm Springs, California, according to a post on the singer’s Instagram account.

The post said Cyrus, 33, and Morando, 28, were wed on Saturday. Photographs show the couple embracing in front of a white backdrop with a palm tree characteristic of the Palm Springs desert in the background, a large dog lying at their feet. In one photo, the couple kisses standing in an aisle of white roses.

The “Party in the U.S.A.” singer wore a long-sleeve silk Saint Laurent gown by Anthony Vaccarello and elegant white silk kitten heels, according to a statement from Saint Laurent. The dress had a low back, and she wore flowers in her hair, which was pulled back into an updo.
Morando wore dark, square shades. His single-breasted tuxedo was also made by the French luxury fashion brand.

The pair have been together since 2021, meeting after they were set up on a blind date, according to an interview Cyrus gave Vogue in 2023. Morando proposed to her while the couple were in Japan late last year, he said in a separate interview with Wonderland Magazine.
“I could feel my heart pounding” before popping the question, Morando said for a profile in the magazine.
Morando is the drummer of the rock band Liily.

title: 9 people shot at a central California concert; 1 in critical condition
summary: Nine people have been shot at a concert in central California, leaving one person critically injured
story: Nine people have been shot at a concert in central California, leaving one person critically injured
Nine people were shot at a concert in central California, leaving one person critically injured with a chest injury, the local sheriff said Sunday.

The shooting broke out around 7:30 p.m. Saturday at a concert attended by about 150 people in Strathmore, a small town in Tulare County, a mountainous region in the center of the state, the county sheriff's department said in a statement. An unspecified number of suspects opened fire on the crowd. No arrests were announced.

One 26-year-old man was shot in the chest and required surgery. He remained in critical condition, the sheriff's department said. Two other victims ages 19 and 22 also required surgery, while six people sustained minor injuries.

Authorities said that they believe the shooting “may be gang-related” but didn't elaborate. The show in the town of roughly 3,000 people featured performers from neighboring states, the department said.
The department didn't immediately respond to emailed questions seeking further details but said there was no longer any immediate threat to the public.

title: Trump targets Newsom and Democrats in Justice Department speech focused on violent crime
summary: President Donald Trump has condemned California Governor Gavin Newsom's decision to commute hundreds of death sentences
story: President Donald Trump has condemned California Governor Gavin Newsom's decision to commute hundreds of death sentences

WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump condemned California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s decision to commute hundreds of death sentences in the state, using a Justice Department visit to sharply chastise an outspoken Democratic critic who is considering his own bid for the White House.

The speech offered the president a platform to showcase what he said was his administration's success in combating violent crime, a favored Trump topic he has repeatedly invoked to rally his Republican base. But the address, Trump's second at the department in less than two years, veered openly into partisan politics as the president lambasted both a governor with whom he has openly feuded and a Democratic Party he depicted as soft-on-crime and part of a “radical left.”

“For years now, we have watched the radical left commit one betrayal of justice and safety after another,” Trump said in a speech that was also interspersed with first-person accounts from relatives of victims of crimes affected by Newsom's clemency who criticized the commutations.

Newsom has said the announcement this month to commute the sentences of more than 500 inmates to punishments of life in prison without parole was among the most difficult choices of his career because it will surface painful memories for crime victims’ families. The state’s Supreme Court would be required to approve the majority of those commutations.

“I won’t take lectures on accountability from a president who has used the pardon power to help wealthy friends and business associates avoid accountability while victims are left fighting to recover what was stolen from them. Justice should be about the people we serve, not the political interests of the people in power,” Newsom said in a statement about Trump's speech.

Asked at an event Monday why he didn't take the death penalty reveal to the ballot, Newsom said he had the “constitutional right” to do what he did. He added: “I may be the first to have received the kind of response from the sitting president of the United States at the Department of Justice with the FBI director — talk about weaponization.”
The speech marked the latest tussle between Trump and Newsom.

In June, Newsom accused the Justice Department of launching a politically motivated investigation into him and his wife, which his office said was focused on “increasingly personal matters involving the governor’s family and professional network.” He has denied any wrongdoing. The president has repeatedly gone after the heavily Democratic California during his second term and the state has pushed back by suing the federal government dozens of times.

The president's address unfolded against the backdrop of sweeping Republican losses in this month’s midterm elections, which gave Democrats control of the House and Senate. The development tees up possible congressional inquiries into everything from the mass firings of federal agents and prosecutors by the Trump administration Justice Department to a series of politically charged investigations into Trump adversaries that have been rejected by grand juries and judges alike.

Trump was introduced by Attorney General Todd Blanche, his former personal defense lawyer who has been unapologetic in his view that the Justice Department as an executive branch agency is an extension of the White House and that the president is free to exert his will over the institution. He said Monday that the Justice Department in the Trump administration was seeking the death penalty whenever appropriate.

“I want to take just a moment and tell every law enforcement member watching or here in this room that we have your back, that President Trump has your back, and he will always have your back,” Blanche said.

Trump has long sought to position himself as a tough-on-crime president who staunchly backs law enforcement. He has taken credit for dropping violent crime rates that experts say have been declining since 2022.

"Our opponents seek an America that empowers the most violent and dangerous elements and celebrates deviancy and enables dysfunction and demands empathy for serial killers and criminals, while hardworking citizens are treated with hatred and scorn and contempt,” Trump said Monday. “In the Trump administration, we believe in the exact opposite.”

As with last year’s speech, Monday’s remarks were delivered inside the ceremonial Great Hall of the Justice Department headquarters, a building whose exterior in the last year was decorated with a massive banner of Trump’s face in a physical demonstration of the president’s sway over the agency.

Trump's March 2025 address was meant to rally support for his administration’s policies on violent crime, drugs and illegal immigration but became a forum for a litany of complaints about the criminal cases Trump faced during Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration — when prosecutors charged him with hoarding classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, and with conspiring to overturn his 2020 election loss to Biden — and to vow retribution for what he described as the “lies and abuses that have occurred within these walls.”

He pledged at the time to expose the “egregious crimes and severe misconduct” of his foes. The Justice Department since then has accelerated efforts to investigate the president's enemies but has encountered multiple setbacks, with cases either thrown out by judges or spurned by grand juries that have refused to issue indictments.
___ Associated Press writers Jonathan J. Cooper and Aamer Madhani contributed to this report.

title: Chinese neuroscientist at Princeton is held by ICE after detention at Washington airport
summary: A Chinese neuroscience researcher at Princeton University is in the custody of immigration authorities after she was detained while trying to get on a flight back from Washington
story: A Chinese neuroscience researcher at Princeton University is in the custody of immigration authorities after she was detained while trying to get on a flight back from Washington

WASHINGTON -- A Chinese neuroscience researcher at Princeton University is in the custody of immigration authorities after she was detained while trying to get on a flight back from Washington, marking another instance of federal enforcement at airports.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year doctoral student at Princeton, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Thursday as she tried to fly back to New Jersey from a conference in the nation's capital, her university adviser Carlos Brody said in a social media post.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, says Xie overstayed her visa and did not have authorization to study in the United States.

“News of Eva’s detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” Rodney Priestley, dean of the university’s graduate school, said in a statement. "We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

Two days after Xie was taken into custody in Washington, masked immigration officers detained a father and daughter on an airport jet bridge in Seattle. ICE has ramped up detentions at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed their visas.

Kerry Doyle, Xie’s lawyer, said she came to the U.S. at age 14 with her family from China and has had an asylum application pending for years. Doyle insisted that Xie has permission to live, work and study in the U.S. while her case is pending.
Doyle said Xie is being held in ICE's Caroline Detention Center in Virginia.

DHS said in a statement that Xie came to the United States on a temporary visa on March 16, 2016, but “chose to violate our nation’s laws by refusing to depart by the required date of September 15, 2016.”
The agency said she did not have valid permission to study in the U.S. and “a pending application does not confer legal status.”
“Xie will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending her removal proceedings," the DHS statement said.

On her professional website, Xie said her research at Princeton Neuroscience Institute “seeks to understand the neural basis of decision-making.” She said she graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024.

title: Pentagon sharply rebukes Canada over defense spending and the F-35 fighter jet review
summary: The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets
story: The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets

TORONTO -- The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets.
In an unusually blunt fact sheet, the U.S. Defense Department on Monday said Ottawa had failed to make the tough decisions needed to modernize its military and meet NATO commitments.
“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves,” it said. “Canada must get serious and focused.”

Simon Lafortune, a spokesperson for Canada’s defense minister, said Canada had committed 81.8 billion Canadian dollars ($56.9 billion) over five years to rebuild its armed forces and reached NATO’s 2% defense spending benchmark five years ahead of schedule.

“Canada is also on track to meet NATO’s new commitment to invest 5% of GDP annually in defense by 2035 and is taking concrete steps to build the capabilities needed to meet that goal,” he said in a statement.
The Pentagon said U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was “laser focused” on modernizing Canada’s military after decades of American taxpayers footing the bill for its defense.

Canada reached NATO’s previous target of spending 2% of gross domestic product on defense and joined allies pledging to reach 5% by 2035, including related security investments. Its latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by 2027-28, but only 2.6% of GDP would go toward core defense.

The Pentagon accused Ottawa of having no credible, fully costed plan to meet NATO’s 5% target and postponing the largest spending increases until after the 2029 federal election. Canada’s parliamentary budget watchdog has also questioned how the government will meet the target.

The criticism follows a classified directive from Hegseth that Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said largely restricts U.S. military officials’ participation in Canadian think tank and social events. Relations have been battered by President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st state.

Wesley Wark, a Canadian national security expert and former government adviser, titled his Monday newsletter “Pentagon Pete strikes again,” calling the criticism “insulting and infuriating.” He suggested Washington was discounting Canada’s NATO deployment in Latvia and its support for Ukraine.
In May, Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby paused a U.S.-Canada defense advisory board established in 1940, accusing Ottawa of failing to make credible progress on its military commitments.
The Pentagon said only 41.9% of Canada’s air force fleet and 53.9% of its naval fleet were serviceable in 2025-26, while army readiness stood at 48%.

It also criticized Ottawa’s review of its planned purchase of 88 American-made F-35s, warning that a mixed fighter fleet could worsen personnel shortages. The Pentagon accused Canadian leaders of putting domestic economic interests ahead of military effectiveness, creating uncertainty for the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, which the countries operate jointly.

Prime Minister Mark Carney put the F-35 purchase under review as Trump threatened Canadian sovereignty and imposed tariffs. Canada has examined Swedish-made Gripen fighters, which could bring manufacturing jobs.
Carney has acknowledged readiness problems, saying only one of Canada’s four submarines was seaworthy. His government plans to buy up to 12 replacements.
“We should no longer send three-quarters of our defense capital spending to America,” Carney said in June.
Other NATO allies also remain short of the new 5% target. Yet Colby praised Germany’s military buildup Sunday as a “tectonic shift” and called Poland a “true model ally.”

The Trump administration had already barred Pentagon officials from attending the Halifax International Security Forum under restrictions imposed in 2025. The forum’s president, Peter Van Praagh, previously served as a senior adviser to a Conservative government in Canada.

Before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Van Praagh warned that Trump might undermine the results if Republicans suffered major losses. If those efforts succeeded, he said, it would mean “the end of the United States as we know it.”
Speaking at the Halifax forum Saturday, Rounds said Hegseth’s directive was not expected to affect joint military operations or intelligence sharing.

title: 3 killed, 1 wounded in shooting at Ohio baby shower, police say
summary: Authorities say an apparent domestic dispute turned deadly at a baby shower.
story: Authorities say an apparent domestic dispute turned deadly at a baby shower.
PARMA, Ohio -- Three people were killed and one was injured at an Ohio baby shower during an apparent domestic dispute, authorities said.
Officers responded to a shooting Saturday evening at Pandora’s Magical Events Venue in Parma, about 10 miles (16 kilometers) south of Cleveland, a police news release said.

Authorities said one of the shooters, a 29-year-old man, was taken into custody, but he wasn't immediately charged. Detectives were trying to determine whether the man was the aggressor or acting in self-defense, police spokesman Scott Traxler said. A second suspected shooter, a 19-year-old man, was one of the people killed, police said.

Officials have identified two of the victims as 17-year-old Leasia England and 45-year-old Jayson Townsend. Police said Townsend was the father of the woman for whom the baby shower was being held; she was not injured.
Officials haven't released the names of the 19-year-old suspected shooter who was killed, or a 39-year-old woman who was shot in the leg.

Preliminary information indicates that the 19-year-old man was the father of the unborn baby, and witnesses told police that he was not invited to the shower, Traxler said. The man in custody appears to be a relative of the expectant mother.

Both firearms involved in the shooting were recovered by police, officials said. Detectives were reviewing surveillance video and witnesses' statements on Sunday to determine what led to the violent confrontation, Traxler said. Ballistics testing might be required to determine which gun shot each victim.
Prosecutors will eventually determine whether the man in custody should be charged with a crime, officials said.

title: Data Centers Flood Black Communities Without Residents Having a Say
summary: Research shows majority-Black communities are over twice as likely to host data centers compared to majority-white ones
story: Research shows majority-Black communities are over twice as likely to host data centers compared to majority-white ones
By the time Zakiya Mabery learned that a $2 billion data center was planned just a 10-minute walk from her house, officials had already approved it.
The 200-acre facility in Augusta, Georgia, was first authorized in 2022 without a public hearing that would’ve allowed the community to voice their concerns.

Just months before the facility known as Project Eisenhower came to be, Mabery bought her home in a new housing development called Hayne’s Station. Since then, two-thirds of the people who’ve moved into the community have been Black.
“We would’ve never purchased a house if we knew a data center was coming,” she said about the project that began construction earlier this year.
Mabery’s experience exposes the racial divide in America’s data center boom — not just in where facilities are built, but in who gets a chance to question them.

Majority-Black communities are more than two times more likely to host a data center than majority-white ones and far less likely to receive the chance to hear about the projects before they’re approved or offer their opinion through public comment.
“It seems like (processes) are being built to silence citizens,” Mabery said at an Augusta Planning Commission meeting this past summer.
In recent years, dozens of AI data centers in communities home to hundreds of thousands of Americans have been approved without a public hearing.
For Black communities, the data center boom is extending a familiar pattern of environmental racism that has plagued families for generations.

Black communities are hosting infrastructure that generates wealth elsewhere. Meanwhile, they live with the pollution and disinvestment that undermines economic opportunity and contributes to poor health outcomes and premature deaths in their neighborhoods.

The stakes are growing as tech companies pour hundreds of billions of dollars into new infrastructure. President Donald Trump has pulled the levers of government in favor of these companies as he’s cast AI dominance as a competition the United States cannot afford to lose to China.

His administration has ordered agencies to exempt data centers projects from federal environmental review and to revise federal rules to accelerate their construction. At the same time, he has pushed federal agencies to limit the opportunities for public comment as the building boom reaches communities already carrying generations of industrial burdens.
The opportunity for residents to speak their mind is consequential to the outcome of a data center project.
On average, communities that have received a hearing before construction are nearly 80% white on average. Those without one are roughly 60% people of color.

When communities have received a public hearing, data centers have been blocked 66% of the time. When they don’t, they’re approved 80% of the time, according to Zoned Out, a tool created by researchers at Harvard University.

“We know disparities already exist in our communities, and now in the case of data centers, we’re seeing the targeting that happens without any say. It is systemic injustice,” said Aino Halonen, a former AI worker who led the Harvard study.

The racial disparities showed up during November’s midterm election. More than 40 jurisdictions nationwide allowed voters to decide if they wanted data centers in their communities via ballot measures. White residents made up an average of over 83% of the population in these places, compared with less than 5% for Black residents.
In Georgia, Mabery and her neighbors want a voice in what happens to their homes, health, and finances.

Data centers have increased PM 2.5 air pollution, which Black Americans die from at the highest rate in the U.S. The pollution can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing respiratory and cardiovascular disease. It is linked to asthma attacks, strokes, dementia, and cancer.

Carbon emissions from data centers are also connected to the intensification of climate change. America’s largest data centers are responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of climate change-causing carbon dioxide emissions annually — more than emissions from entire countries like Kenya and Guatemala.

“These are not emotional concerns. This is where we live. We invested here. We live and bear the impact here,” Augusta resident Charles Zabel said about the data center. “We ought to have a voice in this. So far, we have not had a meaningful voice in this discussion. Representation does not mean protecting a project. Representation means protecting the people who already call this place home.”

Researchers at George Washington University Law School joined American University researchers to analyze the placement of more than 5,200 data centers in the U.S., finding the major racial divide in where they’re found.

Researchers accounted for income, population density, home values, and proximity to major power lines, and compared neighborhoods within the same state to test whether economics or geography explained the racial disparities in where data centers were located and the benefits the communities received.
Even after those adjustments, neighborhoods with larger Black, Latino, and Asian populations remained most likely to have these negative experiences with data centers.
“Even when you control for all of that, race stands out,” said Dhanaraj Thakur, director of the Fair Technology Initiative at George Washington University.
“I think it’s important to show that this is not some anecdotal thing that’s happening in a few cities like Memphis or elsewhere,” he added. “It’s actually happening across the country.”

The difference often comes down to zoning. Due to the long tentacles of segregation and redlining, Black people are far more likely to live in communities that are home to tracts zoned for industrial use.

When a data center requires rezoning from, say, commercial to industrial, the approval process generally includes public notice, a hearing, and a vote. But if the land is already zoned industrial, developers can secure permits through an administrative review without requiring opportunities for residents to intervene.

As Capital B has reported, there have been several incidents where developers have pursued projects in poorer, majority-Black neighborhoods with more lax public hearing requirements after encountering opposition in wealthier, whiter areas.

After a data center was proposed in a wealthy, 65% white community in North Carolina, for example, thousands of residents were able to submit signatures and comments against the project. Then, the developer withdrew the project.

Weeks later, that same developer moved the project to another county in North Carolina, where the closest neighborhood was predominantly Black and had a median income that was just one-third of the former community’s. Commissioners in the county quickly approved the project in a 6-1 vote.

Even as data centers are more likely to be in communities of color, these same communities are less likely to receive major economic benefits, Thakur’s study found. Campuses operated by tech giants such as Meta, Google, and Microsoft are more likely to generate property-tax revenue and implement community benefit agreements, but those campuses are more likely to be in majority-white neighborhoods than communities of color.

That pattern raises the prospect that communities of color are shouldering the financial and environmental burdens of data center development writ large without the same potential financial rewards, the researchers wrote.

“A lot of the rhetoric coming from industry is that there are lots of economic benefits from data centers — tax revenue and job creation,” Thakur said. “These are what the industry groups promise, even though we’ve seen a lot of contradictions to that. But even if you do accept that as fact, the research shows that communities of color are less likely to receive those benefits.”
According to some analyses, Black workers make up just 7% of AI workers compared to 13% of the general population.

As for construction, for one week last fall, Capital B spent every morning and evening outside the site for Meta’s data center in northern Louisiana, the largest project in North America. The two closest towns are over 80% Black. None of the workers Capital B spoke to or saw drive off in their Ford F-150s were Black.

As Black communities bear the brunt of this crisis, increasingly, they’ve also been left out of the imagined face of the opposition. Nationwide, roughly 70% of Americans opposed data centers. As such, the fight has been framed by advocates and politicians as one that crosses all racial and political boundaries.
But researchers found that the flattening of data center opposition to an “American problem” has erased the racial injustices permeating the boom.

Communities that have been highlighted via the media in resistance to data centers were about 79% white on average, compared with 53% white in communities without recorded opposition. They said that the disparity reflects unequal media coverage, political influence, and organizing resources.
“It’s interesting that only some communities are being highlighted as opposing it,” Thakur said. “It is erasing the nuance and racial inequality” at the heart of the boom.
At Capital B, we’ve highlighted Black communities fighting data centers everywhere from Memphis to Maryland and Mississippi.

In Augusta, where the community closest to the massive data center site is 67% Black, residents are committed to fighting for a say. This summer, the board of commissioners approved a temporary moratorium on data center development. The $2 billion construction project was not included in the blockage.
“We are asking for respect,” Mabery said.
This report is a collaboration between Capital B, the Pulitzer Center and The Associated Press.

title: Two central Ohio bus drivers killed, nine others injured after head-on crash
summary: Two Columbus transit bus drivers have been killed and nine others injured after their vehicles collided during the morning rush hour in Ohio's state capital and one bus was struck by a third vehicle
story: Two Columbus transit bus drivers have been killed and nine others injured after their vehicles collided during the morning rush hour in Ohio's state capital and one bus was struck by a third vehicle
COLUMBUS, Ohio -- Two transit bus drivers were killed and nine others were injured after their vehicles collided during the morning rush hour Monday and a third vehicle became involved in the crash.

According to Columbus police, the two Central Ohio Transit Authority buses collided head-on on the city's north side at around 8 a.m. The third vehicle collided with the rear or side of one of the buses or was rear-ended.
“Early indications are that one of the buses, for reasons unknown, crossed a double yellow line and struck the other bus head-on,” said Columbus Police Sgt. Joseph Albert.
COTA identified the drivers as Richard Terry, 53, and Paul Copeland, 60, who had joined the transit authority in 2012 and 2008, respectively.

“We are heartbroken by the tragic loss of Richard and Paul, two valued members of our COTA family who dedicated their careers to serving our community,” Monica Tellez-Fowler, COTA's president and CEO, and Tyson Brown, president of Transportation Workers Union Local 208, said in a joint statement.
Police said one of the bus operators was pronounced dead at the scene, while the second man was transported from the crash site in critical condition before dying at the hospital.

Nine other individuals, either bus riders or passengers in the third vehicle, were transported to area hospitals, according to police. They were all in stable condition Monday with non-life-threatening injuries. No pedestrians were injured, Albert said.
Columbus City Council President Shannon Hardin and council member Lourdes Barroso de Padilla, who chairs the public service and transportation committee, called the accident “heartbreaking.”

“Our hearts go out to all those impacted by Monday’s accident, especially to the loved ones of those killed,” they said in a statement. “While we try to understand how this tragedy happened, we must not forget the lives lost and the families that will be mourning them just as we enter the holiday season.”

COTA said it was working with investigators to determine the cause of the crash and providing support and counseling services to affected employees. Some operators were relieved from work Monday as part of their grief support. COTA asked for patience with any associated cancellations or delays.

title: Natural gas pipeline fire shoots flames in Alabama, cause under investigation
summary: A pipeline in rural Alabama sent a column of flames high into the night sky.
story: A pipeline in rural Alabama sent a column of flames high into the night sky.

WARD, Ala. -- A fire on a natural gas pipeline lit up the night sky in rural Alabama late Saturday with a towering column of orange flame, prompting the operator to shut down part of the line but causing no injuries, the company said.
The cause of the fire is under investigation and customer deliveries were not impacted, Southern Natural Gas Company said in a statement Sunday.

Photos and videos posted on social media appeared to show flames rising dozens of yards (meters) above the trees near Ward, with smoke billowing into the air. People said on social media that the fire was visible from miles (kilometers) away across the state line in Mississippi.

Southern Natural Gas said it “experienced a natural gas release and fire” on the segment of the pipeline at around 11:30 p.m. CST Saturday. Emergency responders and company personnel secured the area and the blaze was extinguished, the company said. The impacted part of the pipeline was shut down and depressurized.
The Sumter County Emergency Management Agency did not immediately respond to a voicemail seeking information.

title: Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo can't undergo surgery after swallowing a hat
summary: The Cincinnati Zoo says staff members are doing everything they can to help its beloved hippo Fiona after she swallowed a knit hat
story: The Cincinnati Zoo says staff members are doing everything they can to help its beloved hippo Fiona after she swallowed a knit hat

Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's famed hippo, underwent a colonoscopy this week, and now veterinarians are trying a new way to help her pass a knit cap that she swallowed after it slipped into her enclosure.
The zoo's animal care team borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, hoping the shaking will help move things along through her digestive tract, the zoo said Wednesday.
Video released by the zoo Wednesday shows Fiona snorting and moving about her indoor enclosure.
Veterinarians sedated her Tuesday for a second time to evaluate her condition, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health.
An ultrasound showed some bunching of her intestines, indicating she is still trying to pass the obstruction, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy, using a 9-foot scope, he said.
Specialists have told the zoo that surgery isn’t an option for full-grown hippos, he said.

Fiona, who became a global sensation as a tiny newborn after her premature birth in 2017, has inspired books, a line of beer and a bobblehead. During her first year, the zoo recorded her progress while fans worldwide followed her growth online.
She initially couldn’t stand on her own and weighed just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms) at birth, 25 pounds (11.3 kilograms) less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species.

The beloved hippo swallowed the hat just over a week ago. A visitor tossed it into the air, and a ceiling fan caught and catapulted it through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows, said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.
Zoo staff are now monitoring her around the clock, trying to keep her hydrated and giving Fiona her favorite foods to help her pass the knit cap, the zoo said.
“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked,” Curley said Wednesday. “And they were happy to see her respond.”

title: Central Park's horse-drawn carriage drivers sue NYC over incoming ban
summary: Central Park’s horse-drawn carriage drivers have sued New York City to stop a new law that will ban the iconic tourist attraction, challenging Mayor Zohran Mamdani just minutes after he signed a bill to wind down the industry
story: Central Park’s horse-drawn carriage drivers have sued New York City to stop a new law that will ban the iconic tourist attraction, challenging Mayor Zohran Mamdani just minutes after he signed a bill to wind down the industry

NEW YORK -- Hold your horses: Central Park's horse-drawn carriage drivers sued New York City on Thursday to stop a new law that will ban the iconic tourist attraction, challenging Mayor Zohran Mamdani just minutes after he signed a bill to wind down the industry.
The law — approved after the death of a teenager last spring — is set to stop the carriage rides by June 2028.
But the union representing carriage drivers filed a federal lawsuit in Manhattan attempting to have the ban struck down, arguing the city is taking away their livelihoods.
“The City’s approach can be summarized in twelve words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate,” the lawsuit reads.

The lawsuit is the latest turn in a long fight over the carriage rides, as animal welfare activists and industry supporters have tussled over whether the carriage rides amount to animal cruelty or are simply a romantic throwback to the city's past.

At a bill signing ceremony at City Hall on Thursday, Mamdani lauded the role of horses in the city’s development but said the animals should no longer be hauling tourists around a perpetually busy Central Park among joggers, cyclists and other passersby.
“Our city has changed and now it is time for our laws to change, too,” said Mamdani, a Democrat.

City lawmakers reignited their push for a ban earlier this year in response to the death of 18-year-old Indian tourist Romanch Mahajan, who died after jumping from a runaway carriage in what appeared to be the first fatality in a horse carriage accident since they were introduced in Central Park.

Over the years, horses have collapsed or gotten startled and run off into cars or other objects. In response, the city has put various safety regulations in place for the industry, including veterinary checkups, vacation time for horses and a retirement age for the animals.

City Hall has promised to release a career transition plan for those in the carriage industry next April that includes job training, educational pathways and stipends, though drivers argue their future remains uncertain.

"Despite the good intentions of the mayor, the protections he outlined recently should have been written into the legislation," said John Samuelsen, head of the Transport Workers Union, which represents carriage drivers.
The union's lawsuit argues the law is unconstitutional and that the city violated local legal procedures when it approved the law. It names the mayor and various other city officials as defendants.
A spokesperson for the city's law department said it is reviewing the case.

title: Iran war costs surpass $48B as lawmakers demand unreleased estimates on base damage
summary: The Iran war’s costs have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13
story: The Iran war’s costs have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13

WASHINGTON -- The costs of the Iran war have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13, but because that total does not include damage to U.S. bases attacked in the Middle East, lawmakers are pushing for the Pentagon to provide those figures.

Arthur Miller, a Pentagon budget official, provided the latest overall cost estimate Thursday to the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is considering his nomination to be Navy comptroller. The $48 billion figure includes the costs of military operations, as well as for replacing equipment and munitions.

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut pressed Miller for an estimate on damage to U.S. installations, which Miller said he didn't have. Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, the committee’s chair, directed Miller to try to provide an answer as soon as possible.
An Associated Press analysis found that Iran attacked aircraft hangars, systems that detect incoming strikes, warehouses, troop housing and more, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage.

The war's price tag has been a flashpoint in Congress, with debates over costs intensifying as the Trump administration asks lawmakers to pass a $1.5 trillion defense budget. After the unpopular war and its economic effects contributed to severe Republican losses in the midterm elections, financial battles over the conflict will only escalate once Democrats take control of Congress in January for the remainder of President Donald Trump's term.
The Pentagon has faced growing calls from Democrats to release estimates on the damage Iran has done to American bases in the Middle East through missile and drone attacks.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on the costs of the war at his confirmation hearing Tuesday for the permanent job.

Citing independent estimates and media reports, Warren said the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian shipping costs about $32.5 million a day, while an Iranian attack on the Navy’s regional headquarters in Bahrain did at least $400 million in damage.

Cao confirmed the figure for the blockade but said he could not offer a full damage assessment in Bahrain because “it’s a nonpermissive area for us to go." Cao told a reporter months ago that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain.”

title: UK, EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, reshaping post-Brexit relationship
summary: UK and EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, pledging an “ambitious and dynamic” post-Brexit relationship
story: UK and EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, pledging an “ambitious and dynamic” post-Brexit relationship
BRUSSELS -- UK and EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, pledging an “ambitious and dynamic” post-Brexit relationship.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.

A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials met with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together.

Burnham said the two sides would agree to a “pragmatic” set of deals that will make it easier for food products and young people to move between Britain and the bloc, but leave big questions about the relationship unanswered. Months — likely years — of negotiations lie ahead on everything from student fees to manufacturing rules.
“The deal is done,” a British government spokesperson said, adding that details would be published in a joint statement later.

Burnham was scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners.

Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.
“The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained,” he said this week.

Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.

Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be “a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security.”
Burnham pitched the package of agreements expected to be agreed Friday as a way of “cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people.”
He said “a closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe.”
The deals are set to include an agreement for up to 100,000 young adults from Britain to live and work in EU countries for up to three years, and the same number of Europeans to come to the U.K.

There will also be an emissions trading agreement and a deal to remove checks on food and agricultural products that will make things cheaper and easier for British exporters to Europe. Burnham said Friday the deals could add 0.5% to Britain’s economy — he'd previously set it at 0.4%.

But nothing in U.K.-EU relations is ever quick or simple. An EU official said the package is contingent on the two sides reaching agreement on university tuition fees in the next six months. EU negotiators want European students to pay domestic fees if they study in Britain rather than the higher fees for foreign students, something the U.K. has resisted. The official said negotiations had not been easy but they sensed good will to resolve the issue.
The official was designated to brief reporters about the summit but only on condition that they not be named.
Talks are also continuing on Britain's desire to have access to the bloc’s “made in Europe” rules for manufacturing.
To get the deals, the U.K. must accept some EU rules and standards that it has no role in setting. Supporters of Brexit say that undermines Britain’s independence.

“I’m afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again,” Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told the BBC. He said “it’s perfectly clear that this very, very soon becomes a debate about: do we rejoin or do we stay out?”

The war in Ukraine, and the U.K.’s military strength, are drawing the two back together, and the summit provides the EU with an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.

“Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential,” Costa said ahead of the meeting. “By deepening our cooperation, we can strengthen our ability to address the challenges of our time, strengthen our resilience and promote stability in Europe and beyond.”

Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want real clarity about the country’s intentions.

Ireland’s ambassador in London, Sonja Hyland, said that when Britain voted for Brexit, “there was a lack of clarity as to exactly what that meant.” If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must “make a clear decision as to what it wants.”
Lawless reported from London.

title: Nations at UN talks on AI killer robots agree to more talks but no firm commitment to rein them in
summary: Efforts to establish rules for AI-powered killer robots and drones have run aground
story: Efforts to establish rules for AI-powered killer robots and drones have run aground
GENEVA -- Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as U.N.-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.

Scores of countries ended the week-long U.N. conference on weapons by agreeing to “elaborate” a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they didn’t commit to binding rules sought by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries, and activists.
The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts and major military powers jockeying for dominance.

Izumi Nakamitsu, the U.N. high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a “significant achievement” but acknowledged a “glass half full or half empty” scenario, citing Guterres’ hopes for a legally binding deal this year.
Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language.

Stop Killer Robots lamented a “watered-down mandate,” and Beatrice Fihn, founder of international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounts to “pushing the can down the road for two more years."

They noted most countries supported work toward a new treaty, and Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said: “States have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue, for the 14th year, while these weapons enable atrocities.”

Before the meeting, seven countries proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook that could prevent or limit the ability of machines to kill without human control or accountability. That effort fell short.

“Technology is moving faster than diplomacy,” said Ambassador Frederico Meyer of Brazil, which joined Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama in proposing such negotiations. “Diplomats are very slow.”

After years of talks on the issue, advocacy groups bemoaned obstructionism largely by Russia, which, like other top AI weapons-developing countries such as the United States, wants a freer hand to develop such high-tech weapons.
Guterres, who leaves office at the end of the year, set a 2026 deadline for launching negotiations toward an agreement on autonomous weapons systems.
Pope Leo XIV and many advocacy and humanitarian groups have framed the issue as an existential debate, urging quick action to rein in AI weapons before they become too commonplace to regulate easily.
Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened.

Talks this week centered on the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, ratified by 128 countries, where decisions are made by consensus. That means any single country can thwart an agreement, and that any deal was likely to be based on a low common denominator.

title: San Francisco braces for massive tides, mayor urges residents to reconsider travel
summary: Scattered rain is exacerbating the impacts of historic flooding across central Florida, as Northern California braces for an unprecedented deluge accompanied by high tides ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday
story: Scattered rain is exacerbating the impacts of historic flooding across central Florida, as Northern California braces for an unprecedented deluge accompanied by high tides ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday

Scattered rain continued to exacerbate the impacts of historic flooding across central Florida on Saturday, even as officials in Northern California braced for an unprecedented deluge during high tides heading into the heavy Thanksgiving travel week.

San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie warned that an “extremely serious” situation was about to hit the city, based on National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and National Weather Service forecasts, and urged people to consider not traveling for the holiday.

“We are expecting tides that the National Weather Service told us they have never seen before in recorded history here in San Francisco,” Lurie said via the social platform X. “Take this weekend to get yourself ready, please stock up on supplies, get your shopping done, and know that the city will be out all weekend doing everything possible to protect our residents and our small businesses.”

Storm systems impacting Florida and California are an offshoot of El Niño, the natural warming of the Pacific near the equator that warps weather patterns worldwide. Florida typically experiences its dry season from October to May, for example.

The expected deluge in California coincides with the highest tides of the year, called king tides. Forecasters said up to 2 feet (0.6 meters) of flooding would be likely in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways through 6 a.m. Monday, and through 4 p.m. Thursday along other areas of the Pacific coast.

Forecasters also warned of dangers Saturday along Florida's Atlantic coast. The weather service issued marine warnings to boaters tied to thunderstorms capable of creating destabilizing waterspouts, and advised beachgoers to beware of rough surf and dangerous rip currents.

NWS meteorologist Melissa Watson in Melbourne said that while the heaviest rains have passed, water levels were expected to continue to rise along the St. Johns River, Florida’s longest, due to continued lighter showers. Near the city of Cocoa, the river rose above a 1953 record Thursday.
“Regardless of any additional rainfall, we are expecting these river floods to continue for an extended period of time,” Watson said.
Heavy rain earlier this week submerged large swaths of Florida’s Atlantic coast, trapping people in floodwaters in the northeastern part of the state.
Associated Press journalist Donna Warder contributed.

title: Prosecutor declines to charge white officer who fatally shot Black man in Wisconsin
summary: A Wisconsin prosecutor is not filing criminal charges against the police officer who shot and killed a 38-year-old Black man in Madison in July
story: A Wisconsin prosecutor is not filing criminal charges against the police officer who shot and killed a 38-year-old Black man in Madison in July

MADISON, Wis. -- The Madison police officer who shot and killed a 38-year-old Black man in July, sparking racial justice protests and renewed calls for police reform, will not face criminal charges, a prosecutor announced Thursday.

Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, a white officer with more than a decade of experience in law enforcement, fired the shots that killed Corey Ruiz on July 22. Baitinger-Peterson was one of four officers who responded to calls about someone checking out parked cars and an alleged burglary attempt, police said. They surrounded Ruiz, who was on a bicycle.

“I conclude it was reasonable for the officer to use deadly force when this person resisted officers, produced a knife, and was not affected by multiple attempts to use Tasers while officers attempted to take him into custody,” Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne said in a statement announcing his decision.

The Wisconsin Department of Justice said immediately after the shooting that two officers attempted to use a Taser on Ruiz but weren’t successful. Ruiz “brandished a knife and injured” Baitinger-Peterson, the department said.

Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who represents Ruiz’s family and had called for the officer to be charged, said in a statement that there was nothing in the videos that the district attorney showed them on Thursday to justify the shooting.

“The medical examiner told the family that if the officer had not fired that shot to his head, Corey would have survived,” Crump said. “It was clearly an excessive use of force. This police killing in Madison, Wisconsin, was unjustifiable, unreasonable, unnecessary, and unconstitutional.”

Ozanne said he reached his decision after reviewing evidence that included police reports, diagrams, surveillance videos, police squad car videos and citizen videos. Madison police officers do not wear body cameras.
“In the video you see they tackle him, they tase him, they kick him and then the police officer executes him,” Crump said during a news conference. “The video is the objective unbiased witness here.”
“That is an execution,” he said. “When you are shooting a man who is on the ground, three (times). It hits him in his chest and the kill shot hits him in his head.”
Crump said the medical examiner told the Ruiz family he would have survived had the third shot not been fired and hit him in the head.
Ozanne said his decision was a correct interpretation of the law.

“A person does not have to like and/or agree with the law, however I am sworn to apply the law to the facts at hand,” the prosecutor said. “The law applies equally to members of law enforcement and to those who are not.”
Baitinger-Peterson has not replied to an email seeking comment.

Executive Director Jim Palmer of Wisconsin Professional Police Association, the police union, said in a statement the decision that the officer's use of deadly force was legally justified “is supported by the evidence and consistent with the legal standards governing the use of force by law enforcement officers.”

It was the third time since 2012 that Madison police had shot and killed someone in the same neighborhood. The killing sparked days of protests and forced the city to reckon with calls for police reform to address racial justice issues.
Baitinger-Peterson and the other three officers who interacted with Ruiz that day have been on paid administrative leave since the shooting.

While bystanders captured the confrontation on video, there is no body camera footage because Madison police officers don’t wear them. All Madison police officers could be equipped with body cameras by the end of 2027 thanks to a $350,000 donation from a local nonprofit that city officials announced in September.
The donation will help cover operational expenses, while other costs are being funded through grants and other means.
Associated Press journalist Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed.

title: Trump administration use of encrypted messaging apps like Signal is scrutinized by House Democrat
summary: A Democratic lawmaker is investigating the use of encrypted messaging apps by Justice Department employees for official business
story: A Democratic lawmaker is investigating the use of encrypted messaging apps by Justice Department employees for official business

WASHINGTON -- A top House Democrat is demanding that multiple government agencies preserve communications created on nongovernment messaging apps and investigate whether any records related to official business have been deleted.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee and the panel's incoming chairman, said in a series of nearly identical letters made public on Friday that he was concerned that President Donald Trump's administration was circumventing record-keeping requirements by using apps like Signal that can be configured to automatically delete messages after a certain time period.

Raskin noted in the letters, which were sent to top officials at the FBI, the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security, the Bureau of Prisons and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, that the agencies were legally required to preserve all records related to their official business, policies and decisions.

But he said: “There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records, seemingly with the express purpose of circumventing federal record preservation laws. This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials.”

The Maryland Democrat cited as an example a Signal exchange that he said he had obtained between the FBI’s general counsel and an associate of the Republican president's oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., in which a potential or ongoing healthcare fraud investigation was discussed.

The Justice Department said in a statement Friday that it “follows all legal requirements for the management of federal records involving its official functions and decisions.” The other agencies cited by Raskin did not immediately return messages seeking comment.

Signal is an app that can be used for direct messaging and group chats as well as phone and video calls. It uses end-to-end encryption for its messaging and calling services that prevents any third party from viewing conversation content or listening in on calls.
Encrypted messaging apps are increasingly popular with government officials, an Associated Press review from last year found.

Their prevalence was demonstrated in vivid fashion last year when journalist Jeffrey Goldberg revealed that he had been inadvertently added to a Signal group chat of U.S. national security officials coordinating plans for airstrikes.

The White House and the Pentagon have said that disgruntled former employees were spreading false claims about the use of Signal, a commercially available app not authorized to be used to communicate sensitive or classified national defense information.

title: Beloved drive-thru worker on making a year's salary on last day of work
summary: When Sighle Williams decided to retire from Mac's Drive Thru after 37 years, she never could have expected the send-off she received, which is the focus of a new Netflix documentary.
story: Sighle Williams keeps it simple.
"I just like to treat people the way I like to be treated," she told "CBS Mornings."

So when Williams, who'd spent her 37-year career making people smile at Mac's Drive Thru in Gainesville, Florida, was approached about having a documentary made about her last day, she was excited but a bit skeptical.
That short film, called "One Last Order," premieres on Netflix Tuesday and has already garnered awards from the Aspen Shortfest, Nantucket Film Festival, Miami Film Festival and more.

The movie documents Williams' final day on the job, but it also shows the side of Williams that her beloved customers didn't see, like how she raised five girls — her sister and niece's children — as her own. The film shares how she lived in a house for a while with no running water or electricity.
"I just did what I needed to do, I knew I needed to make sure they were straight, and I needed to make sure I went to work," she said.
When she went to work, she made everyone feel like she was glad to see them. She remembered people's orders.

On her last day at Mac's, her boss decided that every dollar made would go back into Williams' pocket as a retirement bonus. Community members lined up around the block and waited for up to four hours to say goodbye and give Williams one final order.
The whole thing made her feel on "top of the world," she told "CBS Mornings."

"I didn't even eat all day, I didn't go to the restroom all day," Williams said, "I was just so -- I wanted to acknowledge everybody and thank everybody for coming out, you know, sharing the love with me on my last day."
She ended up making a year's salary on that final day, but won't reveal how much she made.
"I don't want nobody to feel no type of way because, you know, I'm hamburgers and fries," she said.
Now that she's been retired for a couple of years, Williams has some time for herself.
"I'm traveling, I'm ready to go," she said. "With the film fests, I've been going to different places and enjoying myself."
When asked about where her drive comes from, she said, "Just be kind. Just be patient and, you know, don't take everything so serious."

title: Don Toliver concert in U.K. evacuated due to mystery substance
summary: Some 12,000 fans of American rapper Don Toliver had to evacuate his concert in Manchester, England, after a noxious substance spread through the arena.
story: More than 12,000 people were evacuated from an arena in northern England Sunday night after the crowd at American rapper Don Toliver's concert suddenly started screaming, choking and coughing when a powerful smell spread through the venue.
Police said the Co-op Live arena in Manchester was evacuated at about 10 p.m. (5 p.m. Eastern).
There's been speculation online that the mysterious substance that spread through the air in the arena was tear gas, but authorities have not confirmed that.
Don Toliver, who is set to end a world tour with a Tuesday night show in London, left the stage in Manchester and police declared it a major incident.
One person was hospitalized and dozens were assessed for eye and respiratory symptoms according to the local ambulance service.
The arena was being fully decontaminated as a precaution, the emergency medical service said.
Ben Stevenson told the Manchester Evening News newspaper that he was in the audience standing section when he "started coughing and (my) eyes were kind of itchy."

He said the lights came on as Toliver left the stage, but that everyone remained in the venue for almost an hour before an announcement asking people to make their way out was heard over the loudspeaker.
"We will now begin to fully understand what this substance was and how this incident came about," Police Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker told reporters.
The venue opened in 2024 and is only about 2 miles from the Manchester Arena, where 22 people were killed in 2017 by a suicide bomber who blew himself up during an Ariana Grande concert.

title: Tony Shalhoub on food, family, and his book, "We Thought They'd Never Leave"
summary: For the award-winning star of "Monk," food had always been an integral part of family. And now he's teamed with daughter Josie Adams to write a food memoir: "We Thought They'd Never Leave," the story of their family reunions - and their recipes.
story: He was a detective with a quirk in "Monk," and played an alien opposite the "Men in Black." But if you really want to feel the soul of Tony Shalhoub, this character might be it: the stubborn chef Primo in "Big Night," his 1996 film with Stanley Tucci about food, family and … even more food.

Shalhoub is himself an investor in a New York City restaurant, Massara, where he invited us last week to break bread with his daughter, Josie Adams. The act of breaking bread, he said, is very important: "It's part of the family tradition, really. Having bread at the center of the table, it's how we were formed."
He's even made a TV series, "Tony Shalhoub Breaking Bread," about different types of bread from different places.

For him and his family, the passion for food can be traced back to a time when there wasn't any. Shalhoub's father, Joseph, was born in war-torn Lebanon. Orphaned at a young age, he faced hunger and food shortages as a child. "A lot of his early memories were about that hunger," he said, "so that ties into our current family situation and our appreciation for and devotion to preparing food and feeding each other."
The Shalhoubs settled in Green Bay, Wisconsin, and by the time Tony came along in 1953, there were a lot of mouths to feed; he was one of ten children.

The family was close, and stayed that way. Every summer, the entire extended Shalhoub clan – more than 50 in all – gathers in Wisconsin for a reunion. It's a week of big, homecooked meals and intense family bonding. And when the party's over, everyone gets a traditional Shalhoub family send-off: "At the end of the week," Tony said, "as people are loading up their cars, everyone else who's remaining gathers in a line in the drive and raises their hands," and a chorus cries out: "We thought they'd never leave!"
"We Thought They'd Never Leave" became the title of a book Shalhoub co-wrote with Josie, the story of their family and its recipes.

She actually started it during the pandemic, when both of her parents (Tony and actor Brooke Adams) were sick with COVID, and she feared that their memories and recipes would be lost forever. So, she gave them both journals to write it all down. "My dad was like, 'Do you think we're going to die? Why are you giving us this right now?'" Josie said. "He's like, 'I'm better now!' So I said, 'OK, well, will you maybe work on this cookbook with me? I'd like to do the family cookbook for real.' And he said yes."

Shalhoub and his wife raised two daughters in Los Angeles as he navigated the feast-or-famine life of a Hollywood actor. But for every Emmy-winning success like "Monk," there were lesser roles. "Sometimes there were jobs that I did that were just for the money," he said. "Do I regret doing those jobs? Not really. I mean, maybe one or two, but sometimes you just got to eat."
In 2016 he said he wanted to take a break from screen acting, move to New York, and just do live theater. He won a Tony Award for best lead actor in a musical for "The Band's Visit."
But then he got a job offer that was irresistible. As family patriarch Abe Weissman in "The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel," Shalhoub won his fifth Emmy.

In real life, Shalhoub has been married to Brooke Adams for 34 years, and he actually does a lot of the cooking at home. Josie said, "Yeah, you cook for Mom a lot. Every morning my dad wakes up before my mom and makes her a cappuccino and brings it to her in bed. Every single morning."
"Except when I'm not there!" he laughed.
And that's the Shalhoub family's love language: cooking and serving each other, whether it's one loved one, or a crowd of 50.

Josie said, "It's really easy to send a text and say, 'I love you, thinking about you.' But it's a lot harder to do something for someone else. And that's what this whole reunion is about: getting together and showing the people that you love, that you love them."
