title: Trump presents Rudy Giuliani with Presidential Medal of Freedom
summary: Rudy Giuliani, the former mayor of New York City who worked as a personal lawyer to President Trump, said he will be honored in the Oval Office.
story: Washington — President Trump presented Rudy Giuliani, the former New York City mayor who served as his personal lawyer during the 2020 election, with the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday.

The White House praised Giuliani for his work across his career as a federal prosecutor in New York and then as mayor of New York City. The Medal of Freedom ceremony was set to take place in the Oval Office at 11 a.m. ET, according to Mr. Trump's schedule.

"Mayor Rudy Giuliani is a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our Nation," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said in a statement. "As U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Mayor Giuliani took down mob bosses and led a relentless war on crime. As Mayor, he transformed New York from a crime-ridden city into one of the safest big cities in the world, fostering economic opportunity and cultural greatness. And in the aftermath of the tragic September 11th attacks, he displayed strong American leadership in the face of evil."
Giuliani said he is "honored and humbled" to receive the award.

"Any and all distinction I have received in public office is fully the result of following the advice of my boss, Ronald Reagan, who said: 'There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn't mind who gets the credit.' I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together,'" he said in a statement. "And to my family — mother, father, children, ancestors, and extended family, including my friends — what you have done will always mean the most. Doing the right thing for others has been my guiding light."

I am honored and humbled to receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom from my nation and from President Donald J. Trump.Any and all distinction I have received in public office is fully the result of following the advice of my boss, Ronald Reagan, who said: "There is no limit… pic.twitter.com/hKb7qi5Tc8
Giuliani told conservative commentator Steve Bannon on his podcast Monday that he would be receiving the nation's highest civilian honor at the White House.
"I'm of course very, very humbled and very honored not only to receive it, but to receive it from him," he told Bannon during his "War Room" podcast and livestream.

Created in 1945 by President Harry S. Truman, the Presidential Medal of Freedom recognizes individuals who have made significant contributions to the security or national interests of the U.S., world peace and cultural or other public or private endeavors.

Across his two terms, Mr. Trump has so far awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to 26 people, according to the Congressional Research Service. Giuliani will be the third person to receive the honor from Mr. Trump in his second term. The president posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to conservative activist activist Charlie Kirk last year after he was fatally shot on a college campus in Utah, as well as to Welles Crowther, a Boston College graduate who died in the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.

The president has said he plans to award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Ben Carson, a former neurosurgeon who led the Department of Housing and Urban Development during Mr. Trump's first term; Connor Hellebuyck, Team USA men's hockey goalie; and Roger Clemens, former Major League Baseball pitcher.

Mr. Trump announced in September 2025 that he would be awarding Giuliani, 82, with the Presidential Medal of Freedom and said details would be forthcoming. The president hailed Giuliani as the "greatest mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot."
Mr. Trump announced that Giuliani would be honored days after the former mayor was injured in a car crash in New Hampshire and hospitalized.

Giuliani rose to prominence as mayor of New York City in the 1990s and became known as "America's mayor" for his leadership following the 9/11 terror attacks. He mounted a run for the GOP presidential nomination in 2008 but ended his campaign after placing third in the Florida primary.

He became a close friend and adviser to Mr. Trump's in his first term and worked as a personal lawyer to Mr. Trump during the 2020 presidential election, during which he spread baseless claims that the contest was rife with widespread voter fraud and stolen from Mr. Trump.

Giuliani was disbarred from practicing law in New York and the District of Columbia as a result of the false statements he made about the integrity of the 2020 election. He was also found liable by a federal judge in 2023 for defaming two former election workers in Georgia and ordered to pay them $148 million. Giuliani filed for bankruptcy following the decision.

The former mayor also faced state charges in Georgia and Arizona in criminal cases stemming from alleged efforts to overturn results of the 2020 election in both states. He pleaded not guilty, and both cases were dismissed.

title: Federal court releases Rep. Ilhan Omar D.C. home raid documents
summary: A federal court on Monday evening released documents regarding last month's raid at the Washington, D.C. home of Democratic Minnesota U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar.
story: A federal court on Monday evening released documents regarding last month's raid at the Washington, D.C., home of Democratic Minnesota U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar.

The majority of the 169 pages of court documents are heavily redacted and consist of exchanges between federal prosecutors and a magistrate judge over probable cause, constitutional privilege, warrant execution and public unsealing.

According to one of the documents, federal government officials applied for a search warrant on Oct. 2 to search Omar's home for "[a]ll records and information that constitute fruits, contraband, evidence, and instrumentalities of violations of." The document then contains redacted text before stating, "those violations involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present."

Federal officials provided two ex parte briefs in support of the warrant to the court before the judge signed it on Oct. 9. According to Cornell Law School, ex parte refers to "communication with a judge or opposing party without the presence or knowledge of the other party's attorney."
Homeland Security Investigations agents executed the warrant on Oct. 12. HSI has jurisdiction over federal offenses including immigration document fraud, identity fraud and immigration benefit fraud.

The court documents, released by the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, said federal investigators were authorized to seize documents, records, photos, thumb drives, external hard drives, computers and cellphones "registered or used by" Omar.

Three days before the raid, a judge granted a request to have the warrant sealed, stating that "because of such reasonable grounds to believe the disclosure will result in flight from prosecution, destruction of or tampering with evidence, intimidation of potential witnesses, and serious jeopardy to the investigation," according to the court documents.

A document filed by the federal government on Oct. 16 said, "The United States believes ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades—beginning long before she was ever in Congress," though the filing did not identify the alleged crimes.

U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro asked that a judge on Monday not release any of the files because they may be needed in a future trial. WCCO sources have said there are several immigration issues that authorities are investigating.
Criminal defense attorney Joe Tamburino says this case is highly unusual.

"First of all it's unusual because you have a sitting member of Congress, I don't know when that has ever happened, if ever," Tamburino said. "Second, you have a situation where somebody could be in jeopardy of losing their citizenship, and I have never seen that."

WCCO reached out to Omar's office on Monday and has not yet heard back. Her office said in a statement on Oct. 12 that Omar had "done nothing wrong" and called the raid an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."

title: Husband of woman arrested by ICE at airport calls it "unjust"
summary: Jose Castillo told CBS News he felt "useless" seeing his wife and father-in-law be taken into federal custody at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.
story: The husband of a woman whose arrest by immigration agents inside a jetway at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport gained national attention says he felt "useless" when seeing his wife and father-in-law be taken into federal custody, calling the episode "unjust."

Jose Castillo, an American citizen, teared up when recounting the moment on Saturday when masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers detained his wife, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, and his father-in-law, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza.

"You black out. You don't even know what's going on. You don't even know what's happening. Everything is moving so fast. Trying to protect your wife and they're taking your father-in-law," Castillo told CBS News in an interview Monday. "As a U.S. citizen, you feel useless."
Castillo said he felt "disgusted."
"How can you sit with yourself and strip somebody away like that in broad daylight, in front of families?" Castillo added.
The arrest was captured on videos that have gone viral. Hernandez Mejia is heard wailing and saying she has a valid work permit, while bystanders demand answers from the federal agents.

Department of Homeland Security officials identified Hernandez Mejia and Larrondo Mendoza as Mexican nationals living in the U.S. illegally after overstaying their visas. The agency said ICE officers were targeting Larrondo Mendoza for arrest when "other passengers began obstructing federal officers."
DHS accused Hernandez Mejia of assaulting agents, alleging she threw hot coffee on them. Castillo pushed back on the allegations.
"There was no assault on her end," Castillo said. "She did nothing. She was being shoved. They came directly at us."
"When you're coming at me and my wife and you're shoving us, obviously coffee's going to be spilled," he added.
DHS has said Hernandez Mejia "will be charged with assaulting a federal officer."

Castillo said he was traveling with his wife and father-in-law to a family event when they were approached by ICE agents in plainclothes on the jetway to an Alaska Airlines flight. The flight was delayed by over two hours, and the flight crew had to be replaced, the airline said.
Officials at Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle, which runs the airport, said they were not given prior notice of the ICE operation. The Port of Seattle said it was "outraged."
Hernandez Mejia and her father remain in ICE custody in Tacoma, Washington, according to their attorney. Castillo pleaded for their release.
"They don't deserve to be in there," he said. "It was done in such an unjust manner."

The incident is the latest in a string of ICE operations that have gone awry in recent weeks, even after President Trump acknowledged to 60 Minutes that his crackdown on illegal immigration may have been "too tough."

Last week, video captured ICE agents pushing a pregnant woman and U.S. citizen to the ground in Modesto, California. ICE accused her of interfering with the arrest of a man with a criminal record. In Texas, an ICE agent is facing criminal charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after allegedly striking a Mexican immigrant with an unmarked SUV. His attorney has called the incident an "accident."

The detention at Sea-Tac airport is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to send ICE officers to major airports across the country to arrest travelers who are in the U.S. illegally or with a tenuous legal status. Those arrested have included travelers with pending legal immigration applications but whose underlying permission to be in the U.S. expired.

Olia Catala, who is representing the father and daughter detained at Sea-Tac, said her clients entered the U.S. as tourists and that both have pending immigration applications. Hernandez Mejia, Catala said, applied for a green card as the spouse of a U.S. citizen.
She said the family was trying to follow the immigration process prior to being arrested.

"Congress created legal pathways and Sofia and her father were using them," Catala said. "We can't tell immigrants to use the legal pathways, to follow the law and then punish them for doing just that."

title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang still testifying before Congress next week
summary: Jensen Huang is still set to testify before lawmakers next week, congressional panels confirmed, after he was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO Monday, after resigning earlier this month amid allegations of affairs.
story: Washington — Jensen Huang is still scheduled to testify before lawmakers next week, congressional committees confirmed, after he was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO following his resignation earlier this month.

After Huang stepped down less than two weeks ago, amid reports of extramarital affairs — including one with an alleged Chinese spy — Nvidia's board of directors said Monday that it had reinstated Huang as president and CEO. The board's move, for which President Trump claimed some credit, sent shockwaves through the political sphere, with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressing concern, and threw into question whether the congressional hearings would proceed.

Huang is set to appear for a transcribed interview with a trio of panels on Dec. 1, including the House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs committees, along with the Select Committee on China. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter voluntarily agreed to appear before the committees on Dec. 2. A spokesperson for the House Intelligence Committee told CBS News that the reinstatement "changes nothing."

"When Jensen was CEO, our three committees were demanding answers. When he was removed and no longer CEO, we were still pursuing the facts," the spokesperson said. "The fact that he has been reinstated as CEO, changes nothing. There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committees' commitment to oversight."
Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, added, "We expect to see him on Capitol Hill next week."
The Senate Banking Committee also sent out a notice Monday announcing that Huang would still appear before the panel to testify on Dec. 3.
Lawmakers from both parties expressed alarm Monday about Huang's reinstatement, which is taking place as the focus shifts to questions about the chipmaker's compliance with export restrictions.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer vowed that Democrats "will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives." And Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the Banking Committee, said in a statement that Huang's reinstatement "does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers."

She went on to say that Huang's return to Nvidia's top job only "increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who's set to become House Speaker in the new Congress next year, called Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible" and vowed a "swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation" into any potential misconduct by the company and by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who is set to chair the House Oversight Committee in the new Congress, argued that President Trump's alleged involvement in Huang's reinstatement "raises serious national security and corruption questions," which he said must be investigated.

"No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions," Garcia said in a statement. "Congress must come together in swift bipartisan action and demand answers immediately."

On the GOP side, Sen. John Cornyn of Texas questioned the rationale behind the Nvidia board's conclusion that Huang's return poses no national security risk, as did Sen. John Curtis of Utah, who pointed to the board's claim that it received input from "senior levels of the United States government."

"I have some questions," Curtis said in a post on X. "Mr. Huang was right to step down when the affair came to light. Just 11 days after Nvidia announced his departure, the board brought him back while its own independent investigation was still underway. Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him. I'd like to know what changed."

Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota said the "risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who's been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang," while urging Congress to "immediately pass the strictest export controls possible."

"The legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens," Cramer said.
Sen. Pete Ricketts of Nebraska argued that Huang's behavior "does not support reinstatement," citing his own experience serving on a public company board.

"Nvidia's decision today doesn't excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress," Ricketts added. "It also doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December."
A representative for Huang declined to comment about Huang's appearances before Congress.

Caitlin  Yilek
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Trump tells Army to halt detonation for now in Iowa this week
summary: President Trump said he will wait for the courts and Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand to agree with the Army's plan.
story: Update: A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating the explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa. Read earlier developments below.

Washington — President Trump says he has ordered the U.S. military to hold off for now on detonating an explosives site in Iowa, deferring the decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit and Iowa's Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand. The Army had planned to carry out the detonation this week.

The president made the announcement on Truth Social, after the U.S. Army said it planned to move forward with the detonation of tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Middletown, Iowa. That Army decision came in spite of a federal court order pausing it indefinitely, which the Army said it didn't need to follow, citing risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating spontaneously. Community members in the small southeastern Iowa town have voiced concerns about the risk of toxic particles spreading across Iowa and neighboring Illinois.

Last week, two environmental groups filed a lawsuit to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit to block the detonation, challenging the validity of the emergency permit granted by the Environmental Protection Agency. The appeals court issued a stay on Thursday pending a final decision on the validity of the permit.

On Truth Social, Mr. Trump wrote that there is a "substantial chance that this material will explode on its own volition," and he thinks the safer option is to detonate now. But, he said he will follow what the courts and Sand wish to do. The president called Iowa a "very special place" to him.

"I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation," the president wrote. "If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation."
The federal government told the court over the weekend that it needed to conduct the controlled detonation by Tuesday, before the temperature is expected to drop below freezing.
Earlier this year, the Army said dozens of drums of lead azide started recrystallization. The lead has been stored in bunkers in the munitions plant, which was built during World War II.
CBS News has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

Sand said on social media the Trump administration "should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks."
"Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward," Sand said.

Lucia I Suarez Sang

title: Rep. Jimmy Gomez resigning after panel finds evidence of misconduct
summary: The bipartisan committee said Rep. Jimmy Gomez made unwanted sexual advances and sexual contact with a House staffer.
story: Warning: This story contains graphic content.

Washington — Rep. Jimmy Gomez announced Monday that he will resign from Congress, with the announcement coming shortly after the House Ethics Committee released a report saying it found "substantial evidence" that the California Democrat engaged in sexual misconduct, including making unwanted sexual advances and sexual contact with a House staffer.
The committee said Gomez's behavior toward the House staffer "could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse," or sexual assault.

Gomez said he had "strong disagreements" with the findings, but saw "no other alternative than to resign." He said his resignation is effective Dec. 1 "to allow for my staff to close out important constituent casework and needs."

"I recognize the seriousness of the Ethics Committee's report and as I previously stated I take full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage," Gomez said in a statement.
Gomez was set to leave office in early January after losing his reelection bid.
The bipartisan committee announced in August that it was looking into allegations against Gomez.

As part of its investigation, the panel interviewed one woman who said Gomez made unwanted sexual advances toward her while she was a House staffer on two occasions, including one in which he made "sexual contact" with her in public and another where she described him as "forceful" with her in his congressional office, according to the report.

The woman, described as Witness 1 in the report, said she met Gomez at a birthday party hosted by another lawmaker at a bar near Capitol Hill in February 2024. Gomez and the woman eventually left the party with another woman and lawmaker to go to a bar in Chinatown.

According to the report, the woman told the committee that at the Chinatown bar Gomez started to touch her legs and then she said he penetrated her with his fingers. She described the incident as nonconsensual and said she was "mortified" that it had happened.
"I kind of just was really embarrassed by it. I didn't know how to react," she told the committee, adding that she "ran to the bathroom" and "started to cry."
Later outside the bar, the woman said Gomez pushed her against a wall and kissed her, and she said she "kissed him back because I just wanted to go home and I just, like, wanted it to end."

Gomez initially described the encounter outside the bar as "consensual kissing," but later acknowledged that "I put my hand down the top of her skirt." Gomez said the sexual contact happened outside the bar and he had asked her, "yes?"
"And she said yes," he said. He denied penetrating her, but also alleged that "she did not say no, she did not push me away."

The woman also told the committee about a second incident in July 2024 and alleged that Gomez invited her to his office after she had texted him. She said when she tried to leave his office, he grabbed her and pushed his body into hers and "tried to kiss me."

She alleged that she "said no" and that she needed to leave, and told the panel, "I was trying to push off of him, and he wouldn't let go. And, at some point I, like, succeeded in pushing him off of me, and then I just ran out."
Gomez described the incident, saying, "I walked her to the door, gave her a beso, a kiss on the cheek, a hug, and she left."

The committee called Gomez's actions "aggressive and inappropriate" and said his "conduct at various junctures suggests he knew that what he was doing was wrong." The report also said Gomez's conduct caused the woman "significant and ongoing distress" and contributed to her decision to leave her job.
The committee did not recommend any punishment for Gomez, such as censure or expulsion, noting that the California Democrat had lost his reelection campaign.

"[T]he Committee has observed that although there is not enough time for it to pursue an adequate House sanction, it remains essential that the Committee adopt and publish its Report so that the House is aware of Representative Gomez's misconduct and so that the House may determine, in its judgment, whether to sanction Representative Gomez," it said.
In a statement, the woman's lawyers claimed the committee's report "confirms that Representative Gomez sexually harassed and assaulted our client while she was a staffer on Capitol Hill."

Her attorneys, Lisa J. Banks and Sarah E. Nesbitt, said Gomez "abused the power given to him by the voters when he violated this young woman, effectively destroying her dreams of a career in public service," adding that he "seems to believe that the power he wields, both as a man and as a member of Congress, makes him untouchable."
They said that the committee's findings "are a meaningful step toward dismantling that belief."
House Democratic leaders called the report "serious and deeply troubling" and said it is "appropriate that he is stepping down."

"Decisive action to set a new standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Minority Whip Katherine Clark and Democratic Caucus chairman Pete Aguilar said in a joint statement.

title: U.S. adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist after Nvidia scandal
summary: The Trump administration restricted Megaspeed from buying advanced semiconductor chips, after the firm's alleged links to China helped kick-start the scandal surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
story: The Trump administration on Monday restricted Singapore-based Megaspeed from buying advanced semiconductor chips, after the firm's alleged links to China helped kick-start the scandal surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

An operator of data centers in Southeast Asia, Megaspeed has been accused of transferring the high-tech Nvidia chips that power artificial intelligence to China, which the company denies. Huang also admitted earlier this month to having an affair with a former Megaspeed executive who U.S. intelligence agencies believe was a Chinese intelligence asset.

The U.S. Commerce Department added Megaspeed to the Entity List, a designation that prevents it from buying sensitive U.S. technologies — including advanced chips — without a license from the federal government.
Megaspeed has already been on Nvidia's internal "no sell" list since June 2025, the Justice Department and Commerce Department said in a joint statement last week.
CBS News has reached out to Megaspeed for comment.
The crackdown on Megaspeed came just hours after Nvidia's fortunes dramatically turned around — partly at the Trump administration's behest.

The semiconductor giant's board of directors reinstated Huang as CEO early Monday, less than two weeks after Huang resigned following allegations of extramarital affairs with the Megaspeed executive and a subordinate at Nvidia. President Trump told CNBC he personally spoke with Nvidia's board and "convinced them" to rehire Huang, giving the board "assurances" on national security. Nvidia's share price leaped more than 30% after the decision.
The scandal has drawn broader scrutiny of the loopholes that allow China to access advanced chips in spite of U.S. trade restrictions designed to preserve the U.S.' artificial intelligence edge.
Some experts and former government officials have questioned why Megaspeed was permitted to buy Nvidia chips, and have argued Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should have taken action sooner.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly suggested earlier this month that Lutnick's team was to blame, saying on CNBC that other federal agencies "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen."

The Commerce and Justice departments said last week that since launching an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024, Commerce has requested sales records from Nvidia, carried out a site check and conducted interviews.
The Justice Department is now leading the probe, the two agencies said, adding that they "have an extremely strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice."

Separately, the Commerce Department issued a rule last week aimed at preventing Chinese firms from remotely accessing high-tech chips installed in data centers in other countries. The rule tightens chip exports to countries like Malaysia and Singapore.

Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing, saying earlier this month it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and complies with U.S. export control rules. It said Alice Huang, the former executive who allegedly had an affair with Jensen Huang, left the company last year.

title: Trump says he convinced Nvidia board to reinstate Jensen Huang
summary: President Trump claimed the government "has no reason to believe" Jensen Huang's return is a national security risk.
story: Washington — President Trump says that he spoke to Nvidia's board and helped win Jensen Huang's reinstatement as the company's CEO.
He told CNBC in a phone interview Monday about his call to the board. "I spoke to them and I convinced them," he said. "And it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week ago."

The president also claimed in a Truth Social post Monday that the U.S. government "has no reason to believe" that Huang's return to Nvidia as CEO "poses any risk to national security," although he did not elaborate. His social media comment went up shortly after Nvidia announced its board had reinstated Huang. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. China has denied it.

The president said Nvidia's board asked "for assurance on the national security threat" and he gave them "assurance." The president told CNBC he believes his intervention was essential to getting Huang reinstated. Mr. Trump told CNBC Huang "did nothing wrong."
He also said in the interview that he spoke with Huang Sunday night "after the deal was done" and told him to "work hard."

Mr. Trump said in Truth Social his post that U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche "has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." A Justice Department official told CBS News that Mr. Trump did speak to Blanche over the weekend, and the official said the has no evidence of any wrongdoing by either Jensen Huang or Nvidia.

Mr. Trump has been a vocal proponent of returning Huang to the company, after Nvidia's stock tanked in the wake of his resignation. Since his reinstatement was announced Monday morning, the stock has surged over 30%.

Huang has built Nvidia into one of the world's most valuable companies, with its high-powered chips emerging as integral to the race for AI dominance between the U.S. and China. A White House official told CBS News on Monday that the decision to reinstate Huang "will preserve America's technological edge over China, strengthen our national security" and ensure the future of AI will be built in the U.S.

"The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," Mr. Trump wrote. "The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," he continued. "Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security."
Huang had publicly advocated for his return to Nvidia, along with others in the tech industry, including SpaceX's Elon Musk.

Mr. Trump has said he was not told that Alice Huang was suspected of being a spy, although The New York Times reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated a highly classified memo in May about the counterintelligence risk posed by Jensen Huang's affair.

Jensen Huang has agreed to publicly testify before Congress, although the date has not been set, a Senate Banking spokesperson told CBS News last week. Republicans and Democrats are applying increasing pressure to make Huang testify about Nvidia chips making their way into Chinese hands.

On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was asked if the president understood the national security and regulatory risks Nvidia and Huang face, after Bessent had said Nvidia's board of directors needed "to go to the outside" to find a new CEO.
"Well, Jensen is on the outside now, so you know," Bessent said.
"I know the president said he should come back," "Face the Nation" moderator Margaret Brennan said.
Bessent then said of Jensen Huang, "Well, I said they should go to the outside, but he's on the outside now."

                                  Sara  Cook

title: Democrats announce 12 debates starting in June for 2028 race
summary: In announcing the debate framework, DNC chair Ken Martin leaned heavily into one of his signature causes, ending dark money in politics.
story: The Democratic National Committee on Monday unveiled a primary presidential debate plan that includes 12 debates starting in June 2027 and running through early 2028 as the field narrows from what's now a wide-open race.

There are no declared Democratic candidates yet, although several prominent Democrats have indicated their interest in a White House bid. DNC chair Ken Martin said debate participants will be capped at 20, and the party said if a large number of candidates qualify for a debate, it will be split up over two nights with candidates chosen for each night at random.
Martin said the exact dates, media partners and polling and fundraising thresholds would be announced later. Monday's announcement said there would be five debates in 2027 and seven in 2028.

In announcing the debate framework, Martin leaned into one of his signature causes, ending dark money in politics. Candidates are required to sign a pledge to publicly denounce super PAC and dark money flowing into their campaigns.

The debate schedule comes as Democrats are emboldened by big wins in the midterm elections this month. On Sunday, Democrats secured their 258th seat in the House, giving the party its largest majority since 1992. Democrats won 56 seats in the Senate, including wins in red states like Mississippi, Iowa and South Carolina, which is set to hold the first Democratic primary in 2028.

For the 2020 presidential election, the DNC also held 12 debates starting in June in 2019, the last time the party had a competitive primary. The new plan follows the DNC's decision to change the primary calendar, putting South Carolina first and pushing Iowa's decisive caucuses out of the early window.

The DNC says candidates who benefit from certain advertising expenditures by super PACs and "dark money" nonprofits would be required to publicly denounce that support, though the party acknowledges it cannot prohibit such outside spending. The framework also establishes a complaint and review process through which campaigns can raise alleged violations ahead of debate qualification periods.

While the pledge requires candidates to publicly denounce super PAC and dark money spending in support of their campaigns, the potentially more consequential change is new restrictions on coordination between campaigns and Democratic Party organizations.

The neutrality provisions highlight the party's desire to avoid accusations of favoritism that have dogged Democratic primaries since the 2016 cycle, when critics argued party officials tilted the playing field toward former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton over Sen. Bernie Sanders. In 2024, former President Joe Biden faced no serious primary challengers and easily clinched the nomination, only to drop out in July after a disastrous debate performance. The party then coalesced behind former Vice President Kamala Harris, despite the concerns of some influential Democrats, who believed an open, albeit truncated, nominating process would be better.

The neutrality provisions also build on a longer-running debate among Democrats over the role of outside money in presidential campaigns. During the 2020 primary, Sanders and Sen. Elizabeth Warren made opposition to super PAC and dark-money spending major themes of their campaigns, helping turn outside spending into a litmus test for candidates.

Under the 2028 framework, presidential campaigns would be barred from entering into joint fundraising agreements with Democratic Party committees during the primary and could not authorize coordinated spending by state or local Democratic parties on their behalf. In 2015, Clinton's campaign entered into a joint fundraising agreement with the DNC, long ahead of her clinching the nomination.

DNC officials say the changes are intended to limit the influence of dark money and maintain party neutrality during a competitive primary. But because the rules do not prevent outside groups from spending on behalf of candidates, the effect is likely to be one of greater scrutiny, rather than a reduction of the amount of outside money in the race. The DNC said that its effort to limit the role of dark money in the primary is backed by Reps. Greg Casar and Jason Crow, Sens. Andy Kim, Sanders and Warren and former DNC Chair Jaime Harrison.

Still, the new rules stop short of preventing outside groups from participating in the primary. Candidates are only required to disavow a super PAC or nonprofit once, even if that group's spending continues. And because campaigns can file complaints against rivals ahead of debate qualification periods, disputes over compliance could become a recurring feature of the debate process.

title: Inside Trump's gala for $TRUMP meme coin buyers
summary: Over 150 of the largest buyers of the meme coin $TRUMP attended the gala at Trump National Golf Club in Virginia.
story: Washington — President Trump hosted a gala Sunday night at his Northern Virginia golf club for investors in $TRUMP coin, a novelty product whose value rises and falls with the interest of buyers.

The event marked the third $TRUMP coin gala, in which those competing for access to the dinner and proximity to the president can try to do so by acquiring large quantities of the Trump-branded token, renewing questions about the potential for corruption as Mr. Trump's family venture conducts business with investors from around the world.

CBS News got an exclusive look via videos and photos from inside the event, where VIP attendees received Trump-branded watches and "Trump Victory" perfume. Guests mingled with celebrities like Shark Tank's Kevin O'Leary and mentalist Lior Suchard.
When the president took the stage, he spoke about the need for the U.S. to dominate in cryptocurrency, chips and artificial intelligence, which he referred to as "SI," or super intelligence.

"We have to remain number one in everything we do," Mr. Trump said. "If we are not going to do it, China is going to do it." He described himself as "the veto king of the world," to which the audience cheered.

Then, according to a video taken from inside the event, he took questions from the audience, including "What is your favorite Chinese food?" The president answered, "President Xi gave me great Chinese food. I have no idea what it was, but it was very good."

Mr. Trump said in his Q&A that he hoped Jensen Huang would return as Nvidia CEO after departing amid scandal earlier this month. (The following morning, the board announced Huang's return, and Mr. Trump said he'd "convinced them.")
"I'd love to see Jensen be able to go back into the company. I really would. I think that he's a real— he made a mistake. It was a big one, but he's a brilliant guy," Mr. Trump told the dinner crowd.
Regarding Elon Musk, the president said, "I've always said this about Elon, he's 80% super genius and 20% I refuse to say what that is," adding, "He is a very unusual guy."
Mr. Trump also praised the CEO of Anthropic as a "good guy" and remarked on the company's strong opening IPO.
"There should be some checks and balances," he said about the AI industry.
A mysterious attendee
Among those spotted in the crowd Sunday night was a woman who goes by Addy and leads FastX, a Singapore-linked company claiming to want to build a "Chinese $TRUMP coin community."

"We are the number one Trump holder now. We have over 2 million tokens," she said in a video posted to X before the event. "So later this month our team will attend a VIP reception with President Trump. So it's a big moment for us and the FastX community."
CBS News traced FastX's video to an office building in Singapore, but neither Addy nor anyone else was there.

A CBS News investigation found more than half the wallets that invested in $TRUMP coin to attend the gala used exchanges that bar American customers, suggesting they're based overseas. Cryptocurrency wallets are tools that allow users to store and interact with digital currencies.
The mysterious digital finance firm has sparked concerns about a foreign company investing millions to be in the same room with the U.S. president.

Corey Frayer, who works on investor protection at the Consumer Federation of America, a nonprofit public interest group, told CBS News it appears as if the president is "not making choices about public policy and what's in the best interest of the United States. He's making choices about what is most profitable to him."
Mr. Trump told "60 Minutes" earlier this month that he puts the country's needs first and has left his crypto dealings to his sons, who control his businesses through a trust.
"My sons run the company. It's hard to say to them, 'Don't do anything anymore for four years because I'm president,'" Mr. Trump said.
The president's financial disclosures show so far he's earned more than $600 million in royalties from the company that issues the crypto token.

"It is his most profitable, highest income, lowest margin company, and it is exclusively based on buying this access," Frayer said. "You're basically paying for thin air in exchange for this favor of meeting the president."

The website for the gala said no attendees would be granted a private meet-and-greet with the president. The videos obtained by CBS News show the president addressing the crowd, and there's no evidence of one-on-one conversations.
Neither the White House nor FastX responded to requests for comment.  Fight Fight Fight LLC, the company that hosts the gala, also did not respond to requests for comment.
Ramy Inocencio and RJ Carrel contributed reporting.
This story published first on CBS News at 12:51 p.m. on Nov. 23, 2026.

title: ICE officers arrest 2 passengers boarding flight in Seattle
summary: Masked immigration officers arrested two passengers on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday.
story: Masked immigration officers arrested two passengers on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, federal officials said, causing what Alaska Airlines called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.
Videos of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screamed that her daughter was being taken and she has a work permit.
Alaska Airlines said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests."
An Alaska Airlines spokesperson told CBS News on Sunday that the flight, scheduled to depart at 8:45 a.m., left the airport at 11:03 a.m. after some crew members asked to leave.

"Immediately following the incident, some inflight crew members requested to be replaced. As we learned more about what occurred, we ultimately brought in an entirely new crew," the airline spokesperson said in a statement.

In a statement provided to CBS News Saturday evening, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, the parent agency of ICE, said that ICE officers "conducted a targeted enforcement operation" on a Mexican national identified as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza who had "overstayed his visa."

During the arrest, a second passenger "hurled hot coffee" at the officers, the DHS spokesperson said in the statement. That second passenger, identified by DHS as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, is a Mexican national who had also been determined to have overstayed her visa, the spokesperson said.
Mejia was also subsequently arrested and will face federal charges of assaulting a federal officer, DHS said.
A DHS source told CBS News the two people arrested are a father and daughter.

Mendoza and Mejia remained in ICE custody in Washington, immigration attorney Olia Catala told CBS News on Sunday night, saying she was visiting her clients at the Northwest Processing Center in Tacoma.

Democratic Rep. Adam Smith of Washington said in an earlier statement that "masked ICE agents detained at least one passenger waiting to board an Alaska Airlines flight at Sea-Tac Airport. The masked agents forcibly dragged the individual off the jet bridge, taking them into custody."
The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. Videos showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases looked on.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past. ICE sources told CBS News in July that the uptick in arrests stems from increased collaboration between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration.

On Thursday, a Princeton University student and Chinese national was detained by ICE at Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., after attending a neuroscience conference, the school and her colleagues said.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities."

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, called the incident "just the latest example of ICE's deeply un-American tactics."

"ICE is completely and totally out of control," Ferguson said in a statement. "Like many Americans, I'm outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities."

Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington said in a social media post that she was "disturbed by the reports of this detention at Sea-Tac," adding that her office was "working to gather more information on the situation."

DHS numbers obtained by CBS News last week found that ICE arrested 491,000 people in FY 2026, a record, including nearly 475,000 administrative arrests, also a record. Administrative arrests are those in which alleged undocumented immigrants are arrested for civil violations rather than criminal charges.

In a "60 Minutes" interview earlier this month following the heavy losses suffered by Republicans in the midterm elections, President Trump appeared to acknowledge that his administration's immigration crackdown may have contributed to his party's poor showing.

"For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," Mr. Trump told "60 Minutes." "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."
Of his deportation policies, the president said: "I think it was too tough. A lot of people would say that it's great, but a lot of people think it's too tough."

title: Democrats reach historic House majority not seen since 1992
summary: "House Democrats have just secured the largest majority any party in Congress has held this century. BOOM," Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York said Sunday.
story: Democrats secured their 258th seat in the House on Sunday, marking the largest majority either party has won in the lower chamber in a general election in three decades.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Trump's first midterm in 2018. It's an election sweep unseen since 1992 for either party, creating not only vast opportunities for Democrats to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Hubbard led Foxx by 330 votes following a recount, according to the North Carolina Board of Elections.
"House Democrats have just secured the largest majority any party in Congress has held this century. BOOM," Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, of New York, wrote on X Sunday afternoon.

The milestone in the 435-member House exceeded Democrats' own expectations, and they could still gain a few more seats with four other House races remaining outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.
Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The blue wave, or as some have called it, "blue tsunami," sets up a divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address the high cost of living while also confronting Mr. Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term.

The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.
It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

In an interview on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday, Jeffries repeatedly emphasized the need for action, saying, "Can you imagine how angry the American people will be with Washington if, over the next two years, we fail to do anything about affordability, fail to do anything about healthcare, and fail to do anything about immigration?"
Election rout creates a mandate to govern

The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and war with Iran and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Mr. Trump.

Persistent negative views of the economy turned against the party in power. Those who said the economy was bad voted for Democrats in their House races, according to CBS News exit polls. This was the second straight election most voters told CBS News inflation was a hardship for them, and more said their finances are worse now compared to two years ago — these voters also backed Democrats over the Republicans for the House.

Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.
The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.

Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Mr. Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Mr. Trump for a third time.
"This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the Capitol.
The New York Democrat called the big numbers "a mandate for change."
Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.
"Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it's affecting the people," he said.
For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Mr. Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?"

The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality."
A new generation of leaders

After House Speaker Mike Johnson struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority — meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.

Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.
"We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK," said Democratic Rep. Troy Carter of Louisiana, who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.
Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.
"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Jordan said.
The GOP's high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

title: Army delays detonation in Iowa that could send toxic dust into Illinois
summary: The U.S. Army has delayed plans to detonate unstable explosives at a munition plant in Iowa, amid concerns about the risks of a plume of dust containing toxic lead particles that could spread across parts of Iowa and Illinois.
story: The U.S. Army has delayed plans to detonate unstable explosives at a munition plant in Iowa, after elected leaders and environmental groups raised concerns about the risks of a plume of dust containing toxic lead particles that could spread across parts of Iowa and Illinois.
The dust plume is expected to spread across portions of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois, potentially settling on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces.

The detonation was originally scheduled for noon CT Friday, Nov. 20, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, a small community of 360 people, four hours west of Chicago, near the Mississippi River. However, on Thursday evening, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle announced the explosion would be delayed until Monday.

"Public safety is the Army's top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow's controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa until Monday, November 23. This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material," Telle wrote in a post on X.

The Army plans two controlled detonations involving 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive used in military ammunition since World War I. The Associated Press reported the material totals about 5 tons. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, the material has deteriorated during storage, allowing lead azide to recrystallize and become increasingly sensitive to friction and shock.

"In March of this year, the Army uncovered degrading Lead Azide housed in bunkers at the installation and immediately began communicating with stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the modeled impact area about the danger it posed," Telle wrote in a post on X. "In coordination with the Environmental Protection Agency, experts, and the local community, it was determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area. Public communication is essential to public trust. Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information."
In a statement after the Army postponed the detonation, U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois) wrote on X, "The American people deserved better than this."

"This whole operation was poorly planned and poorly communicated. Families were abruptly told to avoid the area, unsure if they would return to broken homes and whether their air and water could be at risk due to toxic lead exposure. This was unacceptable and a failure of leadership of epic proportions," Duckworth wrote. "Moving forward, I will continue to demand answers about how we even got to this point and accountability to make sure the Army never allows unsafe conditions to get this dire again."
U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) called on the Army to hold a community town hall meeting on Saturday to answer questions from the public before proceeding with the demonstration on Monday.

Thursday afternoon, two environmental groups filed a lawsuit in the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to block the detonation. Earthjustice, a nonprofit public interest environmental law organization, filed the suit on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter. They are challenging the validity of the emergency permit granted by the EPA.

"We were very concerned about the very short notice that people in Iowa had to prepare," said Kerri Johannsen, senior director of policy and programs with the Iowa Environmental Council. "We also have not seen the evidence that the EPA used to determine that this was the best course of action, in terms of safety and health."
Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, noted in a news release that the EPA itself says there is no safe level of exposure to lead.

"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal," Schmidt said.
Iowans protested and some made plans to fortify their homes or leave the state.
"I called my daughter and said, 'I'm coming to Chicago,'" said Pam Munce, who lives in Burlington.
Garrett Anthony, who also lives in Burlington, said he plans to put a tarp over his air conditioner.
"And I'm going to try and seal up windows as best I can," he said.

The barrels had been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command. A routine check earlier this year found that some of the water had evaporated, Barati said.

The Army said moving or transporting the material now poses an unacceptable risk of accidentally detonating it, potentially even killing the explosives technicians handling it. After evaluating alternative disposal methods, military officials determined that detonating the explosives in place was the safest available option. Barati said the risk of accidental detonation increases in cold weather. "We're really concerned that it will detonate on its own," Barati said.
The Army describes such operations near populated communities as highly uncommon, it told CBS News Chicago.

"A team of experts from around the nation got together to figure out what the best and safest disposal method was, and they determined that the safest method would be to detonate it in place," Barati said.

The Army says it is taking several steps to limit the amount of lead-containing dust released during the explosions, including earthworks, soil wetting and air monitoring. According to the AP, the barrels are surrounded by concrete and buried under soil, with sand barriers stacked two stories high around them. Barati said the soil will be sprayed with water and the air misted to try to keep the majority of the lead on Army property. EPA's permit also requires environmental monitoring at the installation and off-site locations, along with post-detonation sampling and cleanup measures.

With the detonation delayed until Monday, the winds are expected to be different than Friday, meaning that plume of lead dust could impact a completely different group of people as it moves in a different direction.
Residents urged to evacuate as explosions could shatter windows

The planned detonations are powerful enough that the Army is warning of possible damage to nearby buildings, including shattered windows. Residents in Middletown's City Park neighborhood are being asked to temporarily evacuate their homes from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Friday. Residents who can't leave should stay inside with windows and doors closed, officials said.

In its Nov. 15 public advisory, the Army says residents should expect loud explosions, ground vibrations and a visible dust plume. Temporary accommodations will be available at the Armed Forces Reserve Center in Middletown.

A group of Democratic and Republican elected officials from Illinois and Iowa had urged the Pentagon and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to delay the planned detonation and seek safer alternatives.

"While we understand the urgent need to address these volatile materials, their detonation has the potential to spread lead contamination in and around the region. We call on you to consider delaying this detonation until there is an opportunity to explore safer alternatives," they wrote to Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and U.S. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. "Iowa and Illinois residents understandably are concerned about the potential health impacts of the scheduled detonation."
The elected officials who signed the letter include:

U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois)U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois)U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Illinois)U.S. Rep. Mary Miller (R-Illinois)U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen (R-Illinois)Illinois Gov. JB PritzkerU.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Illinois)U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa)
U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois)
U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois)
U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Illinois)
U.S. Rep. Mary Miller (R-Illinois)
U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen (R-Illinois)
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker
U.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Illinois)
U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa)
They also raised concerns about communication with the public before the detonation.

"Our offices have received reports of poor communication from the Army and EPA about the detonation plans and anticipated monitoring after the detonation. In addition, there are significant concerns about appropriate Army and EPA oversight of this contractor-operated facility, the site of which remains on a Superfund list. We urge you to examine the contractor's handling of this and other hazardous material to prevent any future issues," they wrote.
Toxic lead dust could travel miles downwind

Following the initial blast, airborne toxic dust becomes the main concern. According to the Army's published plume forecasts and public safety advisory, the explosions are expected to release particles containing lead into the atmosphere.

The preliminary maps show a potential airborne plume stretching northward across eastern Iowa, the Mississippi River, and potentially into far northwest Illinois. The Army notified communities as far as 100 miles away Sunday, the AP reported, and thousands of people live along the plume's projected track.

In addition to airborne dust, toxic dust particles are expected to settle on surfaces. That raises concerns about possible lead contamination on agricultural land, residential properties, playground equipment and other outdoor surfaces.
Actual exposure levels and the extent of any contamination will depend on the amount of lead released, atmospheric conditions and how much material settles out of the plume.
Lead is a toxic heavy metal that does not degrade naturally over time. Once deposited, it can persist in soil for decades and may be transported through erosion or runoff into waterways.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that no safe blood lead level has been identified in children. Even relatively low levels of lead in the blood have been linked to learning difficulties, developmental delays and behavioral problems. Lead exposure is also especially dangerous to pregnant women.

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa's Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, told the AP it is encouraging that the Army and EPA are working to minimize the dust, but it's still unknown how much will end up in the air and on surfaces. He said he is particularly concerned about toddlers who put everything in their mouths. Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters, told the AP that high doses over a short period can cause lead poisoning and make people feel sick.

The Army's forecasts do not establish that harmful exposure will occur at every location within the projected plume. The Army says extensive modeling predicted that lead particle levels in the air may be elevated but still well below the level at which the EPA would require protective action, according to the AP. Environmental sampling will be needed to determine where lead was deposited and at what concentrations.
Weather conditions will determine where the plume travels

Wind direction, speed and vertical motion in the atmosphere will play critical roles in determining the plume's eventual path. Officials expect the dust to linger for no more than an hour, depending on wind speed, according to the AP.

Current forecast guidance suggests gusty southerly winds of 20 to 30 miles per hour Friday will carry the plume northward through eastern Iowa, keeping it well west of the Chicago metropolitan area. Communities closer to the Mississippi River and the Illinois border could be more relevant to potential downwind exposure. The exact path remains subject to change as the detonation approaches.

Under the EPA's emergency permit, the operation cannot proceed if certain unfavorable weather conditions are forecast, including surface winds below 1 mph or above 15 mph, strong winds aloft, thunderstorms, precipitation or temperature inversions. There is no word yet on whether Friday's gusty winds could cancel the detonation.
The Army is required to update its plume forecasts six hours before the operation, and hourly thereafter until the detonations are completed.
Army promises environmental monitoring and cleanup

The permit requires soil and surface-wipe sampling to begin within 24 hours in accessible public and consenting private areas where modeled lead-dust deposition meets a specified threshold. The Army must also submit environmental findings and proposed remediation plans to EPA.

For residents potentially affected by dust deposition, the Army recommends wet-cleaning surfaces that people frequently touch, including outdoor toys, playground equipment, patio furniture and windowsills. However, questions remain about the extent of contamination that could occur beyond the ammunition plant, the effectiveness of cleanup efforts and how residents will know whether their properties are safe.
EPA issues emergency permit for detonation

On Nov. 13, the EPA issued an emergency permit allowing the Army to detonate the lead azide at a location not authorized for the activity under the facility's existing hazardous-waste permit. In its Nov. 16 public notice, EPA said the emergency authorization was necessary to address an imminent threat to public safety posed by the unstable explosives.

The detonation is being regulated under the federal Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, or RCRA, which governs the treatment, storage and disposal of hazardous waste. However, federal emergency-permitting provisions allow greater flexibility than ordinary permitting procedures. Under 40 CFR § 270.61, applicable environmental requirements must be incorporated into emergency permits to the extent possible and consistent with the emergency situation.

The emergency permit issued for Middletown includes specific environmental safeguards and incorporates applicable federal hazardous-waste regulations. It remains unclear whether EPA modified or omitted any requirements that would ordinarily apply to this operation because of its emergency designation.
The EPA's authorization does not mean the detonation will produce no environmental contamination.
CBS News Chicago has sought additional information about the EPA's environmental risk assessment and the standards that would trigger cleanup of affected properties.

The Illinois Department of Public Health referred CBS News Chicago's questions about potential health impacts back to the EPA. Environmental and public health officials in Illinois have urged the military to conduct comprehensive sampling in that state after the detonations, the AP reported.

Iowa Health and Human Services told CBS News Chicago it was made aware of the planned detonation only very recently and is coordinating with other state agencies as they assess and respond to the public health concerns. The agency said the Army released two maps showing possible exposure but did not say what conditions the modeling included.
Community concerns grow ahead of detonation

Some residents and environmental advocates are questioning whether the planned detonation has received sufficient independent scrutiny. Protest organizers have called for greater transparency, independent environmental review and assurances that any contamination resulting from the explosions will be properly addressed.
U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek was among those calling for the detonation to be delayed, arguing the public needs a better understanding of the potential health impacts, the AP reported.

Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of the degraded lead azide, after the plant paused operations for a review and the material was discovered, the AP reported. The Army previously held a public open house on Oct. 15, where military officials discussed the safety operation and answered residents' questions.

Some schools in the region canceled classes Friday before the detonation was delayed, including in Danville, a few miles from the plant. Superintendent Pat Wallace said his initial intention was to keep schools open, but the uncertainties made closing "the most responsible decision." He wrote that he is not suggesting the detonation will create unsafe conditions: "The reality is that we simply do not know exactly what conditions will look like Friday afternoon," the AP reported.

In Mediapolis, less than 20 miles northeast of the plant, city officials learned of their potential exposure Sunday, when the Army's map put the town in the center of the dust exposure area, the AP reported. The school district announced Tuesday it will close Friday with no events or sports practices, and the public library will also close. The local fire department plans to hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles. City officials said the EPA will have a command center in Mediapolis to sample air, soil and water during and after the detonation, and the city plans to do its own testing.
"The biggest issue we're having is the lack of information," Deputy City Clerk Amy Stucker told the AP. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds' office said it was first briefed on the public advisory Monday.

The Iowa Department of Agriculture advised bringing animals, bales of hay and water indoors. Staff at the Iowa State University Extension office in Des Moines County fielded calls Thursday from residents "deathly afraid" for their animals and vegetable gardens, staff member Morgan Hoenig told the AP. "We ran out of soil test kits yesterday," she said.

The Army recommends that those within the projected exposure area consider avoiding outdoor activities, remaining indoors with windows closed and setting ventilation systems to recirculate air until officials announce that the exposure period has ended.
The latest official plume forecasts, public advisories and safety instructions are available on the U.S. Army's Iowa Army Ammunition Plant information page.
Residents can sign up for toxic plume forecast updates from the U.S. Army by sending an email request with the subject line "IAAAP Environmental Updates" to usarmy.ria.asc.list.pa@army.mil.
