title: Newly found farthest quasar from Earth is also oldest known to man
summary: Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its center dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.
story: Cape Canaveral, Fla. — Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its center dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.

The quasar formed within 630 million years of the universe-forming Big Bang, a German-led team reported Tuesday. That's considered a very early development in the 13.8-billion-year history of the cosmos, and it smashes previous records.

"This time the leap in cosmic time is huge!" the European Southern Observatory's Julien Wolf, who led the study, said in an email. "The previous two records each took us back by about 15 million years or less. This one takes us back by nearly 40 million years, the biggest advance in nearly a decade!"

Wolf and his team spotted the quasar while digging through millions of observations made by the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope. Launched in 2023, Euclid is surveying galaxies in an effort to shed light on the dark matter and dark energy that fill so much of the universe and keep it expanding.

Finding a quasar so early in the universe is rare, according to Wolf. What makes this one even rarer, he said, is the massive size of its black hole, despite being such a relatively slow eater of everything around it. Scientists are seeing it as it was 13.1 billion years ago - when the universe was less than 5% of its current age.

Wolf nicknamed the quasar Dun Aonghasa after the prehistoric stone fort in Ireland's Aran Islands. His wife and daughter are Irish, and he was awestruck when they visited the fort - a frontier holding "the promise of a vast horizon still to explore," just like this quasar.

His team's findings were corroborated by the Hubble and Webb space telescopes as well as other observatories on and off Earth. Thanks to Webb, scientists learned that the black hole powering this quasar is equivalent in mass to 360 million of our suns, an astounding amount so early in time. The final results appear in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

"Dun Aonghasa gives us a new deadline" for the early universe, Wolf said. "About 630 million years after the Big Bang, its black hole had already grown to about 360 million times the mass of the sun. But how?"
Their prowling of the cosmic dawn continues.
"Honestly, the record could fall again in a few months or it could stand for years," Wolf said.

title: Spacecraft enters Mercury's orbit after 8-year journey despite glitch
summary: BepiColombo was launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency in October 2018.
story: A spacecraft has entered Mercury's orbit after an eight-year journey, overcoming a technical glitch to continue its mission to conduct scientific observations around the planet.
BepiColombo was launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency in October 2018. Since then, it has navigated its way toward Mercury.

On Nov. 21, the spacecraft attached itself to Mercury's orbit. The maneuver started with a scheduled, brief loss of contact with the mission control team at the European Space Operations Center in Darmstadt, Germany, the ESA said in a news release.

As BepiColombo passed over the planet, it fired four axial thrusters that slowed it enough to lock into Mercury's orbit. During this stage of the mission, the spacecraft came within 400 miles of Mercury's surface. The burn was supposed to last for about 37 minutes.

But when the ESA team reestablished contact with BepiColombo, they found the maneuver had been interrupted, causing the spacecraft to enter safe mode, where nonessential activities are stopped. Analysis of trajectory data showed the spacecraft had only completed about 77% of the maneuver.

"Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened," ESA BepiColombo flight operations director Ignacio Tanco said in a statement.
The glitch has been traced to a software issue involving attitude guidance and thruster control, the ESA said. The investigation into the error is continuing.

Despite the error and the incomplete maneuver, ESA scientists were eventually able to confirm that BepiColombo had locked onto Mercury's orbit. It took six hours from the time the maneuver started to confirm that it had been successful, the ESA said.

Over the next few weeks, the spacecraft will continue to make small thruster burns to gradually adjust its orbit around Mercury. Each movement will be adapted by BepiColombo's flight dynamics team using the spacecraft's actual trajectory. This will allow BepiColombo to enter the "optimum point" in orbit. The ESA compared it to "braking a car at just the right moment" to find the "sweet spot." Conducting multiple maneuvers also allows the craft to maximize its fuel supplies.

On Dec. 9, BepiColombo will release two science orbiters. The ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter, or MPO, will spend another few months navigating to find the right spot in Mercury's orbit. It is expected to enter its final orbit in March 2027 and begin science operations in April.
The scientific operations will study Mercury's interior, surface and the space around the planet, Geraint Jones, ESA's BepiColombo lead project scientist, said.

The second science orbiter is the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, or Mio. Mio's studies will include Mercury's magnetosphere, interplanetary dust and electric fields, according to the ESA.

title: 5 questions Nvidia still faces after bringing back Jensen Huang
summary: Despite Jensen Huang's shock return as Nvidia's CEO, experts say it's anything but business as usual for the chipmaker.
story: Jensen Huang's first task in returning to lead Nvidia after resigning last week under a cloud will be to deal with the fallout from his stunning exit and even more surprising reprieve.

Following his reinstatement by the company's board, some lawmakers are calling for investigations into President Trump's role in the billionaire entrepreneur's return and whether Nvidia skirted export rules meant to prevent its advanced chips from reaching China. And while Huang may be viewed as key to Nvidia's success, his return raises a thicket of legal and operational problems, according to financial and governance experts.

"Three tests will now decide how strongly it builds from here: how its leadership sits with Washington, how it handles China and how long AI spending keeps growing at this speed,"  said Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, an investment advisory firm, in an email.
Here are five critical questions facing Nvidia as Huang retakes the helm.
Did Nvidia compromise U.S. national security?

One of Nvidia's major customers, Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, employed a Chinese businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and whom U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China. Megaspeed is also alleged to have smuggled Nvidia's advanced chips into China and provided remote access to the technology in violation of U.S. export controls.

Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter are scheduled to appear on Dec. 1- 2 in closed-door interviews before multiple congressional panels to discuss the company's ties to China. Huang is also scheduled to appear on Dec. 3 at a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on U.S. export rules and global AI competition.

"The Nvidia board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the Republican chairs of the House committees who will interview Huang and Teter said on Monday.
Will Nvidia's board face legal issues?

The board's decision to reinstate Huang is likely to set off a flurry of shareholder lawsuits over questions including whether Nvidia failed to disclose the spying allegations earlier and whether the company was aware of Megaspeed's links to China, according to Charles Elson, founding director of the John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware.

Shareholders could also challenge Huang and Nvidia over their failure to disclose his personal relationships with subordinates at the company, which appears to violate the chipmaker's code of conduct. Earlier this month, Nvidia was sued by shareholders for allegedly failing to disclose information about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive (no relation).
"There's just a whole range of things that they can bring actions," Elson said.
Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment about whether it will continue pursuing an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence.
Will Nvidia face new U.S. export restrictions?
Nvidia is expected to come under increased scrutiny and face greater regulatory hurdles in selling chips to China and companies in Southeast Asia.
"There will definitely be tighter restrictions, and any dealings directly with China will be the government's primary focus," StoneX equity research analyst Cody Acree told CBS News.

Huang has long lobbied U.S. officials to permit Nvidia to sell its most advanced chips to China, with an eye toward growing its market. Earlier this month, the Commerce Department moved to curb sales of U.S. chips to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand.

"Going forward, they'll be subject to more export controls so that their chips don't end up in China and data centers in Asia," Gil Luria, lead tech analyst at investment firm D.A. Davidson, told CBS News. "In that way, Nvidia's market has shrunk, and that business will go away."
Can Huang ease investor fears about an AI bust?

Investors cheered Huang's return partly because it suggests that Nvidia will continue in its role as the de facto "bank of AI," providing financing for companies that buy its chips and otherwise fueling the sector's growth. Huang helped arrange deals such as Nvidia's investment in OpenAI. Through such circular financing, Nvidia invests vast sums in AI companies, which then flow back to the chipmaker through chip purchases.

"Nvidia is more than just a chipmaker — it's heavily involved in the broader AI ecosystem by financing other companies," Capital Economics senior economist James Reilly told CBS News. "Having Jensen back reassures investors that those relationships and that financing will continue."
Still, Huang's return doesn't erase concerns about the sector's debt-fueled spending, or whether AI companies will ever turn a profit and deliver returns to investors.
"There are growing concerns as to whether all of this AI investment will generate the revenue it needs long-term to make it worthwhile," Reilly said. "Those hurdles are very demanding."
What is Nvidia's succession plan?
Developing a succession plan to replace Huang will be the first item on the board's agenda, Elson, a prominent governance expert, told CBS News.

When Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month, he had more than 60 direct reports, a structure that allowed him to wield enormous power. However, his departure made it clear that the company had no succession plan should Huang be unable to lead.
As a result, Elson expects Nvidia to hire an outside consultant to help forge a plan for who might succeed Huang.
Such "key man" risk isn't unique to Nvidia, Acree noted.

"You have other high-profile CEOs at the helm of large companies, but that's the nature of Silicon Valley, unfortunately," he said, pointing to Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and SpaceX's Elon Musk. "There is no way to address that risk entirely or make it go away, but boards will be more sensitive to that in the future."

title: Can Anthropic win hearts and minds by curing hearts and minds?
summary: Anthropic says Claude Science can drive breakthroughs in drug discovery. It could also open lucrative commercial opportunities, experts say.
story: Fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, Anthropic now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits. The company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases.

In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases."

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes "it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!)."
Speeding in the right direction

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts.

"AI can accelerate research. It will help you get there faster, but it's not just speed — it's directional speed," Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News. "Let's say you're at the top of the mountain and your aim is to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley. AI will not just help you get down there faster — it will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is."

For Anthropic, meanwhile, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes. Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.
"If you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable," Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News.
The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits. That could take time, Khan told CBS News.

"How this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and I think it's a question Anthropic hasn't figured out yet," Khan said. "Coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research."
But the potential to move the needle for both Anthropic and its pharma partners is significant.

"If you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference," Khan added. "You'll get asymmetric payouts in the sense that if a model can help with any part of the process, it's very economically valuable."

For example, he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay "hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug 2% better than it is."
A way to win hearts and minds by curing them?

Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic. By applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts.

"If you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that's prevailed for quite some time, I think that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users," Khan said. "Because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large."

title: How Huang's resignation and return unfolded at Nvidia
summary: Jensen Huang's shocking exit as CEO of Nvidia unspooled suddenly, yet signs of trouble had emerged much earlier.
story: Nvidia's board of directors announced on Monday, Nov. 23, that it is reinstating Jensen Huang as the chipmaker's CEO. The move marks an abrupt shift from board members' position only last week that they had no plans to rehire the billionaire entrepreneur at the company he co-founded more than 30 years ago.

Huang's departure from Nvidia on Nov. 12 capped a tumultuous week for the chipmaker, with his resignation coming less than a week after his extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy became public. The woman with whom he had a relationship, Alice Huang (no relation), arrived on the tech scene in 2023, when she became the managing director of Singapore-based data center Megaspeed International.

Megaspeed, which says it has complied with U.S. laws, would proceed to buy billions of dollars in Nvidia chips and servers. Over the past two years, Alice Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, has been photographed and recorded socializing with Jensen Huang, prompting questions in May from one quizzical investor about their "uncomfortably close relationship."

In a statement on Sunday, Nov. 15, Megaspeed said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025, and it denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business." "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.
Below is a timeline of events that led to Jensen Huang's startling resignation, and the board's decision to rehire him:
November 2015

Alice Huang, a former television reporter in China, joins investment firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Management as deputy general manager, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database. Shanghai Hexi was founded by Kang Wei, who became her husband, according to The Wall Street Journal.
March 2023

7Road International, originally incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, is renamed Megaspeed, and ownership of the "neocloud" company is transferred to Huang Le Ltd., an enterprise controlled by Alice Huang. She becomes its managing director.
June 2023
Cloud-computing company Shanghai Century Litong is founded. A company linked to Alice's sister, Huang Yu, held an ownership stake.
October 2023
Nvidia designates Shanghai Century Litong as a preferred cloud partner, giving the Chinese company priority access to Nvidia's chips, according to The Information.
Around November 2023
Megaspeed's shares were transferred to another Singapore company, Swiftdata, and Alice Huang ceased to be listed as a director of the company, according to news site Caixin Global.
June 7, 2024
Information technology firm NetThunder posted a picture on social media of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang with other tech executives at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan.
End of 2024
Megaspeed's assets exploded from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, according to financial filings reviewed by Reuters.

Shipment records from December 2024 through early 2026, analyzed by short-selling firm Culper Research, suggest that Megaspeed's Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, imported about $4 billion in products from a company that builds equipment with Nvidia chips.
Early 2025

Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, jointly pitched Chinese investors on a Southeast Asia data center project, reportedly telling them they had "no problem securing GPUs" — the graphics processing units Nvidia specializes in — and citing Alibaba as a customer, according to the Financial Times.
Jensen Huang meets with President Trump at the White House. It marks their first of many White House encounters in Mr. Trump's second term.
February 2025
Singapore opens an investigation into Megaspeed and several other companies over suspected false declarations related to the purchase of servers and other offenses, according to Bloomberg News.
Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are recorded on video together at a dinner at San Liu Shi Fu restaurant in Taipei, around the time of the Computex tech conference in Taiwan.
July 2025

Jensen Huang says the technology giant has won approval from the Trump administration to sell its advanced H20 computer chips, used to develop artificial intelligence, to China, a reversal of prior administration policy.
"It's so innovative and dynamic here in China that it's really important that American companies are able to compete and serve the market here in China," Huang said at the time.
That same month, Nvidia becomes the first public company to be worth $4 trillion.
February 2026
Chinese police detained Kang Wei, Alice Huang's husband and business partner, in connection with suspected stock manipulation, sources told Caixin.

That same month, Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country after she downplayed her role at Megaspeed amid the country's investigation into its operations, according to a Bloomberg News report.
Jensen Huang boards Air Force One in Alaska to accompany Mr. Trump on a two-day trip to Beijing.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Mr. Trump about the counterintelligence risk posed by Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang, according to The New York Times. The briefing, which occurred before Jensen Huang joined the trip, was the second briefing Mr. Trump had received from U.S. intelligence about the Nvidia CEO's relationship, the Times reported.
Jensen Huang attends Mr. Trump's state dinner for China's Xi Jinping at the White House.
Jensen Huang attends an AI event at the White House and signs a set of voluntary AI safety standards amid calls for tighter guardrails on the technology.

Jensen Huang writes a message to Nvidia employees admitting that he had an extramarital affair. The same day, Nvidia's board said it had launched an independent investigation amid reports that its CEO was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
The New York Times on Nov. 8 reported that U.S. government surveillance suggested Alice Huang was feeding information directly to Beijing.

At an impromptu press conference at the White House, Mr. Trump said he had spoken to Jensen Huang and that the tech exec had indicated he was unaware of Alice Huang's links to China's intelligence services. Mr. Trump also described the Nvidia CEO as an "honorable man" who's "definitely suffering."
Mr. Trump didn't address questions about when he first learned about the spy allegations, only saying "not too long ago" and that "it didn't make much of an impact on me."
The New York Times reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, a subordinate at Nvidia.
Nvidia's board of directors announces that Jensen Huang has resigned, effective immediately.

Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings, with interim CEO Colette Kress hosting the call following Huang's resignation. Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones said the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Nvidia reverses course on Huang's exit, announcing his reinstatement as CEO effective immediately. "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the company said in a statement.

title: Trump, tech CEOs cheer Huang's return, but lawmakers question board
summary: President Trump and prominent tech figures applauded Huang's reinstatement as CEO, though some lawmakers criticized the move as "reckless."
story: President Trump and high-profile business leaders applauded Nvidia's shock move to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after the billionaire entrepreneur's resignation from the chipmaker.
In a post on social media platform Truth Social on Monday, Mr. Trump cheered the board's move, calling it "an absolutely GREAT decision" that would benefit the U.S. economy.

Mr. Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had spoken to Nvidia's board members to encourage them to reinstate Huang. "We have to protect our geniuses, and he is certainly a genius," he told the media outlet.

SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, another prominent supporter of Huang's, said in a post on X that "The mistake has been corrected," referring to the Nvidia co-founder's Nov. 12 resignation following revelations that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair and apologized to his family. Huang also had a relationship with a subordinate at Nvidia, the New York Times reported last week, while Reuters reported that he had an intimate relationship with a second employee at the company.

Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones on Monday announced that Huang's "reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers." Last week, during a quarterly earnings call discussing Nvidia's latest financial results, Jones said the board had no intention of rehiring him.
Sam Altman, CEO of ChatGPT developer OpenAI, in which Nvidia has pledged to invest up to $100 billion, issued a one-word post on X on Monday. "Jensen!" he wrote.
For their part, investors also seem heartened by Huang's return. Nvidia's stock soared $39.80 per share, or 32%, on Monday, quickly adding more than $1 trillion to the company's market value.
Lawmakers keep heat on Nvidia

Not everyone cheered Huang's return to the world's most valuable AI chipmaker. In a statement, Sen. Elizabeth Warren called the Nvidia board's decision to reinstate Huang "reckless." The Massachusetts Democrat also pressed Nvidia's board to offer more details on its decision to rehire Huang.

"Jensen Huang's return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk," she said.

Lawmakers have moved to strengthen controls around U.S. exports to restrict China from gaining remote access to the most powerful chips and chipmaking equipment. On Nov. 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued a new rule to close a loophole to protect sensitive American technology.

"Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain," Sen. Charles Schumer, a Democrat from New York, said in a social media post. "We'll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries."

Sen. John Cornyn, a Texas Republican, also expressed concern on social media about Nvidia's decision to restore Huang, questioning the board's conclusion that rehiring him posed no national security risk.

In addition to existing license requirements for advanced semiconductors, the rule adds new license requirements for exporting, re-exporting or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand. The department said such nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."

Despite Huang's resumption of his duties at Nvidia, the House Intelligence Committee plans to carry on with a closed-door hearing with the executive next week, sources told CBS News. Huang and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter were also expected to appear before other congressional panels in early December to answer questions about the company's export practices, among other issues.
Huang has long lobbied for the federal government to allow Nvidia to sell its most powerful AI chips to China.

title: Anthropic's IPO set for blastoff in key test for AI boom
summary: Anthropic's stock is poised to start trading on Nasdaq Thursday in one of the largest IPOs of all time. The AI world is watching.
story: Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering is set to launch on Thursday, a milestone that will test investor enthusiasm for the company behind the popular Claude chatbot and the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector.

"This is a case where the deal is so large and important, so central to the AI thesis, that it's going to be a turning point for the AI sector," Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, told CBS News. "Even non-AI companies are going to feel the ripple effects, especially in the IPO market."
Anthropic shares are scheduled to start trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT" sometime after markets open Thursday at 9:30 a.m. ET.
Anthropic increases stock price amid high demand

In an announcement on Wednesday night, San Francisco-based Anthropic said it will offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 each. The initial public offering raised around $81 billion and valued Anthropic at $1.5 trillion, making it the largest public offering in history. Elon Musk's SpaceX raised $75 billion when it went public in June.
Anthropic is selling 956.3 million shares, although only 7.4% will be available for public trading (up to 9.8% including Class A shares held by nonfounder employees), according to Renaissance.

The company plans to raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, all of which have a stake in the AI race.

Kennedy thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading, an increase that would represent a "solid pop," he said. If the stock rises closer to $140, "that would tell me that AI enthusiasm has come roaring back," he added.
Great expectations
Although many investors appear eager to own a piece of Anthropic, the IPO comes amid growing concerns about whether the torrid spending on AI will deliver the expected productivity and profit boom.

AI-related stocks have fluctuated in recent weeks following subpar earnings and the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance data center construction. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors, with the chipmaker's stock now down more than 35% from its October all-time high.

"The whole AI sector has sold off from its July peak. Investor enthusiasm was greatest then," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, told CBS News.

Although Anthropic has yet to turn a profit, the company has shown explosive revenue growth over its short time in business. Anthropic raked in nearly $17 billion in the third quarter this year, up 45% from the second quarter, a recent regulatory filing shows. Given that heady rate of expansion, Ritter expects Anthropic to reach profitability quickly.

To justify its projected trillion-dollar valuation, however, the company will need to sustain that momentum while operating under Wall Street's unsparing gaze. Compounding the challenge is how quickly the AI landscape itself is changing. For instance, Anthropic could struggle to maintain its growth rate as consumers shift from pricier AI models like Claude and ChatGPT to cheaper open-source models, Ritter noted.

Anthropic also will have to spend heavily to keep developing its AI models and stay ahead of rivals, from OpenAI, Alphabet and Meta to Chinese platforms. Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Meanwhile, the company has committed to spending nearly a trillion dollars on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045, according to a securities filing.

Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.
"The company is likely to be very successful, but the market is pricing in very lofty expectations," Ritter said. "It could be hard for management to execute."
Wall Street analysts said Anthropic's share offering has broader ramifications for the AI sector, with the IPO's pricing setting a benchmark for other tech companies planning to go public.
Even if Anthropic's stock soars on the first day of trading, it won't necessarily create a swarm of IPO activity, Kennedy said. Still, it could reinvigorate markets, he added.

Meanwhile, by going public, Anthropic is effectively asking investors to discount the threats that Anthropic founder Dario Amodei himself has identified as posed by AI. In September, he called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after a former Anthropic researcher warned of the existential threat AI poses to humanity.

title: Anthropic shares jump in Nasdaq trading debut after record IPO
summary: Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion, catapulting it past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion​ when it went public in June.
story: Anthropic's stock soared in early trading on Nasdaq Thursday before partly shedding those gains in the afternoon, as the artificial intelligence developer completed the largest initial public offering in history.

Trading under the ticker "ANT," Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, up 34% from the $83 offer price, and rose as high as $114.99, valuing the company at more than $2 trillion at the peak. The stock pared those gains over the course of the day, closing at $97.17, a rise of 17%.

"Both the jump from the offer price and the high volatility are not surprising, given the enormous potential of the company and the wildly different opinions about how profitable the company will become," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, said in an email.

Anthropic shares rose on a day when the rest of the stock market took a dive. Late in Thursday's session, the Nasdaq dropped 550 points, or 2.3%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled more than 1,100 points, or 2.2%, and the S&P 500 sank 2%.
"Seminal" moment
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei celebrated Anthropic's market debut at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City on Thursday.
"The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time," Dario Amodei said Thursday in an event to mark the IPO.
"The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better," he added.

San Francisco-based Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its IPO, catapulting past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it went public in June. The IPO values the company behind the Claude chatbot at roughly $1.5 trillion, more than companies such as Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Walmart.

Anthropic's IPO represents an "A-plus success," Dan Ives, a tech analyst and partner of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News. "I think it's a vote of confidence for the market relative to the tech trade," he added.
The public offering delivered a huge payday to the seven Anthropic co-founders, boosting their worth on paper to around $20 billion each. It will also turn many Anthropic employees into millionaires.

Anthropic said Wednesday that it would offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 per share, allowing it to raise a record-breaking amount. Anthropic originally priced its shares in a range of $70 to $78, but raised its per-share IPO price amid strong investor demand.

The IPO price of $83 a share is what Anthropic insiders and other early investors pay to receive an allocation of stock. According to Renaissance Capital, which tracks IPOs, 7.4% of Anthropic shares are available for public trading (or up to 9.8% if Class A shares held by non-founder employees are included).
Even if Americans don't buy shares, Anthropic's IPO could still affect their 401(k), given how exposed the stock market is to AI stocks.

Anthropic has previously said it will raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, bringing its fundraising total to around $107 billion.
Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading.

However, like many companies that go public in a blockbuster, and perhaps overhyped, share offering, Anthropic's stock could well waver in the months to come. In a Truist study of 32 of the biggest ever IPOs, more than half saw their shares slide by at least 50% at some point during their first year of trading.

Anthropic announced its plans to go public in October, inviting investors to be part of what it called one of the "seminal moments in human history." The company is the first frontier AI lab to go public.
Critical time for AI trade

Anthropic's IPO comes at a critical time for the AI industry, as investors are asking harder questions about the sector's growing losses, capital investments and returns, Sam Grelck, an equity strategy analyst at Truist Advisory Services, a unit of Truist Financial, told CBS News.
"I wouldn't view Anthropic's IPO as a verdict on AI, but the reception can give us another indication of investors' appetite for the AI theme after what's been a challenging few weeks," he said.

AI-related stocks have swung sharply in recent weeks as concerns mount about the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance the data center buildout and a potential Democratic-led crackdown on the AI boom following the midterms. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors.
At a time when investors are skittish, the robust demand for Anthropic shares suggests there is still faith that lofty investments in AI will pay off.
"Anthropic's IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Ives said in a research note.
Financing its future

The IPO provides Anthropic with cash to finance its AI development plans. The company, which is yet to turn a profit, has said it wants to use its technology to "improve how humans live" by providing tailored financial and legal advice and speeding up scientific discovery.
"I believe sufficient and powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of medical and scientific progress into a decade," Amodei said at Nasdaq in New York on Thursday.
While the IPO will boost its coffers, Anthropic could quickly burn through cash as it works to keep its AI models on the cutting edge and stay ahead of rivals like OpenAI.

As of Sept. 30, the company had $6.2 billion in debt, according to its regulatory filing. At the same time, it has committed to spending nearly $1 trillion on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045.

title: Stocks enter correction territory, driven by deepening tech rout
summary: The tech-heavy Nasdaq tumbled more than 1,200 points, putting it on track for its second-worst day of the year.
story: Technology stocks plunged on Friday, dimming investor cheer over Anthropic's high-profile IPO this week amid mounting concerns about the health of the artificial intelligence sector.

The Nasdaq Composite Index fell 1,261 points, or 5.3%, to close at 22,618, the tech-heavy index's second-worst day of 2026 and erasing all of its gains for the year. The S&P 500 declined 3.7%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9%.

Both the  S&P 500 and Dow entered "correction" territory, meaning the indexes have fallen more than 10% from their most recent highs. The S&P 500 is set for its seventh consecutive day of losses, its longest losing streak since February 2020, when the pandemic caused investors to sell in a panic.

Investors are fretting over the value of AI stocks, which drove much of Wall Street's gains earlier this year but are now driving the slide. Microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom led Friday's losses over concerns about a possible slowdown in data center construction and over tighter federal policies on exporting chips outside the U.S.

"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."

The S&P 500's decline into correction territory was largely driven by investors selling AI-related companies, but the underlying U.S. economic and business fundamentals remain solid, said Chris Larkin, managing director of trading and investing at E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley, in an email.

"It's impossible to know when any selloff will run its course, but history shows most moves like this don't turn into bear markets —only five of the past 15 corrections from all-time highs since 1983 have done so," he said, referring to when stocks decline 20% or more from the market's most recent peak.
Anthropic can't buck the market

Thursday's big market debut for Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI chatbot, fizzled on Friday, along with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.3% to $88.14, although it remains above its IPO price of $83 per share.

As of early afternoon trading on Friday, Anthropic's stock had fallen about 23% from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive Facebook (now Meta) saw shortly after its May 2012 IPO.
Shares of Nvidia, considered practically synonymous with the AI boom, are falling for the ninth day in the last 10, down 13% in late Friday trading.

The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI buildout, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its co-founder and former CEO. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has shed more than 25% of its value.
Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills jumped 4.4%, and homebuilder Lennar rose 2.5%.

title: White House national cyber director leaving his post
summary: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross will be leaving his position, a White House official told CBS News.
story: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross will be leaving his position, a White House official told CBS News.
Cairncross was fired, multiple sources told CBS News.

White House chief of staff Stephen Miller — who took over for Susie Wiles earlier this month — had long wanted Cairncross out of the job, sources said, telling people he didn't think Cairncross had the expertise needed to be national cyber director.

Miller immediately teed up a search process for a replacement and selected Kirsten Davies, currently the Pentagon's chief information director, to replace Cairncross, the sources said. On Friday, the White House announced President Trump had named her the new White House cyber director. She will, however, require Senate confirmation to serve in the role permanently.
Axios was first to report that Cairncross would leave.

Cairncross' departure comes as the U.S. reels from a series of technological outages over the last week that have hit Microsoft services, air traffic control systems, banks and the National Security Agency's internal network.

Authorities investigating the outages have "seen nothing that would indicate that they are related," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told lawmakers this week. He said he is "98% confident" the outages are not the result of malicious foreign activity, though he acknowledged that he had "absolutely not" seen so many outages in a short period of time.
The national cyber director advises the president on cybersecurity and coordinates cyber strategy across the federal government. An attorney, Cairncross has served in the role since August 2025.
The job was created in 2021. In recent years, the U.S. has faced a series of cyberattacks linked to actors in Iran, Russia, China and other U.S. adversaries.

The Trump administration released its cyber strategy in March, which Cairncross' office oversaw. The seven-page document vowed to "detect, confront, and defeat cyber adversaries before they breach our networks and systems," harden critical infrastructure, maintain a U.S. edge in artificial intelligence and modernize federal tech systems.
In a November 2025 appearance at the Aspen Cyber Summit, Cairncross said one of the administration's primary goals is "introducing costs and consequences" on adversaries.

"I think, as a country, we have not done a terrific job of sending a signal to our adversaries that this behavior is not consequence-free," he said. "And we need to do that because it is scaling and it is becoming more aggressive every passing day."
In a statement, Cairncross called the role "the honor of a lifetime."

"I leave my role as Director of Cyber incredibly proud of our work to strengthen America's cybersecurity, protect our critical infrastructure, confront foreign threats, and position America to lead the world in Super Intelligence. None of it would have been possible without President Trump's extraordinary leadership," he said.

title: Why the Army says it needs to detonate unstable explosives in Iowa
summary: The U.S. Army plans to detonate 68 drums of lead azide in Iowa despite local leaders and residents raising concerns.
story: The U.S. Army's plan to detonate several tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa has been delayed multiple times amid a court battle and community outcry about the risk of toxic lead particles spreading in a dust plume for miles.
The Army said the controlled detonation of lead azide is necessary due to the public safety risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating on their own.

"Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the Army said in a statement.

President Trump said Monday that without the demolition, "a very dangerous situation exists," but ordered the Army to defer its plans until a ruling came down from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit. The court ruled Monday evening that it can go forward.
So why exactly does the Army need to detonate the chemicals and what are the risks to the public?
Why does the Army need to detonate lead azide in Iowa?

In March of this year, the Army said it discovered that 68 drums of lead azide at the site had started "recrystallization." The lead was stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a munitions plant built in 1941, which produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions.
Lead azide is a highly sensitive primary initiating explosive. Due to its extreme sensitivity, even minor external triggers, such as sparks, open flames, friction or pinpricks, can detonate it.
The recrystallization of lead azide can have a high risk of spontaneous explosion, which the EPA said creates a highly unstable and dangerous situation.

Additionally, cold weather would further destabilize the explosive materials. Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command, told CBS News Chicago that the risk of accidental detonation increases in cold weather.
Military officials said it's not safe to relocate the explosive materials.
The Army said it modeled four different ways to try to neutralize the chemicals, and concluded that a controlled detonation was the best method available.

"It was determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a statement.

Army officials said they connected with stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the surrounding area about the approved plan. Critics, however, contend they weren't made aware of the plan to detonate the lead azide until just days before the scheduled controlled explosion.
Local politicians said the decisions were made at the federal level, and poor communication contributed to the outcry and confusion from residents concerned about toxic chemicals.

"The safety of Iowans now and in the future should be the government's top concern. An unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation," Sand said.
What are the risks to residents?
One of the main concerns is that lead particles would be scattered in the dust plume created by the explosion. Lead in any amount is dangerous for humans, and in particular for young children.
"Lead is a really challenging contaminant," said David Cwiertny, a professor at the University of Iowa and director of its Environmental Policy Research Program.
He said there are essentially two ways the lead could be released: moving freely in the air and collecting on the ground.
"We do expect that air to dissipate fairly quickly as it moves with the wind," Cwiertny said.

Lead can enter the body through contaminated food, water or through dust or fumes, according to the U.S. National Institutes of Health, leading to health issues for adults and children. It can impede growth, contribute to learning disorders and damage the brain and nervous system. Children under age 6 are most susceptible to lead poisoning, the CDC says, as their bodies and brains are still developing.

Residents were told to evacuate the immediate area ahead of the planned explosion. But some are worried that afterward, lead would contaminate the environment and infiltrate their groundwater, rendering their communities unsafe.
Middletown resident Sean Byers, whose house is across from the munitions plant, pointed down the street and said, "There's a playground back over there where kids in the community play all the time."
Byers, who has three young children, said he's worried about contamination.
"It's going to linger probably for decades," he said. "It's going to affect everyone."
Are there any steps to reduce the risk?
The Army said it planned to take a number of steps to reduce the risk in a controlled detonation.

The lead azide drums would be detonated inside earth-covered magazines made of concrete, and surrounded with Hesco barriers full of sand, which are approximately two stories high. Before and during the detonation, explosive experts would saturate the soil above with water. Water misters would also be spraying, the Army said.

Residents would be asked to vacate the area at that time, as the controlled detonation "will cause temporary noise, ground vibrations, and a dust plume that will contain some lead," the Army said in a statement.

Byers said he found out about the planned explosion through his neighbor a few days before the planned explosions — not from the U.S. Army. He said he plans to evacuate with his family to Branson, Missouri, where they'd stay for three or four days.
He said the Army told them it would be safe to return to their homes after six hours, but he "highly doubts" that.
Notices were sent out by the Army saying residents' windows could potentially break, and if they do, they'd be replaced by the ammunition plant.

Byers said he got the notice, but says, "The damage at that point has already been done, because it's going to let all that lead enter the house. And the question is, are they going to come in and decontaminate that? Are they going to, you know, are they going to do that? Probably not."

The Army said that due to its mitigation efforts, while there will be some lead particles in the air after the detonation, the levels will be well below the level at which the EPA requires protective actions.

title: Army to detonate unstable explosives in Iowa Wednesday morning
summary: A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa.
story: The Army is set to detonate 5 tons of explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday morning after a back-and-forth that has played out between politicians and in court.

The detonation will take place at 9 a.m. Central time, acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said Tuesday at a press conference. Telle said the unstable explosives become more dangerous as temperatures drop, and the weather forecast for Wednesday is "ideal to protect public health and safety across the region."

"Inaction is no longer an option," Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the commander of the operation, said Tuesday. "It would be irresponsible for us to not take the determined, consensus-based course of action moving forward."
The government has argued the detonation — which is expected to send a plume of toxic lead particles into the surrounding area — is necessary because the lead azide could spontaneously explode.

"There is consensus across the experts, across the country, that a controlled mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to an uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance," Telle said Tuesday.

A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating the explosives. The court's ruling came after environmental groups challenged the validity of the emergency permit granted by the Environmental Protection Agency and argued the EPA hadn't given enough notice to residents.
Following the ruling, the Army noted Monday night that current Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds "has given her support to go forward."

"It is the unanimous judgement of our people — the Army, Navy, EPA, ATF, FBI, DARPA, DoE, CDC, HHS, FEMA and every other agency involved — that the Army should proceed with an extensively mitigated, carefully controlled detonation, which will occur this Wednesday morning, as previously scheduled, based on forecast wind conditions," Telle said on X.

The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily blocked the detonation last week to give itself time to issue a longer-lasting ruling. On Monday, the court said the environmental groups that challenged the plan had failed to show they are likely to succeed.

"We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide," the ruling said. "However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place."

President Trump said earlier Monday the government would not carry out the detonation until the appeals court ruled and unless Democratic Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand signed off. Mr. Trump added that government experts felt detonating the material was the best option.

"If [Sand] or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation," the president said on social media.

Sand, whose input was not required and who is not yet in office, said on social media the Trump administration "should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks."
"Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward," Sand said.

The government has argued that even if the appeals court had stayed its EPA permit, the Army has the legal right to move forward without a permit to "respond to the immediate threat of an uncontrolled explosion."

The Army has stored the lead azide in earthen-covered containers for decades at its ammunition plant in Middletown, a small town located near the Mississippi River in southeastern Iowa. The EPA has said the government discovered earlier this year that the material deteriorated over time, risking explosion if it is moved or disturbed.

As part of an earlier detonation plan slated for Friday, the Army asked some Middletown residents to temporarily evacuate their homes for six hours, and said people could expect loud noises, vibrations and a dust plume.

Environmental groups and Iowa and Illinois politicians from both parties criticized the plan, arguing the detonation could lead to widespread lead contamination in both states and pressing the EPA and Army to consider other options.

The Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council asked the federal appeals court to step in and review the EPA's permit last week. The environmental groups said the EPA failed to fully assess the risks of the detonation or consider alternatives, and argued the Army was operating on an "extraordinarily rushed timeline" that prevented residents from getting enough notice.

On Monday, a panel of three appellate judges sided with the federal government. The court found that the EPA "adequately incorporated safeguards" to mitigate the risks, including barriers and plans for environmental monitoring, and the Army considered a range of alternatives.

title: 5 questions Nvidia still faces after bringing back Jensen Huang
summary: Despite Jensen Huang's shock return as Nvidia's CEO, experts say it's anything but business as usual for the chipmaker.
story: Jensen Huang's first task in returning to lead Nvidia after resigning last week under a cloud will be to deal with the fallout from his stunning exit and even more surprising reprieve.

Following his reinstatement by the company's board, some lawmakers are calling for investigations into President Trump's role in the billionaire entrepreneur's return and whether Nvidia skirted export rules meant to prevent its advanced chips from reaching China. And while Huang may be viewed as key to Nvidia's success, his return raises a thicket of legal and operational problems, according to financial and governance experts.

"Three tests will now decide how strongly it builds from here: how its leadership sits with Washington, how it handles China and how long AI spending keeps growing at this speed,"  said Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, an investment advisory firm, in an email.
Here are five critical questions facing Nvidia as Huang retakes the helm.
Did Nvidia compromise U.S. national security?

One of Nvidia's major customers, Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, employed a Chinese businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and whom U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China. Megaspeed is also alleged to have smuggled Nvidia's advanced chips into China and provided remote access to the technology in violation of U.S. export controls.

Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter are scheduled to appear on Dec. 1- 2 in closed-door interviews before multiple congressional panels to discuss the company's ties to China. Huang is also scheduled to appear on Dec. 3 at a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on U.S. export rules and global AI competition.

"The Nvidia board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the Republican chairs of the House committees who will interview Huang and Teter said on Monday.
Will Nvidia's board face legal issues?

The board's decision to reinstate Huang is likely to set off a flurry of shareholder lawsuits over questions including whether Nvidia failed to disclose the spying allegations earlier and whether the company was aware of Megaspeed's links to China, according to Charles Elson, founding director of the John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware.

Shareholders could also challenge Huang and Nvidia over their failure to disclose his personal relationships with subordinates at the company, which appears to violate the chipmaker's code of conduct. Earlier this month, Nvidia was sued by shareholders for allegedly failing to disclose information about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive (no relation).
"There's just a whole range of things that they can bring actions," Elson said.
Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment about whether it will continue pursuing an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence.
Will Nvidia face new U.S. export restrictions?
Nvidia is expected to come under increased scrutiny and face greater regulatory hurdles in selling chips to China and companies in Southeast Asia.
"There will definitely be tighter restrictions, and any dealings directly with China will be the government's primary focus," StoneX equity research analyst Cody Acree told CBS News.

Huang has long lobbied U.S. officials to permit Nvidia to sell its most advanced chips to China, with an eye toward growing its market. Earlier this month, the Commerce Department moved to curb sales of U.S. chips to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand.

"Going forward, they'll be subject to more export controls so that their chips don't end up in China and data centers in Asia," Gil Luria, lead tech analyst at investment firm D.A. Davidson, told CBS News. "In that way, Nvidia's market has shrunk, and that business will go away."
Can Huang ease investor fears about an AI bust?

Investors cheered Huang's return partly because it suggests that Nvidia will continue in its role as the de facto "bank of AI," providing financing for companies that buy its chips and otherwise fueling the sector's growth. Huang helped arrange deals such as Nvidia's investment in OpenAI. Through such circular financing, Nvidia invests vast sums in AI companies, which then flow back to the chipmaker through chip purchases.

"Nvidia is more than just a chipmaker — it's heavily involved in the broader AI ecosystem by financing other companies," Capital Economics senior economist James Reilly told CBS News. "Having Jensen back reassures investors that those relationships and that financing will continue."
Still, Huang's return doesn't erase concerns about the sector's debt-fueled spending, or whether AI companies will ever turn a profit and deliver returns to investors.
"There are growing concerns as to whether all of this AI investment will generate the revenue it needs long-term to make it worthwhile," Reilly said. "Those hurdles are very demanding."
What is Nvidia's succession plan?
Developing a succession plan to replace Huang will be the first item on the board's agenda, Elson, a prominent governance expert, told CBS News.

When Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month, he had more than 60 direct reports, a structure that allowed him to wield enormous power. However, his departure made it clear that the company had no succession plan should Huang be unable to lead.
As a result, Elson expects Nvidia to hire an outside consultant to help forge a plan for who might succeed Huang.
Such "key man" risk isn't unique to Nvidia, Acree noted.

"You have other high-profile CEOs at the helm of large companies, but that's the nature of Silicon Valley, unfortunately," he said, pointing to Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and SpaceX's Elon Musk. "There is no way to address that risk entirely or make it go away, but boards will be more sensitive to that in the future."

title: Rep. Omar D.C. home search sought evidence going back to 1980
summary: The warrant application covers a 46-year period beginning in 1980, long before Omar was in Congress, according to newly released court records. The documents are heavily redacted, and no criminal charges are listed.
story: A federal magistrate judge questioned whether prosecutors had probable cause for at least two of the offenses they were investigating when they sought to search the Washington, D.C., home of Democratic Minnesota U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, according to court documents released Monday evening.

The records, which cover last month's raid, reveal a behind-the-scenes constitutional dispute between federal prosecutors and U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh. The judge's questions about probable cause surface in a filing prosecutors made Oct. 7. The specific statutes are redacted.

The Justice Department expressly disclaimed any connection to Omar's congressional office, describing the investigation as concerning private conduct, not legislative activity. But the judge, who raised the question independently after reviewing the warrant application, concluded that Speech or Debate Clause protections for members of Congress apply to a search of Omar's home. Prosecutors had argued the privilege covers only congressional offices and certain electronic devices. "That logic does not hold," Sharbaugh wrote.

Sharbaugh also rejected prosecutors' reasoning about how likely it was that congressional materials would be kept at Omar's home, writing: "That perspective blinks reality." The judge noted that many professionals bring work home and that a lawmaker's work happens in many places.

The judge also required the Justice Department to modify its search procedures. Prosecutors had offered two alternative protocols, but the judge found both fell short because agents would have searched before Omar, even with a lawyer present, had a chance to identify legislative materials. The judge required that Omar have an opportunity to identify constitutionally protected legislative materials before investigators searched for them. The judge also rejected the government's suggestion that such protections would make lawmakers immune from prosecution.

The majority of the 169 pages of court documents are heavily redacted and consist of exchanges between federal prosecutors and a magistrate judge over probable cause, constitutional privilege, warrant execution and public unsealing. The redactions obscure the underlying criminal allegations, the supporting evidence and the inventory of seized property. The released docket lists no criminal charges. A 67-page affidavit at the heart of the warrant request remains largely under seal for now.

According to one of the documents, federal government officials applied for a search warrant on Oct. 2 to search Omar's home for "[a]ll records and information that constitute fruits, contraband, evidence, and instrumentalities of violations of." The document then contains redacted text before stating, "those violations involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present." That is a 46-year window, and prosecutors identified Omar in the papers by an alternative name.

Federal officials provided two ex parte briefs in support of the warrant to the court before the judge signed it on Oct. 9. According to Cornell Law School, ex parte refers to "communication with a judge or opposing party without the presence or knowledge of the other party's attorney."
Homeland Security Investigations agents executed the warrant on Oct. 12. HSI has jurisdiction over federal offenses including immigration document fraud, identity fraud and immigration benefit fraud.

The court documents, released by the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, said federal investigators were authorized to seize documents, records, photos, thumb drives, external hard drives, computers and cellphones "registered or used by" Omar.

Three days before the raid, a judge granted a request to have the warrant sealed, stating that "because of such reasonable grounds to believe the disclosure will result in flight from prosecution, destruction of or tampering with evidence, intimidation of potential witnesses, and serious jeopardy to the investigation," according to the court documents.

A document filed by the federal government on Oct. 16 said, "The United States believes ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades—beginning long before she was ever in Congress," though the filing did not identify the alleged crimes.

The search came less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. That drew criticism because the Justice Department customarily avoids public investigative steps involving candidates within 60 days of an election, an unwritten practice.

U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro asked that a judge on Monday not release any of the files because they may be needed in a future trial. Associate Deputy Attorney General Alessandra P. Serano and Pirro's office sought continued secrecy as recently as Nov. 4, according to the documents. WCCO sources have said there are several immigration issues that authorities are investigating.

Multiple relatives of Omar received grand jury subpoenas days before the search, according to sources familiar with the matter, as part of the investigation into possible fraud and false statements in the family's immigration paperwork.
Criminal defense attorney Joe Tamburino says this case is highly unusual.

"First of all, it's unusual because you have a sitting member of Congress, I don't know when that has ever happened, if ever," Tamburino said. "Second, you have a situation where somebody could be in jeopardy of losing their citizenship, and I have never seen that."

WCCO reached out to Omar's office on Monday and has not yet heard back. Her office said in a statement on Oct. 12 that Omar had "done nothing wrong" and called the raid an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."

title: How far lead dust from the Iowa detonation could travel Wednesday
summary: Maps of the planned lead azide detonation in Middletown show the shaded area stretching from near Burlington toward Macon, Missouri, by noon Wednesday. The forecasts will change with the weather.
story: New maps of the Army's planned lead azide detonation in southeast Iowa show a plume of toxic dust drifting southwest toward northeast Missouri between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. Wednesday.

The Army plans to detonate about 5 tons of degraded lead azide, in 68 barrels, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown at 9 a.m. Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving, according to an emergency alert sent to cellphones Tuesday morning. The alert said some people within 5 miles southwest of the plant may be evacuated and told people up to 20 miles away to stay indoors with windows closed. Officials expect the wind to blow southwest, away from Burlington, a city of just under 25,000 people on the Mississippi River.

The Army moved the detonation from Friday, citing more favorable wind and time to add safety measures, according to a government court filing. A federal appeals court cleared the way Monday for the detonation after it had been delayed several times amid lawsuits from environmental groups and concerns from elected officials in Illinois and Iowa.

The maps show the modeled lead dust from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m. Wednesday. At 9 a.m., a red circle is centered near the plant. By 9:45 a.m., the shaded area becomes a long oval running from near Burlington southwest toward the Missouri line.

By early afternoon, the shaded area stretches far into northeast Missouri, passing Knox City. By late afternoon, it narrows to a band running from the Burlington and Keokuk area toward Macon, Missouri, with Quincy, Illinois, just southeast of it.

Wind arrows on the maps point southwest. Illinois officials said Monday that NOAA's latest model showed no Illinois counties would be affected. The Illinois EPA had asked the Army for updated modeling but had not received it, officials said, and Gov. JB Pritzker has directed state agencies to remain on alert.
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said state agencies are setting up additional monitoring of air and water quality.

The maps are forecasts and will change with the weather. Under the EPA's permit, the Army must update its plume forecasts six hours before the detonation and hourly after that until it is finished. The Army's forecasts do not establish that harmful exposure will occur at every location inside a projected plume, and sampling will be needed to show where lead settles on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces.
Officials recommend that people stay indoors during the detonation and rinse outdoor surfaces with water afterward.
Why the Army is detonating the lead azide, and the pushback
"Inaction is no longer an option," said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, who leads the operation.

The Army says the lead azide has been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, in a bath of ethanol and water meant to keep it stable. A routine check this year found some of the water had evaporated, and the material has since recrystallized, making it increasingly sensitive to friction and shock. Army officials say moving the barrels now risks setting them off, and experts say the stockpile will become more volatile as temperatures cool, since less liquid in the barrels makes the solution more prone to freezing, which raises the risk of a chain reaction.

The Army has added blast barriers around the bunkers where the lead azide will be detonated, plans to apply ballistic gels and foams to absorb dust, and will douse the materials with thousands of gallons of water. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the goal is to keep as much of the dust as possible on the plant's grounds. The Army considered "every viable solution," he said, and concluded a controlled detonation is safest. The EPA issued an emergency permit for the detonation Nov. 13.

The plan has drawn criticism from both parties. A bipartisan group of Illinois and Iowa elected officials asked the Army and EPA to delay it and look for safer alternatives, citing poor communication with the public. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, an Illinois Democrat, called the operation a "failure of leadership of epic proportions." Earthjustice sued on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter, challenging the validity of the EPA's emergency permit. The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily blocked the detonation last week, then declined Monday to stop it, saying the groups had not shown they were likely to succeed and that the degraded explosives risk an uncontrolled blast without the permit's safety measures. The judges said the Army evaluated "a full range" of alternatives, including neutralizing the lead azide with other chemicals and thermal treatment.

President Trump said on social media that in addition to the court's go-ahead, he wanted Gov.-elect Rob Sand to approve the detonation. Sand, a Democrat who takes office in January, has said the decision is fully up to the administration. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said Tuesday she supports the plan after speaking with military leaders.

title: Shein to pay $100 million to settle claims it deceived customers
summary: The Singapore fast-fashion company misled millions of U.S. consumers about its products and policies, FTC alleges.
story: Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to settle allegations that the fast-fashion company harmed consumers by misleading them about its products and policies.

The Federal Trade Commission alleges that the Singapore-based retailer made it hard for customers to resolve purchase problems, broke its shipping promises, suppressed negative reviews and engaged in other deceptive practices.

"Shein attracted consumers with promises of affordable clothing, fast delivery and use of suppliers that earned above-average ratings on standards related to child and forced labor, among other representations,"  Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Tuesday. "In reality, the company misled millions of consumers about its products, its suppliers and the authenticity of its customer reviews. Shein further compounded consumer harm by making it extraordinarily difficult to obtain customer service."
Shein, which ships roughly 1 million packages to the U.S. daily, employed only five customer service representatives to field calls from American consumers about their orders, according to the FTC.

Shein also made deceptive claims about its supply chain and the origin of its cotton and failed to provide customers with shipping updates or help them locate late or missing packages, the agency alleged in its complaint.

The $100 million will be used to provide redress to Shein customers, the FTC said. Under the agency's proposed order, Shein is also barred from making misleading claims about shipping and delivery times and from suppressing negative product reviews. The company is also required to provide adequate customer service.

A Shein spokesperson said the agreement "does not constitute an admission of liability, and we continue to disagree with aspects of the FTC's characterization of our business and compliance practices."
Shein went public on the Hong Kong exchange in September. It's built a sizable customer base in the U.S., appealing to shoppers with ultra-cheap clothing styles and fast delivery.

Last year, the White House ended the "de minimis" tariff exemption that allowed low-cost packages, including shipments from Shein, to enter the U.S. duty-free. In April, Shein said it would raise prices for consumers after the loophole closed.
