title: DOJ directs array of litigators to help with ICE detainee lawsuits
summary: Roughly 2,000 DOJ civil litigators are being directed to help with thousands of ICE detainee habeas petitions.
story: The Justice Department has directed attorneys from across its civil litigation divisions to help defend the Trump administration against a growing number of lawsuits filed by individuals in immigration detention.

More than 97,000 detainees have filed habeas corpus petitions challenging their detention since January 2025, including approximately 10,000 new petitions just since October 2026 alone, according to a Nov. 24 memo obtained by CBS News. Habeas petitions are a legal mechanism through which individuals may challenge the lawfulness of their detention.

Prior to the second Trump administration, the federal caseload for habeas immigration detention petitions tended to be much lower — closer to a few hundred in an entire year. It can take weeks or even months to resolve an immigration habeas petition.
The Justice Department says the litigation is straining resources at U.S. attorneys' offices, which have been primarily responsible for handling the cases.

"Many of the Department's U.S. Attorneys' Offices have been overwhelmed by the influx of petitions and impracticable procedures set by the courts," Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote in a three-page memo.

The memo directs attorneys from the department's Antitrust, Civil, Civil Rights, and Environment and Natural Resources divisions and U.S. Trustees Program, to assist with the litigation — roughly 2,000 litigators across its civil components. The memo doesn't specify how many attorneys will be reassigned or how many cases they will be expected to handle.
Attorneys from the offices of the attorney general, deputy attorney general and associate attorney general will also take on additional cases.

Immigration-related habeas cases have skyrocketed since President Trump returned to office, as his administration has placed record numbers of individuals in ICE detention and narrowed the avenues for them to be released, including on bond.
Blanche characterized many of the habeas petitions as "frivolous" in his memo.
"The increase in habeas petitions resulted, in part, from the immigration bar's attempt to thwart President Trump's promise to the American people to prioritize their safety and security," he wrote.

Last year, Stephen Miller, the architect of the Trump administration's deportation policy and now the White House chief of staff, floated the idea of suspending the right of habeas corpus for those detained as part of Mr. Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration. The administration has not moved forward with the proposal, which would likely trigger swift legal challenges.
This story published first on CBS News at 4:43 p.m. on Nov. 24, 2026.

title: Wendy's "pricing scheme" inflated menu prices, lawsuit alleges
summary: In a proposed class action, a California resident alleges that Wendy's conspired with its franchisees to set and raise menu prices.
story: A proposed class-action lawsuit alleges that Wendy's engaged in a pricing scheme that reduced competition across its restaurants, driving up costs for customers.

The lawsuit, filed Monday in a Maryland district court, accuses the burger chain of conspiring with independently owned franchisees to set and raise prices at its U.S. locations over a six-year period between 2016 and 2022. Wendy's collected "competitively sensitive information" from franchisee locations, including transaction data, to coordinate prices, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit was filed by Andy Garcia, a California resident and longtime Wendy's customer, according to the suit. He alleges that Wendy's engaged in "anticompetitive conduct" that resulted in artificially high prices, causing him to pay more than he otherwise would have.
Garcia also sued NCR Voyix, a software company that provides Aloha POS, a point-of-sale system used by Wendy's.

"By delegating pricing decisions to a common decision-maker, it eliminates critical price competition that drives costs down for consumers," Blake Hunter Yagman, the lawyer representing Garcia and founding partner of Yagman PLLC, a class-action law firm headquartered in New York, said in an email.

"This is even more important with respect to food prices, which have never been higher — and Wendy's owes [it to] its consumers to compete on the merits for better service, more innovative products and better pricing," Yagman added.

Wendy's and NCR Voyix did not immediately respond to requests for comment. As of September, Wendy's had 432 company-owned restaurants and 6,762 franchisees across the U.S., according to the company's most recent regulatory filing.

In 2024, Wendy's raised concerns after saying it would test Uber-style pricing. Also known as dynamic pricing, that approach allows companies to set prices based on real-time market conditions and other factors such as weather.
Other restaurants have also faced scrutiny over their pricing practices. Last month, a consumer sued McDonald's over the use of an AI tool that recommends dynamic pricing.

title: Democrats have flipped 48 House seats. Here's the breakdown.
summary: Democrats won control of the House by flipping dozens of Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red.
story: Washington — Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Nov. 3 by flipping more than 40 Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

The 2026 midterm elections were also shaken up by last year's nationwide mid-decade redistricting gambit, with Texas Republicans shifting several districts rightward at President Trump's behest, California Democrats moving districts to the left and several other states tweaking their House maps for partisan purposes. Democrats notched several wins under the new maps, while the GOP's pickups have been more limited so far.
Winners in a handful of House races have yet to be projected by CBS News.
So far, 48 districts have shifted to Democrats and three have shifted to Republicans. Here's a look at the seats that swung:

In several districts, Democrats ousted GOP lawmakers who won by double digits two years ago.

Tennessee's 4th District: GOP Rep. Scott DesJarlais lost to Democrat Victoria Broderick in a deep-red part of Middle and East Tennessee that Mr. Trump won by 24 points, according to the Cook Political Report. The district was made somewhat less red due to redistricting.New Jersey's 2nd District: Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew lost to Democrat Zack Mullock in a South Jersey district that was widely seen as solid red. Van Drew, who won by 16.9 points in 2024, is known for switching from the Democratic Party during the first Trump impeachment saga in 2019. Ohio's 10th District: GOP Rep. Ann Wagner, who won by 12 points in 2024. Republicans tried to make the St. Louis-area seat slightly redder last year, but the new maps were tossed out in the courts. As recently as September, the Cook Political Report viewed it as solid-red.Indiana's 5th District: Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democrat J.D. Spartz won reelection by just over 18 points in 2024.Kentucky's 6th District: The race between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado for the open seat was not expected to be competitive, but the election forecasters moved the GOP-held seat toward Democrats in recent weeks. Outgoing Rep. Andy Barr won it by 26 points two years ago.Wisconsin's 1st District: Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, who was first elected in 2018, lost his race to Democrat Mitchell Berman. A Democrat has not represented the district in more than 30 years. title: Trump presents Rudy Giuliani with Presidential Medal of Freedom
summary: Rudy Giuliani, the former mayor of New York City who worked as a personal lawyer to President Trump, said he will be honored in the Oval Office.
story: Washington — President Trump presented Rudy Giuliani, the former New York City mayor who served as his personal lawyer during the 2020 election, with the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday.

The White House praised Giuliani for his work across his career as a federal prosecutor in New York and then as mayor of New York City. The Medal of Freedom ceremony was set to take place in the Oval Office at 11 a.m. ET, according to Mr. Trump's schedule.

"Mayor Rudy Giuliani is a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our Nation," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said in a statement. "As U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Mayor Giuliani took down mob bosses and led a relentless war on crime. As Mayor, he transformed New York from a crime-ridden city into one of the safest big cities in the world, fostering economic opportunity and cultural greatness. And in the aftermath of the tragic September 11th attacks, he displayed strong American leadership in the face of evil."
Giuliani said he is "honored and humbled" to receive the award.

"Any and all distinction I have received in public office is fully the result of following the advice of my boss, Ronald Reagan, who said: 'There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn't mind who gets the credit.' I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together,'" he said in a statement. "And to my family — mother, father, children, ancestors, and extended family, including my friends — what you have done will always mean the most. Doing the right thing for others has been my guiding light."

I am honored and humbled to receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom from my nation and from President Donald J. Trump.Any and all distinction I have received in public office is fully the result of following the advice of my boss, Ronald Reagan, who said: "There is no limit… pic.twitter.com/hKb7qi5Tc8
Giuliani told conservative commentator Steve Bannon on his podcast Monday that he would be receiving the nation's highest civilian honor at the White House.
"I'm of course very, very humbled and very honored not only to receive it, but to receive it from him," he told Bannon during his "War Room" podcast and livestream.

Created in 1945 by President Harry S. Truman, the Presidential Medal of Freedom recognizes individuals who have made significant contributions to the security or national interests of the U.S., world peace and cultural or other public or private endeavors.

Across his two terms, Mr. Trump has so far awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to 26 people, according to the Congressional Research Service. Giuliani will be the third person to receive the honor from Mr. Trump in his second term. The president posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to conservative activist activist Charlie Kirk last year after he was fatally shot on a college campus in Utah, as well as to Welles Crowther, a Boston College graduate who died in the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.

The president has said he plans to award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Ben Carson, a former neurosurgeon who led the Department of Housing and Urban Development during Mr. Trump's first term; Connor Hellebuyck, Team USA men's hockey goalie; and Roger Clemens, former Major League Baseball pitcher.

Mr. Trump announced in September 2025 that he would be awarding Giuliani, 82, with the Presidential Medal of Freedom and said details would be forthcoming. The president hailed Giuliani as the "greatest mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot."
Mr. Trump announced that Giuliani would be honored days after the former mayor was injured in a car crash in New Hampshire and hospitalized.

Giuliani rose to prominence as mayor of New York City in the 1990s and became known as "America's mayor" for his leadership following the 9/11 terror attacks. He mounted a run for the GOP presidential nomination in 2008 but ended his campaign after placing third in the Florida primary.

He became a close friend and adviser to Mr. Trump's in his first term and worked as a personal lawyer to Mr. Trump during the 2020 presidential election, during which he spread baseless claims that the contest was rife with widespread voter fraud and stolen from Mr. Trump.

Giuliani was disbarred from practicing law in New York and the District of Columbia as a result of the false statements he made about the integrity of the 2020 election. He was also found liable by a federal judge in 2023 for defaming two former election workers in Georgia and ordered to pay them $148 million. Giuliani filed for bankruptcy following the decision.

The former mayor also faced state charges in Georgia and Arizona in criminal cases stemming from alleged efforts to overturn results of the 2020 election in both states. He pleaded not guilty, and both cases were dismissed.

title: Federal court releases Rep. Ilhan Omar D.C. home raid documents
summary: A federal court on Monday evening released documents regarding last month's raid at the Washington, D.C. home of Democratic Minnesota U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar.
story: A federal court on Monday evening released documents regarding last month's raid at the Washington, D.C., home of Democratic Minnesota U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar.

The majority of the 169 pages of court documents are heavily redacted and consist of exchanges between federal prosecutors and a magistrate judge over probable cause, constitutional privilege, warrant execution and public unsealing.

According to one of the documents, federal government officials applied for a search warrant on Oct. 2 to search Omar's home for "[a]ll records and information that constitute fruits, contraband, evidence, and instrumentalities of violations of." The document then contains redacted text before stating, "those violations involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present."

Federal officials provided two ex parte briefs in support of the warrant to the court before the judge signed it on Oct. 9. According to Cornell Law School, ex parte refers to "communication with a judge or opposing party without the presence or knowledge of the other party's attorney."
Homeland Security Investigations agents executed the warrant on Oct. 12. HSI has jurisdiction over federal offenses including immigration document fraud, identity fraud and immigration benefit fraud.

The court documents, released by the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, said federal investigators were authorized to seize documents, records, photos, thumb drives, external hard drives, computers and cellphones "registered or used by" Omar.

Three days before the raid, a judge granted a request to have the warrant sealed, stating that "because of such reasonable grounds to believe the disclosure will result in flight from prosecution, destruction of or tampering with evidence, intimidation of potential witnesses, and serious jeopardy to the investigation," according to the court documents.

A document filed by the federal government on Oct. 16 said, "The United States believes ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades—beginning long before she was ever in Congress," though the filing did not identify the alleged crimes.

U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro asked that a judge on Monday not release any of the files because they may be needed in a future trial. WCCO sources have said there are several immigration issues that authorities are investigating.
Criminal defense attorney Joe Tamburino says this case is highly unusual.

"First of all it's unusual because you have a sitting member of Congress, I don't know when that has ever happened, if ever," Tamburino said. "Second, you have a situation where somebody could be in jeopardy of losing their citizenship, and I have never seen that."

WCCO reached out to Omar's office on Monday and has not yet heard back. Her office said in a statement on Oct. 12 that Omar had "done nothing wrong" and called the raid an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."

title: "We're racing towards huge dangers," AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio says
summary: As one of the "godfathers" of artificial intelligence, Yoshua Bengio helped bring generative AI into the world. Now he worries society isn't ready for what's coming.
story: Yoshua Bengio is the most professionally cited scientist alive, and the most cited computer scientist of all time. He's informally known as one of the three "godfathers" of artificial intelligence, along with Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun, for his foundational work on the deep neural networks that power today's AI models.
In short, Bengio helped usher AI into the world — a technology now being integrated into our schools, our search bars, our smartphones and our wars.
Yet despite being one of the principal minds behind AI, the University of Montreal professor is now urgently calling for a slowdown in its development and a renewed focus on using AI safely.

LawZero, the nonprofit where Bengio is co-president and scientific director, strives to develop AI that is "designed to be trustworthy and safe" — effectively a dissent from the models being released by Anthropic and OpenAI. Bengio wants companies, governments and AI lab employees to stop developing ever more capable AI systems.

What led to such a dramatic turnaround for one of the world's most prominent AI researchers? Bengio spoke with CBS News about AI risks, regrets and responsibility. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.

CBS News: You're considered one of the people most responsible for the early advancement of deep learning, and you're the most cited scientist in the world because of your work in AI. How do you feel about your past work today?

Yoshua Bengio: I feel like I learned a lot. It was exciting. But I should have seen some of the most serious risks earlier. And I think, like most humans, I was focused on the good side of my work. And not enough on the potential consequences.
What was the original goal of your early work on deep learning or AI?

I was trying to understand intelligence and do it in a way that was sufficiently abstract to help us understand human intelligence, animal intelligence and build intelligent machines. That was a very exciting research goal, with the hypothesis that there could be a few simple principles — think of the laws of physics for the physical world — that could explain intelligence.
Do you feel like that goal has been accomplished since then?
Beyond our expectations. There are still people who are in denial, but it's very clear that we have been making very rapid progress towards machines that are intelligent.
Have your personal views on what intelligence actually is changed over time?

It has been refined, but I haven't made a U-turn about the nature of intelligence. In the last few years, I've focused on how it can go wrong, in the sense that intelligence can be in the service of goals that are not ethical.
You've now shifted to advocating for AI safety — that's a markedly different focus than your earlier research. Can you explain that shift?

I was spending a lot of my brain cycles on two things. One was understanding how we can make AI more intelligent, and the other was how to apply AI to fields like medicine or handling the climate crisis, education and so on. I made a big pivot to orient my research to how we can make AI safe because the capabilities, the intelligence, can be in the service of really, really bad goals — whether in the hands of humans with those bad goals or the AI itself.
And as the intelligence of those systems grows, the risks of the very dangerous use of that intelligence grow as well.

Anthropic recently became the first AI lab to go public, turning many of its employees into millionaires and even billionaires. At the same time, these researchers acknowledge they might be building the equivalent of a doomsday device. What should AI researchers think about as they develop new models?

They should try to look honestly at their work, its consequences and at what is the best use of their time to be aligned with their values. If they care about humanity and democracy, I think they should reconsider what they're doing now.

What we've seen in the past few years, and especially since the summer, is that the companies don't really know how to deal with the misalignment problem — in other words, with building AIs that do things that are bad for us.

The risk is growing with capability. I don't think society is even ready. Even if we were to solve this problem — to deal with the existence of machines that are greatly superior to humans —we're racing in a direction that is dangerous. And even the people working in AI safety in those companies, in some ways, are contributing to this.

Many experts think that more powerful AI models far surpassing human intelligence, including in areas like creativity where people excel, will arrive sooner rather than later. Do you agree with that general timeline, and if so, how should we respond to such advancements?

My perception of when things could go wrong has certainly shifted towards earlier than, say, I was anticipating before the Hugging Face incident, and even earlier with the Mythos cyber capabilities. We are moving faster towards more and more capable systems, and we're moving faster towards systems that we don't know how to control.

Because of this, in my own work at LawZero, we have shifted our research program to aim for shorter-term goals that could have an impact earlier — to show that there is a different way of training AIs that will not almost systematically lead to reward hacking. In other words, systems that prefer to cheat and try to hide it rather than do the things we are asking.
What would a more honest AI look like?

I'm going to use an analogy. Right now, the way we're training AIs is like how you would try to teach drivers on the highway to not go over the speed limit. They get rewards when they get to their destination faster. And we're trying to control their bad behavior by putting detectors on the highway.

So what happens? Well, first, drivers are going to try to figure out where the detectors are. They're going to slow down only where the detectors are. And we're already seeing that in AI. In other words, when the AI knows that it's being tested, it behaves well. And if they're really smart, those drivers might even hack the detectors themselves.

Now let's imagine a different kind of way of building the drivers. Imagine a human driver who is in the same situation with the detectors, and they want to get to their destination. But they believe God is watching them, and there is nothing they can do to hide what they do from God. Well, they're going to behave well.
How can society prepare itself for what seems like an inevitable future in which AI is a feature of ordinary life?

The short-term urgency is to stop this crazy advance toward more and more capable systems that we're not sure how to control. It's not just inside the companies. The models can be leaked. The methods can be copied. There are many risks, and they all come from having machines that are very, very intelligent and can do things we didn't know how to do before.

So there's urgency in stopping this. And the place where it's most acute is in the compute resources that are used to train the next generations. Right now, the majority of compute resources are going into training future machines, rather than actually using what we have for the benefit of society. And those new models are bringing more and more danger because intelligence gives power, and that power can be misused.

What is the right way of pacing the frontier, of slowing down? And what kind of regulation and oversight is needed? I think that's an interesting discussion, and we should have it. But it's not going to happen until people understand we're racing towards huge dangers.
What do you think ordinary people who don't work in government or at artificial intelligence companies should do to make a positive impact on AI?

People need to understand this is much more serious than they would typically believe. That's the first thing. The second thing is: Don't fall into desperation and powerlessness, because we can change the future. We still have agency. We can change society. We're in a democracy, where governments can actually do something about all this.

But it's going to take enough people to ask for it, and demand it. And for that, they need to understand their life is at stake, children's lives are at stake, democracy is at stake, peace and stability are at stake. People need to understand that the stakes here are comparable to a war. It's not yet in front of us, but it's coming, and we need to prepare.
I've got a kid, and I know you have children and grandchildren. Do you feel positive about the future despite the dangers posed by AI?

For sure. I'm an optimist by nature. Here is the flip side of all the scary stuff. Humans, when they see danger, can pivot quickly. Think about how quickly we reacted to the pandemic. We didn't wait for an international agreement that would take a decade — we just acted and coordinated.

Because of the risks, I think that we might end up in a much better world, where there is no war anymore. Because we can't afford that kind of risk when there are AIs that can be used to kill everyone, or a large number of people.

I also think democracy is going to have to be much more robust, because the temptation to abuse the power that AI will provide is going to be so great that the only way around it is to have incredibly strong institutions.

So we may end up in a much better world, and that's in addition to, of course, all the scientific advances that AI can bring. But it's not going to happen if we're blind collectively to the current trajectories' risks.

If we were to solve the alignment problem, which is what I'm trying to do as a scientist, we still have to make sure humans don't use very powerful AIs — maybe even superintelligent AI's — against each other in the search for wealth, power and for reasons of hatred. All the bad things that humans are capable of. And I don't think our society is ready for this.

title: Huang's return at Nvidia puts spotlight on chipmaker's board
summary: Nvidia directors' decision to rehire Jensen Huang shows a "lack of courage," according to one prominent governance expert.
story: Nvidia's stunning about-face on Monday to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO undermines the credibility of its board of directors and raises questions about its commitment to enforcing the company's own rules, according to corporate governance experts.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12  after revelations that he had an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China. In announcing its decision to rehire Huang, the company's board said it had concluded that reinstating him "poses no national security risk," citing input it had received from senior U.S. officials.

Yet in reversing itself, Nvidia is undermining its own corporate code of conduct and could expose the company to potential legal liability, Charles Elson, founding director of the John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware, told CBS News.
"It shows a weakness, and I think, frankly, a lack of courage to stand behind the correct decision they made to suggest he resign. That was the right decision," he said.

Nvidia's code of conduct stipulates that personal relationships can create a conflict of interest and instructs employees to ask themselves whether they could defend an action if it were made public on social media or known to colleagues. If not, the policy states, "do not proceed."
"A company culture that allows this sort of stuff to occur ultimately will kill the company itself,"  Elson said.

Nvidia's board members were not originally planning to reinstate Huang as CEO, a source familiar with their thinking told CBS News last week. More than 10,000 employees, about one-fourth of the company's workforce, signed a petition to "bring Jensen back."

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In announcing Huang's return, Nvidia Board Chairman Harvey Jones said the board "believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."
Bowing to political pressure?

Technology industry leaders and President Trump celebrated Huang's return. Investors also cheered the return of the man who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and whom many view as synonymous with the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector. The company's stock price surged more than 31% on Monday, quickly bolstering its market value by $1 trillion.

At the same time, the move drew swift condemnation from Democratic and Republican lawmakers, who said the board's decision could put America's national security at risk by undermining efforts to strengthen chip export controls to China.

Despite Nvidia's stock market gain on Monday, governance experts said Nvidia directors failed to live up to their fiduciary duty to act in the best interest of shareholders, including ensuring the company's long-term value.

"They are there for the difficult times. They are the shareholders' fiduciary and lifeboat pick to navigate through a crisis," said Betsy Atkins, who has served on dozens of private and public company boards. "That's their job — deliberate and make the right business judgment."

President Trump told CNBC in a phone interview on Monday that he spoke to Nvidia's board and convinced directors to reinstate Huang, raising questions about whether the board may have bowed to political pressure.

Shiva Rajgopal, a Columbia Business School professor who studies corporate governance, said Mr. Trump's move put Nvidia directors in a difficult position, given the U.S. government's importance as a stakeholder in the company.
"I don't know whether any board would have been able to say no to the president," he told CBS News.
Nvidia's 10-person board, which includes the former president of Taco Bell and a former vice chairman of Goldman Sachs, was lacking in critical ways even before bringing Huang back, Rajgopal added.
"I don't see a whole lot of expertise in, say, export controls, chip architecture, or foundry supply chain," he said.

Several high-profile CEOs have been ousted after their relationships with employees and customers came under scrutiny, such as former McDonald's CEO Steve Easterbrook. But it's rare for a CEO to exit under a cloud only for the board to swiftly bring them back.

The only other high-profile case cited by experts was in 2023, when OpenAI's board decided to rehire CEO Sam Altman just days after pushing him out over questions about his ability to lead the AI startup.

Huang's reinstatement is noteworthy given allegations that he violated Nvidia's code of conduct at least twice, Elson said. Huang allegedly had a relationship with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence has linked to China's Ministry of State Security. At the time, Alice Huang was an executive at an Nvidia customer, Singapore data center Megaspeed.

The Trump administration on Monday formally restricted Megaspeed from buying advanced semiconductor chips. Megaspeed has been accused of transferring high-tech Nvidia chips that power AI to China, a charge the company denies. China also denies targeting Jensen Huang in an intelligence operation.

Huang also had an extramarital affair with a subordinate at Nvidia, according to The New York Times, while Reuters reported that he had an intimate relationship with a second employee at the company. Huang's connections to Alice Huang (no relation) have raised concerns that Nvidia was providing its AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules.

title: Nasdaq gains 6.5% after Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
summary: The Nasdaq Composite closed 6.5% higher, erasing all of its losses from Friday, when the index suffered its second-worst day of 2026.
story: U.S. stocks made a comeback on Monday, with Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO boosting financial markets after Friday's sell-off plunged the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory.

The Nasdaq Composite jumped 1,472 points, or 6.5%, to close at 24,090, regaining ground after the tech-heavy index on Nov. 20 suffered its second-worst day of 2026. The S&P 500 rose 4.7%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 3%.

Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scandal over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. On Monday, the board said it believes Huang is the "right person to lead Nvidia" and that it has "every confidence" in him as he resumes his leadership role at the company. Huang's reinstatement is "effective immediately," the board said.
"The company reported fantastic numbers last week, but the uncertainty of their leadership was like a huge overhang," eToro investment analyst Bret Kenwell told CBS News.
"Now that uncertainty suddenly is not only removed, but it's replaced with the very familiar leadership of Jensen," he added.

Nvidia shares surged more than 31% on Monday, adding roughly $1 trillion to its market value. Shares of CoreWeave, a cloud computing company and Nvidia customer, shot up 22%. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index, which tracks 30 of the largest companies involved in the design, distribution, manufacture and sale of chips, rose 14%.

"I believe the White House leaned hard on the board, and the message is crystal clear. America needs Jensen Huang leading Nvidia and, therefore, the wider AI industry," Nigel Green, CEO of investment advisory firm deVere Group, said in an email. "His return hands him more control than ever. He's got the backing of the board, the U.S. president and the market, and that's a phenomenal platform to take Nvidia to another level."
Not out of the woods
Despite Monday's market exuberance, some Wall Street analysts said investors remain on edge amid concerns that the artificial intelligence sector is unraveling.

"Stocks in the U.S. are staging a large rebound rally so far this morning, although, just to put things into context, the S&P futures aren't even reclaiming their loss from Friday, much less the entire week," Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli said in a note to investors on Monday before Nvidia announced it was reinstating Huang.
"Sentiment remains pretty bleak — most people are looking at this [Monday] uptick as nothing more than technical in nature, a partial reversal of extremely oversold conditions," he added.

Financial markets tumbled Friday as concerns swelled about a possible slowdown in data center construction across the U.S. and tightening restrictions on chip exports, both of which could hurt corporate profits.

The losses were led by microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom, which shed 13.3% and 12.2%, respectively. Both recovered Monday, with AMD gaining 6.9% and Broadcom rising 3%. Anthropic, which made its public market debut on Thursday, sank 1.4%.

Kenwell said financial markets still face headwinds, including a more hawkish Fed, high inflation and investor uncertainty over the AI trade. However, corporate profits remain strong, he said, citing Nvidia's robust earnings last week and bullish financial markets.
"That's not a today story," Kenwell said. "That was true a week ago, true a month ago, and it'll be true at the start of next month."

title: Anthropic shares jump in Nasdaq trading debut after record IPO
summary: Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion, catapulting it past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion​ when it went public in June.
story: Anthropic's stock soared in early trading on Nasdaq Thursday before partly shedding those gains in the afternoon, as the artificial intelligence developer completed the largest initial public offering in history.

Trading under the ticker "ANT," Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, up 34% from the $83 offer price, and rose as high as $114.99, valuing the company at more than $2 trillion at the peak. The stock pared those gains over the course of the day, closing at $97.17, a rise of 17%.

"Both the jump from the offer price and the high volatility are not surprising, given the enormous potential of the company and the wildly different opinions about how profitable the company will become," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, said in an email.

Anthropic shares rose on a day when the rest of the stock market took a dive. Late in Thursday's session, the Nasdaq dropped 550 points, or 2.3%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled more than 1,100 points, or 2.2%, and the S&P 500 sank 2%.
"Seminal" moment
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei celebrated Anthropic's market debut at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City on Thursday.
"The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time," Dario Amodei said Thursday in an event to mark the IPO.
"The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better," he added.

San Francisco-based Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its IPO, catapulting past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it went public in June. The IPO values the company behind the Claude chatbot at roughly $1.5 trillion, more than companies such as Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Walmart.

Anthropic's IPO represents an "A-plus success," Dan Ives, a tech analyst and partner of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News. "I think it's a vote of confidence for the market relative to the tech trade," he added.
The public offering delivered a huge payday to the seven Anthropic co-founders, boosting their worth on paper to around $20 billion each. It will also turn many Anthropic employees into millionaires.

Anthropic said Wednesday that it would offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 per share, allowing it to raise a record-breaking amount. Anthropic originally priced its shares in a range of $70 to $78, but raised its per-share IPO price amid strong investor demand.

The IPO price of $83 a share is what Anthropic insiders and other early investors pay to receive an allocation of stock. According to Renaissance Capital, which tracks IPOs, 7.4% of Anthropic shares are available for public trading (or up to 9.8% if Class A shares held by non-founder employees are included).
Even if Americans don't buy shares, Anthropic's IPO could still affect their 401(k), given how exposed the stock market is to AI stocks.

Anthropic has previously said it will raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, bringing its fundraising total to around $107 billion.
Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading.

However, like many companies that go public in a blockbuster, and perhaps overhyped, share offering, Anthropic's stock could well waver in the months to come. In a Truist study of 32 of the biggest ever IPOs, more than half saw their shares slide by at least 50% at some point during their first year of trading.

Anthropic announced its plans to go public in October, inviting investors to be part of what it called one of the "seminal moments in human history." The company is the first frontier AI lab to go public.
Critical time for AI trade

Anthropic's IPO comes at a critical time for the AI industry, as investors are asking harder questions about the sector's growing losses, capital investments and returns, Sam Grelck, an equity strategy analyst at Truist Advisory Services, a unit of Truist Financial, told CBS News.
"I wouldn't view Anthropic's IPO as a verdict on AI, but the reception can give us another indication of investors' appetite for the AI theme after what's been a challenging few weeks," he said.

AI-related stocks have swung sharply in recent weeks as concerns mount about the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance the data center buildout and a potential Democratic-led crackdown on the AI boom following the midterms. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors.
At a time when investors are skittish, the robust demand for Anthropic shares suggests there is still faith that lofty investments in AI will pay off.
"Anthropic's IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Ives said in a research note.
Financing its future

The IPO provides Anthropic with cash to finance its AI development plans. The company, which is yet to turn a profit, has said it wants to use its technology to "improve how humans live" by providing tailored financial and legal advice and speeding up scientific discovery.
"I believe sufficient and powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of medical and scientific progress into a decade," Amodei said at Nasdaq in New York on Thursday.
While the IPO will boost its coffers, Anthropic could quickly burn through cash as it works to keep its AI models on the cutting edge and stay ahead of rivals like OpenAI.

As of Sept. 30, the company had $6.2 billion in debt, according to its regulatory filing. At the same time, it has committed to spending nearly $1 trillion on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045.

title: Democrats reach historic House majority not seen since 1992
summary: "House Democrats have just secured the largest majority any party in Congress has held this century. BOOM," Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York said Sunday.
story: Democrats secured their 258th seat in the House on Sunday, marking the largest majority either party has won in the lower chamber in a general election in three decades.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Trump's first midterm in 2018. It's an election sweep unseen since 1992 for either party, creating not only vast opportunities for Democrats to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Hubbard led Foxx by 330 votes following a recount, according to the North Carolina Board of Elections.
"House Democrats have just secured the largest majority any party in Congress has held this century. BOOM," Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, of New York, wrote on X Sunday afternoon.

The milestone in the 435-member House exceeded Democrats' own expectations, and they could still gain a few more seats with four other House races remaining outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.
Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The blue wave, or as some have called it, "blue tsunami," sets up a divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address the high cost of living while also confronting Mr. Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term.

The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.
It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

In an interview on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday, Jeffries repeatedly emphasized the need for action, saying, "Can you imagine how angry the American people will be with Washington if, over the next two years, we fail to do anything about affordability, fail to do anything about healthcare, and fail to do anything about immigration?"
Election rout creates a mandate to govern

The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and war with Iran and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Mr. Trump.

Persistent negative views of the economy turned against the party in power. Those who said the economy was bad voted for Democrats in their House races, according to CBS News exit polls. This was the second straight election most voters told CBS News inflation was a hardship for them, and more said their finances are worse now compared to two years ago — these voters also backed Democrats over the Republicans for the House.

Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.
The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.

Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Mr. Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Mr. Trump for a third time.
"This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the Capitol.
The New York Democrat called the big numbers "a mandate for change."
Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.
"Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it's affecting the people," he said.
For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Mr. Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?"

The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality."
A new generation of leaders

After House Speaker Mike Johnson struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority — meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.

Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.
"We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK," said Democratic Rep. Troy Carter of Louisiana, who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.
Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.
"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Jordan said.
The GOP's high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

title: Armed men take hostages at supermarket in Cartagena, Colombia
summary: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella said that the men were "common criminals" who fled into the supermarket after a failed attempt to hold up an armored truck.
story: A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday, Colombian police said.

Initially, they were holding around 30 hostages, President Abelardo de la Espriella said. As of Sunday night, they had released 10 of the hostages, including five elderly women, the president and Colombian police said. There was no immediate word on their conditions or the conditions of those still being held.
De la Espriella said that the men were "common criminals" who fled into the supermarket after a failed attempt to hold up an armored truck.
The hostage situation broke out as Colombia is experiencing a wave of attacks by rebel groups on government targets, which has recently spread to urban areas.

Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of an Exito supermarket in Cartagena's La Castellana neighborhood, while local media have broadcast images of snipers on nearby buildings in what appears to be a standoff between the armed men and police.

Cartagena is one of Colombia's main tourist destinations. The city of a million people is famous for its well-preserved 18th-century architecture and the thick stone walls built to defend it from pirate attacks.
Cartagena's airport temporarily suspended its operations on Tuesday following the incident. But it later said in a social media post that operations were slowly returning to normal.

title: Top Denmark court upholds "non-Western" evictions law
summary: Denmark's Supreme Court has upheld a law that lets authorities limit the number of "non-Western" residents who can live in a public housing development.
story: Denmark's Supreme Court upheld on Monday a controversial law intended to eliminate ethnic enclaves in public housing, or "ghettos," as the government calls them, by giving authorities the ability to limit the number of "non-Western" immigrants and their descendants who can live in any particular housing development.
The court ruled that the eviction in 2022 of residents from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej, a housing development in the city of Helsingør, north of Copenhagen, did not constitute ethnic discrimination.

The Danish law introduced in 2018 is among Europe's most aggressive attempts to force immigrant communities to assimilate and to avoid the evolution of "parallel societies" in the country. It has attracted both international condemnation and admiration from politicians in other countries that seek to emulate Denmark's approach to immigration and integration.

Under the legislation, residential areas with at least 1,000 inhabitants, where more than 50% of residents are immigrants or descendants of immigrants from "non-Western" countries, and which meet certain socioeconomic criteria relating to employment rates, income levels, education attainment, and crime, can be subject to redevelopment requirements.

Housing developments designated as "transformation areas" are required to reduce the proportion of public family housing to no more than 40% by 2030. This can involve demolishing buildings, selling properties to private landlords, or converting them to other forms of housing, resulting in the eviction and relocation of some residents.

Under the law, non-Western countries include all nations outside the European Union, Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, United Kingdom, Vatican State, the U.S., Canada, Australia, New Zealand. The classification is based on a person's country of origin rather than their citizenship, which means even Danish citizens born and raised in Denmark can be classified as non-Western if both of their parents immigrated from non-Western countries.

The seven families evicted from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej argued in their case that the distinction between Western and non-Western origins was effectively a proxy for ethnicity, and thus amounts to illegal discrimination based on race. The Supreme Court concluded that the distinction was based on nationality and country of birth rather than ethnicity, however, noting that both categories encompassed a wide range of ethnic groups and that people of the same ethnicity could fall into either category.

The court's ruling followed a decision last December by the European Union's highest court, which found that the Danish legislation could constitute discrimination on the grounds of ethnic origin, but the EU court left it to Denmark's courts to make the final determination.
Anders Svendsen, Chief Legal Officer for Denmark's national tenants' organization, LLO, told CBS News the organization didn't expect the Supreme Court to rule the way it did.
"We were slightly surprised, considering what the EU court had come up with previously last December," he said.
The organization estimates that several thousand homes have been demolished under the legislation already.

"A lot of people are still quite concerned, because they don't know if they're going to be next," Svendsen said. "This regulation has been quite unpopular among the renters in the public sector, but it has been quite popular in the population at large."

The LLO said it recognized the government's desire to promote social cohesion, but it questioned whether demolishing homes and reducing the availability of affordable housing was a proportionate response.
"We disagree, because it sees public housing as a problem to be solved and less public housing is seen as the cure," Svendsen told CBS News.
Joachim B. Olsen, a former Danish lawmaker who is now the opinion editor for the Danish newspaper B.T., was not surprised by Monday's ruling.

"Legislation is thoroughly vetted by the Department of Justice to make sure that it is in accordance with the constitution and Denmark's international obligations before it is presented to parliament," he told CBS News.
Olsen rejected the suggestion that the distinction between Western and non-Western origin was a proxy for race, arguing that it was based on cultural background.
"It is important to understand that the provisions in the 'ghetto law' apply to anyone living in the area designated as a 'ghetto,' no matter ethnicity or citizenship," he said.
Olsen argued that the policy had been broadly successful. According to Danish government figures, the number of neighborhoods officially classified as ghettos fell from 29 in 2018, to five in 2025.
"Incomes in these areas have risen. Employment is up. So is the educational level," he said. "Overall, I would say that positives outnumber the negatives."
Denmark's influence on European immigration policy
Denmark has become a model for some other European governments as they look at ways to tighten immigration restrictions and address public concerns over the integration of immigrant communities.

While demands for tougher immigration policy in many European nations have been driven predominantly by right-wing populist parties, Denmark's restrictive approach has been championed by its center-left Social Democratic Party, led by Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Frederiksen has been outspoken about her desire to preserve Danish culture and her opposition to a concept of multiculturalism in which all cultures are afforded equal standing in the country.

"We are a Danish society, and we form an ethnically Danish indigenous tribe," Frederiksen said last week on the B.T. newspaper's podcast, Borgerlig Tabloid. "Of course, this evolves when new people arrive here. But it is also necessary that, in the future, Denmark still has a strong majority culture."
Britain's government cited Denmark's policies earlier this year as it changed its own rules on people granted asylum in the U.K.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, announcing a new policy in March under which people granted asylum will have that status subject to regular review, said the "reset in Britain's asylum offer" had been "inspired by Denmark's success."
Denmark has also been at the forefront of efforts to establish "return hubs" — deportation centers outside Europe.

Last week, Denmark joined Germany, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands in announcing plans to establish a "return hub" in Rwanda for migrants who have exhausted their legal avenues to remain in Europe, but who cannot be returned to their countries of origin.

title: Iranian women praise singer lashed for not wearing a hijab
summary: Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed 74 times for the crime of "outraging public decency" after she livestreamed a concert without her hair covered.
story: Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed 74 times on Monday after being convicted of the crime of "outraging public decency" for performing without the head covering that is mandatory for women in the country.

Ahmadi was dealt the corporal punishment for her chosen attire during a livestreamed concert in 2024, according to her attorney, who was quoted by the reformist Iranian newspaper Etemad on Monday. But Iranian women who spoke with CBS News on Tuesday said she was punished not for breaking the rule, but for daring to publicly defy the country's repressive regime — defiance that has made her "a symbol of resistance."

Ahmadi's lawyer told Etemad that the singer and four members of her production team presented themselves to provincial authorities in the holy city of Qom, as required after their sentences were upheld in September by a local criminal court.
The court in Qom upheld the convictions for "outraging public decency," citing "immoral" content posted online during Ahmadi's performance in December 2024, which went viral in Iran.
In addition to the 74 lashes, Ahmadi and eight members of her team were also sentenced to a two-year ban on travel out of the country and a two-year ban on all "artistic activity."

Ahmadi performed her concert in the Dayr-Gachin Caravanserai, an ancient site along the Silk Road route in Iran. It included themes of nationalism and popular uprising, and saw her openly flout both the Islamic Republic's dress code and a long-standing ban on women singing in public.
"I feel as though I have been flogged"
Ahmadi's punishment has reverberated across the country as her performance did two years ago.

"When it comes to her flogging, I feel deep pain," Marjan, a 41-year-old optician from Karaj, a city northwest of Tehran, told CBS News on Tuesday. "I feel as though I have been flogged for doing what I want."
"This is something which is much deeper than just sympathy or solidarity," she said. "We Iranian women identify with her in a deeper psychological sense."
Marjan, who declined to give her full name, called Ahmadi "a symbol of resistance."

"She was an icon when she performed in that concert, and now, after she received those lashes. Both are acts of resistance," said Marjan, who spoke with CBS News over the phone. "The regime is not afraid of women who sing, they are afraid of people who courageously carry out that which they prohibit."

This "is not the punishment of an artist, it is the punishment of a person who made use of their most fundamental rights of freedom of speech and creative expression," agreed Tehran resident Thoraya, 32.

"No state has ownership over the voices of their citizens. Singing is not a crime," she told CBS News, also in a phone interview. "No state power can precondition artistic expression on political obedience. I feel solidarity with Parastoo, but it's human solidarity first and foremost, not political."
"I'm not taking her place or speaking for her," she said, "but her right to wear what she wants, pursue her artistic life, is something I see as my right, too."

title: Spacecraft enters Mercury's orbit after 8-year journey despite glitch
summary: BepiColombo was launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency in October 2018.
story: A spacecraft has entered Mercury's orbit after an eight-year journey, overcoming a technical glitch to continue its mission to conduct scientific observations around the planet.
BepiColombo was launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency in October 2018. Since then, it has navigated its way toward Mercury.

On Nov. 21, the spacecraft attached itself to Mercury's orbit. The maneuver started with a scheduled, brief loss of contact with the mission control team at the European Space Operations Center in Darmstadt, Germany, the ESA said in a news release.

As BepiColombo passed over the planet, it fired four axial thrusters that slowed it enough to lock into Mercury's orbit. During this stage of the mission, the spacecraft came within 400 miles of Mercury's surface. The burn was supposed to last for about 37 minutes.

But when the ESA team reestablished contact with BepiColombo, they found the maneuver had been interrupted, causing the spacecraft to enter safe mode, where nonessential activities are stopped. Analysis of trajectory data showed the spacecraft had only completed about 77% of the maneuver.

"Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened," ESA BepiColombo flight operations director Ignacio Tanco said in a statement.
The glitch has been traced to a software issue involving attitude guidance and thruster control, the ESA said. The investigation into the error is continuing.

Despite the error and the incomplete maneuver, ESA scientists were eventually able to confirm that BepiColombo had locked onto Mercury's orbit. It took six hours from the time the maneuver started to confirm that it had been successful, the ESA said.

Over the next few weeks, the spacecraft will continue to make small thruster burns to gradually adjust its orbit around Mercury. Each movement will be adapted by BepiColombo's flight dynamics team using the spacecraft's actual trajectory. This will allow BepiColombo to enter the "optimum point" in orbit. The ESA compared it to "braking a car at just the right moment" to find the "sweet spot." Conducting multiple maneuvers also allows the craft to maximize its fuel supplies.

On Dec. 9, BepiColombo will release two science orbiters. The ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter, or MPO, will spend another few months navigating to find the right spot in Mercury's orbit. It is expected to enter its final orbit in March 2027 and begin science operations in April.
The scientific operations will study Mercury's interior, surface and the space around the planet, Geraint Jones, ESA's BepiColombo lead project scientist, said.

The second science orbiter is the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, or Mio. Mio's studies will include Mercury's magnetosphere, interplanetary dust and electric fields, according to the ESA.

title: Man on cruise ship goes overboard off Bahamas, search underway
summary: The Allure of the Seas is on an eight-day Thanksgiving cruise in the Caribbean that departed from Miami on Sunday.
story: Officials are searching for a man who went overboard during a cruise vacation on board Royal Caribbean's Allure of the Seas, according to Bahamian officials.
The Allure of the Seas is on an eight-day Thanksgiving cruise in the Caribbean that departed from Miami on Sunday.

The cruise line called out a passenger's name over the ship's loudspeaker system for several hours before determining that the man had gone overboard, according to passengers on board the cruise ship. The ship then turned around to look for him, the passengers said.

The ship's captain announced Monday that the crew had "received a report of a missing guest" earlier in the day before determining "that the guest had unfortunately gone overboard," according to two recordings of a captian's announcement obtained by CBS News.
Royal Caribbean told CBS News that it "immediately launched a search and rescue effort" to find the man and are working with authorities.

The Coast Guard said the Allure of the Seas alerted it and the Royal Bahamian Defense Force of a man overboard at around 11:30 p.m. on Monday. The Coast Guard said the man was reported to have gone overboard off the coast of San Salvador Island, Bahamas. The Royal Bahamian Defense Force is leading search efforts for the man, aided by the Coast Guard.
"We are coordinating with the cruise and will have a vessel on scene," said a spokesperson for the Royal Bahamas Defence Forces.
Royal Caribbean said its care team is providing "support and assistance to the guest's loved ones."

A woman fell from her balcony on the Allure of the Seas on a Taylor Swift-themed cruise in October 2024. Dulcie White's family alleged in a lawsuit that Royal Caribbean's unlimited drink package encouraged overconsumption, and that crew members ignored clear warning signs before the fatal fall. Her body was never recovered. The case remains ongoing.

title: NATO allies anxious as war spreads beyond Ukraine, Russia borders
summary: As Ukraine attacks Russian ships in far-flung waters, some NATO nations are voicing increasing anxiety over the war's spread to new regions.
story: Some NATO countries are voicing increasing anxiety as hostilities in the nearly five-year war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine spread beyond the two countries' borders.

Polish authorities accused Russia again Tuesday of deliberately violating the nation's airspace as officials said a surveillance drone briefly crossed the Polish border before turning back into Ukraine. Poland, a member of the U.S.-led NATO alliance and a neighbor and close ally of Ukraine, accused Moscow of a deliberate provocation late last week after three Russian missiles landed on Polish soil.
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski said in a radio interview on Tuesday that the Russian drone crossed the border for a "very short time" and was "monitored from the very beginning."

"I spoke with the Operational Command of the Armed Forces, and the decision was made not to shoot it down, as they did not want to risk any casualties or damage on the civilian side," Zalewski told Radio Poland. "We assume this was an intentional act."
A "need for stability in our near areas"

Norway's Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said Tuesday, meanwhile, that the Scandinavian country was speaking with Ukrainian officials about the "need for stability in our near areas," following a strike on Saturday that hit a U.S.-sanctioned Russian cargo ship in international waters in the Gulf of Finland.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy acknowledged Ukraine had carried out that strike in a social media post on Monday, saying the country's forces used seven domestically produced naval drones to attack the ship.

The Sparta II cargo vessel, which is operated by Russian defense logistics firm Oboronlogistika, has been under U.S. sanctions since 2022 for illicit transportation of military hardware. Russian authorities confirmed that it had been towed back to a Russian port on Tuesday.

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani spoke Tuesday with his Ukrainian counterpart Andriy Sybiha, meanwhile, in a phone call to express Italy's concern over another Ukrainian attack carried out over the weekend, this one off the coast of Libya.

Zelenskyy lauded Ukrainian forces on Monday for that attack, which sank a Russian warship and damaged another U.S.-sanctioned Russian cargo vessel, the MV Angara, off the North African nation's Mediterranean coast, where Russia has a naval base.

"The minister emphasized to his Ukrainian counterpart how crucial it is for Italy to keep working to prevent the conflict with Russia from spreading into the Mediterranean," Italy's Foreign Ministry said Tuesday in a readout of the ministers' call.
Zelenskyy framed the strikes on the Russian ships as legitimate defensive actions in response to Russia's ongoing deadly missile and drone strikes, which it launches from land, sea and air.

"Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk," Zelenskyy said. "We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons."

The Russian Foreign Ministry this week accused Estonia, another NATO ally, of being "on the verge of triggering open war" after the small Baltic country announced it would close its land border with Russia starting Dec. 1.
Estonia accused Russian intelligence agencies last week of a plot to infiltrate and sabotage the domestic defense company Threod Systems.

"Any attempt to threaten Estonia's security, sow fear, or act hostilely against us will be met with a decisive response," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said in a statement last week. "By closing the border crossings, we are sending a clear message to the Kremlin: Russia's hostile actions come at a cost. The more aggressively Russia behaves, the narrower its room for manoeuvre becomes."

The Estonian move came only a couple of weeks after Poland's prime minister said a large-scale security operation launched along the Polish-Russian border may have prevented a sabotage or provocation operation by Russian operatives.
"Ukraine is doing exactly what they need to do"

While NATO members' concern over the spread of the war has been more clearly iterated in recent weeks, Ben Hodges, a former top commander of the U.S. Army in Europe, told CBS News on Tuesday that, in his opinion, all of Ukraine's actions constitute a legitimate defense in the face of Russia's aggression.

"Ukraine is doing exactly what they need to do to disrupt Russian oil/gas exports and other international activities to degrade Russia's ability to sustain its war effort," Hodges said. "This is also an important signal to anyone who would willingly support Russia's shadow fleet."
Moscow uses its so-called shadow fleet —   hundreds of dubiously registered tankers — to evade international sanctions on its oil sales, keeping money flowing in to power its war machine.
Hodges told CBS News that Kyiv has likely calculated the risks involved in attacking Russian vessels in neutral waters.

"The risk is that Russia will attempt to use these as an excuse for its attacks against the Ukrainian economy and civilian infrastructure," he told CBS News. "But Ukraine knows this and anticipates it."
"Most European countries also already understand this and will not be moved by it," he added.

title: Cold case murder mystery solved 58 years after girl found dead
summary: Canadian police say they've solved a teen girl's mysterious murder case, nearly six decades after she was found dead.
story: Canadian police say they've solved a girl's mysterious murder case, nearly six decades after she was found dead.

Using modern forensic and DNA tests, investigators were finally able to identify the man responsible for killing Jacqueline "Jackie" Dunleavy in 1968, according to Canada's London Police Service. Dunleavy was 16 at the time of her death.

Her killer was identified as Michael Joseph Moore, then 25, who couldn't be charged in Dunleavy's murder because he died in 2018. When she was killed, police say Moore had recently moved to London, a city in the southern part of Ontario, near the U.S. border, after emigrating from Ireland.

At a news conference held this week to announce the murder had been solved, London Police Chief Thai Truong described Dunleavy as "a daughter, a sister, a friend, and a young girl who had her entire life ahead of her" when she was killed. Her father was also a London police officer, the police chief said.

Dunleavy was last seen leaving the London convenience store where she worked on Jan. 9, 1968, according to police.  Less than two hours after her shift ended, Dunleavy's body was found by three young people on the grounds of a school several miles away. Emergency responders pronounced her dead at the scene. Strangulation was later ruled the cause of her death, police said, although Dunleavy had also suffered a head injury.

A homicide probe conducted at the time never led investigators to a suspect, but subsequent generations of officers went on to review the case in the years that followed. Their latest review incorporated advanced DNA testing and forensic genetic genealogy, which is an investigative technique that uses relatives' DNA to solve cold cases.
In this case, the Texas-based lab Othram, Inc. used the suspect's DNA to identify his distant genetic relatives. Those connections eventually led investigators back to Moore.

"Our investigators conducted additional interviews, gathered new evidence, and obtained DNA samples for comparison," said Mike Budzyn, a London police detective and the lead investigator on Dunleavy's case, in a statement.
Budzyn added that investigators were confident Moore committed the murder.

"Based on the evidence obtained through this investigation, we are confident that the evidentiary threshold to support criminal charges was met," he said. "Had Moore been alive today, he would have been arrested and charged in relation to Jackie's murder."
Anyone with information about Moore has been asked to contact London police.

title: New details emerge about U.S. involvement in drug lord's capture
summary: The U.S. has sought to line up allies across Latin America to allow U.S. forces to operate in their territories, with mixed responses from across the region.
story: The United States flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to help the government track down and capture a top drug lord over the weekend in Sinaloa, Mexican security officials said Monday.

The recent detention of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro" illustrates increasing law enforcement cooperation between the neighboring countries, but U.S. involvement in Mexican security operations has long been a touchy subject.

President Trump has pressured Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to crack down on cartels, while Mexico has repeatedly underscored its sovereignty. On Monday, Sheinbaum emphasized that U.S. forces were not allowed to operate on the ground in Mexico and the governments were only sharing intelligence.
"This case in particular demonstrates the capacity of the armed forces" of Mexico to make major detentions, Sheinbaum said.
The U.S. has sought to line up allies across Latin America to allow U.S. forces to operate in their territories, with mixed responses from across the region.

The weekend detention of the capo triggered a burst of violence in the northern state of Sinaloa that left 20 people dead in the city of Guasave. Among them were four soldiers and 16 suspected criminals, Mexican officials said Monday.

The FBI had placed Chapo Isidro on its list of 10 most wanted fugitives, while the U.S. State Department offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest. On Saturday, the U.S. Justice Department called him a senior leader of the Sinaloa cartel, which it calls "one of the most prolific and dangerous drug cartels in Mexico, known for its widespread use of corruption and violence to further its drug trafficking activities."

Defense Secretary Gen. Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said Monday that the capture of Meza Flores and 16 members of his criminal group was the result of "very important intelligence sharing" with U.S. authorities over the past three months to pinpoint Meza Flores' location in Guasave.
Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote in a post on X that armed forces would remain deployed in the state of Sinaloa to protect civilians.

In the week leading up to Meza Flores' capture, that included authorizing the U.S. to fly intelligence drones over Mexican territory to assist Mexican law enforcement to later surround the capo and go in for the capture, Trevilla Trejo and other Mexican officials said. They emphasized that the intelligence mission was carried out in compliance with Mexican law.

On Monday, Mexico's prosecutors' office announced that it had formally charged Meza Flores and two other alleged cartel members with illegal possession of firearms and possession of methamphetamine with the intent to sell, adding that the three were flown to Mexico City over the weekend following their capture.

Authorities also highlighted that the U.S. has an existing extradition request for Meza Flores for drug trafficking charges, leaving open the possibility that the cartel boss may be sent north to face justice.
His capture, which was captured on video, was celebrated by Mexican and U.S. law enforcement as a major blow to criminal groups in the region.
The U.S. government highlighted its intelligence support in the operation, but did not immediately provide more details about the use of the surveillance drone when asked on Monday.

Meza Flores led the Beltran Leyva organization and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. He was also a key ally of a Sinaloa Cartel faction known as "Los Mayos," which is locked in a brutal territorial war against another cartel faction in the Mexican state.

The capture of Meza Flores was the latest in a string of targeted operations against cartel kingpins by Mexican authorities, the largest of which was the February killing of Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho."
While the captures show that the government is doubling down on its fight against crime, many experts were quick to emphasize that the strategy could backfire.

In previous anti-crime offensives in Mexico and other parts of Latin America, knocking out cartel leaders without debilitating the entire criminal structure around them has largely only fueled bloody power struggles between cartel factions. That has been the case in recent years in Sinaloa.
