title: Prince William and Kate's country home broken into, 2 arrested
summary: Intruders have broken into the country residence of Prince William and Princess Catherine, British media reported Tuesday.
story: Two men have been arrested over a suspected burglary at the royal family's Sandringham Estate, the country residence of Prince William and Princess Catherine, U.K. police said.

Police responded to reports of "suspicious activity" at Anmer Hall on King Charles III's Sandringham estate in eastern England on Monday at about 6 p.m., Norfolk police said. William, Kate and the rest of their family weren't present at the time, Norfolk police said.

The two men were arrested on the estate's property on suspicion of burglary and trespassing and remain in custody, police said. Police dogs, drones and a helicopter were used to search the property and make the arrests, officials said.
Kensington Palace told CBS News it wouldn't comment on security matters.

Anmer Hall, which has 10 bedrooms, was a wedding present to the couple from Queen Elizabeth II. It is used as a country residence on weekends. William and his family spend most of their time at Forest Lodge in Windsor, which they have described as their "forever home."
The reported break-in came as William visited Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the British leader's office, 10 Downing Street.
Meanwhile, Kate recently opened up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.

"Heal" follows the 44-year-old princess as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours. The film will premiere on the BBC in the United Kingdom on Nov. 29, before airing internationally on NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30.

title: Gisèle Pelicot to sue publisher after nude images sent to media
summary: Gisèle Pelicot, who spoke out about being drugged and raped by her husband and 50 other men, says she's been "once again humiliated."
story: Gisèle Pelicot, the French woman who spoke out about being drugged and raped by her husband and dozens of other men, said Monday that she had been "once again humiliated" after nude photos and videos of her were sent to media outlets to promote a book that she said is dismissive of her husband's crimes.
Pelicot, 73, told France's BFMTV that she will take legal action against the publisher, Tinard, and the author of the book, French psychoanalyst Sabine Prokhoris.

The book criticizes the concept of coercive control and questions whether Pelicot was really a victim, suggesting she could have been complicit in her husband's actions despite her having been surreptitiously drugged for years.

"I am deeply shocked that images relating to my most intimate life could be exhibited and exploited for commercial purposes," Pelicot said in a statement to the French broadcaster, adding: "Above all, I refuse to have my story rewritten by implying that I was complicit in what I suffered."

"Today, I find myself humiliated, exposed, and hurt once again. As if the ordeal of the trial wasn't enough," she said. "I fought to regain my dignity and my freedom. I will not let anyone take them away from me."

Pelicot became a global symbol of resilience in 2024 when she waived her right to anonymity in her then-husband Dominique's trial. He was convicted and sentenced to 20 years in prison for his abuse — and for inviting 50 other men to join him in raping his wife while she was incapacitated repeatedly over the course of a decade.

"How can you imagine that your husband is drugging you? It's unthinkable — impossible," she told CBS News in February. "In fact, I was manipulated for about 10 years. Because he was looking me in the eyes every day while knowing he was poisoning me. But I never saw that. I saw a kind, caring man."
She said she waived her anonymity during the trial to show that "shame has to change sides," from victims to perpetrators.

On its website, the publisher Tinard said it had offered "our sincerest apologies" to Pelicot and that it would not be reprinting the book after 280 copies already printed are sold. It said "no images of rape or pornographic videos were leaked to the press."

It is not clear where the publisher got the nude images of Pelicot. In her statements to French media, Pelicot did not question their authenticity. She also did not confirm or deny a report by the French weekly news outlet Le Canard Enchaîne, which said the images were among those taken by her former husband and presented during his trial as evidence.
Prokhoris, the author, said she had given "full responsibility" for the promotional campaign to the publisher, according to French news agency AFP.

AFP said the back-cover blurb on the book asks readers to "think freely" about the notion of coercive control, which Prokhoris describes as "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy" that is "fundamentally ambiguous" and, she says, involves "each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way."

"There are two types of violence that have been committed," Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM. "There is, on the one hand, the fact that intimate images of her were sent without her consent in the context of purely commercial communication, and then there is a book that calls into question her status as a victim."
"It is a clear violation of the law, and she does not intend to let it go unchallenged," he said.

title: Istanbul lioness never existed, Turkish officials say after search
summary: A 24-hour search for a lioness in the Istanbul suburbs that sparked panic among local residents was thrown into fresh confusion late Monday when Turkish officials said the animal didn't exist.
story: Istanbul — A 24-hour search for a lioness in the Istanbul suburbs that sparked panic among local residents was thrown into fresh confusion late Monday when Turkish officials said the animal didn't exist.

Istanbul's governor mobilized teams of animal welfare experts, police and army commandos in the hunt for the lioness after it was "identified" — even releasing two videos of the animal prowling around the upscale neighborhood of Uskumrukoy.
"The location of the lion has been identified, and the necessary care is being taken to capture it alive," the Istanbul governor's office said in a statement posted on social media.
Residents were warned to stay home, and the roughly 20 square mile Belgrade Forest to the north of Istanbul was sealed off.
By Monday evening, however, officials backtracked and said in a statement new images had been examined that showed the animal was "not a lion or any other large cat species."

"The area has been scanned from the air with a drone equipped with thermal cameras and from the ground by our teams," the statement said. "Baiting was also carried out and motion-sensor camera traps used."
"Fieldwork has not yielded any concrete evidence of a lion being present in the area."

The abrupt change left many bewildered, wondering what animal could have been mistaken for a lioness, with some suggesting it was a large dog. Others posted mocking videos of domestic cats on social media, asking if it was the lioness.
Even after the governor's office statement, media outlets published another video of an animal emerging from bushes and asked readers if it could be a lion.

title: Man with Alzheimer's found alive after 11 days lost in jungle
summary: Rescue workers said the man survived in the jungle by eating berries, drinking water from natural sources and making bedlike structures with the leaves of acai palms.
story: An elderly man with Alzheimer's disease who survived 11 days on his own in the Amazon rainforest is currently recovering at a hospital in the Brazilian city of Macapa, as rescue workers reveal more details about his surprising ordeal.

Janarino Ferreira dos Santos, 74, was rescued by park rangers and volunteers on Friday in a thick patch of rainforest about 6 miles from Macapa in northeastern Brazil. Rescue workers said Dos Santos was able to survive in the jungle by eating berries, drinking water from natural sources and making bedlike structures with the leaves of acai palms, where he could rest for the night.
"When he was younger he had worked in the rainforest, so he knew how to get around," said Aniel Cardoso, a park ranger who helped find dos Santos.

Cardoso and a group of volunteers who joined the search for dos Santos on Friday said they were able to find the man after they identified his footprints and realized he had been walking around in circles. As they tracked dos Santos' footprints, the rescuers came across a bed made from acai leaves that looked like it was at least four days old. Later, they came across a second bed with leaves that seemed to have been taken down from a palm tree that same morning.
"That's when we realized he could be alive, and that he could be close," Cardoso said. The rescuers found dos Santos in a thick patch of the forest, sitting down barefoot and wearing only underwear.
"He wasn't able to talk, he was no longer walking and he was very thirsty," Cardoso said.

The search, which started a day after the man went missing, brought together family members, volunteers and public safety teams, who faced difficult conditions in the forest. Firefighters and specialized teams used ground searches, helicopter and drone overflights as well as thermal cameras to look for signs of the missing man.

After nine days of searching and no news of dos Santos emerged, his granddaughter Sara Montes urged firefighters to keep looking for him. In a video posted on Instagram, she said they planned to suspend the search on Sunday, November 22.
"Don't forget about us. Don't forget about Grandpa," she pleaded.

Getting dos Santos out of the forest proved challenging as dense vegetation, flooded areas and swampy grounds prevented him from walking unaided, so rescuers improvised a stretcher using ropes and carried him through the difficult terrain.
A video posted on the G1 news site shows several men carrying him through the forest on the makeshift stretcher.
Cardoso said the man had walked out of his home on the edge of the rainforest while his relatives were visiting a neighbor.

He said that finding dos Santos was "very gratifying" because two months ago, another man had gone missing in the rainforest near Macapa, but had already died by the time he was found by rescue workers.
"This time, thank God, we were able to deliver this citizen alive," Cardoso said.
The dramatic rescue comes just over a week after a 17-year-old boy with autism was found alive after six days lost in eastern Australian woodlands.

title: Pope Francis had visions of devil, "gates of hell," diary reveals
summary: Pope Francis suffered a profound spiritual crisis in 2021-2022 linked to temptations to exercise power omnipotently, his diary reveals, adding that he overcame it by entrusting himself entirely to God's mercy.
story: Vatican City — Pope Francis saw the "gates of hell" when he realized the depths of the clergy sexual abuse scandal and experienced mystical visions of the devil throughout his ministry, according to excerpts of his personal diary published by the Vatican on Tuesday.

"The Private Diary of Pope Francis" also reveals the Argentine pope suffered a profound spiritual crisis in 2021-2022, connected to his own temptations to exercise power omnipotently. He overcame the crisis by entrusting himself entirely to God's mercy.

The book, being released globally in several languages, offers a deeply personal and almost voyeuristic view into the mind and heart of Francis, revealing his innermost fears, insecurities, dreams and temptations that he kept hidden from the world. It shows him as incredibly hard on himself, lamenting his own sense of worthlessness and shame, and his utter trust in God to lead him, even from the depths of despair.

The book was curated by one of Francis' closest aides, Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, the Argentine theologian who heads the Vatican's doctrine office. Fernández is listed as the author, as his comments contextualize Francis' diary entries.

Fernández expressed concern to Francis' successor, Leo XIV, that the book would be "left forgotten in some storage," and was permitted to publish passages, noting that "the spiritual concerns present in his (Francis') heart are very clear and can do us good."

Written in a leather-bound calendar used as a notebook, it starts in 1992, when Jorge Mario Bergoglio was auxiliary bishop of Buenos Aires. It continues through his time as cardinal archbishop of the Argentine capital and finally pope. The last entry is Aug. 18, 2024. He died in April 2025 at the age of 88 after 12 years as pontiff.
Francis, the devil and a disastrous Chile trip

The most moving sections are Francis' revelations of his own spiritual torments and what he described as encounters with the devil - visceral, tangible, seemingly terrifying encounters. Two occurred when he was in Buenos Aires, and the third after his disastrous 2018 trip to Chile.

"A few days after returning to Rome, I was in a meeting. I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant possessing everything. 'Now I've gotten everything I wanted,'" Francis quoted the devil as saying in a Jan. 24, 2021, entry. "Just as I can't forget his eyes from the previous two, in this case, I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice."

During the January 2018 Chile trip, Francis created an uproar for discrediting victims of Chile's most notorious abuser. After journalists, including from The Associated Press, challenged him during the in-flight news conference returning home, Francis commissioned an investigation and realized that the victims were right, that he was wrong and had been misled by the Chilean hierarchy.

"Devastated because of the situation in Chile and the dialogue with the journalists on the airplane," Francis would write later. "I became aware of how serious the problem was. ... It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious."
Francis wrote on June 7, 2018, a few months after he returned, that he "saw the entrance to hell. Pagan seduction in full force" in the Chile scandal.

In July and August of 2018, as he dealt with the fallout, he wrote: "What shame and evil this has brought on the church!" and "Once more the gates of hell. ... May holiness and conversion abound in the midst of so many scandals."
Spiritual crisis followed Vatican financial scandal, introspection
But Francis' spiritual crisis wouldn't come until 2021.
The book dates the onset of the crisis to Jan. 24, 2021. The day before, Francis canceled several upcoming public appearances due to what the Vatican said was a resurgence of his sciatica.

Fernández reveals, however, that Francis was suffering from "insupportable" pain from an intestinal problem that, in July 2021, would land Francis in the hospital for 10 days for surgery to remove 13 inches of his colon.
In January 2021, while the world was still in the throes of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Vatican was in utter upheaval over a massive financial investigation that Francis had authorized.

A few months earlier, in September 2020, Francis had fired a onetime close collaborator, Cardinal Angelo Becciu, convinced Becciu had embezzled money from the Holy See. The scandal - and Francis' belief that a web of corruption had engulfed the Vatican's secretariat of state - led to an unprecedented Vatican investigation and years of legal proceedings through which Francis sought to show his willingness to crack down on financial misconduct.

The trial resulted in some convictions, including against Becciu, but much of prosecutors' theory of a vast conspiracy of corruption was thrown out. The appeals process is ongoing, with Francis' own role in the investigation a key question for the defense.

There is no mention of the trial in Fernández's text, though he hints at it by revealing Francis' later musings that the 2021-2022 spiritual crisis was "mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation."

In the end, Fernández writes that the crisis was primarily related to Francis' exercise of power, the temptation to omnipotence and belief that he was above the world. It's a vice Francis admitted to publicly in 2013, in his first interview as pope, when he acknowledged a tendency to wield power in an "authoritarian" way.

It is significant that Francis was tormented by something his critics often faulted him for: an authoritarian, go-it-alone governing style in an absolute monarch and supreme leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.
For Francis, the temptation to omnipotence was the devil tempting him to "reductive curiosity," or believing he alone could solve everyone's problems, and essentially thinking of himself as God.
Moving on from the crisis

By Dec. 30, 2022, Francis had apparently overcome the crisis, by entrusting himself to God. Fernández writes that by then, Francis realized that what began on Jan. 24, 2021, "was a powerful invitation from the Lord to become aware of an accumulation of interior darkness that he had to overcome so he could be free."

Fernández notes that the final two major teaching documents of Francis' life, a 2023 text on confidence in God's merciful love, and a 2024 encyclical on Christ's human and divine love, are deeply spiritual texts borne out of the crisis. They differ in tone and content from the texts often associated with his pontificate.
While the book reveals some of Francis' innermost thoughts, Fernández says Francis wrote his most confidential thoughts in an indecipherable code, which is not reproduced.
The reader is also left wondering what Fernández left out of his selection of diary entries, and what more context he could have provided as one of Francis' most trusted advisers.

Fernández writes that the diary includes hardly any information about church matters, and is truly a spiritual repository. He said he omitted entries affecting third parties, though he does include some of Francis' personal musings, including about then-Cardinal Robert Prevost, now Pope Leo XIV: "A great pastor, a generous missionary and an irreproachable man."
Fernández said Francis had shown him the diary during one of their meetings and told him, "From this, you will all see," essentially entrusting the writings to him after his death.
Fernández said he mentioned the writings to Leo a few weeks after his election.
"I added that I wished to study these materials — to make them known and interpret the exact meaning of their contents," Fernández wrote. "The Holy Father showed intense interest."
The posthumous publication of popes' innermost spiritual musings is not unusual.

Pope John XXIII's autobiography, "Journal of a Soul," was published by his secretary in 1960. St. John Paul II had wanted his personal notes burned after his death, but his secretary defied his wishes and had the writings published in 2014.

title: Chinese official sentenced to death for spying
summary: According to state-affiliated media, the official received monthly payments in exchange for intelligence.
story: A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying for a foreign country and leaking "top secret" information in return for payment, state-affiliated media reported.

The convicted man, identified only by the surname Ma, had been recruited by foreign intelligence while working abroad, according to a report on Monday in an online account run by Gold Wall Press, a publishing company linked to China's National Administration of State Secrets Protection.
The recruiter, identified only as "Kailin," met Ma frequently, originally on the pretext of learning Chinese.

"Kailin gradually shifted the focus of their discussions to politically sensitive topics," probing for China's operational and personnel details in another country, the report said, without specifying which countries were involved.
"Ma disclosed a large amount of sensitive information concerning China's institutions" in the unidentified country, it said.
Kailin later introduced Ma to a colleague, who threatened to report that he had leaked information to Chinese authorities if he refused to cooperate.
Ma agreed to work for the foreign intelligence network and signed a cooperation agreement that included clauses on "confidentiality" and "loyalty."
He received monthly payments in exchange, and "a laptop for the purposes of sending and receiving intelligence," the report said.
Ma returned to China after he finished his overseas posting and "embarked on a long-term career of espionage."

"He would extract relevant content from classified documents and materials he came into contact with at work; in the evenings, after returning home, he would organize the information and send it via espionage websites," the report said.
Ma stole and leaked "over a hundred pieces of intelligence" during that period, it said, without specifying how, when or for how long that lasted.
He was "eventually apprehended" and a court found that he had received more than 1 million yuan ($150,000) in exchange for 35 pieces of information, some of which were "top secret," the report said.
The report did not specify when or where Ma was sentenced or whether he had already been executed.
"This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call," the report said.
"The tactics employed by espionage and intelligence agencies are becoming increasingly cunning" and included emotional manipulation and blackmail, it said.

title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine sank Russian warship off Libya's coast
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country was behind attacks that sank a Russian warship and damaged a sanctioned cargo vessel off Libya.
story: Kyiv, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country was behind an attack on a Russian warship off Libya on Sunday, claiming Ukrainian naval drones sank the vessel. It marked the latest attack in the North African nation tied to the Russia-Ukraine war.

Zelenskyy said Monday in a social media post that Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made naval drones in the operation, which sank a Russian corvette. The Ukrainian leader described the ship as one of Russia's newest vessels commissioned in 2023 during Russia's invasion.
"Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk," he wrote. He added that a Ka-27 military helicopter was destroyed in the attack.
"We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons," he said.

Ukrainian forces also struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara off Libya on Sunday. Zelenskyy said Moscow had used the vessel to transport weapons. The Angara has been under U.S. and international sanctions for illegally transporting weapons for Russia.

Another Russia-linked cargo ship, the Sparta II, which is operated by Russian defense logistics firm Oboronlogistika, was struck by drones Saturday in international waters in the Gulf of Finland, causing a fire on board. Kyiv has not confirmed or denied any role in that attack, but Finland's military said it was likely a Ukrainian strike. The Sparta is also under U.S. sanctions for illicit transportation of military hardware.
Russian, Estonian and Finnish vessels helped put out the fire and all crew members were rescued from the Sparta, and a Russian ship then started towing it away Sunday, according to Reuters.

Zelenskyy thanked the Security Service of Ukraine, known as the SBU, and other Ukrainian defense forces that took part in the strikes off Libya's coast, which he called "an exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war."
Zelenskyy said he received detailed briefings on Sunday and Monday and that "the targets we set were achieved."
The Kremlin made no immediate comment on the strikes off Libya, but said the Russian defense ministry would provide information later about the attacks.

Referring to the strike in the Gulf of Finland, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that it was "indeed a very dangerous trend — the expansion of terrorist activity in the Baltic region ... This is very dangerous. It is, of course, leading to an escalation of tensions in the region."
Russia "would like to hope that the Baltic states will somehow use their influence" on Ukraine to "warn it against continuing such dangerous terrorist practices," Peskov said.
The operation off Libya's coast, conducted some 1,500 miles from the front line in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv's forces.

Ukraine has at times blindsided Russia during the war with ingenious attacks that embarrass Moscow, such as Operation Spider's Web in June last year, when drones launched from trucks hit over 40 aircraft on bases across Russia.
The latest strike by sea drones severely damaged the Russian navy corvette at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya, according to two Libyan officials.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw fire at the base early Sunday. Civil defense rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Muammar Qaddafi, who was later killed, in 2011. A U.N.-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.
The U.N. mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the latest attack and called for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation."
"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) wrote on social media.

Ukrainian forces are operating in western Libya under a covert deal endorsed by the West. They used the North African country's territory to strike a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in March, according to Libyan officials.

The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, were at the time operating mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also in other military facilities in the capital Tripoli and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press earlier this year.

The SBU described the latest operation as "unique." It said the drones were delivered to a designated location and launched from a so-called "mothership" near the target. Russian defenses tried from air, sea and land to hit the attacking drones, it said.
"Ukraine's defense forces have once again shown that the Russian navy and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea," which borders both Russia and Ukraine, the SBU said.
Russia hammered Ukrainian cities with another deadly round of airstrikes overnight, meanwhile.
Regional authorities said 17 people were killed as a result of Russian attacks on Kyiv and the southern Zaporizhzhia region, including one child. Dozens more have been injured.

title: U.S. man convicted of killing U.K. woman he met on fetish website
summary: Dwain Hall was found guilty of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby, and was sentenced to two consecutive life terms, Florida prosecutors said.
story: A Florida man was convicted by a U.S. jury on Friday of the 2025 murder of a British woman he met on a fetish website.
Dwain Hall, 54, was found guilty of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby, and was sentenced to two consecutive life terms, Florida prosecutors said in a statement.
"This was an extraordinary and deeply disturbing case involving circumstances that are difficult to comprehend," said Bill Gladson, state attorney for the Fifth Judicial Circuit.
According to prosecutors, Hall and the 32-year-old Exelby had communicated for about two years using a fetish website called "Motherless.com" and an encrypted application called Sessions.
The now-defunct Motherless features "content that depicted various fetishes, including extreme BDSM, torture, and rape material," according to court documents.
During their exchanges, Exelby, who reportedly struggled with mental health issues, allegedly expressed a desire to be murdered.
A GoFundMe set up on behalf of her family has raised more than $12,000.

"Sonia struggled with her mental health, and she knew from her own experiences how difficult life could sometimes be," the GoFundMe says. "But Sonia was passionate about using the challenges and experiences she had faced to help others."
Exelby traveled to Gainesville, Florida, on Oct. 10, 2025, and was picked up at the airport by Hall, according to prosecutors.
Hall, who went by the username "AlphaSadist" on Motherless.com, was accused of sexually abusing Exelby during the course of the next week and stabbing her to death.
An ominous message sent by Exelby to an online friend was included in the arrest affidavit, CBS affiliate WPEC-TV reported.

"I'm sorry he keeps taking my phone he doesn't trust me with it. He made it clear there was no way out unless I shoot him. I was questioning it last night. I can't kill anyone," she wrote, adding: "He's in the shower, but I'm locked in, and there is no signal in the middle of nowhere. I thought he'd do it quick and not give my mind time to stew and realise this is the last thing I'll ever say to anyone if I don't take his offer of shooting him. He showed me about to use it and where to aim it."
Hall was arrested after attempting to use Exelby's credit card.
Her body was found on Oct. 17, 2025, in a wooded area of Marion Oaks, Florida, near Hall's residence, days after she was reported missing in the United Kingdom.

Investigators linked Hall to the murder through a receipt found at the scene, for a shovel that was later found at his home. A search of his cellphone turned up explicit images, some of which were used as evidence in the trial.

"Sonia was a truly beautiful person, inside and out," her family said in a statement to British police in July. "She was incredibly talented. Sonia could play the piano so effortlessly, and when she sang, she had the voice of an angel. Being around her felt special—she brought a calmness and warmth that made everything feel a little lighter."

title: U.S. will host the 2031 Women's World Cup, FIFA announces
summary: FIFA has confirmed a United States-led bid to host the 2031 Women's World Cup and a U.K. project led by England for the 2035 edition.
story: The United States will host another World Cup, as FIFA confirmed Monday that the country will lead a regional co-hosting of the 2031 Women's World Cup. The co-hosting group includes Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, while a different U.K. project, led by England, was ratified for the 2035 edition. It will be England's first time hosting the games since 1966.

The winning candidates and FIFA president Gianni Infantino promised commercially successful tournaments — the first editions with 48 teams and 104 games — and to reinvest all that money in women's soccer.

"This will be the largest women's sporting event in history," the U.S. Soccer Federation president, Cindy Parlow Cone, told FIFA members in a pre-vote presentation at the governing body's headquarters in Zurich. "Which means we have to deliver."

FIFA wanted these heavyweights of women's soccer to face no opposition without rival bids and so lead hosting the first expanded tournaments. That will bring parity with the men's World Cup, which expanded to 48 teams this year in the U.S., Canada and Mexico.
The 2027 Women's World Cup will have 32 teams in Brazil.
The U.S.-led 2031 project across the CONCACAF regional soccer body bid offers FIFA a choice of stadiums in 20 cities: 14 in the U.S., four in Mexico plus San José in Costa Rica and Kingston, Jamaica.

Atlanta, which hosted men's World Cup games this year, is among the U.S. cities included in the U.S.-Mexico-Costa Rica-Jamaica proposal for 2031, CBS News Atlanta reported. The station cited a report released by FIFA earlier this month, which gave the proposal a score of 4.4 out of 5 and noted that the bid "exceeded the minimum hosting requirements in the FIFA Women's World Cup 2031 technical evaluation."

The U.S. bid also proposed stadiums in Charlotte, Dallas, Denver, Houston, Kansas City, Los Angeles, Minneapolis and Nashville, in addition to MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where the men's final took place in July.
The U.K. bid joins England with Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales that offers a choice from 19 venues, including Wembley Stadium in London.
The pair of four-nation co-hosting bids had a clear run in the past 20 months and were approved Monday by acclamation in an online meeting of FIFA's 211 member federations.
The U.S. previously hosted the Women's World Cup alone in 1999 and 2003. The national team's tournament win in 1999 was the second of its four titles.
England never hosted a Women's World Cup which started with the 1991 tournament in China, won by the U.S. In the men's World Cup, England hosted for the only time in 1966 and won its only title.

The U.K. bid includes Northern Ireland which has plans for Windsor Park in Belfast for a renovated 23,000-capacity stadium. That is big enough for a Women's World Cup but not for the men's European Championship.
Euro 2028 is being hosted by England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland, which has the 50,000-seat national soccer and rugby stadium in Dublin.
For the second time in less than two years, FIFA is confirming a double award of World Cup hosts without rival bids that gives clarity for the decade ahead.

In December 2024, FIFA member federations were asked to rubber-stamp the unprecedented six-nation, three-continent bid for the men's World Cup in 2030 from Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.
That cleared the way for FIFA to award also the 2034 World Cup to Saudi Arabia in a fast-track process that seemed designed to exclude other candidates.

title: Capture of drug lord on FBI's most wanted list leads to more arrests
summary: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, alias "Chapo Isidro," was captured in Sinaloa during a special forces raid in coordination with U.S. intelligence.
story: Eight suspected members of a gang led by Fausto Isidro Meza Flores have been arrested, Mexico's defense ministry said Sunday, after widespread violence swept across Sinaloa following the drug kingpin's capture.
Meza Flores, alias "Chapo Isidro," was captured on Friday in the northwestern state during a special forces raid in coordination with U.S. intelligence.
The military operation sparked panic in Guasave, sending civilians fleeing from erupting gunfire. Elsewhere in the state, suspected gang members reportedly erected improvised roadblocks.
In clashes with security forces, 16 cartel suspects have been killed since the operation began, Defense Secretary Ricardo Trevilla said Monday. Four soldiers also died.

The fresh arrests took place during a patrol by special forces who "were fired upon by members of a criminal group" linked to Chapo Isidro, Mexico's defense ministry posted on X. The ministry included a short video showing special forces arresting suspects at night.

"In repelling the attack, they arrested eight members of the 'Beltran Leyva' criminal organization ... including one minor, who had participated in the roadblocks on November 20," the ministry's post said.
The military also seized several high-caliber weapons and six vehicles, two of which had "improvised armor and a turret for mounting machine guns."

Chapo Isidro, 44, led a drug trafficking organization affiliated with the Beltran Leyva gang and allied with one of two rival factions of the powerful Sinaloa cartel, according to U.S. and Mexican authorities.
He faces criminal charges in both Mexico and the United States.

The FBI had placed him on its list of 10 most wanted fugitives, while the U.S. State Department offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest. On Saturday, the U.S. Justice Department called him a senior leader of the Sinaloa cartel, which it calls "one of the most prolific and dangerous drug cartels in Mexico, known for its widespread use of corruption and violence to further its drug trafficking activities."
The Mexican defense ministry released dramatic video of the suspects being apprehended and escorted on to a military plane.
U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson said on X that "strategic intelligence sharing" between the U.S. and Mexico "helped make this operation possible."

In a social media post Saturday, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that Meza Flores had been captured "in an operation by the Mexican government supported by a coordinated interagency effort that included" the U.S. Homeland Security Task Force.
Chapo Isidro's capture came just days after Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum met President Trump on the sidelines of a summit in Asia.
Mr. Trump, who has pushed Mexico to do more to tackle drug gangs, said Friday that the two had discussed trade and security.

The Mexican government has knocked out several cartel kingpins. Chief among them was Mexico's most powerful cartel leader, known as "El Mencho," who was killed in February. Similar to the capture of Meza Flores, the dramatic operation resulted in a burst of violence and burning cars.
Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote in a post on X Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in the state of Sinaloa to protect civilians.

title: Why some Europeans have started prepping for doomsday
summary: Amid tech glitches, cyberattacks and climate change, some European governments are urging people to prepare for days without access to basic necessities.
story: European governments are increasingly urging citizens to prepare for up to 72 hours without access to food, water, electricity or communications.

France, the United Kingdom, Ireland and the Netherlands have all launched campaigns encouraging households to take steps to prepare for events caused by anything from extreme weather to cyberattacks that could disrupt digital networks or critical supply chains.

Last month, major French supermarket chains were hit by a cyberattack that caused the temperature in thousands of refrigerator and freezer units to soar, wasting tens of thousands of pounds of food and stoking concerns about food security.

French officials later accused a cyber unit of Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of being behind the attack, which was mirrored several weeks later by a nearly identical cyberattack targeting grocery stores in several other European nations. Belgian authorities blamed that, too, on Iran.

Europe was also hit by a record-setting, continent-wide heatwave last summer, triggering wildfires and severe drought even in areas such as northern England, where sustained, excess heat and a lack of precipitation have long been rare exceptions, not the rule.

The European governments have recommended that citizens buy and store emergency supplies including bottled water and canned foods to last households up to three days, along with AM/FM radios and sleeping bags.
CBS News spoke with residents and tourists on the streets of London to see who, if anyone, was taking the advice to heart.
At the Outdoor Emporium in North London, owner Mehmet Ahmet told CBS News the U.K. government's campaign had been good for business.
"There is an uplift, 100%," he said, noting increased sales of flashlights and gas stoves in particular.

According to a report cited by Getty, compiled by retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator, bottled water sales shot up by 67% in the U.K. in the wake of the government launching its "Be Ready" campaign in late October, while canned and jarred food sales rose 37%.
But on Oxford Street, the epicenter of central London's retail district, some locals just shrugged when asked if they were prepping.
"I think it's ridiculous. It's not going to happen," said South Londoner Ryan. "What's all the fuss about? If it happens, then I'll panic."
Other Europeans visiting London said they were taking a more measured approach.
"It's not a big effort. It's a small risk, but if something really happens, the impact is big," said one man from the Netherlands who declined to give his name, but said he was preparing.
In light of the recent Microsoft outage and the FAA's hours-long grounding of all commercial flights in the U.S. earlier this month, analysts said American wholesaler Costco saw a surge in sales.

"Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote.
In London, a woman visiting from Chicago told CBS News she would be stocking up as soon as she got home.
"I just decided 	I'm going to start now. We were hit with tornadoes, which never have ever touched down in Chicago," she noted. "People were without power for up to 7 to 10 days in the summer."

title: Search on for lioness seen roaming Istanbul's outskirts
summary: Police and animal welfare teams in Istanbul are searching for a lioness seen prowling the city's outskirts, Turkish officials say.
story: Istanbul — Police and animal welfare teams in Istanbul are searching for a lioness seen prowling the city's outskirts, Turkish officials said Monday.

A resident spotted the animal Sunday evening in Uskumrukoy, an upscale neighborhood on the northern edge of Istanbul's European side, surrounded by forests. The lioness was later captured on security camera footage.
"The location of the lion has been identified, and the necessary care is being taken to capture it alive," the Istanbul governor's office said in a statement posted on social media.

Grainy images published by the Demiroren News Agency showed the lioness walking through a grassy area. It was unclear where the animal came from, though some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home. The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office said it launched an investigation focused on identifying its owner.

The National Parks Directorate said specialist veterinarians and teams equipped with thermal imaging cameras were assisting in the search, which was focused on the wooded area. A drone was being used as well, the Anadolu state news agency reported.
Local resident Arda Koc said he saw the lioness after joining the search.

"I took my car and went out for a drive hoping to see it," he said in comments reported by the Cumhuriyet newspaper. "While I was driving, it suddenly jumped out in front of me. At first I was scared. After that, I immediately notified the gendarmerie (police)."
Residents were warned of the danger, and police were stationed on roads leading into and out of the neighborhood.

The search sparked numerous memes on social media, French news agency AFP noted, including one widely shared image showing a lioness sitting outside a gate with the logo of Besiktas FC, one of Istanbul's three major football clubs (soccer teams).

"The lion being sought is under our protection ... it will be tamed and handed over on Monday evening," read a social media post in a Besiktas fan account, referring to the lion being the the symbol of Galatasaray, the club's fierce rivals.

Turkey has become a hub for the illegal trade in wild animals as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia. In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered at Istanbul Airport on a flight from Nigeria to Thailand.

title: Pro golfer, chef arrested for 111 pounds of alleged drugs in luggage
summary: Officials said Grobler and a pro golger and his alleged accomplice, a 25-year-old chef, swapped luggage tags to conceal ownership of the cannabis.
story: Nigeria's anti-narcotics agency Sunday said it had arrested a South African professional golfer with 50.4 kilograms (111 pounds) of cannabis in his luggage on arrival at Lagos airport.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency said 37-year-old Henlo Grobler was arrested on Oct. 11 after arriving from South Africa.

The agency said Grobler and his alleged Kenyan accomplice, a 25-year-old chef named Faiza Njambi Abubakar, swapped luggage tags to conceal ownership of the cannabis. Officials said the golfer traveled in business class while his accomplice flew economy.
While Grobler carried bags tagged in the Kenyan woman's name, she collected two bags bearing his tags and left the airport.
The bags found with Grobler contained 46 parcels of a "strong strain of cannabis," the NDLEA said.
Grobler told investigators he was recruited by a South African associate and was promised $280 upon successful delivery of the drugs.
Abubakar, who was arrested on Oct.15 as she prepared to board a flight to Kenya, told investigators she had been offered $8,000 for her role in the operation.
"Both suspects identified each other during an identification parade," NDLEA spokesman Femi Babafemi said in a statement.
The agency said tracking devices were installed on the luggage and Grobler's mobile phone, allowing the syndicate to monitor its couriers and consignments.

Similar devices were also found in bags abandoned by an American professional basketball player arrested at the same airport on Nov. 11 with 34 kilogrammes of cannabis. Officials said the player, DaMonte Greene, claimed he was visiting Nigeria to "build networks for his basketball career" but examination of his mobile phone showed information suggesting his "knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity."
PGA South Africa lists a player by the name of Henlo Grobler.
Nigeria is considered a trafficking and production hub for drugs destined for other countries, but researchers say the contraband also finds its way into local markets.

Recent discoveries of industrial-scale methamphetamine production laboratories have raised concerns among authorities that Mexican cartels are establishing links in Nigeria to produce and ship the drug abroad.

title: Princess Kate reflects on healing in new documentary: "Cancer does change you"
summary: The princess reflects on her cancer journey in the documentary and speaks to others about their experiences.
story: Britain's Catherine, Princess of Wales, opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.
"Heal" follows 44-year-old Catherine as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours.

The Princess of Wales said at the time she undertook the challenge in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, an organization connected to the hospital where she received her treatment. She was greeted by her husband Prince William, who is heir to the throne, and their children Princes George and Louis and Princess Charlotte, as well as her parents and brother after completing the climb.
In a trailer released Saturday by Prince William and Catherine's Kensington Palace office, the princess reflects on her cancer journey and speaks to others about their experiences.
Catherine announced in March 2024 that she had cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy following major abdominal surgery. She did not reveal what type of cancer she was treated for.

Catherine disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission about 10 months after announcing her diagnosis. At the time, she said in her post on Instagram that she remains focused on recovery: "As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal."
She has gradually resumed her public duties, visiting India with William earlier this month.

In the trailer, Catherine says cancer changes people profoundly, and "healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew, and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty."
She adds that "it's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone" and "often, it is through pain that we realize there's a greater beauty that lies beyond that."
The film will premiere on the BBC in the United Kingdom on Nov. 29, before airing internationally on NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30.

title: Country singer Drake White admits he still fears another stroke seven years after nearly dying
summary: Drake White reveals the fear of another stroke lingers seven years after his hemorrhagic stroke, and how faith and Navy SEALs help him cope.
story: The 42-year-old country music star suffered a stroke that left his left side paralyzed
Seven years after suffering a hemorrhagic stroke that nearly killed him in 2019, country music star Drake White admits he still lives with the lingering fear of suffering another medical emergency.

Speaking exclusively to Fox News Digital at the third-annual Benefit For The Brain event in Nashville, the 43-year-old singer opened up about the lasting physical and mental toll of his health battle — and how he has learned to channel that anxiety into purpose.

"The fear of having another stroke is always there," White said. "Once your nervous system goes through that, it’s imprinted on it. You can work yourself into a tizzy, you can work yourself into anxiety attacks, and your heart rate gets up, your blood pressure gets going. So, it's about learning how to deal with that and breathe through it."
COUNTRY SINGER DRAKE WHITE DESCRIBES ‘GUNSHOT’ MOMENT HIS BRAIN RUPTURED MID-CONCERT: ‘I KNEW I WAS DYING’
Drake White attended a benefit for the brain at Ryman Auditorium in Nashville, Tenn., on Nov. 16, 2026. (Getty Images)

White credited both his background as an athlete and the support of friends — including several Navy SEALs in attendance at the benefit — with teaching him how to manage anxiety and high-stress situations.

"Just being confident in people saying, 'Hey, you're helping, keep going,'" he explained. "Because there are so many days that I don't want to keep going. So yeah, I fear sometimes, but there's a lot of good things in fear, too. You pay attention when you're scared."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Even seven years later, the memory of his near-death experience remains vivid.

"It feels just as real today," White said. "For me, I had a real-life experience where I witnessed a near-death experience. To come through that — that'll never leave me. I'm 43 now; I was 35 when that happened. So for me, it's very, very palpable. Very, very real."
Alex White and Drake White attended Drake White's benefit for the brain at Ryman Auditorium in Nashville, Tenn., on Nov. 16, 2026. (Getty Images)

"The thing is, God meets you where you're at," he added. "I don't care who you are, what you believe or what you think, if you cry out to Jesus, you cry out to God ... God's gonna meet you where you're at, and He's gonna come to you. And that's what happened. It was as clear as that."
In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital earlier this year, White reflected further on that life-changing moment and how leaning on his faith carried him through recovery.
CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND

Before hitting the road with Zac Brown in 2019, White was diagnosed with a rare brain condition called arteriovenous malformation (AVM). Having already undergone four surgeries, White said doctors told him the chance of a rupture was less than 1%. He decided to take the risk and continue touring.
His worst nightmare unfolded while doing what he loved most: performing.
REALITY STAR DR PIMPLE POPPER SUFFERED A STROKE WHILE FILMING HER SHOW, SAYS PART OF HER BRAIN 'DIED'
Drake White performs at his benefit for the brain at Ryman Auditorium on Nov. 16, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. (Getty Images)

"We just took the stage in Roanoke, Virginia. It was probably 98 degrees and cotton candy skies, beautiful, 2,500 people out there. And I tore into three or four songs and I just felt a tick," White recalled. "I felt my left arm, my fingers tingling, kind of numbness. And then I heard what I call a gunshot. It literally sounded like an audible gunshot behind my left ear. And when it snapped, if you look at the video back, you can see me trying to push through it."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"I grew up in Alabama where you just kind of keep pushing, keep going, and I tried to do that, and I couldn't speak," he continued. "I couldn't think, and the cotton candy sky became the grass, and the grass became the sky. Everything flipped upside down ... Everything slowed way down, and it just felt like I was walking in quicksand, and everything was heavy. My left arm was heavy, my left foot was heavy, and I knew right then, I was like, 'Well, dang, I'm having a stroke.'"
White immediately remembered his doctors' warnings about what would happen if the AVM ruptured.

"They told me, 'If it ruptures, you would have a very good chance of death,'" he said. "Death was kind of it. And so I just remember thinking: Keep breathing, keep praying, and get me to the hospital."
RUDY GIULIANI REVEALS HE HAD 'SPIRITUAL EXPERIENCE' WHILE IN PNEUMONIA-RELATED COMA
White was rushed to a local hospital and administered a coagulant that stopped the brain bleed.
Drake was mid-performance during his 2019 stroke. (Jo Hale/Redferns)

"That ultimately saved my life, but in that process, [I] saw angels, had the whole near-death experience, talked to God, the whole thing," he said. "It humbled me down to my knees. I realized that rock bottom had a basement. It really got me to a spot where I didn't know if I was gonna survive."
At the time, the country singer was left paralyzed on his left side and uncertain of his future.

"That was when the mental battle started," White said. "The doctors came in and told me that I'd had a hemorrhagic stroke and that I had a long road ahead of me. They didn't say this directly, but I heard them murmuring that I'd be lucky to walk again, much less get back on stage."

"That's when my world kind of crashed in around me," he added. "I was thinking, 'I've put so much time into this, and I've been so passionate about it. What am I going to do now? I've got a bedpan and I can't even feed myself.'"
Amid his recovery, White and his wife, Alex, were hit with another tragedy six years after his stroke.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
In September 2025, the couple — who are parents to a 3-year-old son — announced the death of their newborn daughter, Della Elizabeth.
During this time, White leaned heavily on his family, friends and faith. Looking back, he describes his previous interaction with God during his near-death experience as "very peaceful."
Drake White credits his faith to pushing through tough times. (Danielle Del Valle/Getty Images)

"My faith, I like to describe it like this: The sun feels different on my cheek than it does on your cheek," he said. "I am a Jesus-following guy that believes in that wholeheartedly. Met Him, saw Him, talked to Him. It's as real as me and you talking right now ... He was like, 'What's going on? Tell me what's up. ' It was the most peaceful I'd ever been in my life in that moment."

"I was not scared," he continued. "It's just like a transition. I could feel it. It was palpable. You know what I mean? I could touch it ... Whatever faith is for you, it meets you where you are. It meets you where you are in a hospital bed or in a car wreck or whatever it is. It met me where I was."

Now, White is turning his new perspective into action through his Benefit For The Brain concert. Following two consecutive sold-out shows, the event’s third installment once again united major musical talent and passionate advocates to raise awareness and funds for brain and mental health.
For White, hosting the event is the fulfillment of a vow he made while fighting for his life.
Drake White performs at his benefit for the brain at Ryman Auditorium in Nashville, Tenn., on Nov. 16, 2026. (Getty Images)

"For me, it was just a promise to myself and a promise to God that if He let me out of the hospital — if He would get me to a place where I could live again — that I would help give back to people and show people how I got from the darkness to the light," White said.

"That promise was just something I could drive towards," he continued. "If you have a purpose, and you find that purpose and push towards it, then your life starts to make sense. None of that stuff made sense to me when I was going through it — there were a lot of whines and a lot of howls. But when you start seeing other people come up and say, 'Hey, you helped me through this,' or 'You helped me through cancer,' or 'You helped me through losing my son or daughter' — who am I to even be complaining about what I had to go through if I get an opportunity to help people? "

title: Billy Bob Thornton says he’s a holiday ‘purist’ as he brings back ‘traditional’ Thanksgiving at home
summary: Billy Bob Thornton says one restaurant Thanksgiving was enough, as his family returns to traditional cooking, football and holiday rituals at home.
story: "The Mayflower" host Billy Bob Thornton tells Fox News Digital why eating out on Thanksgiving just doesn’t hit the same.
Billy Bob Thornton tried to have Thanksgiving dinner at a restaurant in the past, and he'll never do it again.

During an interview with Fox News Digital about his new Fox Nation series, "The Mayflower," Thornton opened up about his own Thanksgiving traditions and how his newest gig shows the actual events that unfolded in 1621, not what is taught in schools.

"Well, I've always been a little bit of a purist in terms of holidays and, especially when you have kids, you want to kind of, you know, keep that tradition going. So my early thanksgivings were in Arkansas, and then after high school I moved to Texas and Houston," he began. "I've always wanted traditional holidays and particularly Thanksgiving and Christmas. And we have that, my family and I always have a traditional Christmas and Thanksgiving."
Billy Bob Thornton hosts "The Mayflower" on Fox Nation, which premieres on Nov. 23. (Fox Nation)
He continued, "But for Thanksgiving, a couple of times over the last decade, we went to a restaurant, and it just didn't seem right."
BILLY BOB THORNTON PUSHES BACK ON CELEBRITY ACTIVISM: ‘I DON'T KNOW ANYTHING ABOUT POLITICS’
Thornton said his wife and sister-in-law were tired of the mess that Thanksgiving creates in the kitchen, so they proposed the idea that they go out for dinner instead.

"We get there, and it was just like, we do this all the time, what's special about it, you know? And so this year, we're going back to the traditional thing and there's going to be a lot of cooking going on and a lot of football-watching," Thornton said.
Thornton hosts and narrates "The Mayflower," which is a three-part historical docudrama. It premieres Monday, Nov. 23, on FOX Nation.
Thornton said that part of the series was shot on a replica of the Mayflower. (Matei Horvath/Getty Images)
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Speaking to Fox News Digital, the Academy Award-winning actor explained that once he was brought on to this project, he learned about the reality of the journey on the Mayflower and the extent of the "pain, suffering and sickness" people endured.
WATCH: BILLY BOB THORNTON SAYS HE REFUSES TO DO THANKSGIVING AT A RESTAURANT

"I would say the fact that not everybody who came over here, they weren't all exactly buddies. You know, there were people who just hitched a ride and all this kind of stuff. And also just learning to what extent there actually was pain and suffering and sickness. By the end of the first winter, half of those people were gone. I mean, that was surprising," he said.
Thornton explained that the Fox Nation series created a replica of the ship, which was much smaller than he expected.
Thornton told Fox News Digital he learned a lot about the first Thanksgiving when creating this series. (Scott Dudelson/Getty Images for Stagecoach)

"We did stuff on the replica of the Mayflower. It's not a big ship, I mean, at all, and to go down below deck there and see where these people were, and they were literally on top of each other – I mean, it was crowded getting the crew down there to film anything. And so it really brings it home to you about how difficult this really was," he said.
Thornton said he wasn't aware of the "bloodshed" that surrounded the Mayflower's journey to America.
WATCH: BILLY BOB THORNTON ON THE DARK HISTORY BEHIND THE FIRST THANKSGIVING

"I mean, I've heard things, but you know, like it says in the documentary, most of us, in terms of Thanksgiving, know what we learned in the third and fourth grade," he continued. "And it was all just like, 'Oh, look, look at the Native people. Let's invite them over for dinner, you know, and make peace.' And it wasn't like that. I mean, there was a war involved in this."
Thornton told Fox News Digital one of the main reasons he signed on to this series was because it was intended to educate people.
Billy Bob Thornton is an Academy Award-winning actor. (Jim Smeal/Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

"To be a part of something like this, to actually host something that educates you – and believe me, it educated me. I learned as I went along – I did not know this story. And so I just love being a part and telling a story that people don't know about," he said.

The actor is really hoping this docudrama hits home with young people, so they can remember the true meaning of Thanksgiving.
Billy Bob Thornton said he loves being a part of something that tells a story "that people don't know about." (Fox Nation)

"I think the more young people that watch this, the better. I think it would be really good for young people to see this and to understand where we come from and exactly how difficult it was and to maybe appreciate their forefathers and even within their own families," he told Fox News Digital.

title: 'Platoon' star Tom Berenger disses Hollywood as a 'company town,' praises Florida life
summary: Tom Berenger explains why he never lived in Hollywood, calling it a tedious "company town," and shared why he vastly prefers Florida and South Carolina.
story: The "Platoon" actor spoke to Fox News Digital about his new docuseries "Ronin 3: The Battle for Sangin."
Tom Berenger said he never liked the idea of living in Hollywood because he always felt that it was like a "company" town where everyone had the same job and talked shop constantly.

"I never lived in Hollywood," the "Platoon" actor told Fox News Digital recently. "I started in New York in the theater, and I always lived there. And I knew all those New York actors, you know, John Heard, Chris Walken. And a few guys are gone: Brian Dennehy, Peter Weller. They all saw Los Angeles as a "company town where all people did was talk about it all the time," he explained. "I guess it'd be like being in Detroit if they all talked about cars constantly. I don't know. But it was boring to us. It was tedious… it wasn't about anything."

These days, Berenger calls Florida home, which he said he vastly prefers to L.A.

"And South Carolina, it was better too," he said of where he lived for three decades. "They have other jobs and real jobs, for one thing, and it's not the same old chit-chat, I guess. They look different. The people are nicer… I could go on probably for hours if I had to."

title: John Malkovich recalls losing 'pretty much everything' to Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme
summary: John Malkovich opens up to "60 Minutes" about losing his entire fortune to Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme and the moment he told his wife the news.
story: FOX Business' Charlie Gasparino joins 'Your World' to discuss the downfall of the former American financier
John Malkovich recalled once losing his entire fortune to disgraced financier Bernie Madoff.
Malkovich, 72, told "60 Minutes" that he had recently returned from directing a play in Mexico City when he found out about Madoff's Ponzi scheme.

"I got home from that and I saw this photograph of Bernie Madoff in handcuffs, and I thought, 'Oh, well that could prove interesting,'" Malkovich said. "I went in and said to my wife, you know, 'I'm just going to go around the corner, buy a pack of cigarettes.'"
FRAUD MASTERMIND BEHIND MULTIMILLION-DOLLAR PONZI SCHEME THAT VICTIMIZED TRAVIS KELCE IS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT
John Malkovich was one of many victims of late disgraced financier Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme. (Swan Gallet)
He added, "I said, 'We have a little problem. Bernie Madoff just got arrested.'"
Malkovich, a previous smoker, hadn't indulged in nicotine "for a while" when he left the house that day, he said.

"That was pretty much everything I'd ever made," he admitted before coming to terms with his situation. "You know, you look to blame, you're going to do this and that, and then you realize, 'Look, why don't you shut up?'"
FORMER DISNEY STAR ERIK VON DETTEN SUED FOR ELDER ABUSE AFTER COUPLE POURED $2.1M RETIREMENT SAVINGS INTO GOLD
"Whatever you lost, most people who were ever born will never have a 10th of that, no matter what they do. No matter what they do. Get on with your life and that's it."
Madoff died in April 2021 while serving a 150-year sentence at the federal medical care center in Butner, North Carolina, where his attorney said he was being treated for terminal kidney failure.

A decades-long force on Wall Street, Madoff shocked the world when he pleaded guilty in 2009 to running a vast Ponzi scheme that prosecutors said swindled thousands out of their life savings. The scheme began in the early 1970s, and by the time Madoff was arrested in December 2008, had defrauded as many as 37,000 people in 136 countries out of up to $65 billion.
His victims included the famous – director Steven Spielberg, actor Kevin Bacon and Nobel Peace Prize winner Elie Wiesel – as well as ordinary investors.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Madoff said he started the fraud, in which he appeared to deliver steady returns to clients, but was actually using money from new investors to pay off existing shareholders, in the 1990s because he felt "compelled" to give investors solid returns despite the recession and weak stock market. Prosecutors contend he started defrauding investors much earlier.
Bernard "Bernie" Madoff pleaded guilty in 2009 to running a massive Ponzi scheme. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

"When I began the Ponzi scheme, I believed it would end shortly and I would be able to extricate myself and my clients," Madoff told the judge at his plea hearing. "However, this proved difficult, and ultimately impossible, and as the years went by, I realized that my arrest and this day would inevitably come."

Prior to his downfall, Madoff was viewed as a self-made and respected figure among financial professionals as the head of the seemingly successful Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities firm. He also served as the chairman of the Nasdaq Stock Market in 1990, 1991 and 1993.

In addition to being sentenced to the maximum 150 years in prison, Madoff and his family took a major financial hit: A judge issued a $171 billion forfeiture order in June 2009 requiring the disgraced financier to give up his interests in all property, including real estate, investments, cars and boats. Under the arrangement, the government also obtained his wife's interest in all property, including $80 million that she claimed belonged to her, leaving Ruth Madoff with $2.5 million in assets.
Madoff died in April 2021 while serving a 150-year sentence at the federal medical care center in Butner, North Carolina. (Bureau of Prisons)

The decline and fall of Madoff also took a toll on his family. The oldest of his two sons, Mark Madoff, died by suicide on the second anniversary of his father's arrest in 2010. His other son, Andrew, died from cancer at age 48 in 2014.
Mark Madoff's suicide prompted his mother, Ruth Madoff, to cut off all communications with her husband.

"I was responsible for my son Mark's death and that's very, very difficult," Madoff said during a 2013 interview with CNN. "I live with that. I live with the remorse, the pain I caused everybody, certainly my family, and the victims."

"I don't go to the gym anymore," she revealed, adding that when she did, it was "spinning class for an hour, and then I worked with a trainer for a half hour, lifting weights."

Eden said she still lifts weights a little. "Not as heavy as I used to." She added that weightlifting is especially good for women and their bones.
"You have to be disciplined about being active when you’re an actor," she laughed when asked. "My husband and I both have a trainer that comes in and helps us out."
4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS
Eden said she wasn’t sure what to credit for her longevity and energy, "but I'm glad I'm here, and I'm glad I'm still working."
Eden starred as Jeannie on the sitcom, which ran from 1965 until 1970. (Getty)

"I'm careful about what I eat, but I'm not overly stupid about it, you know?" she said when asked about her diet and philosophy on health. "I've never smoked. I don't know if that means anything. But, I think one of the things that's most important in your life is that you recognize other people. You realize that they're not so different than you are and that you have to get along. And when you do that, you find life is much more interesting, and people are much more interesting."
The actress also has a simple beauty routine which she said is what she’s always done. It involves washing her face at night and putting on moisturizer.
"That's about it," she revealed.

One thing the timeless beauty said she wished she had known about when she was younger was "the damage the sun could do to your skin. We didn't know that when I was growing up. And I think it really helps, if you know, to put sunscreen, you know, on your face during the day. Or if you're working."
The actress’ career spans more than 70 years, but she is best known for her titular role in the iconic sitcom "I Dream of Jeannie," which she said she never expected to become a phenomenon.
‘I DREAM OF JEANNIE’ STAR BARBARA EDEN TURNS HEADS AT 94 IN NEW PHOTO WITH HUSBAND
Barbara Eden poses for a photo as Jeannie on "I Dream of Jeannie." (Getty Images)
"It makes me so happy, really so happy that people still enjoy her," Eden said. "I really never expected the show to have the longevity it has."
The "Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea" star said that she gets fan mail from all over the world, including China and Russia.
‘CHARLIE’S ANGELS’ STAR JACLYN SMITH LIVED APART FROM HER HUSBAND FOR 17 YEARS DURING THEIR 35-YEAR LOVE STORY
"I'm just flabbergasted when I get the mail, and very, very proud. I just didn't expect it this long to be around."
Some fans even tell her that the show helped them through a difficult childhood.
WILLIAM SHATNER SAYS HE'S 'TAKING CARE OF BUSINESS' AT 95: 'THE LEAST OF ALL I WANT DO IS DIE'

"People will come up to me and say, ‘Oh, my God, you saved me when I was a child, because I had such a terrible childhood,’ and they just pour out what happened to them during their growing up period," she explained. "And so many of them were hurt either physically or mentally, and the show helped them. And I'm so happy to hear that."
Barbara Eden poses as Jeannie at an event in June. (Getty Images for Project Angel Food's Lead with Love 7)
One fan even revealed that they had turned their bedroom into a bottle as a refuge from the difficulties of life in the opulent style of Jeannie’s — where she slept on the show.
Eden also fondly remembers her "wonderful" co-star Larry Hagman, who played her love interest and "master" astronaut Anthony Nelson on the show.
"You never knew what was going to happen with Larry," she laughed, explaining that he was a bit of a prankster.

"He was just fun and unexpectedly fun, you know, for a lot of people." she added. "He was a dear guy. Yes, he was. He was like working with a 12-year-old boy. That's what it was, yes."

Eden said she rarely hears criticism of the series, but one thing that does bother her is when people wonder: "‘Why did you call him your master? You know, you're not supposed to call him a master.’ You know, and that's so foolish. Look, it's a fantasy, you know, and it's magic. She treasures her five seasons on the show, but the one creative difference she had was Jeannie and Tony getting married in the last season.
