title: ‘Dukes of Hazzard’ star Catherine Bach says co-star stripped naked except for cowboy hat to cheer her up
summary: Catherine Bach recalls James Best's hilarious naked prank on the "Dukes of Hazzard" set that lifted her homesickness, ending with 30 crew members bowing to him.
story: Catherine Bach tells Fox News Digital how her "Dukes of Hazzard" co-star James Best surprised her with a naked prank when she was feeling homesick while filming in Georgia.
"Dukes of Hazzard" star Catherine Bach recalled a wild behind-the-scenes prank that her co-star, James Best, pulled on her while they were filming the iconic 1980s sitcom.

The 72-year-old actress recently spoke with Fox News Digital at Cure Addiction Now's third annual Fundraising Evening at the Beverly Hills Hotel, which raised money for research into treatments for substance-use disorder.

During her interview alongside her daughter, Laura Lopez, Bach revealed that Best, who played Sheriff Rosco P. Coltrane on the show, stripped down naked to cheer her up when she was struggling with homesickness on the "Dukes of Hazzard" set.
‘DUKES OF HAZZARD’ STAR CATHERINE BACH STUNS FANS IN NEW PHOTO AFTER REPORTED HOSPITALIZATION
Catherine Bach recalled how her "Dukes of Hazzard" co-star James Best stripped down naked to cheer her up during filming.  (Paul Archuleta/Getty Images; CBS via Getty Images)
"I was a little depressed," Bach remembered. "I was so far away from home. I'm in Georgia and it's all guys."
However, Bach said her spirits were lifted after Best enlisted the help of a makeup artist for an outrageous stunt, which unfolded during what appeared to be a routine touch-up.

"He has the makeup man. He goes, ‘Catherine, we need to get the makeup underneath your eyes. We need to straighten it out,'" Bach recalled. "And I said, ‘OK.' Close my eyes. He goes, ‘No, open your eyes so I can get underneath,' and I was like, ’What are you talking about?' So he goes, ‘Just look at my hat.' And I say, OK.’"
‘LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE’ STAR SAYS BRUTAL FILMING CONDITIONS LEFT CAST MEMBERS UNCONSCIOUS
"And there's Jimmy, naked, except for his cowboy hat and his holster and guns," Bach remembered with a laugh.
WATCH: ‘DUKES OF HAZZARD’ STAR CATHERINE BACH SAYS CO-STAR PULLED NAKED PRANK TO CHEER HER UP
According to the actress, her co-star received an enthusiastic reception from the men on set afterward.
"So then, when he came to set, 30 people were waiting for him, and they all bowed down, all the guys," she said. "But he got a laugh out of me because I hadn't been laughing very much."

"The Dukes of Hazzard" aired for seven seasons on CBS from 1979 to 1985 and initially filmed in Georgia before production moved to California. The action comedy series followed cousins Bo and Luke Duke, played by John Schneider and Tom Wopat, and their adventures in fictional Hazzard County. Bach played their cousin Daisy Duke, while Best's Sheriff Coltrane frequently found himself outmaneuvered by the Duke boys.

The series was a major hit, drawing in as many as 20 million viewers per episode. By its third season, "The Dukes of Hazzard" had become the second-biggest show on TV, according to The Hollywood Reporter.

"The Dukes of Hazzard" catapulted the cast to stardom, especially Bach, whose short shorts made her a sex symbol. The cast members also became genuinely close both on and off set, forming lifelong friendships that have lasted decades after the show ended.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
James Best, as Sheriff Rosco Coltrane in "The Dukes of Hazzard," holds Flash, a basset hound, in Los Angeles on Jan. 1, 1982. (CBS via Getty Images)
Best died in April 2015 at age 88 due to complications from pneumonia. While speaking with Fox News Digital, Bach shared how Best's sense of humor remains part of her memories of making the series.
Asked to name the biggest troublemaker on set, Bach declined to limit the distinction to one cast member.
"Everybody, everybody. Jimmy Best, he was hilarious," she said.
The actress has previously said that practical jokes were a regular part of life on the "Dukes of Hazzard set."
"We all became such a family; there were so many pranks," Bach told the audience at a 2025 Hollywood Museum event with Schneider and Wopat, according to Remind magazine.
Bach has previously said that the cast "became such a family." (Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

During her interview with Fox News Digital, Bach also recalled how Daisy's wardrobe became a defining part of the series. The character's denim cutoffs became so closely associated with her that the style became widely known as "Daisy Dukes." During her time on the show, Bach posed as Daisy Dukes for a poster that sold five million copies, and her legs were insured for $1 million.
The actress said she had a hands-on role in creating the clothes audiences saw onscreen, saying that she "made them all," including the Daisy Dukes.
"And the bathing suit and the shirt," she added.
‘DUKES OF HAZZARD’ STAR JOHN SCHNEIDER BREAKS SILENCE ON EX-WIFE'S COURT BATTLE: 'EVERYTHING'S A NEGOTIATION'
Bach explained that her sewing skills came from her mother's insistence that she learn a practical skill alongside pursuing acting.
"My mother said I needed to have a craft in case I didn't make it as an actress," she said.
Bach's short shorts, known as "Daisy Dukes," became a fashion sensation. (Getty Images)

Bach previously discussed her influence over her character's costume choices in a 2019 interview with Fox News Digital. She said producers initially wanted her to wear a poodle skirt, but she suggested the denim shorts that became a fashion sensation.
However, Bach shared that the Daisy Dukes presented a familiar problem when it came time to put them on, saying that "gaining weight" in between seasons was "impossible."

"Every year I would say, 'Wait a minute, you guys wash these in the washing machine, and you dried them, I know it. You're supposed to dry-clean them,'" she recalled. "They said, ‘No, we did, we do.’ I said, 'No, you didn't. See, I can't zip them up.'"
"It might be me," she admitted with a laugh.
The actress rose to fame starring on the show, which ran from 1979 to 1985. (Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images)
The famed Daisy Dukes are not the only pieces of "Dukes of Hazzard" that remain part of Bach's life.
"I'm building a General Lee," she told Fox News Digital. "A Charger."

The orange 1969 Dodge Charger nicknamed General Lee that was driven by Bo and Luke was a signature part of the series, appearing in the high-speed police car chases and long stunt jumps that helped define the show.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Bach said her own car began as a surprise gift from her husband, although she suspected he had another reason for choosing it.
"I think he wanted it for himself," she said.
She told Fox News Digital that the vehicle has since become connected to her charity activities, with students currently getting an opportunity to work on it.
Bach told Fox News Digital that she owns a "General Lee." (Getty Images)
"Anyhow, I got it, and it's been a continuation of charity events," Bach said. "It's at a college right now, and all the kids are working on it."
Once the work is completed, Bach said she plans to bring the car to a hospital and offer children rides around the parking lot.
"You know, just stuff like that. It's fun," she said.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Weighing in on what she missed about classic television, Bach said "wholesome" entertainment.

"But funny, and a little edgy, but that you can watch with the whole family, because that's what you can do with ‘Dukes of Hazzard’ and with many other shows," she said. "The whole family can sit around without getting, you know, getting ruffled. Grandma, grandpa, the kids, the mom and dad, everybody. That's what I miss."

Catherine Bach and her daughter, Laura Esmeralda Lopez, attend Cure Addiction Now's 3rd Annual Fundraising Evening at The Beverly Hills Hotel in Beverly Hills, Calif., on Nov. 9, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

While attending the Cure Addiction Now's third annual Fundraising Evening, Bach also shared a health update during an interview with People alongside her daughter, Laura. Bach was hospitalized for an embolism in October 2025, according to multiple reports.
"I’m good... Everything’s on the up and up," she said. "It was very serious. Yeah. It was a very serious situation."
The actress told the outlet that Laura, 28, "took care of me during that time." Bach shared Laura and daughter Sophia, 30, with her late husband Peter Lopez, who died in 2010.

"She’s back and better than ever," Laura said of her mother.

title: Famed NYC restaurateur Keith McNally hospitalized after getting caught in France protest chaos
summary: Balthazar founder Keith McNally says he broke his hip and shoulder after getting caught in a Paris riot, and now must lie horizontal for 8 to 12 weeks.
story: Violent clashes heat up between police and protesters in Paris, France. Former Black Hawk helicopter pilot Lieutenant Colonel Darin Gaub discusses the high-intensity footage showing officers deploying tear gas as crowds demonstrate in the streets.
Keith McNally — a New York restaurateur known for "inventing downtown" with hotspots such as Balthazar and Pastis — claimed he suffered severe injuries after his involvement in the Paris protests.
On Thursday, the 75-year-old took to social media to share a photo of himself from a hospital bed.

"In a Paris hospital with a broken hip bone, broken shoulder bone and broken heart," he wrote in an Instagram post. "Went to Paris to see the Cézanne exhibition and got caught in a huge f------ riot."
FRENCH WOMAN RECOUNTS 'HORROR MOVIE' AS MOB OF RIOTERS TURNED ON HUSBAND IN STREETS OF PARIS
Famed restauranteur Keith McNally hospitalized after involvement in French protests. (Keith McNally Instagram; Getty Images)
"Je ne regrette rien," he added, a French phrase meaning, "I regret nothing."
In a statement to the New York Post, McNally said he "accidentally got caught up" in a protest that turned wild after police arrived and people scattered in a panic.
PHOTOS SHOW AFTERMATH OF RIOTS AS MASKED GROUPS CLASH WITH POLICE ACROSS FRANCE
"Unfortunately, as a result of my stroke I can barely walk let alone run and during the chaos I got pushed to the ground and broke my hip bone and shoulder bone also," the chef said.

FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE

title: Robert Pattinson becomes seventh actor to play James Bond in franchise's 60-year history
summary: Robert Pattinson becomes the seventh James Bond, joining a legacy from Sean Connery's 1962 "Dr. No" to Daniel Craig's 2021 "No Time to Die."
story: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said the team was "slightly biased a little against" Robert Pattinson because of his fame before screen tests made it "so obvious."
Robert Pattinson officially stepped into cinema’s most famous tuxedo as the seventh actor to play James Bond, joining a group of Hollywood legends who defined 007 for generations.
The casting marks the latest chapter in a more than 60-year cinema legacy that began with Sean Connery in 1962 and most recently saw Daniel Craig retire the tuxedo in 2021's "No Time to Die."

Before Pattinson takes his first sip of a shaken martini, we are looking back at every actor who previously held the iconic license to kill — from the modern-day action stars to the original 1960s trailblazers.
Robert Pattinson will take over the James Bond role from Daniel Craig. (Getty Images)
ROBERT PATTINSON NAMED NEXT JAMES BOND
Daniel Craig (2006-2021)
Daniel Craig was unveiled as legendary British secret agent James Bond 007 in the film "Casino Royale." (Greg Williams/Eon Productions via Getty Images)

Daniel Craig took over as James Bond in "Casino Royale" in 2006, delivering one of the franchise's most dramatic reinventions. The English actor's casting initially sparked debate among the spy's fans, but his intense physical performance and emotionally layered portrayal helped establish a new direction for the iconic spy.

Craig starred in five Bond films: "Casino Royale," "Quantum of Solace," "Skyfall," "Spectre" and "No Time to Die." His version of Bond was more vulnerable and psychologically complex, with an interconnected storyline exploring the character's relationships, personal losses and loyalty to MI6.
Craig concluded his 15-year run with "No Time to Die," marking one of the most consequential endings in the franchise's history.
Pierce Brosnan (1995-2002)
Pierce Brosnan stars as 007 in the 1999 James Bond film "The World Is Not Enough." (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)
Pierce Brosnan became James Bond in 1995 with the release of "GoldenEye." The Irish actor helped introduce the legendary spy to a new generation of moviegoers.

Along with "GoldenEye," Brosnan starred in "Tomorrow Never Dies," "The World Is Not Enough" and "Die Another Day." Following his departure from the franchise, Brosnan continued his Hollywood career with projects including "Mamma Mia!," "The Ghost Writer" and "Black Adam."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Timothy Dalton (1987-1989)
Timothy Dalton poses as 007 in a publicity still for the 1987 James Bond film "The Living Daylights." (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)

The year 1987 brought yet another James Bond, played by Timothy Dalton. The Welsh actor brought a darker and more serious tone to the franchise. Dalton developed his acting career through theater, television and film before becoming 007.

Dalton appeared in two Bond films, "The Living Daylights," and "Licence to Kill." His portrayal moved away from the humor associated with Roger Moore and focused more heavily on espionage, revenge and realistic action.
Roger Moore (1973-1985)
Sir Roger Moore as James Bond. (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)

Roger Moore took over the role in 1973 with the premiere of "Live and Let Die." The British actor brought a lighter, more humorous approach to the spy, differing from Connery's original tougher interpretation.

Moore portrayed Bond in seven films, more than any other actor in the franchise. In addition to "Live and Let Die," he starred in "The Man with the Golden Gun," "The Spy Who Loved Me," "Moonraker," "For Your Eyes Only" and "Octopussy"
His final appearance as Bond came with "A View to a Kill" in 1985.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
George Lazenby (1969)
George Lazenby aiming a gun for the James Bond film "On Her Majesty's Secret Service," directed by Peter Hunt, 1969. (United Artists/Getty Images)

George Lazenby took over the role of James Bond after Sean Connery left the franchise. The Australian actor appeared in "On Her Majesty's Secret Service." At 29 when the film premiered, he became the youngest actor to portray Bond in the official film franchise.
Lazenby's portrayal of Bond focused more on his romantic side, particularly through Bond's relationship with Tracy di Vicenzo.

Although the film received mixed reviews upon release, it has since developed a strong following among Bond fans. Lazenby chose not to return for another installment, making him the only actor to portray Bond in just one official film.

Sean Connery (1962-1971)
Sean Connery as James Bond in 1964. (Screen Archives/Getty Images)

Sean Connery became the first official James Bond when he starred in "Dr. No" in 1962. The Scottish actor helped turn Ian Fleming's fictional British spy into Hollywood's most recognizable action star.

Connery starred in six official Bond films, including "From Russia with Love," "Goldfinger," "Thunderball," "You Only Live Twice" and "Diamonds Are Forever." He also appeared in the unofficial Bond film, "Never Say Never Again."

title: Kate Middleton's unexpected house rule for George, Charlotte and Louis: author
summary: Like Queen Elizabeth II, who washed dishes at Balmoral, Kate Middleton uses chores, baking and gardening to keep her royal children grounded in normalcy.
story: Royal boadcaster Ian Pelham Turner discusses Kate Middleton's love for freezing cold water swimming and late-night birthday cake baking as part of her modern royal family life.
Being born into royalty doesn't mean getting a free pass at home.

Kate Middleton is reportedly determined to make sure Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis don't grow up expecting everything to be done for them. And the future queen consort has a surprisingly ordinary way of keeping her three children grounded.
It all starts in the family kitchen.
PRINCE LOUIS' 8TH BIRTHDAY PORTRAIT SHOWS 'RELATABLE' FAMILY VACATION MOMENT: EXPERT
The Prince and Princess of Wales are seen with their three children on April 5, 2026, at St. George's Chapel in Windsor, England. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"When it comes to household chores, Kate is extremely organized," Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!," told Fox News Digital, citing his own sources. "She wants to impart her ingrained sense of normalcy to the children by having them do all their own chores. There is a schedule that she draws up and posts in the kitchen, dividing up daily tasks among the kids."

"Kate!: The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen" by Christopher Andersen is available now. (Gallery Books)

"They make their own beds every morning, prepare their own breakfasts and clean up after themselves," said Andersen. "It’s a good thing that Prince George was accustomed to making his own bed at home, because that’s one of the chores he’s expected to do at Eton College. It’s a valuable lesson for any child growing up under such abnormal circumstances."
Fox News Digital reached out to Kensington Palace for comment. A palace spokesperson previously told Fox News Digital that the palace does not comment on books.
Royal experts told Fox News Digital that Kate Middleton loves to garden and she gets her family involved. (Getty Images)
Kate has made no secret of her fondness for one household chore in particular.
"I love washing up. I really do," the princess said during a visit to a community transport organization in West Sussex.

Prince George, Prince Louis, Catherine, Princess of Wales and Princess Charlotte watch a flypast from the balcony of Buckingham Palace to mark the 80th anniversary of VE Day on May 5, 2025, in London, England. (Getty Images)
When asked whether William lends a helping hand, Kate replied, "He does the drying. We are a good double act. And we get the children involved," The Times of London reported.

Catherine, Princess of Wales laughs as she talks with Lynda Jones at a weekly lunch club at Pulborough Village Hall in Pulborough, southern England, on Sept. 30, 2026. West Sussex Minibus, a volunteer-led community transport group and member of the Community Transport Association, transported attendees to the event. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
Andersen wasn't surprised.

"Kate and William have been a dishwashing duo since their days rooming together at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland," he explained. "They bonded over simple domestic chores like making beds, taking turns doing the laundry, whipping up simple pasta dishes and shopping at the local supermarket. It's really part of their DNA as a couple — a bit of normalcy in an otherwise very high-pressured, anything but normal life."

New graduate Kate Middleton wears a traditional gown to the graduation ceremony at St. Andrews University to collect her degree on June 23, 2005, in England. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
William was no stranger to getting his hands dirty before meeting his future wife.
Prince William cleans a lavatory during his Raleigh International expedition in Tortel, Chile, on Dec. 7, 2000. (Getty Images)

During his gap year in Chile, the prince took part in charity work that involved chopping wood, making beds, washing dishes and doing laundry, Andersen said. The experience may have helped prepare him for the everyday household responsibilities he would later share with Kate.

For William and Kate, those everyday household habits didn't end when they married. In 2024, a source told the U.K.'s Daily Mail that giving their children daily chores was important to the Prince and Princess of Wales.
Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, smile as they attend The Earthshot Prize Awards Ceremony at the Jio World Convention Centre on Nov. 17, 2026, in Mumbai, India. (Getty Images)

"I think it would surprise people to see how ordinary things are at home," the insider told the outlet. "The children help with laying the table, clearing their plates when they’re finished eating and helping with tidying up. There is no preferential treatment."

Prince Louis pulls on Prince William's uniform aiguillettes as they attend a military procession down The Mall to mark the 80th anniversary of VE Day on May 5, 2025, in London. (Getty Images)
The source also said the couple rely on daytime staff to "manage their busy working schedules" and help during "after school" time.
But it's not all work and no play for the royal children, British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital.
Catherine, Princess of Wales visits the Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital in Mumbai, India, on Nov. 18, 2026. (WireImage)

"Princess Catherine cooks regularly and is known to bake birthday cakes, pizza dough and other family meals," said Fordwich. "She also gardens. She declared, while at a Welsh denim factory last year, that she 'loves making things,' referring to knitting and sewing."

Prince William and Theresa Connor, owner of The Welsh Cake Shop, watch as Catherine, Princess of Wales, places rolled and cut Welsh cakes onto a tray for baking during a visit to Pontypridd Market in south Wales on Feb. 26, 2025. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

William and Kate want their children to grow up with a sense of normalcy. Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that the couple's down-to-earth approach reflects the kind of royal family they believe the British public wants to see.
WATCH: KATE MIDDLETON EMBRACES COLD WATER SWIMMING, LATE-NIGHT BAKING: EXPERT

"The reality these days is that William and Kate are a modern family," he said. "And the children do chores at the same time. William makes sure that they understand exactly what life is like in modern-day Britain. So, the children will do things like gardening. They'll do things like baking cakes. They'll do things like other household chores as well, keeping the house clean and tidy. Prince George, who is now at Eton, has learned that domesticity is necessary."
Kate Middleton and Prince William walk with their 13-year-old son, Prince George, as he arrives for his first day at Eton College on Sept. 8, 2026. (Getty Images)
Kate isn't the first royal to find satisfaction in an ordinary household chore.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Princess Catherine and Queen Elizabeth II watch part of a children's sports event while visiting Vernon Park during a Diamond Jubilee visit to Nottingham on June 13, 2012, in Nottingham, England. (Phil Noble/WPA Pool/Getty Images)
The late Queen Elizabeth II was also known to roll up her sleeves and wash dishes at Balmoral, her beloved Scottish retreat, according to royal experts who previously spoke with Fox News Digital.

Dickie Arbiter, a former Buckingham Palace press secretary who worked for Queen Elizabeth II and the then-Prince Charles, recently published a book, "On Duty with the Royals." He told Fox News Digital that one encounter with the queen left a lasting impression.
"On Duty with the Royals" by Dickie Arbiter is available now. (W. F. Howes Ltd.)

"After I joined Buckingham Palace, I was invited up to Balmoral," Arbiter recalled. "We went for a picnic. It had been raining. The picnic was in a log cabin and she got everything ready. I was left outside with Prince Philip. And the lunch was really four people: the queen, Prince Philip, the lady-in-waiting and myself."

"At the end of it, we had to clear up," said Arbiter. "At least I had to clear up, being the newbie. She didn't tell me to, but I took it upon myself, and I started washing up. And I heard these footsteps behind me, thinking it was the lady-in-waiting coming in to give me a hand."

title: Ty Pennington calls out 'excessive' home renovation trend people do in kitchens
summary: Ty Pennington calls renovation trend overkill, while sharing why kitchens and baths still build equity.
story: Ty Pennington, who suffered from an abscess in his throat that nearly took his life in July 2023, told Fox News Digital that it allows you to "really appreciate the people that love you, because sometimes we take that for granted."
Ty Pennington has built and maintained a successful career with his extreme home makeovers, but there's one renovation trend he believes homeowners are taking a little too far these days.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, Pennington — who has recently partnered with Insmed on the "Suspect BE" campaign to encourage people with unresolved respiratory symptoms to pursue further testing — weighed in on where homeowners should and shouldn't put their renovation budgets, calling out oversized kitchen islands packed with redundant appliances as a trend that has crossed into overkill.

"I would probably say the island with three dishwashers," the veteran HGTV star, 62, said when asked about renovation trends that go overboard. "It's maybe a little excessive. This is coming from somebody who was a personal dishwasher for many years of my life."
JOANNA GAINES REVEALS WHY SHE AND CHIP WALKED AWAY FROM 'FIXER UPPER' AT THE HEIGHT OF ITS SUCCESS
Ty Pennington attends the "Americans With No Address" red carpet premiere at Harmony Gold in Los Angeles on Oct. 3, 2024. (Getty Images for Robert Craig Films)

"There is a point that you almost get too big," he continued. "Is there an island that's almost the size of a small court? Possible. So I think sometimes we may be sort of outgrowing things. We may be just going too big. I know that's hard to believe, but I think sometimes we've got to scale back not only in budget, but also maybe in size. Cozy is cool."
Ty Pennington left "Trading Spaces" after the show launched his career in 2000. (Mark Peterman/WireImage)
While Pennington advocates for dialing back the scale, he still acknowledges that kitchens and bathrooms remain the smartest investments for homeowners looking to build equity.
"The most expensive are the kitchens and the bathrooms, but I do think they're kind of necessary if you plan on selling, because that's what people look at first," he explained.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Ty Pennington renovating a home in 2007. (GC Images)
When tackling home projects and renovation with his wife, Kellee Merrell, Pennington said compromise can prevent them from budding heads.
TIM MCGRAW WARNS OF ‘MOST DANGEROUS’ TIMES IN MARRIAGE AFTER 30 YEARS WITH FAITH HILL

"Sometimes you have to divide and conquer," Pennington said. "If somebody is passionate about a certain project that they know exactly what they think they want it to look like, sometimes you have to just use a different room in a different project. We don't always agree on everything. I don't think that happens in any aspect of life. What I try and do is lend my perspective and also throw out a couple of crazy ideas that hopefully sometimes lead to something sort of midway between."
"When you're dealing with a spouse and their plans, you sort of have to just be like, well, you just have to trust," he added. "And I think that's the key."
Ty Pennington and Kellee Merrell tied the knot in November 2021. (Ty Pennington Instagram)
These days, Pennington is splitting his time between his home in Georgia with Merrell and his mother’s home in Florida, where he has stepped into a caretaker role.
Nearly 20 years ago, his mother was officially diagnosed with bronchiectasis, or BE—a chronic, progressive lung condition that causes permanent widening and scarring of the airways.

Pennington, who has partnered with biopharmaceutical company Insmed as a spokesperson to raise awareness and educate others about BE, said his mother's diagnosis—combined with his own past health scare involving a life-threatening throat abscess—fundamentally shifted his perspective on life.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Pennington has taken the role of caretaker for his mother, who was diagnosed with BE 20 years ago. (Ty Pennington Instagram)

"[The diagnosis] certainly is an eye-opener, and you realize, 'My God, you really don't know what life's going to throw you around the next corner,'" Pennington said. "Just having the thing that happened to me on my throat and finding out that people can die of that just makes you realize everything is fleeting. Honestly, what it reassures you is that you really have to live life to the fullest, and you have to make every moment you can share with your loved ones the best."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"You have to get more of that laughter and more of that fun in your lives," he continued. "I think having clarity and understanding what you're dealing with is so important so that you can focus on those better, fun times. I have a little bit of regret because we didn't realize what was going on for so long with my mom. We only have so much time in life. Let's make the best of it."
Pennington says his mother's diagnosis changed the way he thinks about his own health. (Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images for SCAD)
Watching his mother navigate a chronic respiratory condition has also shifted his own mindset when it comes to staying physically active.

"I think it's really important to make sure you take time to focus on your body and make sure you're constantly moving," he said. "The one thing I've noticed with my mom is because you're battling and struggling with some health issues, you don't keep your body as strong as it should be because you get winded."

"What I've learned from that is if you have the capability of keeping your body in shape—constantly moving, constantly exercising—it is going to make sure you can add a few extra years to your life," Pennington added. "That's what I'm trying to do, as well as trying to motivate my mom to keep moving as well. Luckily, I stay very active and I've always been really active. You have to worry a little bit more about injuries because of that, so it's never too late to wear a helmet every day. I'm kidding, but you get the idea."

title: Tommy Lee Jones says ‘God loved me’ by putting him in Texas, opens up about life on his 6,000-acre ranch
summary: Tommy Lee Jones said he knew God loved him "because he put me on the ground in Texas," where he now lives and is raising 25 horses and has two polo fields.
story: Jones moved back to Texas in the early 2000s. (Rick Kern/Getty Images)
Tommy Lee Jones is discussing his decision to live on a ranch in his Texas hometown and one of his hobbies that has carried over since the '70s.

During a recent interview with The New York Times, the 80-year-old actor shared how he decided to move back to San Saba, Texas, in the early 2000s, saying, "I knew that God loved me because he put me on the ground in Texas."
"There came a time when I became aware that I could live anywhere I wanted to," Jones said. "So, in my wisdom, I went home."

The actor now lives on a 6,000-acre ranch in a two-story home originally built in 1856 and has turned it into the home he always wanted, noting he wanted to live somewhere that didn't have "any fences around the house."
Jones moved back to Texas in the early 2000s. (Rick Kern/Getty Images)
ANTONIO BANDERAS SAYS HE ALWAYS KNEW LOS ANGELES WASN'T WHERE HE BELONGED

When speaking to the outlet, the "No Country for Old Men" star shared that living on the ranch also allowed him to enjoy playing polo. The actor grew up riding horses and began playing polo in the 1970s.
Since moving onto his ranch, Jones has built two polo fields on the property, which now also holds 25 horses, and the actor and his wife, Dawn Laurel-Jones, host many polo events throughout the year.
Jones and Dawn Laurel-Jones have been married 25 years. (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)
Although Jones doesn't compete anymore, his wife continues to participate in competitions.
"She’s one of the better female polo players in the United States," Jones said of his wife.
Jones was an avid polo player and has two polo fields on his ranch. (Chris Weeks/Getty Images)
Jones began playing polo in the 1970s and grew up riding horses. (Chris Weeks/Liaison)

Jones started his acting career in the 1970s, making a name for himself as a cast member on the soap opera "One Life to Live," and appeared in many acclaimed television projects, winning an Emmy Award in 1983 for his work on "The Executioner's Song."

He cemented his status as a leading man and Hollywood heavyweight in the 1990s, earning his first of four Academy Award nominations in 1992 for his role in "JFK." He won the award for best supporting actor in 1994 for his work in "The Fugitive."
Jones won an Academy Award for his supporting role in "The Fugitive" in 1994. (Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

Jones is not concerned with his legacy. (Phillip Faraone/Getty Images)
He is starring in the FX show, "The Lowdown," alongside Ethan Hawke, Betty Gilpin and Jeanne Tripplehorn.

title: Bo Derek stands by falling for married John Derek at 16 despite 30-year age gap: 'It all worked out'
summary: Bo Derek reflects on meeting married director John Derek at 16, while "Dynasty" star Linda Evans recalls the devastation of losing him on a Greek film set.
story: John and Bo Derek pose together in Qatar on March 23, 1996. (Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images)
Bo Derek believes "it all worked out" when it comes to her marriage to John Derek, the director who was 46 and married when she met him as a 16-year-old up-and-coming actress.
She spoke about their relationship — as did John's former wife, "Dynasty" star Linda Evans — in a new profile for The Hollywood Reporter.
John, best known for appearing alongside Charlton Heston in "The Ten Commandments," had shifted into filmmaking later in his career.
In the early 1970s, he'd set out to cast a movie he'd written, "Fantasies," about a relationship between a teenage girl and her adoptive brother.
CAMERON MATHISON SAYS HE HAS ‘TONS’ IN COMMON WITH NEW GIRLFRIEND TAELYR ROBINSON DESPITE 24-YEAR AGE GAP
Bo Derek met John Derek when she was 16 at an audition for a movie he was directing. (Getty Images)

Bo, who went by her birth name, Mary Cathleen Collins, at the time, auditioned and was given the part. The film was shot in Greece, but John asked Evans to give Bo acting lessons before they departed.
As Evans recalled, Bo was "beautifully independent," and she had "zero, zero, zero" suspicions that anything romantic might develop between the teen and her husband at the time.
"I was with him 25 years until he died. He was a very ridiculously honest, good man. And it all worked out, didn’t it?"
Bo told the outlet her relationship with John and the age gap they shared is "not the natural way of things.
"If it were my daughter, I would have kidnapped her and taken her away from him, of course," Bo said.

It was 1973 when Bo left with John for Europe to shoot the film. A few weeks later, Evans traveled to visit John on the set, which was when she'd learned that he'd fallen for Bo.
Linda Evans with John Derek in 1972, a year before their marriage ended when he started seeing Bo Derek. (Getty Images)

She later added, "It was a favor they both did to me, because I ended up having an extraordinary life going off on my own."
And Bo, as she said, went on to have a long relationship with John that ended when he died in 1998.
John Derek and Bo Derek are interviewed by Barbara Walters in 1980. (ABC)

BO DEREK REVEALS WHY SHE FELT LIKE AN 'IMPOSTOR' AND WALKED AWAY FROM HOLLYWOOD DESPITE BLOCKBUSTER FAME

He said at the time that he was on good terms with Evans, and that she was the one who researched the legalities of returning to the U.S. with Bo. After wrapping up the film in Greece, they stayed in Germany for some time, because, as he explained, "In the United States you have statutory rape and the Mann Act to contend with."
John and Bo Derek pose together in Qatar March 23, 1996. (Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images)
"It was definitely more acceptable there," Bo admitted to The Hollywood Reporter.
They were married in Las Vegas in 1976, and, three years later, "10" was released, and Bo became an international sex symbol.

Bo Derek walks along the beach in swimwear as Samantha Taylor in the 1979 movie "10," directed by Blake Edwards. (Bettmann Archive)

She recalled telling him, "I just want to go make little films like we were doing before," referring to "Fantasies," which was finally released in 1981. She then starred in "Tarzan, The Ape Man," which John directed, and a couple other films helmed by her husband.

John Corbett and Bo Derek in 2002 at the Oscars party where they had their first date and in 2026. (Sebastian Artz/Getty Images; Vivien Killilea/Getty Images for the Shania Twain Foundation)

title: Chuck Norris’ ‘Firewalker’ co-star doesn’t regret quitting Hollywood: ‘I’m glad I’m out of it’
summary: Melody Anderson, the "Flash Gordon" star who shared the screen with Chuck Norris, reveals why she quit acting to become a therapist helping families heal.
story: Fox News' Carley Shimkus provides details after Chuck Norris' family released a statement on the American legend's death.
Melody Anderson knew when it was time to say goodbye to Hollywood.
The "Flash Gordon" star, who once shared the screen with Chuck Norris, grew tired of the uncertainty of showbiz and the constant pressure to land her next role.
So, she traded acting for a new calling: helping families as a therapist.
And she hasn't looked back.
DAVID CHARVET ADMITS HE WALKED AWAY FROM HOLLYWOOD AFTER 'BAYWATCH' TO FOCUS ON FATHERHOOD
"Firewalker," which starred Louis Gossett Jr., Melody Anderson and Chuck Norris, premiered Nov. 21, 1986. (TCD/Prod.DB/Alamy)
"I saw the writing on the wall," the former actress, who is marking the 40th anniversary of her Norris action-adventure comedy "Firewalker," told Fox News Digital.

"Part of it was aging out," she explained. "There was also the financial insecurity of always having to wait for a job. I thought, 'I've got to start organizing my life by the time I got into my mid-30s because I realized this is not something I can count on unless I win the lottery.' I still haven't. I still buy tickets, though.
Melody Anderson and Sam J. Jones appear in a scene from the movie "Flash Gordon." (Alamy)

"It wasn't really that scary for me to make that decision," Anderson continued. "The work was getting slower. My brain was getting duller. I wanted to pursue a career that would keep me growing. The curiosity and desire to learn keeps me young."
WATCH: CHUCK NORRIS DEAD AT 86

"Do I miss Hollywood? I miss being on the set. The crew was always so great. I loved the creative energy. I loved acting. But the actual business? I'm glad I'm out of it. I don't miss the business at all. There's always the anxiety of, 'When will my next job come in? Will it come in time so I can pay my mortgage?' All that extra stress becomes more intense as you get older in the business.
"I am so glad I don't have to deal with that anymore."
"Flash Gordon" (1980) is widely regarded as a cult classic. Although the sci-fi adventure received mixed reviews upon its release, it developed a devoted following over the years. (Getty Images)
Anderson stopped acting in 1995. Today, she is a licensed clinical social worker and therapist who specializes in addiction and recovery, trauma treatment and family therapy.
Actress Melody Anderson attends the West Coast premiere of "Life After Flash" at 2018 Beyond Fest at the Egyptian Theatre Oct. 3, 2018, in Hollywood, Calif. (Getty Images)

"When you're on a set, you hear a lot of stories from people," Anderson said. "I loved listening to people, hearing about their triumphs and struggles. I remember someone told me, 'You're pretty good at this. Have you ever thought about going back to school and getting a master's degree in social work?'
"I thought, 'Never.' But it really spoke to me. That's when I started working at a treatment center in New York and taking courses. I learned I loved family therapy.
Jeff Goldblum as Ernie Kovacs and Melody Anderson as Edie Adams appear in the ABC TV movie "Ernie Kovacs: Between the Laughter." (ABC)
"One of the reasons I love this career is because you can get really old, fat and wrinkled, and you can still help people," she said.

"I've been doing this for over 30 years now, and it's just so rewarding. I work with my clients to help them find peace and some healing. It's a wonderful life to live. On my deathbed, I'll know I did a good job, not for being the greatest actress, but for wanting to help others find peace."
Melody Anderson, circa the 1980s. (MediaPunch via Getty Images)
Still, Anderson has fond memories of her time in Hollywood, especially working opposite Norris. The actor died March 19, 2026, at 86.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Iconic martial artist and actor Chuck Norris died March 19, 2026, at the age of 86. (Gilbert Carrasquillo/Getty Images)

"Chuck loved doing tricks on set," she said with a laugh. "He loved to tease me. I remember he had this fake poop thing, and he put it right by my chair. But I immediately identified that it was from him because I'm also a prankster. I love spiders and bugs so it takes a lot to spook me. I just thought, 'Oh my God, he thinks I'm going to fall for this?'
Chuck Norris loved doing pranks on co-star Melody Anderson. (Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic, Inc)

"I thought, 'I'm going to tell him this is stupid,'" she recalled. "But then he was going to punish me with an even greater prank. I wanted to make sure he never knew there would be a day when I would come and get him. I was going to get back at Chuck Norris. And he wouldn't suspect a thing."
During a break from filming, Anderson came across a wooden sculpture at a local market. She had an idea.
Melody Anderson and Chuck Norris appear in a scene from the 1986 movie "Firewalker." The two were known pranksters on set. (Alamy)

"I remember telling him that I had found the most beautiful sculpture I've ever seen," Anderson said. "Its head was loose. So, I showed it to him with so much pride. Of course, he grabs it and the head falls off. I pretended to cry. He felt horrible.

"And just when he started to feel really bad, I smiled at him. I told him, 'If you want to do pranks on me, be prepared. I'm better than you.' We had a good laugh about it. He was a huge prankster with a big sense of humor. I think that's why he wanted to do a comedy. And he did such a good job at it."
But Norris' fitness routine was no laughing matter.
Chuck Norris lifts weights in New York City, circa April 1993. (Getty Images)

"He really showed me how to ride a bike for exercise," Anderson said with a smile. "He told me the faster I go, the better it will be, because it will get my heart pumping. It will also build up my thighs without bulking them up. It helped me lose weight quickly. We had a ball working out together.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
President George H.W. Bush jogs with actor Chuck Norris and his son Michael Norris at the U.S. Naval Observatory in Washington on March 21, 1990. (AFP via Getty Images)

"You have to remember, he was in Korea," Anderson continued. "He was a veteran. He knew the importance of taking care of yourself, defending yourself. He had that discipline of always working out, staying in shape. He saw it as an art form, taking care of your body. He was so disciplined.
Chuck Norris and Lou Gossett Jr. attend the 16th annual Shelby Awards at the Beverly Hilton Hotel in Beverly Hills Dec. 4, 1986. (Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

"He would get up every morning and work out for an hour, sometimes an hour and a half. I wanted to learn from him, so I started waking up early to work out with Chuck. And I'm so grateful for it because now I know how to exercise properly."
But there was one time when trying to stay healthy backfired on Norris and co-star Louis Gossett Jr.

Despite its star power, "Firewalker" failed to win over most critics when it hit theaters in 1986. Roger Ebert gave it just one out of four stars. However, the Los Angeles Times offered a more favorable review, praising the movie's humor and Norris' willingness to embrace a lighter role. (Alamy)

"These were two very, very macho men," Anderson said with a laugh. "When they came to Mexico, they were just, 'I'm not going to get sick. No ice, no anything. We're only eating the hotel food.' My belief has always been that if you eat the food, you'll get over it quickly. So, I was eating off the taco carts right outside the studio. They kept warning me, 'You're going to get sick.'

Best known for his tough guy roles in action movies (seen here), Chuck Norris showed off his comedic chops in the 1986 action-adventure comedy "Firewalker," embracing a more playful side of his on-screen persona. (Cannon/Getty Images)
"Well, they both got sick — terribly sick. They were unable to work. And me? I was fine. I remember I approached them and said, 'How are we feeling now, boys? Want some more hotel food?'"
Forty years later, Anderson remembers Norris as more than the tough guy audiences saw on screen.

Melody Anderson stopped acting in 1995. (ABC)
"He was a very gregarious, happy guy," she said. "I miss him."

title: Ashton Kutcher on track for billionaire status after ignoring wife Mila Kunis' early tech warnings
summary: Ashton Kutcher's Sound Ventures saw its $435 million Anthropic investment grow to $7 billion after the AI company's stock market debut on Nov. 19.
story: Ashton Kutcher is on his way to becoming a billionaire after investing in tech despite Mila Kunis previously warning him not to. (Taylor Hill/FilmMagic)
Ashton Kutcher is on his way to becoming a billionaire after going against his wife's advice and investing his money in tech.

According to Newsweek, the 48-year-old actor's venture capital firm, Sound Ventures, made a $435 million investment in the artificial intelligence company, Anthropic, in 2023, an investment that is now worth $7 billion.
Bloomberg reports that the company owns 0.5 percent of Anthropic, which has an estimated IPO valuation of $1.4 trillion. Anthropic went public on the stock exchange Nov. 19.

Kutcher co-founded Sound Ventures in 2015 and, since then, has invested in a number of successful companies. He previously invested in Spotify, Uber and Airbnb with his investment firm, A-Grade Investments, which he co-founded in 2010.
Ashton Kutcher is on his way to becoming a billionaire after investing in tech despite Mila Kunis previously warning him not to. (Taylor Hill/FilmMagic)
WHO IS DARIO AMODEI, THE ANTHROPIC CEO PUSHING INDEPENDENT AI OVERSIGHT?
Kutcher has since relinquished his position as partner at Sound Ventures but has stayed on as a senior advisor.
Although the "Two and a Half Men" actor has found success with his investments, his wife, actress Mila Kunis, wasn't always on board with him investing in certain companies.

"Early in our dating, two things came up. He was like, ‘Hey, there’s this company, it’s kind of a rideshare,'" she said on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert Show" in 2021, referencing his investment in Uber.
"He’s like, ‘There’s this company, it’s kind of like a cab company, but anyone can drive the cab.’ I was like, ‘That's the worst idea ever.'"
Anthropic went public on the stock exchange Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The actor decided to convince Kunis by suggesting she try the service herself, an idea that left her "furious."

"He is, like, ‘Let me get you this thing, called Uber, let me order it, you can test it out,’" she said. "And I was like, 'You are going to put me in a car with a stranger. What is wrong with you? Like, I was furious at him."

He later approached her about investing in Bitcoin, saying he told her, "I gotta explain this thing to you, tell me if I’m crazy," and then he told her about "this thing, mining for money. It’s called cryptocurrency."
Kunis told Kutcher not to invest in Uber or Bitcoin, thinking they weren't going to be successful. (Taylor Hill/WireImage)
"I was like, ‘Then who is going to make sure it’s safe?’ He was like, ‘That’s the point,'" she said. "He didn’t listen to me. ... This happens all the time."

When speaking with Business Insider in April 2017, Kutcher admitted he initially passed on Uber when the CEO of the company approached him but then realized "there was a product market fit there" and immediately called the CEO back.
He also admitted to having the same feelings about Airbnb, noting his initial thought was, "Who's going to want a stranger sleeping on their couch?"
Kutcher was unsure about investing in Airbnb and Uber in the beginning. (Kate Green/Getty Images)

"Oftentimes, the foundation of great companies are extraordinarily counterintuitive where the founders have some data nodes that would suggest that the intuition relative to a certain sector is wrong or that there's some fundamental intuition that is wrong," he explained.

"And that we when you unveil that fundamental intuition to be wrong, you actually find an entire pasture of green grass that nobody else is building in because there's a fundamental intuition … that has been an assumption of so many people for so long that they've never actually built into that sector."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
During her interview with Stephen Colbert, Kunis said it is not uncommon for her husband to approach her with a "ludicrous" idea, but somehow he is always right.
Kunis joked that she's never been happier to be wrong. (Todd Owyoung/NBC via Getty Images)

"There are companies all the time that he will talk about that, to me, seem so ludicrous," she said. "Why would I want to sleep on someone's couch and pay for it? Like, it is ludicrous, and yet here we are. And I Airbnb everything and Uber everywhere, and I use cryptocurrency. So, guess what? I have never been happier to be wrong."

Kutcher and Kunis first met when they were both cast on "That '70s Show" when he was 20 years old and she was 14. Although they played love interests on the show, their real-life friendship never crossed the line into romance at the time.
Kunis and Kutcher met when they were both cast on "That '70s Show." (FOX Image Collection via Getty Images)

They began dating in April 2012 after they reconnected at the Golden Globe Awards in January 2012. Kutcher was married to Demi Moore from 2005 to 2011, while Kunis was in a long-term relationship with Macaulay Culkin from 2002 to 2011.

"The people that we were back then would never be together. But it's just such a bummer that we missed out on 20 years together. I look back, and I think, ‘We could have spent 20 years together,’" Kunis said on the "WTF with Marc Maron" podcast in July 2018.
"But we would have never been together if we didn't both go what we went through in order to be the people that we were when we met."

The couple reconnected at the Golden Globes in 2012 and tied the knot in 2015. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images)
The two got engaged in February 2014 and got married in July 2015. During their relationship, they have welcomed two children together: Wyatt, 12, and Dimitri, 9.

Kutcher told Esquire in January 2023 he believes his relationship with Kunis "accelerat[ed]" the way it did because "I had always admired her."
"Her talents, her skills, her gifts," he said. "But I knew that she didn't need me. And she knew that I didn't need her."

title: Meghan Markle’s brand gets Oprah push, but expert says duchess still has ‘a credibility problem’

Meghan Markle may have Oprah Winfrey's stamp of approval, but experts say even the queen of daytime television can't guarantee the Duchess of Sussex something money can't buy: credibility.

title: FDA approves first new breast cancer hormone therapy in over two decades
summary: Genentech says its oral drug Wilserdly reduced recurrence or death risk by 30% compared to standard endocrine therapy in the Phase III lidERA breast cancer trial.
story: National Cancer Institute Director Tony Letai joins ‘America’s Newsroom’ to discuss an NIH study linking exposure to ‘forever chemicals’ to an increased risk of aggressive breast cancer.
A new early-stage breast cancer therapy has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration for the first time in more than two decades.

Wilserdly (giredestrant), an oral hormone therapy from San Francisco-based drugmaker Genentech, received the approval after positive trial results in treating adults with early-stage ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer.
This subtype is the most common form of the disease in which tumor growth is fueled by the hormone estrogen rather than excess levels of the HER2 protein.
NEW DRUG APPROACH OFFERS HOPE FOR PATIENTS WITH RECURRENT AGGRESSIVE CANCERS

The Phase 3 lidERA study showed that the drug reduced the risk of disease recurrence or death by 30% compared to standard endocrine therapy, including generic pharmaceuticals like tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors, according to a Genentech press release.
Wilserdly by Genentech has been approved by the FDA to treat early-stage and advanced breast cancer. (Genentech)
Patients were also less likely to quit treatment because of side effects like joint pain and hot flashes compared to standard options, the researchers noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The study found a reduction in cancer returning in distant parts of the body, like the bones, liver or lungs.

Aditya Bardia, M.D., global principal investigator of the lidERA breast cancer trial and professor of medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, noted that this finding is "particularly significant" because once breast cancer spreads to distant organs, it is "generally no longer curable."
The phase III lidERA study showed the drug reduced the risk of disease occurrence or death by 30% compared to standard endocrine therapy. (iStock)
The foundational hormone therapies used for early-stage breast cancer have remained "largely unchanged" since the 2000s, Bardia told Fox News Digital.
"These medicines have saved countless lives, but there has been room for improvement, both in terms of effectiveness and tolerability," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Now, for the first time in more than two decades, we have a new foundational hormone treatment that has been shown to be more effective than our existing standard therapies in early-stage breast cancer."
Because most breast cancers are caught early and fall into the hormone receptor-positive subtype, the new therapy has the potential to help a large number of patients, Bardia added.
Genentech plans to continue developing how Wilserdly can serve breast cancer patients. (iStock)

Earlier this year, the FDA also approved Wilserdly combined with everolimus, an oral cancer medication, for the treatment of adults with ER-positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer whose disease had recurred during or after completing endocrine-based therapy.
This makes Wilserdly the "first and only" SERD (selective estrogen receptor degrader) that is FDA-approved to treat both early-stage and advanced ER-positive breast cancer.

Levi Garraway, M.D., chief medical officer and head of global product development, commented in a statement that the FDA approval is due to the drug showing "superior efficacy" against other therapies that have long been the standard of care.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Genentech, a member of the Roche Group, plans to continue investing in "broad development" of Wilserdly, exploring its potential across disease stages and in new treatment combinations, according to Roche Pharmaceuticals CEO Teresa Graham.

Bardia encouraged patients to speak with their oncologists about the new treatment option, particularly those whose recent diagnosis is "consistent with the regulatory label and approval of the drug. "

title: Popular actor says bladder cancer discovery followed one strange bathroom symptom
summary: Jonathan Frakes says the sight of pink urine led to a cystoscopy and a high-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer diagnosis caught in time.
story: Board-certified physician Dr. Janette Nesheiwat joins 'Fox News Live' to break down the American Cancer Society's updated prostate screening protocols for men aged 50 to 69.
For "Star Trek: The Next Generation" star Jonathan Frakes, a life-altering health scare began not with physical pain, but with a strange sighting during a regular trip to Phoenix.
"My pee was pink," Frakes shared during an episode of his podcast, "Dropping Names with Brent and Jonny," alongside his co-star Brent Spiner and urologic surgeon Dr. Ram Narayanan. "I was unnerved."
Searching for an easy explanation, Frakes said he considered blaming his diet. Maybe it was beets, he mused, before realizing he hadn't touched one in six years.
MAN GOES TO DOCTOR TO PROVE HE’S 'IN PERFECT SHAPE,' TEST REVEALS SHOCKING DIAGNOSIS
Frakes ultimately called his doctor, a decision that may have saved his bladder.
According to Narayanan, Frakes experienced what is clinically known as painless gross hematuria, or visible blood in the urine without accompanying pain.
Painless visible blood in the urine can be a medical red flag requiring a trip to the doctor for urological evaluation.
"When it’s painless blood that you see with your eyes, that’s always a red flag," the doctor said on the podcast.

While blood in the urine can stem from benign causes like urinary tract infections or kidney stones, painless visible hematuria is the most common symptom of bladder cancer. It always warrants an immediate urological evaluation, according to both Cleveland Clinic and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
DIAGNOSTIC TEST COULD FLAG WHICH MEN NEED AGGRESSIVE PROSTATE CANCER TREATMENT AND WHICH DON'T

Days after finishing a fan convention, Frakes underwent an in-office cystoscopy, a quick procedure in which a thin camera examines the lining of the bladder. Inside, Narayanan spotted small, fern-like growths.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Three days later, Frakes was in the operating room to undergo a blue light cystoscopy — a specialized exam that uses an imaging dye to make hidden tumors glow — and tumor resection to scrape away the abnormal tissue.
The biopsy confirmed high-grade, non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
Jonathan Frakes credited his wife, Genie Francis, for saving his life by encouraging him to act quickly and get evaluated right away. (Getty Images for Hallmark Media)

To illustrate why early timing was so critical, Narayanan compared the bladder to a layer cake — scraping away the surface "icing" removed the tumor before it could invade the deeper muscle wall, which often forces surgeons to remove the entire bladder and fashion a new one from a piece of intestine.
"At the end of it, he says, 'I think we got it all,'" Frakes recalled.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
To prevent the cancer from returning, Frakes underwent six weekly rounds of intravesical therapy, where a liquid medication is placed directly into the bladder.
While immunotherapy is the standard first-line treatment, a nationwide shortage led Narayanan to administer a combination of two chemotherapy drugs, gemcitabine and docetaxel.
"At the end of it, he says, ‘I think we got it all.’"
According to medical experts, this dual-agent chemotherapy has proven to be a highly effective alternative during immunotherapy shortages.

While inspecting Frakes’ bladder, Narayanan noticed a secondary issue: an enlarged prostate. As Frakes joked on air, his surgeon told him, "While I was in there, I noticed your prostate is the size of a small town."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The enlarged prostate was forcing Frakes’ bladder muscle to work overtime, a condition called trabeculation, which can eventually lead to bladder failure.
After ruling out prostate cancer via MRI, Narayanan performed a surgery to remove roughly 135 grams of obstructing tissue through a single tiny incision.

The cast of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" poses in California in 1987. Front row, from left: Marina Sirtis (Counselor Deanna Troi), Patrick Stewart (Captain Jean-Luc Picard), and Gates McFadden (Dr. Beverly Crusher). Back row, from left: Jonathan Frakes (Commander William T. Riker), Brent Spiner (Lt. Commander Data), Whoopi Goldberg (Guinan), LeVar Burton (Lt. Commander Geordi La Forge), and Michael Dorn (Lt. Worf). ((Photo by CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images))
As a result, Frakes was able to stop taking his daily prostate medications, and his urinary symptoms vanished.

Other than immediate family, the actor kept his diagnosis private until deciding to share his story during Men’s Health Awareness Month to encourage other men to overcome their reluctance to see a urologist, whom Narayanan affectionately calls "primary care doctors below the belt."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"If something happens like [what] happened to you, check it out immediately," the doctor urged listeners. "Don't be shy. Don't be afraid."

The Fox News senior medical analyst joins hosts Bill Hemmer and Dana Perino to discuss the rise to over 5,000 cases in 2026. Siegel outlines what is driving the decline and explains how communities can protect public health.

Pennsylvania health officials announced Monday that a resident unvaccinated against measles died from the virus after testing positive, making it the ninth measles-related death in the state this year.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed the death less than a week after the United States lost its measles elimination status, ending a public health achievement that had been maintained since 2000.
Officials said the victim was a resident of Centre County, located in the middle of the state and most known for being home to Penn State University.
The state has 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties this year, including 49 new infections that were reported Monday.
A measles screening sign is posted at the entrance of Geisinger's Hospital for Advanced Medicine in Danville, Pennsylvania, on Nov. 21, 2026. (Paul Weaver/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
CHILD’S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE’S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK
Hospitalizations rose from 315 to 330, according to the state’s measles dashboard. Just five of the confirmed infections involved vaccinated residents.
Last week, officials confirmed the state’s eighth measles death, an unvaccinated Clinton County resident.
Pennsylvania and federal health authorities continue to urge residents to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, saying it the best defense against the disease.
Pennsylvania has been battling a measles outbreak since April and now leads the nation in cases, accounting for more than a quarter of all U.S. infections.

One-year-old River Jacobs is held by his mother, Caitlin Fuller, while he receives an MMR vaccine from Raynard Covarrubio, at a vaccine clinic put on by Lubbock Public Health Department on March 1, 2025, in Lubbock, Texas. (Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images)
TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK BACKS MMR VACCINE, REJECTS LINK BETWEEN CHILDHOOD VACCINES AND AUTISM
The sharp rise in cases — largely in rural and Amish communities with historically low vaccination rates — has prompted state health officials to ramp up immunization efforts.

The state health department has administered more than 7,400 doses of the MMR vaccine at nearly 300 pop-up clinics. Officials plan to set up dozens more of these temporary immunization sites over the coming weeks and months.
For months, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have sparred over the response to the ongoing measles outbreak in the state.
Shapiro has accused Kennedy of spreading misinformation about the MMR vaccine and vaccines in general, something the nation's top health official has denied.

Josh Shapiro, governor of Pennsylvania, speaks during the Bradford County Democrats Breakfast at the Sayre VFW in Sayre, Pennsylvania, on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026. (Photographer: Heather Ainsworth/Bloomberg)
AMISH FACE NEW YORK VACCINE MANDATE IN SUPREME COURT FIGHT, MIGHT HAVE TO ‘PACK THEIR WAGONS’
Overall, Kennedy has given a mix of answers about his stance on the MMR vaccine. When testifying before the House in May 2025, he said he would "probably" vaccinate his children against measles.
When he was asked the same question in August 2024, prior to becoming HHS secretary, Kennedy said he would not give his kids the MMR vaccine.
Kennedy, meanwhile, has accused Shapiro of politicizing the outbreak and suggested that some of Pennsylvania’s reported measles deaths may have been "fabricated."

Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks during an event at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services building on Oct. 5, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Pan American Health Organization’s decision last Wednesday to revoke the U.S.’ measles elimination status means the virus is once again considered endemic in the country. This means it is circulating regularly at a relatively predictable level, much like the seasonal flu and chickenpox.
The difference is, measles is around 12 times more contagious than the flu and twice as contagious as chickenpox, according to Unicef.

People infected with measles — especially babies and young children — also face the risk of severe complications, including a weakened immune system or encephalitis, a type of brain swelling that can cause seizures and intellectual disabilities.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Alzheimer’s risk jumps 53% for millions living with common blood sugar condition
summary: New research suggests people with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease, with experts pointing to blood sugar control.
story: Dr. Caghan Kizil, professor of neurological sciences at Columbia University Department of Neurology, discusses new research showing that people living with type 2 diabetes may face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease.
People living with type 2 diabetes may face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease compared to those without the condition, a new study suggests.
Researchers from Curtin University's School of Population Health in Australia reviewed 40 observational studies including people with Alzheimer’s disease and type 2 diabetes.

After accounting for other health and lifestyle factors, the researchers found that individuals with this condition have a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer's. That translates to roughly 4.7 new cases for every 1,000 people tracked over a year.
3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS

"It doesn't add newer experiments or show that diabetes directly causes Alzheimer's disease, but how we should read it is that someone with diabetes has about one and a half times more chance of getting Alzheimer's disease compared to someone without it," Dr. Caghan Kizil, professor of neurological sciences at Columbia University Department of Neurology, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
People living with type 2 diabetes may face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease compared to those without the condition, a new study suggests. (iStock)
The findings were published in the journal Alzheimer’s Research & Therapy on Nov. 9.
ALZHEIMER’S BLOOD MARKER COULD PREDICT COGNITIVE DECLINE RISKS, MAYO CLINIC SAYS

Unlike earlier reviews that often combined different forms of diabetes and dementia, the new analysis looked specifically at type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease to calculate the rate of new cases, according to lead study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, a researcher at the Curtin School of Population Health.
Researchers found that individuals with type 2 diabetes have a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer's. (iStock)

"Reporting both relative risk and incidence measures helps explain not only whether risk is higher, but how frequently new cases occur," Adewuyi told Fox News Digital. "What stood out was the fuller picture that emerged when we examined how often Alzheimer’s disease developed alongside how risk compared between groups."
Experts point to a few key ways that poor blood sugar control harms brain cells over time.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY PREVENT PREDIABETES FROM TURNING INTO DIABETES

Excess blood sugar can stiffen and narrow blood vessels in the brain, causing a decrease in blood flow and oxygen to brain cells, according to Dr. Nikhil Palekar, director of Stony Brook Medicine's Center of Excellence for Alzheimer's Disease in New York.
"Insulin resistance prevents the brain cells from utilizing glucose, resulting in reduced cellular energy and neuronal functions," Palekar, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
To protect brain health, a doctor advises monitoring blood sugar, getting 150 minutes of weekly moderate aerobic exercise and eating a balanced, Mediterranean-style diet. (iStock)
Maintaining optimal blood sugar levels can reduce the risk for Alzheimer’s, the doctor confirmed.
"GLP-1 agonists have been shown to lower elevated blood sugar levels as well [as] decrease brain inflammation, which is a risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease," Palekar said.
Limitations of the analysis
There were some limitations, including extreme variation across the studies.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Because the individual studies reported vastly different rates — ranging from fewer than one to nearly 30 new cases per 1,000 people each year — the researchers could not pinpoint a single, exact risk rate.
Additionally, the analysis relied on real-world observational data rather than controlled clinical trials.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Importantly, these are population-level findings," Adewuyi said. "They cannot predict whether a particular person will develop Alzheimer’s disease."
Variations in where the studies were conducted, how long patients were tracked and which outside health factors were considered all influenced the outcomes.
The early signs and symptoms of Alzheimer’s are most often related to becoming more forgetful, according to a doctor. (iStock)
Alzheimer's is one of the most prevalent dementia types, comprising almost 70% of all cases, Kizil noted, which is why the studies are heavily focused on that condition.
However, as diabetes can deprive the brain of essential nutrients, it can contribute to a wide range of neurological diseases beyond just Alzheimer’s.
Lowering the risk
For people who have diabetes along with an increased risk of developing dementia, Kizil recommends undergoing cognitive screenings much earlier, alongside blood sugar control and other measurements.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

People with diabetes or any type of cardiovascular risk factors, including high blood pressure, should work proactively with their doctors on metabolic control and earlier cognitive monitoring, he advised.
Adewuyi emphasized that the study provides no basis for changing medication or adopting tighter blood glucose targets specifically to prevent Alzheimer’s disease.
To support brain health, a doctor recommends following a primary care physician’s guidance to closely monitor blood sugar levels alongside key lifestyle modifications. (iStock)

"If someone notices persistent changes in memory or thinking – particularly if these are affecting medicines, glucose monitoring or daily activities – they should discuss them with their healthcare team," he advised.
The early signs and symptoms of Alzheimer’s are most often related to becoming more forgetful, according to Palekar.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Some of those include "short-term memory loss, such as forgetting recent events or conversations, misplacing things routinely, having difficulty managing finances or performing complex daily tasks," the doctor told Fox News Digital.

To support brain health, Palekar recommends following a primary care physician’s guidance to closely monitor blood sugar levels alongside key lifestyle modifications — "specifically, moderate-intensity aerobic exercise 150 minutes a week and a balanced diet, such as the Mediterranean diet."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Who owns your body parts after surgery? Doctors uncover the complicated rules
summary: Surgical patients are asking hospitals to hand over removed organs, teeth and joints as keepsakes, but pathology rules and release forms stand in the way.
story: Dr. Raymond Lynch, director of the Division of Transplantation at HRSA, discusses how updated federal organ donation guidelines seek to protect patients and improve communication with families facing difficult end-of-life decisions.
Most people want to forget their time in the operating room, yet some surgical patients insist on bringing their removed body parts home as souvenirs.

While hospitals usually throw away removed tissue as medical waste, a small number of patients asks doctors to pack up their organs, teeth and worn-out joints after surgery, according to TIME magazine.
Doctors say these patients want keepsakes for many reasons, from marking personal milestones to honoring cultural traditions.
ORGAN HARVESTING BEGAN WHILE PATIENTS STILL SHOWED ‘SIGNS OF LIFE,’ FEDERAL INVESTIGATION FINDS

Examples included a patient who kept her removed uterus in a jar after a hysterectomy as a reminder of the pain she survived, and another who dried her removed fallopian tubes to display in a box with flowers, according to the report.
While hospitals typically discard removed tissue as medical waste, some surgical patients ask to bring their organs, teeth or joints home as souvenirs. (iStock)
Other saved items included a pulled wisdom tooth fashioned into a calligraphy pen and a piece of medical tubing saved from a hospital stay and later given to a future spouse, the magazine said.

Dr. Robyn Power, a gynecologic surgeon in South Florida, told TIME that only about five of her patients finished the paperwork to take tissue home over the past year, though more people are asking about it.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
She said patients living with painful conditions like endometriosis sometimes want the removed tissue as physical proof of what disrupted their lives.
"It means something different to everybody," Power said.
Hospital rules and safety

Taking a body part home takes more than asking a surgeon in the recovery room.Dr. Kenneth Perry, an emergency room physician based in South Carolina, told Fox News Digital that rules surrounding who owns removed tissue vary widely.
Before any surgical tissue can be released to a patient, pathologists must examine the specimen for disease. (iStock)

"As odd as it sounds, the ownership of tissue and other things removed from a person’s body is actually not settled law," Perry said. "Each state and each institution will have its own views on how to handle different tissues."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

In the emergency room, Perry said doctors often let patients take home low-risk items like passed kidney stones, salivary gland stones or splinters, as long as the objects are not tied to a police case, like a bullet.
Larger organs or body parts carry more risk because doctors must rule out infection or serious disease before releasing them.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"For instance, if an extremity or an organ has been removed due to infection or bleeding, it is often required that it goes through pathology testing to ensure it is safe," Perry said.

He added that for pregnancy-related tissues, such as a placenta or remains from a miscarriage, hospitals typically have different rules and separate steps involved for families who ask to take them home.
Patients debate the rules online
Some surgical patients have taken to Reddit to share their confusion and experiences with trying to keep removed body parts.
Surgeons say patients request removed tissue for varied reasons, from honoring cultural traditions to keeping physical proof of chronic conditions. (iStock)

"Seeing as the hip bone is coming from my own body, I don't understand why I cannot," one user wrote ahead of a hip replacement in Washington State after a surgeon claimed that state law rejected his request to keep the bone.
"My best friend's son got to keep one of his tonsils to take to school for show and tell," the user added.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Others pushed back, pointing to health hazards and hospital rules.
"It's considered medical waste. Yes, bones can carry risks," one commenter wrote.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It really depends on the state laws, but most will not allow it," wrote another user who said they worked in pathology. "You can have a funeral home bury it if you like, but probably not take it home."
