title: Popular bedroom supplements often fail to deliver, says longevity physician
summary: Dr. Pablo Prichard shares why most sexual enhancement supplements fail and how L-arginine and L-citrulline may help blood flow and erectile dysfunction.
story: Dr. Pablo Prichard, an Arizona-based surgeon who focuses on longevity and preventative health, warns that most over-the-counter sexual enhancement products are ineffective — and some carry health risks.

Pharmacy aisles and social media feeds are crowded with capsules, powders and gummies promising to boost libido and sexual performance. Yet according to physicians and clinical research, most over-the-counter sexual enhancement products are ineffective — and some carry health risks.
It's a mistake to treat all sexual health concerns as a single problem, according to Dr. Pablo Prichard, an Arizona-based surgeon who focuses on longevity and preventative health.
Before reaching for a bottle, patients should understand the difference between low sex drive and physical performance issues like erectile dysfunction or vaginal dryness, he told Fox News Digital.
WHY STACKING SUPPLEMENTS WITHOUT A BLOOD TEST FIRST CAN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD
"When you're looking at supplements, you have to think, ‘Is this supplement affecting what my problem is individually?’" Prichard said.
"Because if you have a hormonal issue, and you take a supplement that supposedly increases your blood flow, that doesn't necessarily improve your condition."
Hundreds of unregulated "all-natural" supplements have been found by the FDA to contain hidden, undeclared prescription drugs like sildenafil and tadalafil, the doctor said. (iStock)

If performance issues stem from restricted circulation, certain amino acids may offer modest support. Supplements like L-arginine and L-citrulline target the nitric oxide pathway, which helps relax and widen blood vessels, Prichard said.
According to Cleveland Clinic, L-citrulline converts into L-arginine in the body to boost nitric oxide production, and small clinical studies suggest it may help improve mild erectile dysfunction.
VIAGRA COULD DO MORE THAN ADVERTISED AS STUDY REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH SUPERPOWER
Still, the clinic notes that overall scientific evidence remains mixed, larger clinical trials are needed, and the supplements are less reliable than prescription treatments.

"If you actually have a blood-flow issue, then taking a supplement like this … that improves your blood flow could actually help," Prichard said. "If you don't have a blood-flow issue, and it's another problem, then taking a supplement like this probably won't help."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

While certain herbal extracts, such as Panax ginseng and saffron, have shown potential in small trials to improve erectile function and sexual satisfaction, experts urge caution with unregulated sexual enhancement blends.
"The FDA has repeatedly seen actual Viagra in these 'herbal Viagra' medications," Prichard said.

Mixing hidden prescription ingredients or certain herbs with heart medications, blood pressure drugs or blood thinners can trigger life-threatening drops in blood pressure or elevated bleeding risks. (iStock)

Laboratory testing by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has identified hundreds of over-the-counter products marketed as "all-natural" sexual enhancers that secretly contain prescription drug ingredients — most commonly sildenafil (the active ingredient in Viagra) and tadalafil (found in Cialis).

Because these hidden drugs aren't listed on the label, the agency warns that consumers risk dangerous side effects or severe drops in blood pressure, particularly if they take heart medications containing nitrates.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Taking unknown doses of prescription erectile dysfunction drugs can trigger dangerous side effects.

Prichard warned that combining hidden sildenafil — or even high doses of L-arginine — with heart medications like nitroglycerin or hypertension drugs can cause life-threatening drops in blood pressure. Similarly, mixing herbs like ginkgo biloba with blood thinners can elevate bleeding risks.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
For both men and women experiencing low desire or dryness tied to shifting hormone levels, consulting with a physician is more effective than guessing at the store, the doctor advised.

Fundamental lifestyle habits such as getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, managing stress and consulting a doctor for underlying medical conditions are far more effective than relying on pills. (iStock)
Any new or worsening changes in sexual function warrant a medical checkup, as they could be a warning sign of cardiovascular disease, diabetes or depression.
"I think a lot of times, people take the easy way out and say, 'Yeah, I have this problem, I'm just going to take this pill ... and that's going to fix my problem,'" Prichard said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Foundational habits like prioritizing sleep, managing stress and getting both aerobic and strength exercise "can have a much bigger influence on your sexual health than just taking a supplement," the doctor added.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Common sleep habit linked to 50% higher death risk in heart patients, recent study finds
summary: A PLOS One study of 3,287 US adults with heart disease links sleeping nine or more hours to a 51% higher risk of all-cause mortality over 15 years.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses a new study challenging the traditional eight hour sleep rule on America Reports.

Adults with heart disease who sleep nine or more hours per night could be at a higher risk of death from both heart-related and non-heart-related causes than those who sleep seven to eight hours, according to a recent study.

The cohort study in the journal PLOS One, titled "Sleep duration and cause-specific mortality among US adults with heart disease," analyzed data from 3,287 adults with heart disease from the 2004 National Health Survey linked to the National Death Index running until Dec. 31, 2019.

In the National Health Survey, participants answered whether they had heart disease based on if they had ever been told they had coronary heart disease, a heart attack or a heart condition or disease, according to the study.
MORE NAPS, HIGHER RISK? RESEARCH LINKS DAYTIME SLEEP TO HEALTH WARNINGS IN AGING ADULTS

"Sleep affects blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, inflammation, and appetite hormones, and all of these influence cardiovascular risk," Erin Palinksi-Wade, a New Jersey-based registered dietitian and Certified Diabetes Care and Education Specialist (CDCES), told Fox News Digital.
Sleeping too much or not enough could be warning signs of various health problems and worth mentioning to a doctor. (iStock)
The study authors adjusted for health factors and lifestyle behaviors such as body mass index (BMI), alcohol consumption, smoking, physical activity, diabetes, hypertension and more.
Sleep per 24 hours was categorized into durations of six hours or less, seven to eight hours and nine or more hours.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Over approximately 15 years of follow-up, 49.4% of participants died.
Out of all participants, 16.7% died from heart-related causes and 32.6% died from non-heart-related causes.
Sleep impacts blood pressure, blood sugar regulation and inflammation, which all influence cardiovascular risk. (iStock)
After adjusting for all lifestyle factors, researchers found that sleeping nine or more hours was linked to a higher mortality risk, compared with sleeping seven to eight hours.
There was a 51% increased risk of all causes of death, a 53% increased risk of heart-related causes of death and a 50% increased risk of non-heart-related mortality.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
Sleep duration of six hours or less was significantly associated with non-heart-related death only in the least-adjusted model, and the connection weakened with further adjustment.

"Because the study is observational, it shows an association, not cause and effect. Long sleep may be a symptom of underlying problems like more advanced heart disease, depression, sleep apnea, or medication side effects, and the study couldn't fully account for those," Palinski-Wade said.
It's important to monitor heart health, which includes paying attention to sleep quality and quantity, registered dietitian Erin Palinski-Wade noted. (iStock)
The authors noted that their findings do not invalidate the negative cardiovascular effects of getting too little sleep.

"I'm not aware of a convincing biological mechanism by which extra hours of sleep damage the heart," Antony Chu, MD, a cardiologist and clinical assistant professor at Brown University’s Warren Alpert School of Medicine, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"What I see clinically is that patients sleep longer because something is pulling on their reserve: worsening heart failure, untreated obstructive or central sleep apnea, depression, sedating medications, anemia or frailty," Chu said.

Sleeping too much or too little are both potential red flags, Palinski-Wade noted, so it’s important for people to pay attention to how rested they feel rather than only focusing on the number of hours they slept.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Because the study only tested people with pre-existing heart conditions, it should not be used to suggest that prolonged sleep leads to heart disease in the general population, she added.
Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Social media users are eating huge amounts of carrots and shrimp for a natural tan
summary: Dr. Navin Arora says the viral carrot tan from eating carrots, tomatoes and shrimp is real but no substitute for sunscreen and basic sun safety.
story: Dermatologist Dr. Jody Levine joins 'Fox & Friends' to discuss critical sun safety topics during Wellness Week. Dr. Levine explains why a base tan offers minimal protection and compares different types of sunscreen and the protection they provide.
Some social media users are "carrotmaxxing," "tomatomaxxing" and "shrimpmaxxing," in the hopes of getting a sun-kissed glow that lasts them all winter long.

The trend, which calls for eating large quantities of carrots, tomatoes and shrimp, or taking supplements packed with their compounds, relies on carotenoids, natural pigments found in certain foods, the New York Post recently reported.

The outlet highlighted wellness creators promoting raw carrots as a way to get a "carrot tan," including one who said she no longer gets fake tans, and followed two Atlanta moms who said they take a daily carotenoid supplement for a "healthy glow."
COULD 'HUMANMAXXING' ACTUALLY HELP YOU LIVE LONGER? HERE'S WHAT EXPERTS SAY
The supplement they take is a blend of three carotenoid pigments: beta-carotene, lycopene and astaxanthin, the compounds that give carrots, tomatoes, shrimp and salmon their color.
Carrots contain beta-carotene, a pigment that can affect skin tone. (iStock)
Wellness influencer Lee Tilghman Pollis, meanwhile, recently said on Instagram that raw carrots have given her "the best skin of my life and I will die on this hill."

Another influencer went viral on TikTok for her carrot tan, telling followers that she no longer gets fake tans or stays out in the sun and instead eats three to four large carrots a day for several months to build up her tan.
DOCTOR REVEALS 4 HIDDEN HEALTH RISKS OF SPENDING TOO MUCH TIME INDOORS
Experts say the skin-color change is real and generally harmless, but it's no substitute for basic sun-safety measures.
Carotenoids in tomatoes, shrimp and salmon can also give foods their yellow, orange or red hues. (iStock)

"Beta-carotene, lycopene and astaxanthin are fat-soluble pigments, and when you eat a lot of them they build up in the outermost layer of the skin," Dr. Navin Arora, a board-certified dermatologist and medical director of Borealis Dermatology in New York, told Fox News Digital.
NEW CALIFORNIA LAW WILL RESTRICT SALES OF SOME MUSCLE-BUILDING SUPPLEMENTS TO MINORS
The buildup can create a yellow or orange tint, often first visible on the palms, soles and around the nose.

There is no reliable dose for achieving a cosmetic change, Arora said. Small studies have found visible changes after about six weeks of eating extra servings of fruits and vegetables, though results can vary. The color also fades gradually after a person cuts back, he noted.
Dermatologists warn that a carotenoid glow does not protect skin from UV exposure. (iStock)
That pigment buildup, known as carotenemia, is generally harmless, Arora said, but skin that turns yellow-orange without a dietary change should be evaluated by a health care professional.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The food trick does avoid skin damage caused by UV exposure, which also raises the risk of skin cancer and premature aging.
"The carotenoid glow involves no UV damage at all, but it also gives you no meaningful sun protection," Arora warned. "'Carrot color' is not a substitute for sunscreen."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Dermatologists also caution that carotenoid supplements taken for a tan may carry risks for certain people. (iStock)

Arora cautioned against taking high-dose carotenoid supplements for appearance, though. High-dose beta-carotene supplements have been linked to increased lung cancer risk in people who smoke or used to smoke, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
For people seeking a bronzed look, Arora recommends self-tanners, professional spray tans, bronzers or tinted sunscreen. He advises pairing them with broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher every day.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Eating a colorful, carotenoid-rich diet is great for your overall health," he said. "I’d treat the glow as a bonus, not the goal."
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Iconic MTV star turns 60, shares her no-guilt approach to fitness, food and aging well
summary: Daisy Fuentes shares her 20-minute strength training routine, menopause sleep tips and the guilt-free "anti-hustle era" that keeps her strong at 60.
story: As Daisy Fuentes turns 60, the TV personality and lifestyle entrepreneur has traded superficial beauty pressures for a low-key wellness routine — built on 20-minute workouts, a "magical" sleep trick and a guilt-free "anti-hustle era."
During her 1990s rise as an MTV icon and supermodel, Daisy Fuentes admitted that "being cute" was her top priority.
Now, as she enters her 60s, the TV personality and lifestyle entrepreneur has traded superficial beauty pressures for a more grounded approach to health.

Speaking with Fox News Digital, Fuentes, who is primarily based in Los Angeles, opened up about embracing a guilt-free "anti-hustle era" — sharing her 20-minute workouts, a "magical" sleep trick and the surprisingly simple habits that keep her rested and strong.
JENNIFER ANISTON’S SECRET TO STAYING FIT AT 57 STARTS WITH ONE SIMPLE WORKOUT ROUTINE
Fuentes’ health and wellness priorities have shifted a great deal in the decades since she started modeling and appearing on TV in her late teens and 20s, she shared.

"In that era, I was more focused on, how can I look better? How can I lose a few pounds to look better in certain clothes? It was very superficial. And as the years have passed, health and wellness has started to become an inside job," Fuentes said.
As Daisy Fuentes turns 60, the TV personality and lifestyle entrepreneur has traded superficial beauty pressures for a low-key wellness routine. (Daisy Fuentes Instagram/Celeste Canino)

"When you start realizing that most of your life has already happened, how you want to live your life now … becomes more about being present and being able to enjoy the time that you have left," she added.
LONGEVITY DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR AGING WELL, BEYOND PRICEY BIOHACKS
Amid the litany of longevity-focused tips and tricks circulating online, Fuentes said she strives to keep it simple and not be "obsessive" about health and wellness.
"On social media, depending on your algorithm, you can get bombarded and overwhelmed with all the [things] that you're supposed to be doing and not doing," she said.
Model and TV personality Daisy Fuentes poses for portraits around September 1993. (Getty Images)

"Yes, some of those things are smart … I do a lot of the things, but I also realized at a certain point that it's much more important to have fun, to be present, to not obsess, and to leave a little room for the unexpected."
Optimizing sleep
As Fuentes entered her 50s, she started to experience some sleep challenges, which she attributed to fluctuating hormones during menopause.

"Balancing out my hormones [and] going on HRT [hormone replacement therapy] helped tremendously," she said. "It got me feeling back to my old self, where the minute I got in bed, I would do a little scrolling and all of a sudden my eyes would start closing."
10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG

Although Fuentes admits that she breaks a few traditional "sleep hygiene" rules — such as scrolling on her phone in bed – she does wear red-light-blocking glasses and strives to keep her social media algorithm strictly positive.
Fuentes said she relies on what she describes as a total "sensory experience" to stay asleep, including wearing a silk eye mask.
Fuentes said she strives to keep it simple and not be "obsessive" about health and wellness. (Celeste Canino)
"Right as I'm going to sleep, I pop that mask on, and it's almost like magic," she said. "It does something to your brain. It relaxes you." She also uses an air purifier that provides white noise.
"Our room is set up for sleep," Fuentes said. "We don't hear anything, we don't see anything and it is a sensory experience … a routine that instantly prepares your mind for what it needs to do."
Moving through life
When it comes to fitness, Fuentes said she strives for consistency, but, above all, listens to her body.

A key component of her routine is strength training, which she does four or five times a week. "That doesn't mean it has to be long … I can do a full-body weight training in 20 minutes, and that's what's important to me right now," she said.
WOMEN WHO START COMMON HORMONE THERAPY IN THEIR 50S MAY HAVE 23% LOWER DEMENTIA RISK
Other mainstays of Fuentes’ fitness regimen include Pilates, walking and staying active outdoors. "That's what keeps me and my mind really feeling better," she said.
A key component of Fuentes' fitness routine is strength training, which she does four or five times a week. (iStock)
"Sometimes I get on a vibration plate with my weights and just do 15 minutes of that, doing a plank, doing some sit-ups on it, some squats — I just try to do whatever I can," Fuentes said.
"Some days I have more energy, some days I don't, and I don't beat myself up about it. I do what I feel like doing and as long as I'm doing something, I'm OK."
Eating for longevity

When it comes to nutrition, Fuentes’ biggest shifts over the last decade were driven by physical changes during menopause. Noticing stubborn weight gain around her midsection in her mid-50s, she said she scaled back to about two meals a day and eliminated mindless snacking.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"I try to make it very protein-based," she said. "I start my day with a coffee that already has 20 grams of protein in it ... And if I'm having a snack in the middle of the afternoon, it's going to be protein-packed yogurt with some nuts and berries."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

While Fuentes adopted a vegetarian, plant-based diet in her mid-40s, she emphasized that healthy eating doesn't require an "all-or-nothing" mindset, encouraging others to lean into more whole foods that match their lifestyle and preferences.
Embracing an ‘anti-hustle’ lifestyle
After decades of fast-paced working – both on and off-screen – Fuentes made a conscious decision in her late 40s to embrace a slower pace of life.
Fuentes shared her gratitude for being able to enjoy time with her husband, musician Richard Marx, whom she met in her mid-40s. (Getty Images)

"Ambition that never ends is something that I think needs to be adjusted as we flow through life," she said, adding that she no longer desires to "be out there and be chosen" the way she did in her 30s.

"I started embracing the fact that I am in this era of my life where I don't want to work like when I was 30 … and it's OK to feel proud of myself for what I have accomplished," she said. "I don't want to feel guilty for enjoying the fruits of my labor, for enjoying my life now."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

When it comes to decompressing, Fuentes said she recharges by spending quiet time in the home spaces she loves decorating. Some of her favorite ways to unwind include reading, having tea with a friend, sitting in her backyard or taking an hour-long walk.
"I don't want to feel guilty for enjoying the fruits of my labor, for enjoying my life now."
Fuentes shared her gratitude for being able to enjoy time with her husband, musician Richard Marx, whom she met in her mid-40s.

"Finding love and finding your person later in life made me feel so grateful to have the time to spend with him," she said. "Why would I want to pretend to be busy doing something when what really fills my heart is to be with him, to have fun, to do what I want to do right now?"
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While Fuentes acknowledged that she is in a "privileged" and fortunate position, she pointed out that she spent decades sacrificing to earn it.
Stepping into her "anti-hustle era" in her 50s and 60s, she said, is about questioning whether you are staying busy out of habit — or are ready to embrace a new, more fulfilling stage of life.

title: Jennifer Aniston’s secret to staying fit at 57 starts with one simple workout routine
summary: Jennifer Aniston trains three to four times a week with PVOLVE, and a trainer says consistency, plus added weight training, are key to her fitness success.
story: Melanie Ramos, PVOLVE trainer, reveals that Jennifer Aniston trains three to four times a week, focusing on consistency and incorporating more weight training.
At 57 years old, Jennifer Aniston seems to be defying the laws of aging — but it doesn’t come without hard work.
The "Friends" actress has been public about practicing PVOLVE, a functional fitness method grounded in movement longevity.

The workouts prioritize mobility and stability through twisting and reaching motions that translate directly to everyday life. Combining sculpting, cardio and weight training, the method is designed to build muscle mass and support bone density.
10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG
According to PVOLVE trainer Melanie Ramos, what keeps Aniston looking and feeling her best isn't a specific workout buzzword, it's consistency.

"She's very consistent," Ramos told Fox News Digital. "She trains about three to four times a week doing PVOLVE, and she trains in all our modalities. … She specifically is adding a lot more weight training into her routine."
Jennifer Aniston is pictured with her trainer Dani Coleman, VP of Training at PVOLVE. (Instagram @dani_bcoleman)
As people age, especially women, muscle mass begins to decline, according to Ramos, who serves as lead trainer at PVOLVE Soho in New York City.
"So, I think for [Aniston], the consistency and just adding that extra weight training really helps her look amazing," she said.
WANT TO AGE BETTER? RESEARCHERS SAY 4-MINUTE ROUTINE MAY HELP PREVENT DANGEROUS FALLS
According to research published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, only about 20% of women regularly engage in strength training, with many opting for aerobic exercise instead.
While walking offers major benefits for overall health, pairing cardio with simple resistance work can lead to significantly stronger heart and longevity outcomes.
Jennifer Aniston, pictured in 2025, has been adding a lot more weight training into her routine, a PVOLVE trainer shared. (Rodin Eckenroth/FilmMagic)

Rather than feeling pressured to commit to a full-hour workout to see results, Ramos advised simply getting started, adding, "Something that [Aniston] really prioritizes is even just getting 15 minutes of movement. "
Starting with "baby steps" — aiming for at least three workouts per week, even if they're short — will help you feel "like you can achieve the goals you want," the trainer said.
YOUR WALKING SPEED MAY HOLD A CLUE TO HOW LONG YOU’LL LIVE, STUDY SUGGESTS

"And then build more of that lifestyle habit where it feels that you need that movement every day," Ramos continued. "Movement is a part of life, and as we age, we have to look at how we're moving our body."
Exercises for mobility and stability can help aging adults maintain balance and independence, the trainer said. (iStock)
Prioritizing strength training and gradually increasing muscular load helps build lean mass and improve bone density, according to the trainer.

As the body naturally stiffens with age, Ramos noted, targeted mobility and stability exercises become essential for maintaining balance and independence.
3 core pillars of Aniston’s routine
To show how simple it is to get started, Ramos demonstrated three signature moves from Aniston’s routine — targeting mobility, strength and stability, using just a pair of dumbbells.

Bending the knees deeper with each curl will target more leg strength, while also toning the upper body and increasing arm strength.

Dropping one dumbbell, stand in the same wide-leg position and hold the weight with two hands.
Bring the dumbbell over the right shoulder as if slinging a laundry bag.

Bend the front knee for extra leg strength.

Standing in a high lunge, hold the dumbbell in one hand at the shoulder. Hold the other arm straight out to the side.
Bend the knees to lunge deeper, then straighten. While coming up from the lunge, press the dumbbell up to the ceiling.
Getting into a deeper lunge will activate the quad muscles, while the overhead shoulder press targets the upper body.

Modification: Hold the weight with two hands, tucking the elbows in and bringing it up in an uppercut punch style.

title: New drug combo shrinks tumors in most patients facing aggressive cancer type
summary: The pancreatic cancer pill daraxonrasib shrank tumors in 60.7% of patients when paired with chemotherapy, and 8.2% saw tumors vanish on scans.
story: Pancreatic cancer treatment received a major boost, and Dr. Monique Yohanan analyzed clinical trial results for Rasonque, a breakthrough drug from Revolution Medicines.

Pairing an experimental pill with standard chemotherapy shrank tumors or halted growth in most patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, according to early clinical trial results presented Friday at a major international cancer conference.

The findings, shared at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium in Barcelona, come from a phase ½ trial testing a daily oral medication called daraxonrasib, along with two standard intravenous chemotherapy drugs, gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel.
The trial focused on 61 patients whose pancreatic cancer had already spread to other organs and who had not yet received treatment for their advanced disease.
PANCREATIC CANCER PATIENT BEN SASSE SEES 'MASSIVE' TUMOR REDUCTION WITH EXPERIMENTAL NEW DRUG
Pancreatic cancer is notoriously difficult to treat because more than half of patients are diagnosed after the disease has already spread, research shows.

In major clinical trials for metastatic pancreatic cancer, chemotherapy alone shrinks tumors in about 23% to 42% of patients, but the disease typically begins growing again after five to six months, and most patients survive between 8 and 11 months.
Combining an experimental daily pill called daraxonrasib with standard chemotherapy shrank tumors or stopped cancer growth in 90.2% of patients with untreated, advanced pancreatic cancer. (iStock)
According to National Cancer Institute data, only about 3% of patients with distant-stage disease live five years past diagnosis.

In the new study, which tracked patients for a median follow-up of 18 months, tumors shrank in 60.7% of cases, including 8.2% where they disappeared entirely on scans. Overall, the combination stopped tumor growth in 90.2% of participants.
FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE

Patients went a median of 12.8 months before their cancer worsened, almost double the timeframe typically seen with standard chemotherapy, and 76.6% were still alive at the one-year mark, the study found.

"We are now seeing not only substantial tumor shrinkages, including complete responses, but also durable disease control, with median progression-free survival exceeding one year," study lead Dr. Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, said in a press release.
Most side effects, including rash, diarrhea, fatigue and low blood cell counts, were manageable with standard care, and only 5% of patients stopped treatment due to daraxonrasib. (iStock)

More than 90% of pancreatic cancers are driven by a faulty gene called RAS, which allows tumors to keep growing. Daraxonrasib is designed to turn off that growth signal, something scientists long thought was impossible to fix with medication.

Dr. Elena Garralda, chair of the symposium and co-director of the clinical research program at the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology in Spain, who was not involved in the research, said the results show that RAS-targeted drugs can be combined with existing treatments at the start of treatment to potentially achieve longer-lasting benefits.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Side effects included rash, diarrhea, fatigue and low blood cell counts linked to chemotherapy, most of which were manageable with standard care.
Only 5% of patients stopped treatment because of side effects tied to daraxonrasib.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Researchers emphasized that the findings carry some limitations.

Because this was an early-phase, single-group study involving 61 people, all participants received the experimental combination. Without a direct comparison group of patients receiving standard chemotherapy alone, doctors cannot yet confirm how much better the new regimen performs or whether it definitively extends overall survival.
Researchers are now running a larger, randomized Phase 3 trial to directly compare the new treatment against standard chemotherapy. (iStock)

The findings also apply strictly to metastatic pancreatic cancer, even though RAS mutations drive several other cancers, including certain lung, colorectal and gynecological cancers. Separate studies would be needed to test whether the combination works in those diseases.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The trial was funded by Revolution Medicines, the California-based developer of daraxonrasib.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

To determine whether these early findings translate into a durable survival benefit, researchers have launched a larger, randomized Phase 3 trial, called RASolute-303, which directly compares daraxonrasib — both on its own and combined with chemotherapy — against standard chemotherapy alone.

title: Mysterious illness tied to breast implants shares symptoms with MS, but key questions remain
summary: Christina Applegate suspects her breast implants could be behind joint pain and other symptoms, saying she plans to discuss it with her doctors.
story: Diana Zuckerman, Ph.D., president of the National Center for Health Research and a breast implant safety advocate in Washington, D.C., said breast cancer illness has been taken more seriously in recent years.
Weeks after Christina Applegate revealed she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS), the actress has shared a suspicion that her breast implants could be to blame for her symptoms.

On a Nov. 10 episode of the podcast "MeSsy," which she co-hosts with actress and MS advocate Jamie-Lynn Sigler, Applegate — who underwent a double mastectomy in 2008 after a breast cancer diagnosis — said she believes she is overdue to have her implants replaced.
Applegate also said she recently saw a study suggesting that implant-related symptoms could resemble MS.
CHRISTINA APPLEGATE'S MS MISDIAGNOSIS AFTER 5 YEARS OF TREATMENT EXPOSES ALARMING MEDICAL REALITY
"And I swear, over the last five years or whatever, I thought, ‘What if they’re leaking, and they’re like poisoning me?’" she said.
Applegate said she plans to discuss the possibility with her doctors. She did not say that her implants had been confirmed as the cause.

Weeks after Christina Applegate (pictured in 2022) revealed she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, the actress has shared a suspicion that her breast implants could be to blame for her symptoms. (AFP via Getty Images)
Some of her symptoms have included joint pain, difficulty lifting her right arm and pain that can make it hard to get out of bed, she shared during the episode.
"I don’t know what’s going on in my joints, but I can’t move my right shoulder at all now," she said. "I can’t lift my arm."
NYC MARATHON RUNNER, 24, DIES JUST 2 MILES FROM FINISH LINE AFTER SENDING DAD CHILLING TEXTS
Other possible conditions that could contribute to these symptoms include rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and Lyme disease, Applegate said.

"We’re going into square one, just doing some testing and going one by one [through] the sister diseases to MS," she added. "It’s overwhelming because there are so many different things that could be going on and this pain stuff."
What is breast implant illness?

Diana Zuckerman, Ph.D., president of the National Center for Health Research and a breast implant safety advocate in Washington, D.C., said that breast implant illness hasn’t always gotten a lot of attention, but is being taken more seriously in recent years.

"It’s a range of symptoms, and not everybody has the same symptoms," she told Fox News Digital. "And some of them are pretty common, such as joint pain or chronic fatigue. Some women talk about feeling like they've had the flu for [months]."
Research has shown that in some cases, if the implants are taken out, women recover "almost miraculously and immediately and dramatically," a health expert said. (iStock)
Brain fog, memory issues, anxiety, insomnia, muscle pain and weakness are additional symptoms that could potentially overlap with various viruses or conditions.

Women with breast implant illness tend to have many symptoms all at once, Zuckerman said. "They're often very young women who are in their 20s, and suddenly they feel like they're in their 50s — that's how they describe it."
Research has shown that in some cases, if the implants are taken out, women recover "almost miraculously and immediately and dramatically," Zuckerman said.
A difficult diagnosis
Jonathan Kaplan, M.D., a board-certified plastic surgeon at Pacific Heights Plastic Surgery in San Francisco, agrees that breast implant illness symptoms are real.

"While patients may have abnormal blood tests to support their concerns about having some type of illness, these lab tests would not predict ahead of time if the patient is more or less likely to have issues if they choose to get implants," he told Fox News Digital.
"The cause could be due to breast implants, but the only way to confirm that is to remove the implants and see if the patient improves."

For those experiencing symptoms such as fatigue, joint or muscle pain, and cognitive concerns, Kaplan recommends starting by looking for other treatable causes, which might include MS or effects of medications.

"The cause could be due to breast implants, but the only way to confirm that is to remove the implants and see if the patient improves," he said. "If they do not, then they may have unnecessarily undergone a surgical procedure that did not benefit them."
MYSTERIOUS DISEASE SENDING YOUNG, HEALTHY TEXAS WORKERS INTO KIDNEY FAILURE
For women who are considering explant surgery, Kaplan asks them how they would feel if they removed the implants and the symptoms persist.

"If they've run out of other options or causes of their illness, they may feel like it is worth the risk of having a procedure even if it doesn't help their illness," he said. "There's no evidence at this time that MS would be affected by the presence or absence of implants."
In 2021, the FDA issued strict new labeling rules requiring a boxed warning and a mandatory patient decision checklist for all breast implants. (iStock)
Kaplan shared that he once had a patient who received breast implants and then several years later experienced fatigue and had abnormal bloodwork suggestive of kidney failure.

"Once she removed her implants, she felt better and labs returned to normal," he said. "But we couldn't have gotten any lab ahead of time that would have predicted her risk of breast implant-associated illness."
What the research shows

Patricia McGuire, M.D., a St. Louis-based plastic surgeon and chair of the Breast Implant Emergency Task Force, noted that over 100 symptoms have been reported by patients in association with breast implant illness.
"They have no abnormal labs or physical findings, and there is no diagnostic criteria," she told Fox News Digital. "It is a diagnosis of exclusion and is not a currently recognized illness."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Symptoms can occur with all types of implants, she noted – silicone gel, saline, smooth and textured implants, by all manufacturers.

"We do not know the cause," McGuire said. "The suggestions have been heavy metals from the implants entering the body, bacterial biofilms, fungal infections, allergic reactions, immune response to a foreign body and neuropsychiatric conditions."
"We also know that some patients may get better with implant removal."

In a prospective, blinded study that McGuire co-led with Dr. Caroline Glicksman, researchers found no biological differences — such as heavy metals, bacteria or inflammatory blood markers — between women reporting breast implant illness and asymptomatic control groups.

Instead, the research revealed that while patients experienced genuine symptom relief after implant removal, the condition was strongly linked to elevated anxiety, somatic symptom patterns and a heavy reliance on social media for medical information, she said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"To be honest, we were disappointed that we did not find an easily reversible cause, or that we did not find a blood value that could be used to make a diagnosis or point to the cause of symptoms in these patients," McGuire added.
"We have a couple of pilot studies in the works, hoping we can find something definitive."
What patients should know
In 2021, the FDA issued strict new labeling rules requiring a boxed warning and a mandatory patient decision checklist for all breast implants.
The warning explicitly lists systemic symptoms, such as fatigue, memory loss, rash, "brain fog" and joint pain, and notes that symptoms may resolve after removal.

For those experiencing symptoms such as fatigue, joint or muscle pain, and cognitive concerns, a surgeon recommends starting by looking for other treatable causes, which might include MS or effects of medications. (iStock)

Breast implants are not considered lifetime devices. The FDA recommends routine MRI or ultrasound screenings starting five to six years after surgery (and every two to three years after) to check for "silent" ruptures.
However, implants do not have a strict 10-year expiration date if they are intact and the patient is asymptomatic.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Anyone with breast implants who experiences symptoms should undergo a full medical work-up to rule out reversible causes before having surgery, McGuire advised.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"For a patient considering implant removal, they should see a board-certified plastic surgeon who has experience in breast surgery," she added.
Fox News Digital reached out to implant manufacturers requesting comment.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Popular alcoholic drinks linked to sudden kidney damage in 14-year study
summary: Beer and hard liquor drinkers face a sharply higher risk of acute kidney injury, a UK Biobank study finds, while red and white wine showed no such link.
story: Josh Gowin explains how research has shifted the understanding of alcohol's health risks, including its association with reduced brain volume, as drinking habits and social norms continue to change.

People who regularly drink beer or hard liquor face a significantly higher risk of sudden kidney damage than light drinkers, while wine drinkers do not show the same increased risk, according to a large British study.
Researchers at Anglia Ruskin University analyzed health and lifestyle data from 250,791 adult drinkers in the UK Biobank database, tracking them for an average of 14 years.
Over that time, 10,335 participants developed acute kidney injury, a serious condition in which the kidneys suddenly stop filtering waste from the blood properly.
IS DRINKING EVERY DAY ALCOHOLISM? EXPERTS EXPLAIN WHERE CULTURE AND ADDICTION COLLIDE
The study, published in the journal Scientific Reports, challenges a longstanding medical assumption that alcohol harms the kidneys mainly as a secondary consequence of liver disease.
The elevated risk among beer and liquor drinkers continued even after researchers considered liver disease and a wide range of other health and lifestyle factors.

The elevated risk for beer and liquor drinkers persisted even after accounting for liver disease, suggesting alcohol may damage the kidneys directly through inflammation rather than solely as a secondary effect of liver harm. (iStock)

"Acute kidney injury is a serious condition that can lead to chronic kidney disease, kidney failure and an increased risk of dying early," lead author Rudolph Schutte, an associate professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Anglia Ruskin University, said in a university news release.

"While alcohol has traditionally been linked with kidney injury through its impact on the liver, our research suggests that spirits and beer may contribute directly to kidney damage through inflammatory pathways."
HEAVY DRINKING SURGES AMONG AMERICANS IN ONE AGE GROUP AS OTHER GENERATIONS CUT BACK
To compare drinking habits, the researchers divided participants into three groups based on their average weekly consumption of each type of alcohol.
In the U.K., one unit of alcohol equals 8 grams of pure alcohol — a little more than half of a standard U.S. shot of liquor or about half a pint of lower-strength beer.
"Acute kidney injury is a serious condition that can lead to chronic kidney disease, kidney failure and an increased risk of dying early."

Among liquor drinkers, those in the lowest consumption group drank an average of 1.22 units per week. Compared with that group, people who averaged 2.69 units per week were 8.1% more likely to develop acute kidney injury.
Those in the highest tier, averaging 8.73 units per week, had a 25.5% higher risk.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Beer drinkers showed a similar, though smaller, pattern. Compared with light beer drinkers averaging 2.67 units per week, people who drank an average of 6.81 units had a 5.7% higher risk of acute kidney injury.
Those in the highest group, averaging 23.6 units per week, faced a 14.8% higher risk
Regular consumption of beer or hard liquor is linked to a significantly higher risk of sudden kidney damage, whereas wine shows no significant overall association. (iStock)
Researchers found no significant link between red or white wine consumption and a higher risk of acute kidney injury overall.
The authors noted that higher levels of internal inflammation appeared to drive the increased risk seen with other drinks.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"The results provide important population-level evidence supporting laboratory research that has suggested alcohol can directly affect the kidneys," Schutte said.
Beer drinkers saw a smaller increase in risk, rising by 5.7% at an average of 6.81 units per week and 14.8% at 23.6 units per week compared to light beer drinkers. (iStock)
Because the study is observational, it can only identify links between drinking habits and kidney injury, and cannot prove that beer or liquor directly caused the damage.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The authors also warned that the findings do not prove wine protects the kidneys, noting that drinking above 14 units per week, the U.K.’s recommended limit, was tied to higher risk across all drink types, including wine.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Additionally, participants relied on memory to report their average weekly alcohol intake, which can lead to inaccurate estimates or underreporting.
The study also only included adults ages 40 to 69, meaning the results may not apply to younger or older people.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' mania comes with serious health risks, doctors warn
summary: Experts warn Grand Theft Auto VI marathon sessions can trigger eye strain, sleep deprivation and problematic gaming amid the PlayStation 5 launch.
story: Psychotherapist Jonathan Alpert addresses concerns surrounding major video game releases, noting that while violent games do not cause real-world crime, excessive screen time can strain health and relationships.

As millions of players prepare for the long-awaited release of "Grand Theft Auto VI," mental health and medical experts are warning that marathon gaming sessions, skipped sleep and obsessive playing habits could have physical and psychological effects.
The latest installment in the blockbuster franchise launches Thursday, Nov. 19, on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, according to New York-based maker Rockstar Games.
"Grand Theft Auto VI" is an action-adventure game set in the fictional state of Leonida, which includes Vice City. Players follow a story while exploring the game’s world and taking on missions.
SKIPPING SLEEP MAY PACK ON POUNDS FASTER THAN YOU THINK, NEW STUDY FINDS
The release is prompting questions about how much time players may devote to the game — including during the workweek.
According to a survey of 1,000 full-time employed U.S. gamers conducted by gaming and esports media company GameSquare, 10% plan to skip work for the game’s launch.
The latest installment in "Grand Theft Auto" launches Thursday, Nov. 19, on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, according to New York-based maker Rockstar Games. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)

Another 30% are considering taking time off, and 36% said they would call in sick rather than use planned vacation days. Meanwhile, 42% expect to be less productive at work because of the release, according to the survey.
TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME MAY TRIGGER LASTING BRAIN DELAYS, TOP HEALTH OFFICIAL WARNS

Jonathan Alpert, a psychotherapist based in New York and Washington, D.C., compared the excitement around major game releases to overnight lines for new smartphones, saying fans want to be part of the moment.
DOCTOR REVEALS 4 HIDDEN HEALTH RISKS OF SPENDING TOO MUCH TIME INDOORS

"Video games and social media can be a great distraction from the stress of real life and relationships, but it shouldn't become real life," Alpert, author of "Therapy Nation," told Fox News Digital. "In other words, it shouldn't dominate. It should just be an escape."
Health risks of extended play

"Grand Theft Auto" is an open-world game, meaning players can freely explore a large virtual environment rather than follow a set path from one level to the next. Cleveland Clinic says that freedom, along with the game’s fast-paced action and rewards, can make it hard to stop playing.
"It shouldn't dominate. It should just be an escape."
That constant stream of stimulation can raise a player’s threshold for excitement, making ordinary offline interactions feel flat by comparison, according to Alpert.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Pulling an all-nighter to explore Vice City can also take a toll on the brain. According to the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute, sleep deficiency impairs concentration, slows reaction times and makes it harder to regulate emotions.

While a single late night is unlikely to cause lasting harm, Alpert said, repeated sleep loss can leave players more vulnerable to anxiety, irritability and difficulty completing basic tasks at school or work.
Sitting at a screen for eight or more hours can trigger neck and back pain, as well as digital eye strain, experts warn. (iStock)

Extended gaming sessions can take a physical toll. Sitting at a screen for eight or more hours can contribute to neck and back pain, repetitive-motion injuries and eyestrain, according to Mayo Clinic.
Research cited by the clinic found that eyestrain affects up to 56% of competitive gamers. Symptoms can include headaches and blurred vision.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Prolonged, uninterrupted sitting can reduce blood flow to the brain and legs, while also affecting blood-vessel function.
"People can get sick if they are sitting at a computer for eight or more hours a day playing games," Alpert cautioned.
Signs of problematic play

The American Psychiatric Association lists nine proposed symptoms of internet gaming disorder, a condition included in the DSM-5-TR for further study. A proposed diagnosis requires five or more of the following symptoms within a year.

Becoming preoccupied with gamingFeeling irritable, anxious or sad when unable to playNeeding to spend more time gaming to feel satisfiedMaking repeated unsuccessful attempts to cut backLosing interest in other activitiesContinuing to play despite problemsLying to family members or others about time spent gamingUsing games to escape or relieve a negative moodJeopardizing or losing a significant relationship, job or educational opportunity because of gaming

"When I look at addictions or people spending too much time online, I look at how [it] has impacted relationships, their work, school, family relations, their health and their finances," Alpert said. "So, when we start to see those suffering, there's a problem."

Adolescents and young adults may be more vulnerable to problematic gaming, while anxiety and depression can co-occur with it, according to Cleveland Clinic.
Ensuring safe play
To participate in launch week in a healthy way, experts recommend setting the following boundaries.

Take regular movement breaks: Stand, walk or stretch for at least five minutes every hour to restore circulation and ease muscle tension, Alpert suggests.Set firm time limits: Alpert advises parents to keep consoles out of teenagers’ bedrooms and limit play to an hour or two after homework is finished. For adults, he recommends prioritizing work and relationships over late-night sessions.Create a mental buffer: After logging off, take a brief breather before jumping back into daily responsibilities.
Take regular movement breaks: Stand, walk or stretch for at least five minutes every hour to restore circulation and ease muscle tension, Alpert suggests.

Set firm time limits: Alpert advises parents to keep consoles out of teenagers’ bedrooms and limit play to an hour or two after homework is finished. For adults, he recommends prioritizing work and relationships over late-night sessions.
Create a mental buffer: After logging off, take a brief breather before jumping back into daily responsibilities.
"You almost have to do a gut check and a reset and remind yourself that what you just saw is fantasy and what you're experiencing now is reality," Alpert added.
Sitting at a screen for eight or more hours can contribute to neck and back pain, repetitive-motion injuries and eyestrain, according to Mayo Clinic. (iStock)
The psychotherapist added that concerns about gaming’s physical effects should be separated from claims that violent games lead to real-world violence.

"Millions of people play violent video games, and they don’t go out there and commit crimes," he said, adding that there is no evidence linking gameplay to real-life violence.

title: Obama judge's Omar warrant unsealing directly contradicts his own decision in Trump case, DOJ says
summary: Justice Department lawyers say Judge James Boasberg contradicted his ruling by unsealing search warrant records in Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C. case.
story: Former Acting ICE Director Jonathan Fahey joins 'Fox & Friends' to discuss the newly unsealed search warrant records revealing a decades-long federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.

Government lawyers argue unsealing documents related to the warrant used to search the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is at odds with a ruling made by the same Obama-appointed federal judge in a high-profile case against President Donald Trump.

Lawyers for the Justice Department pleaded in the filings with Judge James Boasberg, who has frequently found himself at odds with the Trump administration, not to unseal search warrant materials in the Omar case due to the ongoing nature of the investigation,.
The DOJ also argued it has not yet finished executing that search warrant.

Still, Boasberg ordered last week the redacted documents to be released. The DOJ submitted their redacted and the materials were made public Monday night. The only document Boasberg ordered to remain sealed was the government's affidavit presented to a magistrate court judge in order to secure the search warrant.

James Boasberg, incoming chief judge of the US District Court, in Washington, DC, US, on Monday, March 13, 2023. Boasberg, who starts a seven-year term as chief judge on March 17, will oversee the court's secret grand jury proceedings, including pending and future legal fights related to Special Counsel Jack Smith’s probes of Trump, among other duties. mong other duties. (Valerie Plesch/Bloomberg via Getty)
'RADICAL LEFT LUNATIC' JUDGE TRUMP WANTED IMPEACHED TAKES UP ILHAN OMAR WARRANT FIGHT

"Just a few years ago, Chief Judge Boasberg ruled that search warrant proceedings and related documents should not be made open to the public while an investigation is ongoing," the DOJ said in an emergency ex parte brief in opposition to the unsealing.
"The Chief Judge was merely echoing many other courts—like the D.C. Circuit, the Ninth Circuit, the Fourth Circuit, and others when he said that," the brief continued.

The case to which the DOJ referred — where Boasberg ruled that search warrant documents should remain under seal during active investigations — was none other than Special Counsel Jack Smith's probe into Trump for alleged election interference after his 2020 presidential loss, and for the alleged retention of classified documents.
Trump was indicted in both of those investigations. All the charges were eventually dropped.
Judge James Boasberg, President Donald Trump (Valerie Plesch, Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
ILHAN OMAR RECORDS SHOW JUDGE, DOJ OFFICIALS DEBATING BEFORE RAID OF HOME

In that case, like the Omar case, media organizations sought to unseal a warrant related to the search. Specifically, the press wanted to view a warrant obtained by Smith related to Twitter's records associated with Trump's account, @realDonaldTrump.
Boasberg's tune was much different in that case, when, like in the Omar case, the government asked him to keep the warrant under seal due to the ongoing nature of the case.
Notably, Trump had already been indicted when Boasberg ruled that the records needed to remain sealed while Omar has not been indicted.
"Ultimately, the undeniable need to protect an ongoing criminal investigation tips the balance toward the Government’s request to continue sealing," Boasberg wrote in his Nov. 29, 2023 ruling.
The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on the apparent u-turn from the judge.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is denying that federal agents have told her what she is under investigation for and speaks to Fox News Digital about the status of her items that were seized after her Washington, D.C., home was raided Oct. 12, 2026. (REUTERS/Elizabeth Frantz)

In the Omar case, government lawyers said they weren't opposed to releasing the documents at an appropriate future date, but did not want them unsealed while the case is ongoing. Boasberg didn't find that argument compelling.
But in the case against Trump, he did.
"There may yet come a time when press access becomes appropriate, but at present the Application is a premature bid for sensitive information pertaining to an active investigation," he wrote in 2023.
Throughout his 2023 ruling in favor of the government's bid to keep the warrant in the Trump case sealed, Boasberg continually noted the government's ability to keep warrants under seal.
ILHAN OMAR HUDDLES WITH HER DC-BASED LAWYERS DURING HER FIRST DAY BACK ON CAPITOL HILL AMID FEDERAL PROBES

He said in a second instance: "When it comes to an active investigation, the Government 'has always been able to restrict access to warrant materials by requesting a sealing order, which courts have granted freely upon a showing that a given criminal investigation requires secrecy,'" Boasberg's ruling said.
In response to the media's claim that the First Amendment should be a deciding factor in unsealing the Trump warrant, Boasberg disagreed.

"The historical practice is somewhat muddled, but it suggests that the First Amendment does not open search warrants and related documents to public examination when an investigation is ongoing. Search-warrant applications traditionally have been filed ex parte and thus out of the public’s view."

The DOJ confirmed in a brief statement to Fox News Digital on Tuesday that the characterization that Boasberg contradicted himself in unsealing the Omar documents "is accurate and a point we have made in our court filings."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

One issue distinguishing Boasberg's ruling in the 2023 Trump case from the Omar case is the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause, which shields lawmakers from certain government intrusions into their legislative work.

In the Omar case, the Justice Department argued that searching her home did not involve those protections. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh disagreed and required safeguards for potentially privileged materials.

Boasberg later questioned why the legal arguments over those constitutional protections should remain sealed when sensitive investigative details could be redacted. He nevertheless agreed to keep the government's warrant affidavit sealed to protect the ongoing investigation.

Boasberg has also faced scrutiny over investigative secrecy during the Biden-era Arctic Frost probe, when he signed nondisclosure orders tied to subpoenas for Republican lawmakers' phone records. Unlike the Omar and Trump rulings, those orders restricted telecommunications companies from revealing the subpoenas rather than deciding whether court documents should be made public. Court officials have said Boasberg may not have known lawmakers' records were involved.
The District Court for the District of Columbia declined to comment. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia did not return a request for comment.

Omar's home was raided in the early morning hours of Oct. 12, 2026. Fox News Digital confirmed that the investigators are probing whether Omar or her father fraudulently filled out her citizenship paperwork, though the full scope of the investigation remains under wraps.

The unsealing of last night's documents revealed that investigators are seeking evidence dating back as far as 1980, and that investigators believe Omar committed "crimes over decades— beginning long before she was ever in Congress."
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Trump pauses turkey pardon to salute US troops guarding Strait of Hormuz: 'Watch over and protect'
summary: President Donald Trump paused the White House turkey pardon to thank U.S. troops enforcing what he called the greatest naval blockade against Iran.
story: President Donald Trump thanked U.S. service members enforcing the naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz during Tuesday’s annual White House Thanksgiving turkey pardoning ceremony, asserting no Iranian ships have gotten through and vowing Tehran will never obtain a nuclear weapon.

President Donald Trump paused Tuesday's annual White House Thanksgiving turkey pardoning ceremony to offer a special tribute and thanks to U.S. service members defending the Strait of Hormuz and enforcing a naval blockade against Iran.

Speaking from the White House South Lawn during the 79th National Thanksgiving Turkey presentation, Trump thanked American troops deployed overseas and praised those working to prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
"We want to say a special thank you to them, the people that are guarding the strait know or the blockade we call it," Trump said. "It’s a blockade, the greatest naval blockade in history."
TRUMP DARES IRAN TO BREACH US PORT BLOCKADE AS TEHRAN REPORTEDLY READIES 14 OIL TANKERS

President Donald Trump speaks prior to pardoning the National Thanksgiving Turkey during a ceremony on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Trump asserted that the U.S. maritime cordon has stopped every Iranian vessel from passing through since its establishment, save for a brief pause earlier in the standoff.

"Not one Iranian ship has gotten through to the blockade since we established it, other than we had a little moratorium. And we learned that you can’t trust them," Trump said. "But not one ship from Iran has gotten through. Our naval blockade is the most incredible naval blockade, probably in the history of the world. It’s amazing."
IRANIAN ‘GHOST FLEET’ FILMED EVADING US BLOCKADE EN ROUTE TO CHINA, UANI SAYS

President Donald Trump grants a presidential pardon to Freedom during the 79th annual National Thanksgiving Turkey Presentation on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

Trump also contended that U.S. forces have severely degraded Iran's conventional military capabilities and restored oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to levels higher than before the conflict began.
The U.S. naval blockade targeting vessels entering and leaving Iranian ports began in April amid the Strait of Hormuz crisis and resumed in July following a temporary pause.
Before returning to the holiday ceremony, Trump offered a Thanksgiving prayer for deployed U.S. troops and expressed pride in the country.

President Donald Trump, center, pardons Freedom the turkey as, from left, Deans Gap Farm co-owner Scott Rightsell, National Turkey Federation chairwoman Christy Puffenbarger, first lady Melania Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., look on during the 79th annual National Thanksgiving Turkey Presentation on the South Lawn of the White House. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"And we send them all our best wishes, Thanksgiving, and is very special. It’s a very special time for me for a lot of reasons," Trump said. "And I ask God to watch over and protect all of our military and all of our people. I’m so proud of our people, and I’m so proud to be your president because we’ve never had a time like this."

Following his remarks, Trump pardoned this year's National Thanksgiving Turkeys, Freedom and Feathers — though Feathers briefly ran into the bushes during the presentation — before sending them to retire at Texas A&M University.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Kamala Harris' former political mentor and boyfriend delivers stinging warning about 2028 comeback
summary: Willie Brown says Kamala Harris is "not a communicator" and doesn't want her to run in 2028, as Pete Buttigieg and Gavin Newsom eye the Democratic primary.
story: Tyrus and Ryan return for another round of News or Noise on Planet Tyrus, putting bizarre studies, viral animal headlines, and Kamala Harris’s brutal 2028 straw poll numbers to the test. Can Tyrus spot the real news from Ryan’s fabricated headlines, including a shameless New York Giants Super Bowl trap?
Willie Brown, a longtime California Democrat and a power broker in the state party, said former Vice President Kamala Harris lacks the communication skills needed to run for president again in 2028.
"She’s not a communicator," Brown said in an interview with Tara Palmeri, an independent journalist.
"No Baptist preacher flavor in her soul," he added.
Although Harris remains one of the country’s most recognizable Democratic figures, Brown’s skepticism comes from a longtime political ally and casts doubt on her potential candidacy.
DEMOCRATS SHY AWAY FROM QUESTIONS ON WHETHER HARRIS SHOULD RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028

Kamala Harris, former vice president and 2024 presidential candidate, speaks with Al Sharpton during the National Action Network (NAN) Convention in New York, April 10, 2026. (Angelina Katsanis/AP Photo)
"I’m sorry that she even thinks about running for president. I don’t want her to run," Brown said.
"She’s reached the highest electoral level for any woman in America," he added, referring to her post as President Joe Biden’s vice president.

Brown, who once served as San Francisco mayor and California state Assembly speaker, has a long history with Harris. Early in her career, he appointed her to the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board and then the Medical Assistance Commission.
The two were also romantically involved between 1994 and 1995.
Brown, in a San Francisco Chronicle op-ed, openly discussed their relationship and his role in her political career in an article titled, "Sure, I dated Kamala Harris. So what? "
GAVIN NEWSOM SAYS HE WON'T RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 IF KAMALA HARRIS RUNS

Former Mayor, Willie Brown laughs with District Attorney Kamala Harris at the reception before the rededication ceremony for Twenty-First Century Academy in 2005. (Carlos Avila Gonzalez/The San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images)
"Yes, we dated. It was more than 20 years ago. Yes, I may have influenced her career by appointing her to two state commissions when I was Assembly speaker," Brown wrote.

"And I certainly helped with her first race for district attorney in San Francisco. I have also helped the careers of House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Gov. Gavin Newsom, Sen. Dianne Feinstein and a host of other politicians," he added.
Representatives for Harris did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital about Brown’s comments about her prospects for 2028.
Several other Democrats have already hinted at their own interest in a 2028 bid, crowding the potential field.

Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., a top progressive in the House of Representatives, has hinted at a run. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg has said he is "inclined" to run, and California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans to decide on a presidential bid at the beginning of the new year.
DEMOCRATS DEBATE KAMALA HARRIS 2028 RUN AS SURROGATE SAYS PARTY WANTS TO 'MOVE ON' FROM 2024 LOSS

California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris both said in separate media interviews that they're keeping their options open for potential 2028 presidential runs. (Patrick T. Fallon/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Harris has not officially announced plans for 2028, though she chose not to run for California governor last year, keeping her options open for a possible presidential bid. In April, she said in a CNN interview that she had not made up her mind.

title: CIA hit by cyber breach that exposed unclassified data on intelligence analysis network: sources
summary: Sources confirm a cyber breach hit the CIA, exposing unclassified data on a network used to analyze open-source intelligence as the FBI weighs in.
story: Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin has the latest on a cybersecurity breach involving an unclassified system on 'The Story.'
A cyber breach exposed unclassified information on a CIA network last week, the same day the FBI was hit by a cyberattack on a database used by law enforcement agencies across the country.
Multiple sources told Fox News that the CIA, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the FBI were breached on the same day.
The New York Times first reported that the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence discovered the breach.
FBI PROBES SECOND CYBERATTACK IN MONTHS AS HACKERS BREACH KEY CRIME DATABASE, SOURCES SAY
A cyber breach hit the CIA the same day the FBI last week. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images, File)
The CIA system was used to analyze open-source intelligence, which draws on publicly available information. No classified systems were affected, and the issue has been resolved, sources said.
RETIRED FBI AGENT WARNS NCIC BREACH COULD THREATEN POLICE SAFETY DURING TRAFFIC STOPS
It remains unclear who was behind the CIA breach or whether the intrusions were connected.  (Samuel Corum/AFP via Getty Images, File)

TECH OUTAGE CASCADE EXPOSES US VULNERABILITIES TO FOREIGN CYBER THREATS

title: Biden admin weighed quitting Twitter after Elon Musk purchase, new HHS doc drop reveals
summary: HHS launched a searchable public records trove with Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s calendars and Biden-era memos, promising transparency for health agencies.
story: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Medicare Chief Dr. Mehmet Oz announce the first 15 organizations receiving federal funding to combat chronic disease through nutrition and lifestyle care.

Amid a push to bolster transparency, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) launched a searchable trove of public records, including previously unreleased memos from the Biden administration and Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s calendars.

While the website will be updated over time, the initial drop includes a Biden-era memo detailing how the National Institutes of Health (NIH) considered no longer having a presence on Twitter after billionaire Elon Musk acquired the platform in October 2022, renamed it X and promised to scale back moderation amid free expression concerns.
Also included within the department's so-called Radical Transparency dashboard are Kennedy’s calendars, which reporters have previously requested and have not been publicly disclosed before now.
HHS BUREAUCRATS ACCUSED OF 'SABOTAGING' RFK JR'S EFFORTS TO EXPOSE FAUCI RECORDS
Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. delivers remarks during an event at HHS headquarters Aug. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"When President Trump asked me to lead HHS, I promised to bring transparency back to the American health agencies," Kennedy said in a video announcing the launch of the website. "If the government makes decisions that affect your health, you deserve to see the evidence behind them. Not simply to be told, ‘trust the science.’"

Kennedy claims that HHS’ previous method of presenting public records was disorganized and confusing to use. He said public accountability would be aided by consolidating the documents in one simplified dashboard.

The Cabinet secretary noted that his department plans to upload more documents to the website during his tenure and the first drop includes previously available documents that are now easier to search and locate.
TRUMP ORDERS FEDERAL CONTRACTORS TO ALERT WHITE HOUSE ON CONGRESSIONAL RECORD REQUESTS
Though many on the political right are likely to hail the move as HHS’ increasing transparency efforts, Democrats have criticized the agency for lacking transparency under Kennedy's leadership.
Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks during an announcement at HHS headquarters in Washington, D.C., on July 21, 2026. (Tierney L. Cross/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Congressional Democrats, for instance, have repeatedly said Kennedy stonewalls their oversight inquiries and claim that HHS, under his leadership, has provided incomplete responses to their questions. A letter sent by 18 Democratic lawmakers on Nov. 19, 2026, called out "an alarming lack of public transparency" following a delay to the disbursement of rural healthcare grants.

In early 2025, HHS reduced staff working on Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests and public records at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and Food and Drug Administration (FDA) — another move Democrats claim stifles or at least slows transparency.
Previous releases of public records by the Trump administration have enabled journalists to uncover millions of dollars in welfare fraud.

President Donald Trump has charged Vice President JD Vance, seen by some as his heir apparent, with leading the White House charge against fraud, signaling the high importance of the issue to the administration.
WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, left, President Donald Trump, Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Education Secretary Linda McMahon attend an event at the White House on May 22, 2025. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
In addition to public records releases, HHS has also pushed regulations requiring that healthcare companies make more information public about their pricing practices.

While the administration focuses on fraud, concerns about corruption within its ranks have taken root with voters amid press reports regarding conflicts of interest and alleged self-dealing. A Fox News survey found that 60% of Americans were concerned about government corruption ahead of the recent midterm elections.

title: Republican senator's husband dead: 'Our family is heartbroken'
summary: Sen. Deb Fischer announced her husband, Bruce Fischer, died Nov. 22 while doing what he loved most, spending time outdoors at their Nebraska Sandhills ranch.
story: Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., on Tuesday announced that her husband, Bruce Fischer, passed away over the weekend.
Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., announced Monday that her husband, Bruce Fischer, died over the weekend.

"It is with a heavy heart that I share the passing of my beloved husband, Bruce," Fischer said in a statement posted on X. "Bruce was my partner in life, my greatest source of strength, and the heart of our family. His kindness, integrity, and quiet strength left a lasting impression on all who knew him.
"On November 22, Bruce passed away peacefully while doing what he loved most, spending time outdoors," the statement continued.

"Our family is heartbroken by his passing, but we find comfort in the life we shared with him. I will cherish the decades we spent building a family in the Nebraska Sandhills. Above all, Bruce was a loving husband, a devoted father and grandfather, a man of faith and a rancher."
BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS
Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., is sworn into office by then-Vice President Mike Pence alongside her husband, Bruce Fischer, who died Sunday. (Sen. Deb Fischer; Facebook)
Fischer met her husband when the pair were students at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, the Lincoln Journal Star reported. They married in 1972 and had three sons.
Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee reacted by saying, "This is truly heartbreaking."
"Bruce Fischer was a good man, with whom Sharon and I have been privileged to interact over many years," Lee wrote on X.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen also offered his condolences following news of the death.
Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., second from left, stands alongside husband Bruce, third from left, and then-Vice President Kamala Harris. (Sen. Deb Fischer; Facebook)
FROM NEBRASKA TO WEST VIRGINIA TO NEW JERSEY: PRIMARY CLASHES SET STAGE FOR FIERCE MIDTERM FIGHT
"Suzanne and I are keeping Sen. Fischer and her family in our thoughts. We share our prayers as she deals with this great personal loss," he wrote on X.

"I am very sad to hear of the passing of Bruce Fischer," Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts said. "Bruce left his mark on this world through his love for family, his faith, and his ranch. Susanne and I send our deepest condolences to Deb, the entire Fischer family, and all their loved ones during this difficult time. The Fischer family is in our prayers."
Chair Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., gavels to order the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on the Legislative Branch hearing April 15, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Bruce Fischer's cause of death has not been disclosed.
Bruce Fischer went viral in January 2025 when he appeared to decline a handshake from then-Vice President Kamala Harris as his wife was sworn into office.
After administering the oath to Fischer and shaking her hand, Harris turned to Bruce Fischer to extend her hand. He appeared to respond with "Thank you" without extending his hand back.
