title: Boston marks Thanksgiving as ‘Day of Mourning’ while historic Plymouth battles anti-Thanksgiving activists
summary: The Boston City Council's Day of Mourning resolution honors Indigenous peoples as Plymouth officials and activists clash in court over their own observances on Thanksgiving.
story: Boston City Council slams Thanksgiving Day narrative taught in American schools.

The Boston City Council recognized Thanksgiving as a "National Day of Mourning" ahead of the holiday, continuing a recurring acknowledgment from city leaders as nearby Plymouth, home of the "first Thanksgiving," battles activists in court over their Indigenous peoples observances.

Last week, the Boston City Council passed a resolution designating Thursday, Nov. 26, as a "National Day of Mourning" in Boston after it was introduced by Councilor Benjamin Weber and co-sponsored by 11 other councilors. While the resolution carries no legal weight or changes to city operations, it reflects an annual tradition for the Boston City Council, which has passed similar ceremonial recognitions ahead of Thanksgiving in previous years.

"The story of Thanksgiving that so many of us grew up learning in school fails to acknowledge the devastating consequences that colonialization had and continues to have on Indigenous peoples, " Boston City Councilor At-Large Julia Mejia said in favor of the resolution during a city council meeting on Nov. 18.
HOW VIRGINIA SCHOOL DISTRICT SHAMES KIDS TO MARK THANKSGIVING
Boston City Councilor Julia Mejia listens during a Boston City Council meeting at Boston City Hall on June 3, 2026. (Erin Clark/The Boston Globe via Getty Image)

"I think it's important that we recognize that these are not simply injustices of the past," Mejia continued. "And as a city, we have a responsibility to ensure that our commitment to equity and justice includes the Indigenous peoples whose lands we live on."

Meanwhile, in nearby Plymouth — the famed site of the 1621 "first Thanksgiving" feast between the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag people, where the United American Indians of New England (UAINE) has held the annual National Day of Mourning every year since 1970 — town officials and organizers appeared in court Monday over a dispute about this year's event logistics.
ARIZONA MAN THREATENED WITH ARREST FOR PREACHING AT HOLIDAY FESTIVAL FILES LAWSUIT
Illustration of a pilgrim celebration held in Plymouth, Massachusetts on August 01, 1853. (Kean Collection/Getty Images)
The legal battle centers on a 1998 settlement, signed after a clash between police and demonstrators the year prior, that requires Plymouth to make a mobile stage available for the event.

According to CBS Boston, town officials now say they will not set up a stage on state property without proof of insurance or an outside vendor, citing liability concerns, while UAINE argues the demand violates the decades-old agreement.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Demonstrators march on Main Street during the 56th National Day of Mourning on Cole's Hill in Plymouth, Mass., on Nov. 27, 2025. (Boston Globe via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Plymouth Independent reported that Plymouth Superior Court Judge Brian Glenny took the arguments under advisement Monday, leaving a ruling pending just days before Thursday's 57th annual gathering on Cole's Hill. According to the outlet, Glenny did not express when a ruling might come, though lawyers involved indicated he understands "time is of the essence."
However, regardless, a UAINE leader told the Plymouth Independent that the event would continue as planned. "I can assure you we will be there Thursday," Mahtowin Munro told the local outlet.
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Biden's first-year fundraising fails to crack 1% of Obama's library haul as questions swirl over legacy
summary: Joe Biden raised just $1.5 million for his presidential library in 2025, per tax filings, a fraction of the $232.6 million Barack Obama brought in 2017.
story: Ohio State accounting professor Brian Mittendorf examines the Obama Foundation's financial health, assets and endowment as construction costs hit $1 billion.
Former President Joe Biden has raised a shockingly small amount of funds for his presidential library compared to former President Barack Obama.
The figures are fueling skepticism about how history will remember Biden's single term in the White House.

In 2017, Obama’s first year out of office, the two-term president managed to bring in $232.6 million in donations and contributions to fund the foundation behind his presidential library. By comparison, Biden secured just $1.5 million in 2025 for his presidential library foundation, per tax filings.
This is less than 1% of what his former boss raised in the same amount of time after leaving office.

Even before leaving office, President Donald Trump’s library foundation has already dwarfed that of his predecessor by raising tens of millions of dollars from a variety of sources, including companies that settled lawsuits with him.
OBAMA CENTER ISN'T A TRADITIONAL PRESIDENTIAL LIBRARY. CRITICS SAY IT'S AN ACTIVISM CENTER.
Former US presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden shake hands during the opening of the Barack Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, Illinois, on June 18, 2026. (Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images)

Though the Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation has yet to decide on a construction site, it’s already running a deficit, spending $600,000 more than it raised in 2025. A Biden library official claimed that it wasn’t actively fundraising in 2025 in a statement shared with CBS News.
The lack of enthusiasm for Biden’s legacy has led some to claim that Americans may simply forget about his presidency as the years go on.

"Presidencies usually fade," Axios’ Zachary Basu wrote of his legacy. "But in just one year, Biden’s has been reduced to a footnote by a successor committed to dismantling every pillar of Washington’s old liberal order."
Heritage Action press manager Doug Blair told Fox News Digital, "Joe Biden spent half a century in Washington and did nothing to benefit the American people."

"The anemic fundraising for his presidential library is a fitting bookend for a failed presidency Americans are eager to forget," he added. "Joe Biden left Americans worse off by every conceivable measure and his legacy will be a southern border blown wide open, the disgraceful image of him checking his watch as fallen American troops returned home from Afghanistan, and endless scandals and investigations surrounding him and his corrupt family.'
BIDEN'S BATTLE WITH ADVANCING CANCER RENEWS FOCUS ON PROSTATE DISEASE

Allies of the former president point to the fact that Biden presided over the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, influential pieces of domestic legislation and America’s withdrawal from Afghanistan, parts of his legacy that could contribute to historical staying power.
A January 2025 Gallup poll found that 54% of U.S. adults believed history would remember Biden as a "below-average" or "poor" president.
Former U.S. President Joe Biden attends the dedication ceremony for the opening of the Barack Obama Presidential Center in John Lewis Plaza (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)
A source close to Biden’s foundation told CBS News that it ramped up its fundraising in 2026, pulling in multiple multi-million-dollar contributions, including two $5 million donations.
Another source told the outlet that some of Biden's close allies are frustrated that Democratic donors aren’t stepping up to support the former president’s library.
Further complicating Biden’s fundraising efforts, and his ability to nurture his public image, is his advanced age and Stage 4 prostate cancer, which has metastasized to his bones.
OBAMA CENTER OPENS AFTER YEARS-LONG SAGA AS LOCALS WARN ‘MONSTROSITY’ COULD PRICE THEM OUT

Former President Barack Obama and the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, where construction costs are now projected to reach approximately $1 billion, nearly triple the upper end of the original estimate. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images; Talía Sprague/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
While the increase in funds is no doubt encouraging for Biden’s allies, it still puts them far behind Obama, who raised $164.8 million for his foundation in 2018.
Obama ultimately spent nearly $1 billion on his presidential library in Chicago, a sum Biden likely will not be able to reach given his current fundraising levels.

title: DOJ recovers $8B, charges more than 800 suspects in largest anti-scam surge in history
summary: U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche says the Justice Department charged more than 800 defendants and recovered $8 billion in intended victim losses.
story: The Department of Justice on Tuesday announced the largest anti-scam enforcement surge in its history, charging over 800 defendants and recovering more than $8 billion in intended losses.

Federal prosecutors have charged more than 800 defendants and recovered over $8 billion in intended victim losses as part of the largest anti-scam enforcement surge in Justice Department history, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Tuesday.

Speaking alongside FBI Director Kash Patel at a news conference in Washington, Blanche said the enforcement blitz follows President Donald Trump's March executive order directing a government-wide crackdown on fraud and predatory schemes targeting Americans. Since that directive, the Justice Department has filed more than 400 criminal cases across 85 federal districts, resulting in charges, extraditions, guilty pleas and prison sentences.
"We are not just going after individual scammers," Blanche said. "We are dismantling the criminal networks that have been stealing from the American people for far too long."
INSIDE OPERATION BLACKOUT: PATEL REVEALS GLOBAL SCAM ‘CITIES’ TARGETING YOUR PARENTS’ LIFE SAVINGS

A board with data, labeled "2026 Anti-Scam Surge," is displayed during a press conference with U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva about recent efforts against cyber fraud at the Justice Department in Washington, D.C., Nov. 24, 2026. (Reuters/Jonathan Ernst)

Patel detailed the FBI's global offensive under Operation Blackout, an interagency campaign targeting international fraud syndicates. According to Patel, federal agents and international partners have seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, confiscated more than 14,000 digital devices and dismantled 29 scam compounds across four continents.

Those compounds operate as self-contained towns where criminal networks force human trafficking victims to run online fraud schemes against Americans, Patel said, noting that joint operations have freed more than 2,200 trafficked workers.

"They thought they could get away with it in Southeast Asia. They moved to Africa. They moved to the Middle East," Patel said. "We annihilated them on every single continent that they chose to operate and attack American citizens."
FBI OPERATION TARGETS SCAM COMPOUNDS IN AFRICA WITH ARRESTS, ACCOUNT TAKEDOWNS

The crackdown comes as online and phone fraud continue to hit U.S. households at staggering rates. Blanche cited a recent Gallup study finding that 10% of Americans reported that they or a household member fell victim to a scam in 2025, resulting in an estimated $68 billion in losses in a single year.

Officials pointed to a wide range of schemes disrupted since March, from felony inmates using contraband cellphones and handwritten scripts to run jury-duty extortion scams to Mexico-based timeshare fraud allegedly operated by major drug trafficking cartels.

FBI Director Kash Patel speaks alongside U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche during a news conference to announce the results of a crackdown on cyber-enabled scams, at the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 24, 2026. (Ken Cedeno/AFP via Getty Images)

In the past two weeks alone, federal authorities worked with Mexican officials to extradite a list broker accused of selling the names of more than 1 million elderly Americans to international scam networks, resulting in at least $15 million in victim losses. Agents also dismantled websites impersonating U.S. federal courts and arrested nine suspects in an alleged sweepstakes scheme that defrauded seniors of millions of dollars, Blanche said.

Overseas, a recent enforcement push coordinated in London yielded 28 arrests across Africa, $11 million in seized assets, the rescue of 120 trafficked workers and the removal of 3.7 million fraudulent Facebook and Instagram accounts, Patel said.

Beyond arrests and asset seizures, federal officials are also intervening before money leaves victims' bank accounts. Through Operation Level Up, a joint effort with the U.S. Secret Service, agents have prevented nearly $700 million in potential losses across 11,000 targeted Americans, 77% of whom did not realize they were being scammed, Patel said.

"The United States government and President Trump does not tolerate organized theft perpetrated against the American people," Blanche said. "No matter where these criminals are in the world, we will find them and hold them accountable."

title: Draft plan to overhaul Smithsonian spotted on White House staffer's laptop: report
summary: A commuter's photos of a White House adviser's laptop show a draft plan to overhaul the National Museum of American History, ProPublica reported.
story: Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., discusses controversies surrounding the Smithsonian Institution and President Donald Trump calling on the museum to replace a sculpture with a statue of George Washington on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’

Photos taken by a commuter on Washington, D.C.'s Metro system appear to show a White House advisor’s laptop displaying a draft plan to overhaul the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, ProPublica reported.

Last month, a commuter riding the Orange Line from Northern Virginia noticed a man in a suit working on a laptop displaying a document titled "Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan." The commuter photographed the screen and sent the images to ProPublica.

The multipoint draft proposed firing museum Director Anthea Hartig, creating new museum-wide exhibit guidelines that omit the Smithsonian’s diversity style guide, reviewing its traveling-exhibition strategy — including ending "The Bias Inside Us" — and reassessing grants to what the draft called "woke third parties," including the American Alliance of Museums. A separate handwritten note that was also pictured proposed a policy against "X-rated" exhibitions. ProPublica said it likely referred to an exhibit the White House criticized for displaying a two-piece chrome-and-rubber harness designed for sadomasochism.
INSIDE THE BEHEMOTH SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM NETWORK DRAWING FIRE FROM THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION

The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 12, 2025. Photos taken on a D.C. Metro train appear to show a White House advisor's laptop displaying a draft plan to overhaul the museum's leadership, exhibits and K-12 curriculum. (Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The draft renewal plan pictured on the staffer's laptop surfaced amid a broader Trump administration effort to reshape how the Smithsonian presents American history. The White House released a 162-page report on July 4 accusing the National Museum of American History of "ideological capture." Two congressional hearings followed, and a July executive order directed officials to post signs outside the museum informing visitors of the report’s findings about "ideological capture," though ProPublica reported the signs had not yet gone up as of publication.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment on the photographed document and whether any of its proposals are under consideration, but did not receive a response by publication. The photographed document does not establish whether the proposals were approved or put into effect.
TRUMP GIVES SMITHSONIAN DAYS TO REPLACE 'STRANGE MODERNIST SCULPTURE' WITH FOUNDING FATHER

ProPublica reported that it identified the White House staffer as Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy advisor with the White House Domestic Policy Council — which produced the July report — after spotting the initials "B.S." or "S.B." on the laptop screen and following a man matching his description from the Metro to a White House employee checkpoint. ProPublica reported that Bock did not respond to its messages and that the Smithsonian declined to comment.

ProPublica reported that the proposals on Bock’s laptop envisioned a permanent exhibit celebrating Western civilization, a display on prominent American families, a large George Washington statue at the museum entrance and new museum-wide interpretive guidelines written without reference to the Smithsonian’s diversity style guide. A separate handwritten note photographed alongside the laptop also floated a potential new D-Day exhibit.

The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C.. A July White House report accused the museum of "ideological capture," and a draft renewal plan photographed on a White House advisor's laptop proposed replacing its diversity guidelines and adding a George Washington statue at the entrance. (Kevin Carter)

In addition to the proposed exhibit changes, the draft called for the firing of National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig and about a dozen senior administrators and curators. That proposal came as Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch, who leads the broader institution, was preparing to retire at year’s end. ProPublica reported that White House criticism of the Smithsonian helped prompt Bunch’s departure.
TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED

The draft plan also called for overhauling the museum’s online curriculum for K-12 students, including dropping a module on immigration and creating new material focused on the Founders, according to ProPublica, which noted the document floated possible titles for the new curriculum, including "Architects of Liberty" and "Profiles in Liberty."

Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch poses for a portrait at the Smithsonian Castle on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., on May 28, 2026. Bunch is preparing to retire at the end of the year amid White House criticism of the institution, according to ProPublica. (Al Drago/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

The administration’s push to reshape how the Smithsonian presents American history began picking up steam in March 2025, when Trump signed an executive order directing Vice President JD Vance, through his role on the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, to help remove what the order called "improper ideology" from the institution. The Smithsonian, which encompasses 21 museums and D.C.'s National Zoo, is governed by a 17-member Board of Regents that consists of the vice president, the chief justice of the Supreme Court, members of Congress and private citizens. It receives more than $1 billion in federal funding annually.

The White House’s July report cited, among other examples, a museum exhibit that raised the possibility Benjamin Franklin had used enslaved people in his household as subjects in electrical experiments. It also criticized staff training based on a social-action toolkit that the report said linked museums to White supremacy and other forms of oppression.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The report said the museum should not erase slavery, Jim Crow or other national failures. Its broader charge was that the museum was not giving visitors a coherent account of how the country developed, including both its achievements and its wrongs.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
The criticism from the Trump administration came amid a longer-running debate over how the museum should tell the nation’s story, which has stretched back to at least 2001.

ProPublica reported that in response to earlier criticism, the Smithsonian convened a blue-ribbon commission in 2001, whose 2002 report urged the museum to present a more unified account of American history. The outlet also reported that after George Floyd’s murder in 2020, Bunch and other leaders began an institution-wide reassessment of the Smithsonian’s priorities and how it tells the nation’s story.
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Ilhan Omar records show judge, DOJ officials debating before raid of home
summary: Court documents reveal Judge Matthew Sharbaugh warned the DOJ its search warrant for Rep. Ilhan Omar's D.C. home could violate the Speech and Debate Clause.
story: Newly unsealed search warrant documents reveal a decades-long federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., going back to 1980. Former federal prosecutor Jonathan Fahey joins 'Fox & Friends' to analyze the records and the Department of Justice's search for evidence of redacted crimes. Fahey discusses the legal implications of the unsealed warrant for her Washington, D.C. home.

Court documents released Monday night showed U.S. Department of Justice prosecutors battling with U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew J. Sharbaugh to obtain a search warrant for the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.
The DOJ applied to the magistrate for a search warrant on Oct. 2, eventually receiving the warrant which led to a Homeland Security Investigations search of the home on Oct. 12.
However, the newly released petition for the warrant reveals the court raised concerns that the DOJ could be violating the Constitution’s Speech and Debate Clause.
FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION

"The search warrant here is directed to a sitting member of the United States House of Representatives. This means that, even after ensuring that there exists probable cause to issue the warrant, see Fed. R. Crim. P. 41(d)(1), the Court must separately balance any necessary constitutional considerations under governing precedent," the court wrote in a memorandum.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is seen on Capitol Hill in Washington D.C., on Tuesday for the first time since two federal investigations were opened against her, looking into her immigration status and financial filings. (Reuters/Tim Evans)
The DOJ, for its part, argued that the requested warrant did not relate to any speech Omar had made as a Congressperson or to her legislative duties at all.
'RADICAL LEFT LUNATIC' JUDGE TRUMP WANTED IMPEACHED TAKES UP ILHAN OMAR WARRANT FIGHT

The memorandum, according to the document, affirms a previous oral ruling from the court which questioned the government’s assertions that the search would be independent of Omar’s Congressional business.

"The issue that remains and the issue this Court independently raised with the government after its initial review of the warrant application is whether the search of residence implicates the Speech or Debate Clause. The government says no. This Court sees it differently. It concludes that the proposed search of the residence of a sitting Member of Congress, at least on the facts here, requires the balancing of interests that the D.C. Circuit explicated in Rayburn," the memorandum read.
ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS
The court specifically cited the warrant’s request to search Omar’s cell phone, arguing that most adults now bring some portion of work home with them, particularly on their electronic devices.

Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital. (Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)

"The Court has no trouble concluding that the presence of at least some legislative materials along those lines is 'inevitable' in the residence of a sitting member of Congress, whether in a formal home office setting, a work bag inside the home that travels back and forth to Capitol Hill, or otherwise," the memorandum read.
REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES

Despite the pushback, Sharbaugh ultimately granted the DOJ the search warrant but with the caveat that Omar could invoke Congressional privilege over any seized items that could relate to legislative activity and require prosecutors to obtain a separate warrant to search the content of electronic devices.
The documents also reveal that U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro is searching for documents related to any crimes going back to the 1980s.
OBAMA ADMIN FIRST LAUNCHED THE INVESTIGATION INTO ILHAN OMAR'S ALLEGED BROTHER MARRIAGE
Though parts of the document released Monday were heavily redacted, it revealed that prosecutors believed Omar committed "[redacted] crimes over decades."
According to Fox News legal analyst Jonathan Turley, the scope and time frame "confirms the broad sweep of the investigation back to her birth."
ILHAN OMAR HUDDLES WITH HER DC-BASED LAWYERS DURING HER FIRST DAY BACK ON CAPITOL HILL AMID FEDERAL PROBES
The documents were released by Judge James Boasberg, the chief judge for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, against DOJ wishes.
Boasberg denied a federal prosecutor's request to keep the records sealed.
WHAT'S NEXT FOR ILHAN OMAR? FORMER IMMIGRATION JUDGE BREAKS DOWN LEGAL RISKS AMID FEDERAL PROBES
James Boasberg, incoming chief judge of the U.S. District Court, in Washington, D.C., on Monday, March 13, 2023. (Valerie Plesch/Bloomberg via Getty)

The DOJ had previously argued in the documents that unsealing the records could prompt potential suspects into fleeing or witness tampering. Sharbaugh apparently agreed, signing off on the documents' sealing on Oct. 9.

However, Boasberg signed off on the unsealing and ordered the release of the heavily redacted 170-page documents. He also indicated that a further release could be coming in the future with significant reductions in redactions.
Boasberg excluded the 67-page search warrant affidavit, the search warrant itself, and a list of seized items from the release, citing an ongoing investigation.

Fox News Digital contacted the DOJ and Rep. Omar's office for further comment.

title: Trump to award Giuliani Presidential Medal of Freedom
summary: President Donald Trump is set to award former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday, honoring his public service and 9/11 leadership.
story: Andrew Giuliani described his father, former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani, receiving the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Donald Trump in a closed-press ceremony Tuesday.

President Donald Trump will award former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday during a closed-press ceremony at the White House, honoring the longtime prosecutor and "America's Mayor" for his lifetime of public service.

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is the nation's highest civilian honor, alongside the Congressional Gold Medal, awarded to individuals who have made especially meritorious contributions to U.S. security, national interests, world peace, or significant public and private endeavors.
"I am honored and humbled to receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom from my nation and from our Commander-in-Chief, President Donald J. Trump," Giuliani, 82, said in a statement.
FOX NATION REVEALS HOW RUDY GIULIANI BROKE THE MAFIA'S GRIP ON NEW YORK
Rudy Giuliani is often coined "America's Mayor" by political pundits. (REUTERS/Joshua Roberts)

Quoting his former boss, President Ronald Reagan, Giuliani added: "'There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.' I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together."
After the ceremony, Giuliani's son Andrew Giuliani described the day as "incredibly special."

"To see your father receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom is an unbelievable honor," Andrew Giuliani told reporters on the White House grounds. "It's tough to describe. But to see him receive it from such a consequential president like the 45th and 47th president, it makes it all the more special."

White House assistant press secretary Olivia Wales praised Giuliani’s decades-long record in law enforcement and city leadership, noting that his work had "left a lasting impact on New York City and our Nation."

"As U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Mayor Giuliani took down mob bosses and led a relentless war on crime," Wales said. "As Mayor, he transformed New York from a crime-ridden city into one of the safest big cities in the world, fostering economic opportunity and cultural greatness. And in the aftermath of the tragic September 11th attacks, he displayed strong American leadership in the face of evil."
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
"President Trump will proudly honor Mayor Giuliani – America’s Mayor – with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for his lifetime of service to the American people," Wales added.

title: Former chief of staff to Pentagon chief Hegseth says 'it’s time for Pete to call it quits': report
summary: Politico reported that Joe Kasper, former chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, said that the Pentagon leader should resign.
story: Impeachment efforts against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth fail in the House after 11 Democrats miss the vote. Host Paul Gigot joins Kim Strassel and Kate Odell to discuss the roll call that referred the matter to the House Judiciary Committee. The panel also explores political setbacks for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and President Donald Trump's negotiation strategy.
Joe Kasper, who served as chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth during the early days of the Trump administration last year, has now said that Hegseth should resign.

"Pete's ability to be effective has been constrained and very soon he’ll have lost any ability to be effective," Kasper said, according to Politico. "For that reason and others, it’s time for Pete to call it quits."
"Pete's been belligerent in his stewardship of an office that will outlive him or any memory of his service," Kasper asserted, the report states.
The outlet reported that Kasper suggested that Hegseth would not be able to work with the nation's legislature or obtain appropriate funds for department priorities.

"He’s not just burned bridges up on the Hill," Kasper reportedly said. "He’s napalmed them. … He’s going to be suffocated, and it’s not like it’s going to be a slow suffocation. It’s going to be a quick asphyxiation."
PENTAGON SUED BY THE INTERCEPT, FREEDOM OF THE PRESS FOUNDATION OVER ALLEGED 'BLACKLIST' OF NEWS OUTLETS
U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth attends a Halloween event hosted by first lady Melania Trump at the White House on Oct. 29, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

According to Politico, Kasper noted that he understood within a week of joining the Pentagon that Hegseth's focus was "all about Pete rather than the institution and the men and women who support it."

"There’s quite an emphasis on the showmanship," Kasper reportedly said. "The virtues of humility and basically service before self and those things have disappeared. I didn’t see those at the start, and see them ever less so now."
The Pentagon chief "overindulged in ego, in attitude, and in entitlement," Kasper said, according to the report.
He noted that he would rate Hegseth near the bottom 10% of defense secretaries in U.S. history, Politico reported. "I think history will be much crueler to him than I could be," he said.
MASSIE'S PUSH TO IMPEACH HEGSETH SPLITS CONSTITUENTS IN HIS OWN BACKYARD: 'PURE SPITE'

War Secretary Pete Hegseth and President Donald Trump during a roundtable in the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Due to an executive order that was issued last year, the administration now refers to the Defense Department as the Department of War and to Hegseth as the secretary of war.

A senior department official said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital, "It’s no surprise that a disgruntled former staffer—someone who could barely survive ninety days in the building—is now peddling made up gossip to the media. Secretary Hegseth is laser focused on restoring lethality to the force and supporting our warfighters, while Mr. Kasper is more focused on rewriting history to cover for his own failed tenure."
PETE HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT EFFORT DIES IN THE HOUSE AS ABSENT DEMOCRATS COULDN'T BEAT THE TRAFFIC
U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth takes questions from reporters during a news conference at the Pentagon on Nov. 10, 2026 in Arlington, Va. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

title: US Army to proceed with Iowa detonation of degraded bomb materials: ‘A consensus decision’
summary: The Army will detonate 68 barrels of crystallized lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown after a federal appeals court ruling.
story: American Military Project director Will Thibeau reacts to the federal approval of a controlled detonation of expired explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Thibeau also breaks down a Wall Street Journal report indicating the U.S. suspects Iran is behind dozens of recent cyberattacks targeting commercial ships in the Middle East.

The U.S. Army will detonate 68 barrels of unstable, degraded bomb-making chemicals in Iowa on Wednesday morning after a federal appeals court rejected a legal challenge and allowed the controlled blast to move forward.

In a statement late Monday, Army officials confirmed they are proceeding with destroying the crystallized lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown in coordination with state, local and federal authorities.

"This is a consensus decision," Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle posted on social media. "Every expert agency agrees, and both Iowa’s current and incoming Governors say the call belongs to the experts."
FEDERAL APPEALS COURT CLEARS ARMY TO DETONATE VOLATILE IOWA EXPLOSIVES AS DEM GOV-ELECT REFUSES TO SIGN OFF
A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Nov. 19, 2026 in Middletown, Iowa. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

Hours earlier, a three-judge panel of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals lifted a temporary pause and denied an emergency request from the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club to block the operation. The judges found that the Environmental Protection Agency built adequate safeguards into its emergency permit to limit lead dust dispersal.

"Here we are faced with a situation in which the risk is between a controlled detonation and an unplanned explosion, not between the risk of a controlled detonation and no explosion at all," the court wrote.

The ruling followed a Truth Social post from President Donald Trump declaring he had ordered the military to hold off unless both the appeals court and Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand signed off. Trump warned he would hold Sand "responsible for any and all death or destruction" if the operation were blocked.

Sand, who takes office in January, declined to approve or reject the blast on Monday evening. He posted on X that the Trump administration should make the call based on the experts it brought in months ago and urged federal officials to release their briefing details publicly.
DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT
Meanwhile, a flight carrying Army officials departed Joint Base Andrews for Iowa just before Trump's post went live.
The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. (U.S. Army via AP)

The operation has already been postponed three times amid public concern over toxic lead dust. Munitions specialists warned in court filings that dropping temperatures increase the risk that crystallized material inside the barrels could trigger an accidental, fatal explosion if left untreated.
In a public advisory, the Army said Wednesday's blast will produce two rapid detonations, ground vibrations and a dust plume expected to linger for no more than an hour.
An aerial view shows homes on Nov. 20, 2026 in Middletown, Iowa. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
People living near Middletown, some of whom have already sealed their windows and doors, have been advised to stay indoors and wash outdoor surfaces with water afterward.
Fox News Digital’s Alex Nitzberg and Sophia Compton, along with The Associated Press, contributed to this report.

title: Trump welcomes turkeys to the White House for Thanksgiving pardon as farmer dishes on prep for the big day
summary: West Virginia farmer Scott Rightsell trained "Freedom" and "Feathers" for the White House turkey pardon, getting the 40-pound birds used to loud noises.
story: Turkey farmer Scott Rightsell and National Turkey Federation head Christy Puffenbarger explain the lifecycle of the turkeys receiving a presidential pardon on Tuesday.

President Donald Trump will participate in the annual Turkey Pardon on Tuesday, and the West Virginia turkey farmer responsible for raising this year's two birds helps walk Fox News Digital through the process from hatch to White House ahead of the light-hearted event.

"We spent a little bit more one-on-one time with each of these birds to get them trained to loud noises, a lot of people present, flashing lights — just being handled — so when they get to the president, hopefully they'll act like they have some sense," Scott Rightsell told Fox News Digital about raising the birds for Tuesday's National Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon.

Rightsell, who owns and operates Deans Gap Farm in rural Fort Seybert, West Virginia, with his wife Becky, found out during the summer that he would raise the turkeys for the ceremony. He received the young turkeys in July — shortly after the celebration for America 250.
A White House spokesperson tells Fox News Digital that Trump will deliver remarks about "how well our nation is doing" during the event just two days of the holiday.
The turkeys were named Freedom and Feathers through a White House public opinion poll, beating out the options for Commander and Chief or Honey and Ham.
Freedom and Feathers, the two turkeys chosen for the 2026 Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon at the White House, on a farm where they were raised in West Virginia. (National Turkey Federation)
TRUMP'S THANKSGIVING TURKEYS ARRIVE AT LUXURY DC HOTEL AS AMERICANS VOTE ON THEIR NAMES
"We've had them from the middle of the July until now," said Rightsell. "The turkeys weigh probably 40 to 45 pounds right now."
He added that besides the aforementioned training, the birds receive the same treatment as all the others that he raises on the farm, which he and his wife founded in 2015.
"Being on national TV, that's a big deal," Rightsell said when asked what he was looking forward to most about his trip to the nation's capital this week.

"I mean That's probably what we're looking forward to the most is being on national TV, actually meeting the president, which everybody does not get to do that. And getting to converse with him and the first lady, that's gonna be a real treat for us."
Typically, the pardon event is held in the Rose Garden. However, Trump will host the pardoning on the new South Lawn helipad Tuesday afternoon.

First lady Melania Trump, Vice President JD Vance and a litany of Cabinet secretaries, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Education Secretary Linda McMahon. Attorney General Todd Blanche will also attend. So will new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

From left to right, Becky Rightsell, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, Scott Rightsell, Gov. Patrick Morrisey, R-W.Va., and Christy Puffenbarger pose for a photo in West Virginia. (National Turkey Federation)

"President Trump will participate in the time-honored American tradition and grant a Presidential Pardon to two turkeys, Freedom and Feathers. Guests will enjoy the 79th annual event on the new South Lawn Helipad for the first time this year, bringing a change of scenery to this enduring ceremony," White House spokesperson Allison Schuster told Fox News Digital.
"Tune in to see President Trump spare these two birds from the Thanksgiving table and send them into retirement."
The National Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon has been a tradition for 79 years, recurring annually since President Harry Truman occupied the White House, according to Christy Puffenbarger.
Puffenbarger is this year's National Turkey Federation chairwoman, a position that rotates annually. She's the first woman to hold the role.
Both turkeys receive a pardon, but which turkey participates in the ceremony depends on the American people, who vote for their preferred bird on the White House's website.
INSIDE THE THANKSGIVING TURKEY HOTLINE THAT'S BEEN SAVING HOLIDAY DINNERS FOR 45 YEARS

Neither bird will end up on the Thanksgiving dinner table. The turkey that doesn't receive a pardon remains behind the scenes at the White House, "for moral support," as Puffenbarger put it. If the chosen bird gets stage fright or cannot carry out the ceremonial duties, the second bird is on standby.
Freedom and Feathers, the two turkeys chosen for the 2026 Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon at the White House, on a farm where they were raised in West Virginia. (National Turkey Federation)

"What I'm really looking forward to… is meeting the president and his wife and representing this industry," Puffenbarger told Fox News Digital. "[I] would like to thank the president for continuing this tradition. Because I do think it is a very nice event. It showcases not only our industry, but the tradition of turkey at Thanksgiving."
Puffenbarger says the industry as a whole will provide 30 million pounds of turkey to Americans enjoying the Thanksgiving holiday this year.
"And to be able to showcase it at a positive, fun event like that ... it'll be quite an honor for myself and my family," she said.

After spending their first few months of life like any normal turkey, the royal treatment for Feathers and Freedom began on Thursday. They left for Washington, D.C., after a star-studded send-off from a local elementary school in Brandywine, West Virginia, where Becky Rightsell is also a teacher.
Secretary Rollins attended the sendoff, as did West Virginia Governor Patrick Morrisey.

"It’s so humbling for West Virginia to be named to have two of the turkeys that get pardoned. This is history in the making, only the second time that’s happened," Morrisey told WDTV during the ceremony.

Freedom and Feathers, the two turkeys chosen for the 2026 Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon at the White House, walk on a red carpet at the Willard Intercontinental Hotel in Washington, D.C. (Department of Agriculture)
BROOKE ROLLINS, MONICA CROWLEY: AMERICA’S FAMILY FARMS HAVE KEPT US STRONG FOR 250 YEARS

Sunday night, the birds arrived at the five-star Willard InterContinental Hotel in Washington, D.C., where they received "presidential treatment," according to the Department of Agriculture (USDA), which posted photos of the turkeys sitting on the beds in a hotel room.
A red carpet was rolled out as they strolled through the lobby of the hotel to much fanfare. Once in the room, the birds were greeted by a layer of crunchy fall leaves lining the floor.
But the fun doesn't end after Tuesday's pardoning. Instead, the turkeys will be whisked away for their next adventure.

"Immediately afterwards, another cool thing, these birds will get on an airplane and fly to beautiful College Station, Texas, where they will retire to live out the rest of their lives at Texas A&M University," Puffenbarger explained.

Freedom and Feathers, the two turkeys chosen for the 2026 Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon at the White House, sit on beds at the Willard Intercontinental Hotel in Washington, D.C. (Department of Agriculture)
Friday night, Texas A&M's football team is scheduled to host rival Texas, the fifth-ranked college football team in the country.
Feathers and Freedom will be the guests of honor at the game.
"I don't know how much they know about football, but I feel sure they will have a good time," Puffenbarger said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"And then Texas A&M ... their poultry science department, will take care of the birds. They built quite a beautiful facility for them to spend their days in."
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: What the US gets from Israel alliance as support for aid to the Jewish State erodes on left and right: report
summary: A new report calls Israel "the largest U.S. aircraft carrier" in the Middle East, citing missile-defense co-production across 34 states as a key return.
story: Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed was confronted on NBC's "Meet the Press" Sunday over his opposition to Israel's existence as a Jewish state.

The U.S.-Israel alliance was tested when Washington and Jerusalem found common cause against Iran — and when defending Israel drew heavily on American weapons stocks. Meanwhile, that ongoing conflict has now sharpened a question for Washington: what does the alliance deliver, and what does it demand in return?

A new report from Advancing American Freedom (AAF) and the Zionist Organization of America (ZOA) argues that Israel’s military reach and regional role make the alliance a strategic asset for Washington.

Its authors call Israel "the largest U.S. aircraft carrier" in the Middle East. But this is in direct opposition of critics who say that the alliance costs the U.S. a lot and delivers very little in return.
The report, dated Oct. 26, 2026, arrives as public support for Israel continues to fall across the political spectrum — even among Republicans and MAGA supporters.
FROM INTELLIGENCE SHARING TO MISSILE DEFENSE, HOW ISRAEL'S PARTNERSHIP PROTECTS AMERICAN SECURITY
President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced joint military action targeting Iran. (REUTERS/Kevin Mohatt)

President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have discussed ending direct U.S. military aid, but the U.S. leader has also called Israel "a great ally, much more reliable than most" and said Washington would help if Israel needed it.
The report specifically points to intelligence sharing, joint weapons development and military cooperation as returns on what the U.S. gets for providing support to Israel.

One of the clearest examples is missile defense. The U.S. and Israel develop systems including David’s Sling and Arrow, while American companies manufacture components for several programs. More than 100 companies across 34 states participate in missile-defense co-production, according to the Congressional Research Service. In August, a Raytheon-Rafael facility in Arkansas delivered the first Iron Dome Tamir interceptor built entirely in the U.S.

Those programs support U.S. manufacturers and give the Pentagon a role in developing missile-defense systems. During the Iran conflict, however, U.S. forces also expended large numbers of interceptors — costly weapons that can take years to replace.
US REBUILDING WEAPONS STOCKPILE COULD DELAY ORDERS FROM ALLIES

In September, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated that the U.S. had probably used between half and two-thirds of its combined inventory of Patriot, THAAD, SM-3 and SM-6 interceptors since June 2025.

The estimate includes weapons used during the earlier 12-day war with Iran and is based on publicly reported expenditures compared with the number of those interceptors the War Department has purchased. CBO said rebuilding stocks could take at least five years, even if production increased.

President Donald Trump, left, meets with Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, as CIA Director John Ratcliffe, from second left, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, and from second right, Netanyahu's wife Sara Netanyahu, Israel's Strategic Affairs Minister Ron Dermer, Israel's National Security Council head Tzachi Hanegbi, obstructed, and Israel's Cabinet Secretary Yossi Fuchs listen in the Blue Room of the White House, Monday, July 7, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

Intelligence sharing is another return cited by supporters of the alliance. Former CIA Director John Brennan said Israeli intelligence was among the "thousands of bits" considered during the years-long effort to find Usama bin Laden. He did not specify what Israel provided or how much it contributed to the operation.

A more recent exchange shows how Israeli reporting can prompt U.S. action even when its accuracy is uncertain. Israeli officials warned the U.S. of a possible Iranian plot to kill Trump during a trip to Turkey. The Secret Service took precautions, including moving him to another aircraft. U.S. intelligence agencies could not independently verify the threat, however, and the CIA assessed some of the Israeli reporting with "low confidence," according to Reuters and The Washington Post.
NETANYAHU REVEALS HE WANTS AMERICAN FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL TO 'DRAW DOWN TO ZERO'

The financial relationship has also become part of the debate. Under the current agreement, the U.S. provides Israel with $3.3 billion annually in Foreign Military Financing and $500 million for joint missile-defense programs. Most of the military aid pays for weapons and services from U.S. contractors, according to CRS. Israel’s ability to spend a portion of the funding on domestic purchases is scheduled to phase out by 2028.
The report's authors call the $3.8 billion in annual U.S. military aid "one of the highest returns on investment of any U.S. foreign assistance."

Trump has said he wants to end annual aid, while Netanyahu has also publicly called for phasing it out over time. U.S. and Israeli officials have been negotiating a new agreement that could wind down direct assistance while expanding joint defense projects and weapons production. The current agreement runs through 2028, Congress controls appropriations, and no successor deal has been reached.
TRUMP WANTS LARGEST-EVER ISRAELI HEAVY BOMB TRANSFER — BUT PROPOSAL HAS CONGRESS PREPARING FOR $2.8B FIGHT
The Israeli Iron Dome air defense system fires to intercept missiles during an Iranian attack over Tel Aviv, Israel, early Wednesday, June 18, 2025. (AP Photo/Leo Correa)
The debate is also becoming more politically consequential as Americans question the relationship’s terms.

A 2026 Chicago Council survey found that 56% favored reducing or ending U.S. military aid to Israel. Republicans remain more supportive than Democrats and independents, but the right is divided: Joe Kent blamed Israeli pressure for the Iran war, Rep. Thomas Massie has pushed to cut aid, and Vice President JD Vance has called for changing the relationship while continuing to describe Israel as a strategic ally.

The two countries have cooperated against Iran and developed defenses against missile attacks, but their goals have not always matched during the war. A Stimson Center analysis says Israel sought to broaden the conflict beyond what Washington preferred. That does not establish that Israel drew the United States into a war it opposed. It does show how cooperation can leave Washington managing military costs even when its preferred limits differ from Israel’s.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The next agreement will help determine whether the alliance continues to rely on direct grants or shifts toward joint weapons development and production. Either way, the military and intelligence cooperation described in the report comes with commitments of U.S. money and weapons — and leaves Washington weighing those costs against the advantages it expects the alliance to deliver.

title: Massachusetts sues Trump admin to stop ICE's courthouse arrests: 'Unnecessary fear'
summary: Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration over ICE's courthouse arrests without judicial warrants, saying they violate a new state law.
story: Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell filed a federal lawsuit Monday seeking to block ICE from making civil immigration arrests inside state courthouses without a judicial warrant.

Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration on Monday to block Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from carrying out civil arrests in the state's courthouses, arguing that such arrests without judicial warrants are illegal under state law.

The lawsuit filed by Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell challenges a 2025 ICE directive that authorizes agents to conduct civil arrests in or near state courthouses without judicial warrants, which she says violates the PROTECT Act, a new state law passed ​by the Democratic-led legislature that prohibits civil immigration arrests in state courthouses without judicial warrants. The courthouse protections took effect Nov. 3.

Campbell said the ICE directive interferes with the state's authority to operate its judicial system, disrupts court proceedings, undermines constitutional principles and public safety and spreads fear, chaos and confusion.

"The Massachusetts PROTECT Act makes it illegal for ICE to conduct civil arrests in our courthouses without a judicial warrant. ICE’s intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable," Campbell said in a statement.
DOJ SUES TO STOP OHIO COURT BLOCKING COURTHOUSE ARRESTS
Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration to block ICE agents from carrying out civil arrests in the state's courthouses. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images)

"ICE is misleading the public by suggesting that these arrests make us safer when, in fact, ICE's actions are preventing criminal cases from moving forward, denying a victim’s ability to obtain accountability, violating a defendant’s due process, and leaving open the possibility that someone facing serious criminal charges could ultimately be released from ICE custody without their criminal case ever being resolved," she continued.

The attorney general said more than 1,110 people have been arrested at her state's courthouses since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, including more than 600 people in 2025 and more than 500 during the first 10 months of 2026.

Campbell said ICE has ignored the new state law and arrested at least 38 people in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants in the two and a half weeks since the courthouse protections went into effect.

"I, along with our district attorneys, share the goal of holding defendants accountable for crimes, yet ICE’s unlawful tactics to arrest someone for a civil immigration violation is not the same as holding them accountable for a crime," Campbell said.
FEDERAL JUDGE IN NEW YORK TIES TRUMP ADMIN HANDS ON ARRESTS AT IMMIGRATION COURTS
The attorney general said more than 1,110 people have been arrested at her state's courthouses since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. (Getty Images)

Campbell said that ICE's courthouse arrests have continued in Massachusetts despite a federal ruling handed down in June by U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in California that vacated the Trump administration's courthouse arrest policy ​in a separate class action lawsuit.

In Monday's lawsuit, Campbell argues the ICE policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act since it was adopted without taking into account the impact it would have on states and because the Immigration and Nationality Act does not explicitly authorize courthouse arrests.
The lawsuit also alleges that the ⁠policy violates the U.S. Constitution's Tenth Amendment, which protects states' rights to maintain authority over their own judicial systems.

"The Trump Administration’s ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses are interfering with our justice system and undermining public safety. When people are afraid to go to court, victims are less likely to report crimes, survivors are less likely to seek protection, and our communities are less safe," Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey said in a statement. "We expect ICE and all federal agents to follow Massachusetts law."
The lawsuit challenges a 2025 ICE directive that instructs agents to conduct civil arrests in or near state courthouses without judicial warrants. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

In a statement to Reuters, a DHS spokesperson argued that making immigration arrests at courthouses "conserves valuable law enforcement resources because they already ​know where a target will ​be," adding that "the ability of law enforcement ⁠to make arrests of criminal illegal aliens in courthouses is common sense."
A similar lawsuit against ICE arrests at state courthouses was filed in October by California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

title: Unsealed warrant documents for Ilhan Omar's DC home raid reveal decades-long scope of investigation
summary: The redacted search warrant for Homeland Security Investigations' raid on Ilhan Omar's Washington D.C. home was released, with phone and passport seized.
story: Fox News legal analyst Gregg Jarrett joins 'Fox & Friends' to explain what a federal judge's expected release of redacted search warrant records could reveal about the investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.
Heavily redacted versions of documents used to justify a search warrant and raid on the Washington, D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., were released to the public Monday evening.
Despite the level of redaction, the documents provide more insight into the scope of the investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman.

In an ex parte brief in support of an affidavit for a search warrant, federal prosecutors say they're searching for all "records and information that constitute fruits, contraband, evidence, and instrumentalities of violations of [redacted], those violations involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present (the 'Target Offenses)."

While accounts vary, even from the congresswoman herself, Omar was born in 1981 or 1982. She does not have a birth certificate. She came to the United States in 1995 with her father. Fox News Digital confirmed just after the Oct. 12 raid of her home, that investigators were looking into alleged immigration fraud, potentially related to how Omar and her father filled out her immigration paperwork.
In another document, arguing that the court mischaracterized the government's arguments in ex parte proceedings, prosecutors make it clear that the investigation into Omar spans decades.
"The United States believes that ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades— beginning long before she was ever in Congress," the document says.
Fox News Digital reached out to a spokesperson for Omar.

In a rare move, Obama-appointed federal Judge James Boasberg ordered the documents' release last week, telling the Department of Justice (DOJ) to submit proposed redactions before the materials were made public on Monday. Judge Boasberg, in order dated October 9, 2026, agreed initially to seal the documents due to "such reasonable grounds to believe the disclosure will result in flight from prosecution, destruction of or tampering with evidence, intimidation of potential witnesses, and serious jeopardy to the investigation."
Search warrants typically remain sealed until there is an arrest in a criminal case.

Fifteen media outlets, led by The New York Times, along with watchdog group Judicial Watch, sued President Donald Trump's DOJ for the release of the documents used to conduct the raid of a sitting congresswoman's residence. The outlets claimed that viewing the documents was in the public interest, while the government attempted to block the release by arguing that it was a violation of investigative protocol.
Rep. lhan Omar, D-Minn., continues to generate headlines related to her finances.  (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE PAVES WAY TO UNSEAL ILHAN OMAR SEARCH WARRANT IN BLOW TO TRUMP'S DOJ

Omar's Washington, D.C., home was raided on Oct. 12, 2026 — an unprecedented action to take against a sitting lawmaker, especially when there is less than a month until the Election Day where they are seeking reelection. The raid did not impact Omar in winning a fifth term in the House of Representatives.

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the chief investigative body of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), conducted the raid last month. Omar's personal phone, computer and passport were seized as evidence in the search. Authorities are also in possession of her DNA.

Additionally, the lawmaker's sister, Sahra Noor, voluntarily submitted to questions from investigators during the week of the raid. Investigators are probing whether Omar or her late father — or both — lied on her citizenship paperwork, sources told Fox News Digital.

In a motion seeking to prevent the federal search warrant for the raid from being unsealed, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia referred to Omar as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar." Sources later told Fox News Digital that Ilhan Omar is not the congresswoman's "real name."

Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Oct. 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. According to reports, the search is part of an ongoing criminal investigation. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES
That news caused speculation that Omar married her brother, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, to resurface. The pair married in 2009, and divorced in 2017.
Omar has not been charged with a crime and has repeatedly denied wrongdoing. She has characterized the investigation as politically motivated, saying President Donald Trump is targeting her.

"For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," her office said in a statement after the raid. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."

The Somali-born congresswoman came to the United States as a child in 1995, after decades of civil unrest in her home country. Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, served as a colonel in the Somali National Army under the brutal Siad Barre regime.

Barre's regime systematically killed between 50,000 and 200,000 members of the Isaaq clan in what is known as the Isaaq genocide. He was deposed in 1991.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Former Navy SEAL says New Jersey’s Islamophobia bill puts protected speech in the crosshairs
summary: A former Navy SEAL and lawyer warns that New Jersey's Assembly Bill 1146 could function as a "backdoor blasphemy law" chilling public debate.
story: Bill Brown, a Parlatore Law Group partner and former Navy SEAL, tells Fox News Digital why he believes New Jersey’s Islamophobia bill could make people think twice before criticizing religious and political ideas.
A New Jersey proposal aimed at combating anti-Muslim discrimination could make Americans think twice before criticizing religious and political ideas, a lawyer and former Navy SEAL warned.

Bill Brown, a partner at Parlatore Law Group, told Fox News Digital that Assembly Bill 1146 contains language broad enough to discourage public debate, even though the legislation expressly preserves First Amendment rights.
"The mere threat of state scrutiny is a direct assault on public debate," Brown said.
TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS
A New Jersey bill would create a state definition of Islamophobia for officials to consider in certain civil and criminal matters. An unrelated photo shows Muslim men praying in Marseille, France.

The proposal would establish a state definition of Islamophobia and require public officials and law enforcement officers to consider it when determining whether alleged discriminatory acts were motivated by anti-Muslim bias.
Brown argued that requiring officials to use a definition that includes harsh criticism and other speech could make people afraid to speak openly.
CHRISTIAN GROUPS AND PASTORS SAY NEW CALIFORNIA LGBT HATE SPEECH LAW IS DISGUISED AS INDOCTRINATION
Shiite Muslims stand over a representation of an American flag during a rally to condemn Israeli strikes on Iran, in Karachi, Pakistan, Sunday, June 22, 2025. (Fareed Khan/AP Photo)
"The First Amendment guarantees that no religion or theology is immune to criticism," he said.

Democratic Assemblyman Joe Danielsen sponsors the bill, which is co-sponsored by fellow Democrats Assemblywomen Verlina Reynolds-Jackson and Mitchelle Drulis and Assemblyman Roy Freiman. The legislation describes a uniform definition as a tool to help officials identify and investigate anti-Muslim crime, harassment and discrimination."
Fox News Digital made multiple attempts to contact Danielsen and all three co-sponsors for comment but did not receive a response.
Its definition includes "hatred or severe disparagement towards Muslim persons or their culture," as well as "rhetorical, violent, or physical anti-Muslim manifestations."
Other examples include pulling hijabs from Muslim women, discriminatory treatment and blaming Muslims collectively for wrongdoing committed by an individual or group.
CONNECTICUT BARS NATIVITY DISPLAY IN STATE CAPITOL BECAUSE IT'S 'RELIGIOUS,' LAWSUIT THREAT SAYS

The bill would create no standalone criminal offense for criticizing Islam. It directs officials to consider the definition when reviewing an alleged violation of an existing policy, law or regulation prohibiting discriminatory acts.
It also explicitly says nothing in the legislation should diminish or infringe on rights protected by the First Amendment or New Jersey’s Constitution.
AMERICA'S FIRST MUSLIM SENATOR EXPOSES A POLITICAL BLIND SPOT
Asked about that safeguard, Brown maintained that the prospect of scrutiny itself could discourage people from speaking, regardless of whether a case ultimately succeeds.

He also singled out a provision in the bill’s legislative findings that lists "anti-Islamism" among terms that may describe the same characteristics as Islamophobia. Brown argued that the wording risks blurring the distinction between prejudice against Muslim people and criticism of a political movement.
JONATHAN TURLEY: FRANCE'S FREE SPEECH CRACKDOWN SHOWS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN POLITICIANS DEFINE TRUTH

Former Navy SEAL and attorney Bill Brown warns that New Jersey’s proposed Islamophobia bill could discourage Americans from criticizing religious and political ideas. (Jahi Chikwendiu/The Washington Post via Getty Images)
"Islamism is a distinct geopolitical movement," he said. "It’s not just a religious faith."
Brown described the proposal as a "backdoor blasphemy law," arguing that government should protect people’s rights while allowing their religious beliefs to face public scrutiny.
PASTOR UNLEASHES ON DEARBORN AS RELIGIOUS TENSIONS ERUPT AT CITY COUNCIL MEETING: 'ENOUGH IS ENOUGH'

The measure would require officials to consider its definition when reviewing alleged violations of existing anti-discrimination laws, while also preserving First Amendment protections. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)

The legislation excludes criticism of Muslim-majority countries comparable to criticism directed at other countries. Brown argued that criticism of religious and political ideology also needs protection.
Brown said his concerns are informed in part by his military service. He recalled responding to two suicide bombings in Iraq and said he remains committed to speaking out against jihadist ideology.
He also recalled studying Arabic at Rutgers after leaving the military, where Muslim American classmates helped him when he struggled with the language.
For Brown, the broader concern is whether Americans will feel free to challenge ideas they oppose.
