Fox News Digital has reached out to Van Drew's office for comment on the indictment. A spokesperson previously told Fox News Digital after Greene's initial arrest that she was "no longer associated with the Congressman's government office," adding, "our thoughts and prayers are with her" and "we hope she's getting the care she needs."
Fox News Digital reached out to attorneys for Greene and Ventnor.

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

title: Iran to execute 2 anti-regime protesters at dawn after 3 days in death row holding cells
summary: Iran Human Rights urges UN intervention as two political prisoners await execution at Ghezel Hesar Prison in Iran's high-profile "Ekbatan case."
story: Fox News reports on Iran's escalating human rights abuses as the regime executes protestors, with 13 killed since the conflict started.

Two Iranian anti-regime protesters face execution within hours after spending three days in pre-execution holding cells at Ghezel Hesar Prison, according to a human rights organization warning that the men were sentenced to death following torture, forced confessions and unfair trials.
Milad Armoun, 27, and Navid Najaran, 34, are scheduled to be executed in the early hours of Wednesday, Nov. 25, according to Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO).
The men were transferred to solitary confinement on Nov. 21 after Iran's Supreme Court upheld their death sentences.
IRANIAN BOXER ON DEATH ROW WINS HUMAN RIGHTS AWARD AS ATHLETES PUSH TO SAVE HIS LIFE

An armed member of Iran's police special forces adjusts a country flag on an armored military vehicle during a pro-government rally in downtown Tehran, Iran, on Jan. 12, 2026. The rally was held against recent anti-government unrest and in support of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. (NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Both men were arrested during Iran's 2022 "Woman, Life, Freedom" uprising and are defendants in the high-profile "Ekbatan case," which stems from the killing of a member of Iran's Basij paramilitary force during nationwide anti-government demonstrations.
Exiled Iranian crown prince Reza Phahlavi said on X on Tuesday that the execution would take place at dawn.
IRANIAN REGIME CRITIC WARNS TRUMP DEAL COULD BE 'LIFELINE' FOR REGIME, CLAIMS PEOPLE ARE 'NERVOUS'
Iranians gather while blocking a street during a protest in Tehran, Iran on January 9, 2026. (Mahsa/ Middle East Images / AFP via Getty Images)
"Despite being acquitted of the murder charge, Milad Armon and Navid Najjaran have been sentenced to death by "hanging judge" Abolqasem Salavati.
"The execution orders for these two political prisoners have been sent to their lawyers, to be carried out at dawn on Wednesday, Azar 4."
"Milad and Navid were held in Ward 33 which houses those accused of murder before being transferred to solitary confinement in preparation for their executions today," a source told IHRNGO.

The men were sentenced to death in May by Branch 15 of Tehran's Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Abolqasem Salavati, on charges of efsad-fil-arz , or "corruption on earth," a capital offense under Iranian law.
Salavati has faced longstanding criticism from human rights organizations over his handling of political cases and the harsh sentences imposed on government opponents.
Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of Iran Human Rights, condemned the sentences and called for immediate international intervention.

"Milad Armoun and Navid Najaran were sentenced to death following torture, forced confessions and grossly unfair trials. Their executions would be an irreversible injustice and another example of the Islamic Republic’s use of the death penalty as a tool of political repression.
IRAN HANGS 2 PROTESTERS IN PUBLIC, CROWD CRIES 'DISHONORABLE' AS SECURITY FIRES TEAR GAS

Protestors burn images of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei during a rally held in Solidarity with Iran's Uprising, organised by The national Council of Resistance of Iran, on Whitehall in central London Jan. 11, 2026, to protest against the Iranian regime's crackdown on internet access and "recognise their right to self-defence against the regime's forces". (Carlos Jasso/AFP via Getty Images)

"Strong international reactions may be the only way to save their lives. We urge the UN and all governments with diplomatic relations with the Islamic Republic to intervene immediately to stop their executions," Amiry-Moghaddam said in a statement.
The Ekbatan case centers on the death of Arman Aliverdi, a member of the Basij, a volunteer paramilitary force affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Aliverdi was injured during unrest in Tehran's Ekbatan neighborhood in 2022, and died two days later. Iranian authorities accused several protesters of involvement in his death.
Armoun was arrested in Tehran in November 2022, while Najaran was detained the following month in Ahvaz.
Iran Human Rights alleged that both men were tortured and subjected to ill-treatment to obtain self-incriminating confessions subsequently broadcast by Iranian state media.
IRAN JAILS PSYCHOLOGIST OVER TRUMP PLEA AS REGIME DEMANDS HE MAKE AMERICANS ‘LOOK STUPID’: FAMILY

People attend a protest against the Iranian regime, in Berlin, Germany, Saturday, Oct. 22, 2022, following the death of Mahsa Amini in the custody of the Islamic republic's notorious "morality police." (Markus Schreiber/ AP Photo)
Defense attorneys also accused judicial authorities of barring lawyers from hearings, withholding case documents and obstructing appeals.

Earlier death sentences tied to murder charges were overturned, and Najaran was acquitted of involvement in the killing in a separate proceeding. However, the Revolutionary Court subsequently imposed death sentences under Iran's national security laws.
The death sentences of two other defendants, Mehdi Imani and Seyed Mohammad Mehdi Hosseini, were overturned, and their cases referred for retrial, according to human rights organizations.

The "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement erupted in 2022 following the death of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish Iranian woman detained by morality police over allegations that she improperly wore her hijab.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The demonstrations spread nationwide, becoming one of the most significant challenges to Iran's clerical leadership in decades.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Vatican releases Pope Francis' private diary detailing spiritual crisis, encounters with the devil
summary: Pope Francis' private diary reveals a two-year spiritual crisis from 2021, with the late pontiff writing he felt tempted by the devil and saw hell in 2018.
story: Vatican releases Pope Francis' private diary, detailing a spiritual crisis and encounters with the devil, as theologian Jonathan Morris joins Stuart Varney to react. They also analyze actor Mark Ruffalo calling to oust Sen. Chuck Schumer and replace him with Sen. Chris Van Hollen.

Excerpts from the late Pope Francis' private diary published Tuesday reveal that the pontiff endured a two-year spiritual crisis beginning in 2021, writing that he felt tempted by the devil and struggled with the weight of wielding power over the Catholic Church.

The 160-page volume, "The Private Diary of Pope Francis," was compiled by Cardinal Victor Fernandez and spans entries from December 1992 through August 2024 — eight months before Francis died in April 2025 at age 88 — marking the first papal diary made public since the 1960s.

In a December 2022 entry, Francis described his crisis as "all mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation," adding that he resisted becoming a leader "who uses others like puppets."
MYSTERIOUS BLOOD-SOAKED RELIC LINKED TO HISTORY'S MOST BELOVED SAINT, ST. FRANCIS OF ASSISI, GOES ON DISPLAY
Pope Francis celebrates a mass with members of different religious orders in St. Peter's Basilica at the Vatican, Friday, Feb. 2, 2018. (The Associated Press, File)
Across the entries, Francis wrote that he believed he had seen the devil three times — including during a Vatican meeting — and recalled a June 2018 vision of hell.
"Last night I saw the entrance to Hell," he wrote in the 2018 entry. "I peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me. I grabbed the Rosary as a weapon. I thank the Lord for this help."

Reacting Tuesday on "Varney & Co.," Fox News contributor and theologian Jonathan Morris said he was most struck not by the late pope's spiritual struggles, but by the Vatican's decision to publish them.
POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL
Pope Francis officiates at the General Audience in Saint Peter's Square with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle. (Grzegorz Galazka/Mondadori Portfolio via Getty Images)

"I think the most surprising part is that this was actually published, not so much that it happened, " Morris said. "Spiritual warfare is a very basic Christian doctrine, and even the last things — death, judgment, heaven, hell. And apparently he saw the gates of hell. Those are the core beliefs of the church across all sorts of denominations within Christianity."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Morris added that Francis' successor, Pope Leo XIV — whom Francis praised in the diary as "a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man" — approved releasing the writings so they might help others facing similar trials.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Israel raises prospect of preemptive strike over emerging Iranian chemical weapons threat
summary: Israel Katz says Israel and the U.S. hold intelligence on Iran's alleged chemical weapons program, warning a preemptive strike remains possible.
story: Asked by Fox News senior White House correspondent Jacqui Heinrich about a reported dirty bomb plot targeting D.C., Trump says Iran is looking at biological weapons and says "we’ll see what happens" after Jan. 1, 2027.

Israel accused Iran of developing chemical weapons Tuesday and raised the possibility of a preemptive strike to prevent Tehran from using them, warning that the regime seeks a strategic advantage after major setbacks in its war with Israel and the United States.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz told reporters in Tel Aviv that Israel and the U.S. have intelligence indicating Iran began developing chemical weapons after their joint military campaign launched Feb. 28.

Katz declined to disclose how far the program has progressed or where the weapons are being developed, though he noted Israeli intelligence has monitored Iran's effort for months and said that operational plans are in place.
BLINKEN WARNS US GROUND INVASION OF IRAN WOULD BE 'ABSOLUTE DISASTER' AS TEHRAN ESCALATES ATTACKS

Joint press statements by the Greek Minister of National Defense, Nikos Dendias, and the Israeli Minister of Defense, Israel Katz, at the Ministry of National Defense, Athens, January 20, 2026. (Nick Paleologos / SOOC / AFP via Getty Images)
"Iran is in the process of developing chemical weapons," Katz said, according to Israel's i24NEWS.
"This intelligence information reached both the United States and Israel," he said.
"Israel is determined not to allow Iran to acquire this kind of chemical weapons capability that would threaten the country and the entire region," he added.

Katz described the program as a potentially game-changing threat to Israel and the broader Middle East, warning that the weapons could give Tehran leverage to rebuild its depleted military infrastructure, including its nuclear program.
LIVE WWII-ERA GRENADES TURN UP IN UNLIKELY PLACE; BOMB SQUAD WARNS OF DANGER

Iranian flags fly as fire and smoke from an Israeli attack on Sharan Oil depot rise, following Israeli strikes on Iran, in Tehran, Iran, June 15, 2025. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via Reuters)
"They came out of the tunnels and saw what happened to them," Katz said of Iranian forces following the April ceasefire, according to comments reported by The Times of Israel.

"They are looking for a weapon that gives them some balance against us. This process in Iran is new and comes in the wake of the damage they suffered. True, it is not nuclear, but it is still unconventional weapons."
"If we thought this was already an unfolding event, we would act," Katz said.
Katz also said that Israel must maintain the ability to act preemptively if intelligence shows an Iranian attack is imminent.
"If the Iranians attack us first, it will be a failure," Katz said, according to Israel's Ynet news outlet.
ISRAEL’S LEADING CONTENDER FOR PRIME MINISTER CLASHES WITH NETANYAHU OVER IRAN STRIKES
President Donald Trump and an image of an Israeli strike on Iran. Trump said he believes Israel and Iran can strike a deal to halt the fighting between both nations. (Getty Images/AP)
The allegations come amid heightened U. S. intelligence concerns over Iranian threats against the American homeland.

CNN reported Nov. 16, citing seven U. S. officials, that American intelligence indicated Iran was developing plans to potentially target senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a radiological "dirty bomb" or chemical weapon.
Sources familiar with the intelligence described the planning as an effort to preserve potential retaliatory options rather than evidence of an imminent strike.
The White House said at the time that it was monitoring potential threats but had identified no credible threats to the U.S. homeland.
President Donald Trump subsequently warned that Iran would face severe consequences if it carried out such an attack.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the reporting as "Iraq War-style propaganda" with "Israeli fingerprints all over it."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Nobody is buying it," Araghchi wrote on X.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: NATO fighter jet cleared to shoot down Russian missile over Poland as Warsaw pushes for US troops
summary: Poland renewed its push for permanent U.S. troops after a Russian drone entered its airspace Nov. 24, days after three Kh-101 missile violations.
story: Fox News anchor Jon Scott reports on NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warning the alliance will defend every inch of Polish territory after a suspected airspace breach by Russia on ‘Fox Report.’

Poland announced Tuesday it had renewed its push for a permanent U.S. military presence in the country after two Russian airspace incursions in four days, including one in which a Swedish fighter jet under NATO command was cleared to shoot down a Russian cruise missile but held its fire.

The latest incursion came overnight Nov. 24, when a Russian drone briefly entered Polish airspace during attacks on Ukraine, four days after three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles had crossed into Poland, prompting NATO to scramble fighter jets and bolster air defenses along its eastern flank.

Poland's chargé d'affaires in Washington, Bogdan Klich, said Tuesday that he briefed the White House National Security Council on the violations and renewed Warsaw's call to permanently station American troops in the NATO member country.
US URGES AMERICANS IN HISTORIC REGION TO STAY ALERT AFTER 'DANGEROUS' AIRSPACE INCIDENT

"Yesterday, I briefed the U.S. National Security Council on the violation of Polish airspace by Russian Kh-101 missiles and once again discussed the issue of the permanent deployment of U.S. troops in Poland," Klich wrote on X.
The new diplomatic push follows the incidents involving Russian assets and heightened concerns that Moscow's war in Ukraine will spill into NATO territory.

The Nov. 20 incursion involved a Swedish JAS 39 Gripen pilot operating under NATO command who was authorized to engage a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, according to Lt. Gen. Ireneusz Nowak, commander of Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command, as reported by The Kyiv Independent.

NATO's Combined Air Operations Centre in Uedem, Germany, issued conditional authorization to fire, but the pilot could not positively identify the object visually or through the aircraft's onboard electro-optical systems because of severe weather, Nowak said. No weapons were fired.
SUPERSONIC RUSSIAN JETS TRIGGER JOINT SCRAMBLE BY NATO ALLIES AMID PUTIN 'CLOWNS' JAB

Russian President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting aboard the missile cruiser Varyag in Russia's far eastern Sakhalin region Aug. 12, 2026. Putin previously said Russia is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe. (Reuters/File)
Polish authorities monitored 11 potentially threatening aerial objects during the attack, three of which entered the country's airspace, according to Nowak.
The Swedish Armed Forces said its jets had tracked several unidentified objects over Poland during the mission, which lasted several hours under difficult weather conditions.
Polish F-16 fighter jets, a Swedish Saab 340 early warning aircraft, a Dutch aerial refueling aircraft and ground-based air defense systems were also supporting the operation.

Polish prosecutors confirmed Sunday that debris recovered at three locations belonged to Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles, revising an initial military assessment that one of the objects might have been a drone, according to reports.
RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS

His warning comes as NATO confronts a series of airspace violations, drone incidents and hybrid activity along its eastern flank. NATO’s military leadership said Friday that Russia’s actions continue to "test Allied resolve." (Olena Bartienieva/Getty Images)
Preliminary findings indicated the missiles were manufactured in October or November 2026 at a factory in Dubna in Russia's Moscow region, prosecutors said.
The second incursion happened overnight Nov. 24, when a Russian drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine during another wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine.

Polish forces tracked the unmanned aircraft and received authorization to shoot it down but did not fire after it changed course and headed east, citing potential risks to civilians and property on the ground.
Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski said Polish authorities believed the violation was deliberate.
"It's hard to imagine this being a coincidence, so we assume it was an intentional act," Zalewski told RMF FM, according to Reuters.

After an emergency meeting of the North Atlantic Council on Monday, Nov. 23, NATO's supreme allied commander in Europe went on to authorize the forward deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System, or AWACS, aircraft to Poland.
NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski addresses a joint news conference at a meeting of the foreign ministers of the so-called Weimar Triangle of France, Germany and Poland with Ukraine's foreign minister in Warsaw Sept. 29, 2025 (Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images)

"All Allies stand in full solidarity with Poland. NATO remains united, ready, and committed to defending against any threat," NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said on X and as Warsaw summoned Russia's ambassador, according to Reuters.
In September, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said U.S. and Polish officials were working toward an agreement that could accommodate up to 10,000 American troops.
Roughly 7,000 U.S. troops were stationed in Poland on a rotational basis at the time while a permanent installation would expand Washington's military commitment along NATO's eastern flank.
"We want the kind of U.S. presence that would reassure us but not be threatening to Russia," Sikorski said during a Council on Foreign Relations event in New York, Bloomberg reported.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
President Donald Trump has previously voiced his support for a permanent U.S. military base in Poland, although Washington has also reviewed American troop deployments across Europe.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: European leader warns Russian aggression could escalate within weeks or months
summary: Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs warns Russia is escalating sabotage, arson and assassination plots against NATO countries that could worsen in weeks.
story: In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs warns of growing Russian threats against NATO and says the West misunderstands Putin’s ideological ambitions.

Russia is growing increasingly willing to take risks against NATO countries, with a mounting campaign of sabotage, arson attacks and assassination plots that could escalate within weeks or months, Latvia’s president warned in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs said Western leaders may be underestimating the threat posed by Russian President Vladimir Putin because they fail to fully understand the ideological and historical beliefs driving the Kremlin’s foreign policy.
"The appetite for the risk is growing in Russia," Rinkēvičs said. "We see numbers of arson attacks. Some assassination plots. Acts of sabotage."
BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT
Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs chairs and addresses the U.N. Security Council meeting on Ukraine Nov. 23, 2026 (Dāvis Doršs/ Chancery of the President of Latvia)

While Russian provocations have so far remained below the threshold that would trigger NATO’s collective defense mechanism under Article 5, Rinkēvičs warned that the situation could deteriorate rapidly.
"We see that the number of attacks is rising, but we still see that, at this point, it may change very quickly. It may change maybe in weeks or months or a couple of months' time," he said.
The Latvian leader pointed to recent cooperation between Latvian and Estonian intelligence services that he said resulted in arrests in Estonia and prevented an attack against a defense factory.
He said the escalating campaign is part of Moscow’s strategy to discourage European countries from continuing to support Ukraine.
DENMARK ACCUSES RUSSIA OF PLOTTING TO KILL UKRAINIAN AMERICAN RAPPER ON DANISH SOIL

Russian President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting aboard the missile cruiser Varyag in Russia's far eastern Sakhalin region Aug. 12, 2026. Putin previously said Russia is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe. (Reuters/File)

His warning comes just days after President Donald Trump met with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 19, for unprecedented talks that addressed the war in Ukraine and nuclear arms control.

On Monday, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said Ukraine and NATO countries had already created circumstances in which Moscow could contemplate using nuclear weapons.

Medvedev also raised the possibility of a preemptive nuclear strike if Western countries supplied Ukraine with nuclear weapons, while acknowledging that Russia’s nuclear doctrine does not explicitly provide for preventive strikes, Anadolu reported.
TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE

Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump attend a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 19, 2026. (Reuters)

Rinkēvičs argued that Western governments need to reconsider how they interpret Putin’s motivations, suggesting that conventional military, economic and political calculations alone cannot explain the Kremlin’s determination to continue the war.
"We are too pragmatic and rational in the West," he said.

The Latvian president pointed to Putin’s recent interviews, saying he was struck by the Russian leader’s ideological and religious references, including the historical concept of Russia as the "Third Rome" and its perceived mission to safeguard Christianity.
"I think that this kind of belief also drives the war," Rinkēvičs said, describing a "missionary approach that we in the West do not understand because we are too rational and too pragmatic."
While Rinkēvičs welcomed continued engagement between Washington and Moscow, he said last week’s summit had not produced a diplomatic breakthrough on Ukraine.
"Russia is not willing to end this war," he said.
He argued that Moscow is using diplomatic engagement to extend the conflict in the hope of securing further gains both militarily and at the negotiating table.

Rinkēvičs said the combination of Russian ideological ambitions, escalating operations against Western countries, upcoming European elections in France, Poland and Italy and political debates in the U.S. could encourage Moscow to continue the fighting.
ZELENSKYY PRESSES US FOR EXPANDED RUSSIA TALKS AS KUSHNER ANNOUNCES BREAKTHROUGH

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ukrainian Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko visit the Dormition Cathedral of the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, which was hit during Russian missile and drone strikes, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine, June 15, 2026. (Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Handout via Reuters)

The Latvian State Security Service confirmed that eight Latvian nationals were detained in Estonia on Nov. 14, after authorities thwarted an attempted arson attack against Threod Systems, an Estonian drone manufacturer.
Estonian security officials attributed the operation to Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU.

Estonia subsequently announced it would close its land border with Russia beginning Dec. 1, for at least six months. Russia’s Foreign Ministry responded Monday by accusing Estonia of hostile actions "on the verge of triggering open war," Reuters reported.

British security officials also warned Tuesday that companies supporting Ukraine’s military should prepare for potential Russian sabotage attempts after a series of incidents across Europe, The Associated Press reported.
The Kremlin has consistently denied conducting sabotage operations against NATO countries.

As Fox News Digital reported Monday, new Western intelligence assessments suggest Russia could launch a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon within weeks, potentially threatening thousands of satellites used by the U.S. and its allies.

Rinkēvičs said he could not confirm the intelligence assessments but warned that Russia’s pursuit of advanced weapons requires greater Western investment in missile defenses, drones and emerging technologies.
"Russia is developing nuclear weapons, developing new technologies and we have to be extremely, extremely careful," he said.
However, he cautioned that Moscow has previously overstated its military capabilities.
"Whether that weapon in space, nuclear weapon in space is going to be the real thing or just a kind of fake news, remains to be seen," he said.

Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs warned in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital that Russia’s growing appetite for risk could lead to further escalation against NATO countries. (Davis Dorss/ Chancery of the President of Latvia)

Despite his warnings, Rinkēvičs said an opportunity for meaningful negotiations could emerge next spring or summer if Ukraine withstands Russia’s winter offensive against its civilian and energy infrastructure.
"I'm quite confident Ukraine is going to survive. Unfortunately, the big question is at what human cost," he said.

Speaking at a U.N. Security Council meeting on Ukraine Monday, Rinkēvičs said Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure had reached their highest level since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
He warned that millions of Ukrainians face the prospect of spending the winter without electricity, heating or running water.
"Winter must never be a weapon of war," he told the council.
Rinkēvičs also praised the Oleshky ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump as evidence that diplomatic pressure and political will can produce results.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Emergency employees work at the site of a Russian missile strike during Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv region, Ukraine, July 24, 2026. (Press service of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine/Handout via Reuters)
For now, however, he remains skeptical that Moscow is genuinely seeking peace.
"Currently, Russia explores diplomatic efforts in order to prolong the war, not to end the war," he told Fox News Digital.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this article.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Ex- Ukraine prosecutor general accuses Zelenskyy's office of interfering in anti-corruption investigation
summary: Former prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko alleges political interference, while Zelenskyy defended his removal and anti-corruption agencies rejected the accusations.
story: Fox News correspondent Stephanie Bennett reports on the Trump administration’s push for a deal between Russia and Ukraine on ‘Fox Report.’

Ukraine's former prosecutor general is accusing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's administration of interfering in a criminal investigation involving the head of the country's anti-corruption bureau after the president demanded his removal from office in September.

In an extensive interview with Fox News Digital, Ruslan Kravchenko alleged that Zelenskyy's decision to remove him came under pressure from the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), whose officials he said his office had been investigating.

"The signature on the resignation letter was mine. The decision was his," Kravchenko said. "You do not have to put handcuffs on the president himself to tie his hands. It is enough to put the people he relies on at risk."
BILLIONS IN US AID TO UKRAINE UNDER MICROSCOPE AS CORRUPTION ROCKS ZELENSKYY’S INNER CIRCLE
Former Prosecutor General of Ukraine Ruslan Kravchenko attends a press conference in Kyiv, Ukraine July 23, 2025. (Thomas Peter/Reuters)
Kravchenko's most serious allegation concerns what happened afterward. He claims the president's office instructed prosecutors to close a criminal case involving NABU Director Semen Kryvonos.

"The Office of the President began issuing instructions to the Office of the Prosecutor General to immediately close the criminal case against the head of NABU," he said. "In my assessment, that amounts to deliberate interference in an investigation."
"The authority to investigate crimes becomes the ability to determine government policy and even geopolitics," he argued.

Kravchenko did not identify who allegedly issued those instructions or provide documentary evidence of the communications in the materials supplied to Fox News Digital. His allegation of presidential interference has not been independently verified.
UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY ON DEFYING US IN ATTACKING RUSSIAN OIL: 'OUR RESPONSE MUST BE PAINFUL'
Prosecutor General of Ukraine Ruslan Kravchenko attends a press conference in Kyiv, July 23, 2025. (Thomas Peter/Reuters)

Kravchenko's departure followed a September investigation known as Operation Carthage, in which NABU and SAPO accused officials connected to the Prosecutor General's Office of helping protect fraudulent call centers and laundering criminal proceeds.

According to a Sept. 8 report in The Guardian, the investigation centered on fraudulent call centers whose employees impersonated banks, police officers and investment advisers to steal money from victims in Ukraine, Russia and Europe. NABU alleged that a senior official in the Prosecutor General's Office protected the operation and helped launder its proceeds.

Law enforcement sources told Ukrainska Pravda that individual call centers paid approximately $7,000 a month in protection money. Investigators also released recordings suggesting that the principal suspect had overseen repairs at Kravchenko's home while allegedly collecting bribes.

Kravchenko, who has not been charged in the investigation, denies wrongdoing and rejects the allegations against his office. He claimed the operation was intended to seize investigative materials concerning misconduct by anti-corruption officials and prevent him from pursuing those cases.

He said he initially refused to resign but changed his position following a Sept. 7 meeting with Zelenskyy, attended, according to Kravchenko, by Davyd Arakhamia, leader of the president's parliamentary faction.

"When the president wants your resignation and the leader of his parliamentary faction, which commands a majority, is sitting beside him, believe me: a prosecutor general's room for maneuver is extremely limited," he said.
Zelenskyy publicly confirmed that he had demanded Kravchenko's removal.
"There is only one path for this Prosecutor General: removal from office. That is what I told him," Zelenskyy said in a Sept. 14 statement, according to Reuters.

Zelenskyy also said that if Kravchenko considered the decision political pressure, he was free to characterize it that way. The president suspended him on Sept. 14, and parliament approved his dismissal the following day.
ZELENSKYY PRESSES US FOR EXPANDED RUSSIA TALKS AS KUSHNER ANNOUNCES BREAKTHROUGH
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during a briefing in Kyiv, Jan. 3, 2026. (Danylo Antoniuk/AP)
The confrontation intensified when Kravchenko announced on Sept. 14 that he had signed a notice of suspicion against Kryvonos over alleged misconduct predating his appointment as NABU director.

Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office disputed the validity of the notice, stating that Kryvonos had not been formally notified of suspicion under Ukrainian law and that relevant entries in the investigative register had been deleted.
Kravchenko alleges those actions followed pressure from the president's administration. The claim remains unverified.

NABU and SAPO have rejected Kravchenko's broader accusations, describing them as a campaign against independent anti-corruption institutions. In a Nov. 4 announcement, the agencies said Operation Carthage had uncovered an alleged criminal network involving senior law-enforcement officials accused of protecting fraudulent businesses. Those allegations have not been proven in court.

The controversy comes amid widespread public concern about corruption. A September survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that 72% of Ukrainians held Zelenskyy politically responsible for corruption among his associates, although the findings did not suggest respondents believed he was personally involved.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and former head of the presidential office, Andriy Yermak, in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Jan. 22, 2024. (Maxym Marusenko/NurPhoto via AP)

Zelenskyy has publicly condemned the widening investigation's allegations. In a Nov. 7 address, he described alleged misconduct involving senior security officials as "frankly shameful, absolutely unacceptable," according to Reuters, and called for a full investigation.

His former chief of staff, Andriy Yermak, defended him in an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, amid an earlier corruption scandal in November 2025, describing Zelenskyy as "not corrupt" and saying he had allowed independent anti-corruption investigations.
Zelenskyy's office did not respond to multiple requests from Fox News Digital for comment on Kravchenko's latest allegations.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The offices of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine, on Oct. 1, 2019, in Kyiv. (Sean Gallup/Getty)

The former prosecutor general maintains that his removal prevented him from pursuing investigations into the leadership of the anti-corruption agencies. Ukrainian authorities, meanwhile, have publicly defended the investigation that preceded his dismissal.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. title: Former Florida mayor urges American Jews to fight back against rising antisemitism
summary: In "The Jewish Fight for America," Gabe Groisman says forces on the left and right are trying to distance American Jews from Israel and unlearn Zionism.
story: Hunter College was the site of a protest after the school’s student government canceled an event that involved a Jewish organization.

As antisemitism surges across the United States and around the world in the wake of Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, massacre, policy strategist and public speaker Gabe Groisman is urging American Jews to stand their ground and fight for the future of their community — and the soul of the nation.

In his new book, "The Jewish Fight for America," Groisman, a former mayor of Bal Harbour, Florida, explores the history of American Jews and their contributions to the country, arguing that despite rising antisemitism, they should confront the tide of hate and stand firm in their rightful place.

"The first fight we have to take on here in the U.S. is to strengthen the community, to try to teach our brothers and sisters about who we are as a people," Groisman told Fox News Digital. "Then we can get to the part of why the Land of Israel is important to us, why Jewish sovereignty over the Land of Israel, which is the State of Israel today, is an integral part of who we are as Jews in America or anywhere in the world."
CHRISTIAN ZIONISTS TAKE ON ANTI-ISRAEL ‘PROPAGANDA’ FROM BIBLICAL HEARTLAND
Anti-Israel activists march with banners during a protest on May 15, 2025, in Brooklyn, New York. (Alexi Rosenfeld/Getty Images)

One of the book’s chapters opens with quotes from Genesis. Groisman explained that powerful forces are seeking to distance American Jews from Israel. On the left, he said, a movement is seeking to "unlearn Zionism," while on the right, critics attack Zionism through the lens of dual loyalty.

"These days, people are afraid to connect things to the Bible, but it is critical to do so. It is the only way to honestly understand where our connection to that land begins. It begins with the Bible and the words of God himself," Groisman said.
Gabe Groisman holds a copy of his new book, "The Jewish Fight for America." (Gabe Groisman)

He noted that only 26% of American Jews say they believe in "God as described in the Bible," per a Pew Research Center study published in May 2021. According to the study, another 50% believe in some other spiritual force.
"Most American Jews don't hold a biblical or Judeo-Christian understanding of God, and I think that's a huge reason why most don't look to the Bible for their connection to the land," said Groisman.
"When they are asked to defend their connection to the Land of Israel or to the State of Israel, they can’t begin to respond in a proper way because they don’t believe in God," he added.
Groisman has practiced law for more than 20 years, litigating cases nationwide and participating in legal challenges on behalf of the Jewish community.
A NEW CHAPTER FOR AMERICA’S 250TH: 'J250' INITIATIVE PUTS JEWISH CONTRIBUTIONS IN THE SPOTLIGHT
A close-up image of a Jewish man wearing a traditional tallit (prayer shawl) and tefillin during morning prayers. (iStock)
During his tenure as mayor, Groisman passed what he describes as the nation's first anti-Israel boycott ordinance, as well as the first municipal ordinance adopting a definition of antisemitism.

Groisman said the book seeks to address a question American Jews across the country are asking privately: What is the future of Jews in America, and is it time to leave? His answer, he said, is an emphatic no.

"Jewish American history is not well taught, not even in Jewish circles. We need to understand that this community has been here since before day one and has played integral roles in this country. The religious liberties established in this country from the beginning were meant to benefit groups explicitly like the Jews, who were here from day one," he said.

For American Jews, Groisman said, the solution lies in helping young people reconnect with their identity. He argued that a strong sense of identity and purpose, rooted in their Jewish religion and national heritage, can help them become confident American Jews and thrive in the United States.
"America is not about freedom from religion; it’s about freedom of religion. You are allowed to be who you are as an American and still be as American as everybody else," he said.

In his book, Groisman examines developments over the past several years that he believes have contributed to the surge in antisemitism, including the rise of intersectionality and critical race theory on the left and their growing influence in academic and intellectual circles, which he says have received significant funding from foreign actors.
SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

Members of the NYPD’s Counterterrorism Unit stand guard outside the Jewish Museum in New York City, May 22, 2025, part of an increase in security at Jewish organizations nationwide after an Israeli couple was killed in Washington, D.C. (Kevin C. Downs for Fox News Digital)

Groisman pointed to foreign funding flowing into American universities, warning that "that money comes with strings attached" and is intended "to create chaos in our country." He argued that foreign actors unable to defeat the United States militarily seek to weaken it by creating internal divisions, with antisemitism serving as "a useful tool" in that effort.

"When we saw actors in this country, in the aftermath of Oct. 7 and even before Israel responded in Gaza, being coordinated and directed by foreign actors in the United States, all the way down to small chapters on college campuses across the country, that requires years and years of coordination," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
People hold an Israeli and U.S. flag in front of a large group of anti-Israel protesters outside The Grove shopping center in Los Angeles, Nov. 24, 2023. (David Swanson/AFP via Getty Images)
Groisman said his book offers a message of optimism, emphasizing his faith in America, its political system and the American people’s ability to confront these challenges.

"For the American Jewish community, this book will hopefully help swing the pendulum back, encouraging people to recalibrate and put our country — and the American Jewish community as an integral part of it — back on track," he said.
Amelie Botbol is a freelance field reporter based in Tel Aviv, Israel, who reports on Israel-related news.

title: Iran flogs female singer 74 times for performing without hijab in viral YouTube concert
summary: Lawyers said singer Parastoo Ahmadi and members of her concert team received 74 lashes each in Qom after performing without a hijab. They also face two-year bans.
story: Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi faces 74 lashes and a travel ban for performing without a hijab, sparking international outrage. Zineb Riboua joins Fox News to discuss the regime's brutal crackdown on dissidents, attributing it to the Islamic Republic's growing weakness amid internal protests and external pressures. She emphasizes the need for international pressure on the Iranian regime.

Iranian authorities subjected a female singer and four members of her concert team to 74 lashes each Monday after she defied the Islamic Republic’s restrictions on women by performing without a hijab in a viral YouTube concert, their lawyers said.
Parastoo Ahmadi, 29, and her four male co-defendants were flogged in the Iranian city of Qom, defense attorney Mostafa Nili told Iranian news outlet Emtedad, according to Reuters.
The five were also banned from traveling abroad and engaging in artistic and musical activities for two years.
IRAN'S REGIME CAME FOR TEENAGE TWINS. THEIR FATE OFFERS A GLIMPSE OF TEHRAN'S WIDENING DEATH CAMPAIGN
Parastoo Ahmadi sings in a live performance filmed near Qom, Iran, in December 2024. (Parastoo Ahmadi/YouTube)

One of the defendants’ lawyers told the BBC Monday that efforts to overturn the ruling, reduce the punishment or suspend its enforcement had failed. Defense attorneys also sought to postpone the flogging, but authorities insisted on carrying out the sentence immediately.
The punishment sparked outrage among Iranian artists and human rights advocates, who condemned the regime’s restrictions on women and artistic expression.

Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the U.S.-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI), told the BBC that Ahmadi’s flogging was "a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights" and demonstrated the authorities’ determination to suppress women’s freedoms and punish those who challenge discriminatory laws.
Those flogged alongside Ahmadi were musicians Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri and Amirali Pirnia and producer Mohsen Lashkari.
IRAN REGIME'S EXECUTION SPREE CONTINUES AS TWINS FACE DEATH PENALTY, DECADES IN PRISON AFTER ALLEGED TORTURE

Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi performs alongside her band without a hijab during a concert released on YouTube on Dec. 11, 2024. Iranian authorities subjected Ahmadi and four members of her concert team to 74 lashes each on Nov. 23, 2026, according to their lawyers. (Parastoo Ahmadi/Youtube)

The case stems from a Dec. 11, 2024, performance in which Ahmadi appeared in a sleeveless black dress with her hair uncovered, accompanied by male musicians at the historic Deir Gachin Caravanserai in Qom province.
With no audience physically present, Ahmadi shared the performance, known as the "Imaginary Concert," on her YouTube channel.
The video of the concert has garnered over 3 million views on YouTube.

Iran’s judiciary swiftly opened a criminal case over the performance, and Ahmadi was arrested three days later. Two musicians involved in the concert were also arrested. All three were subsequently released on bail, according to the Norway-based Hengaw Organization for Human Rights.

In June 2026, a criminal court in Qom sentenced Ahmadi and eight others involved in the production to 74 lashes each on charges of "offending public decency by producing and publishing obscene and immoral content online," according to Hengaw.
The defendants denied the charges. An appeals court upheld the flogging sentences in September, clearing the way for their enforcement, Iran International reported Sept. 25.
IRAN JAILS PSYCHOLOGIST OVER TRUMP PLEA AS REGIME DEMANDS HE MAKE AMERICANS ‘LOOK STUPID’: FAMILY

Maryam Shariatmadari was detained by Iranian security forces after removing her hijab in protest against mandatory veiling laws during the "Girls of Revolution Street" demonstrations in Tehran. Shariatmadari was later sentenced to one year in prison for what authorities described as "encouraging corruption by removing her hijab." (Fox News)

Amnesty International urged Iranian authorities in October to abandon plans to carry out the sentences, arguing that judicial flogging amounts to torture and violates international human rights protections.

Ahmadi, a native of Nowshahr in northern Iran who studied film directing at Soore University, had previously faced restrictions from Iranian security authorities over her performances of protest songs and regional folk music during the Woman, Life, Freedom movement, according to Hengaw.

The movement erupted in September 2022 following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Iranian Kurdish woman detained by the country’s morality police for allegedly violating mandatory hijab rules.
Many Iranian women have since openly defied the compulsory dress code, despite periodic arrests, warnings and other enforcement measures.
Of the nine people originally sentenced over Ahmadi’s concert, five were reported to have been flogged Monday. The status of the remaining defendants’ punishments remains unclear.

A protester holds a photo of Mahsa Amini during a demonstration against the Iranian regime and in support of women in Istanbul on Oct. 2, 2022. Amini died after being arrested in Tehran by the Islamic Republic's morality police. (Bulent Kilic/AFP via Getty Images)

Ahmadi’s punishment comes amid a broader human rights crackdown in Iran that has intensified since nationwide anti-regime protests erupted in January. In addition to years of restrictions on women, artists, journalists and political dissidents, Iranian authorities have increasingly resorted to mass arrests, torture in detention and executions to suppress opposition, as previously reported by Fox News Digital.

Human Rights Watch reported in February that Iran’s executions in 2025 had reached levels unseen since the late 1980s, while rights groups have documented a further escalation in political repression throughout 2026.

Earlier this month, the Norway-based Iran Human Rights organization reported that at least 121 people arrested in connection with January’s protests had been sentenced to death, including at least 30 whose sentences had been upheld by Iran’s Supreme Court.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Women members of the Basij paramilitary, affiliated with Iran's Revolutionary Guard, hold weapons during a parade in Tehran, Iran, April 17, 2026. (Sobhan Farajvan/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Iranian authorities did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Reuters contributed to this report.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Ukraine’s drone strike on Russian warship in Libya risks ‘serious escalation,’ former official warns
summary: Morgan Murphy warned the Ukrainian sea drone strike on the Russian corvette Mercury in Benghazi risks a serious escalation of the nearly five-year war.
story: Former White House official Morgan Murphy says Ukraine’s strike on Russian warship in Libya signals major shift in war.

The Ukrainian sea drone strike that capsized and sank a Russian warship in Libya on Sunday risks a "serious escalation" of the nearly five-year war, a former U.S. national security adviser warned Monday, calling the operation a "giant tantrum" by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Morgan Murphy, a former press secretary to the secretary of defense, also told Fox News Digital that the nighttime attack on the Russian corvette Mercury in the Libyan port city of Benghazi could further strain relations between Zelenskyy and President Donald Trump, while echoing frustrations that he said also plagued former President Joe Biden's administration.
"The strike on the Russian corvette Mercury in North Africa — in Libya specifically — is a serious escalation of the war in Ukraine," Murphy claimed.
"Calling the Benghazi strike a giant tantrum could be one interpretation of it, and it's not unusual behavior for him," Murphy said of Zelenskyy.
RUSSIAN WARSHIP SINKS OFF LIBYA AS SUSPECTED UKRAINIAN STRIKES TAKE WAR BEYOND BLACK SEA
The port of Benghazi after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi naval base. (Vantor/Handout via REUTERS)
Murphy also argued that Zelenskyy's willingness to pursue military objectives that complicate Washington's diplomatic priorities has frustrated previous administrations.

"This is why I think the Biden administration was frustrated with Zelenskyy, and why the Trump administration has been frustrated with Zelenskyy: he's acting like an independent player and not an ally," Murphy said.

Biden had reportedly lost his temper during a June 2022 phone call after Zelenskyy requested additional military assistance shortly after the White House announced a $1 billion aid package for Ukraine.
In his recently released memoir, Biden also revealed private frustrations with Zelenskyy, describing the Ukrainian leader as moody, stubborn and less grateful than expected.
UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC

U.S. President Biden and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine's president, left, meet in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Sept. 1, 2021. Photographer: Doug Mills/The New York Times/Bloomberg via Getty Images (Doug Mills/The New York Times/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Murphy went on to suggest the Benghazi drone strike could also complicate Trump's efforts to broker an end to the war, particularly after the president met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a historic summit without Zelenskyy.

"The President just had a successful meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, and he met them without Zelenskyy present, as is the right of the President of the United States to meet with whom he likes when he pleases," Murphy said.
"Zelenskyy was clearly upset about that, and this attack is him showing the President of the United States that he's still very relevant."

The operation, coordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and armed forces, targeted the Russian vessel in port, raising questions about where the drones originated and whether the conflict could spread further beyond Ukraine's borders.
Zelenskyy praised the strike Monday in a post on X, calling it "An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war."
Murphy argued that the Ukrainian leader is increasingly under pressure to demonstrate Kyiv can still deliver significant military victories as Trump pursues a diplomatic resolution.
"What he's looking for here is, I believe, a victory, because Ukraine has found more aid and sympathy on the world stage when it's winning," Murphy said.
Ukraine initially drew widespread international support after resisting Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, defying expectations that Moscow would quickly overwhelm Kyiv.
"Ukraine performed much better against an enemy five times its size, and human nature loves an underdog."
"There was a deep outpouring of sympathy — and more importantly, support — for Ukraine after that initial flop of a Russian invasion," Murphy said.
UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS
President Donald Trump met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the White House Aug. 18, 2025, where Trump said a ceasefire agreement is not necessary.  (Getty Images)

But as the conflict has dragged on, Murphy argued, Ukraine has struggled to sustain the enthusiasm that followed Russia's initial setbacks, with the fighting descending into what he described as a "stalemate and a war of attrition."
"Zelenskyy is having a harder time building support," he said of the current state of play.
"As he saw the President meet with Russia and meet with Xi Jinping in China, he needed a victory, and he needed a dramatic attack — so an asymmetric attack was on the board."

The Benghazi strike also underscores Ukraine's expanding ability to target Russian military assets thousands of miles from its territory, although questions remain about how the operation was carried out.
"Ukraine has taken credit for it, but they've been coy about where it was launched from," Murphy said.

"There's some speculation that it was launched from within Libya. Others say that it came from a mothership, which is totally plausible — that they took an innocuous-looking cargo ship and launched these drones out of it."
Murphy said the operation reflects a broader transformation in modern warfare, with military planners still grappling with the implications of increasingly sophisticated drone attacks.
"What we are watching unfold in real time is a total shift in the nature of warfare. It's really unheralded," he said.
UKRAINE’S DRONE REVOLUTION SHOWS RUSSIA IS DANGEROUSLY UNPREPARED. BUT, SO IS AMERICA
A Russian corvette before and after the explosion in Benghazi and with Libya's eastern-based government saying the explosion was caused by a suspected drone attack. (VANTOR/ Reuters)
"It will take time — planners' time and nations' time — to understand how to react to this kind of aggression."
Beyond the military implications, Murphy warned that the strike could undermine diplomatic efforts in Washington to negotiate an end to the conflict.
"There is a very concerted group of diplomats and thought leaders in D.C. who want to see a diplomatic end to this conflict sooner rather than later," Murphy said.
"They see that as being in the best interest of the United States and the world, but most importantly, they see it in the best interest of the Ukrainian people."
Murphy said those pushing for a negotiated settlement would likely view the reported strike in Libya as a setback to Trump's peace efforts.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"A lot of thinkers in Washington want this to end, and they'll see this escalation in Libya as counterproductive to what the President is trying to do."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: NATO warns Putin could strike before European army responds, points to US as military model
summary: NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte warned Russia's war machine runs at full speed and could threaten Europe long after the war in Ukraine ends.
story: Polish airspace violations by suspected Russian missiles trigger a stern warning from NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, as Jon Scott reports. Rutte declares that the alliance will defend every inch of Polish territory. This escalation coincides with a devastating Russian missile strike on a residential apartment building in Kyiv, where rescuers search the ruins.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte warned Monday that creating a separate European army could undermine the alliance’s ability to respond quickly to a Russian attack, as Moscow continues to ramp up its military capabilities during the ongoing war in Ukraine.

Speaking at the 72nd annual session of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin, Rutte cautioned that competing military command structures could hold up decisions in a crisis, warning that Russia’s "war machine" is running at full throttle and could also pose a threat to Europe long after the war ends.

"What I would counsel against is having all the nations with their own militaries working together in NATO and then on top of that having a big European structure, because then if Putin attacks, we will first need two or three weeks to agree who will do what, and then he will probably end up in Rotterdam before we have decided. So that has been my argument," Rutte said, according to Ukrainska Pravda.
NATO JETS SHOOT DOWN DRONE IN LITHUANIAN AIRSPACE AS RUSSIA GROWS 'INCREASINGLY RECKLESS,' RUTTE SAYS
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte speaks to the media during a joint news conference with the members of the Bosnian Presidency in Sarajevo, Bosnia, Monday, March 10, 2025. (Armin Durgut)
Rutte pointed to the United States as a model for an integrated military, arguing that European countries would also need to move beyond separate national forces to establish a unified army.
"My point has always been that if you have a European military, you cannot also have national militaries. The United States has one military."
"There is not a specific army or navy for the state of New York or for the state of California. It is an integrated United States military. If Europe is able to pull that off, fine," Rutte said.
Rutte said it was Russia's expanding military production and cooperation with China, Iran and North Korea that pose a long-term threat to NATO, regardless of how the war in Ukraine ends.

"We face great dangers coming from Russia and the fact that Russia works so closely together with Iran, China, and North Korea, we know that Russia's war machine at the moment is running at full speed," Rutte also said at the assembly in Berlin.
FOREIGN LEADER ON PUTIN’S DOORSTEP SOUNDS ALARM OVER IRAN FUELING MOSCOW’S WAR MACHINE

Plumes of smoke rise from fires at an oil refinery following what authorities said was a Ukrainian drone strike during the Russia-Ukraine conflict in Moscow, Russia, on Sept. 20, 2026. (REUTERS/Stringer)
"Its war economy keeps growing, and it won't stand still when the war against Ukraine hopefully will end one day. That whole machine is there and will continue."

Rutte also rejected the idea that only countries bordering Russia or Ukraine face a direct military threat, warning that Moscow's long-range missiles put capitals across Europe within striking distance.

"Let me say once again to everyone here who is not on the eastern flank: I have news for you. You are on the eastern flank too. These latest Russian missiles need only five minutes longer to reach Lisbon, Rome or The Hague, my hometown, than to reach Tallinn, Warsaw or Helsinki," Rutte said.
"So we are all on the eastern flank here. Let's put an end to this discussion about whether or not you are on the eastern flank. We are all on the eastern flank."

The NATO chief's remarks came amid plans to deploy an early-warning aircraft to Poland after Polish prosecutors said three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles landed on Polish territory Friday during strikes against Ukraine.
NATO WARNS RUSSIA: 'WE WILL BREAK' FORCES, DESTROY 'ANYTHING AND EVERYTHING' IF YOU ATTACK
Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski during an inteview with Fox News Digital in Warsaw, Poland. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)

Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said that NATO would deploy an Airborne Warning and Control System, or AWACS, aircraft to strengthen surveillance along the alliance's eastern flank, according to Reuters.
"This is a very good system that gives us even deeper... operational awareness which allows us to respond better to this kind of threat," Zalewski told reporters following a NATO meeting in Brussels.

The aircraft can monitor large areas of airspace and provide allied forces with a shared picture of potential aerial threats, improving NATO's ability to detect and respond to missile and aircraft activity.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also warned Monday night that intelligence indicated Moscow was preparing a new wave of strikes against Ukraine.
Beyond Russia's ongoing military threats, Rutte said that Europe's interconnected infrastructure, including energy networks and communications systems, is vulnerable.
RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT
Smoke rises in the city during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine August 31, 2026. (Gleb Garanich/Reuters)
"We are all targeted, that we are all affected when it comes to our pipelines, our cables, our energy grids, and our economies."
"They are all interconnected, and that means that we are all in this for the long term. And therefore, we must step up to the plate to ensure that we stay ahead of danger."
Rutte said defending NATO countries demands civilian preparedness, pointing to northern European nations that have begun teaching residents about their responsibilities in the event of war.
"This really takes the whole of society," he said.

"And that's in the end, I think, still Norway and Sweden, and Denmark and Finland, and maybe one or two others who are really ahead of the pack here, and having made clear to their citizens what they need to do in case war breaks out, at least not to get in the way of the military, but to be helpful and also how they make sure that the police and the ambulance services and fire, the fire fighting departments work together, supporting the military wherever possible."

Rutte's warnings come amid uncertainty over Ukraine's long-term security arrangements and whether Western allies will offer guarantees resembling NATO's Article 5 collective defense commitment as part of a future peace agreement.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

U.S. special envoy Jared Kushner said Sunday that President Donald Trump was willing to consider Article 5-style security guarantees for Ukraine as part of a broader postwar security arrangement for Europe.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Russia warns of 'preventive nuclear attack' as Medvedev claims Ukraine, NATO crossed line
summary: Dmitry Medvedev claims Ukraine and NATO have crossed thresholds that could make a preventive nuclear attack by Russia possible, warning Kyiv's allies.
story: Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reports on Russian President Vladimir Putin's warning to NATO regarding the use of long-range weapons in Ukraine on ‘America Reports.’

Russia warned Monday that it could carry out a "preventive nuclear attack" under certain circumstances, with former President Dmitry Medvedev claiming Ukraine and NATO allies have already crossed certain thresholds that could push Moscow to consider using nuclear weapons.

"The massive use of non-nuclear means that cause catastrophes makes a preventive nuclear attack by the Russian Federation possible," Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, wrote in an article published Monday in the Moscow Journal of International Law and excerpted by the state news agency TASS.
Medvedev also warned that "secret or hidden supplies of nuclear weapons from the West to Kyiv will provoke a legitimate preventive nuclear attack by Russia."
MOSCOW THREATENS NUCLEAR RESPONSE OVER TINY FORTRESS WEDGED BETWEEN US ALLIES AS CLASH FEARS GROW

Dmitry Medvedev takes part in a wreath-laying ceremony marking Defender of the Fatherland Day at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier by the Kremlin Wall in Moscow, Russia, Feb. 23, 2024. (Yekaterina Shtukina/Sputnik/Pool via Reuters.)
"Kyiv and its allies must remember that the Russian Federation not only has the right, but in various situations has the obligation to use nuclear weapons," he wrote.
Medvedev's warning came amid continuing tensions between Moscow and the West over the nearly five-year war in Ukraine and NATO's military support for Kyiv.

He argued that Ukraine and its Western allies have already created circumstances under which Russia could consider a nuclear strike, though he said Russian President Vladimir Putin carefully weighs the consequences before making such a decision.

"Formally, in a number of cases, the parties collectively opposing us (Ukraine, NATO countries, and several Western countries outside the alliance) have already created situations in which Russia considers the possibility of launching a nuclear strike," Medvedev wrote in the article, titled "State Sovereignty and Nuclear Weapons: International Legal Aspects of Ensuring National Security".
TRUMP HOLDS THE NUCLEAR CARDS TO PLAY AGAINST CHINA AND RUSSIA ON ARMS CONTROL
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin (Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images; Contributor/Getty Images)

Despite those warnings, Medvedev wrote that Putin "is always guided by a comprehensive analysis of all factors and the proportionality between the actual damage inflicted and the retaliatory measures."
Medvedev also said Russia has not used nuclear weapons during the war with Ukraine because it has not considered them necessary, though he warned that calculation could change.
"Obviously, so far the course of events in the Ukrainian crisis has not created a state of direct necessity to use nuclear weapons," he wrote.

"The decision on Russia's use of nuclear weapons during the special military operation was not taken due to the lack of a direct necessity to do so," he added, using the Kremlin's preferred term for the war in Ukraine.

Medvedev argued that while Russia's nuclear doctrine does not explicitly authorize preventive nuclear strikes, certain scenarios — including catastrophic attacks using conventional weapons or the transfer of nuclear arms to Ukraine — could justify preemptive action.
He said any final decision rests solely with Putin.
TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE

Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump meet during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19, 2026. (Reuters)

"In making such decisions, the Russian president is always guided by a complete analysis of all factors and the proportionality between the actual damage caused and the retaliatory measures," Medvedev wrote.
"The Kyiv regime and its sponsors must not harbor dangerous illusions," he warned.

"If the scenarios mentioned above were to occur, the head of state not only has the right, but also the obligation to use nuclear weapons. All those who are currently fanning the flames must fully realize this".

Medvedev's remarks came within days of President Donald Trump meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Nov. 19 in Shenzhen, China, where the leaders of the three nuclear powers agreed to pursue talks aimed at reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.
While the summit produced no major breakthrough on arms reductions, the leaders reaffirmed in a declaration that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.
TRUMP WILL FACE REPORTERS AFTER HISTORIC XI-PUTIN TALKS AS WAR QUESTIONS LINGER
Dmitry Medvedev, Russian Security Council deputy chairman, speaks at a meeting of the United Russia party programme commission in Moscow, Oct. 1, 2025. (Ekaterina Shtukina, Sputnik Pool Photo via AP)

To support his argument, Medvedev cited a 1996 International Court of Justice advisory opinion, contending that international law does not categorically prohibit the use of nuclear weapons when a state's survival is at stake.

The court concluded that the threat or use of nuclear weapons would generally violate international humanitarian law, but it did not definitively resolve whether such use would be lawful in extreme circumstances of self-defense.

Medvedev, who served as Russia's president from 2008 to 2012 and later as prime minister under Putin, has become one of Moscow's most outspoken voices on nuclear escalation since Russia invaded Ukraine.

Medvedev accused NATO members of undermining nonproliferation efforts, criticizing Germany's participation in nuclear deterrence arrangements and arguing that NATO's nuclear-sharing policies do not represent a universally accepted interpretation of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT)

title: Russia could launch nuclear-capable satellite within weeks, Western intelligence warns: report
summary: Western intelligence reportedly warns Russia's nuclear satellite could launch in 60 days, threatening thousands of United States and allied satellites.
story: Chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin joins ‘The Faulkner Focus’ to discuss the growing threat of orbital warfare after the U.S. confirmed it has deployed weapons in orbit. She examines the security implications as concerns over China and Russia’s space capabilities continue to mount.

Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit within less than 60 days according to new Western intelligence assessments reported Monday, raising fears that Moscow is preparing to deploy a weapon capable of crippling thousands of satellites used by the United States and its allies.

The intelligence reports emerged just four days after President Donald Trump met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a high-profile summit in Shenzhen, China, where nuclear arms control was a central topic.
The three leaders issued a joint declaration affirming that nuclear war should never be fought, but stopped short of announcing binding arms-control commitments.
NEXT GENERATION OPIR GEO: BUILDING AMERICA’S GATEWAY TO THE FUTURE OF SPACE-BASED MISSILE WARNING AND TRACKING
Advanced satellite launch (Amazon)
On Monday, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz publicly addressed the reports, while the Kremlin dismissed the allegations.

According to a joint investigation published Nov. 23 by German broadcasters WDR and NDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, Western intelligence agencies believe Russia has assembled a satellite known as "Sputnik-S," which has reportedly been stored in the Moscow region for several years.

Intelligence warnings shared among several NATO countries in early November indicated that the satellite, reportedly designed to carry a nuclear warhead, could be launched within 60 days. Germany's military Space Command reportedly assessed that a December launch was possible.
The German investigation also reported that military officials had briefed senior government figures, including German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, about the threat.
The reports prompted an immediate response from European leaders.
Speaking alongside Rutte in Berlin on Monday, Merz described the allegations as "shocking," while noting that concerns about Russia's nuclear space ambitions were not entirely new.
PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz sparked backlash while remarking about the country's migration policies. (Thomas Traasdahl/Ritzau Scanpix via AP)
Rutte, meanwhile, stressed that NATO was continually assessing its defensive capabilities.
"I can assure you, we will always make sure that we defend every inch of NATO territory," Rutte said, according to Reuters.
He added that the alliance's defense planning included threats in space and said NATO had response options that were not always visible to the public.

The Kremlin rejected the allegations. Russian presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov questioned the credibility of the intelligence reports, saying they contained numerous unsubstantiated claims that were "hardly worth taking seriously," according to The Moscow Times.

"We haven’t seen the report. But there are so many ‘alleged’ and ‘possible’ claims in it, attributed to who knows whom, that it’s certainly hardly worth taking them seriously," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.

Russia's Embassy in Berlin separately dismissed the reporting as part of a propaganda campaign and maintained that Moscow's space activities were peaceful and consistent with international obligations.

The latest warnings follow an earlier assessment by the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency , which publicly identified Russia's development of a nuclear-capable satellite in October. "Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon," the DIA stated in its 2026 Challenges to Security in Space assessment.
NATO WARNS RUSSIA: 'WE WILL BREAK' FORCES, DESTROY 'ANYTHING AND EVERYTHING' IF YOU ATTACK

FILE - Russian President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting aboard the missile cruiser Varyag in Russia's far eastern Sakhalin region on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Putin previously said Russia is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe. (Reuters)
As Fox News Digital reported on October 29, the agency warned that such a weapon could cause the rapid loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by governments and private companies.

Unlike a conventional anti-satellite weapon targeting an individual spacecraft, a nuclear detonation in orbit could potentially disable large numbers of satellites through radiation and electromagnetic effects.
The consequences could extend far beyond the military. Satellites support GPS navigation, international communications, financial transactions, weather forecasting and critical infrastructure.
The threat also has implications for Ukraine, whose military relies heavily on satellite communications, including SpaceX's Starlink network, during its war with Russia.

The concern was initially addressed on February 2024 when the Biden administration publicly acknowledged that Russia was developing a troubling anti-satellite capability, although officials said at the time that no such weapon had been deployed.
Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which prohibits stationing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in space.

The latest German reporting suggests the threat could be approaching a more immediate stage, but critical questions remain unanswered, including whether the satellite already carries a nuclear warhead and whether Western intelligence has independently verified the reported launch preparations.
