The facility is part of Indonesia's United Family Food company – founded in 1981 and employing roughly 5, 000 people – and manufactures Milkita, a popular Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snacks. The tragedy adds to a string of deadly industrial fires in Indonesia in recent years that have raised ongoing concerns over workplace safety and emergency preparedness.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

title: Zelenskyy says Russia strikes hometown, criticizes Putin-Trump meeting
summary: Zelenskyy says a Russian strike on his hometown of Kryvyi Rih killed two people, including 7-year-old Tykhon, and wounded 58 others in a civilian area.
story: Steve Yates defends President Donald Trump's meetings with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping following criticism. Yates outlines the strategic value of maintaining communication lines between the three global leaders, arguing that dialogue is essential to national security.
A Russian strike on Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown of Kryvyi Rih killed two people and wounded 58 others, the Ukrainian leader said Saturday.
A 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman were killed in the attack Friday night in the central Ukraine town, according to Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration.
Zelenkskyy said in a social media post the woman was an emergency medical worker and the boy was named Tykhon.
PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE

"He was born in 2019, and, sadly, most of his life was lived during a war like this. And the Russians took his life with their strike. My condolences to their families and loved ones," Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks at a news conference after a phone conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump in Kyiv, Ukraine, May 19, 2025.  (Danylo Antoniuk/Anadolu via Getty Images)
On top of the civilian deaths and injuries, the strike sparked four fires and damaged roughly 25 apartment buildings, along with a hospital, schools, an industrial facility, businesses and vehicles.
RUSSIA'S PUTIN VOWS A RESPONSE 'FAR MORE PAINFUL' AFTER UKRAINE ATTACKS PRIZED BRIDGE IN CRIMEA
Zelenskyy claimed the Russian strike hit an area of the city with no military targets.

"The strike hit an ordinary civilian area of the city – there are no military facilities nearby, and there never have been," he wrote. "Russia is waging war against life, and there can be NO justification for this."
TRUMP WILL FACE REPORTERS AFTER HISTORIC XI-PUTIN TALKS AS WAR QUESTIONS LINGER
The Ukrainian leader later commented on President Donald Trump's recent meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, Aug. 15.  (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

"Putin didn't get his 'Yalta 2,'" Zelenskyy wrote, referring to the famed 1945 Yalta Conference between former U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin.
TRUMP’S PROPOSED RUSSIA DEAL RAISES NATO ALARM AS EX-COMMANDER WARNS PUTIN SEEKS INFLUENCE OVER EUROPE

"As far as I understand, he recently commented: 'What's wrong with Yalta? Those were the victories over Nazism, over fascism, and so on, that were sealed there.' First of all, indeed, this was no Yalta. Did Putin want a real Yalta? Yes.

"In the sense of carving up the world and changing borders. China didn't let itself be drawn into it. I don't know what happened between the United States and Russia in their bilateral, but Ukraine wasn't discussed. Nothing came out publicly. So the redrawing of borders didn't happen," Zelenskyy wrote.

"If there really was an intention to reaffirm the victory over fascism now, then the participants at this summit would have to be the United States, Europe, and Ukraine. Definitely not Russia. I think this trilateral summit turned out very badly for Russia. Not only did Putin fail to get the results he wanted, but we also saw his reaction.

"And, unfortunately, we saw that reaction in Ukraine. There was a massive attack that night – 111 missiles. If Putin wanted to remind the world once again who he is, there was no need – we haven't forgotten that he's a terrorist and a killer."
UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR 'VICTORY'

U.S. President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China’s President Xi Jinping stands beside then before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, southern China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)
The strike on Zelenskyy's hometown is far from uncommon, with periodic Russian attacks targeting the industrial steel town dozens of times since the start of the war in 2022.
The incident also occurred as a Russian ship was struck by drones on Saturday, setting it ablaze in the Gulf of Finland.
The Russian-flagged Sparta II was struck by a drone shortly before 9 a.m., according to Finnish Coast Guard Commander Mikko Simola.
The damaged Russian cargo ship Sparta II in a location given as the Gulf of Finland Nov. 21, 2026. (Finnish Border Guard/Handout via Reuters)
"Generally it should be noted that it is known that this Sparta II vessel has been used for transports for the Russian state, including the armed forces," Simola said.
As a result of its damage, the craft entered Finnish territorial waters. Simola also noted that Finland believed a Russian helicopter crossed Finland's sovereign borders as well.
Finnish officials believe that Ukraine was behind the attack.
"It is likely that Ukraine ... is behind (the attack)," Finnish armed forces spokesperson Aki-Mauri Huhtinen said.

title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to kill Ukrainian American rapper on Danish soil
summary: Denmark's PET accuses Russia of an assassination plot against Kyivstoner, expelling Moscow's defense attache as two gang-affiliated men plead guilty.
story: Denmark’s security and intelligence agency accused Russia of attempting to kill Ukrainian American rapper Kyivstoner on Danish soil in September.
Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) accused Russia of attempting to kill Ukrainian American rapper Kyivstoner on Danish soil in September.
Authorities arrested two individuals on charges of attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
As a result of the alleged plot, Denmark will expel Russia's defense attaché from Copenhagen, the Danish foreign minister said.
NATO MEMBER BOOTS 10 RUSSIAN DIPLOMATS

"We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and notified him of the government's decision to expel the Russian defense attaché from Denmark [within seven days]," Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said during a press conference Friday.

Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen holds a news conference at the Ministry of Justice in Copenhagen, Denmark, Nov. 20, 2026. Two Danes were charged with the planned murder of a Ukrainian rapper. (Ritzau Scanpix/Emil Nicolai Helms/via Reuters)
Russia denied any involvement in the alleged plot, calling the accusations "unsubstantiated" in a statement.
RUSSIAN SPIES ORCHESTRATED $40K MURDER PLOT IN NATION’S CAPITAL, US ALLEGES

Russia's intelligence agency, FSB, accused Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasilyev, of plotting a drone attack on Moscow in July, an accusation Vasilyev denied, according to Russian media outlet Meduza.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reproached Russia for the alleged scheme.
SHE GREW UP UNDER SOVIET RULE; NOW, EU'S TOP DIPLOMAT WARNS EUROPE AGAINST GIVING RUSSIA WHAT IT WANTS
"I strongly condemn the assassination attempt against a U.S.-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services," she said in a statement.
"This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable," she continued. "Russia's hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real."
GERMANY BLAMES RUSSIA AFTER EXPLOSIVE-LADEN DRONE FOUND NEAR UKRAINIAN CARGO PLANES AT MAJOR AIRPORT
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen as she meets with Iceland's Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir (not pictured), in Brussels, Belgium, April 9, 2025.  (Reuters/Yves Herman)

Danish security services said the pair who tried to carry out the attempted hit were affiliated with the Danish gang Loyal to Familia, which is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity," according to PET.

Danish police stopped three individuals in a car near a music venue in Hellerup, where Kyivstoner was performing in September. Inside the vehicle they found guns and knives. Both men charged pleaded guilty.
TRUMP SIDELINES SWEEPING RUSSIA SANCTIONS AS GOP ALLIES WARN PRESSURE ON PUTIN IS SLIPPING
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Denmark would issue fewer visas to Russians as a result of the incident.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Toughen the sanctions against Russia, including a halt to all non-essential visas to Russian citizens, and these visas should only be valid in the issuing country," Frederiksen said.

Denmark's Justice Minister, Nicolai Wammen, and Danish Foreign Minister Lars Loekke Rasmussen hold a news conference at the Ministry of Justice in Copenhagen, Denmark, Nov. 20, 2026. Two Danes are charged with the planned murder of a Ukrainian rapper. (Ritzau Scanpix/Emil Nicolai Helms/via Reuters)
The foreign ministries for Ukraine, Russia and Denmark did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital for comment.
Reuters and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Congress reacts with anger and skepticism about Jensen Huang reinstatement
summary: Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle vowed to press ahead with investigations into the once-again Nvidia CEO, who’s scheduled to meet with them next week.
story: The stock market was thrilled with the announcement that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO of Nvidia, but lawmakers on both sides of the aisle reacted with shock — and said they still expect him to answer questions next week on Capitol Hill.

“You gotta be kidding me,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told MS NOW when he learned of Huang’s reinstatement 11 days after he resigned in the wake of revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy.
In its announcement, the board said it reached the decision after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
“No national security risk? Based on what?” Cornyn asked in a post on X.
President Donald Trump told CNBC he’d spoken to the board “directly and indirectly.”

“One of the things the board wanted to know, is there a national security problem?” Trump said. “And after a lot of research, we — you know, we’ve been looking at this for more than a couple of days, right? This has been a story for a few weeks. We said no, it’s not a problem.”
Lawmakers made clear they still need answers.
The Senate Banking Committee, chaired by Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced that Huang was scheduled to testify publicly Dec. 3.

“The national security concerns and adherence to export controls will be central to the committee’s oversight and the congressional hearing. Our markets demand transparency. Americans deserve the truth. Our committee will deliver answers,” Scott said in a statement.

A spokesperson for the House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO “changes nothing” for the three House committees that are set to conduct a closed-door transcribed interview with Huang on Dec. 1.

For Subscribers

“There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee’s commitment to oversight,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

In a joint statement later Monday, the chairs of the House Select Committee on China, the Intelligence Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee said Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter “have confirmed they will appear for their transcribed interviews on December 1 and December 2 as previously planned.”

“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” said the three Republicans, Reps. John Moolenaar of Michigan, Rick Crawford of Arkansas and Brian Mast of Florida.

The speedy reinstatement and assurances of the lack of a security risk came after the Justice and Commerce departments last week shared details about their investigation into Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company tied to Alice Huang, the suspected spy with whom Huang was allegedly involved.
Megaspeed reportedly acquired billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is also being investigated over concerns that it — and its subsidiaries — smuggled chips to China.

Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said in an X post that “the legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens. The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who’s been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang.”
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told NBC News in a phone interview “It’s not my job as a public official to tell a private company who to pick for their CEO. That’s up to the board of directors.”

But, he added, “What I want to know is whether Nvidia violated the export controls of our country with respect to advanced chips. And I want to know if the Department of Commerce did. That will be the purpose of the Banking Committee hearing.”

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said in a statement that the administration appears to have known about the Chinese espionage efforts targeting the Nvidia CEO for the past year and his reinstatement “without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the administration’s “rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act.”

“Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat,” Schumer said in a statement. He added that “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.”
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., called the board’s decision “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.”

“Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce,” Jeffries said.
Lutnick agreed earlier this month to testify before Congress about the Huang scandal amid lawmakers’ scrutiny of China’s access to advanced AI chips.

Democrats pointed Trump’s financial ties to Nvidia, with Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the ranking member on the Oversight Committee, noting the president has a sizeable amount of Nvidia stock. “No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions,” Garcia said.
Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., cited Nvidia’s donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project as a reason to give the board’s decision extra scrutiny.

“Trump’s assurances cannot be taken at face value, especially after Nvidia’s $25 million donation to his ballroom. Huang must testify at a full public congressional hearing, with every member of the relevant committees allowed to question him,” he posted on X.
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., questioned the Nvidia board’s decision in a post on social media.

“Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy,” Ricketts wrote. “His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement.”

“Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress,” he continued. “It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.”

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., called the president’s actions “Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration’s big tech and AI policy.” He told reporters it was a “good sign” that Republican senators and lawmakers have spoken out because they “realize this is a threat to national security.”

title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia is leaving the U.S. a ‘free man,’ Van Hollen says
summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia has been ordered by a federal judge to leave the United States by Tuesday, a U.S. official confirmed to NBC News.
story: Kilmar Abrego Garcia has been ordered by a federal judge to leave the United States by Tuesday, a U.S. official confirmed to NBC News.
In a statement Tuesday evening, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, said Abrego Garcia  is “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.”
The Salvadoran national became a central figure in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown last year after he was mistakenly deported to his home country.

The Washington Post reported earlier in the day that Abrego Garcia voluntarily agreed to leave the United States under an agreement with U.S. authorities who had sought his removal. The agreement, it said, would end those proceedings.
Court records in Maryland have yet to reflect such an order. There have been a handful of sealed filings in his civil case against the administration over the past several weeks, however.
The 31-year-old man immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager, but has been in the United States for years, is married to an American, and has a child with her.
He had lived and worked in Maryland for years under the regular supervision of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from gang members.
He was deported there anyway in 2025, but returned to the U.S.  ICE officials admitted in court filings that his deportation there was an “administrative error.”
Not long after his return to U.S., he was charged with human smuggling in a case stemming from a traffic stop in Tennessee in which he was driving a van with multiple immigrant passengers.
Tennessee did not prosecute him. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying the Trump administration failed to rebut the “presumption of vindictiveness.” The government appealed.

title: Fort Hood mass shooter makes legal move to stop Pentagon’s firing squad execution
summary: The former Army officer whose scheduled military execution by firing squad provoked outrage over an initial proposal to livestream his death is planning to file a constitutional challenge that could halt his December execution, his lawyers said Tuesday.
story: The former Army officer whose scheduled military execution by firing squad provoked outrage over an initial proposal to livestream his death is planning to file a constitutional challenge that could halt his December execution, his lawyers said Tuesday.

Nidal Hasan, convicted in the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, that claimed 13 lives, filed a motion for a stay of execution so he can submit what’s known as a habeas corpus petition, which requires the government to justify a person’s detainment.

“There is no question that the violence committed at Fort Hood caused unimaginable pain and loss,” Anna Arceneaux, deputy director of the ACLU’s Capital Punishment Project, said in a statement. “But the gravity of that loss does not change the government’s obligation to uphold the principles that define our justice system. Mr. Hasan, like every person facing an irreversible punishment, must have a chance to pursue federal review of his case.”
Hasan, 56, had officially exhausted his military justice appeals, opening the door to President Donald Trump in October approving his death sentence and the Army setting an execution date.

Hasan’s request was filed in civilian court, which is another process available to military prisoners. Military experts told NBC News the legal maneuver to file a habeas corpus petition would all but assure Hasan’s case will be tied up in a lengthy review process that could effectively stall his pending execution to well beyond the end of Trump’s term. At that point, they say, Trump’s successor may avoid setting another execution date.
The motion was filed on behalf of Hasan by the ACLU of Kansas. Pentagon and Army officials could not immediately be reached for comment.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth first raised the prospect of livestreaming Hasan’s execution, telling a conservative news outlet that he would ensure “people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”
For Subscribers
But John Baker, the federal public defender for the Western District of North Carolina whose capital habeas unit is assisting Hasan, said the case deserves further review by a federal court.

“The President, the Secretary of Defense, and others have turned Mr. Hasan’s case into a political spectacle,” Baker said in a statement. “Our government cannot be permitted to execute Mr. Hasan until his death sentence has received full and fair review, which the Constitution safeguards through our federal courts.”

Few details were made available about how a firing squad execution could unfold, although Army officials said it would occur at 1 p.m. Dec. 3 at Fort Hood — around the time the attack occurred at the military base. During the shooting, Hasan was injured by responding officers and paralyzed and now requires a wheelchair.
For Subscribers

Within days of Hegseth’s announcement, Trump said he would ultimately decide whether Hasan’s death could potentially be watched by millions of people online. He subsequently said in a Truth Social post that while livestreaming the execution “might have been a strong deterrent,” there are other people who “would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”
“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad,” the president said, “but this event will not be streamed.”

Hegseth’s announcement had set off immediate backlash from a bipartisan group of lawmakers, human rights organizations and religious leaders, many of whom said a livestreamed execution would be “medieval” and “barbaric,” echoing public killings conducted by the most brutal totalitarian regimes and terror states and harkening back to the nation’s dark period of public lynchings and racism.

In the U.S., the last large-scale gathering for a lawfully public execution occurred in 1936 in Kentucky, where a Black man convicted of raping a white woman was hanged in front of thousands, according to news reports.

Opponents of livestreaming Hasan’s execution also warned it could be used as propaganda by jihadist militants, while playing into the desires of Hasan, an American-born Muslim who had become radicalized.
“I’m paraplegic and could be in jail for the rest of my life,” Hasan told a mental health panel following the shooting spree. “However, if I died by lethal injection, I would still be a martyr.”
The U.S. military has not put a service member to death by firing squad since 1945 and last executed a service member in 1961, by hanging. Both were conducted privately.
Currently, four people, including Hasan, are on the military’s death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

title: Chinese tech giant Huawei convicted of federal charges, including fraud
summary: Chinese tech giant Huawei was convicted of multiple federal charges in New York on Tuesday after prosecutors accused the company of stealing technology from U.S. companies, abusing the American financial system and helping Iran spy on its citizens.
story: Chinese tech giant Huawei was convicted of multiple federal charges in New York on Tuesday after prosecutors accused the company of stealing technology from U.S. companies, abusing the American financial system and helping Iran spy on its citizens.

A jury in New York’s Eastern District found the company and three of its subsidiaries guilty of seven conspiracy counts that included bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering, defrauding the United States and conspiracy to steal trade secrets.
In the roughly two-month trial, Huawei was also convicted of bank fraud and wire fraud. Huawei was acquitted of two counts, a racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice.

“For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft and deception,” Assistant Attorney General Tysen A. Duva said in a statement. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security.”
In a statement, Huawei said the charges are “without legal or factual merit,” and it said it welcomes the racketeering verdict.
“We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests,” the company said.
Huawei attorney Brian Heberling said the company plans to appeal. At sentencing, which is scheduled for Sept. 14, Huawei could face fines, forfeiture and restitution.

Prosecutors accused the company, which makes smartphones and has telecom networks around the world, of encouraging its workforce of 200,000 in 170 countries to lie, cheat, and steal “for a competitive advantage to grow and protect its business.”

Huawei was accused of misappropriating intellectual property like source code, user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology and robot testing technology, prosecutors said. T-Mobile, Cisco, Quintel and CNEX were among the companies whose technology was stolen, federal prosecutors said in a news release Tuesday.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

In Iran, the company assisted the regime with “turnkey” internet services and mobile networks, prosecutors said, and it provided surveillance cameras that allowed officials to monitor protests. Huawei also helped intelligence agents monitor and censor the internet, prosecutors said.

Huawei then lied to banks about the nature of its business in Iran, allowing the company to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and become what prosecutors described as “a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services.”

In an interview Tuesday, Heberling rejected the government’s allegations, saying prosecutors presented a “caricature-like portrait” of Huawei of as a corrupt organization with company policies that condoned crime.

“That was just profoundly inconsistent with the company that I experienced in my work, but more importantly, [with] the evidence, which really showed a series of isolated events over a 20-year period,” he said. “No company can insure perfection over that period of time.”
Heberling argued that the racketeering acquittal — the most serious charge the company faced — showed a “profound rejection of the narrative the United States pursued in this case.”

Huawei was previously banned from selling equipment to U.S. carriers over fears that it poses a security risk, according to the Associated Press, and it was blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.

title: ‘Shocking’ decline seen in hep B vaccination against incurable virus, including babies with infected mothers
summary: Fewer newborns are being vaccinated against hepatitis B, an incurable infection that can lead to liver disease, a large new analysis has found.
story: Fewer newborns are being vaccinated against hepatitis B, an incurable infection that can lead to liver disease, including babies whose mothers are known to have the virus, a large new analysis has found.

As of June, just 66% of newborns got the hepatitis B vaccine within a day of their birth, down from 80% in 2022. The birth dose serves as a safety net especially for babies whose pregnant mothers are unaware they’re infected with the virus and unknowingly transmit it during childbirth.
Up to 90% of babies with the virus develop chronic infections, putting them at risk for liver failure and liver cancer later in life. Vaccinating them at birth dramatically lowers those odds.
The new study from Truveta, a health care and analytics company, included medical records from more than 1.3 million babies born in the United States from January 2018 through June this year.
During that time period, newborn vaccination rates increased from 76% in 2018 to 80% in 2022 before declining in mid-2023, falling to 66% by June this year.

“It’s shocking to see a nearly 15% decline in three years,” said Nina Masters, lead author and principal applied research scientist at Truveta. “Infants born to mothers with hepatitis B have a 90% chance of perinatal infection. That can mean a lifetime of chronic liver disease, cirrhosis and early death. This is a real preventable tragedy.”

The decline began before federal vaccine advisers voted in December to abandon a decades-old recommendation that all babies be vaccinated against hepatitis B at birth. (That decision was later halted by a federal judge in response to a lawsuit filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics. The block remains in effect.)

The findings mirror increasing trends in anti-vaccine behavior in general. A recent NBC News data investigation found three-quarters of U.S. counties that track kindergarten immunization rates no longer meet the minimum threshold to prevent measles outbreaks.

Now, measles outbreaks are popping up nationwide, with nearly 6,000 cases and at least 13 deaths, according to state health departments. The U.S. lost its measles elimination status Nov. 16, reversing one of the country’s greatest public health achievements this century.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“We talk about measles being the canary in the coal mine. We’re seeing those outbreaks,” said Dr. Richard Besser, a pediatrician and president of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. “This one — hepatitis B and the rise in unvaccinated newborns — these are the kinds of things that are silent, that you don’t see for years and years until these babies grow up and end up having liver disease.”

The study, published Tuesday in NEJM Evidence, also revealed that hepatitis B vaccination rates have fallen among babies born to mothers known to be infected with the virus. Up to 98% of those babies were vaccinated between 2018 through 2025. But between January and June, that rate dropped to 94%.

Cases of acute hepatitis B fell dramatically in children after the the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began recommending a universal birth dose in 1991, falling 99% from 1990 to 2019. A CDC analysis of children born from 1994 to 2023 estimated that hepatitis B vaccination prevented more than 6 million infections and nearly 1 million hospitalizations.

Last year, the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project published a review of more than 400 studies, finding no evidence of short- or long-term health problems from the hepatitis B shot after birth.
“Reversing the successes of previous public health programs puts individuals’ lives at risk,”
Dr. James Conway, a pediatric infectious disease physician and medical director of the UW Health Immunization Program in Madison, Wisconsin, wrote in an email. “It’s sad, tragic and preventable.”

title: Meet the ‘GTA’ superfans who turned the game’s release into a major life event
summary: From transforming their homes into “Grand Theft Auto”-inspired playgrounds to clearing their calendars at all costs, die-hard fans of the franchise pulled out all the stops for the arrival of “GTA VI.”
story: From transforming their homes into “Grand Theft Auto”-inspired playgrounds to clearing their calendars at all costs, die-hard fans of the franchise pulled out all the stops for the arrival of “GTA VI.”

The Rockstar Games title, which launched Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, generated a whopping $3.79 billion in first-day sales, which the company said makes it the “biggest entertainment launch in history.”
The latest installment pushes the boundaries of realism, immersing players in the photorealistic world of Vice City, where they can take the wheel as Jason or Lucia, the pair that leads the story.
NBC News spoke with six devoted “GTA” fans to find out what preparations they made for the blockbuster franchise’s return after a 13-year gap between games.
Nara Mont

It wasn’t enough for Nara Mont to just purchase the game and a new Xbox gaming system to play it on. She wanted to immerse herself in the fictional state of Leonida by getting into the mindset of female protagonist Lucia.

In the weeks leading up to launch day, Mont tore down the decorations in her bedroom in an effort to re-create Lucia’s bold, kitschy apartment based only on a glimpse of it she caught from the extended look released this summer. The color pink was prominent everywhere in the teaser, including in the bedding, accent lighting and flamingo wallpaper.

title: Authorities drop criminal charge against incoming House Democrat over unreturned rental car
summary: The summons for Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack was issued in 2020, but law enforcement didn’t serve the warrant until last month, at a campaign event, court records show.
story: Prosecutors in North Carolina announced Tuesday that they are dropping a 2020 felony charge against Democratic Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, who flipped a House seat this month, over allegations that she failed to return a rental car.
Womack was charged six years ago after a vehicle first rented by Womack in August 2019 was not returned to Budget Car Rental, according to Mecklenburg County District Attorney Spencer Merriweather.

Merriweather said in a news release that Womack renewed the rental two more times over the next few months but never returned the car. Instead, it was returned in December 2019 after law enforcement agents recovered the vehicle, he said.
Womack’s attorney, Harold Cogdell Jr., said in a statement Tuesday that his client had been “unaware a criminal summons had been issued” for “almost seven years.”

“Upon learning of this unresolved matter, Ms. Womack promptly and fully resolved this matter with the rental car company,” Cogdell said. “The vehicle was returned to the owner, undamaged, forty-one days prior to the charge being issued on January 14, 2020.”

According to the court documents, the summons was first issued in 2020, though it was not served until last month, when law enforcement officers provided Womack with the warrant at a campaign event on Oct. 11.
It is not clear why it took years to deliver the summons.
For Subscribers
Merriweather said Tuesday that the state moved to voluntarily dismiss the charge against Womack after his office was informed on Nov. 16 that she had reached an agreement with Budget.

Merriweather said his office confirmed that Budget had received “a sum of money” from Womack that was “equal to an assessed rental cost from the day the vehicle was deemed overdue until the day it came back into the possession of the victim corporation.”
Representatives for Budget then “explicitly” said that they did not wish to continue with prosecution as it considered the matter resolved, Merriweather said.
Budget did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
For Subscribers
According to the court summons, the car was valued at $20,000.

Womack has previously talked about experiencing housing insecurity after she moved back to Charlotte, North Carolina, in 2016, saying she lived in a hotel for a period of time and did not have a regular address for receiving mail.
After receiving the summons during a campaign event last month, Womack criticized the timing of the move.

“In the seven years that this has been kind of lingering, Mecklenburg County couldn’t find me or, you know, send me any paperwork?” Womack said in an Oct. 12 interview with the NAACP’s Gastonia branch.
The felony charge was used in campaign ads that sought to boost GOP Rep. Tim Moore, who lost his re-election bid to Womack.
“LaKesha Womack talks about integrity, but she’s charged with a felony,” one ad said. “Served a court summons at a campaign rally. Her court date: a week after the election.”
“Don’t let Democrats hand this seat to a felony defendant,” the ad continued.

Womack won North Carolina’s 14th Congressional District in the midterm elections by 2.2 percentage points, with the district swinging 17 points to the left compared with the 2024 election. She bested Moore, who was running for a second term, with a progressive campaign that emphasized affordability and healthcare.

Her victory contributed to Democrats’ sweep in the midterm elections, where they won both the House and Senate. As of Tuesday, Democrats will hold 259 of the House’s 435 seats in January after flipping 47 seats, losing only three.

title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia is leaving the U.S. a ‘free man,’ Van Hollen says
summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia has been ordered by a federal judge to leave the United States by Tuesday, a U.S. official confirmed to NBC News.
story: Kilmar Abrego Garcia has been ordered by a federal judge to leave the United States by Tuesday, a U.S. official confirmed to NBC News.
In a statement Tuesday evening, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, said Abrego Garcia  is “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.”
The Salvadoran national became a central figure in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown last year after he was mistakenly deported to his home country.

The Washington Post reported earlier in the day that Abrego Garcia voluntarily agreed to leave the United States under an agreement with U.S. authorities who had sought his removal. The agreement, it said, would end those proceedings.
Court records in Maryland have yet to reflect such an order. There have been a handful of sealed filings in his civil case against the administration over the past several weeks, however.
The 31-year-old man immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager, but has been in the United States for years, is married to an American, and has a child with her.
He had lived and worked in Maryland for years under the regular supervision of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from gang members.
He was deported there anyway in 2025, but returned to the U.S.  ICE officials admitted in court filings that his deportation there was an “administrative error.”
Not long after his return to U.S., he was charged with human smuggling in a case stemming from a traffic stop in Tennessee in which he was driving a van with multiple immigrant passengers.
Tennessee did not prosecute him. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying the Trump administration failed to rebut the “presumption of vindictiveness.” The government appealed.

title: Wisconsin reports 3rd measles death, as illnesses spread to the general public
summary: A third person has died of measles in Wisconsin, state health officials reported Tuesday, as cases across the state soared to 920 since the outbreak began in late summer.
story: A third person has died of measles in Wisconsin, state health officials reported Tuesday, as cases across the state soared to 920 since the outbreak began in late summer.
The Wisconsin Department of Health Services said the death occurred in an adult, but declined to provide additional details. Earlier this month, two children with measles died in the state.
The state’s outbreak had been concentrated in largely Amish populations in the southwestern corner of Wisconsin, but has now spread into counties in the central and northern part of the state.

There are growing signs that cases are spilling over into the general population, said Dr. James Conway, a pediatric infectious disease physician and medical director of the UW Health Immunization Program in Madison, Wisconsin.

“What we’ve started to see is pop-up clusters in a number of counties, and not all of them can be directly drawn to the Plain community,” Conway said. “It’s a brush fire turning into a forest fire pretty quickly right before our eyes.”
Nearly all of the people who’ve tested positive, 99.2%, were unvaccinated. Twenty people have needed hospitalization.
For Subscribers

During a media briefing Tuesday, Stephanie Schauer, immunization program manager for the Wisconsin Health Department, said that 14 women have tested positive while pregnant and there’s been one reported case of congenital measles.
For Subscribers
The state is also requesting a second round of help from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. A CDC team previously deployed to the area in mid-August.

“We are going to be receiving additional staff to do case investigation, public communication and management of data,” Wisconsin’s state epidemiologist for communicable diseases, Dr. Ryan Westergaard, said during the meeting. “We decided to do this now, several months into the outbreak, when it became clear that the outbreak was growing rather than shrinking.”

Tuesday’s announcement marks the 14th measles death this year, according to a tally from state health departments in New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Wisconsin. At least six have been reported in children.

title: How Democrats are gaming out the timing of their 2028 bids: From the Politics Desk
summary: In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki explores when we might see Democratic presidential contenders launch their campaigns.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki explores when we might see Democratic presidential contenders launch their campaigns. Plus, Sahil Kapur interviews DSCC Chair Kirsten Gillibrand about the 2028 Senate map.
Programming note: We are taking a holiday break the rest of the week and will be back in your inbox on Monday. Have a happy Thanksgiving!
— Adam Wollner
How Democrats are gaming out the timing of their 2028 bids
Now that the midterm elections are all of three weeks behind us, Democratic White House hopefuls can get real about their 2028 campaigns.

With that comes one of the first big decisions they’ll need to make: exactly when to enter the race. Jump in early and face the harsh national spotlight and a possibility of burning through cash too soon. Wait too long and risk getting left behind in what’s expected to be a crowded field.

We talked to advisers to potential candidates, donors and outside strategists who laid out the major considerations that go into deciding the right moment to officially announce a campaign for president. Here are some of the key factors to keep an eye on.

A mad rush in two phases: Several strategists said to expect to see two main phases of rollouts (with the potential of it starting even before the end of the year). The first is in January, after the new party superstars in Congress settle in. And the second is in February and March, with the bulk of the field likely to be in place by March 31, just as the first quarter of fundraising ends.

“The minute you jump in, you need to start paying people, raising money, all of those things,” a senior Democratic strategist who worked on a presidential campaign in 2020 said. “But time is also your friend in a crowded field. … You need to distinguish yourself.”

Governing: Voters just re-elected Govs. Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania, JB Pritzker in Illinois and Gov. Wes Moore in Maryland to four-year-terms. It’s unlikely they’d announce before their own January swearing-in ceremonies. And they might even have to clear legislative sessions and state of the state addresses from their plates first.

Money: Locking down donors is vital to demonstrate fundraising strength early. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear is asking his donors to convene in December before any decision happens. Some potential contenders, like Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, are already sitting on a pile of cash. And while Pritzker, a notorious self-financier, is expected to fundraise for the first time, the billionaire can reliably lean on personal wealth.

Staffing up: Some nascent campaigns have already locked down their hired guns, but with so many Democrats competing for talent, there are some potential contenders still wrangling over some important hires. “There are a lot of factors,” said a person working with a potential 2028 candidate. “It’s a conversation I know everybody is having.”

Book releases: Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg is due out with a book in January. Moore has a scheduled March release for his book. Conventional wisdom (though it isn’t always accurate) is that candidates will seek to tap into momentum from the publishing tours to then shift into campaign mode.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The X factors: As we reported this week, what Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and former Vice President Kamala Harris decide to do looms particularly large over the rest of the field. Someone like Rep. Ro Khanna may want to jump in sooner rather than later to get a leg up in the progressive lane over AOC.

For his part, California Gov. Gavin Newsom has said he would not run for president if Harris does — though not everyone is buying that. “When he said it, it was total bull----,” said billionaire Democratic donor John Morgan. “Put this down for my prediction: Even if she runs, he’s running.”
🔵 Related: Democrats grumble about the DNC’s plan for the 2028 primary debates, by Jonathan Allen and Natasha Korecki
DSCC chair says it’s ‘definitely possible’ for Democrats to win 60 Senate seats in 2028
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y. is seeking another two-year term as chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee after her party flipped nine seats on its way to securing a 56-seat majority.

In an interview with NBC News, Gillibrand said she’s bullish that Democrats can expand the map again in 2028, calling it “definitely possible” to capture 60 seats and win a very rare, filibuster-proof majority.

“It’s on the table. There’s some easy targets that I’m very excited about — obviously, Wisconsin and North Carolina,” Gillibrand said. “But I would also suggest any state that was in play last cycle is in play this cycle. Waves tend to be two cycles long, and this is a very large blue tsunami.”

If Democrats hold all their seats in 2028, their best pickup opportunities are seats in the highly competitive states of Wisconsin (held by Sen. Ron Johnson) and North Carolina (held by Sen. Ted Budd). From there the hill gets steeper, requiring victories in redder states.

“I think we can put a lot of these states that we put in play last time that are exciting states like Kansas and South Carolina and Iowa,” all of which Democrats won in November, Gillibrand said. “There’s no reason why we can’t find extraordinary candidates, again, who have the right message to fight for their states to run in these very red and purple places.”

title: Four former detainees allege they were raped, subject to forced labor at a Louisiana ICE facility
summary: Four formerly detained immigrants said they were subjected to rape, sexual assault, anti-LGBTQ harassment and a forced labor scheme at an ICE detention center in Louisiana.
story: Four formerly detained immigrants said they were subjected to rape, sexual assault, anti-LGBTQ harassment and a forced labor scheme at an ICE detention center in Louisiana.

The four filed a federal lawsuit Monday against GEO Group, the private prison company behind the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Basile, Louisiana, as well as former assistant warden Emmanuel Reyes and former detention officer David Courvelle. The detention center is the largest in the nation for female immigrant detainees.
They “endured a months-long nightmare of rape, sexual abuse, degrading harassment, and hard manual labor that targeted primarily transgender and non-binary detained people,” according to the lawsuit.

Luis Renteria-Gonzalez, Mario Garcia-Valenzuela, Kenia Campos-Flores and Jane Doe said in the lawsuit that between 2023 and 2025 they were repeatedly abused by Reyes and Courvelle and forced to perform sex acts and hard manual labor under threats to themselves and their families. Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela are transgender men and Campos-Flores is nonbinary.
“They suffered horrific, abusive conditions at the hands of employees of the GEO Group,” Susan Meyers, the senior supervising attorney with the Southern Poverty Law Center, told NBC News.

GEO Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment. NBC News was unable to reach Reyes and Courvelle. Courvelle was sentenced to three years in federal prison in June after pleading guilty to sexual abuse of a different detainee.

“Reyes coerced plaintiffs to perform hard physical labor, sex acts, or both, threatening them with death, deportation, further sexual abuse, physical harm, and harm to their families and loved ones,” according to a statement announcing the lawsuit.

The physical labor and custodial work involved stripping floors, sanitizing housing units and facility spaces and moving heavy supplies and machinery without protective equipment, the lawsuit said, adding that the plaintiffs suffered physical injuries and exposure to toxic fumes. Reyes is accused in the lawsuit of telling Renteria-Gonzalez, “If you think you are a man, I’m going to treat you like a man.”

Reyes abused his power to sexually assault the detainees in areas hidden from surveillance cameras, stalk them, view their naked bodies on surveillance camera footage and harass people in the middle of the night, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit also alleges that after Doe turned down an offer to join Reyes’ “cleaning crew,” he stalked and harassed her, groped her and forced Doe to perform sex acts on him under threats to her life if she refused.
Reyes left the facility voluntarily in 2024, Meyers said. It was unclear if he was employed at another facility.
GEO Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Reyes’ employment status.

The lawsuit also accused Courvelle of sexually assaulting Garcia-Valenzuela multiple times and forcing Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela to stand guard outside a closet while he raped a woman who was also detained there.
For Subscribers

“The treatment and the conditions that they had us living in, nobody should go through that,” Renteria-Gonzalez said in the statement. “It’s unbelievable that this happened under the care of the people who are supposed to protect us.”
For Subscribers
Sarah Decker, a senior staff attorney at the Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, said the four former detainees did not suffer in silence.
“They screamed for help. They filed a complaint with every avenue that was available to them,” she said.

Meyers said that despite them coming forward with the allegations, “in many cases things got worse, because what they found was that it opened them up to retaliatory actions” such as solitary confinement.
Garcia-Valenzuela said in a statement, “We were looked down upon like the sole of someone’s shoe.”
“What we experienced there was a true nightmare,” Garcia-Valenzuela said. “For the rest of my life, I will live with the aftereffects of the torture and abuse I endured.”

There have been previous accusations of sexual abuse at the facility, including in 2022, when a Prison Rape Elimination Act audit by the Department of Homeland Security documented four sexual abuse allegations that included one staff-on-detainee allegation and three detainee-on-detainee allegations. Two of the sexual abuse allegations were substantiated, including one against a staff member who resigned the day the allegation was made, according to the audit report. All four cases were investigated and closed.
The report does not say how GEO Group responded to the four cases.

The auditor found in the report that the detention center met 36 standards, exceeded one standard, and was out of compliance with two standards: accommodating detainees with disabilities and detainees who are limited English proficient, and detainee education.
The facility entered into a 180-day corrective plan for those two standards and was later found to be in compliance.

title: Chinese tech giant Huawei convicted of federal charges, including fraud
summary: Chinese tech giant Huawei was convicted of multiple federal charges in New York on Tuesday after prosecutors accused the company of stealing technology from U.S. companies, abusing the American financial system and helping Iran spy on its citizens.
story: Chinese tech giant Huawei was convicted of multiple federal charges in New York on Tuesday after prosecutors accused the company of stealing technology from U.S. companies, abusing the American financial system and helping Iran spy on its citizens.

A jury in New York’s Eastern District found the company and three of its subsidiaries guilty of seven conspiracy counts that included bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering, defrauding the United States and conspiracy to steal trade secrets.
In the roughly two-month trial, Huawei was also convicted of bank fraud and wire fraud. Huawei was acquitted of two counts, a racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice.

“For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft and deception,” Assistant Attorney General Tysen A. Duva said in a statement. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security.”
In a statement, Huawei said the charges are “without legal or factual merit,” and it said it welcomes the racketeering verdict.
“We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests,” the company said.
Huawei attorney Brian Heberling said the company plans to appeal. At sentencing, which is scheduled for Sept. 14, Huawei could face fines, forfeiture and restitution.

Prosecutors accused the company, which makes smartphones and has telecom networks around the world, of encouraging its workforce of 200,000 in 170 countries to lie, cheat, and steal “for a competitive advantage to grow and protect its business.”

Huawei was accused of misappropriating intellectual property like source code, user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology and robot testing technology, prosecutors said. T-Mobile, Cisco, Quintel and CNEX were among the companies whose technology was stolen, federal prosecutors said in a news release Tuesday.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

In Iran, the company assisted the regime with “turnkey” internet services and mobile networks, prosecutors said, and it provided surveillance cameras that allowed officials to monitor protests. Huawei also helped intelligence agents monitor and censor the internet, prosecutors said.

Huawei then lied to banks about the nature of its business in Iran, allowing the company to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and become what prosecutors described as “a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services.”

In an interview Tuesday, Heberling rejected the government’s allegations, saying prosecutors presented a “caricature-like portrait” of Huawei of as a corrupt organization with company policies that condoned crime.

“That was just profoundly inconsistent with the company that I experienced in my work, but more importantly, [with] the evidence, which really showed a series of isolated events over a 20-year period,” he said. “No company can insure perfection over that period of time.”
Heberling argued that the racketeering acquittal — the most serious charge the company faced — showed a “profound rejection of the narrative the United States pursued in this case.”

Huawei was previously banned from selling equipment to U.S. carriers over fears that it poses a security risk, according to the Associated Press, and it was blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.

title: Family of teen killed by Georgia police officer demands release of body camera footage
summary: The family of a Black teenager in Georgia who was killed in a police shooting said Tuesday that it wants transparency and called on the police department to release the officer body camera footage.
story: The family of a Black teenager in Georgia who was killed in a police shooting said Tuesday that it wants transparency and called on the police department to release the officer body camera footage.

The 16-year-old, identified by the family and its attorneys as Tyrie Howse, was shot and killed Nov. 3 following an encounter with a Henry County police officer outside a Krispy Kreme in Stockbridge, about 21 miles southeast of Atlanta.

Howse’s mother said Tuesday at a news conference that her son had left his cellphone somewhere the night before and went to get it. She was a few minutes from picking him up from the Krispy Kreme parking lot when he was shot, she said.
“There was no reason, no reason at all for this to happen to him,” Taneshia Puckett said.

Preliminary information released by the Georgia Bureau of Investigation said a Henry County police officer approached Howse and a 17-year-old in the parking lot of a Krispy Kreme, a news release states.

The officer briefly spoke with the teens “before giving verbal commands for the 17-year-old to take his hands out of his pockets,” the release says. Authorities have not said what prompted the officer to approach the teens.
The GBI said the 17-year-old “passed a handgun” to Howse, who allegedly ran away from the area with the gun, according to the release.
For Subscribers

“The 16-year-old did not drop the gun, and the officer shot at the 16-year-old, hitting him. Medical aid was provided to the 16-year-old. The 16-year-old was pronounced deceased on scene,” the GBI said.

No officers were injured, and a firearm was recovered from the scene, according to the GBI. The officer involved in the shooting was placed on administrative leave pending the conclusion of the investigation, police said.

Attorneys Ben Crump and Harry Daniels, who are representing Howse’s family, said they have viewed witness video showing the aftermath of the shooting and cannot see a firearm in the video they viewed. They called on officials to release the body camera footage.
For Subscribers
“There’s nothing stopping this Henry County Police Department or this Henry County district attorney from being transparent and showing the video,” Crump said at the news conference.
He said Howse, a junior at Woodland High School, was an honor roll student who dreamed of becoming a pediatric nurse.
“I fail to understand why the most dangerous thing in America to police seems to be young Black people running away from them,” he said.

The Henry County Police Department said in a Nov. 10 statement that it asked the GBI to investigate the shooting and that it was aware of calls to release the body camera footage and other evidence, but “any potential release must be evaluated in coordination with the appropriate investigative and legal authorities.”
The department did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
The GBI said the investigative case file will be turned over to the Henry County District Attorney’s Office for review once completed.
The district attorney’s office said in a Nov. 19 statement that it had not yet received the case file and was not in possession of the body camera footage.

“Once the GBI completes its investigation and submits its findings, our office will conduct a thorough and independent review of the entire case file to determine whether criminal charges are warranted,” the district attorney’s office said. “Our decision will be guided solely by the facts, the evidence, and the applicable law.”

title: ‘Shocking’ decline seen in hep B vaccination against incurable virus, including babies with infected mothers
summary: Fewer newborns are being vaccinated against hepatitis B, an incurable infection that can lead to liver disease, a large new analysis has found.
story: Fewer newborns are being vaccinated against hepatitis B, an incurable infection that can lead to liver disease, including babies whose mothers are known to have the virus, a large new analysis has found.

As of June, just 66% of newborns got the hepatitis B vaccine within a day of their birth, down from 80% in 2022. The birth dose serves as a safety net especially for babies whose pregnant mothers are unaware they’re infected with the virus and unknowingly transmit it during childbirth.
Up to 90% of babies with the virus develop chronic infections, putting them at risk for liver failure and liver cancer later in life. Vaccinating them at birth dramatically lowers those odds.
The new study from Truveta, a health care and analytics company, included medical records from more than 1.3 million babies born in the United States from January 2018 through June this year.
During that time period, newborn vaccination rates increased from 76% in 2018 to 80% in 2022 before declining in mid-2023, falling to 66% by June this year.

“It’s shocking to see a nearly 15% decline in three years,” said Nina Masters, lead author and principal applied research scientist at Truveta. “Infants born to mothers with hepatitis B have a 90% chance of perinatal infection. That can mean a lifetime of chronic liver disease, cirrhosis and early death. This is a real preventable tragedy.”

The decline began before federal vaccine advisers voted in December to abandon a decades-old recommendation that all babies be vaccinated against hepatitis B at birth. (That decision was later halted by a federal judge in response to a lawsuit filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics. The block remains in effect.)

The findings mirror increasing trends in anti-vaccine behavior in general. A recent NBC News data investigation found three-quarters of U.S. counties that track kindergarten immunization rates no longer meet the minimum threshold to prevent measles outbreaks.

Now, measles outbreaks are popping up nationwide, with nearly 6,000 cases and at least 13 deaths, according to state health departments. The U.S. lost its measles elimination status Nov. 16, reversing one of the country’s greatest public health achievements this century.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“We talk about measles being the canary in the coal mine. We’re seeing those outbreaks,” said Dr. Richard Besser, a pediatrician and president of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. “This one — hepatitis B and the rise in unvaccinated newborns — these are the kinds of things that are silent, that you don’t see for years and years until these babies grow up and end up having liver disease.”

The study, published Tuesday in NEJM Evidence, also revealed that hepatitis B vaccination rates have fallen among babies born to mothers known to be infected with the virus. Up to 98% of those babies were vaccinated between 2018 through 2025. But between January and June, that rate dropped to 94%.

Cases of acute hepatitis B fell dramatically in children after the the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began recommending a universal birth dose in 1991, falling 99% from 1990 to 2019. A CDC analysis of children born from 1994 to 2023 estimated that hepatitis B vaccination prevented more than 6 million infections and nearly 1 million hospitalizations.

Last year, the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project published a review of more than 400 studies, finding no evidence of short- or long-term health problems from the hepatitis B shot after birth.
“Reversing the successes of previous public health programs puts individuals’ lives at risk,”
Dr. James Conway, a pediatric infectious disease physician and medical director of the UW Health Immunization Program in Madison, Wisconsin, wrote in an email. “It’s sad, tragic and preventable.”

title: Todd Blanche calls Nvidia a ‘good corporate citizen’ while dodging questions on investigation
summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche praised Nvidia as a “good corporate citizen” while sidestepping questions about the Justice Department’s role in the president’s controversial decision to push for the reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang.
story: Attorney General Todd Blanche on Tuesday praised Nvidia as a “good corporate citizen” while sidestepping questions about the Justice Department’s role in the president’s controversial decision to push for the reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang.
President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he’d spoken to Blanche and “they did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he himself was exonerated,” referring to Huang.

Asked at an unrelated press conference about Trump’s remarks, Blanche said, “What the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him,” before adding, “I’m not going to get into communications I have with the president about it.”
He then said that what Trump was saying “is exactly right.”

“To the extent that, that the department, that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that is, that is, that’s just not, that’s something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true,” Blanche said.

NBC News previously reported that Trump sought Blanche and Vice President JD Vance’s help in convincing Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back. An administration official said the attorney general told the president that the DOJ had no evidence of wrongdoing by Huang or the company. Trump and Vance gave Nvidia’s board information that informed its decision to reinstate Huang, a person familiar with the conversations said. The company’s announcement of the move cited input from “senior levels” of government that convinced the board members that Huang posted “no national security risk.”

When asked if Huang — who’d resigned as CEO earlier this month after reports of extramarital affairs,  including a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy — had been investigated, Blanche told reporters, “What does that mean?”
“Had Huang been investigated for what?” he continued.
“I don’t understand the question,” he said, adding, “It’s certainly not fair to him to just speculate about, about things or answer hypothetical questions. And so, so no.”
Asked about whether an investigation into the the chip exporter, Singapore-based Megaspeed, that the alleged spy worked for was ongoing, Blanche continued in a similar vein.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“I don’t know what you’re talking about,” he said. “So, we have hundreds, if not more, export investigations going at any time at the Department of Justice.”
When a reporter pointed out that Blanche had said last week that he was looking into the Nvidia situation, he then said, “We look into things all the time.”

“How do you look at things? You look at things by subpoenaing. You look at talking to witnesses, examining public information, and that’s the way you run investigations, and that’s the way this investigation was run,” Blanche said.
Pressed on whether Nvidia or Jensen were aware of efforts to send high-tech chips to China, Blanche said, “Nvidia is a good corporate citizen.”

“Obviously if Nvidia was, was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation, or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn’t be the message that, that the president is saying to the American people,” the attorney general said.
FBI Director Kash Patel, who also attended the press conference on cyber scams, was asked what the agency had spoken to Huang about or whether it had information about the alleged spy.
“I don’t have anything to add,” Patel said, without stepping up to the microphone.

title: Army to detonate lead explosives in Iowa on Wednesday morning as officials insist the plan is necessary
summary: The Army will detonate a large cache of lead azide explosives at an Iowa ammunition plant at 9 a.m. local time Wednesday, officials said, insisting that the plan is the best and only option because the chemical is unstable and at risk of exploding on its own.
story: The Army will detonate a large cache of lead azide explosives at an Iowa ammunition plant at 9 a.m. local time Wednesday, officials said, insisting that the plan is the best and only option because the chemical is unstable and at risk of exploding on its own.

A host of federal officials — from the Army, the Environmental Protection Agency, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and other agencies — said at a news conference Tuesday that extensive safety precautions are being taken to protect the public.

The detonation is expected to send a plume of lead dust southwest across Iowa and into neighboring Missouri, according to the Army’s forecast map. Officials recommended that anyone in the immediate vicinity evacuate.

The plan has prompted widespread distress and confusion among local residents, many of whom say they have not had enough time to prepare for the possible health and environmental consequences. Lead is a potent neurotoxin and there is no safe level of exposure.

The 68 drums of the deteriorating, toxic lead azide, once used to make bombs, are stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The Army has said it needs to detonate them because the chemical has undergone a process of “recrystallization,” making it highly unstable and dangerous.
The cold weather increases the risk of a spontaneous explosion, officials said.
“It’s just a matter of time when we have an uncontrolled detonation,” ATF Director Robert Cekada said. “It’s not a matter if, it’s a matter of when, and that would not be a great place for us to be.”
In response to a lawsuit challenging the detonation plan, a federal appeals court on Monday gave the Army the green light to proceed.
Army officials said they discovered the problem following an inspection in March.

“This is not something that just happened overnight. We’ve been really working hard to figure out the best way to get this done as safely as possible for the surrounding communities and our personnel here,” Cekada said.

Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the Army and other federal partners were taking “unprecedented, innovative” measures to contain the blast, with the goal of keeping as much lead dust as possible within the ammunition plant site.

In its communications about the detonation plan, the Army has described a two-story structure of “HESCO” barriers — modular, collapsible structures filled with sand — built around the blast site. The Army also said it would saturate the sand and apply a mist as the blast went off.

Telle described additional measures on Tuesday: The Army plans to use a “water wall” to help absorb small particles, he said, as well as foam barriers to help absorb the blast and “state-of-the-art gel blocks in huge quantities.”
It wasn’t immediately clear if those new strategies were added to the plan recently or if the Army had intended to use them all along.
The Army did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

According to emergency permitting documents submitted to the EPA, the Army thinks chunks of concrete could land up to 3,000 feet away from the blast site and smaller objects could go farther. The blast is expected to leave a crater 38 feet wide and about 5 feet deep.
Telle said the Army had explored other options to neutralize the lead azide but determined that none were safe.
“We wanted to prevent having a high-order detonation because there is risk associated with that,” he said. “However, we were never able to find a viable alternative.”

The Army at one point did pursue a plan to neutralize the chemical a different way, which would have avoided an explosion. It awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, which uses a chemical product that dissolves in water and can be sprayed onto the explosives to neutralize them, company CEO Valentine Nzengung told NBC News.
But the Army canceled the contract shortly after initiating it, Nzengung said.
The New York Times first reported on the contract.
Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the Army’s 71st Explosive Ordnance Disposal Group, said Tuesday that this neutralization approach proved to be unsafe.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“The barrels of lead azide have deteriorated rapidly over the past eight months. We’ve observed a significant accumulation of crystallized lead azide on the exterior of the barrels, including the barrel lids,” he said. “So it prevents those barrels from being able to be moved. It prevents us from removing the lids of the barrels.”
Nzengung, who is also a professor of environmental geochemistry at the University of Georgia, said he did not understand the Army’s conclusion.

“We have performed the same exercise before, with the same lead azide in the same packaging and storage deemed unstable. So I don’t understand the assessment,” he said. “If it doesn’t work, I would not be alive ...  I have opened more lead azide barrels that are deemed unstable than anybody using a chemical method.”
Nzengung added, however, that he did not have the latest details about the degradation from the Army.
The weather conditions expected Wednesday morning make it an optimal time for the planned blast, officials said.
“The forecast weather patterns are ideal to protect public health and safety across the region,” Telle said.
An Army-produced map indicates that the lead dust could be deposited at meaningful concentrations about 40 miles away, toward the community of Farmington and into northeastern Missouri.
The Army described the evacuation zone as a “5-mile cone extending southwest” of the ammunition plant.

“If there are women who are pregnant, children under the age of 6 or children in general, and individuals who may have chronic disease, you definitely want to be out of that area,” said Sean Kaufman, the principal deputy assistant secretary for preparedness and response at the Department of Health and Human Services. “I would evacuate that area.”
Short-term hotel lodging is being provided for Middletown residents and others in the evacuation zone through Friday, the Army said.

Anyone who remains in the area is urged to stay indoors. Those residents “will certainly hear and potentially feel with the rattling windows,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commanding general of the U.S. Army Sustainment Command.
Richard Fordyce, a U.S. Agriculture Department undersecretary, said that approximately 350 farms could be impacted, based on the anticipated direction of the plume.
Any concerned residents in Iowa, Illinois and Missouri can ask for their property to be examined for lead contamination, officials said.

“If you want your home sampled, your property sampled, your school sampled, you will get that sample,” said Tom Croci, the EPA’s associate administrator for national security and operations coordination.

Once Army and contractor cleanup personnel are allowed to re-enter the facility following the detonation, they are expected to spend up to three months remediating the site. According to the Army’s permit, workers might have to move as much as 13 tons of fencing, sand and other debris to a hazardous waste facility. Cleanup crews will wear full-body Tyvek safety suits and a respirator, the documents say.

Lead azide, once commonly used in military explosives, was phased out about 15 years ago, Cekada said, “because of how sensitive it is and how difficult it is to maintain in storage and also in transportation.”
The nation’s stockpile, previously spread across multiple locations, was moved to the Iowa plant in 2009, he added.

title: Black Friday deals are already here, and I’m tracking the best ones live: Walmart, Apple, PlayStation and more
